We are the opinion team of the Kyiv Independent. We publish analysis, commentary, and arguments from Ukrainian and international voices. Feel free to contact us via email with pitches and responses.

title: Lukashenko explains why Belarus holds military inspections
body:
MINSK, October 13. /TASS/. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, at a meeting with law enforcement and security officials, explained why regular inspections of military personnel and training are necessary – especially for those who, in the event of wartime, will be called up from the reserve.
"I won’t hide this from my potential adversaries in a future conflict – God forbid, of course – but I constantly remind the defense minister that today the country must have designated points where armed forces will be deployed instantly, within 24 hours – and our logistics allow us to do this in Belarus – and these points will be occupied. Fortified areas, as we used to call them. There are a certain number of them on the western border," his press service quoted him as saying.
Lukashenko said that every military serviceman must know every point, especially those who will be called up from the reserve.
"I remember this from my own military service in the army. We were taught back then: if something happens, you must be in that trench with that weapon. We are doing the same today so that our military personnel know which direction to act in. We’ve been there more than once, we’ve visited this fortified area, and we know what weapons they’ll use to defend our country," he explained.
"And our foes should know: we know our Belarus well. We know whether tanks can pass through the wooded and swampy terrain somewhere or not. If they can’t, we know where they’ll go. We clearly understand where we need to deploy our armed forces."
Lukashenko noted that under the current conditions, it will not be possible to build roads through the swamps, as it was done at the beginning of Operation Bagration in 1944. According to him, modern weapons, in particular drones, will not allow this to be done.
Thus, there is a clear understanding of where a potential adversary might cross the border, the head of state pointed out.
"That’s where we must block everything. It’s simple and clear; no grand strategy is needed from the Defense Ministry. I say it again: this is very important for those whom we will call up from the reserve, so that they know where they are," he said. "Because [Deputy Interior Minister, Commander of Interior Troops Nikolay] Karpenkov will transfer its flying detachments to the right place within a few hours. But when they are fully equipped, having conducted combat coordination from conscripts, they should know which trench they will be in.
"I’m saying this so that the Defense Ministry and the minister understand what I expect from you. This isn’t even about the experience of the special military operation in Ukraine – it’s just ordinary experience in the armed forces. We’re working through it, and we need to work through it carefully, without haste."

title: Eisenkot wants a new direction. His Palestinian policy has a problem - opinion
body: Gadi Eisenkot's significance lies not only in the possibility that he may become Israel's next prime minister, but also in the nature of the political alternative he offers. He opposes the full annexation of the West Bank and criticizes settler violence and the policies of the far Right, yet remains opposed to a fully sovereign Palestinian state and insists on overriding Israeli security control. In one interview, he raised the possibility of Palestinian self-government or what he described as a “minus state,” without a Palestinian army and without a large-scale evacuation of existing settlements.This vision raises a question that goes beyond the differences between Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu: Can Eisenkot offer a political alternative that opens the way to a lasting settlement, or would his proposals simply manage the conflict more efficiently without changing its underlying causes?Improvements in security and economic management, however necessary, do not guarantee a political settlement unless accompanied by tangible progress on settlements, Palestinian sovereignty, rights, and mutual security. Nevertheless, some of his proposals could open a different political path if translated into clear and implementable commitments.The real test of Eisenkot's vision, therefore, is not how moderate his rhetoric appears compared with Netanyahu's, but whether it can bring about meaningful changes in political, geographic, and economic realities while expanding the options available to Palestinians and Israelis. The issue is not simply how to manage the existing situation more effectively, but whether his policies would address the conditions that perpetuate the conflict or merely make its continuation easier to manage.Constrained politics: Can Eisenkot change the direction or merely manage the constraints?On August 27, 2026, Eisenkot argued that implementing the two-state solution after the October 7, 2023 attacks was unrealistic. At the same time, he opposed the settlement project known as E1, which threatens geographic continuity between Palestinian communities. In further statements in September, he reiterated his opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state.These positions illustrate the limits of the political approach he represents. He recognizes the dangers of annexation and uncontrolled settlement expansion, yet does not explain how the possibility of political separation can be preserved without a clear vision for Palestinian sovereignty.Eisenkot therefore needs to answer a fundamental question: If the two-state solution is currently unacceptable to him, what viable political alternative does he propose? Does he regard existing security arrangements as a transitional phase or as a permanent model for relations with the Palestinians?Postponing difficult decisions may appear to reduce immediate risks, but it can also narrow future options until a political settlement becomes even harder to achieve.After the Israeli elections: Will the government change, or will policy change?A change of government in Israel should not automatically be taken as a change in policy toward the Palestinians. Heightened security concerns since October 7, 2023, may continue to limit prospects for a settlement, even if Israeli leaders differ in their approaches to security, settlements, and relations with the Palestinian Authority.Findings published by the Jewish People Policy Institute in August 2026 illustrate this political environment. Among Israeli Jewish respondents, 38% selected scenarios involving the annexation of the entire West Bank, while 35% chose scenarios based on partition. Another 22% selected a scenario involving annexation accompanied by the relocation of the Arab population to other countries. These were long-term strategic options presented in a survey, not direct measures of immediate support for annexation or population transfer.In this context, Eisenkot rejects annexing millions of Palestinians and governing them directly, while also opposing a fully sovereign Palestinian state. His challenge, therefore, is not simply to change the way the conflict is managed, but to clarify whether the self-government he proposes is a transitional arrangement leading toward a settlement or a permanent condition of limited sovereignty. The real test for any future Israeli leadership is whether its policies create new, verifiable political possibilities or simply manage the status quo differently.Settlements: Where does confronting violence end and addressing the underlying problem begin?In an interview with The Jerusalem Post on September 24, 2026, Eisenkot pledged to reorganize the Civil Administration and policing in the West Bank under military coordination and restore enforcement measures against settlers who engage in violence. In another interview, he reaffirmed his support for settlements he considers consistent with Israeli law and Israel's security interests, while rejecting a large-scale evacuation of existing settlements.Confronting settler violence, however, is not the same as addressing settlement expansion itself. Nor does the classification of settlements under Israeli law determine their legality under international law.Eisenkot needs to clarify whether he is prepared to halt projects that undermine Palestinian geographic continuity, rather than merely remove outposts that Israel itself considers illegal. A practical measure of his policy would be whether Palestinians can remain in their homes, access their land, and work safely, alongside effective protection of Israeli civilians from attacks.Protecting civilians is essential for both peoples, but that responsibility does not relieve political leaders of the need to address the conditions that allow violence and control over land to remain enduring features of the conflict.Palestinian sovereignty: Could a “minus state” become a permanent solution?Eisenkot wants Palestinians to continue managing their own affairs, but opposes a Palestinian army or foreign military forces between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, while insisting on Israeli security superiority. His approach raises a question that goes beyond political terminology: How much independence can an entity exercise if it lacks ultimate control over its security, borders, and resources?The Palestinian experience since the Oslo Accords has shown that self-administration does not automatically develop into political sovereignty. Eisenkot therefore needs to specify the powers he would be willing to grant Palestinians, the limits of Israeli intervention, and the guarantees that would prevent a transitional arrangement from becoming permanent.Without a clear path toward addressing rights and self-determination, his proposed model could become a more orderly means of maintaining control rather than ending it.The Palestinian Authority: Preserving it for what purpose?Eisenkot opposes dismantling the Palestinian Authority or replacing it with a direct Jordanian role. He has also made clear that he does not want Israel to govern millions of Palestinians. This distinguishes his approach from those calling for the Authority's dissolution or a reduction in its role.But preserving an institution does not necessarily mean empowering it. Does Eisenkot envisage a Palestinian Authority capable of exercising meaningful political and economic powers, or an administrative body whose responsibilities remain limited to public services and security coordination?At the same time, the Palestinian leadership faces responsibilities that cannot be postponed, including renewing political legitimacy, holding elections, strengthening accountability, and reforming institutions. Yet successful reform also requires political conditions in which Palestinian institutions can exercise their powers.Eisenkot therefore needs to create room for the Palestinian Authority to develop into a genuine political partner, rather than merely preserve it to avoid an administrative and security vacuum.The economy: Between work permits and the ability to build a futureEisenkot advocates improving Palestinian living conditions by allowing certain groups to work in Israel, subject to strict security approvals, while encouraging foreign investment, including investment from Arab countries.Such measures may provide important income and opportunities, but they do not, on their own, address the structural problems facing the Palestinian economy, including clearance revenues, banking relations, freedom of movement, trade, and access through crossings.A survey conducted by the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion between June 24 and July 5, 2026, among 503 respondents in the West Bank, including east Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip, found that 92.6% reported weakened purchasing power, while 90.7% believed poverty and unemployment had increased.These findings reflect the economic pressures as perceived by respondents, without independently establishing their causes. They raise an important question for Eisenkot: Is his objective to ease immediate economic hardship, or to enable Palestinians to develop an economy capable of producing, investing, and planning for the future?Economic stability depends not only on increasing the number of work permits, but also on creating conditions in which businesses and households can make economic decisions with greater stability and independence.Gaza: The limits of a security-based SolutionIn his October 6, 2026 interview, Eisenkot expressed his commitment to advancing US President Donald Trump's 20-point plan for Gaza, while insisting on the complete disarmament of Hamas before the restoration of civilian governance, the deployment of an international force, and the start of reconstruction.This approach reflects the priority he gives to security, but it raises questions about whether lasting stability can be achieved if rebuilding institutions and restoring essential services are delayed until all security conditions have been fulfilled.The long experience since 1967 has demonstrated that military superiority alone has not brought the conflict to an end. Eisenkot needs to present a vision that links security arrangements with civilian governance, reconstruction, and Palestinian participation in determining the future, while preventing the political separation of Gaza from the West Bank from becoming permanent.Rebuilding homes and infrastructure is a humanitarian necessity, but it cannot be sufficient if Gaza's political future remains unresolved.Palestinian public opinion: Is there still an opportunity?Palestinian public opinion reveals a dimension that may receive insufficient attention in Israel's security debate. A telephone survey conducted by the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion between July 5 and 18, 2026, among 309 respondents in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, found that 92.9% selected non-military means as the most effective way to gain international support for Palestinian rights, compared with 3.2% who chose military action.The survey also found that 68.9% believed coexistence could be possible if based on justice and equal rights, while 77.7% regarded the lack of trust as an obstacle to peace.These findings do not indicate support for Eisenkot's vision or acceptance of a “minus state.” They do, however, suggest a conditional openness that could provide a basis for political progress. Eisenkot needs to recognize that addressing security concerns alone will not build trust if political rights remain without a credible future.In this context, Prof. Raphael Cohen-Almagor's 2026 book, Resolving the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, offers an important perspective grounded in trust, fairness, political courage, and mutual recognition. The book goes beyond these principles to discuss practical arrangements, beginning with the restoration of civilian and economic cooperation and moving toward a settlement in which the two-state solution remains central.The comparison is revealing: If an Israeli scholar sees a way to combine security guarantees with a political settlement, the question facing Eisenkot is why overriding Israeli security control should remain an open-ended substitute for resolving Palestinian sovereignty.Regional normalization: Can peace be achieved without the Palestinians?Eisenkot sees opportunities to expand regional cooperation through US mediation, strengthen relations with Egypt, Jordan, and countries already participating in normalization agreements, and potentially extend those relationships to additional Arab states. He has acknowledged that these countries seek changes in the West Bank and in Israel's treatment of Palestinians, while emphasizing that his decisions would be guided by Israeli interests.This raises a fundamental question: Can Eisenkot use regional cooperation to open a path toward a political settlement, or does his approach aim to strengthen Israel's regional position without substantially changing its relationship with the Palestinians?Normalization may create economic, security, and diplomatic opportunities, but it cannot replace the need to address Palestinian rights. Nor are Arab positions identical: Saudi Arabia's position on Palestinian statehood reflects considerations that differ from Jordan's more immediate interests in the West Bank and Jerusalem.Eisenkot needs to clarify whether he is prepared to turn regional cooperation into an incentive to halt settlement expansion, strengthen Palestinian institutions, provide mutual security guarantees, and establish a political process with clearly defined objectives.Conclusion: The real test of Eisenkot's visionEisenkot should not be treated as identical to Netanyahu. There are differences in their approaches to institutional management, confronting settler violence, relations with the Palestinian Authority, and engagement with the international community. Yet differences in governance do not necessarily translate into differences over the nature of a political solution.His vision should therefore be assessed through observable outcomes: Will settlement expansion that undermines geographic continuity stop? Will Palestinian powers be expanded? Will the Palestinian economy become more capable of sustaining itself? Will civilian protection become more effective? And will a political process emerge that addresses sovereignty, rights, and mutual security?Security without a political horizon may develop into a permanent system for managing the conflict, while justice without capable institutions and credible security arrangements may remain a difficult goal to achieve. Nevertheless, some of Eisenkot's proposals could mark the beginning of a political shift if accompanied by clear, verifiable commitments that move the relationship from managing the conflict toward addressing its causes.The real test for Eisenkot is not whether he can manage the conflict more efficiently than Netanyahu, but whether he is prepared to make decisions that bring a political settlement within reach. The question is not simply how the existing situation is managed, but whether the proposed policies change the conditions that keep it in place.Dr. Nabil Kukali is the founder and president of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion (PCPO) and a specialist in public opinion research and survey methodology. He has more than three decades of experience in social, political, and economic research and has supervised numerous national and international studies throughout Palestine and the Middle East.

title: The US targeting the International Criminal Court is a slippery slope to nowhere good
body: The US government’s moves to sanction the International Criminal Court represent an unwelcome distraction that sets a dangerous precedent for the rest of the world. The ICC is certainly an elitist organisation, and it is intrusive in certain areas to the point of justifying reforms and new safeguards. But that should not disguise the wider harms that come from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s latest pushback against the court. Mr Rubio has warned that Washington will demolish the ICC “brick by brick” unless it ends the overreach of prosecuting US citizens for alleged battlefield crimes. “Republicans and Democrats alike rejected the idea that the International Criminal Court had the power to prosecute American citizens, military service members or political leaders,” he said earlier this month. “America never joined the court. We don’t need it. And we don’t want it.” Washington is undoubtedly entitled to resist the wildest demands of the court, but it is in principle setting a precedent that the US and the rest of the world could come to regret. Overarching global bodies perform a necessary function in a world where scores of nations are growing and interacting in pursuit of common development. There is a well-established set of benefits that stems from having a common point at which countries establish rules and guidelines on how to co-operate better together. The people who work in these international systems are more often motivated to carry forward the principles and ideals of global co-operation than the pursuit of a narrow agenda or ideology. In any event, the need for this architecture is the most important element to remained focused on. It is not just courts and the highest echelons of international law that come under a shadow when the US takes this sort of action. There is also the UN, which has a number of agencies under its umbrella, such as the World Bank Group. There are also a number of private and public institutions that are dedicated to a “force for good” impact. There are even areas of scientific and research co-operation to tackle issues such as health, metrological developments and geographic changes. To some critics, this is an archipelago of the legal industry that has become a historical aberration. Calling out poor performances or abuses of powers is, therefore, a natural effort that restores balance in the international system. As an unchallenged superpower, the US had an outsized role in judging how the far the balance had tilted one way or another – even in situations where it had not subscribed to the international body, such as the ICC. But President Donald Trump has gone even further across his two terms. For a sample of his view on global institutions, his reaction to the Nobel Peace Prize given last week to Navi Pillay – the jurist who has carried out inquiries for the UN – was tellingly dismissive. “In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations. They were of no help to me,” he said. Leaving aside the record of settling or initiating wars, you have in Mr Trump’s statement the fundamental starting point of the US administration. The problem is, when the fabric of global co-operation starts to get worn down by sanctions, it has to rely on the willingness of people to volunteer to undertake any given mission. That is a wider point than suggesting that people will no longer work for free or give their backing to appeals that are led by international institutions. The campaign amounts to an attack on those who offer their professional skills, talent and dedication to the inner workings of the world. For many, the difference between signing up for good works and suffering the penalties of a powerful system that turns against international work is a dividing line they would not cross. Just for personal reasons, including to insulate themselves and their families, they will find that the appeal of making a contribution has diminished or been extinguished. The ethos that dies, then, becomes impossible to replace. What come next are the cynical and the exploitative instincts of those with an agenda. That sets the international system on a collision course within itself and among the nation-states that have a clear need for good rules of the road. Also, as frustrating as it might be for the US to suffer constant challenges, there is a reflection of its own strength across the international system. Undermining that extension of its own powerful role in the world is, ultimately, not in its interest. It is the quiet death of the best people not turning up that will be the consequence of applying system-wide sanctions. Mission creep will follow, too, as sanctions tend to be addictive for policymakers with few tools as easy to embrace in a world of grey choices and negative developments. Other countries might even emulate the US government’s actions, which would lead to the worst sort of competitive dynamic. Within the global system, the leadership is bound to go into defensive mode. Co-operation could succumb to confrontation. Reform could become an illusory platitude. There is little positive to say about what might follow. A bad idea begets worse ones, so don’t be surprised if the world ends up in the worst possible situation.

title: UK intelligence chief warns of 'major shift' after Iran attacks military bases
body: Iran has raised the stakes in its sabotage efforts against military bases in the UK with Tehran behind multiple plots, the head of the UK's domestic intelligence service warned. Authorities have arrested scores of people suspected of working for Iran, as the level of state-backed threats against the UK exceeds terrorism and extremist activity, Ken McCallum, the director general of MI5, revealed on Tuesday. “Over the last 12 months, our Iran-linked operations have led to more than 50 arrests in the UK,” he said. “The other major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tehran was "highly likely" behind a suspected plot against RAF Fairford on Monday. The base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran since the war was launched in February. The plot prompted a security alert and led to US President Donald Trump withdrawing planes from the air base. Seven people have been arrested on suspicion of involvement in the incident. Two more suspects were arrested last week at the RAF Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire, which is known to be used by US intelligence agencies. Mr McCallum warned an even greater threat existed elsewhere, raising the prospect of more "aggressive and sophisticated" tactics spreading to the UK. "Clearly it is the case that in countries closer to its own homeland, the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary ​Guard Corps] has quite ‌deep experience of using more conventional and hybrid technology," he said. Iran has previously attempted attacks at UK bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean and Akrotiri in Cyprus. The UK has prosecuted dozens of people for carrying out attacks on Jewish sites and on dissidents active in London and other parts of the UK. Mr McCallum's last national security update a year ago revealed that there were 15 active plots disrupted within the UK. In his latest his annual report he added that all state threats, including from Russia and China, had quadrupled. He referred to interconnected financial systems, energy grids, supply chains and manufacturing bases – designed during simpler times for maximum efficiency – as key vulnerabilities to disruption and coercion by foreign actors. EU support Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign affairs minister, expressed solidarity with the British government on Tuesday, following Mr Burnham's statement. "UK has now concluded that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard was almost certainly behind the threat to Fairford airbase," she said. "Iran’s campaign of intimidation and chaos extends well beyond the Middle East. "The EU has already designated the Revolutionary Guard as a terrorist organisation. We have sanctioned Iranian officials for undermining freedom of navigation and serious human rights violations. The UK is a close partner, and we stand firmly with them."

title: GoldBod initiative has created over 1,300 public and private sector jobs – Sammy Gyamfi
body: The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), Sammy Gyamfi, says the government’s GoldBod initiative has created more than 1,300 jobs across the public and private sectors. He made the disclosure when he appeared before Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. “On top of my head, I can tell you that in terms of mainstream public sector jobs, nothing less than 300. “In terms of the private sector jobs, close to a thousand through the license reforms that have introduced four-tier licenses, tier one, tier two, self-financing aggregators, who are all employing more workers, and also the refineries that we’ve contracted to refine gold locally, employing workers. The private sector component of jobs created under the GoldBod initiative should be more than a thousand,” he told the committee. He added that GoldBod will publish the official figures of the jobs created through the initiative by December 2026. He explained that the licensing reforms had introduced four categories: Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3, and Tier 4 of gold-buying licences, creating opportunities for more people to participate in the gold trade and employ additional workers. Mr Gyamfi said the Tier 2 category currently had more than 700 licence holders, many of whom employ between three and five people. He identified Tier 2 licence holders as a significant source of employment for young people, explaining that eligible buyers could access financing indirectly through licensed aggregators.

title: Financial wellness key to retaining Ghana’s skilled workforce – Merban Capital CEO, Benjamin Ackah-Nyamike
body: The Chief Executive Officer of Merban Capital Ltd, Benjamin B. Ackah-Nyamike, has called on employers and institutions across Ghana to prioritise financial wellness as a key component of employee welfare and retention, stressing that financial security plays an important role in building a motivated and sustainable workforce. He made the call during a presentation at the Ghana Health and Labour Summit 2026, organised by Mentapulse Africa in collaboration with the University of Ghana Business School and the Ministry of Labour, Jobs and Employment. Speaking on the topic “What Makes a Pasture Greener? Achieving Financial Stability in a Volatile Economy,” Mr Ackah-Nyamike highlighted the growing importance of financial security in addressing workforce challenges, particularly the increasing migration of skilled professionals seeking better opportunities abroad. He explained that the search for greener pastures extends beyond higher salaries to include long-term financial security, career development and improved quality of life. According to him, while employers may not be able to prevent every skilled professional from seeking opportunities elsewhere, they can create an environment where employees see greater value in building their futures in Ghana. Financial security as a tool for employee retention A key focus of his presentation was the need for employers to look beyond traditional salary structures and introduce financial benefits that help employees build wealth throughout their working lives. Mr Ackah-Nyamike encouraged institutions to consider structured investment and savings programmes as part of their employee welfare strategies. Among the solutions highlighted were Tier 3 provident funds, staff welfare investment funds, long service investment plans and workplace financial wellness programmes. He explained that these initiatives could provide employees with opportunities to accumulate savings, prepare for retirement and develop greater confidence in their financial futures. Building financial stability in an uncertain economy Beyond institutional interventions, the Merban Capital CEO emphasised the importance of individual financial discipline in achieving long-term stability, particularly in an economy characterised by changing market conditions and financial uncertainty. He encouraged employees to adopt practical financial habits, including setting aside a portion of their income before spending, maintaining emergency savings, making voluntary pension contributions and investing additional income from bonuses and allowances. He also highlighted the importance of starting early, using a practical illustration to demonstrate how delaying retirement savings by even a few years could significantly reduce the amount accumulated by retirement. The role of professional investment management Mr Ackah-Nyamike also underscored the value of professional investment management in helping individuals and institutions navigate financial uncertainty. He highlighted the importance of developing investment strategies that reflect an individual’s financial objectives, risk tolerance and investment horizon, while stressing the need for diversification, regular portfolio reviews and professional financial guidance. A shared responsibility Concluding his presentation, Mr Ackah-Nyamike called for greater collaboration among employers, employees and financial institutions in promoting financial wellness. He encouraged employers to assess whether their employee benefit structures merely address immediate financial needs or contribute meaningfully to long-term financial security. He reiterated Merban Capital’s commitment to partnering with institutions to design and manage financial wellness programmes that support employees throughout their working lives and into retirement. The presentation reinforced the message that retaining Ghana’s skilled workforce requires more than competitive salaries. It also requires creating opportunities for employees to build financially secure futures within the country.

title: DLSS 5 gets toned down for its Hogwarts Legacy debut next month
body:
When Nvidia originally showed off DLSS 5 earlier this year, the technology immediately got branded as gen AI for video games. To gamers, Nvidia had lost the plot. I personally couldn’t get over how faces were transformed using DLSS 5. The 15-year-old student from Hogwarts Legacy suddenly looked much older, and Grace from Resident Evil Requiem looked yassified.
Now more than six months later, DLSS 5 is about to debut properly in Hogwarts Legacy, and it looks like it has been seriously toned down. Nvidia published new comparison screenshots today, where the changes to faces are as subtle as they are in NBA 2K27. Teenagers no longer look like middle-aged men, and even the environmental changes look more subtle.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/nvidia-dlss-5-geforce-rtx-hogwarts-legacy-comparison-001-off.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/nvidia-dlss-5-geforce-rtx-hogwarts-legacy-comparison-001-on.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Nvidia’s DLSS 5 in Hogwarts Legacy in March.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/hogwarts-legacy-nvidia-dlss-5-3d-guided-neural-rendering-geforce-rtx-50-series-comparison-002-off.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/hogwarts-legacy-nvidia-dlss-5-3d-guided-neural-rendering-geforce-rtx-50-series-comparison-002-on.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Nvidia’s new Hogwarts Legacy DLSS 5 comparisons.
Nvidia has always maintained that developers have “detailed artistic control” over DLSS 5, and ultimately make the choice on how to implement the technology in their own games. DLSS 5 will now appear in Hogwarts Legacy on November 5th, and it’s also coming to Where Winds Meet late next month.
Nvidia is also improving the performance hit of DLSS 5 with an October update to the neural rendering system that should make it twice as fast on RTX 50-series GPUs and the upcoming RTX Spark laptops. “The DLSS 5 October update shrinks the footprint by 24 percent to roughly 118 million parameters while reducing 4K VRAM usage by 20 percent,” says Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes. This new DLSS 5 model will debut first in NBA 2K27 on October 16th and “will ship by default with future DLSS 5 games.”
Alongside the DLSS 5 updates, Nvidia has also shipped a new Nvidia app beta update that includes a faster performance mode for Frame Generation on RTX 40- and 50-series GPUs. The updated AI model uses a “faster and lighter algorithm to boost frame rates” for Frame Gen, Multi Frame Gen, and Dynamic Multi Frame Gen. Nvidia says it has “minor trade-offs in image quality,” and that performance mode for Frame Generation should now be up to 35 precent faster.

title: Situation around Zaporozhye nuclear plant tense, pressure palpable — director
body:
MELITOPOL, October 13. /TASS/. The situation around the Zaporozhye nuclear power plant remains stable but very tense, Director Yury Chernichuk said.
"It’s a stable but extremely tense situation, because the situation has been escalating since April and it continues to escalate. It's a real pressure cooker there. Unfortunately, we haven’t seen any radical improvements or positive changes," Chernichuk said in an interview with the Energodar TV channel En TV.
He noted that only "individual changes" in the repairs of one of the two power supply lines and periodic cargo deliveries can be seen.
However, the ongoing Ukrainian attacks prevent stable and safe transportation of personnel and materials necessary for the nuclear power plant, the director said. Chernichuk said that since April Ukraine has killed nine employees of the Zaporozhye nuclear power station and injured more than 50 people.

title: Venice Commission Criticizes Georgia’s New Foreign Funding Restrictions, Urges Review of Criminal Penalties
body: The Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on constitutional law matters, has criticized Georgia’s March 4 legislative amendments that restricted foreign funding and political activities. The Commission has warned that the legislation imposes disproportionate and unnecessary restrictions on the fundamental rights and political freedoms of the Georgian citizens. In its newly adopted 24-page opinion , prepared at the request of the chairperson of the Monitoring Committee of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, the commission assessed the amendments adopted by the Georgian Dream-dominated parliament on March 4. The legislative package imposes additional restrictions on receiving foreign funding, criminalizes so-called external lobbying, restricts political activities, imposes limits on businesses and introduces penalties for “systematic acts” directed at “establishing the perception” of the government’s illegitimacy. The changes include amendments to the Law on Grants , Law on Political Associations , Criminal Code and Administrative Offenses Code . They have drawn widespread criticism over provisions that observers say are vaguely worded, open to arbitrary enforcement and restrictive of political participation. In its opinion, the Venice Commission recalled its 2025 assessment , which concluded that Georgia’s legislative framework “risked undermining the rule of law, civic space and democratic freedoms” and recommended repealing restrictive legislation and improving the existing legal framework. The Commission said the March 4 amendments failed to address those concerns. “Rather than addressing the concerns identified in previous opinions, they further strengthen governmental control, broaden the scope of the restrictions and reinforce the legislative framework through extensive monitoring powers and criminal sanctions,” the opinion reads. The commission warned that the cumulative effect of the restrictions could discourage individuals and organizations from exercising their fundamental freedoms, even when their activities are lawful. “Faced with prior governmental control, extensive monitoring powers and the prospect of investigation, criminal prosecution and imprisonment, individuals and organisations may reasonably refrain from engaging in lawful activities protected by the Convention,” the commission said. “The exercise of freedoms of association and expression as well as the right to political participation is thereby likely to be curtailed, not only through direct prohibitions, but more importantly through the creation of a legal environment in which the risks associated with civic engagement become too great to assume.” The commission raised concerns about the compatibility of the restrictions with international human rights standards, particularly the extensive use of criminal penalties for violations related to foreign funding and political activities. “The Commission recommends strongly reconsidering the use of criminal-law sanctions in the framework of the procedures and breaches of obligations under the Law on grants, as well as for conduct involving the broad concept of ‘political matters concerning Georgia’, the activities of foreign legal entities, or transactions characterised as intended to circumvent the grant’s regime,” the opinion reads. According to the commission, such conduct “should be dealt with by purely administrative means, accompanied by robust procedural safeguards.” It added that even if Georgian authorities decide to retain criminal penalties, “it should be ensured, as a minimum, that criminal liability remains limited to situations where it is strictly necessary and proportionate, and that both the conduct attracting such sanctions and the applicable sanctions are precisely defined.” The commission also challenged the legislation’s lack of legal certainty and foreseeability, warning that several key provisions are so broadly formulated that they could allow excessive discretion in their enforcement. It identified the notions of “grant”, activities “relating to political matters”, “organisation representing the interests of a foreign power” and a “person with a declared party-political aim”, “establishing a perception of illegitimacy” or “harming the interests of the state”, as concepts that “are formulated in overly broad and imprecise terms, creating uncertainty as to the persons subject to the restrictions and conferring excessive discretion on the authorities.” The commission recommended that these concepts be clarified and narrowly defined to ensure greater legal certainty and prevent arbitrary application. Beyond the substance of the amendments, the Venice Commission criticized the legislative process and stressed the need for broader public participation in future lawmaking. “The Venice Commission further considers that in the future the process of adopting legislation in Georgia must take an appropriately inclusive approach so as to ensure its legitimacy and broad acceptability,” the opinion reads. It also stressed that the legislative process “should be conducted in a context of deliberation, the expedited procedures being the exception, involving and permitting the expression of the opinions of all relevant actors.” In its concluding assessment, the commission rejected the argument that the amendments serve to protect Georgia’s sovereignty from foreign interference. “In light of these conclusions, the Venice Commission is of the strong view that the legislation under examination does not pursue the aim of protecting and strengthening the sovereignty of Georgia and political parties from foreign influence and external interference,” the opinion reads. “It rather imposes disproportionate and unnecessary restrictions on the fundamental rights and political freedoms of the Georgian citizens, concerning in particular freedom of association and expression and preventing the formation and survival of a political opposition – especially when considering the cumulative and systemic impact of the 4 March 2026 legislative framework as a whole, including recent amendments assessed in the Venice Commission Opinion on the amendments of 16 October 2025 to the Organic law on political associations of citizens and related laws.” The commission further concluded that the legislation contradicts international standards on democracy and pluralism, warning that rather than protecting Georgia’s sovereignty, “the constitutional system and political parties from foreign influence and external interference, the legislation at stake risks undermining them profoundly.” The Venice Commission also expressed regret over the Georgian authorities’ lack of engagement during the preparation of the opinion. The March 4 Amendments The legislative package adopted by the Georgian Dream-led disputed parliament on March 4 introduces sweeping restrictions on foreign funding, political participation and activities considered to be linked to foreign influence. Under the amendments, the definition of a “grant” requiring government approval is significantly expanded to include technical assistance, free-of-charge assistance and funding transferred from foreign organizations to their local branches. The legislation also broadens the categories of grant recipients, including foreign-based organizations working on Georgia-related issues, and introduces criminal penalties for grant-related violations. The amendments to the Law on Political Associations introduce eight-year bans on political party membership for individuals who have worked in foreign-funded organizations. They also replace the concept of a “declared electoral goal” with the broader notion of a “declared party-political goal,” potentially subjecting more individuals and organizations to financial restrictions applicable to political parties. Party leaders may also face criminal penalties for receiving foreign funding. The package further criminalizes so-called external lobbying, introducing prison sentences of up to six years, and establishes penalties for businesses that “publicly carry out such political activity that is not related to [their] principal entrepreneurial activity.” Another provision introduces an “extremism” offense carrying prison sentences of up to three years for “systematic acts” aimed at promoting nonrecognition of the government’s legitimacy. The March amendments follow a series of earlier laws restricting foreign funding and civil society activities, including previous changes to the Law on Grants that introduced fines for receiving foreign funding without government approval. They also follow Georgian Dream’s version of the U.S. Foreign Agents Registration Act, or FARA, which introduced prison sentences for foreign-funded entities and individuals who fail to register as foreign agents. Discovery Plus is raising prices across its ad-free and ad-supported plans. Starting Tuesday, the ad-supported plan will go from $5.99 to $6.99 / month, while the ad-free tier will jump from $9.99 to $11.99 / month.
The price hike comes just one week after Paramount closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery , which owned Discovery Plus and HBO Max. The combined companies, known as Skydance, plan to merge Paramount Plus and HBO Max into “a single service over time,” though it’s not clear whether Discovery Plus will remain a standalone streamer.
Discovery Plus streams shows from networks like TLC, The Discovery Channel, HGTV, Food Network, and Investigation Discovery. Many shows from the platform are also included within an HBO Max subscription , such as 90 Day Fiancé , Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives , and Deadliest Catch . Discovery Plus last raised prices in January 2025 .
This latest Discovery Plus price increase will go into effect immediately for new subscribers, while existing ones will see the increase in their next billing statement on or after November 12th.

title: As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now
body:
A police officer photographs the engine of a Shahed drone in front of a multistory residential building damaged in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 12, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Despite the recent failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The attack came as Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the U.S. to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, in turn, publicly said that intelligence sharing with the Americans continued, saying on Oct. 13, "Yes, we continue this cooperation."
Multiple sources told the Kyiv Independent that there was no decision to cut intelligence sharing. The incident instead appears to have involved a failure to detect or communicate the missile launch in time to warn Kyiv.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either."
The S-400 is a Russian air defense system with secondary ground-attack capabilities. Since 2022, Russia has repeatedly used the system, as well as its older version, the S-300, to strike Ukrainian cities.
One senior Ukrainian official familiar with the matter said Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said.
"The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
The official alleged that the incident might have been "a game" to test Ukraine's reaction. Ukraine's military leadership also warned senior officials that if similar incidents became a pattern, they could indicate that Washington was using intelligence assistance to pressure Kyiv.
There is, however, no evidence in the information provided that the incident resulted from a deliberate decision to withhold intelligence.
Detection of ballistic missile launches is largely carried out by a network of sophisticated infrared detecting spy satellites, which identify the thermal spikes caused by the launch of ballistic missiles , Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
The system is generally extremely reliable but not infallible, Hoffmann said, explaining that certain environmental conditions, such as dense, unusually high cloud coverage, could impair its functioning.
Like any system, Hoffmann said, it was susceptible to "human or technical failure" or "extraordinary circumstances" that could impair its functioning.
Missile attacks on Kyiv , which precede air raid warnings, are uncommon but have occurred several times since 2022. In almost all cases, it was the ballistic missiles, which fly at extremely high speeds, that escaped detection by radar.
"Friends, this is not the first time that the intelligence services of our partners have not recorded the launch of the S-400," Zelensky's advisor, Sergey Beskrestnov, said on Oct. 12. "You should not draw conclusions prematurely."

title: Russian drone hits supermarket roof in Kharkiv, injuries reported
body:
Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, reported the incident on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
"The enemy attacked the Shevchenkivskyi district of Kharkiv with a drone. Preliminary reports indicate a strike on the roof of a supermarket. We are establishing the circumstances," Syniehubov wrote.
He later clarified that people had been injured.
"Two people were injured as a result of an enemy drone strike in the Shevchenkivskyi district. Medical personnel are providing all necessary assistance," the regional administration chief said.
Meanwhile, Russian forces also attacked the Osnovianskyi district during the day. According to Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov, the enemy targeted an infrastructure facility.
As previously reported, on the evening of October 12, Russian forces launched missile strikes on two districts of Kharkiv.
In the Kholodnohirskyi district, a strike on a residential building caused one of its entrances to collapse. Four people were confirmed dead, and their bodies were recovered from the rubble. Search and rescue operations are ongoing.
According to the regional office of Ukraine's State Emergency Service, 41 people were injured in the attack.
Illustrative photo: State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS)

title: Scottish Tourist Stranded in Greece After Three-Storey Balcony Fall
body: A Scottish tourist who suffered serious injuries after falling from a balcony on the Greek island of Rhodes faces an uncertain recovery and an expensive journey home, with her family fundraising for a specialist medical flight. Denby McLaren, from Larkhall in Scotland, was visiting Rhodes with her mother to celebrate her 30th birthday when the accident occurred on October 6. McLaren, who works as airline cabin crew, has been unable to use her legs following the three-storey fall. She has suffered a fractured vertebra and multiple fractures to her foot, while her family awaits further information about the extent of her injuries. Family fears possible permanent paralysis McLaren has remained in hospital in Greece since the accident. Her partner, Craig Anderson, has travelled to the island to be by her side. Family friend Leeanne Weir told BBC Scotland News that the situation had been devastating for those close to McLaren, with the greatest concern surrounding her inability to move her legs. The family is waiting to learn whether the injuries have caused permanent damage to her spine. Weir said McLaren was fortunate to have survived the fall, but stressed the uncertainty surrounding her recovery. Specialist medical flight costs thousands McLaren’s family is now seeking to arrange a specialist medical flight to return her to Scotland. The journey requires an air ambulance equipped to transport her on a stretcher with appropriate medical assistance. However, despite having medical cover, her travel insurance does not cover the cost of the specialist repatriation. The situation is placing additional financial pressure on her family, with hospital-related expenses and other costs continuing to accumulate while she remains in Greece. Weir also highlighted the challenges of navigating the situation overseas, including the language barrier and the pressure of arranging the journey home while dealing with the severity of McLaren’s injuries. Fundraiser approaches £28,000 target Anderson has established a GoFundMe campaign to help pay for the medical flight and bring McLaren home to Scotland. According to the BBC report, the fundraiser has raised approximately £19,000 towards its £28,000 target. Weir said the family had been overwhelmed by the response, with donations of all sizes helping them work towards the goal. The immediate priority is to get McLaren back to Scotland, where she can continue her recovery closer to her loved ones. Her long-term prognosis remains uncertain as her family waits for further medical information. Source: The fundraiser’s progress reflects the figures reported at the time of publication. title: IN BRIEF: Lukashenko comments on preparations for war to avoid it, Latvia’s insinuations
body:
MINSK, October 13. /TASS/. Belarus is currently inspecting its armed forces, but this does not mean it is preparing to attack its neighbors, the republic’s President Alexander Lukashenko said at a meeting with senior security officials.
He also disavowed Latvia’s accusations alleging that an armed group from Belarus had infiltrated the Baltic state.
TASS has compiled the key statements from the Belarusian leader.
Belarus is currently inspecting its armed forces, but this does not mean preparations for an attack on its neighbors, Lukashenko stated: "I have said candidly and honestly that we are preparing for war in order to avoid that [scenario]. And we are not going to attack anyone, as has been claimed recently by our Western 'friends' in a media campaign alleging that Russia will attack the Baltic states, and Poland too perhaps, from Belarus or alongside Belarus."
Belarus must be prepared for the most negative scenario amid international tensions, he argued: "We must be ready for a scenario that is the most negative for us. And we have calculated these scenarios. But a new bout of aggression must be prevented. Nobody needs that today."
Lukashenko emphasized the need for unity in wartime, not only in the army but also nationwide.
Europe is speculating about nuclear arsenals, making nuclear weapons a double-edged sword, Lukashenko argued: "They have been overtly mulling upgrading nuclear capabilities, or a European nuclear shield, as they call it. Nevertheless, given the aggressive plans by certain European countries and their leaders that have been repeatedly announced, it would be more appropriate to talk about a sword in the hands of reckless politicians, not a shield. They must understand and realize that this sword is double-edged. I mean nuclear weapons."
The West is spreading false claims about preparations by Russia and Belarus for an attack on the Baltic states, Lukashenko said: "This nonsense [about arrangements toward an attack] which is aimed at us is constantly mounting in the media."
According to the Belarusian leader, the three Baltic states and Poland have been feeding the media rumors about the republic planning an attack, as they need money: "They need money. Neither the three Baltic states, nor former Soviet republics or Poland have enough power to meet their wishes, especially military."
As regards the incident involving an allegedly Belarusian armed group that infiltrated Latvia, it was staged by the Latvian side, Lukashenko insisted: "We are well aware - and I have already been briefed about it - that all that was orchestrated as a media ploy to solicit funds from the European Union by the Latvians themselves. We have no connection whatsoever to this [plot] of military people wearing masks penetrating into their soil and seizing or throwing someone into a group of migrants. No plot could be sillier."

title: Haruna Iddrisu calls for ‘Big Push’ investment in health, education, sports and agriculture
body: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has called for the government’s Big Push infrastructure programme to diversify and include increased investment in health, education, sports, agriculture, and irrigation. He says while the programme’s focus on road infrastructure is important for economic growth, spreading the resources across other critical sectors would support the country’s overall development. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, October 13, Mr Iddrisu said the government must show Ghanaians tangible development outcomes, particularly as it approaches the 2027 and 2028 financial years and seeks a renewal of its mandate. “If you look at our debt service obligations, it’s huge. And particularly for 2027 and 2028, going back to the electorate for the renewal of our mandate, we need to show proof on the ground,” he said. Mr Iddrisu said the government was making progress with the implementation of the Big Push programme but argued that its spending priorities should be broadened. “So far, we’re doing well with the execution of the Big Push. My view is that the Big Push implementation itself must be diversified,” he said. He explained that part of the resources allocated to the programme should be directed towards health, sports, education, agriculture and irrigation to ensure that development efforts go beyond road infrastructure. “Diversified in a sense that some of those resources should go into health, should go into sports, should go into education, should go into agriculture and irrigation,” he added. According to the Education Minister, such an approach would allow the government to pursue a more comprehensive development agenda rather than concentrate spending largely on road projects. He acknowledged the importance of road infrastructure to economic growth but maintained that investment in other sectors was also necessary to achieve balanced national development. “But the road infrastructure will itself spur growth. But I’m for diversified spending of it,” he said. He maintained that although road infrastructure is essential for economic growth, investment in other key sectors is necessary to achieve holistic national development.

title: AI hacking will be more common if changes aren’t made, scientists warn
body:
Dozens of Canadian academics are among an international group of scientists calling for better containment measures for AI models.
“Multiple organizations have disclosed high-profile security failures: their AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments to compromise the systems of external organizations,” they say in an open letter.
The letter, released Tuesday, says that unless immediate changes are made to how AI is developed and deployed, “such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure.”
They say there is a need for more research on AI safety as well as emphasis on containment technologies and procedures. The scientists also want to see an international body that standardizes best practices.
“In the short term, strong sandboxing mechanisms including airgapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” the letter says.
The Canadian signatories to the letter include AI pioneers Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, as well as Nicolas Papernot and Catherine Régis, who co-lead the research program at the Canadian AI Safety Institute. Johns Hopkins University professor Gillian Hadfield, who was recently named to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s new AI advisory council, is also on the list.
Reports of r ogue AI agents have helped fuel widespread public alarm about AI safety. OpenAI disclosed over the summer that its AI agents hacked AI startup Hugging Face without being instructed by any human to do so.
That was followed by other disclosures. Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing. Meta disclosed that one of its AI models accessed the internet on its own and hacked another company. And Google confirmed its Gemini AI model hacked three companies as part of a test of its cybersecurity capabilities.
A San Francisco-based lab that monitors AI activity said in a report on Sept. 30 that the website for Library and Archives Canada was one of the targets of a failed hacking attempt by an artificial intelligence agent.
Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said in September he spoke with his international counterparts in the G7 about setting up a “technology stability board” that would evaluate AI models for testing.

title: Israeli extremist settlers use sheep farms, intimidation to expand West Bank control, CBS reports
body: Extremist settler sheep farmers in the West Bank have been using their flocks in an attempt to drive out Palestinians living in the area, according to a CBS News 60 Minutes investigation, broadcast on Sunday.According to the investigation, the settlers' flocks have "taken over" around 20% of the West Bank."Over 100 Palestinian communities have been displaced or erased by the settler violence and the ever-encroaching sheep," CBS's Lesley Stahl said in a voiceover at the end of the broadcast.A local Palestinian mayor told CBS that the settlers "actually seized the land with their sheep.""They enter, they open the gate of the house and take the sheep inside to eat the trees around the house," a man identified as a Palestinian schoolteacher added.Sheep grazing 'delineates' border, Jewish West Bank farmer arguesStahl spoke with Mordehai Minster, one of the co-founders of a sheep farm in the area."Sheep are amazing. They're dumb, but they're amazing creatures," Minster said."So the idea is you send your sheep down to graze, and then you can say, 'That's my land because my sheep are grazing on it?'" Stahl asked."When you have sheep, everyone understands. Arabs tend to fight over grazing land among themselves. It's a language that we understand, and they understand. And it's a way to delineate the border. This is where I graze my sheep. You don't take your sheep here. You don't plant here. You don't build here," Minster said in response."A lot [of the farms], including this one, have used violence against the [Palestinian] villages down around you," Stahl said."Whenever you have ethnic religious communities, especially in the Middle East, fighting over land and resources, that conflict sometimes gets ugly. The fact that violence exists doesn't change the merit of the right that we have to this land," Minster responded.Stahl asked Minster about a group of extremist settlers, often called the "Hilltop Youth," who formed part of the movement."Those are kids that are ranging [in] age between, I don't know, 15 and 25. They don't do great in school. They don't get into the army that easily because maybe behavioral problems. So some of them end up in places like this, taking care of sheep, doing construction. Some of the kids may have drug problems. They smoke [and] grow pot (Cannabis)," Minster said.Stahl raised that US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee had called violence against Palestinian farmers "terrorism," as well as "thuggish and disgusting.""I wouldn't classify it as terrorism, but are there some children who overreact and act in thuggish ways and need to be controlled and held in? Yeah, definitely," Minster said.Stahl flagged that Palestinians have died as part of the violence."Yes. None of this is great, and none of this changes the fact that our right to be here is legal and it's ancient," Minster said.Hilltop Youth 'succeeding' in pushing out Palestinians, Arab family says Stahl also spoke to Palestinians living in the area.Mahmoud Faraj, his cousin Hassan, and Hassan's daughter Salma, spoke about their village, Jannatah [Arabic for Paradise], and how residents of the area feel amid rising extremist settler violence."They come over here, and they shepherd here," Mahmoud said."Actually, it was a paradise until March 26 when a group of settler invaders entered our land, our property, private property, and they established a tent. They were something like 20 people, 25 people, and they started to behave like they owned everything," Hassan said."This is my cousin's house over there. He's not allowed to go there at all," Mahmoud said.Hassan said that Hilltop Youth are "succeeding" in getting Palestinians to leave. "If you go around them, you will see many houses they [Palestinians] just left really empty. Abandon; they abandoned their property. They [Hilltop Youth] steal electricity from the locals, and they also steal water. This is their strategy: to make the area unlivable."The Faraj family also claimed that every time they try to approach their house, teens from the hilltop outpost "rush down to beat them up.""Within few seconds, they started to attack us in small groups with wood sticks and with stones. And they have tear gas. And three of them, they were armed. So one of the armed guys, he started to shoot. He shot my cousin in his head. And it didn't stop here. They came, and they started to beat my uncle and his son, who was dead, with wood sticks," Hassan said.The Faraj family took Stahl to the family's house they were discussing, but were intercepted by Hilltop Youth teens wearing black hoodies.CBS highlighted that the Hilltop Youth were not the only Jewish activists at the scene.Sons of Abraham act to protect Palestinians from extremist settler violenceMembers of Bnei Avraham (Sons of Abraham), a group of Jewish activists who attempt to protect Palestinians from extremist settlers by stepping in between the extremists and Palestinians, were also present."They are trying to push us back. They don't want us to enter with cameras. So they are pushing and waiting for someone to react with their hands, so they have an excuse for more extreme violence," Roie, one of the Sons of Abraham, said.According to the Sons of Abraham, "Judaism calls on them to protect, not expel, their neighbors," Stahl said."When the settlers see you, they get even angrier because they see you as traitors," Stahl said to one of the activists."I think they are angrier because we threaten them ideologically. And also, I'm not coming from outside [the movement]. I also grew up as a settler. I tell them I changed my ways. I know what you're doing, and I know it's not the right way," she answered, adding that sometimes they know and recognize each other when she interacts with the extremists.One of the Hilltop Youth asked Stahl who she was, with the reporter replying that she is "an American journalist - television.""Are you in with Hamas?" the extremist asked, to which Stahl replied, "No."This extremist settler was then shown in the broadcast headbutting Hassan Faraj in the face."This is my land, and you won't stay. These are my roots," Hassan replied, before the same extremist settler headbutted him again.The Palestinians and Sons of Abraham then attempted to leave. An IDF captain and squad of soldiers appeared, "seemingly out of nowhere," according to Stahl. The soldiers went to rescue the two Sons of Abraham activists trapped by extremist settlers, before the captain instructed everybody to leave the scene.Stahl noted that the IDF allowed the Hilltop Youth to return to the disputed house but did not let the Faraj family pass through."The army's priority is the settlers. Some soldiers are settlers themselves and occasionally join the violence. Though there've also been cases where the soldiers have been attacked by the young settlers," Stahl said in a voiceover.Stahl voiceover continued by saying that the Israeli government has "poured tens of millions of dollars into expanding the sheep farms, arming them and giving them American-made off-roaders.""People call it 'settler violence.' I don't agree with that. It is state violence. There is a violence of a government," Roie, one of the Sons of Abraham activists, said.Sons of Abraham released a statement following the 60 Minutes broadcast."Last week, we went to the village of Jannata, near the 'Kochav Yehuda' outpost, an offshoot of the violent 'Eitam Farm' outpost, to accompany a Palestinian man to the home from which he had recently been evicted," the statement said."The structure has since been 'converted' into the outpost's latrine. Settlers blocked our path and injured the homeowner, while soldiers forced both us and the homeowner away from the area," the Sons of Abraham said, noting that the 60 Minutes crew were at the scene, documenting it."At Sons of Abraham, we are a group of over 200 activists who head out into the field four times a week. We believe the Torah commands us to rescue the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor, driven by the conviction that this Holy Land can bring blessing to all who dwell in it," the group said.Stahl asked Minster if he cares about US public opinion towards extremist settler violence, and possible ramifications of Israel losing American military aid."I do...I am bothered by the fact that America's turning on us, and we're turning on America. It's like, I see it as losing a friendship. And I'm also concerned that, as a military ally, as a political ally, we may lose America as well. It looks like it's going in that direction. But Israel will find other allies," Minster said."You're not worried enough about it to dial back?" Stahl asked."No. I am worried about that. But I don't look at it as an existential threat," he replied.

title: NATO exercise involves potential countries for nuclear weapons deployment — expert
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Countries under consideration for expanding the program for hosting and storing US nuclear weapons in Europe (Nuclear Sharing) are participating in the NATO exercise Steadfast Noon, taking place in Italy, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security of the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
"Italy is hosting the latest phase of the exercise, which brings together 17 participating nations, including countries potentially under consideration for expanding the Nuclear Sharing program in terms of nuclear weapons deployment," he said. The expert noted that these countries are primarily located along NATO's eastern flank--the Baltic states and Finland.
According to Stepanov, the exercise aims to ensure coordination during strategic operations, primarily involving the air force component. "These maneuvers involve 60 aircraft to provide both strategic reconnaissance capabilities and cover for the main delivery systems as part of a combined nuclear-use scenario across various sectors," the expert added.
Starting October 13, NATO is conducting nuclear deterrence exercises in Italy without the use of live munitions. Seventeen nations are participating, the NATO press service reported. It emphasized that "no live weapons are used in Steadfast Noon. The exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country."
The Steadfast Noon exercise is held annually as "part of NATO’s efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the Alliance’s deterrence and defense." It involves dual-capable aircraft designed to carry both conventional and nuclear munitions.

title: Seven OPEC+ countries scale up oil production by 977,000 bpd in September
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Seven OPEC+ countries voluntarily reducing oil production lifted 26.123 million barrels per day (bpd) in September 2026, which is 977,000 bpd more than in August, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) reported.
According to the agreement, the seven countries were to increase oil production by 188,000 bpd in September compared to August on account of increasing quotas. The OPEC+ countries also extended the possibility to compensate earlier surplus oil production by the end of this year but no updated scheduled has been released.
Oil production increase among the seven OPEC+ countries was the highest for Saudi Arabia, by 744,000 bpd to 8.001 mln bpd. Iraq scaled up production by 386,000 bpd to 3.92 mln bpd. Oil production in Kazakhstan had an uptick by 22,000 bpd to 1.851 mln bpd.

title: US Army aspires to create Indo-Pacific manufacturing hub in Korea
body: In the Pacific, a single bolt can become a giant headache and the source of months of delay. The bolt that Col. Scott Carpenter held up Monday during the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting belonged to a Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station turret, and it is back-ordered until February 2027. At U.S. Army Materiel Support Command — Korea, the unit Carpenter commands, soldiers built the bolt through the drill-out process of subtractive manufacturing for a cost of $1.27, avoiding months of delay and saving more than $300 in the process. As the Eighth Army in Korea builds out its logistics capability, it’s investing in advanced manufacturing with an eye to supplying spares, not only to local Army forces, but also to troops across the Pacific region . “I want to be the advanced manufacturing center for INDOPACOM,” Carpenter said at an engagement with reporters at the AUSA meeting. “That’s my goal.” Eighth Army officials spoke earlier this year about how establishing a Korea-based regional sustainment hub, or center for logistics, maintenance and supply, could cut down the burden and cost of long-distance sustainment. At a roundtable event Monday, Eighth Army Commander Lt. Gen. Joseph Hilber indicated the force was moving out to build that sustainment hub. “Now, rather than taking equipment that might need a major overhaul and send it back to the United States, we’re looking at ways that we can overhaul it there in Korea and keep it in the fight longer. Keep it west of the [International Dateline] longer,” Hilber said. “That’s going to involve everything from some added manufacturing capabilities to additional repair capabilities that we’ve got in there in terms of being able to fabricate parts, being able to fabricate materials, and then being able to return that equipment back into the fight.” The Eighth Army has already resourced maintenance support teams that cross service and regional boundaries, departing the Korean Peninsula to support the III Marine Expeditionary Force in Okinawa, Japan, and to Hawaii to support Army rotational units, Carpenter said. Through additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, and subtractive manufacturing, or cutting a part out of a solid block of metal, the Eighth Army is manufacturing an increasing number of critical parts, Carpenter said. The materiel support command recently acquired a metal 3D printer and is now building out infrastructure to house it. “But we think come January, February, the metal 3D printer [will be] in, and my goal is … I would like to get to a point where I can 3D print the bolt,” Carpenter said. By next summer, he said, the Eighth Army is set to receive $3 million worth of advanced manufacturing machines, with some $10 million worth of additional machinery set to be requested in the Army’s fiscal 2028 budget. “I’ll be able to print bumpers; I’ll be able to print doors,” Carpenter said. “These are not just desktop printers.” Recently, he said, a Guam-based military unit requested an assembly that would have cost $36,000. The Korea-based team built it through subtractive manufacturing for $82. Through a request system, Carpenter said, any joint forces member can now request a part and get routed to the Army’s logistics hub in Daegu, South Korea. “If you’re the Marines operating in Okinawa and you need this bolt … I get this bolt back over to the Marine at a fraction of the cost, and a lot quicker than if they were to order through the supply system,” he said. “So again, we’re maintaining combat power inside the First Island Chain.” Hilbert said some hurdles remained for the Eighth Army, including intellectual property restrictions with manufacturers; data-sharing to ensure the advanced manufacturing processes deliver components that are up to spec; and seamless connection into existing Army logistics systems not designed for these new modes of parts production. “We’re continuing to work through those pieces to enable us to fix faster,” Hilbert said.
