title: Ghanaian youngster Prince Amoako Jnr reaches new milestone with FC Nordsjælland
body: Ghanaian prospect Prince Amoako Junior has reached 50 appearances for Danish Superliga club FC Nordsjælland. The 19-year-old forward achieved the milestone after coming on as a substitute against Odense Boldklub in the league last Friday. Amoako Jnr has scored 11 goals and provided seven assists since joining the Danish side from the Right to Dream Academy in February 2025. “Prince Amoako Junior turned 50 yesterday with the tiger on his chest. Big congratulations on the anniversary, Prince!” the club posted on social media to celebrate the youngster. The Right to Dream Academy graduate has been one of the standout young prospects in the Danish Superliga, attracting significant interest from major European clubs. His impressive performances for Nordsjælland earned him his maiden call-up to the Ghana national team as the Black Stars prepared for the World Cup in North America. However, he ultimately did not make the final squad for the tournament, which is being hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico.

title: Five Things To Know Today
body: 1. INEC faces ultimatum over Pantami’s exclusion as fresh errors emerge in candidate lists The Peoples Democratic Party and former Communications Minister Isa Pantami have given the Independent National Electoral Commission until Wednesday, October 14, to include his name on the final list of governorship candidates in Gombe State. In a legal notice dated October 12, Pantami’s lawyers argued that INEC had no authority to exclude him after he won a court-ordered rerun of the PDP primary. The commission has not publicly resolved the dispute. Meanwhile, a separate review of INEC’s final list for the Edo State House of Assembly elections has identified two candidates whose names appear under both the PDP and Allied Peoples Movement. INEC’s Edo office acknowledged the duplication and said it had referred the matter to its headquarters. Why it matters: The developments raise questions about the accuracy of candidate lists and the handling of nominations ahead of the 2027 elections. Watch : INEC’s response to Pantami’s ultimatum, corrections to the Edo list and possible legal proceedings. 2. Dangote Refinery extends ₦2.15 trillion share offer as subscriptions exceed target Dangote Petroleum Refinery has extended its initial public offering by two weeks, moving the closing date from October 13 to October 27, 2026. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the extension, which the company says will allow more investors across Africa to participate. Aliko Dangote said subscriptions had exceeded the original fundraising target by more than three or four times, although the company has not disclosed independently verifiable final subscription figures. The offering comprises 4.1 billion shares priced at ₦525 each, with a potential fundraising value of approximately ₦2.15 trillion. Why it matters : The transaction represents a major test of Nigeria’s capital-market capacity to finance large industrial projects. It also highlights regulatory barriers preventing investors in other African countries from participating easily. Watch : Verified subscription figures, participation by investors outside Nigeria and the proposed listing on the Nigerian Exchange. 3. Lassa fever deaths reach 268 as Nigeria records higher fatality rate Meanwhile, Nigeria has recorded 268 deaths from Lassa fever in 2026, according to the latest situation report from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC). The agency reported 1,138 confirmed infections through epidemiological week 40, compared with 924 during the corresponding period last year. The case fatality rate has risen to 23.6 per cent, against 18.6 per cent in the comparable period of 2025. Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue states account for approximately 88 per cent of confirmed cases. Although weekly infections have recently declined, the NCDC identified late hospital presentation, treatment costs and inadequate awareness among factors contributing to the high death rate. Why it matters: The figures indicate a worsening mortality burden despite improvements in recent weekly case numbers. Watch : Expanded access to early diagnosis, treatment availability in affected states and measures to protect healthcare workers. 4. Police investigate Enugu opposition campaign shooting as accounts of airport incident differ The Enugu State Police Command has ordered an investigation into Saturday’s shooting outside the Nigeria Democratic Congress secretariat during activities surrounding the party’s governorship campaign launch. Police confirmed that one person sustained a gunshot injury and five vehicles were damaged. The Commissioner of Police in Enugu, Bitrus Giwa, has directed the State Criminal Investigation Department to identify and apprehend those responsible. The police also addressed a separate confrontation involving party supporters at Akanu Ibiam International Airport. While opposition supporters reported an attack, police said a disagreement involving party members escalated into a disturbance that required security intervention. The circumstances remain disputed. Why it matters: The incident raises concerns about security at political gatherings and the protection of lawful campaign activities ahead of the 2027 elections. Watch : Arrests, findings from the investigation and whether security agencies introduce additional safeguards for political events. 5. Tinubu orders changes to Lagos-Calabar highway route as project faces fresh scrutiny The Federal Government is revising sections of the 700-kilometre Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, a project estimated to cost approximately ₦15 trillion. Works Minister Dave Umahi said President Bola Tinubu had directed that portions of the highway should follow the existing East-West Road between Ondo and Edo states rather than create an entirely new alignment. Umahi attributed the decision to difficult terrain, challenging soil conditions and engineering considerations that could significantly increase construction costs. However, representatives of affected coastal communities have raised concerns that the changes could exclude them from the highway’s anticipated economic benefits. The decision has also renewed questions about the project’s original engineering assessments, environmental reviews and procurement arrangements. Why it matters: Changes to a major infrastructure project can affect construction costs, delivery schedules, environmental impacts and the communities expected to benefit. Watch : Publication of revised route maps, updated project costs, environmental assessments, and consultations with affected communities. title: Ukraine says it hit 12 Russian refineries in September. No refinery strikes reported since Trump’s “energy ceasefire”
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukrainian forces hit 12 large Russian refineries in September, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said, according to ArmyInform on 12 October. The farthest on the ministry’s list, Lukoil’s refinery in Perm, lies about 1,500 kilometers from Ukraine’s border. Since Trump's 11 October announcement, Euromaidan Press has found no reports of new Ukrainian refinery strikes in the official and unofficial Ukrainian and Russian sources it monitors. A refinery-for-refinery pause would limit Ukraine’s ability to disrupt Russia’s oil industry while leaving Moscow free to keep attacking Ukraine’s energy system, giving Russia an advantage in a war where both sides use energy infrastructure as a target. The issue has become urgent since Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October, after which Ukraine reported holding off strikes on Russian energy facilities while Zelenskyy said Russia attacked several Ukrainian energy sites. The campaign continued into October. Ukraine’s General Staff said Ukrainian forces struck the Samara oil pumping station overnight into 10 October, the third attack on the station that month, according to Radio Svoboda. Ukraine held off, Russia hit six energy sites Zelenskyy said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian energy facilities overnight on 11–12 October following Trump's announcement. Monitoring channels and official Russian sources did not report any new refinery strikes on 13 October. “Last night, we did not attack any energy facilities on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there would be an energy ceasefire,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He added that Ukraine does not announce its next operational steps. Zelenskyy said Russia attacked six Ukrainian energy facilities on 12 October alone, according to Radio Svoboda. Refineries first, power plants possibly later A White House official told Axios that the proposal would begin with both sides halting attacks on oil refineries, with a possible agreement covering power plants to follow. Axios reported that Russia had not accepted a ceasefire. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said the proposal, as described, would give Russia a major concession without offering Ukraine anything in return: Russia has scores of operating refineries, while Ukraine has one. ISW also said the proposal would allow Russia to continue its winter strikes on Ukrainian power stations. title: Ho Teaching Hospital to get cardiology centre under Ghana Medical Trust Fund
body: The Ho Teaching Hospital is expected to see a significant boost in cardiovascular care following the announcement that a cardiology centre will be constructed at the facility under the Ghana Medical Trust Fund programme. The initiative is part of the programme’s objective to improve infrastructure, logistics and specialist care, and to move the country towards achieving universal health coverage. A health policy adviser, Dr Norbert Kipo, made the announcement at a stakeholder engagement in Ho, the Volta Regional capital. The engagement was part of a nationwide campaign aimed at informing the public about the objectives, operations and vision of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund. Dr Kipo explained that construction of the cardiology centre is intended to enhance the logistical capacity of selected health facilities across the country. “For 2027, on this same project of cardiology centres, the President has given an express directive to establish one at the Ho Teaching Hospital and also establish one at the Effia Nkwanta Regional Hospital.” “So adequate provision has been made for this project for next year and once approval has been made by Parliament, construction will commence. So, that people in the eastern corridor as well as those on the western side can also benefit from this Fund”, he said. Corporate partnership He added that a $10 million partnership with the corporate sector would fund the construction of an ultra-modern diagnostic centre at the Greater Accra Regional Hospital. He further said that other engagements were ongoing to secure funding to retool health facilities across the country based on needs assessments, ensuring that patients receive the best possible care, irrespective of the disease, in their respective jurisdictions. Expanding cancer care He disclosed that the Ghana Medical Trust Fund aims to establish a state-of-the-art oncology centre at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, adding that the model would be replicated at Komfo Anokye and Tamale Teaching Hospitals. This, he said, was to ensure that the country could provide comprehensive, integrated cancer care. The facility would feature advanced diagnostic imaging, including CT, MRI, PET-CT and nuclear medicine with isotope production capacity. It would also have dedicated chemotherapy suites, a comprehensive radiation oncology department, a brachytherapy facility and at least two linear accelerators (LINACs), among other ancillary facilities. Specialist training The Administrator of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, hinted at plans to upgrade logistics at the Ho Teaching Hospital and other health facilities, as well as provide at least 10 medical specialists in each of the 16 regions by the end of 2028. “We are training 100 pharmacists; they can be trained at the same time, but for the nurses and midwives’ college, they told us that they had to do it in 3 instalments. So, this year in October, they started; they are training 40 of them, next year they will train 30; the following year they will train another 30.” “So, at the end of the day, what the President wants to do is that by the time that he is done with his mandate and he is going, every region in this country should be able to boast of 10 specialists per region”, she explained. She added that the Ghana Medical Trust Fund would also finance the training of biomedical engineers, who would be responsible for installing and maintaining medical equipment supplied to the various facilities by the Fund. “Every piece of equipment we are giving to this teaching hospitals will be managed by us [Ghana Medical Trust Fund]. The facilities are not managing it. So, from the sales and service agreement to servicing, if there’s an equipment replacement, if the 10-year tenure is over and the equipment has to be replaced, everything is done by the Ghana Medical Trust Fund and not by the facilities themselves.” “And we think that that’s how we can maintain this equipment and look after it well. So, that we can take the load off the facilities”, she said. Effective cooperation and transparency The Volta Regional Minister, James Gunu, underscored the importance of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund in improving the quality of healthcare delivery and urged effective cooperation and transparency in its operations. “The Ghana Medical Trust Fund is an important intervention intended to strengthen financial access, to treatment, for chronic and life-threatening diseases, in line with its mandate and approved procedures.” “Its success in the Volta Region will depend on public awareness, transparent administration, effective coordination with healthcare providers, and fair access for eligible beneficiaries”, he said. Appreciation The Chief Executive Officer of Ho Teaching Hospital, Dr Hintermann Mbroh, lauded the Fund’s efforts, explaining that about 33 patients were receiving care under the Fund, which had been integrated into the facility’s electronic medical records system. He acknowledged the commitment to improving human resources, following the sponsorship of four staff members of the Ho Teaching Hospital for post-basic certificate training in specialties related to non-communicable diseases. “We look forward to the anticipated equipment support, particularly mammography, MRI, general X-ray and dialysis equipment. These will improve diagnostic and treatment capacity and reduce avoidable referrals outside the region.” “The proposed Cardiology Centre, promised by His Excellency President John Dramani Mahama, is also under review in collaboration with the Ghana Medical Trust Fund. We remain hopeful that this important project will be realised”, he said. The Ghana Medical Trust Fund aims to provide financial support for patients receiving treatment for chronic diseases, invest in infrastructure, logistics and human resources, and undertake specialist medical training and research.

title: Atiku’s aide challenges Wike to publish invoices for media chats
body: Paul Ibe, media adviser to former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, has challenged the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, to disclose how much public money is spent on his media chats. Ibe made the call in a post on X on Tuesday, shortly after Wike’s latest media chat, which was broadcast live by several television and radio stations. He questioned the cost of the broadcasts and urged the minister to publish invoices showing the amounts paid to the participating stations, the sources of funding and the relevant budget lines. According to Ibe, at least eight broadcast outlets aired Tuesday’s session, including Arise Television, Channels Television, TVC, News Central, AIT, JDK, Aso TV and Radio, and ADBN. Estimating the cost of airtime at between ₦10m and ₦20m per station per hour, Ibe said a two-hour broadcast across eight stations could cost between ₦160m and ₦320m. He further estimated that holding such a session monthly for a year could amount to between ₦1.92bn and ₦3.84bn. “FCT residents deserve to know how much is being spent on these broadcasts and how much airtime is devoted to FCT development, rather than Wike’s political disagreements with Atiku, Amaechi, Obi, ADC and NDC,” he wrote. Ibe said he had no objection to Wike explaining his stewardship as minister but argued that public funds should be used for purposes that directly benefit residents of the territory. “There is nothing wrong with a minister explaining his stewardship. But public resources must serve public purposes, not personal political battles,” he said. He urged Wike to disclose the payments made to the stations and explain how the broadcasts were funded. “Minister Wike, publish the invoices. Identify the stations paid, the amounts, the funding sources and the relevant budget lines,” Ibe added. The former vice-president’s aide also argued that the minister’s media engagements should focus more on issues affecting FCT residents, including roads, water supply, schools, hospitals, sanitation and security. “Atiku and Amaechi are not infrastructure projects. ADC and NDC are not departments of the FCT Administration,” he said. Ibe concluded that public funds should not be used to finance what he described as personal political publicity. “The FCT treasury is not Wike’s personal political broadcasting account. Public office is not a licence to convert public funds into private political publicity,” he wrote. The post Atiku’s aide challenges Wike to publish invoices for media chats appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: EU expresses regret over Trump-Putin 'diesel deal,' but dialogue will continue – European diplomat
body:
The European Union expresses regret over the so-called "diesel deal" between US President Donald Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, noting that this is not the first time differences have arisen between Europe and the United States regarding the war Russia is waging against Ukraine. Dialogue will continue.
A European diplomat informed journalists in Brussels on Tuesday on the eve of the European Council meeting scheduled for October 15-16 in Brussels—where continued support for Ukraine in standing against Russian aggression will be among the agenda items—answering a question on whether European Council President António Costa intends to raise this issue for discussion among EU leaders.
"Regarding the announced deal: we consider it regrettable, we regret its conclusion. It contradicts the strategy we have followed over the past four and a half years, which involves not only pressure on Russia, but also rejection of Russian energy sources—and not just fossil fuels," he said.
Demonstrating the dynamics of phasing out Russian fuel, the source noted that in 2021 Russia's share in imports of fossil fuels—both oil and gas—dropped sharply. "Regarding oil, we went from a level of around 45% of imports to 12% today, so the reduction is obvious. And thanks to full implementation of the REPowerEU strategy, we plan to completely sever this connection. Regarding gas, the figure dropped from 26% to, I believe, 2%. So I repeat: this is a European strategy," he stated.
The diplomat noted that such measures are "not only a way to stop Russia from funding its war machine, but also a means of pressure on Russia to stop this war."
At the same time, he drew attention to the fact that the agreement announced by US President Donald Trump with Russia is "not the first time we have had differences with the US regarding the war in Ukraine." "The experience of recent years—and certainly the period following President Trump's taking office—shows that dialogue with the US does not always lead to full agreement on the vision of the situation between the European Union and the United States, but such dialogue is in any case better than its absence. We have also seen many cases where, thanks to this dialogue, the US changed its position or the positions of the parties moved closer together. Therefore, in my opinion, such practice should continue; it is a completely natural and necessary process," he expressed confidence.
The diplomat emphasized that all EU leaders "share a common position regarding the situation in Ukraine." For this reason, according to him, it makes no sense for European Council President Costa to "singling out this specific moment." "I think the European Council will express regret over this [Trump-Putin deal] decision," the journalists' interlocutor added.

title: PAC pushes for effective use of GH¢25m by Tree Crops Development Authority
body: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has urged the Tree Crops Development Authority to make productive use of about GH¢25 million in its account to support its operations and growth. The Authority regulates the cashew, coconut, oil palm, rubber, mango and shea sectors and has provided training for farmers to improve their yields. The Committee made the call on the fifth day of public hearings on the 2025 audit reports, during which it commended the Authority’s Chief Executive Officer, Dr Andy Osei Okrah, and his management team for their work. The Committee, however, urged the management to sustain its efforts and obtain vehicle ownership documents for vehicles purchased for the institution. In a related development, the Committee directed Dr Benedict Bonaventure Aligeba, former Managing Director of the Irrigation Company of Upper Region Limited (ICOUR), to vacate the official bungalow after the one-year retirement period. The Cocoa Processing Company Limited was also cited for procurement breaches in the 2025 Auditor-General’s Report. The Committee advised the company to comply with the Public Procurement Act, 2003 (Act 663), as amended, which regulates the procurement of goods, works and services using public funds. It also advised the company to enrol on the Ghana Electronic Procurement System (GHANEPS).

title: Kano govt speaks on status of major projects
body:
The Kano State Government has monitored 106 projects valued at N48.9 billion across six local government areas to assess implementation, quality and service delivery within the year.
The Commissioner for Public Procurement, Projects Monitoring and Evaluation, Nura Iro-Ma’aji, disclosed this at a press briefing on Monday in Kano.
Mr Iro-Maaji said 80 of the projects, representing 75.5 per cent, recorded 100 per cent progress, while the remaining 20 were at various stages of completion, and six were recently awarded.
He said the monitoring exercise covered Kabo, Dawakin Tofa, Tofa, Shanono, Gwarzo and Bagwai Local Government Areas.
“The inspections covered roads, classrooms, school renovations, healthcare facilities, neighbourhood security offices, solar-powered streetlights, drainages, water supply and other essential facilities,” Mr Iro-Ma’aji said.
He said the exercise was aimed at assessing the physical implementation of projects, identifying challenges and determining their potential benefits to the communities.
The commissioner said the government would conduct follow-up inspections to address delays, incomplete works and quality concerns, while ensuring compliance with approved specifications and contractual obligations.
He said the monitoring records showed levels of progress on some major road projects.
The projects included the Janguza-Durum-Kabo-Karaye road corridor in Kabo, which recorded 48 per cent completion; the Hawan Ganji-Badari-Kadere road in Gwarzo, 67 per cent; and the five-kilometre road project in Shanono, which attained 65 per cent.
He also identified some education projects requiring further attention.
The projects, he said, included classrooms at Government Junior Secondary School (GJSS), Badau, in Bagwai, which recorded 55 per cent, and the GAA/GGSS Badau project at only 16 per cent.
He said the Government Technical College (GTC), Gwarzo, project stood at 72 per cent completion.
The commissioner added that rehabilitation of Shanono Primary Health Centre stood at 84 per cent, while neighbourhood security divisional offices had attained full completion in several LGAs.
“Dawakin Tofa recorded 85 per cent, while solar street lighting projects in Bagwai and Shanono stood at 35 per cent each,” he said.
He also announced that the state’s Digital Public Procurement Platform had gone live at procurement.kn.gov.ng.
According to him, the platform is expected to promote transparency, improve procurement documentation, strengthen audit trails, reduce administrative bottlenecks and enhance value for money.
Mr Iro-Ma’aji said the initiative supports the objectives of the Kano State Public Procurement Law, 2021.
He added that its success would depend on adoption by the 10 pilot Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs), capacity development and regulatory compliance.
The commissioner said the ministry would continue routine and follow-up monitoring across the state’s 44 LGAs and engage contractors and implementing agencies to resolve outstanding issues.
He added that the ministry would strengthen quality assurance, geospatial project reporting and public communication through town hall meetings across the LGAs.
The commissioner reaffirmed the government’s commitment to transparency and accountability, saying public projects must deliver measurable benefits to residents.
Mr Iro-Ma’aji called on implementing agencies, contractors, professional bodies, CSOs and the media to support the government’s efforts to improve project delivery and ensure responsible use of public resources.

title: Olympiacos Fans Banned from Marseille Europa League Clash in Late French Security Order
body: French authorities have prohibited Olympiacos supporters from attending Thursday’s UEFA Europa League match against Marseille at the Stade Vélodrome, a decision the Greek club described as unacceptably delayed. The Prefecture of Bouches-du-Rhône issued the ban citing public order and security risks. The fixture was rated at the highest danger level (5/5) by France’s national anti-hooliganism unit. Officials pointed to potential clashes involving identified hooligan elements among the travelling support, known ultras rivalries—including links between Marseille groups and AEK Athens—and concurrent student protests in the city. The order also covers Red Star Belgrade fans and bars access to the stadium plus movement in several central Marseille districts from Wednesday morning until early Friday. Olympiacos said it had cooperated fully with Marseille, UEFA and local police throughout the previous month, with no suggestion of a full ban ever raised. The club learned of the intention only the day before the official order and immediately protested to UEFA and the hosts. UEFA also contacted the French authorities, but the decision stood. “We condemn the delay with which they condemn our fans to expenses and inconvenience,” the club stated, noting that supporters had already bought tickets and some were already travelling or in Marseille. Approximately 3,500 Greek fans had been expected. Olympiacos has begun cancelling tickets and will refund purchasers. The club referenced a similar last-minute French ban on Sevilla fans for a 2023 Champions League tie at Lens, which was later suspended by a court—though it noted there is now no time for such an appeal. It has formally asked UEFA to examine compensation for affected supporters and protection for those already in France. The post Olympiacos Fans Banned from Marseille Europa League Clash in Late French Security Order appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: New Russian trade ban on Georgian goods: why now, and what risks do Georgian experts see?
body: Russian embargo on Georgian goods Russia has banned imports of products from seven Georgian companies. Alongside this decision, Moscow has again demanded that Tbilisi guarantee it will not use force against the occupied regions of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali, and agree to the demarcation of what Russia calls state borders. Some Georgian experts believe Russia is using Georgia’s economic dependence as a lever for political pressure. Meanwhile, the Georgian government says it does not know why Russia has imposed the trade restrictions and expects Moscow to reverse its decision. These developments take on particular significance against the backdrop of the policies pursued by the Georgian Dream party. For years, the government has justified maintaining economic ties with Russia and refusing to join international sanctions on the grounds that this protects Georgia’s national interests. Experts, however, argue that this policy has failed to shield Georgian companies from Moscow’s unilateral trade decisions. The key questions are why Moscow has acted now, what it may be seeking from the Georgian government, and how far this economic pressure could go. What happened: ban targeting seven companies A document issued by Russia’s consumer protection watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, and dated 9 October 2026, announces the temporary suspension of imports and sales in Russia of products from several Georgian companies. News of the decision emerged on 10 October. The restrictions affect major Georgian companies Teliani Valley, Tbilvino, Askaneli Brothers, Wineman and Georgian Beer Company , as well as Coca-Cola and Nabeglavi beverages produced in Georgia. The list of banned products includes wine, brandy, beer, soft drinks and mineral water. It is important to note that Russia has not imposed a blanket ban on Georgian wine or other beverages. The restrictions apply only to products from specific manufacturers. The Russian document describes the decision as a sanitary measure. However, it does not specify which violations the authorities allegedly found in the companies’ products or explain why they selected these particular manufacturers. On 12 October, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the government was working on the issue and hoped Russia would reverse the decision. Parliamentary Speaker Shalva Papuashvili called the decision unexpected and said the Georgian authorities did not understand it. However, he stressed that the ban targeted specific companies rather than Georgian products as a whole. Why now? Experts on Moscow’s possible motives Georgian politicians and experts have linked Moscow’s decision to political pressure. Giorgi Rukhadze, founder of the Centre for Strategic Analysis, believes Russia is reminding the Georgian government that it can use economic leverage against the country. In his assessment, Moscow has already secured significant foreign policy concessions and may now be seeking further steps. All you need to know about Georgian wine boom The Georgian economy is increasingly dependent on Russia. Numbers and analysis “I think events are unfolding as one would expect. You know the saying: ‘Appetite comes with eating.’ Russia has secured all the concessions that Georgian Dream was willing to make on the Western front,” Rukhadze said. The expert believes that Moscow benefits from Georgia’s deteriorating relations with the EU and its Western partners. At the same time, Georgia has become increasingly dependent on Russia economically and in the energy sector. Rukhadze believes the new restrictions are a way of demonstrating this dependence: “I am convinced that Georgian Dream already understands what the Kremlin wants from it. In my view, this is Russian blackmail — a way of showing that Moscow can completely destabilise Georgia’s economy. Clearly, this move did not come out of nowhere: there are issues on which the two sides cannot agree. It appears that Georgian Dream is dragging its feet on something and failing to meet certain commitments.” Rukhadze identifies two possible issues: restoring rail links between Russia and Armenia through occupied Abkhazia, and providing guarantees of non-use of force to Sukhumi and Tskhinvali. However, he stresses that more information is needed to establish the specific reason behind Moscow’s decision. Abkhazia, non-use of force and the Russian embargo: what is the connection? On 9 October, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin met with the co-chairs of the Geneva International Discussions. They discussed preparations for the next round of talks, scheduled for November. According to an official statement from Russia’s Foreign Ministry, Moscow continues to demand that Georgia provide guarantees of non-use of force against Sukhumi and Tskhinvali. It also wants Tbilisi to begin delimiting the so-called state borders and subsequently demarcate them. These demands have two distinct aspects. The first concerns the non-use of force. The Geneva International Discussions were established after the August 2008 war, and security and non-use of force have remained permanent items on the agenda. However, Tbilisi and Moscow fundamentally disagree over who should make the relevant commitments. Russia demands guarantees regarding Sukhumi and Tskhinvali, thereby placing responsibility on Tbilisi. Georgia, by contrast, insists that the main security problem is Russia’s military presence and occupation. The second issue is even more serious. By demanding the delimitation of so-called state borders, Moscow treats Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region as states independent of Georgia. This contradicts the principle of Georgia’s territorial integrity, which the overwhelming majority of the international community recognises. Expert Teona Akubardia sees these two demands as part of Russia’s broader political strategy. In her assessment, Moscow is trying to formalise its influence over Georgia in legal and political terms. “Its ultimate goal is to formalise its strategic control over Georgia — control that Russia already exercises in practice, even though it has not been legally formalised,” she said. Akubardia believes that Russia’s economic restrictions, the issue of the occupied regions and Georgia’s deteriorating relations with the West should not be viewed as isolated developments. In her view, opening a transit corridor through Abkhazia may also be linked to Moscow’s demands. Giorgi Rukhadze has also pointed to this possibility. Georgia’s parliamentary speaker, Shalva Papuashvili, offers a different interpretation. He notes that Russia’s demands are not new and that Moscow has raised them at the Geneva talks for many years. “There is nothing new in this statement. At every meeting within the Geneva format, Russian representatives raise exactly the same issue. We, in turn, raise the questions of the return of displaced people, the withdrawal of Russian occupation forces and other matters,” he said. Nevertheless, experts believe this does not rule out the possibility that Moscow is using new economic levers to pursue its long-standing objectives. Gia Khukhashvili: ‘Dependence on the Russian market carries the risk of constant pressure’ Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili describes Russia’s decision as a familiar form of economic coercion. “This is Russia’s brazen ‘sledgehammer’ approach,” he said. Khukhashvili believes Moscow’s actions could have two consequences: increased pressure on Georgia’s government and business sector, and conditions that encourage informal deals and corruption. He argues that companies may try to cultivate ties with influential figures in Russia to circumvent the restrictions. However, he has provided no specific evidence of corrupt deals. Khukhashvili is particularly critical of business models that rely heavily on the Russian market. “The problem is that our businesses — constantly chasing short-term gains and worrying about how to please the authorities — have still failed to understand that they cannot tie themselves to the market of an enemy country. They should have done everything possible to diversify these risks,” he said. In his view, short-term profits from operating in Russia could ultimately lead to much greater losses. “I would tell winemakers this: you cannot ‘reach an agreement’ with Russia. Today, you may make a few pennies, but tomorrow you could lose ten times as much. Leave the Russian market alone. Find people who speak English and target other markets. Forget Russia and explore new opportunities — otherwise, you will remain trapped in this situation forever,” he said. Khukhashvili’s recommendation draws directly on economic data showing just how heavily Georgia’s wine industry depends on the Russian market. Russia accounts for almost two-thirds of Georgian wine exports Between January and August 2026, Georgia exported $102.2 million worth of wine to Russia. Total Georgian wine exports over the same period amounted to approximately $163.6 million. Russia therefore accounted for around 62.5% of the total value of Georgian wine exports. By volume, its share stood at approximately 66.6%. Russia remains the largest export market for Georgian wine, despite a decline in sales compared with the previous year. Poland ranks second, with Georgian wine exports worth around $10.7 million. Ukraine, China, Kazakhstan and Germany follow, but export volumes to these countries remain far below those to Russia. Losing the Russian market would affect producers differently. Tbilvino offers a clear example. According to the company’s chief executive, Zurab Margvelashvili, who spoke to BM.ge , Tbilvino exports wine to around 30 countries and has relatively little dependence on the Russian market. A potential ban would therefore cause some financial losses, but the company does not expect serious damage. Margvelashvili also notes that the company exports to markets with strict quality standards, while the Russian side has provided no detailed information about any specific violations. Energy dependence: a more powerful lever than wine Roman Gotsiridze, an opposition politician and former head of Georgia’s National Bank, has highlighted natural gas imports in the context of the current developments. According to figures he cited, Russia accounted for 1.7% of Georgia’s natural gas consumption in 2018. That share rose to 20% in 2023 and 25% in 2024. Estimates put it at around 28% in 2025. Gotsiridze believes this growing dependence gives Russia an additional lever for economic pressure. Unlike wine exports, natural gas supplies directly affect energy security, industrial operations and people’s everyday needs. Gotsiridze has therefore warned the government about possible scenarios involving more severe pressure from Russia. Could Russia expand the embargo? Mamuka Pipia, leader of the openly pro-Russian party Solidarity for Peace, says the ban on Georgian beverages represents only the first wave of restrictions. In his view , further measures will target other companies and product categories. His prediction deserves particular attention because Pipia represents a political force that takes a favourable view of Russia. Teona Akubardia also points to an earlier statement by Pipia. She notes that he mentioned a list of Georgian companies accused of supporting anti-Russian activity as early as June. If such a list did exist, it would be important to establish whether the companies named on it overlap with those now facing restrictions. Georgian experts also consider it possible that Russia will expand its measures. Gia Khukhashvili believes Moscow could use new restrictions to pressure Georgian businesses into exercising political caution. Giorgi Rukhadze suggests that the initial decision may be intended to demonstrate Russia’s capacity to exert economic pressure. These assessments point to several possible scenarios. The restrictions could remain limited to the seven companies and be lifted following negotiations. They could spread to other producers. Alternatively, Russia could make the use of trade restrictions a permanent instrument of pressure. How is Georgian Dream responding, and has its strategy worked? The Georgian government insists that maintaining economic ties with Russia serves the country’s interests and that businesses should not give up profitable markets for political reasons. Georgian Dream also argues that other countries have economic leverage over Georgia. Commenting on Russia’s latest restrictions, parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili also raised the risks associated with trade relations with the European Union. He pointed to issues involving sanctions, tariffs and the port of Kulevi. The Georgian Dream government justified its decision not to join international sanctions against Russia by arguing that it needed to protect the Georgian economy. Kobakhidze described the decision as correct and pragmatic. However, Georgian Dream’s opponents ask what additional security Georgia has gained by maintaining economic ties with Russia. The restrictions introduced on 9 October have shown that economic relations with Russia do not guarantee Georgian companies unrestricted access to the Russian market. Moscow continues to demand the establishment of so-called state borders with the occupied regions. At the same time, Russia’s sanitary watchdog has restricted imports of products from Georgian companies. Opposition politician Shalva Kereselidze, a member of the For Georgia party founded by Giorgi Gakharia, links the situation to Georgian Dream’s foreign policy. He argues that the government has damaged relations with the European Union while failing to protect Georgia’s economic and political interests in its dealings with Russia. “Do not think that the more you concede to Russia, the more favourably it will view you or the sooner it will take your interests into account. No — the outcome will be even worse,” he said. Russian embargo on Georgian goods

title: UK MEET Fellowship challenges journalists to look beyond AI hype
body: Journalists and digital content creators have been challenged to scrutinise claims about emerging technologies and demand evidence before presenting them to the public. The call was made on Monday, October 12, during the opening of the UK Media Excellence for Emerging Technologies (UK MEET) Fellowship in Accra. The five-day programme brings together selected media professionals to strengthen their capacity to report on science, technology and innovation, with a focus on distinguishing evidence-based findings from exaggerated claims. As artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies become increasingly prominent in healthcare, education and other sectors, the programme seeks to equip journalists with the skills to examine what these innovations can deliver, their limitations and their potential impact on society. Welcoming participants on behalf of the British High Commission, Ryan Davies highlighted the need for stronger and more sustainable connections between researchers and media practitioners. He stressed that as technological developments advance rapidly, trusted journalism is essential to helping the public navigate misinformation and understand the implications of scientific discoveries. Separating scientific evidence from marketing claims The opening day featured a fireside conversation on artificial intelligence in healthcare, with Darlington Akogo, founder of Mino Health AI Labs examining the difference between real-world clinical applications and marketing hype. The discussion placed the spotlight on the questions journalists should ask when reporting on technological innovations, including what evidence supports developers’ claims, how a tool performs in practice and whether its benefits can be independently verified. The issue is particularly important as AI systems are increasingly promoted for applications that could affect people’s health, education and access to essential services. For journalists, reporting on such developments requires more than explaining how a technology works. It also involves examining its reliability, limitations and consequences for the people expected to depend on it. Connecting research to public understanding The fellowship also highlighted the importance of making scientific knowledge accessible beyond academic and research institutions. Delivering the opening keynote, Director of the Ghana National Research Fund, Professor Abigail Opoku-Mensah, called for increased domestic investment in research and innovation, alongside closer collaboration between journalists and researchers. Abigail Opoku-Mensah, GNRF. She said stronger local financing would help Ghana build a sustainable research ecosystem and reduce long-term dependence on external support. Established under Act 1056 and officially launched in June 2025, the Fund is mandated to support research and innovation in priority areas, including health, food systems, climate sustainability, digital and industrial technologies, and governance. Prof. Opoku-Mensah urged journalists to help translate scientific developments into information citizens can understand and use, stressing that public communication is essential to turning research investments into meaningful outcomes. From training to investigative storytelling The UK MEET Fellowship is delivered by Imperial College London through Imperial Global Ghana, with support from the British High Commission. It seeks to strengthen science, technology and innovation reporting among journalists and digital content creators in Ghana and Nigeria. Participants will engage with researchers, policymakers and technology experts while developing original story pitches on emerging technologies. Ten participants with the strongest pitches will be selected for an educational visit to Imperial College London. The programme covers areas including artificial intelligence, climate and environmental risks, biomedical innovation and the circular economy. Its broader ambition is to strengthen evidence-based journalism and ensure that public conversations about technological progress are informed by credible information rather than unverified promises.

title: Kurt Okraku’s regime has ‘failed to perform’ – Kudjoe Fianoo demands resignation of GFA Executive Council
body: Former Ghana League Clubs Association (GHALCA) chairman Kudjoe Fianoo has called on Ghana Football Association (GFA) president Kurt Okraku and the entire Executive Council to resign, accusing the current administration of failing to deliver on expectations since taking office in October 2019. According to the former AshantiGold CEO, the present administration has “failed to perform” on expectations since taking office in October 2019. “You can give him an excuse in your first four years, or even in your first two years. But if it is not progressing, it is rather regressing,” Fianoo told Graphic Sports. “He headed a body that failed to perform. So they should all leave,” he added. Kurt has come under increasing pressure amid the Black Stars’ recent struggles, with Ghana suffering a disappointing start to their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign. The Black Stars lost 4-2 at home to The Gambia in their second Group C match, following a defeat by Ivory Coast in their opening qualifier. Those results have left Ghana without a point from their first two matches and bottom of Group C, while Ivory Coast and The Gambia lead the standings with six points each. The Black Stars, who are currently undergoing technical changes, are scheduled to return to action in November when they face Somalia at the Accra Sports Stadium.

title: Indian Navy to commission first multi-purpose vessel Samarthak on October 16
body:
By Aroonim Bhuyan

New Delhi, Oct 13. The Indian Navy will commission Samarthak, the first of four indigenously built multi-purpose vessels (MPVs), at Naval Base Karwar on October 16, marking another milestone in India's drive towards defence self-reliance.



Built by Larsen & Toubro Ltd under the government’s ‘Make in India’ initiative, the vessel is designed to undertake a wide range of maritime missions and is expected to play an important role in the Navy’s future operational requirements.

Primarily intended for maritime surveillance and patrol, Samarthak can also conduct low-intensity maritime operations (LIMO), serve as a platform for target deployment and trials, and function as a mothership for unmanned and autonomous systems.

The vessel is also equipped to undertake humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR) missions. Its design allows for conversion into a limited-capacity hospital ship and supports salvage operations, adding to its versatility during both routine deployments and emergencies.

The ship’s integrated combat suite combines indigenously developed sensors, weapons and electronic systems tailored to operate in challenging maritime conditions, reflecting the growing emphasis on domestic defence manufacturing and technology.



With its multi-role capabilities, Samarthak is expected to serve as a utility platform for a range of strategically important naval operations, enhancing the Indian Navy’s operational flexibility.

The vessel’s crest features an Indian elephant emerging from the waves, symbolising strength, intelligence and agility. Its motto, ‘Vijayartham Eknishthata’ (Victory Is Our Sole Aim), underscores its commitment to mission accomplishment.

The induction of Samarthak marks the beginning of the Navy’s planned acquisition of four multi-purpose vessels, strengthening its capacity to perform diverse maritime tasks while advancing India’s indigenous shipbuilding capabilities.

title: Russia remains key supplier of oil to China, India in August — OPEC
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia was again the largest supplier of oil to India (accounting for 45% of the country's oil imports) and to China (30% of the country's oil imports) in August 2026, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) said in its report.
In particular, Russia provided 45% of India's oil imports in August, while another 12% came from the UAE, and 9% from Venezuela, the OPEC reported, citing data from Kpler analytical firm.
India's total oil imports in August 2026 decreased relative to July, averaging 4.5 million barrels per day (bpd) compared to 5.05 million bpd the month before.
In the meantime, China's oil imports continued to recover in August, increasing from 8.38 million bpd to 8.89 million bpd, which is 6% more than the previous month. Russia remained the largest supplier of oil to China, with its share of supplies during the reporting period standing at 30%, while Brazil provided another 10% of supplies, and Saudi Arabia accounted for 8% of supplies.

title: Ukrainian Startup Zvook Secures Investment From Czech DEPO Ventures
body:
Czech venture capital firm DEPO Ventures invested an undisclosed amount in Zvook, a Ukrainian defense startup developing a hardware and software system that uses artificial intelligence (AI) and passive acoustic sensors to detect aerial targets.
DEPO Ventures Co-founder and Managing Partner Petr Šíma revealed the deal to Defender Media on Monday, Oct. 12. The investment was made through the firm’s new Ukraine Fund, which was announced separately on Oct. 2. The deal marks the first investment from the new fund.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The fund, which also backs startups from Moldova and Georgia, was established by National Development Investments, a subsidiary of the Czech National Development Bank together with the Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade. Its stated objective is to attract innovative companies from the region while creating skilled employment and strengthening the Czech innovation ecosystem.
Amid the ongoing war, defense tech has emerged as the country’s fastest-growing tech sector, attracting more than $129 million in investments, according to AVentures Capital’s DealBook of Ukraine.
Zvook is conducting research and development on hydrophones for passive underwater acoustic monitoring. The company cites maritime security, the monitoring of shipping and ports, and the protection of critical underwater infrastructure as potential applications for the technology, according to the company’s post on LinkedIn .
The fund plans to allocate $4.25 million to startups from Ukraine, Moldova, and Georgia, offering tickets of up to $559,000 per company. The total fund volume could increase to $6.5 million if conditions around private capital and deployed investment are met, as per The Recursive.
DEPO Ventures has previously invested in several companies with Ukrainian founders, including $1.3 million in 2023 for Masthead Data, a real-time platform for analyzing and monitoring errors in large datasets, and $1.1 million in 2024 for Talsec, a startup developing mobile app security solutions.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Afenyo-Markin’s influence is limited by minority numbers in Parliament – Haruna Iddrisu
body: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu says Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin is doing his best in Parliament but faces limited influence because of the numerical strength of his caucus. The former Minority Leader reflected on the challenges of leading an opposition caucus against a substantially larger majority. “For instance, the current minority leader, Afeyo Makin, is doing his utmost best, but he’s simply overwhelmed with the numbers,” he said while discussing on JoyFM’s SMS on Tuesday. “Very little to do, very little influence with those numbers,” he added. Mr Iddrisu compared the situation with his own experience in a Parliament where the distribution of seats significantly limited the opposition’s ability to influence proceedings. “So it reminded me of my days when we had 169, 106 kind of Parliament, where you can be told that even if you walk out, it made no meaning and made no consequence,” he said. Despite those numerical differences, the Tamale South MP stressed that democracy required space for dissent and constructive criticism. “But I think that for the good of our democracy, it’s good to tolerate dissent, and it’s good to tolerate constructive criticisms,” he said. He explained that such criticism should help improve governance and the quality of life of Ghanaians, adding that making life easier for citizens should be the primary objective of public office holders. Mr Iddrisu also underscored the importance of consensus in parliamentary leadership, noting that leaders sometimes needed to allow backbenchers to take the initiative before intervening to manage disagreements. “Consensus is the beauty of any democracy,” he said. His remarks came in response to questions about whether he missed parliamentary leadership and how he viewed the conduct of parliamentary business.

title: Russian forces attempt to advance toward Riasne in Sumy region, Trehubov says
body:
Viktor Trehubov, spokesperson for Ukraine's Joint Forces Group, made the statement during a televised broadcast, according to Ukrinform.
"In the eastern part of the Sumy region, the Russians are actively trying to push toward the unfortunate settlement of Riasne and take full control of it. They are also attempting to expand their area of control somewhat, both along the border and deeper into Ukrainian territory," he stated.
"They have been unable to advance farther into Ukraine, but there are some indications that they are preparing to expand their presence in areas of the immediate border region that are not under Russian control. They are moving some additional forces into those areas. However, once again, we can see this, and we know what they intend to do," Trehubov said.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian forces carried out more than 40 strikes against 30 settlements across 20 territorial communities in the Sumy region during the 24-hour period from the morning of October 12 to the morning of October 13. Two people were injured.

title: Education Ministry denies approving trip through restricted area following deadly explosion
body: The Education Ministry approved the route of Monday's deadly explosion of a Hezbollah ordnance in northern Israel that killed a 14-year-old student and wounded more than 20 others, even though it was deemed unsafe by the Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF), Army Radio reported on Tuesday.KKL Chairman Eyal Austrinsky told Army Radio on Tuesday that the Education Ministry's situation room should have known the area was unsafe. The Education Ministry denied the it had approved a school trip through an area closed by KKL-JNF, claiming that it "acted in accordance with KKL-JNF restrictions and prohibited activity in the area in question due to war damage, and the planned hiking route was not within the prohibited area."The ministry added that explicit safety instructions had been issued when the trip was approved, including an absolute prohibition on touching unexploded missiles or ammunition and a requirement to report any such objects immediately.The statement did not establish whether the students followed the approved route throughout the trip, an issue investigators are now examining."The circumstances of the incident and the route actually taken are currently being examined as part of an IDF and police investigation, in cooperation with the Education Ministry and the relevant professional authorities," the ministry said."It is necessary to await the findings of the investigation before the full circumstances of the incident can be determined."The ministry said it would continue reviewing the procedures for approving school activities and their accompanying safety instructions with the relevant authorities over the coming days.Hezbollah cluster munition detonates, killing one, wounding dozensOn Tuesday, the student killed in the blast was identified as Elazar Yair Wilensky, 14, from Ma'alot-Tarshiha. The explosion also wounded students and staff members, several of them seriously.According to a preliminary investigation, one of the students had reportedly picked up an unexploded munition and placed it in his bag before it detonated. The circumstances surrounding the handling of the munition remain under investigation.Education Minister Yoav Kisch said Monday that the trip and its route had received the required approvals. Following the explosion, the ministry announced that school trips to areas along the Israel-Lebanon border on Tuesday and Wednesday would be diverted to other locations.Additionally, the Home Front Command has announced it would be stepping up its public information efforts regarding the dangers of unexploded ordnance, including public awareness campaigns and safety instructions.Metula mayor decries decisions to suspend trips to northern IsraelMetula Mayor David Azulay strongly criticized proposals to suspend hiking routes, warning that such a move would deal another devastating blow to tourism and daily life in the Galilee."The decision to suspend trips is wrong," Azulay stated emphatically.He compared the public debate to previous crises that had harmed the region."I remember the amoeba incident in the Sea of Galilee – they killed tourism at the Sea of Galilee. Do they want to kill tourism in the Galilee, which already doesn't have many visitors? As painful as this is, people need to be alert and careful, and walk only on marked trails. There shouldn't be anything on the trails because inspections were carried out."Azulay stressed that the dangers in the area extend far beyond a single type of weapon."It's not just cluster munitions. A cluster bomb like that contains between 39 and 69 bomblets, depending on the type. Most of the bomblets eventually explode, but there is other unexploded ordnance, mortar shells, rockets of various types that were fired, drones and UAVs."

title: Sifnos: The Quiet Cycladic Island of Pottery, Trails and Exceptional Food
body: Any Sifnos travel guide starts with the island’s quiet appeal: whitewashed villages, old stone paths, a living pottery craft and some of the best food in the Cyclades. Church of the Epta Martiri. Its charms are not loud. However, visitors who know Sifnos well rarely swap it for another Cycladic island, and locals call it the “quiet power” of the Aegean. Elegance, balance and gentle growth define the place. In addition, respect for the landscape shapes how the island has developed, so travellers who want nightlife and crowds usually look elsewhere. Apollonia, Kamares and Vathi in a Sifnos travel guide Apollonia has served as the island’s capital since 1836. It takes its name from Apollo, who was worshipped there as a protector of farmers. Banks, pharmacies and shops cluster in the hilltop village, while flower-filled courtyards line its lanes. Visitors can also find the church of Panagia Ouranofora, renovated in 1767, and Agios Sostis with its carved wooden screen. At night, life moves to the Steno, the narrow main street of Apollonia, with its restaurants, old coffee houses, bars and boutiques. During peak season, it is packed. Ferries dock at Kamares, a port that grew in the 19th century as a loading point for ore. Unlike many Cycladic harbours, Kamares has seen only modest development. Traces of old kilns survive there, as well as a pier from 1909. Today the bay offers cafes, fish tavernas, rooms to rent and a sandy, family-friendly beach. On the south-west coast, Vathi wraps around a sheltered bay with shallow water and the small church of the Taxiarchis. Tavernas sit right on the sand, so lunch is never far from the sea. An island shaped by clay Sifnian pottery remains the island’s best-known craft. Rich clay deposits still lie under the hills, and potters say the local clay makes their wares unusually durable. Kostas Depastas, a potter since 1948, works in a seaside workshop at Cherronisos in the north. He recalls a time when the whole island worked as one big pottery. “Everything you see on the coast today, shops, hotels, rooms, all of them were workshops,” he said, because potters needed to be near the sea to load their wares onto ships. In Artemonas, the Lembesis family pottery now runs into its fourth generation. Most of its bowls, mugs and plates leave the island, although tourism keeps the decorative work alive. Look out, in particular, for the flaros, a clay chimney pot that has become a symbol of Sifnian pottery. The island’s craft heritage also earned Sifnos a place in the UNESCO Creative Cities Network , which it joined the network in December 2025 . Walking the old stone paths Hikers can explore more than 350 kilometres of footpaths and stone-paved mule tracks on Sifnos. Many survive because islanders still use them to reach their fields. Since 2012, the Municipality of Sifnos has marked about 100 kilometres of trails as 10 numbered routes. Even so, some signs need repair, so walkers often carry the detailed 1:20,000 map from Terrain Editions . Route 5 from Apollonia to Vathi is one of the most rewarding. It runs for 9 kilometres, mostly downhill, through old farmland, and takes close to four hours. Route 10 instead follows the old mule road from Apollonia down to Kamares over 5.7 kilometres. Meanwhile-free options abound, too: Route 2 links the medieval village of Kastro with the famous Chrysopigi monastery. Much of western Sifnos also falls within the Natura 2000 network. Specifically, the protected zone runs from Profitis Ilias, the island’s highest peak, to the west coast, and it hosts 39 bird species. Autumn and winter turn the interior green, which makes the cooler months a good time for any Sifnos travel guide to recommend walking. Chickpeas, cheese and a famous chef Food is a big part of any Sifnos travel guide, because cooking here carries real history. Nikolaos Tselementes, the chef who reshaped Greek home cooking in the 1920s , came from the village of Exampela. Many families still eat revithada, a slow-baked chickpea stew, on Sundays after church. Taverns in Artemonas also serve mastelo, a local dish of meat baked in a clay pot. Local manoura cheese turns up across menus, from traditional meze to modern restaurant dishes. In 2026, the island’s kitchens drew Australian chef Shannon Bennett’s Culinary Wonderland team for a feature on its food. Sweet tooths should visit the Theodorou patisserie in Artemonas, which opened in 1968. Its third generation still makes almond sweets, pastelli and halva pies to the old recipes. Where to stay on Sifnos Accommodation suits most budgets, and the right base depends on the trip. Apollonia and Artemonas put visitors close to restaurants, trailheads and the island’s bus links. By contrast, Kamares offers many rented rooms and small hotels within walking distance of the ferry. Kastro has small hotels and rooms inside a village that dates back to 1635. Beach lovers often choose Vathi or Platys Gialos, the island’s longest beach. Several boutique hotels and villas have opened in recent seasons, so it pays to book early for summer. Before booking, check ferry times to Kamares, since the timetable shapes the whole stay. For anyone who follows this Sifnos travel guide, the reward is the same: a slower island where villages, paths and kitchens still keep their own rhythm. Source: travel.gr The post Sifnos: The Quiet Cycladic Island of Pottery, Trails and Exceptional Food appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Police administration is doing a yeoman’s job – President Mahama
body: President John Dramani Mahama has commended the current Police administration under the leadership of COP Tetteh Yuhuno for improving the fight against crime. The President said there has been an improvement in public safety with reduced highway robberies and unresolved murders. Speaking at the commissioning of an 85-bed ward complex at the Police Hospital in Accra on Tuesday, October 13, President Mahama praised the administration and advised officers to do more to protect lives and property. “This police administration is doing a yeoman’s job, and as Commander-in-Chief and President of the Republic, I want to express the gratitude of our nation to all of you and urge you to keep up the good work,” he said. He reiterated the commitment of the government in resourcing the administration with the right logistics to deliver on its mandate effectively. “It is no wonder everybody wants to visit Ghana, because people say it is the safest country in the whole of West Africa, and I can assure you that we will continue to provide you with the logistics that you need to continue to do your job,” he added. President John Dramani Mahama announced the termination of the Police Hospital expansion contract after 22 years of delays, citing prolonged disagreements with the contractor and cost overruns. He said the government would take responsibility for completing the project, with about GH¢200 million to be provided in the 2027 Budget to bring the expanded facility into service before the end of that year.

title: GoldBod tells PAC Bank of Ghana authorised its foreign exchange transactions
body: The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), Sammy Gyamfi, says the institution’s foreign exchange transactions are conducted within a market regulated by the Bank of Ghana (BoG), which has provided guidance and authorisation for GoldBod to sell foreign exchange. Speaking before the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), Mr Gyamfi explained that generating foreign exchange for Ghana was one of GoldBod’s primary statutory responsibilities. However, he said the institution needed to sell the foreign exchange it generated to obtain cedis to finance its gold purchases. “First of all, we are set up to generate foreign exchange for Ghana. But in generating foreign exchange for the country, you need to sell that foreign exchange for the country to benefit, so that we can get cedis back to buy gold,” he said. He stressed that the institution’s foreign exchange transactions were subject to the central bank’s regulatory oversight. “We operate within an FX market that is regulated by the Bank of Ghana. The sale of that FX is regulated by the Bank of Ghana,” he told the committee. To explain the regulatory basis for the transactions, Mr Gyamfi said GoldBod formally approached the Bank of Ghana for guidance and authorisation after securing policy approval for its funding model from its supervising minister, the Minister of Finance. He said the approval was obtained under Section 12 of the Gold Board Act before the institution wrote to the central bank on 23 September to seek guidance on its foreign exchange operations. According to him, the request was made in recognition of the Bank of Ghana’s role as the regulator of the foreign exchange market. Mr Gyamfi said the central bank had since responded to GoldBod’s request and provided the necessary guidance and authorisation for the institution to sell foreign exchange. “And I’m happy to inform the committee that the Bank of Ghana has given us that guidance and authorisation,” he said. BoG authorisation recognises GoldBod’s mandate Mr Gyamfi said the Bank of Ghana’s guidance and authorisation recognised GoldBod’s statutory role as a foreign exchange earner. He told the committee that the central bank’s letter expressly acknowledged the institution’s authority to sell foreign exchange. “The authorisation and guidance from the Bank of Ghana recognise Gold Board’s statutory role as a foreign exchange earner,” he said. He added that the letter from the central bank was available for inspection and offered to share a copy with the committee. “The Bank of Ghana made it clear in that letter that the Gold Board is allowed to sell foreign exchange,” he said. Mr Gyamfi maintained that selling foreign exchange was necessary for GoldBod to convert its foreign currency proceeds into cedis to finance gold purchases, while ensuring that its transactions remained within the regulatory framework established by the Bank of Ghana.

title: 2027: Tinubu Turns To Opposition Figures In Re-Election Survival
body: President Bola Tinubu’s bid for a second term is taking on a broader political character. The ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) is turning to influential figures outside its ranks to help build a winning coalition ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The inclusion of Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) chieftain and Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike; Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord Party; and Anambra State Governor Chukwuma Soludo of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) as coordinators of Tinubu’s campaign in their respective territories points to an effort to extend the president’s reach beyond the APC’s traditional political machinery. The appointments come as Tinubu faces the challenge of converting his administration’s control of federal power and growing political reach into an electoral mandate. This is amid public discontent over economic hardship and security concerns, and an opposition struggling to consolidate into a common front. Rather than restricting the campaign to party loyalists, the revised presidential campaign council appears designed to draw on political figures whose influence, local structures and relationships could prove useful in states where the APC cannot rely solely on its own organisation. Wike’s appointment is particularly significant. Despite remaining a PDP member, the former Rivers State governor has been one of Tinubu’s most consequential political allies outside the ruling party since the 2023 election. His support for Tinubu has also become part of a wider debate over whether politicians can back the president nationally while retaining separate political interests at state level. Speaking on Tuesday, Wike said the president’s approach was to accommodate people outside the APC who were willing to contribute to his re-election. “My thinking is that the president, in his wisdom, said there are those who are not members of our political parties but have something to offer to his re-election, and it’s proper to accommodate them,” he said. Wike added that the campaign should not be confined to APC members. He argued that people who wanted Tinubu to continue in office should be allowed to contribute regardless of their party affiliations. His position, however, comes against the backdrop of disagreements within the ruling party over his proposed Rainbow Coalition and the extent to which non-APC politicians should influence the president’s re-election machinery. Some APC state chapters have questioned the arrangement, insisting that those genuinely committed to Tinubu should formally join the party. Adeleke’s appointment presents another striking dimension. The Osun governor, who secured re-election under the Accord Party, has been named to coordinate Tinubu’s presidential campaign in the state. It placed him in a position to mobilise for a president whose party is his rival in the state’s political contest. The choice could help the APC reach beyond its established Osun network, but it also raises questions about how presidential support will coexist with competition for governorship and legislative seats. APGA, meanwhile, has publicly backed Soludo’s inclusion. The party said the arrangement reflects its position that Tinubu should be supported for president while the party maintains its separate identity and pursues other elective offices. The appointments suggest that the APC’s immediate calculation is to assemble a wider electoral support base around Tinubu. Whether that translates into votes will depend on the willingness and ability of the appointees to mobilise their constituencies, rather than their names appearing on a campaign document. The strategy also unfolds against a fragmented opposition landscape. With opposition parties and political blocs yet to establish a unified challenge, Tinubu’s camp has an opportunity to cultivate alliances across party lines. But such arrangements can be fragile where allies have competing ambitions, particularly in states where the presidential and governorship contests may pull political actors in different directions. The revised council also reshapes the ruling party’s internal command structure. Senate President Godswill Akpabio and House of Representatives Speaker Tajudeen Abbas have been elevated to deputy vice-chairmen, while Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq occupies another deputy vice-chairmanship position. Senator Abdulaziz Yari remains director-general, with other senior party and government figures assigned responsibilities across the campaign structure. Former Kwara Senator Gbemisola Saraki is among the new entrants, listed as zonal secretary in the Contact and Mobilisation Directorate for the North-Central. Not all prominent figures appearing in the revised document are new entrants. Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, for instance, was already listed as Director of Finance and Treasury and retains that responsibility while also appearing as Delta State campaign coordinator. Former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Fashola had previously been assigned to South-West stakeholders’ mobilisation, while Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo was already part of the media and strategic communications structure. The changes also leave questions about some appointments in the original document. Abdulfatai Yaya Seriki, who was listed as North-Central Zonal Director of Youth Mobilisation, does not appear under that assignment in the revised list, although the Youth Mobilisation Directorate remains in the structure. Similarly, the six zonal directors previously named for election planning, coordination and mobilisation — Olushola Adeyeye for the South-West, Ngozi Olejeme for the South-South, Uche Ekwunife for the South-East, Muntaqha Rabe for the North-West, Ahmed Muhammed Ketso for the North-Central and Sani Danladi for the North-East — are not reproduced under their former assignments. The Directorate of Election Planning, Coordination and Monitoring remains in place under Faleke, with secretaries and members listed. The absence of the earlier zonal appointments, however, does not by itself establish that the individuals have been formally removed from the campaign council. The changes follow the controversy surrounding the original list in August, when questions were raised over its status. APC National Publicity Secretary Felix Morka dismissed reports that the list had been withdrawn, saying, “Rumours are not news,” and indicating that any adjustments would be announced properly. The Presidency also maintained that the original list remained valid, while acknowledging that adjustments were possible as the campaign structure developed and its subcommittees were constituted. The revised document now presents a more detailed state coordination arrangement, changes the responsibilities of senior officers, expands the advisory network and includes prominent politicians whose party affiliations extend beyond the APC. The council is scheduled to be inaugurated by Tinubu at the Banquet Hall of the Presidential Villa, Abuja, on Wednesday, October 14, at 11am.

title: Russia ready to share knowledge in tax sphere — Deputy PM
body:
BANGKOK, October 13. /TASS/. Russia is ready to share its knowledge in the tax administration sphere with the developing economies in the first instance, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk told reporters on the sidelines of the fall session of the governing authorities of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
Russia's work in the field of tax administration generates high interest and the Russian side is holding two seminars in Bangkok to share the best Russian practices, he said.
"Here, we propose establishing an exchange platform based on Russian knowledge and say that we are open to sharing our experience, our knowledge, primarily with the countries of the Global South, with developing economies, which today are more interested than ever in solving the challenges they face. Specifically, developing their own economies, raising people's living standards, and creating new jobs. This is one of the main recurring themes of the current meeting of shareholders of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank," Overchuk noted. "Russia can indeed contribute a great deal here so that all this positive experience will be used by the international community," the deputy prime minister added.

title: Russian drones strike university in Ukraine’s Rivne, injuring 20
body: Russian drones struck the Rivne region in western Ukraine on the morning of October 13, hitting the city of Rivne. Ukraine’s National Police said in a statement that a Russian drone struck an educational institution. A fire broke out in one wing of the building after drone debris fell on it, according to data from the State Emergency Service. Twenty people were injured, according to the latest data. Ukraine’s Education Minister Andrii Butenko clarified that the building hit was part of Rivne State University of the Humanities. The Department of Musical Arts building burned down completely. All students were in shelters, Butenko said, but members of the university’s administrative staff were injured.
