title: Elgato takes on DJI with a tiny wireless mic for creators on the go
body:
Elgato already dominates the market for hardware built for creators that use powerful desktop PCs, and it’s now turning its attention to creators on the go with its first wireless microphone. The $99.99 Wave Go clips onto your clothes just like DJI’s Mic Mini, with hands-free recording for vlogging and content creation.
The Wave Go is tiny, about the size of an AirPod, so it disappears on camera and only weighs seven grams. Despite the tiny size, Elgato is promising “broadcast-quality” audio, with a condenser capsule that supports EQ shift, auto gain, and noise cancellation.
The Wave Go clips onto clothes with a magnetic clip and plate, and a single button lets you power on the microphone or mute it. You can also double-press the button to launch the camera app on your phone.
[Image: The Wave Go can slot into the top of Elgato’s Smart Handle to transform into a full-size interview mic. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Wave_Go_Lifestyle_Shot_07_vswrku.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Elgato has also created a Smart Handle for the Wave Go, a bundled accessory that turns it into a full-size interview mic. The Wave Go simply slots into the top of the Smart Handle, which has a power and mute button with an LED indicator for power, mute, and pairing status. The handle also acts as a charger for the Wave Go, adding five more charges, which at around eight hours per charge gives you 48 hours in total. You can also quick-charge in 10 minutes to get around an hour of recording time.
The USB-C receiver is made for phones, so it works with iPhones, Android devices, and iPads. It connects to the microphone over a 2.4GHz wireless signal, so there’s no Bluetooth here, and the latency is around 24ms or less. The Smart Handle, mic, and USB-C receiver can all be secured inside the included case, but the case doesn’t have an integrated battery, so the Smart Handle is the main way to charge on the go.
[Image: The Wave Go has a carry case that houses the mic, USB-C receiver, and Smart Handle. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Wave_Go_Device_Shots_08_ezgxud.png?quality=90&strip=all]
Elgato has also created a Wave Go mobile app that lets you monitor live audio levels, enable noise reduction, toggle automatic leveling, and check battery status. You can even use the Wave Go on a desktop PC with Elgato’s Wave Link 3.0 software, simply by plugging the receiver into a USB-C port.
The Wave Go is available today priced at $99.99 (€99.99 / £99.99), and a second mic transmitter is available for $29.99 if you want to record a second voice.

title: Apple launches HomeView, its first smart display for the home
body:
It’s finally here: Apple’s long-rumored smart display, the Apple HomeView, has arrived. I got a first look at the device in New York City this week, and it’s gorgeous. The HomeView puts a small, vibrant screen atop a speaker base for taking video calls, beautifully displaying photos, and providing information at a glance with Apple’s Siri AI voice assistant. The device’s square shape makes it feel less imposing than larger smart displays like Google’s Nest Hub Max or Amazon’s Echo Show 11, and I can see it fitting nicely on my kitchen counter — though it might be a hair too big for my bedside table.
The HomeView is the centerpiece of Apple’s new push into the home. It costs $299 and launches alongside a new collection of cameras, thermostats, and a door lock designed for Apple Home. As a smart home hub, Matter controller, and Thread Border Router, the HomeView can orchestrate these and other Apple Home and Matter smart home devices. It’s available in eight countries at launch: the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and India. Preorders are open now, with devices shipping November 13th. 
[Image: The HomeView can sit on a table or counter and display customizable widgets. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-lifestyle-living-room.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The new smart display has Siri AI built in, enabling natural-language voice interactions to ask general knowledge questions, control smart home devices via voice and touch, and get information using personal context from your text messages, calendar, and emails. Personal context requires facial recognition and for your Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone to be on the same network, so your kids can’t peek at your texts over breakfast.
The HomeView can display neatly formatted recipes for following along as you cook, keep you in the picture on FaceTime video calls with Center Stage, and show live feeds and footage from HomeKit Secure Video cameras.  
The HomeView’s 7-inch square screen sits atop a surprisingly small aluminum speaker base, attached by an adjustable stainless steel arm. It has no physical volume or power buttons, and no cover for the 12-megapixel FaceTime camera, which Apple says is used only for video calls and facial recognition.  
[Image: The many faces of HomeView. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-collection-of-faces.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The screen offers a variety of customizable “faces” that feel more like a big Apple Watch than a small iPad. When idle, the HomeView can display photo faces, clock faces, and Snoopy faces, or you can use a modular face to show widgets from your most-used apps, such as your to-do list, world clock, and podcasts. A home widget face offers controls for lights, climate, cameras, and other devices.  
I haven’t had a chance to try the device yet, but I saw a demo showing how swiping up from the bottom of the screen pulls up a familiar app grid with Apple’s core apps — like Messages and Apple Music — all available.  
[Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hkrYiZ_g9tw]
Apple also showed a video demoing how it envisions a family of five using the HomeView around the kitchen counter during the morning rush. From pulling up a French toast recipe for breakfast to checking the calendar for the day to receiving a FaceTime call to asking it to find lost keys, Apple pictures the HomeView stepping in to help with common minor household crises.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-color-family.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-screen-angles.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-rear-USB-C-port.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-Apple-Podcasts-Lyrics-Apple-Music.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-custom-engineered-acoustic-system.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The video shows the daughter sending a text message to her secret boyfriend from the HomeView, and the younger brother being foiled from attempting to read it because it shuts off when it doesn’t see her face, and then everyone views a live feed of said boyfriend arriving at the front door. The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.  
I’ve always seen smart displays as a good option for controlling smart home devices without having to pull out my phone and open an app. Apple’s vision for the HomeView takes that to its natural conclusion: you don’t have to pull out your phone for anything when you’re home since it’s all available on the HomeView (well, at least all of Apple’s apps). It’s an iPhone for your home.
[Image: The HomeView can be wall-mounted, with the option of POE. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-wall-mounted.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The HomeView comes in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. It features two speaker drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base for bass. Based on initial listening, the sound hits a few notches above the HomePod Mini but doesn’t compete with the HomePod.  
There’s a wall-mountable version without the speaker base that also costs $299 and comes with three mounting options: plug-in, in-wall power, and in-wall PoE. Apple says the audio is tuned for wall placement, but I didn’t get to hear it in action.  
The screen is wrapped in an aluminum case and has no physical buttons; the frame is just dotted with a speaker grille and microphone holes. It has a Liquid Retina display —  that usually means LCD in Apple’s language, though the company didn’t clarify  — with True Tone support and ambient light adjustment, and it can go up to a bright 500 nits and down to a super-low 0.3 nits, which Apple says makes it usable as a bedside clock. The screen is large enough to see clearly from across the room but doesn’t adjust as you approach. You tap widgets to access different apps and controls, or use voice to tell it what to do.  
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-home-touch.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-Timer.png?quality=90&strip=all]
While the HomeView functions as an Apple Home Hub — it enables local control of supported devices, creation of scenes and automations, and support for HomeKit Secure Video — the device feels less like a focused smart home controller and more like a way to use your iPhone less when you’re at home.
The HomeView supports a number of Apple’s own apps, including Calendar, Reminders, Messages, and Music. Apple says it also works with third-party audio and video apps that support the CarPlay architecture. A few audio apps, such as Spotify and Audible, are available, but no video apps yet.  
[Image: You can pick up conversations started with Siri AI on the HomeView in the Siri AI app on the iPhone. And vice versa. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-Siri-AI-app.png?quality=90&strip=all]
Siri AI on HomeView is the same voice assistant as the upgraded version that arrived on the iPhone with iOS 27. It has no smart display-specific features or home-control features; it offers broad world knowledge, personal context, and natural language understanding. I saw a demo where it accepted chained requests and retained the context throughout, such as adding an event to the calendar, then setting a reminder for that same day, and adding an item to a grocery list. However, chained requests for home devices are limited to specific device types — you can turn on the lights in the living room and the bedroom, but you can’t lock the front door and adjust the thermostat with one command.  
Both the tabletop and wall-mounted devices have the same features; only the mount differs, but where you place them will likely dictate how you use them. A HomeView on the kitchen counter feels more tailored to content consumption, music, and cooking, while a wall-mounted version fits more of the smart home control center role.
In its demo space, Apple mounted a HomeView near a front door with the smart home widget enabled, allowing touch control of locks, the thermostat, and lights. It can push a live feed from a doorbell camera when someone rings the bell and display up to nine live streams from HomeKit Secure Video cameras. When you tap on a widget, it becomes a full-screen controller. I saw the thermostat controls, and they were large and easy to use. I haven’t yet gotten to play with any other widgets or try controlling it with voice commands.  
[Image: HomeView supports up to six profiles and uses facial recognition to switch between them so only you see your personal information. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-user-recognition.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The HomeView’s key software feature is intelligent switching that lets the screen move from a household device to a personal device. It uses facial recognition and the presence of your recently unlocked iPhone on the home Wi-Fi network to authenticate you. Once it knows who you are, it can show your customized HomeView layout and, if you have an AI-capable iPhone, use personal context to pull up that recipe Mom texted you or play that song your friend sent. Without recognizing the user, Siri AI on HomeView can show the live doorbell feed, answer general questions, control some smart devices, display recipes, and play audio and video.  
Apple allows the device to support up to six profiles, but each user must have an iPhone or iPad updated to the latest OS. Apple says the microphone and camera data used for profile recognition is processed on a Secure Exclave running on the device’s A18 chip, which Apple says it can’t access, the OS can’t access, and apps can’t access.  
[Image: You can hand off recipes from Safari on your iPhone to the HomeView, and it formats them for following along while cooking. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomeView-Cooking_73277b.png?quality=90&strip=all]
My concern is how seamlessly it will switch between profiles and how limited it will be when it doesn’t recognize you — I’ve had too many instances of yelling at Siri on my HomePod because it refuses to find my iPhone until I authenticate on the iPhone I’m asking it to find. Some smart home controls, like viewing recorded footage or controlling security accessories, require an authenticated user, which I can see causing problems if it’s too slow or if you’re trying to get things done without standing in front of the device.  
Based on early impressions, and without yet getting my hands on the HomeView, I think success here hinges on how much people really want to use a communal device for personal interactions. The demos I saw were engaging and fun, and its deep integration with your iPhone gives it more to work with than a device like Amazon’s Echo Show, which has a similar profile feature but less personal information to offer.
However, all the demos work just as well with Siri AI on your iPhone, and the whole system seems precariously tied to said phone. Beyond the personal context features, I didn’t see a compelling smart home use case that I haven’t seen on competitors’ smart displays. In classic Apple style, the HomeView looks gorgeous as well as intuitive to use, and if it can actually keep phones off the kitchen counter at meal times, that might just be its killer feature.

title: The new Apple Home Collection includes a video doorbell, smart lock, and more
body:
Apple has partnered with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to launch the Apple Home Collection, an assortment of smart home devices meant to be easy to set up and use. The collection is something of a smart home starter pack, including security cameras, a video doorbell, a door lock, and two thermostats.
Apple is announcing the products as part of a major push into the smart home space, led by its new Siri AI-powered HomeView smart display. The devices are the first smart home gadgets the company has made for Apple Home; previously, it relied on third parties to make products for the platform. While third parties manufactured these, Apple co-developed each product and says they are designed to work seamlessly with Apple Home. Apple introduced the collection at its Welcome Home event in New York City today, where it also showcased the new Apple TV 4K and the HomePod Mini 2.    
[Image: The LG lock and doorbell camera. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-lifestyle-01.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The collection shares a similar design aesthetic; Apple says it and its partners designed each product with a simple, clean look in mind. The devices come in black or silver with some white touches and options. The cameras share a tubular design; I saw them installed in Apple’s smart home in New York’s Tribeca neighborhood this week, and they are largely unremarkable — not ugly but not showpieces, seemingly designed to blend in as much as possible. They remind me of products from French smart home manufacturer Netatmo, but not quite as stylish.
Apple said its main focus with the collection was to make the accessories easy to set up, reliable for everyday use, and capable of keeping your data private. All the products work with the Apple Home app (no third-party apps or accounts are needed), and Apple says they are as easy to pair as a HomePod or AirPods; just tap them with your iPhone, and it will recognize them using Bluetooth and NFC. Apple says all accessories in the collection are managed by Apple products, like an iPhone or a device that can act as an Apple Home Hub, and communication is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can say who has access to your data.   
[Image: The LG floodlight camera. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-lifestyle-02.png?quality=90&strip=all]
Ultimately, while easier setup is a nice touch, installation and ongoing connectivity issues with smart home devices like cameras and door locks are what give people headaches. I hope Apple has addressed those here, too, but we won’t know until we test them. The collection does fill a gap in Apple’s offering, giving it a line of products blessed by the platform. Amazon with Ring and Google with Nest both have products they can point users to when they are looking to set up a smart home. Now Apple has the same.
There are six devices in total, with the UWB-powered door lock being the most interesting — it’s only the third lock on the market to support Apple’s hands-free unlocking using UWB.    
LG deadbolt lock
[Image: The LG smart lock is available in silver and black. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/lg-lock.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The LG smart lock costs $349 and supports Apple Home Key, including hands-free unlocking via UWB, so you don’t need to tap your phone or watch (though you can); if it’s in your pocket or bag, the door unlocks automatically. It also has a keypad for PIN code entry and a physical keyhole hidden under the rotating keypad.    
This is a full replacement door lock for a US-style deadbolt that uses Matter-over-Thread for connectivity and supports the Aliro smart lock standard. It has a circular exterior design and a more traditional rear housing for the batteries (standard AA) and motor, as well as a physical thumbturn for manual operation. It comes in black and silver for the housing but only black for the front, and will be available in the US and Canada starting in December.
LG smart doorbell camera
[Image: LG doorbell camera. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-LG-Video-Doorbell-Wired.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The video doorbell will cost $249 and features two cameras: one front-facing for viewing visitors and one pointing down for packages, both cameras support up to 2.5K resolution. The camera comes in silver or black and has a long, tubular design, and sticks out slightly from the wall. It also features a motion-activated light that illuminates the floor to help it see packages and light the area when you approach the door at night.
The doorbell needs to be wired into your home’s doorbell wiring and can ring your HomePods as a chime. It will be available in the US, Canada, and the UK, but Apple hasn’t given a release date. It supports Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, so it can send smart notifications for Familiar Faces, pets, packages, and vehicles.    
If you have an iCloud subscription, recorded video is automatically saved there. Footage is processed locally on an Apple Home Hub and sent to the cloud end-to-end encrypted. If you enable Apple Intelligence on the camera via a supported phone (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer), you can get AI-powered text descriptions that give you more details about what the camera saw than standard notifications. These clips use Apple’s Private Cloud Compute and require a higher iCloud storage tier.    
LG indoor and outdoor security cameras
[Image: LG indoor security camera. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-LG-Indoor-Cam-Plug-In.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The indoor camera has a similar tubular look; the model I saw was white and looked a bit like a desk lamp. It costs $199, is compatible with HomeKit Secure Video, and records up to 2.5K resolution. Its signature feature is that it can move up and down automatically, so you can set it to tilt down when you arrive home. Combined with HomeKit Secure Video’s ability to shut off video and audio recording when anyone arrives home, this can provide assurance that you aren’t being recorded.
[Image: LG floodlight security camera. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-LG-Floodlight-Cam-Plug-In.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The outdoor camera shares a similar design to the indoor camera, is wired, and comes in two models: one without lights for $299 and one with motion-activated floodlights for $399. There’s a black version and a silver one. Both support up to 2.5 K resolution and are compatible with HomeKit Secure Video. All three cameras will be available in the US, Canada, and the UK, but no release date has been announced.
[Image: The LG camera without lights. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-LG-Outdoor-Cam-Plug-In.png?quality=90&strip=all]
All the LG cameras work with Apple’s new HomeView smart display, which can show a live feed when someone presses the doorbell or if you drop in on a camera, as well as play back recorded footage. The HomeView can display up to nine live camera feeds at once.    
Smart thermostats and sensors
[Image: The LG thermostat https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-LG-Smart-Thermostat.png?quality=90&strip=all]
Apple announced two smart thermostats: a round LG model and a square Schneider Electric model. Both cost $199, are designed for North American HVAC systems, and work with or without a C-wire. They will be available in the US and Canada starting in December.    
[Image: The Schneider Electric thermostat. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-Home-Collection-Schneider-Home-Smart-Thermostat.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The two thermostats have similar designs, with an opaque screen overlaid by touchscreen controls. I saw a glowing orb visual on the Schneider model when it adjusted the temperature, but they seem designed to blend in, unlike Google’s latest Nest thermostat, which feels more like a statement piece.
The thermostats support Matter, so they can work with other smart home ecosystems, and each comes with remote sensors for monitoring temperature and humidity. The thermostats should support Apple Home’s adaptive temperature features; we are confirming with Apple.

title: Apple announces the HomePod Mini 2, but it isn’t ready for Siri AI at launch
body:
Apple is announcing the long-awaited HomePod Mini 2 with a new chip that can power Siri AI — but support for those new AI features won’t be available at launch. The speaker is also getting a new sound glow feature that syncs its LED lights with a song’s album art, and it can now be your Mac’s default speaker. Up to four can also pair with the new Apple TV 4K for surround sound. And like everything this year, it’s more expensive, too. 
The HomePod Mini 2 comes in pink, green, and a new shade of blue, along with white and black. It costs $149, $20 more than its predecessor, which is being discontinued. Preorders open today, October 13th, and it will ship on October 30th. Apple announced the smart speaker alongside a suite of new products for the home, including the new HomeView smart display ($299), the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K ($299), and a new collection of smart home devices developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric starting at $199.
[Image: The HomePod Mini 2 in pink. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomePod-mini-2-connected-home.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The biggest upgrade inside the HomePod Mini 2 is the S10 chip, which debuted in the Apple Watch Series 10 in 2024. Here, it will enable Siri AI and bring smarter, more conversational responses to the speaker. However, the Mini 2 won’t ship with Siri AI at launch; instead, Apple says it will arrive in a later software update. It will be available in English in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and India. You’ll need an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone — an iPhone 15 Pro or newer — to enable the upgrade.
Once upgraded, you’ll get the same Siri AI as on compatible iPhones, capable of understanding natural language commands and accessing what Apple calls “broader world knowledge,” as well as your personal context, such as your calendar and text messages. Apple’s examples include: if you ask Siri to set a reminder to buy flowers for mom’s birthday, it can check your calendar, identify when mom’s birthday is, and set the reminder. It can also scan your text messages for music recommendations so you can ask it to play that song your friend sent. 
[Video: Apple HomePod Mini 2 Sound Glow]
Personal context will be available only on the Mini if you have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, and will rely on voice recognition to keep your personal information private, but anyone in the home can talk to the HomePod to ask questions, play music, and control most smart home devices. Apple confirmed that Siri AI will not be coming to existing HomePod Minis.
The speakers don’t appear to have been upgraded from the original Mini, with Apple saying they offer the same great sound, but they do get three new audio features: sound glow, audio companion capability for your Mac, and surround sound support on the new Apple TV 4K.
[Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xLL4UnrLNWs]
Sound glow matches the colors of a song’s album art with the LEDs on top of the speaker. I saw a demo in a brightly lit room, and it was subtle, but the colors clearly changed in sync with the music. It also works with Apple’s ambient soundscapes, such as rain, forest, and ocean sounds.
The Mini 2 can now serve as your Mac’s default speaker and work as a surround-sound pair with the new Apple TV 4K, also announced today for $299. The new colors match a few of the current iMacs; I saw the pink pairing, and it was very pretty. Apple says the Mini uses a new audio companion feature that enables a persistent AirPlay setup and optimizes the streaming architecture for low-latency, responsive sound. It works on any model that supports Wi-Fi 6E or higher. I saw a demo of Angry Birds and the fruit-flinging on screen synced seamlessly with the splat sounds emanating from two Minis.
[Image: Some of the HomePod Mini 2 colors match the current iMac line. You can pair two as the default speakers for your Mac. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-HomePod-mini-2-with-Mac.png?quality=90&strip=all]
You’ll be able to pair up to four of the Mini 2 speakers with the new Apple TV 4K for a surround sound home theatre setup. Two Minis can also work with a pair of the second-gen full-sized HomePods for fuller sound. Apple says the speakers automatically calibrate with the Apple TV 4K to understand where they are in the room and relative to each other, then tune the audio levels to fit the space. 
The first-generation HomePod Mini launched six years ago today, so a full upgrade was long overdue. The jump from the S5 chip the OG Mini ran on to the S10, and the bump up to Wi-Fi 6E and BLE 6.0, should also improve speed and responsiveness.
It’s disappointing that the Mini hasn’t gotten a significant audio upgrade, but the addition of a smarter Siri, when it arrives, should make the speaker more useful at home. However, it’s surprising that Apple launched this without Siri AI, meaning even if you spend $149 on a new Mini, you’ll still have a disconnect between Siri on your phone and Siri in your home. Combined with the fact that Siri AI is in beta on the new Apple TV 4K, it sounds like Apple’s smart voice assistant isn’t quite ready for primetime after all.

title: The new Apple TV 4K has built-in microphones so you can talk to Siri AI
body:
Apple is introducing a refreshed Apple TV 4K today with a pair of interesting new hardware features: far-field microphones to talk to Siri hands-free and Find My built into the remote. The fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, announced at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York City, is the first model to support the Siri AI voice assistant and has a new home theatre feature that lets you pair up to four second-gen HomePods or HomePod Mini 2s for surround sound. 
The new Apple TV 4K costs $299, more than twice the price the prior-generation Apple TV 4K debuted at and $50 more than the current top-of-the-line model (which is being discontinued). The fourth-gen model matches that version’s specs with 128GB of storage, an Ethernet port, and support for Thread and Matter, but it’s getting a bump up to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. It will be available on November 13th, with preorders opening today, October 13th. 
[Video: Apple TV 4K far field microphones]
Apple announced the device as part of a major new push into the smart home, which includes the new HomeView smart display ($299), HomePod Mini 2 ($149), and a collection of smart home devices developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
The new Apple TV comes with an A19 chip, first seen in last year’s iPhone 17, which adds Siri AI support out of the box. It will launch in beta and be available in English in eight countries — the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and India. Apple says Siri AI lets you use natural language to talk to the voice assistant through the remote or the new microphones and ask for recommendations, such as “What are the best nature docs on Apple TV right now?”
[Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bNdmGYamiWM]
Unlike on the HomePod or HomeView, Siri doesn’t speak its responses aloud on Apple TV; they appear either full screen when you search for content or in a text bubble when you ask general knowledge questions. In the demo I saw, someone asked if the soccer team we were watching in an episode of Ted Lasso was real, and Siri displayed a few sentences answering the query (no, it’s fictional) that covered the top-right corner of the screen.
We’ve already seen AI-powered search features on Google’s TV Streamer with Gemini and Amazon’s Fire TV with Alexa Plus, but Apple is taking its streaming box’s AI capabilities further with the addition of personal context. Personal context uses information from your Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone, so you can say “Play that show my friend texted me,” and it will pull from your text messages and find what you were sent.
[Image: The Apple TV 4K can pair with up to four compatible HomePod speakers for surround sound. The group of four consists of two pairs, and each pair must use comparable speakers. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-TV-4K-home-theater-setup.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The design of the streaming box and its remote hasn’t changed, but the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K now supports an expanded surround-sound setup. You can use four compatible HomePod speakers in pairs, up from the two you can use with current Apple TV models. Compatible speakers include the HomePod second-gen and the HomePod Mini 2, also announced today for $149. 
There are three available configurations: four HomePod second-gens, four HomePod Mini 2s, or a pair of HomePod second-gens and a pair of HomePod Mini 2s. The feature is exclusive to the new Apple TV 4K, and Apple says the speakers automatically calibrate with the device to understand where they are in the room and relative to each other, then tune the audio levels to fit the space. 
I’m most excited to be able to say “Hey Siri, can you find the remote?” Apple has finally added Find My to the Siri Remote. It can now play that familiar ringing sound so you can find which cushion it’s fallen under. If for some reason you can’t hear it, you can now use the Find My app on your iPhone to track its precise location, thanks to  Apple adding support for Bluetooth channel sounding, a location technology similar to ultra-wideband, but without the need for a UWB chip.

title: Zionist Iranian dissident Ramin Parsa granted residency in Israel after years-long battle
body: Ramin Parsa, an Iranian dissident and pro-Israel activist living in Jerusalem, was granted a one-year temporary residency permit last month, after a legal and bureaucratic battle with the Interior Ministry that lasted three and a half years.Parsa, who was born in Shiraz before converting from Shia Islam to Christianity and fleeing the Islamic Republic of Iran, is a public speaker and activist who has spent years volunteering and advocating for Israel. Nevertheless, despite his Israeli wife and child, he was twice denied legal status in Israel by the Interior Ministry. Last month, however, following what Parsa credited to an intervention by God, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, that finally changed.“It was a miracle, actually, a miracle of God,” Parsa told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday. “But Ambassador Huckabee really helped. He took our case and presented it to the government, to Prime Minister Netanyahu and his office, and they took it seriously.”According to Parsa, the intervention prompted officials to look again at his case after years of legal proceedings and repeated applications.“They basically had an inquiry into the case – what's happening – and then they realized that it had been stuck there for a while,” he said. “So they granted me my temporary residency after three and a half years.”Parsa said he credited Huckabee, Netanyahu, and members of the prime minister's national security team with helping bring the matter to a resolution.The permit gives Parsa temporary status for one year. After that, he said, he will have to apply again, with the possibility of eventually seeking permanent residency.“We have one year, and then after a year I will reapply again, and so this is one good step in the right direction, and I'm grateful for that,” he said.“I believe that next year we will also apply and will get it. I'm confident of that, but you never know,” he continued. “I believe that it's going to work out, and we're going to have another miracle. And eventually, I can apply for permanent residency.”Parsa said his temporary residency was granted through a discretionary provision that he referred to as “Section Nine,” rather than through the ordinary process based on his marriage to an Israeli citizen.“The way my residency was granted was not based on marriage, but based on Section Nine,” he said, adding that the decision was based on his being considered a benefit to the state.“I've been a Zionist, a Christian Zionist, for almost 20 years,” he said. “I've been supporting Israel even before I met my wife, before I got married, before I even imagined I would be living in Israel.”Parsa stressed that, as he understood the decision, it did not automatically establish a pathway for other applicants in similar circumstances.“It's not a law that basically they have to give it to everyone based on the same rule,” he said. “It's discretion, so they can decide to do it or they can decide not to do it.”The change in status has already opened doors that had previously been closed to him.Parsa has booked trips to South Africa, Germany, United States to speak on Israel's behalfWhen the Post interviewed Parsa earlier in the process, he said his uncertain legal situation had prevented him from traveling abroad, including to events where he had been invited to speak in support of Israel. Now, he has already booked trips to South Africa, Germany, and the United States to speak on Israel's behalf.“A few days ago, I got a message from the Foreign Ministry that they want me to speak to a group of pastors who came from South Africa,” Parsa said.“I want to use my time in the best way possible, in the wisest way possible, to support Israel, to combat antisemitism, and to basically tell the world [about] the real Israel that I live in.”Parsa said he did not view his experience with the Interior Ministry as representative of Israeli society as a whole.“I don't want to blame Israel for the mistake of a few people in the Ministry of Interior because that doesn't represent the country,” he said. “What represents the country is the good people of Israel.”For Parsa, the case also has personal implications beyond his legal status. His wife is an Israeli Jew, the couple has a young son, and they are expecting another child.He described their family as symbolic of what he hopes could one day become a broader reconciliation between Israelis and Iranians.“My marriage with my wife is a prophetic picture of two nations coming together,” he said. “We have a beautiful son, and we have one on the way, so the fruit is so beautiful when these two nations come together.”Asked what he hoped that relationship might look like in the future, Parsa mentioned his hometown: “I'm hoping and praying for a day that we have a direct flight from Tel Aviv to Tehran, from Tel Aviv to Shiraz,” he said. “I see the day that the regime will fall and Israelis and Iranians will become friends.”

title: 2027: Rainbow Coalition Has Come To Stay, Nothing Anybody Can Do About It — Wike
body: The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has again defended his multi-party Rainbow Coalition platform as campaigns ramp up for next year’s general elections. Wike spoke on Tuesday during a media chat with select journalists in Abuja, insisting the Rainbow Coalition has come to stay, saying he supported some contestants in the All Progressives Congress (APC) despite being a member of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). “ What I’ve said to Nigerians and to Almighty God is, ‘I’m going to support Tinubu for him to realise his second-term ambition.’ I did not promise any governor. And two, let me tell you, no governor can say Wike has come to him for this and this,” the minister said. “Some of the governors there, I supported him, but I gave this example now about Hope [Uzodimma of Imo State], so you know that people cannot just come and accuse you. I don’t do that. If you have any problem with me, come out back and face Wike. Don’t go on under the Rainbow Coalition. For the Rainbow Coalition, it has come. It will stay. There’s nothing anybody can do about it.” Some governors in the ruling APC have asked Wike, a member of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), to either join the party or declare his stand. The governors faulted the Rainbow Coalition floated by Wike, saying the former Rivers governor needs to resign from the PDP and join the APC. “Our message is very very clear: be on one side. You can’t be on two sides. If you are in APC, please come out and support the APC, not you are supporting APC here, and you are supporting some other political parties somewhere else,” Zamfara State governor Dauda Lawal told Channels Television’s Inside Sources. “We maintain our stand, and the message is very clear. He can speak; he can say whatever he wants to say, but our position has been very clear: APC all the way from head to toe,” he said. The Rainbow Coalition is a cross-party political platform aimed at mobilising support for President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 re-election bid. However, Wike has maintained that his support is primarily for the president for next year’s election. The post 2027: Rainbow Coalition Has Come To Stay, Nothing Anybody Can Do About It — Wike appeared first on Channels Television .

title: University staff injured in Russian drone attack on Rivne, students took shelter
body:
According to Ukrinform, Ukraine’s Minister of Education and Science, Andrii Butenko, reported the incident on Facebook .
He said the Russian attack sparked a fire in an academic building at Rivne State University of the Humanities. According to preliminary information, the premises of the Faculty of Musical Arts were almost completely destroyed by fire.
Russian drone attack on an educational institution in central Rivne / Photo: National Police of Ukraine
The fire has been extinguished, and debris-clearing operations are continuing.
“According to information from the university, all students were in shelters. There are injured people among the university’s administrative staff,” the minister emphasized.
He noted that the damaged building was no longer suitable for classes and would require reconstruction.
Neighboring academic buildings were also damaged, including windows that were blown out. The full extent of the damage is still being assessed.
According to Butenko, the university is considering switching entirely to remote learning through the end of the week. Decisions about how classes will be organized afterward will depend on the availability of suitable premises and safe locations.
Butenko said the Ministry of Education and Science’s priority was to ensure people’s safety and provide conditions for education to continue. Students and university employees must receive the support they need.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian forces attacked an educational institution in central Rivne on October 13. At the time of that report, 20 people had been reported injured, and the fire in the academic building had been extinguished.

title: Mbah speaks on shootings at NDC secretariat
body:
Governor Peter Mbah of Enugu State has vowed to ensure prosecution of those responsible for Saturday’s attack on the supporters of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in the state.
PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported the sporadic shootings at the NDC secretariat in Enugu State on Saturday during the party’s governorship campaign flag-off.
Reacting in a video clip uploaded on his Facebook page on Monday night, Mr Mbah said he expects the police to “conduct a thorough and impartial investigation” into the violence.
The governor assured he would seek a “formal briefing” on the progress of the police investigation.
“Anyone found responsible for criminal acts must be held accountable through the proper legal process regardless of their political connections,” he said.
“We must allow the evidence to establish what happened.”
Mr Mbah stressed that every citizen should be able to exercise their lawful right irrespective of political affiliation without fear of violence or intimidation.
“I will continue to work with the relevant security authorities to ensure that citizens can go about their lives and participate in lawful political activities safely,” he said, emphasising that political differences are part of democracy.
Mr Mbah said his immediate concern was for those who experienced fear and the families affected during the attack.
“I want to assure them that their safety and well-being matter to me personally,” he said.
The governor added: “Enugu belongs to all of us and I remain committed to protecting the security, dignity and democratic rights of every person who calls this state home.”
PREMIUM TIMES reports that apart from the secretariat, suspected political thugs also attacked NDC supporters at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport in Emene.
The NDC supporters had attempted to gather at the airport to welcome the party’s 2027 governorship candidate, Chinyeaka Ohaa.
On Sunday, the Secretary to the Enugu State Government, Chidiebere Onyia, claimed findings showed that the NDC attempted to gather at the airport without approval.
Mr Onyia, a professor, also denied allegations that the state government was responsible for the attack.
But in a statement on Monday, the Secretary of the NDC in Enugu State said the government’s claim that the party attempted to hold the campaign flag-off at the airport without approval was false.
The police have ordered an investigation into the violence.

title: US rejects Kiev’s quid pro quo ask to end attacks on Russian refineries — NYT
body:
NEW YORK, October 13. /TASS/. US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have told Ukrainian representatives that they do not intend to offer anything in return for stopping attacks on Russian oil refineries, The New York Times quoted sources as saying.
When asked by a Ukrainian representative during Friday’s negotiations in Miami what Kiev would get in return, the US negotiators replied that Washington "was doing a lot for Ukraine already" and should not have to make a trade for Ukraine to stop its refinery attacks.
The newspaper’s sources added that some in the room heard Kushner’s and Witkoff’s words as a veiled threat. The US negotiators mentioned the American intelligence assistance considered vital for Ukraine.
On October 13, Vladimir Zelensky said Ukraine did not receive any notifications from the United States last night about the launch of Russian missiles.

title: Oil-Covered Birds Found Along Russia’s Black Sea Coast After Tanker Fire
body:
Seabirds covered in oil have been found along Russia’s Black Sea coast following a fire aboard a tanker linked to the country’s so-called shadow fleet, a wildlife rehabilitation center said Monday.
The center in the coastal resort of Anapa said it had begun receiving oil-coated birds from coastal towns and appealed for additional volunteers to help treat and feed them.
The reports came after the Liberia-flagged Aframax Rio caught fire in an attack off the coast of Sochi on Oct. 6. The 247-meter (810-foot) tanker has been linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
The blaze was extinguished on Oct. 7 and the vessel was then towed to Novorossiysk, about 200 kilometers (124 miles) northwest of Sochi. Workers started pumping oil out of the damaged tanker Monday, according to local reports .
Sochi authorities denied reports of oil-covered birds, saying beach inspections had found no traces of petroleum products.
Satellite images, however, showed an expanding oil slick in the days after the fire. A radar image from Saturday showed the slick stretching northwest toward Novorossiysk.
Independent environmentalist Zhora Kavanosyan said Novorossiysk’s chief rescuer Alexei Oderov had confirmed that petroleum products had washed ashore but that he described the scale of the contamination as “nothing catastrophic.”
Meanwhile, Russian transportation and maritime rescue authorities said Tuesday that inspections along the Krasnodar region’s Black Sea coast had found no oil spills.
The latest reports come nearly two years after a major oil spill in December 2024, when two Russian tankers released thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil into the Black Sea after being damaged in a storm in the Kerch Strait. The spill polluted beaches around Anapa and prompted authorities to declare a federal emergency.
