title: Four international deals clinched at Moscow Fashion Week
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russian brands will present their collections abroad in conclusion of the seventh Moscow Fashion Week and the event organizer, the Fashion Fund, agreed on cooperation with relevant associations from four countries, said the Department of Culture of the Russian capital.
"International agreements were signed with partners from Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kenya, and Bangladesh. Thanks to them, Russian designers will showcase their collections in these countries," Moscow Deputy Mayor Natalya Sergunina was cited as saying.
The total amount of deals discussed by the participants of the seventh Moscow Fashion Week already amounts to nearly 350 million rubles ($4.2 mln). According to the agreements reached in previous seasons, Russian fashion designers will travel to India and Spain by the end of 2026. Trips to China and Armenia are scheduled for next year.
The seventh Fashion Week took place in Moscow from September 26 to October 1, and was attended by more than 65,000 people. It brought together brands from 12 foreign countries and 24 Russian regions.

title: Standard Chartered Bank delivers strong returns and sustainable shareholder value
body: Standard Chartered Bank Ghana PLC has held its 2026 Facts Behind the Figures stakeholder engagement session at the Ghana Stock Exchange, bringing together investors, brokers, fund managers, regulators and the media. The bank provided an overview of its business and financial performance for the full year 2025 and the first half of 2026, reaffirming that delivering sustainable shareholder value remains a key priority. In 2025, the bank achieved a strong return on equity of 28 per cent, while earnings per share increased to GH¢5.97 from GH¢5.31 in 2024. In line with this performance, a total dividend payout of GH¢673.48 million was declared at the 2025 Annual General Meeting. The balance sheet remained strong and resilient, expanding by 15 per cent in 2025, while meeting all regulatory and capital requirements. The bank also outlined its distinctive operating framework as an international bank, underpinned by a robust regulatory environment and global standards. This framework shapes its approach to risk management and capital allocation and has contributed to a measured approach to business in recent years. Against this backdrop, the bank recorded a resilient performance in the first half of 2026, with total revenue of GH¢798 million. Profit after tax increased by 10 per cent to GH¢320 million. Building on this performance, the bank outlined its strategy, aligned with its core strengths: combining differentiated cross-border capabilities with leading wealth management expertise to connect clients to global growth opportunities. Xorse Godzi, Chief Executive, Standard Chartered Bank Ghana PLC, speaking at the engagement, emphasised that the bank remains firmly focused on its next phase of growth and on delivering sustainable value for shareholders. He said: “We will continue to maximise our strongest competitive advantages while harnessing market opportunities to accelerate growth. As a super-connector bank, we will leverage our international network and cross-border capabilities to connect corporates, financial institutions and individuals to some of the world’s most dynamic and rapidly growing markets.” Albert Larweh Asante, Chief Financial Officer, Standard Chartered Bank Ghana PLC, said: “Our resilient performance reflects the strength of our balance sheet and our disciplined approach to risk management and capital allocation. We remain focused on driving sustainable income growth, maintaining operational efficiency and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.” Beyond its financial performance, the bank highlighted progress in its sustainability and social impact initiatives. In 2025, the bank advanced inclusive growth and climate action by investing GH¢4.6 million in youth empowerment through the Standard Chartered Foundation, focusing on disadvantaged young people, especially young women and persons with disabilities, through employability and entrepreneurship support. Additionally, the bank mobilised $30.5 million in climate finance for Ghana through a $200 million World Bank Clean Cooking Outcome Bond, benefiting 1.3 million people and reducing emissions by more than 1.8 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, while demonstrating the potential of carbon finance to drive impact at scale. This year marked 130 years of uninterrupted operations by Standard Chartered Bank in Ghana. The bank reaffirmed its commitment to Ghana’s socio-economic development by supporting a diverse range of sectors, facilitating capital to underpin infrastructure development, and supporting the trade and investment ambitions of businesses and individuals. The bank is firmly established in Ghana and has been listed on the Ghana Stock Exchange since 1991.

title: The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology. Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems . —Grace Huckins This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here . 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power Fervo Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places. Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? Read the full story to find out . —Eshan Raul Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from sustainable cement to shipping containers packed with old EV batteries. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets Temperatures rose to 120°F, spoiling food and sparking fires. ( BBC ) + The attack has sparked alarm about cyber threats to food security. ( FT $) + It joins a recent wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes. ( CNBC ) + AI is exacerbating the threats. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Meta has launched a bunch of new AI models It hopes the models, built for complex, multi-step tasks, will rival OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s.( BI ) + They scored well on tests of reasoning, writing, and coding. ( NYT $) + Mark Zuckerberg says they bring Meta to the “frontier” of AI. ( FT $) + And will soon power the Muse agent. ( Verge ) 3 Anthropic warns that AI models may soon self-replicate across devices Without even requiring access to data centers. ( Reuters $) + It says models could spread through smart TVs and appliances. ( CNBC ) + We’re putting too much faith in AI saying no. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Police have a new AI tool that finds homes from interior photos It can match single pictures to Airbnb and Zillow listings. ( 404 Media ) + Police-tech giant Flock is tightening its rules. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 The world’s first utility-scale enhanced geothermal plant is online Fervo Energy’s Utah facility will supply carbon-free electricity. ( IEEE ) + AI is uncovering hidden geothermal resources. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Did drone strikes on Yandex data centres blitz Russian bots? Zelenskyy claims the attacks quietened Kremlin-funded social media accounts. ( Euronews ) + But troll farm experts aren’t convinced. ( Verge ) 7 NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a Mars driving record It’s covered 28 miles since landing in 2021. ( Reuters $) + The rover passed Opportunity after detouring to study ancient rocks. ( NYT $) 8 Elon Musk has become the 2026 midterms’ biggest known donor He gave $158 million to a Republican Senate super PAC. ( AP News ) 9 Anduril and Palantir founders have backed execution livestreams Palmer Luckey and Joe Lonsdale support Pete Hegseth’s plan. ( Mother Jones ) 10 A spacecraft has traced how a mysterious solar switchback formed The Solar Orbiter’s discovery could improve space weather forecasts. ( Gizmodo ) Quote of the day “Many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI.” —Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar tells CBS News that Silicon Valley’s “social delusion” has convinced researchers to smoke because they expect AI to cure cancer. One more thing A brain implant changed her life. Then it was removed against her will. Sticking an electrode inside a person’s brain can do more than treat a disease. Take the case of Rita Leggett, an Australian woman whose experimental brain implant changed her sense of agency and self. She told researchers that she “became one” with her device. She was devastated when, two years later, she was told she had to remove the implant because the company that made it had gone bust. Her case highlights the need for a new category of legal protection: neuro rights. Explore how they could be protected . —Jessica Hamzelou We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Astronomers have captured the clearest image yet of a medieval supernova. + Watch centuries-old Chinese paper-cutting techniques create a spectacular work of art . + Artist Josh Gluckstein creates astonishing animal sculptures from recycled cardboard, including this great white shark . + An endangered sea turtle named Pancake has returned to the ocean for the first time in months after recovering from hypothermia.

title: How DBP botched Duterte-era contractor loans: lax checks, billions overdue
body: MANILA, Philippines – Lapses in lending safeguards and years-long delays in collection left the Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) with more than P4 billion in overdue contractor loans under a program meant to support the Duterte administration’s Build, Build, Build infrastructure drive, state auditors found. The overdue loans amounted to 61.4% of the P6.67 billion still owed to DBP under the Infrastructure Contractor Support (ICONS) program. Launched in 2017, the program allowed contractors to borrow against expected payments from infrastructure projects, but the Commission on Audit (COA) found cases where loans were released without adequate verification of construction progress. DBP’s board eventually approved the termination of ICONS on June 3, 2026, citing the high level of overdue loans. The closure, however, still leaves the bank with billions of pesos in debt that it may never recover. What was ICONS supposed to do? Launched in 2017, ICONS helped finance contractors undertaking infrastructure projects under the Duterte administration’s Build, Build, Build initiative, including public-private partnership projects. Contractors need money for construction before they receive full payment from project owners. ICONS helped bridge that gap by lending against expected contract payments, or receivables, assigned to DBP as security. For that arrangement to work, the bank needed to verify that the projects were progressing and that the payments backing the loans could actually be collected. Under its own lending guidelines, loans were supposed to be released in stages as construction progressed, with account officers required to visit project sites before disbursing funds and continuously monitor borrowers. But COA found that DBP’s safeguards were not always followed. Must Read [Vantage Point] DBP’s bad loans: The failures behind the billions A P300-M loan that went wrong One P300-million loan shows how the ICONS program went wrong, from DBP’s failure to properly check the projects before releasing the money to its struggle to collect from the borrower years later. In August 2019, DBP approved a P300-million credit line for a contractor undertaking five projects for a government-owned or -controlled corporation (GOCC). The contractor drew the full amount by March 2020, with repayment supposed to come from payments it expected to receive as construction progressed. On paper, the projects appeared to be well underway. The two biggest projects backing the credit line – each with a contract value of more than P217 million – were reported to be 75.37% and 80.89% complete, respectively. But DBP released the loans without actually checking how much work had actually been completed. Instead, the bank relied on the value of the contractor’s expected project payments, which covered at least 150% of the outstanding loans. OVERDUE . A comparison of the reported and actual completion rates of five projects used as security for the P300-million DBP loan, based on findings from the Commission on Audit’s 2025 report. “There was no verification of the actual project accomplishment prior to loan release of the loans, as required by the Circular,” state auditors said in their 2025 report. By June 2020, just three months after fully drawing its credit line, the contractor had already fallen behind on payments. It was only in March 2021, a year after the full amount had been released, that DBP checked the actual construction progress with project engineers. The findings revealed substantial discrepancies between the accomplishments the contractor had reported and those subsequently verified. Two of the projects, Projects 3 and 4, had already been ordered terminated in September 2020 due to construction delays. “No principal repayment was collected from Borrower 1 despite repeated collection efforts and demand letters, resulting in an outstanding principal balance of P300 million as of December 31, 2025,” the COA said. By January 2026, the situation had worsened. The GOCC confirmed to COA that four projects had been terminated, while the fifth had been fully paid in December 2021. The government company said it no longer owed the contractor anything from the five projects. More than five years after the contractor first defaulted, DBP had yet to recover any of the P300-million principal. The bank had already set aside an allowance for the entire amount to account for the expected loss. Must Read [Vantage Point] DBP’s ₱36.2-B NPL exposure emerges as a state-level credit risk Subcontracted work, delayed collections The P300-million loan was not an isolated case. Another contractor still owed DBP P490.46 million at the end of 2025, even though the infrastructure projects whose expected payments had been pledged to the bank as security were already completed. COA found that the contractor had subcontracted most of the work to other companies, leaving it with a financial stake averaging just 3.5% of the projects’ contract costs. Despite the projects being completed between 2017 and 2021, the contractor continued requesting loan extensions instead of repaying the principal. The audit did not establish what happened to the project payments or why they had not resulted in repayment to DBP. COA also flagged significant delays in DBP’s efforts to recover overdue loans. At DBP’s Albay lending center, a borrower defaulted in June 2021, but the first demand notice was sent only by email in July 2025, more than four years later. By the end of 2025, the borrower still owed P97.24 million of its original P100-million loan, with the bank already setting aside provisions for the possibility that the entire remaining amount would never be recovered. The account had also passed through six different officers between 2021 and 2026. In Tacloban, foreclosure proceedings had yet to begin on a P82.21-million loan that had been overdue since September 2021 because the lending center lacked a full-time lawyer. Its cases were instead being handled by DBP’s Zamboanga legal team. What has DBP done about the bad loans? COA recommended investigating possible negligence among bank officers and employees handling ICONS loans, with administrative or legal cases to follow where warranted. It also urged DBP to act faster in recovering unpaid loans, particularly from borrowers still in operation or those with real estate pledged as collateral. DBP told auditors that its management committee had directed its Legal Services Group to “investigate possible negligence in the credit administration of the loan accounts mentioned.” But DBP had been looking into some of its largest bad loans for years before it decided to shut down ICONS. As early as January 19, 2022, the bank’s board had ordered an inquiry into its 20 largest nonperforming loans, including the P300-million ICONS account. Yet it was only on June 3, 2026 – more than four years later – that DBP’s board approved the termination of ICONS. Meanwhile, DBP’s loan problems extend beyond ICONS. Its gross nonperforming loan (NPL) ratio, which measures the share of loans classified as nonperforming, rose from 7.05% in December 2025 to 9.52% in March 2026, before easing slightly to 9.17% in June, according to data published by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas . These figures cover DBP’s entire loan portfolio, and it is unclear how much ICONS contributed to the deterioration of the bank’s NPL ratio. Rappler sought DBP’s comment on how much of the P4.09 billion in overdue ICONS loans it has recovered as of present, what is driving its elevated NPL ratio, and what became of the 2022 inquiry, including why the program was terminated only in 2026. The bank has yet to formally respond as of press time, although a representative told Rappler that it stood by the explanations it had submitted to COA. This story will be updated if the DBP responds. – Rappler.com [Vantage Point] Why a DBP–LandBank merger has become urgent

title: The web needs interactive lists
body:
One of the priciples of creating new web platform features is "pave the cowpaths" -- figure out what cursèd UI developers and designers are already creating with third party HTML/CSS/JS, and brainstorm how to pull it into the web platform. Maybe with an exorcism or two to fix any particularly egregious accessibility problems.
When the same principle is applied to web accessibility specs, it generally means ensuring any widely used UI patterns can be marked up with an appropriate semantic pattern (i.e. roles and aria-* attributes) and documented interaction patterns that are understandable and operable across different devices, user settings, color modes, zoom levels, and assistive tech. Whether web developers actually do any of that is an entirely separate problem, but it should at least be possible.
Developers and designers will always create new innovative ways to be weird and inaccessible in their UI (intense side-eye at stuffing tabs and tables into comboboxes), and spec authors will always struggle to decide how far to support the chaos. However, every once in a while developers and designers create a perfectly normal, understandable, and theoretically accessible UI pattern that for whatever reason is not supported on the web.
One of those patterns is an interactive list.
One way to think of an interactive list is as the one-dimensional version of a data grid. Just as a data grid is the interactive version of a table (i.e. <table> or role="table" ), an interactive list would be the interactive version of a static list (i.e. <ul> , <ol> , or role="list" ).
An interactive list, like a data grid, would be a single tab stop composite widget, where arrowing between list items would be expected. As such, it would more commonly be useful within interfaces that lean more towards web applications than content-focused websites.
Here are a few more concrete examples of UI where an interactive list role could benefit accessibility:
Normally navigation should be a simple, tabbable set of links, often in a static list. However in environments that function more like traditional desktop applications than websites (think email inboxes or Powerpoint online), it can be beneficial to have navigation be a single tab stop.
A tablist can sometimes be appropriate here, but an interactive list with child links would allow users to both arrow through items and also keep highly beneficial link functionality (e.g. using a screen reader's links dialog from anywhere in the app). Tablists also do not support static content like section/group headers, which often exists in navigation regions.
Multi-level navigation in apps like email inboxes sometimes use a tree, but nested lists of links can offer a significantly lower learning curve than a tree along with preserving virtual cursor access and use of the links dialog.
Pagination is another navigation-like component that would be a good interactive list use case, especially when there can be a large number of pages. If linking to a specific page is possible, then it could be an interactive list with nested buttons. If not, then no nested interactives would be needed.
h/t to Sylvia Villegas for bringing up pagination as a use case.
In this case, each individual chat message is usually not interactive in the sense that they do not have a single primary action and are not selectable. However, users should not need to tab through all content in a chat pane in order to reach the chat input. Most chat applications also allow users to arrow (and often use page down/page up to skip) through past messages.
Yes, everyone knows you shouldn't use a carousel . However, they continue to be built, and sometimes as in the case of streaming services, have become somewhat standard. Especially in UIs like this one from Netflix where there are many carousels in succession, users should be able to quickly tab to their desired category and then arrow through each item in that carousel.
The interactive list role wouldn't be appropriate for all carousels -- only ones similar to the pictured streaming service categories or other product carousels where each item has a primary action, and the context calls for arrowing between items. As with most accessibility choices, there is no one-size-fits-all.
This applies not just to lists of files, but any other list of items where each item does one primary action. While listbox is a tempting role to reach for here, it is not ideal for several reasons: it enforces a selected state on options, it does not robustly support virtual cursor navigation of options, and it does not support having a non-selection primary action.
Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android all have native versions of an interactive list, which matters for two reasons: assistive tech users are already familiar with the paradigm and wouldn't need to learn anything new, and from a technical/spec perspective, accessibility API mappings already exist.
Native platforms already providing this UX pattern is also compelling evidence that there are valid use cases for interactive lists.
There are three places to reference when determining semantic requirements for interactive lists:
At the most basic level, it should be possible to create a horizontal or vertical arrow-navigable set of interactive items that do some general action when pressed. This alone would be enough to create the Netflix-style carousel example from earlier.
We can also come up with a few more requirements just from referencing the examples above:
In addition to the specific requirements above, basic features of both static lists and typical composite widgets should also be supported, such as:
ARIA already has a number of one-dimensional composite widget roles, but no combination of them can cover all the existing common use cases for interactive lists. Even in cases where you can hack together something with existing roles, there are shortcomings.
The existing somewhat list-like linear composite widget roles are: listbox , menu / menubar , radiogroup , tablist , and toolbar . Of those, radiogroup and listbox are both form controls specifically designed only for selection, which prevents usage for any control where the main click handler does a non-selection action. menu and menubar are intended only for application-style menus or context menus, and additionally do not support virtual cursor navigation across all screen readers ( listbox has the same issue, for that matter). tablist is designed for swapping visible content in an associated tabpanel , and toolbar is slightly more flexible but still intended only for buttons and form controls that affect some associated area of the page.
None of those roles allow nested structured content or secondary interactive controls.
Some clever developers might think of simply using a static list and managing focus between listitems, but that approach will not correctly trigger mode switching for Windows screen readers, nor will it allow screen readers and voice control to directly trigger a click event on the list items, as they are spec'd as static container elements.
Hopefully by now you've either gotten bored and left, or are convinced that we should have interactive lists on the web. The good news is that there's already work around making that happen, and you (the now super-informed reader of my pedantic blog post) can help!
There is an active proposal in ARIA to add interactive lists that will be discussed at the end of October 2026:
If added to ARIA, an interactive list can also easily be added to HTML by creating a new focusgroup token. This would make authoring as easy as doing:
For anyone who has their own examples of UI that could be an interactive list, or can think of other features that I've missed, I will pay attention to responses on Bluesky between now and the discussion on October 26th. Commenting on the ARIA github issue also works.

title: Russia invites China to invest in its hospitality sector — envoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia has invited China to invest in its domestic hospitality infrastructure, jointly manage existing hotel chains, and expand bilateral organized tourism, Boris Titov, Russia’s presidential envoy for sustainable development goals, told TASS on Tuesday.
The statement followed a meeting between the Russian delegation from the Russia-China Committee for Friendship, Peace and Development and the leadership of the state-owned Beijing Tourism Group in Beijing.
"Our colleagues from Tourism.RF corporate group proposed that their Chinese counterparts invest in Russian hospitality facilities and jointly manage existing hotel networks," Titov said.
He noted that the initiative aims to double the number of organized Chinese tourists within a year through more extensive outreach. Titov acknowledged that China remains less familiar to Russian travelers than Turkey, while Chinese tourists are similarly unfamiliar with Russian destinations outside Moscow and St. Petersburg.
Beijing Tourism Group is a major state-owned conglomerate with operations in the lodging, retail, and entertainment sectors, Titov explained. "This includes the historic 'Moscow' restaurant in Beijing. We have proposed closer cooperation at this venue with prominent Russian restaurateurs, specifically the Arkady Novikov Group," he added, noting that a branch of Russia's National Center could also open at the Beijing Exhibition Center in the future.

title: Akufo-Addo’s role in the artificial cedi stability is indisputable — Facts do not bend to political convenience
body: One of the least intellectually defensible arguments is the tendency to ridicule experts for describing “THE CURRENT STABILITY OF THE CEDI AS ARTIFICIAL WHILE ALSO INDICATING THAT AKUFO-ADDO’S ADMINISTRATION HAS A HAND IN IT”. Supporters of the government must understand that individual ignorance does not imply universal ignorance. Economic phenomena are often more complex than political rhetoric suggests. To begin with, the Bank of Ghana (BoG) intensified its foreign exchange interventions in April 2025, when the US dollar was trading at approximately GH¢14.90. These aggressive interventions were facilitated, in part, by the foreign exchange reserves accumulated before the change of government. Ghana reportedly had reserves of approximately US$9 billion at the end of the Akufo-Addo administration. Without sufficient reserves, the BoG would have faced significant constraints in financing interventions on that scale. THIS IS NOT AN ENDORSEMENT OF THE AGGRESSIVE INTERVENTIONS; RATHER, IT IS AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT OF THE ECONOMIC CONDITIONS THAT MADE THEM POSSIBLE. Foreign exchange market interventions by central banks are neither unusual nor inherently problematic. Central banks routinely intervene in the foreign exchange market to moderate excessive volatility and maintain orderly market conditions. Our principal concern has never been the mere existence of such interventions, but their magnitude, sustainability, and potential consequences for the broader economy. Injecting approximately US$1 billion monthly into the secondary foreign exchange market is an exceptionally aggressive strategy. Beyond concerns about its sustainability, excessive reliance on such interventions risks diverting policy attention from the structural reforms required to strengthen domestic production and export competitiveness. We must not mistake the temporary management of symptoms for the permanent resolution of underlying economic problems. The concept of artificial currency stability requires careful explanation. When a domestic currency appreciates or maintains its value primarily because of sustained central bank interventions, rather than improvements in the economy’s underlying productive capacity and foreign exchange-generating potential, such stability may be considered intervention-dependent and potentially unsustainable. This does not mean that every central bank intervention is artificial or undesirable. The critical question is whether the stability can be maintained without continued, substantial injections of foreign exchange. The BoG’s capacity to sustain its interventions was also influenced by developments beyond its direct control. First, the substantial increase in international gold prices in 2025 improved Ghana’s potential to generate foreign exchange from gold exports. These additional inflows helped ease foreign exchange pressures. Second, Ghana’s external debt restructuring reduced immediate debt-servicing pressures, creating some fiscal and external-sector relief. THIS IS ANOTHER REASON THE ECONOMIC LEGACY OF THE AKUFO-ADDO ADMINISTRATION REMAINS RELEVANT TO AN ASSESSMENT OF CURRENT CURRENCY STABILITY. The restructuring provided temporary breathing space that helped ease external financing constraints. However, debt restructuring does not eliminate a country’s external debt obligations; it generally changes their timing and terms. As the relief associated with the restructuring diminishes and external debt-service obligations increase, the BoG may find it increasingly difficult to sustain interventions at the current scale, particularly if foreign exchange inflows weaken. The anticipated return of substantial external debt-service obligations from 2027 therefore raises legitimate questions about the long-term viability of the present intervention strategy. The precise timing and magnitude of these pressures, however, depend on Ghana’s revised debt-service schedule and future foreign exchange earnings. The fundamental issue is that currency stability cannot sustainably depend on the central bank’s ability to supply dollars INDEFINITELY. A more durable solution requires expanding domestic production, reducing avoidable import dependence, and strengthening export capacity. When an economy produces more of the goods and services it consumes, it reduces its demand for foreign exchange. When it also exports competitively, it generates the foreign exchange needed to finance essential imports and meet external obligations. This creates a stronger foundation for currency stability than persistent reliance on central bank interventions. Ghana has experienced episodes of currency stability supported by favourable external conditions and policy interventions before. Consequently, the present appreciation of the cedi should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that the structural challenges facing the economy have been resolved. The relevant test is whether the currency can withstand renewed external shocks, increased debt-servicing obligations, and changes in global commodity prices without experiencing severe depreciation. If conditions similar to those that precipitated the 2022 currency crisis were to recur, the cedi could come under substantial pressure again. The extent of that pressure would depend on the strength of the country’s reserves, export earnings, fiscal position, and policy response at the time. The BoG’s initiative to facilitate direct trade with China using the cedi is therefore a potentially important development. By reducing the need to convert the cedi into a third currency for eligible transactions, such arrangements could help reduce transaction costs and some demand for US dollars. However, the overall benefits will depend on the settlement mechanism, the balance of trade between the two countries, and the extent to which the arrangement genuinely reduces Ghana’s net foreign exchange requirements. Similarly, the GoldBod’s role in the gold value chain and its foreign exchange intermediation activities could contribute to improving foreign exchange supply. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of this approach must be assessed against its operational costs, the net foreign exchange it generates, its implications for the BoG’s balance sheet, and the sustainability of its financing arrangements. These initiatives should complement, rather than substitute for, broader structural reforms. In conclusion, Ghana must move beyond an excessive preoccupation with short-term currency appreciation and concentrate on the fundamentals that determine long-term exchange rate stability. The agricultural and manufacturing sectors must be at the centre of this strategy. Expanding agricultural production, strengthening agro-processing, supporting local manufacturers, improving productivity, and promoting competitive exports would reduce import dependence while increasing the economy’s capacity to generate foreign exchange. Ultimately, the most sustainable currency stability is one supported by strong domestic production, diversified exports, adequate foreign exchange earnings, and sound macroeconomic management—not one that depends disproportionately on the central bank injecting enormous amounts of dollars into the market every month. That is the structural transformation Ghana must pursue if it is to achieve lasting exchange rate stability.

title: Show HN: AI Crimes, a game where you spot the bug an AI wrote
body:
Point to the line, say what is wrong, and why it matters. Sloppy naming counts too.
Every case on AI Crimes is a snippet an AI wrote, and every one of them hides a crime. It might be a misleading name, an off-by-one, a missing await or a full-blown security hole. Some of these crimes really happened. Read the code, point to the line, and say what's wrong in plain words. The Division rules on your report and shows you exactly what the AI did.
Cases come in TypeScript, Python, Go, Java, Ruby and C++ . It's code review practice, and practice for the tech interviews that now test whether you can catch an AI's mistakes. Solve cases to build a clean streak and climb the leaderboards .

title: Kremlin spokesman addresses US-Europe ‘peace plan’ for Ukraine, diesel deal
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Media reports about the alleged preparation of a US-European "peace plan" for Ukraine, the diesel agreement between Moscow and Washington, and the situation surrounding the provision of intelligence to Kiev were among the main topics discussed during Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov’s briefing on October 13.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.
- Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet with Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin at the Kremlin today.
- The Russian leader will also have an international telephone conversation.
- The Kremlin has seen a report in The Washington Post about the United States and Europe moving toward a joint peace proposal on Ukraine but has received no information about it: "We have seen media reports but we have heard nothing about it."
- Moscow continues contacts on a possible "energy ceasefire," but there have been no new developments since yesterday: "We discussed this issue yesterday, and for now I have nothing to add to what we said then. Contacts on this matter are continuing."
- There is no connection between the diesel agreement with the United States and Russia’s position on Ukraine; rather, it is a mutually beneficial example of Russian-US cooperation: "I don’t see any connection here. In fact, it is an example of Russia-US cooperation that benefits both parties a lot."
- European Union sanctions and other unilateral actions could hamper the implementation of the fuel deal between Russia and the United States: "That it could interfere is beyond doubt."
- European cynicism is a subject of widespread discussion in international media: "The issue of European cynicism, as [US Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent put it, is being widely discussed in global media."
- European countries themselves remain major purchasers of Russian crude oil and petroleum products: "The fact is that European countries, just like all other nations, are heavy buyers of Russian oil and Russian petroleum products."
- Diesel fuel supply agreements serve the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets: "This corresponds to interests of the United States, this corresponds to interests of international energy markets, and is in line with interests of the Russian Federation, and so it takes place."
- Russia is selling and will continue to sell energy resources, its competitive commodity, on international markets: "Russia in this aspect is a country presenting its competitive commodity to global markets. We will continue doing that."
- The Kremlin is not aware of US President Donald Trump’s alleged plans to suspend intelligence sharing with Kiev or disable the Starlink internet service in Ukraine if Kiev continues strikes on Russian refineries: "We know nothing about it."
- Moscow’s position regarding a potential meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky or the need for Ukraine to hold an election is well known and unchanged: "Yesterday, we repeatedly talked about it and I have nothing to add. No changes here. Our position on all these issues is very well known."
- It is too early to discuss a compensation mechanism for financial losses that users of Yandex services may have incurred following Ukrainian attacks on the company: "It is premature to talk about financial losses at this point. You know that the company is strong and powerful. Yes, it is facing difficulties now. Of course, this issue is currently being discussed in the government, but the company is taking emergency measures to deal with the aftermath of this attack."

title: Intel. Min. nabs 2 members of arms smuggling in western Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence announced on Tuesday that two members of an arms smuggling network were arrested in western Iran.
The Public Relations Office of the Intelligence Department of Sistan and Baluchestan, southeast Iran, had earlier announced the dismantling of three operational cells linked to a Takfiri terrorist group in this province.
These three terrorist cells were identified in Iranshahr, Sarbaz, Saravan, and Zahedan counties and also in Qeshm city of southern province of Hormozgan, in cooperation with Hormozgan Province General Department of Intelligence and were dismantled before carrying out any acts of sabotage or terrorist activities.
Two of these terrorists were killed in clashes with security and intelligence forces, and ten other members of the terrorist teams were arrested.

title: Kazakhstan’s Economy Grows 4.2% as Manufacturing and Private Investment Drive Expansion
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s economy grew 4.2% in the first nine months of 2026, supported by non-oil sectors, rising private investment and expanding industrial production, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said at a government meeting on Oct. 13. Photo credit: Shutterstock The non-resource sector grew 5.4%, while construction, manufacturing, transport services and trade accounted for more than 75% of overall gross domestic product (GDP) growth, according to Zhumangarin. The figures point to continued economic expansion beyond the extractive sector, although inflation remains elevated despite a slight slowdown in September. Private investment drives economic growth Investment in fixed capital reached 16.1 trillion tenge (US$35.7 billion), increasing 7% year on year over the first nine months of 2026. “The distinctive feature is that private investment, which increased by 18.2%, is the main factor driving investment growth,” Zhumangarin said. Gross foreign direct investment inflows reached $9.4 billion in the first half of the year. The strongest investment growth was recorded in manufacturing, up 40.1%, followed by construction at 32%, information and communications at 29.2%, healthcare at 20.4% and agriculture at 9.1%. Kazakhstan’s economic structure has also continued to shift. The oil sector accounted for 7.8% of GDP in 2025, while manufacturing’s share rose to 14.1% and mining’s reached 12.4%, according to Zhumangarin. Manufacturing expands as new plants open Manufacturing output grew 8.6% in the first nine months of 2026, with particularly strong growth in light industry, which increased 62.4%. Chemical production rose 23.4%, while machinery manufacturing grew 22.8%. Deputy Minister of Industry and Construction Kuandyk Kazhkenov attributed the expansion largely to new production facilities. Since the beginning of the year, Kazakhstan has launched 106 industrial projects, creating approximately 8,000 permanent jobs. “Thanks to the implementation of these projects, the country has established production of new goods that were not previously manufactured domestically. These include sodium sulfate, drip irrigation systems, laminate flooring, aluminum capsules for coffee machines and other products,” Kazhkenov said. A further 200 investment projects worth a total of 1.7 trillion tenge (US$3.77 billion) are planned for completion by the end of 2026. Inflation slows, but price pressures remain Annual inflation eased to 9.3% in September, down from 9.8% in August, Zhumangarin said. The government and the National Bank are continuing coordinated measures to reduce inflationary pressure. First Deputy Chairman of the National Bank Yerulan Zhamau­bayev said the country’s business activity index reached 50.4 points in September, compared with 49 points in December 2025. The National Bank plans to maintain a moderately tight monetary policy alongside the government’s anti-inflation measures. Kazakhstan’s financial buffers strengthened as well. Gold and foreign exchange reserves stood at $66.2 billion at the end of September, up 1.2% from the beginning of the year. National Fund assets reached $66.7 billion, an increase of 4.3%. Exports and transit traffic gain momentum Exports of goods and services increased 25.4% to $55.3 billion in the first half of 2026, according to figures presented at the government meeting. Transit cargo moving through Kazakhstan rose 13.1% in the first nine months of the year, underscoring the importance of the country’s transport networks to regional trade. Railways carried 241.7 million tons of cargo, up 3% year on year, while road freight reached 270.4 million tons, an increase of 5.6%. Kazakhstan’s airlines transported 12.4 million passengers during the same period, up 4.2% from a year earlier. The business activity index and rising lending also suggest continued economic activity across several sectors, although the figures alone do not establish how evenly growth is distributed across businesses or households. Energy capacity expands to address supply constraints Kazakhstan generated 91.7 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in the first nine months of 2026. To help reduce electricity shortages, the country plans to commission approximately 2.4 gigawatts of conventional power capacity this year, Deputy Energy Minister Yerlan Akbarov said. The planned projects include modernization of Almaty’s CHPP-2 and CHPP-3, with capacities of 557 megawatts and 544 megawatts, respectively, as well as a 1,000-megawatt combined-cycle power plant in the Turkistan Region. Additional upgrades are planned at the Atyrau combined heat and power plant. Renewable energy is also contributing to the power supply. Renewable energy facilities generated 7.8 billion kilowatt-hours in the first nine months, against a full-year target of 8.8 billion kilowatt-hours. Seven renewable energy facilities with a combined installed capacity of 212.6 megawatts have entered operation this year. By year-end, the government plans to commission two solar power plants with a combined capacity of 30 megawatts and one hydropower plant with a capacity of 3.2 megawatts. The post Kazakhstan’s Economy Grows 4.2% as Manufacturing and Private Investment Drive Expansion appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Central Asia in the Global Innovation Rankings: Supercomputers, Engineers, and the Economics of Government Ambitions
body: In the Global Innovation Index (GII), published on September 29 by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), Kazakhstan climbed eight places to rank 73rd among 139 economies. Uzbekistan ranked 77th and Kyrgyzstan 92nd. Tajikistan placed 112th, while Turkmenistan was not included in the study. The overall rankings, however, conceal some interesting details. Uzbekistan ranks second worldwide in the share of graduates in science and engineering. Kyrgyzstan ranks second in labor productivity growth, while Tajikistan leads in utility model applications relative to the size of its economy. Utility models are a simpler form of patent protection, usually for smaller inventions. Such strong results in individual indicators stand in contrast to the countries’ relatively modest overall rankings. Part of the explanation lies in the study’s methodology. WIPO evaluates education and scientific capacity alongside infrastructure and investment. It also considers business activity and research output. A country may train large numbers of engineers or register technical innovations while lagging in research output and investment, with limited commercial activity. For Central Asia, the rankings also offer a way to compare economic performance with the scale of governments’ technological ambitions. Kazakhstan: Supercomputers in Search of Customers In recent years, Kazakhstan has assembled an impressive portfolio of digital projects. The Alem.Cloud and Al-Farabium supercomputers, along with the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, are intended to improve the country’s computing infrastructure. The Alem.ai artificial intelligence (AI) center and the KazLLM and AlemLLM large language models are designed to develop its AI capabilities. Training opportunities are also expanding through AI-Sana and Tomorrow School , with TUMO Astana offering education in AI and other digital fields. However, the wider use of AI remains relatively modest. The Digital Qazaqstan strategy through 2029 cites figures for the second half of 2025 showing that generative AI adoption in Kazakhstan stood at 13.7%, compared with a global average of 16.3%. Kazakhstan ranked 24th in the United Nations (UN) E-Government Development Index in its 2024 survey but 73rd in the 2026 GII. Kazakhstan’s digitalization model has long centered on government services. The country’s high position in the UN study reflects this focus. Commercial technologies present a more complicated picture: here, the government must rely on research teams, private developers, investors, and customers willing to pay for their services. The arrival of supercomputers expands the country’s technical capabilities. How extensively they will be used outside government projects remains to be seen. Uzbekistan: Engineering Education and IT Services Exports The country has long focused on workforce development for the IT industry. An export-oriented digital services sector is growing around IT Park. Foreign companies are operating in the country, while training programs in programming and AI are expanding. Tashkent intends to support its workforce development policies with domestic computing infrastructure. Under the AI development strategy adopted in 2024, Uzbekistan plans $50 million in AI infrastructure spending and the training of one million specialists. AI laboratories are also planned at 15 universities. A smaller supercomputer is already operating, and preparations are underway to acquire a more powerful system. The high share of technical graduates demonstrates Uzbekistan’s workforce potential but says little about the structure of its domestic IT industry. Developing software for foreign clients generates export revenue and creates jobs. Producing its own software products requires more investment in research and marketing, including reaching customers abroad. Kyrgyzstan: Global Leaders in Individual Indicators Kyrgyzstan climbed four places to 92nd. It also ranks eighth in education expenditure and 15th in microfinance. That said, in most cases the country is developing from a low base. In October 2024, then-Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Akylbek Japarov reported that only three of the 49 measures planned for that year under the digital transformation program had been completed. At a government meeting, agencies were criticized for delays and poor coordination. While those figures from two years ago do not necessarily describe the program’s current state of implementation, they illustrate the problems encountered during its rollout. Tajikistan: Clean Energy Amid Seasonal Electricity Shortages Tajikistan ranks 112th overall but stands out in two categories. WIPO places the country first in utility models and 12th in the use of low-carbon energy. A high ranking for utility model applications does not mean these inventions have been manufactured or sold. Tajikistan’s reliance on hydroelectric plants gives its electricity mix a high proportion of low-carbon energy. Behind these figures lies a familiar problem for Tajikistan’s industry: seasonal restrictions on electricity supply. The share of hydropower in the energy mix and the reliability of electricity supply measure different aspects of the energy system. Construction continues on the Rogun Hydropower Plant , the country’s largest energy project. How effectively the country can turn its energy potential into reliable power for industry will likely influence its future innovation performance. Turkmenistan: Outside the Rankings Turkmenistan is absent from the GII, leaving a significant gap in the regional picture. Nevertheless, Ashgabat has also announced a transition toward a digital economy. In October 2025, the authorities approved the Concept for the Development of the Digital Economy in Turkmenistan for 2026–2028 . The stated priorities include electronic government services and industrial digitalization, along with AI and workforce training . Technology Plans and Economic Realities For all the differences between Central Asian countries, technology policy across the region still relies heavily on government initiatives and investment. The private sector, however, follows its own economic logic. Governments can pay for computing capacity or engineering programs, but the use of this equipment or the employment prospects for graduates depend on demand from customers and businesses. Kazakhstan’s Economic Research Institute, in its analysis of the GII 2026 results , points to the need to expand venture capital financing and turn more scientific research into commercial products. There is also a timing issue. Many programs run through 2028–2030, while the innovation index draws on statistics from previous years. The impact of recently launched projects will become apparent later, provided they find practical applications in the economy.

title: US Navy seeks shipyards for SSN(X) submarine construction
body:
The US Navy is assessing domestic shipyard capacity to support construction of its next-generation SSN(X) nuclear-powered attack submarine, seeking information from potential prime contractors on their infrastructure, technical capabilities and future investment requirements.
The Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA), through its Team Submarine organization and the SSN(X) program office (PMS 351), issued a sources-sought notice on October 9 to gather industry information for market research and acquisition planning. Responses are due by October 15, 2026.
The notice is intended to establish a baseline of domestic industrial capabilities, identify potential capital investment needs and inform the Navy’s plans for the SSN(X) construction pipeline. It does not constitute a solicitation for proposals or a commitment to award a contract, according to the officials.
The assessment focuses on facilities and workforce capabilities needed to support complex nuclear submarine construction over an extended period.
Required capabilities include complete hull fabrication, modular outfitting, precision systems integration, reactor compartment installation and post-delivery testing. The Navy is also seeking information on available drydock capacity, specialized fabrication equipment and the availability of qualified shipbuilding design personnel.
Critical infrastructure identified in the notice includes certified graving or floating drydocks, heavy-module fabrication shops and gantry crane systems capable of lifting and moving major submarine modules.
The sources-sought process is an early market-research step rather than a competition for a construction contract. The US Navy will use the information to assess the industrial base available for SSN(X) construction and inform its future acquisition strategy, it was concluded.
The announcement comes as the Trump administration pursues a broader overhaul of the US naval shipbuilding industrial base.
In an August presidential memorandum, President Donald Trump directed the development of measures to expand domestic shipbuilding capacity, increase competition and establish a fifth public Navy shipyard to improve submarine and aircraft carrier maintenance capacity.

title: Solenn review: Come for the setting, stay for the Wagyu lasagne that keeps selling out
body: Known for his work at some of Dubai’s most acclaimed restaurants, chef Gregoire Berger now has his sights on Abu Dhabi. Solenn, which opened in August at The Arcades at Al Khail Square and overlooks Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club , is Berger's first restaurant in the capital. A departure from the fine dining for which he is known, the relaxed Mediterranean eatery is built around the idea of long lunches, quality produce and a slower pace. First impressions The Arcades at Al Khail Square is busy on a Friday evening, with people strolling along its corridors and between cafes, but Solenn is surprisingly quiet when we arrive, leaving us free to choose a table. Inside, colourful sofas and chairs, terracotta walls and pale pink tables give the space a warm and relaxed feel, like sitting in a cosy living room. Tall arched windows overlook the equestrian area, making the window seats a good spot to watch the activity outside over a meal. Chef Gregoire previously described his vision for Solenn as a “beautiful springtime in the South of France, there's great music outside and an amazing fragrance of lemon trees, and you just chill over a long lunch”. The inviting surroundings make it easy to settle in. The menu The extensive menu offers plenty of choice, from breakfast dishes such as eggs, sandwiches and baked-to-order filo, to bowls, bakery items and manakish. My dining partner and I are here for dinner, so we turn our attention to the mains, although with so many options it makes deciding what to order a bit daunting. We are persuaded to try the Solenn Passion (Dh39) and Blanc Lychee (Dh38), two mocktails that we find quite refreshing, especially after coming in from the heat. Our meal starts with the burrata “Puglia” illusion (Dh95), a dish that is recommended by Gregoire himself. Adapted from one of his signature creations, it features a delicate tomato shell created from white chocolate and cocoa butter filled with a tomato salad and locally made burrata. It’s creamy, with the shell of the tomato offering a touch of sweetness. There is a long list of choices when it comes to mains to try. After some time, we decided on the marrow melt Wagyu burger (Dh160), whole sea bass (Dh220), truffle Wagyu lasagne (Dh85) and, after some persistence from our server, the Solenn baby chicken (Dh135). We’re told the lasagne regularly sells out, and we can see why. Generously portioned and full of flavour, it quickly becomes a favourite at the table, setting a high bar for the other mains. The sea bass is another highlight. Although I am not the biggest fan of seafood, I’m impressed by its tenderness and colourful presentation. It comes on a plate with two sauces – miso beurre blanc and curry – offering different flavours to accompany the fish. Unfortunately, the Wagyu burger is less successful. Neither of us feels it justifies the Dh160 price tag. The patty is small and with fries on the side it feels like an item that doesn’t really fit with the rest of the menu. However, the baby chicken fares better, although by the time we turn to it, we’re already rather full. We finish with two desserts. The caramel millefeuille (Dh55) combines baklava with crunchy vanilla pastry and cinnamon cream caramel, served with vanilla ice cream. The noisette velours (Dh65) is a more chocolate-heavy option, pairing sponge with mousses and hazelnut crunch for texture. It comes with vanilla ice cream and a milk chocolate spray finish. By this point, we’re already full, so the manageable portions are welcome. The millefeuille is the less sweet of the two, while the noisette velours will hit the spot for anyone craving a sugary finish. Standout dish For us, the truffle Wagyu lasagne royale is the standout, with distinct layers that allow each component to come through. The rich flavour of the Wagyu beef also comes through clearly in each bite. Big enough to share, it also offers better value than some of the pricier mains. Save or splurge A three-course meal at Solenn can cost between Dh178 and Dh547. At the high-end of the price spectrum are the beef carpaccio “truffle vinaigrette” (Dh120), solo meuniere “Turkish Riveira” (Dh355) and luxe mango (Dh72). Meanwhile, those who would like to save can order the black lime hummus (Dh48), crispy chicken burger (Dh75) and caramel millefeuille (Dh55). The verdict Solenn is an easy place to settle in for an unhurried meal with friends or family, with its comfortable seating and views of the equestrian area adding to the appeal. The extensive menu could benefit from a tighter focus, and some dishes offer better value than others, but the Wagyu lasagne and sea bass give us reasons to return. Contact information Solenn is located at The Arcades in Al Khail Square at the Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club. It’s open Monday to Thursday, 8am to 10pm and Friday to Sunday, 8am to midnight. Reservations can be made by calling 54 328 9899. This review was conducted at the invitation of the restaurant

title: “Now it’s your turn”: US envoys planned to show Moscow a refinery pause and a diesel deal, then ask for something back, a source tells Reuters
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); US President Donald Trump’s envoys told Kyiv that letting Russia sell diesel could draw Moscow back to peace talks, Reuters reported . In the same meeting, they said Russia’s leader was not ready to negotiate. Since then, Moscow has offered nothing in return, and Trump has brushed off claims that Russia helps Iran. Washington is pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries and offering Moscow economic incentives to return to peace talks, even though Russia has made no commitment in return. Yesterday, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before air raid sirens sounded, amid disputed warnings that the US could cut intelligence support. Meanwhile, Ukraine is being asked to halt its long-range campaign against the oil infrastructure that fuels and finances Russia's war. The pitch: a diesel deal as a signal to Moscow Trump’s Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met the Ukrainian delegation in Miami on 9 October. They described Russian President Vladimir Putin as unprepared to negotiate but said the diesel deal could help restart three-way talks, two of the sources said. The third source said the deal could “soften” Moscow because it “sends a signal that Trump is open to do things” with Russia. One of the sources described the plan: “The idea was that the US could go back to Russia and say ‘See, the Ukrainians stopped striking and we gave you this deal. Now it’s your turn to do something.’” Ukraine’s part was to stop hitting Russian refineries. Kushner repeated Trump’s request at the meeting, noting the administration had made it several times, two sources said. Explore further EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow Kyiv was asked to hold its fire on Russian oil The Ukrainians agreed to nothing formally, Reuters’ sources said. They signaled they would accept an energy ceasefire if Russia did the same, but saw the US approach as an attempt to appease Russia with business deals. Two days later, Trump declared an energy ceasefire, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready if Russia reciprocated. Euromaidan Press has monitored official and unofficial Ukrainian and Russian sources and found no reports of new Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries after Trump’s announcement. One of the last, on the night of the diesel announcement, knocked out more than half the tanks at a fuel-export terminal in Rostov-on-Don. Three sources told Reuters the envoys did not threaten to cut US support over the refinery strikes. A Ukrainian official told Axios, however, that the envoys warned Trump could cut Ukraine off from US intelligence, which a US official denied. US officials are also believed to have told European allies that Trump would halt PURL, the NATO scheme for Europe-funded US weapons for Ukraine, unless the strikes stopped, according to FT. Explore further Ukrainian journalist asks Trump’s envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from “international criminal” Putin. Witkoff wouldn’t answer directly What Moscow has offered in return A person close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin would return to the table only when he gets “the remaining 11% of Donbas.” Ukraine refuses to cede more land. During the 9 October call that produced the deal, Putin declined to commit to resuming talks, his aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, Axios reported. Moscow has not confirmed the energy ceasefire either. Trump insisted on 12 October that the sides had agreed “because I said they agreed,” RFE/RL reported . On the evening of 12 October, Russian munitions collapsed an apartment stairwell in Kharkiv, killing four people . Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak, meanwhile, claimed diesel exports could reach 3.0–3.5 million tons a month by year-end, above the volumes Trump announced. “Too much to lose”: Trump on Russia and Iran Late on 12 October, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he did not believe Russia and China were helping Iran, since they have “too much to lose.” In March, he told Fox News that Putin “might be helping them a little bit.” Asked about Russia’s possible support for Iran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on 2 September that his message to everyone was to “stay away.” That month, a Financial Times investigation found Russia secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles that could threaten US warships. title: Russia’s extra non-oil-and-gas budget revenues to reach 1 trln rubles ($11.92 bln) in 2026
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s federal budget revenues from both energy and non-energy sectors are tracking ahead of target for 2026, with non-oil-and-gas windfalls expected to reach approximately 1 trillion rubles ($11.92 billion), Finance Minister Anton Siluanov announced on Tuesday.
"As for 2026, we see that the projected targets for both non-oil-and-gas and oil-and-gas revenues are overall being outperformed," Siluanov told a plenary session of the State Duma.
The minister attributed the 1-trillion-ruble ($11.92 billion) revenue overshoot primarily to robust domestic economic growth. For the January-September period of 2026, non-oil-and-gas budget revenues surged 18.8% year-on-year to 24.2 trillion rubles ($288.37 billion), according to ministry data.

title: Drone carrying M250 machine gun completes firing test
body: A heavy-duty quadcopter carrying Sig Sauer’s new M250 light machine gun has completed a test requiring it to identify and engage targets from the air, the company announced Tuesday. Sig Sauer completed the test in concert with Israel Aerospace Industries, maker of the Fire Storm 250, a reusable drone that can stay airborne for two hours and is designed with a stabilized machine-gun mount. According to a Tuesday announcement from the companies, the test required the system to hover over a simulated battlefield, ID targets with an onboard camera and fire on them using both single-shot and semi-automatic firing modes “from varying distances and altitudes.” It’s a fast development timeline for the drone, which was first unveiled last October. The defense publication Janes reported in February that flight tests for the system were scheduled for summer 2026. The system, as Janes reported, incorporates Sig’s micro-remote-controlled weapon system along with the M250, a version of which is set to replace the Army’s M249 squad automatic weapon as part of the service’s Next-Generation Squad Weapon program. According to Tuesday’s announcement, the system can carry 200 rounds of ammunition and the 53-pound RCWS. It can take off and land vertically, lending itself to operation in austere forward locations. “Sensor information and fire-control data are combined into a unified targeting solution, giving the operator a continuous operational picture and supporting a rapid sensor-to-shooter cycle,” the companies said. An internal combustion engine can accept a variety of jet fuels, allowing the drone to be reused in the field, per the Janes report. It’s designed, according to the company, to accompany tactical units “with limited manpower and support requirements.” While it’s previously been reported that the system incorporates artificial intelligence to automate components of tracking and detection, the companies emphasized its human-in-the-loop fire control system, allowing human operators to make engagement and fire decisions while receiving imagery and tracking data from the Fire Storm 250’s onboard sensors. “FIRE STORM 250 brings together the most advanced technologies in the world,” Sali Okanin, Israel General Manager for SIG SAUER, said in an announcement. “We’re proud of the new SIG SAUER M250, which is combat-proven technology. It is a belt-fed platform with greater range than legacy systems and weight savings that not only provide squad-level benefits but also make drone capabilities possible.” Sig Sauer executives told Military Times earlier this month that fielding for the M250 is expected to begin in the first half of next year. While the Army’s version of the weapon is chambered in Sig Sauer’s internally developed 6.8X51mm ammo, the Israel Defense Forces began using a 7.62X51mm variant in 2025. The Fire Storm 250 reportedly can carry either.
