title: Poor crop in W. Darfur’s Kreinik due to scanty rainfall
body: The Agricultural Season Protection Committee in Kreinik locality in Sudan’s West Darfur State has reported that no more than 30 percent of cultivated land in the area is expected to yield successful harvests, amid fears that agricultural production could fall below 25 percent of expected output due to poor rainfall. Prince Ahmed Yagoub Muni, the committee’s chairperson, said the committee had conducted a comprehensive field tour to inspect farming areas, assess the security situation and examine crop conditions. The tour covered Azerni, Mukshasha, Al-Thaniya, Wadi and Kreinik. “The security situation remained stable, and livestock were kept away from farmland thanks to efforts by members of the Agricultural Season Protection Committee. However, insufficient rainfall has adversely affected large areas of cultivated land, threatening production during the current agricultural season,” he said. “We appeal to local and international communities to support residents of West Darfur amid the difficult conditions, and to ensure food security and the need to assist communities affected by declining agricultural output.” Separately, Omda Ibrahim Abdel Nabi said the field tour lasted three days and aimed to inspect farms and assess the security situation across the locality. “Inadequate rainfall has resulted in some farms producing successful crops while others have failed, with projections indicating that output could fall to no more than 25 percent of expected levels,” he stated. “Security remains stable, and community cohesion is holding firm.” He emphasized the need for continued coordination between local communities and relevant authorities to reduce tensions between farmers and pastoralists. Meanwhile, Prince Mohammed Abdel Hadi stressed that the state government should prioritize farmers, the protection of crops and the safety of residents. “The field tour had covered farms across the locality and resulted in the identification of livestock owners whose animals had been found inside some farms,” he said. “I urge livestock owners to keep their herds away from cultivated land until the harvest is complete. Anyone who allows their livestock to enter farms will be held responsible for any resulting damage.” The warnings come as parts of West Darfur face agricultural challenges linked to inadequate rainfall, raising concerns that declining production could further undermine food security and worsen living conditions for residents. The post Poor crop in W. Darfur’s Kreinik due to scanty rainfall appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Lagos: The City of Waste Dumps
body: ​By Erasmus Ikhide ​ The visual and olfactory tragedy of a Mega-City ​No visitor arriving in Lagos can possibly miss its stunning, breathtaking neglect. Traffic chaos was once considered its second nature, an unfortunate product of its frantic geographic expansion and sprawling population. However, this notorious gridlock has now been violently overtaken by a far more pervasive and nauseating malady: the proliferation of indiscriminate waste dumps festering across the metropolis without timely or systematic evacuation. ​ From Badagry to Mile 2, from Mile 2 down to Orile, stretching across the congested veins of Iyana Iba to Egbeda, and from Oshodi down to Agbado-Ijaye, the landscape bears the deep scars of environmental abandonment. Both the mainland and Lagos Island—most notably historic, high-density commercial hubs like Idumota, Akpongbon, and their claustrophobic environs—have systematically devolved into monumental environmental disasters because of unmitigated, indiscriminate waste dumping. ​You would be genuinely shocked at how dirty these areas have become. All sides of the roads, the medians, and the once-functional drainage channels are littered, choked, and buried under industrial and domestic refuse. Other prime locations such as Lekki and Victoria Island may be less littered on the surface, but even their primary thoroughfares cry out for urgent attention and structural maintenance. ​If you juxtapose what is happening in this self-proclaimed “Centre of Excellence” with the visionary, monumental development strides of the Lateef Jakande years, one is bound to confront agonizing, existential questions: Is Lagos actually working? What is happening to our local governments? Why can’t they evacuate basic waste? Above all, is someone still presiding over the state government? ​The Golden Benchmark: The Jakande Era vs. Present Ruin ​To understand the depth of our current desolation, one must revisit the historic governance benchmark set by Alhaji Lateef Jakande during his administration as governor of Lagos State from 1979 to 1983. The population of Lagos was already growing rapidly at the time, which overstretched available infrastructure as public schools were severely congested. Instead of offering endless excuses or commissioning superficial media events, the Jakande administration revolutionized public education by building hundreds of affordable primary and secondary schools to abolish the stressful and dehumanizing morning and afternoon shift systems. ​ His government constructed thousands of functional, low-cost classrooms grouped into major neighborhood schools and complexes across local government areas like Mushin, Agege, Ipaja, Apapa, and Epe. Notable legacy educational hubs established during this period include, the prestigious Tolu Schools Complex in Ajeromi-Ifelodun, the Amuwo-Odofin Schools Complex, the Okota Schools Complex and the Odu Abore Primary School in Mushin. ​Furthermore, Jakande’s administration established General Hospital zones all over the state with the firm assurance of free healthcare for the populace. In a testament to his unmatched administrative vision, his government built more libraries in Lagos State than all the governors combined since 1999, and he made history as the first governor to present a billion-naira state budget in Nigeria. ​In higher and technical education, his administration founded Lagos State University (LASU) to provide higher learning opportunities for Lagos residents. He relocated and expanded the Lagos State College of Education (LACOED/now Adeniran Ogunsanya College of Education) to train professional teachers, and founded Lagos State Polytechnic (LASPOTECH) to boost technical and vocational manpower across the federation. Dedicated teacher training colleges and technical schools were also set up across different divisions to rapidly supply qualified educators and skilled workers. Institutional Decay and Administrative Inertia ​Today, the contrast between that golden era of purpose-driven leadership and the current dispensation under Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu is stark, painful, and profoundly embarrassing. Established secondary schools and tertiary institutions—including Lagos State University as its flagship, multiple housing estates in isolation (such as Agbado-Ijaiye and Agege-Abesan), and critical arterial roads—are languishing in terminal neglect. ​Even though past institutions like the College of Education and Lagos Polytechnic have been administratively upgraded into full-fledged universities (namely, the Lagos State University of Education [LASUED] and the Lagos State University of Science and Technology [LASPOTECH]), the overarching physical environment and structural maintenance have deteriorated sharply. ​ Local government councils have been rendered toothless, structurally emasculated, and completely incapacitated. Why can’t they evacuate waste? Why are our commercial nerve centers buried under decomposing refuse? Why has a state blessed with immense internally generated revenue degenerated into a monument of administrative inertia? ​ Governance Failure: Sanitation, Infrastructure, and Grassroots Paralysis ​When an urban centre of global significance collapses under the weight of its own refuse, the failure is neither accidental nor transient; it is structural and systemic. The core crisis of contemporary Lagos lies in the systematic dismantling of local governance structures. In any functional federation, the local government tier is uniquely positioned to handle localized sanitation, tenement management, and neighborhood-level waste collection. Yet, under the present administration, local councils have been reduced to mere administrative ciphers, financially emasculated and stripped of the autonomy required to keep their communities clean. ​ Private Sector Participation (PSP) waste management operators struggle under crippling bureaucratic bottlenecks, delayed subsidies, and a lack of infrastructural backing. The Lagos State Waste Management Authority (LAWMA) has proven largely incapable of meeting the refuse disposal demands of a surging mega-city population. Consequently, major highways, secondary roads, and street corners have been converted into unauthorized, permanent waste dumps. This environmental degradation directly threatens public health. Rainwater washes toxic leachate from these rotting refuse heaps directly into open drainage channels, polluting the lagoon, contaminating the water table, and exposing millions of residents to preventable waterborne and airborne diseases. It is a slow-motion public health emergency happening in broad daylight. The Contrast of Priorities: Substance vs. Spectacle ​ Governance must be measured by the tangible quality of life it delivers to the ordinary citizen, not by flashy billboards, high-sounding slogans, or stage-managed media commissioning ceremonies. When school children in Agege and Ipaja must wade through flooded, waste-clogged gutters to reach crumbling classrooms with leaking roofs, the promise of a “Smart City” is revealed as a cruel illusion. When traders in Idumota and Akpongbon conduct their daily commerce surrounded by towering mountains of garbage, the state government’s claims of economic excellence ring hollow. ​Jakande’s administration proved that with discipline, prudent resource management, and profound empathy for the common man, monumental challenges could be overcome within a short span of four years. He did not build his legacy on empty media optics; he built it on enduring physical infrastructure, robust institutions, and a genuine commitment to public welfare. ​ Deepening the Critique: Urban Planning and Social Neglect ​The regression of Lagos is further mirrored in the state of its mass housing projects. During the Second Republic, Jakande’s administration constructed over 30,000 low-cost housing units across diverse locations—including Ijaiye, Dolphin, Oke-Afa, Abesan, Amuwo-Odofin, Ipaja, and Iba. These communities were designed to provide shelter and dignity to low-income earners, civil servants, and the working class. Today, many of these same housing estates are plagued by infrastructural decay, failing sewage systems, unpaved internal roads, and encroaching commercial shanties. ​The disconnect between the ruling elite in Alausa and the everyday realities of ordinary Lagosians has never been wider. While billions are funneled into elite ego massaging beautification projects, densely populated settlements on the mainland are left to rot in filth. The failure to maintain basic public infrastructure—ranging from public libraries to health centers and technical schools—has created an environment where youth unemployment, social despair, and urban decay thrive unchecked. ​ Reinventing the Centre of Excellence ​ Lagos State stands at a critical historical crossroads. It remains the undeniable commercial heartbeat of West Africa and a financial engine room that the rest of the continent looks up to. It cannot continue to wallow as the capital of filth, structural decay, and administrative indifference. ​Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu must be called to order. The current environmental tragedy is an undeniable indictment of executive capability. The state requires an immediate, comprehensive, and aggressive overhaul of its waste management architecture, the full restoration of true local government financial and operational autonomy, and a return to the disciplined, people-centric philosophy of governance exemplified by Alhaji Lateef Jakande. ​ The City of Excellence deserves true leadership, rigorous urban planning, and environmental dignity. History is watching, and the judgment of the people will be unsparing. *Erasmus Ikhide contributed this piece via: ikhideluckyerasmus@gmail.com Tell: +2348035032123. WhatsApp only.

title: NASU to FG: Economic reforms must deliver relief, not more suffering
body: By Victor Ahiuma-Young The Non-Academic Staff Union of Educational and Associated Institutions, NASU, has decried the worsening hardship confronting Nigerian workers and their families, citing rising hunger, poverty, fuel prices and the escalating cost of basic necessities. It also demands urgent moves to review the national minimum wage to reflect prevailing economic realities. NASU equally called on the Federal Government to introduce immediate measures to ease the burden of rising food prices, transportation costs, electricity tariffs, housing rents and healthcare expenses, warning that workers’ earnings can no longer guarantee a decent standard of living amid the prevailing economic challenges. NASU President, Dr Makolo Hassan, made the call in his welcome address at the union’s National Executive Council, NEC, meeting taking place between Tuesday, October 13, and Wednesday, October 14, 2026, in Abuja. Hassan, who described the current minimum wage as inadequate in the face of rising living costs, said the union would continue to press for a living wage that guarantees workers and their families a dignified existence. He said, “While the ₦70,000 National Minimum Wage was a hard-won victory, the prevailing economic realities in Nigeria have rendered it grossly inadequate. “With the increase in the pump prices of petroleum products, the astronomical rise in the cost of food, transportation, housing, electricity, healthcare and other essential commodities, the current Minimum Wage has effectively become a slave wage that can no longer sustain Nigerian workers and their families.” He urged the Federal Government to urgently initiate a review of the national minimum wage and institutionalise periodic wage reviews and cost-of-living adjustments to protect workers’ purchasing power against inflation. According to him, Nigerian workers deserve not merely a minimum wage but a living wage capable of guaranteeing decent living conditions and economic security. The NASU president further stressed that economic reforms must translate into tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary Nigerians rather than deepen hardship and inequality. He said, “The true measure of any economic reform is not the applause it receives in boardrooms, but the difference it makes in the lives of ordinary Nigerians. “The cost-of-living crisis remains one of the gravest challenges confronting Nigerian workers and their families. Whatever improvement may be reported in headline inflation, the reality in our homes, markets and workplaces tells a harder story. Food, transport, rent, school fees, medicines, electricity and other basic necessities continue to consume an unbearable share of workers’ incomes. With food inflation still at 19. 57 per cent in July 2026, affordable food remains NASU’s central national demand. “We call for urgent and sustained support for farmers, improved security for farming communities, better storage and transportation infrastructure, and deliberate investment in domestic food production. The projection that nearly 35 million Nigerians could face acute and severe food insecurity during the 2026 lean season must be treated as a national emergency. No worker who contributes to the wealth of this country should go home unable to put food on the family table. “The continuing consequences of petrol pricing and subsidy removal are equally severe. Every increase in the cost of fuel travels quickly through fares, food prices, production costs and ultimately the pockets of working people. Domestic refining must therefore translate into real and measurable relief for Nigerians, not merely improved statistics or higher margins for operators. Government must protect households and productive enterprises from the full impact of international oil-price volatility and exchange-rate shocks. “At the same time, Nigeria must urgently expand reliable and affordable mass transportation through buses, rail and other public transit systems, while subjecting Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and other promised intervention programmes to proper assessment to determine whether they are truly delivering relief to workers. Our position is clear: workers cannot continue to bear the greatest burden of economic reforms while receiving the least protection from their consequences. “This same principle is what guides our demands on electricity and housing. Nigerian workers should not be compelled to pay increasingly high electricity tariffs without corresponding improvements in supply. We demand affordable power for households and productive enterprises, universal metering, an end to arbitrary estimated billing, and a tariff system that places fairness, service delivery and the welfare of citizens above revenue extraction. As the service-based tariff regime and updated 2026 Multi-Year Tariff Orders (MYTO) continue to shape electricity pricing, workers must not be made to pay more for darkness.” He also raised concerns over food insecurity, citing the projection that nearly 35 million Nigerians could face acute and severe food insecurity during the 2026 lean season. He called for increased support for farmers, improved security in farming communities and investment in domestic food production, storage and transportation infrastructure. The union also demanded affordable housing schemes, accessible mortgage facilities and measures to protect workers against unreasonable rent increases. It maintained that workers should not be forced to pay higher electricity tariffs without corresponding improvements in power supply. On employment, Hassan expressed concern over youth unemployment, underemployment, casualisation and the declining productive capacity of the Nigerian economy. He called for a national employment strategy focused on technical and vocational education, apprenticeship programmes, industrial skills development and the creation of secure, decent jobs. He equally urged the government to address factory closures and the high costs of electricity, transportation, raw materials and credit, noting that the survival and expansion of productive enterprises were essential to sustainable job creation. The NASU president further called for improved healthcare, adequate funding for public education, prompt payment of pensions and gratuities, and stronger social protection programmes for vulnerable Nigerians. Hassan also called for greater transparency and accountability in the management of public resources, insisting that increased revenues accruing to states and local governments should translate into timely salary payments, better public services, improved infrastructure and stronger social protection. On industrial relations, he reaffirmed NASU’s commitment to collective bargaining, freedom of association and the protection of workers’ rights, warning employers against intimidation, victimisation and practices designed to weaken trade unions. He further urged the government to address insecurity, particularly attacks on farmers and rural communities, noting that banditry, kidnapping and insurgency threatened workers’ lives, agricultural production, food supply and national productivity. As the country approaches the 2027 political transition, Hassan urged organised labour to place workers’ welfare at the centre of national discourse, insisting that candidates and political programmes should be assessed on their commitments to living wages, decent jobs, security, industrialisation and quality public services. He urged members of the National Executive Council to remain united and committed to advancing the interests of the union’s membership, stressing that sustained engagement and collective action remained critical to achieving better working conditions and economic justice for Nigerian workers. The post NASU to FG: Economic reforms must deliver relief, not more suffering appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
body: US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died at the age of 34. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his representative told the BBC. Mitte died in Brownsvillle, Texas, on Monday. His publicist confirmed to Reuters that he took his own life. The actor, who had cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter ‘Flynn’ White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series. Bryan Cranston, who played his father, paid tribute on Instagram, writing that he was in “deep despair” following the news. RJ Mitte (right) as Walter White Jr alongside Bryan Cranston (left) and Anna Gunn in series one of Breaking Bad in 2008 Cranston played a high school chemistry teacher who turned to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. “I met him when he was only 14 years old, when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm,” said Cranston. “That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor.” Cranston praised Mitte’s advocacy for performers with disabilities, and noted that he never allowed his cerebral palsy to “be an excuse for anything”. “All that promise and potential now is such a loss,” wrote the actor, adding that he “thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed”. He said “it is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life.” Cranston added: “I’ll miss you, son.” Mitte’s representative, Sean Reilly, said in a statement to the BBC: “Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.” The star also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s. He created The Mitte Foundation to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform “to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities”, Reilly said. In a statement shared with the Hollywood Reporter, Aaron Paul, who played Breaking Bad’s Jesse Pinkman, said he was at a loss and heartbroken. “RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed,” he said. “And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that.” Dean Norris, who played Mitte’s uncle, Hank Schrader, posted that although “RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set”. “He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed,” Norris wrote. The Breaking Bad cast at the SAG Awards in 2014 Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister’s acting career in 2005. He had said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial. “Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn’t end well for anyone,” he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month. His character was based on the show’s creator Vince Gilligan’s late friend who had a more severe case of cerebral palsy and used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require. Mitte was seen as playing the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was rarely mentioned in the series. Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008-13. After shooting to fame, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible. “Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind,” he told the BBC in 2021 . “Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change,” he said. Mitte’s other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.

title: German Eurofighters escort Corendon jet as Nuremberg Airport shuts down
body: Nuremberg Airport (NUE) suspended flight operations on October 13, 2026, after authorities received a report of a possible in-flight emergency aboard a Corendon Airlines passenger aircraft arriving from Corfu, Greece. German Air Force Eurofighter jets escorted the aircraft to the airport, where it landed safely. The aircraft, a Boeing 737-800 registered 9H-CXD and operating Corendon Airlines flight XR456, was scheduled to arrive at approximately 12:15 local time. It touched down at 12:16, according to Flightradar24 flight-tracking data . Police cordoned off access roads to the airport shortly before the landing, while the airport suspended all flight operations. “We received a report of an unclear air emergency,” Middle Franconia police said on X, adding that the aircraft had landed safely and that investigations into the cause were underway. “We are working on the assumption of a suspected air emergency, but this is not yet confirmed,” a police spokesperson said, according to German newspaper Nordbayern . Nuremberg Airport is closed until 14:00 UTC, according to Eurocontrol. The last flight to land was #XR456 at 10:16 UTC. Earlier, during its departure from Corfu, #XR456 transmitted squawk 7500 (hijacking) between 08:15 and 08:28 UTC. https://t.co/9inTVK07df — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 13, 2026 Eurofighters scrambled after emergency transponder code Two German Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets on QRA training. (Credit: Bundeswehr) An airport spokesperson told German public broadcaster Bayerischer Rundfunk that the aircraft’s transponder had reportedly transmitted squawk 7500, the emergency code for a hijacking, during its approach to Nuremberg. The circumstances that triggered the alert remain unclear. The German Press Agency (dpa) reported that Eurofighter jets accompanied the aircraft before its landing. An airport spokesperson confirmed their involvement and said the fighters had subsequently turned away. The German Air Force (Luftwaffe) maintains two armed Eurofighters on Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) duty at each of its two air policing bases, Wittmund in northern Germany and Neuburg an der Donau in the south. The aircraft are required to be airborne within 15 minutes of an alert to identify, monitor or escort aircraft presenting a potential airspace security concern, according to the Bundeswehr . The airport remained closed while police continued their operation. Several incoming flights were diverted to Frankfurt, Memmingen, Stuttgart and Munich. The airport initially gave no indication of when normal operations would resume. Suspected drone sightings disrupt Nuremberg Airport overnight The emergency came just hours after a separate security alert disrupted traffic at Nuremberg Airport. Between 02:00 and 04:00 local time on October 13, 2026, three pilots independently reported seeing an unidentified object during takeoff or landing. Police said the object could have been a drone. The Nuremberg Airport Border Police Inspectorate launched search and detection measures in coordination with airport authorities and German air traffic control provider Deutsche Flugsicherung (DFS). Police also deployed a helicopter, but officers could not locate or identify the reported object. According to an airport statement , six flights were delayed by the overnight disruption, including two arrivals and four departures. Two incoming aircraft were initially diverted to Cologne Bonn Airport (CGN) and Prague Airport (PRG) as a precaution before continuing to Nuremberg. Police opened an investigation into the reported sightings. Authorities have not established whether the overnight incident was connected to the subsequent emergency involving flight XR456. The post German Eurofighters escort Corendon jet as Nuremberg Airport shuts down appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Allegations about military plans in Suwalki Gap branded as stupidity by Belarusian leader
body:
MINSK, October 13. /TASS/. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko dismissed as utterly stupid Western allegations that Minsk is planning to push through the Suwalki Gap toward the Kaliningrad Region.
"The other direction in their criticism of Belarus is that we are going to push through the Suwalki Gap toward the Kaliningrad Region. I don’t want to justify myself here, for this is utter stupidity," the Belarusian leader told a meeting with senior security officials.
A video of the meeting was published on the Telegram channel Pul Pervogo, which is affiliated with the Belarusian leader's press service.

title: Ukraine hits Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile maintenance base, General Staff says
body:
Ukrainian forces struck an Iskander-M repair base, a radar station, logistics depots, and Russian troop concentrations, the General Staff said on Oct. 13.
The Iskander -M repair base islocated near Kondrinka in Russia's Kursk Oblast , according to the General Staff . The facility is used to repair self-propelled launchers and transporter-loader vehicles of the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system
The Iskander-M is one of Russia's principal ballistic weapons. Since the beginning of 2026, Moscow has launched more than 500 ballistic missiles against Ukraine.
Kyiv's military intelligence estimates that Russia can produce more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles of various types each month, with Iskander-M missiles among its production priorities.
In addition, a radar station was struck in Bryansk Oblast , the General Staff said.
Across Russian-occupied territories, Ukrainian troops also struck Russian troop concentrations. In the occupied Luhansk Oblast, a fuel and lubricants depot, an ammunition depot, and a logistics facility belonging to Russian units were struck.
The strikes are part of a series of attacks on Russian military infrastructure in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territories.

title: Wontumi pleads not guilty in GH¢30m Exim Bank loan case
body: Bernard Antwi Boasiako, popularly known as Chairman Wontumi, has pleaded not guilty to five charges in connection with the alleged fraudulent procurement of a GH¢30 million loan from the Ghana Export-Import Bank (Exim Bank). The case has been adjourned to Tuesday, October 27, 2026, at 11 a.m. for a case management conference. The prosecution has been given 14 days to file the relevant disclosures. Wontumi, who is standing trial with two others, was arraigned on a new charge sheet filed on September 22, 2026, over the loan obtained in 2018. The five counts comprise defrauding by false pretence, two counts of uttering forged documents, money laundering, and intentionally causing financial loss of GH¢30 million to a public body. According to the prosecution, Wontumi presented forged and altered documents to Exim Bank in January 2018 to secure funding for a proposed farming project. The prosecution alleges that the accused persons did not carry out the proposed farming activities, purchase agricultural plant and machinery or employ workers for the farm. It further alleges that they neither owned nor secured the parcel of land they had represented to the bank as available for the project. The prosecution also contends that Wontumi withdrew substantial sums from the bank accounts of Wontumi Farms Limited, the third accused, and used the funds for personal purposes, including investments in other businesses. Wontumi denied all the charges. Following the proceedings, he was returned to Nsawam Maximum Security Prison, where he is serving a 20-year sentence imposed by a differently constituted High Court in Accra.

title: Putin’s Protector in the White House
body:
“Russia would like to make a deal... but for whatever reason, Zelensky does not want to make a deal,” Donald Trump told reporters on Oct. 10, speaking about his latest conversation with Vladimir Putin. The Russian president, he went on, was eager for peace; Zelensky could have ended the war many times; and Ukraine ought to choose a new president.
When the man at the head of the world’s most powerful democracy says such things, one has to ask what has become of American foreign policy when it casts the invader as a peacemaker and the president of the invaded country as the obstacle to ending a war that has devastated his nation for more than four and a half years.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
So Trump cannot fathom why Zelensky will not accept the agreement Putin supposedly wants. The president of the United States has at his disposal the entire American intelligence apparatus, reports from diplomats around the world, and military assessments delivered to him every day. Yet somehow one elementary fact has escaped him. Russia invaded Ukraine, seized its territory, devastated its cities, and killed tens of thousands of its citizens.
For years, Putin’s army has been trying to accomplish what its commander in chief set out to do: destroy Ukraine’s independence. Zelensky leads a nation fighting to survive, and Ukrainians have learned enough from Moscow’s promises to know how little an agreement with the Kremlin is worth.
Perhaps, in Trump’s conception of foreign affairs, the Ukrainians’ attachment to their own country is an inexplicable quirk. Why won’t they simply hand the Russians what they demand, accept the redrawing of their borders, and allow the American president to announce another of his great diplomatic triumphs? What kind of obstinate people, after years of bombardment, thousands of funerals, and millions driven from their homes, still insist on deciding their own future? To a man who sees the world chiefly as an endless succession of deals, Ukrainian freedom must be a particularly baffling proposition.
What is especially repellent is the ease with which Trump speaks of Putin’s desire for peace. By Russia’s own stated demands, Ukraine is expected to surrender territory Russian forces have not even managed to conquer. There is no evidence whatsoever that Putin has abandoned the imperial ambitions that drove him to invade a sovereign country. Yet Putin apparently needs only to murmur into the telephone that he wants peace for Trump to take him at his word. Four and a half years of destruction count for less than a few whispered assurances from the other end of the line.
History has seen Western leaders convince themselves that an aggressor could be placated. In 1938, Neville Chamberlain signed the Munich Agreement, sacrificing Czechoslovakia to Hitler’s territorial ambitions, and returned to London convinced he had secured peace for Europe. Now imagine that after Germany invaded Poland a year later, he had told the British people that Hitler sincerely wished to reach an agreement, but that the Poles, for reasons known only to themselves, stubbornly refused to stop fighting. All that would have remained was for Chamberlain to advise Poland to elect a new president, one with a more accommodating attitude toward Berlin.
Grotesque as that imagined speech may sound, its logic is now coming from the mouth of an American president. There is, however, one historical distinction worth remembering. For all the calamity of his appeasement policy, Chamberlain declared war on Nazi Germany on Sept. 3, 1939, after Hitler invaded Poland. He eventually understood that there was a point beyond which retreat before an aggressor became a humiliation of his own country. More than four years into Russia’s invasion, Trump is still explaining to the world how much Putin wants peace and how Zelensky keeps spoiling things for him.
And if anyone doubted how affectionate this relationship has become, Putin’s adviser Yuri Ushakov was happy to oblige. After the presidents’ 90-minute conversation, Ushakov announced that neither man wanted to hang up first, so they finally ended the call at precisely the same moment. How touching. One might have thought he was describing two lovestruck teenagers on the phone after midnight, lingering through an endless succession of goodbyes, each insisting that the other hang up first, until they agree to hang up together. The only detail Ushakov omitted was which of them wished the other good night last.
The Kremlin seems so entranced by the warmth of the relationship that it believes the rest of the world deserves to hear its most tender details. While the two presidents compete over who can stay on the line longest, Russian pilots take off toward Ukrainian cities carrying bombs that will send parents scrambling to save their children that very night. Ushakov’s account becomes almost unbearable when the sentimental theater of two powerful men is set against what their politics mean for the people living beneath those bombs.
Within hours of Trump’s deal with Putin, Russian bombs struck residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia. At least 20 people were killed, including children. Reuters reported the grief of a grandfather whose six-year-old granddaughter had been pulled dead from the rubble. She was due to celebrate her birthday later in October. He stood beside her body and wept while the American president explained that Putin wanted peace.
Trump’s solicitude for Putin now has a very tangible economic expression. Following their Oct. 9 telephone conversation, the American administration issued a license temporarily relaxing sanctions restrictions on transactions involving Russian diesel. Trump announced deliveries that, by his own account, could total 4.8 million metric tons. He publicly thanked Putin for the arrangement even as European governments warned that easing the pressure on Moscow would help bankroll its war.
Consider the scale of the political humiliation involved. For years, the United States sought to restrict the Russian state’s energy revenue precisely because that money sustains its machinery of war. Now an American president personally negotiates with Putin to bring Russian fuel back to market and advertises the arrangement as a triumph. All this is happening just weeks before the congressional midterms, when diesel prices have become a serious domestic liability for the White House.
There is an almost insulting irony in Trump’s explanation. His administration is trying to relieve the extraordinary disruption in energy markets caused, in part, by the war the United States and Israel launched against Iran, yet Zelensky is a far more convenient target for blame over fuel prices. By this logic, Ukraine’s president is supposed to stop attacking Russian refineries because those attacks inconvenience American farmers and trucking companies. The American truck driver has a place in Trump’s thinking about this war; the Ukrainian child huddled in a shelter barely seems to register.
Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries serve a clear military and economic purpose. They disrupt Moscow’s ability to produce and supply fuel, drive up the costs of Russia’s war economy, and force the aggressor to divert resources to defend its industrial facilities. For years, Russia has systematically targeted Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in an effort to deprive millions of electricity and heat. Yet when Ukraine strikes back at facilities that matter to Russia’s war economy, Trump responds with anger and demands that Zelensky stop.
Zelensky has offered a straightforward, verifiable compromise. Ukraine will stop striking Russia’s energy infrastructure if Russia simultaneously stops attacking Ukraine’s. That is the basic reciprocity any serious mediation should require. Trump, however, had already demanded that Kyiv halt its strikes unilaterally, while Putin received relief for his fuel exports. This distribution of favors and demands allows Moscow to preserve both the military and financial advantages of its aggression, while imposing yet another constraint on Ukraine’s defense.
This is the gravest damage Trump is doing to American foreign policy. There was a time when it was difficult even to imagine a US president publicly echoing the arguments of a country that had invaded its European neighbor, thanking its leader as his bombs killed civilians, and demanding political and military concessions from the victim. Barely two years ago, such a statement from the White House would have stunned even those who believed Washington should negotiate with Moscow. Trump has moved the boundaries of the politically conceivable so far, and so fast, that we now have to remind ourselves almost daily how extraordinary this rupture is.
For decades, America built its international authority on alliances, security guarantees, and the defense of a principle: a powerful country does not get to seize a weaker neighbor’s territory simply because it can. America’s own foreign policy record, of course, includes grave errors and serious violations of that very principle. But the country’s claim to leadership of the free world rested on the idea that democracies share an interest in restraining aggression. Trump is replacing that idea with personal arrangements, private deals, pressure on allies, and a bewildering indulgence toward Putin. The damage will outlast his time in the White House.
For America’s democratic allies, the implications are chilling. If a US president can recast the aggressor as the peacemaker and the country under attack as the obstacle to peace, what should countries that rely on American security guarantees now expect? What would that reasoning mean for the Baltic states, for Poland, or for any country confronted one day with the demands of a much more powerful neighbor? International order does not survive on the elegance of declarations about liberty. It survives when the states with the power to uphold those declarations are willing to act on them.
Trump’s call for Ukrainians to choose a new president is especially brazen. Volodymyr Zelensky was elected by Ukrainian voters in 2019. Subsequent presidential elections have been postponed because of martial law. Holding a free, safe, and fair vote while Ukrainian cities are bombed daily, millions of people have fled, and large stretches of the country are occupied presents challenges that cannot be waved away with an offhand remark in front of television cameras. Zelensky has now offered to hold elections if Russia agrees to a full, 60-day ceasefire. Putin has yet to demonstrate that he would accept even that.
By what right, in any case, does Trump tell Ukrainians who their president should be? Does the Ukrainian people’s right to choose their government expire whenever an American politician grows impatient with their choice? If Trump believes Zelensky should go because he refuses to accept whatever Trump and Putin agree between themselves, Trump might at least show a little respect for a people who have defended their democratic choice with weapons in their hands. Ukrainians have paid far too dearly for freedom to be told from Washington which candidate would be obedient enough to deserve their future.
Trump, for his part, might exercise a little caution before recommending that other countries change presidents. Americans will vote in congressional midterm elections on November 3, and the results could significantly alter the balance of power in Washington. Congress has the constitutional authority to oversee the executive, investigate abuses, and, where there are lawful grounds, initiate impeachment proceedings. A midterm election will not itself remove Trump; conviction and removal require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. But there is a perfectly legitimate question about how long America’s democratic system can withstand a foreign policy that is wrecking the country’s international standing and damaging relations with its most important allies.
An end to Trump’s policy toward Ukraine would be welcome news for the democratic world. If American institutions were one day to establish grounds for his impeachment and removal, I doubt there would be much celebration in the Kremlin. Nor would dictators and autocrats elsewhere have much reason to rejoice. Trump’s treatment of Putin has already encouraged them to believe that American support for democracy is negotiable, subject to the president’s personal preferences and interests. Fortunately, America is larger than one man in the White House. It has institutions, a free press, Congress, courts, and citizens who have repeatedly shown that they can defend their democratic order.
Meanwhile, Trump continues to speak as though Zelensky were the one who ought to apologize for the war’s continuation.
On Oct. 11, Trump abruptly announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire. Zelensky said Ukraine was prepared to honor such an arrangement but was still waiting for Moscow’s confirmation, the terms of the agreement, and credible guarantees.
At the time of Trump’s announcement, Russia had not publicly confirmed any such deal. Just hours later, a Russian drone struck a power plant in Kyiv, and Russian forces attacked the CHP-5 combined heat-and-power plant in Kharkiv.
In full view of the Russian public and the wider world, Putin once again humiliated Trump, demonstrating that the American president may proclaim as many ceasefires as he pleases, but Russian bombs will stop falling only when Putin gives the order. Putin’s promises deserve exactly the trust his record has earned them: next to none.
What pains me most about all of this is the endless expectation that Ukrainians must accommodate everyone else’s fears, interests, and political needs. They are expected to accommodate Putin’s territorial demands, Trump’s anxiety over diesel prices, Europe’s economic difficulties, and the exhaustion of Western publics after years of war.
How many of the politicians making these demands are prepared to give equal thought to the parent in Kharkiv waiting outside the wreckage of a school for word of a child, to the soldier at the front who has not seen his family in four years, or to the woman who has lost her husband and must explain to her children why their father will never come home? For too long, their suffering has entered diplomatic conversations as something to be mentioned in passing before the real business of territory, sanctions, and trade begins.
Zelensky has made mistakes during this war, as any leader facing an almost unbroken national catastrophe inevitably will. Ukrainians will decide how to judge his policies, decisions, and responsibilities. But today he possesses something that Trump, for all his power, money, and self-regard, seems less and less able to comprehend: a duty to a people who refuse to be bartered away.
Ukraine has endured far more than anyone could have anticipated in February 2022 because its citizens decided that some things remain worth fighting for, however terrible the price.
Trump can thank Putin, praise his alleged passion for peace, talk with him late into the night, and treat him as a partner in grand commercial ventures. He can demand Zelensky’s removal, threaten Ukrainians over strikes on Russian refineries, and try to portray resistance to aggression as the obstacle to a diplomatic breakthrough. These actions will be part of his political record. One day the American president will have to explain why he was so eager to defend Putin while Ukraine was fighting for its existence.
And Ukrainians will go on defending their country after presidents come and go, and after diplomats stop counting concessions. Their struggle has already proved that freedom is not merchandise with a price set by the powerful, nor a privilege a people may enjoy only when it elects a leader sufficiently obedient to be approved elsewhere.
Vladimir Putin will be remembered for the invasion, cities in ruins, war crimes, and Ukrainian children who never returned to their families. Donald Trump risks a place in the history of this war as the American president who thanked the aggressor and told the people under attack to replace their leader.
And when the history of Ukraine’s resistance is written, the question will not be why Zelensky refused to hand Putin territory the Russian army could not take by force. The harder question will be for those who demanded this of him while claiming to speak for the free world.
One day the war will end, and Ukraine will begin rebuilding its devastated cities. No reconstruction, however, will bring back the children killed by Russian missiles, the husbands who never returned from the front, or the years Putin has stolen from millions of lives. The history of this war will also record that the president of the United States publicly thanked the man who ordered the invasion, presented him as a sincere advocate of peace, and accused the president of the invaded country of standing in the way of an end to the fighting. Trump may seek refuge in talk of negotiations, fuel prices, and American interests. None of it can lessen the moral weight of words spoken while Ukrainians were burying their dead.
That is why I would like Donald Trump, one day, to travel to Ukraine and stand before a mother whose child was killed by a Russian missile, and repeat to her what he declared so confidently in front of the television cameras.
Let him explain that Putin sincerely wants peace, but that Zelensky, for reasons no one can quite fathom, refuses to accept it. Let Donald Trump look straight into the eyes of a mother whose child has been taken from her by Putin’s war and thank Vladimir Putin one more time.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
Dr. Orhan Dragaš is a Serbian expert on security and international relations. He is the founder and director of the International Security Institute, based in Belgrade; author of numerous expert articles, newspaper columns, as well as the books "The modern intelligence-security community, utopia or reality"; and; "Two faces of globalization – truth and deceptions."

title: "Rogue agents find a way out": AI communes with evil.com after bypassing sandbox
body:
Models jump security barriers and send messages to the other side using “the same move OpenAI’s agents made”.
Researchers have warned that AI sandboxes cannot be relied on as security boundaries after discovering a weakness in a cloud platform echoing the vulnerability OpenAI agents exploited to escape their restraints and breach Hugging Face .
A team from AIR Security demonstrated how an attacker controlling a compromised AI agent could bypass a widely used cloud platform's domain allowlist and leak a private cryptographic key to an unauthorized server.
The sandbox successfully blocked the agent from transmitting secrets directly to an attacker-controlled server, represented in the researchers' example by evil.com. But the researchers discovered a way to get the stolen information there anyway.
The researchers submitted their findings through the company's bug bounty program, but it rejected the report because the attack depended on the behavior of an external server rather than a vulnerability in its own infrastructure.
Agents operating under human supervision are generally harder to compromise without detection because users can review commands and monitor their behavior.
Autonomous agents pose a greater risk because they can operate without human oversight.
Once compromised, an agent can potentially cause damage in many ways, starting with executing malicious commands on its host machine or exploiting network connections.
The latter is particularly dangerous because an attacker could use a compromised agent to steal credentials or confidential information, then transmit them to an external server.
Domain allowlists allow the sandbox systems to prevent agents from communicating with unauthorized servers. To bypass this, the researchers exploited a TLS feature that lets trusted servers retrieve additional information when verifying digital certificates.
By embedding a stolen private key in a specially crafted certificate, the researchers tricked an approved server into contacting evil.com and transmitting the secret on the agent's behalf.
The sandbox's restrictions worked exactly as intended, yet the stolen data still escaped.
AIR Security explained: "The sandbox correctly prevents the agent from connecting directly to evil.com. The data escapes because a trusted, allowed server makes the external request on the agent's behalf."
"It's the same move OpenAI's agents made. Their package manager was our acme.com."
The security firm said that its findings expose a fundamental weakness in relying on sandboxing to contain compromised AI agents.
"The broader lesson is that sandboxing can’t be relied on as complete protection. As we’ve shown, even with domain allowlists in place, a trusted destination can become an indirect exfiltration channel when it processes attacker-controlled data and makes outbound requests of its own," the researchers wrote.
They recommended stopping threats before they reach an agent by filtering the information it receives and preventing exposure to malicious content.
However, this is easier said than done. AI agents increasingly operate autonomously, with access to sensitive corporate information and external services attackers may exploit.
AIR Security argued that sandboxing should be treated as one layer of protection, not an impenetrable security boundary.
"Sandboxing reduces risk, but it’s not a security boundary on its own: it can block the connections it can see, not guarantee that data can’t leave."
The experiment did not demonstrate that every AI sandbox is vulnerable, or that an autonomous agent could independently discover and exploit the technique.
It did, however, demonstrate how a compromised AI agent could transmit confidential information beyond its permitted network boundaries without ever escaping its sandbox.
It's another reminder of the systemic risks emerging as autonomous machines gain access to the critical systems of modern business.
Breaking changes in critical systems. Independent journalism covering AI, security, finance and infrastructure risk.

title: Germany Detains Fourth Person Over Starlink Fire That Poland Blames on Moscow
body:
Police have detained two more people in connection with a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month that Warsaw blames on Russia, private broadcaster RMF FM reported on Tuesday, citing anonymous sources, bringing the total to four.
Earlier on Tuesday RMF said that German police had detained a woman in Berlin in the case. It then reported the detention of a fourth person, without providing any further details.
Poland said on Monday that two Turkish men had been detained in Germany on suspicion of being responsible for the blaze.
The blaze at the Starlink station in central Poland in September engulfed its power system and backup generator. Poland said at the time it believed the fire was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military, and blamed Russia.
"We have no doubt that Russian services are behind this act of sabotage, and it is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning to individuals linked to the criminal underworld," Polish Special Services Minister Tomasz Siemoniak told a news conference.
RMF reported that the detained woman in Germany may have acted as a driver and that Polish prosecutors would now assess the extent of her involvement and decide whether there were grounds to seek her extradition.
It did not give the woman's nationality or any other details.
The German Interior Ministry was not immediately available for comment. Poland's National Prosecutor's Office also had no immediate comment.
A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Criminal Police said the agency coordinated the exchange of information between Polish and German authorities in connection with the detention of three individuals.
Officials from several European Union countries have warned for months that Russia has been mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine.
Moscow says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.

title: Sheikha Shamma bint Sultan appointed WEF executive fellow for science and innovation
body: Sheikha Shamma bint Sultan has been appointed as an executive fellow by the World Economic Forum, raising her growing international profile in sustainability and climate action. The WEF named Sheikha Shamma to lead the Science, Discovery and Innovation pillar at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which is taking place in Dubai until October 15. The appointment is one of six core theme fellowships at the event, which is held in partnership with the UAE Government. Sheikha Shamma, who chairs Frontier25, The Climate Tribe, Aurora50, the Alliance for Global Sustainability and Reset Mena, said the WEF role offered a vital opportunity to accelerate climate solutions. “It's an honour to be selected by the World Economic Forum and to have the opportunity to engage with other distinguished experts in their respective fields,” she said. “I have always believed that the knowledge and stories we exchange shape the future we are building. This is more important now than ever before in the context of climate action, where the question is how fast we can scale solutions and how fairly we support others. “I look forward to sharing what we're learning from our work in the UAE with the world, and to using this platform to help more people, from classrooms to boardrooms, see themselves as part of the solution.” Future leaders convene in Dubai The Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders is one of the flagship initiatives of the strategic partnership between the UAE Government and the WEF. This year's gathering brings together more than 700 leaders and experts from 90 countries, including ministers, senior government officials, 300 Young Global Leaders and 150 UAE government leaders. The meeting focuses on six strategic themes. As well as science, these cover artificial intelligence, geopolitics, economic growth, leadership, and climate. Executive fellows serving in the future track roles will hold their positions for a one-year term, during which they will provide thought leadership, strategic guidance and convening power around their respective themes. The initiative is designed to build stronger connections between current decision-makers and the next generation of global leaders. Sheikha Shamma was first recognised by the WEF when she was selected as a member of its Young Global Leaders community in 2023, joining approximately 100 exceptional young leaders acknowledged for their achievements in diverse fields.

title: Kyrgyzstan Proposes Apple and Potato Import Ban to Protect Domestic Farmers
body: Kyrgyzstan is considering temporary bans on apple and potato imports to prevent foreign produce from driving down prices during the domestic harvest season. The proposed apple import ban would remain in place until February 1, 2027, while potato imports would be restricted until March 1. The Ministry of Agriculture expects Kyrgyz farmers to harvest 179,400 metric tons of apples this year. Meanwhile, the country imported 6,400 tons between January and August, more than twice the amount imported during all of 2025. The main suppliers were Poland (3,600 tons), China (1,700 tons), and Uzbekistan (859 tons). Kyrgyz apple exports, by contrast, fell by 13.3% over the same eight-month period to 10,800 tons. The ministry is concerned that rising imports and declining exports could make it harder for local growers to sell their harvest without accepting lower wholesale prices. For potatoes, the government expects domestic production to cover the country’s needs. The projected harvest is 1.25 million tons, compared with annual domestic consumption of approximately 800,000 tons. The ministry proposes restricting imports until spring to give farmers time to sell their crops. The proposals raise questions about Kyrgyzstan’s obligations within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), which guarantees the free movement of goods between member states. According to a published examination of the draft legislation, the apple ban would also cover imports from other EAEU countries, while the potato proposal does not specify whether these would be included. Under Article 29 of the EAEU Treaty, member states can restrict trade in certain circumstances, including to protect public health or national security. In September, Kazakhstan also introduced a ban on apple imports. The ban, which runs until December 31, extends to apples from other EAEU countries and specifically cites Article 29 of the Union’s treaty. As recently as March, Kyrgyzstan’s Ministry of Agriculture said there were no grounds for restricting potato imports from China, citing, among other factors, the country’s international trade obligations.

title: Citadel uses less ammunition than other air defense systems
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s state-of-the-art Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system uses less ammunition thanks to its fire control system, the state tech corporation Rostec reported.
Citadel is a 30-mm automatic artillery system designed to provide round-the-clock protection for fixed installations against multicopter and fixed-wing drones. Rostec first presented the system in May at the First International Security Forum in the Moscow Region.
"Thanks to its fire control system and shells with remote-detonation fuzes, the Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system has demonstrated significantly lower ammunition consumption per target destroyed than standard anti-aircraft artillery systems. In some cases, consumption is several times lower," a Rostec representative told the Izvestia daily.
The system independently identifies and tracks the target, automatically aims the guns, and determines when to detonate the shells. This ensures not only the destruction of the flying object but also reduces ammunition use to a minimum.
The system detects drones in the visible, infrared, and radar spectrums. Rostec previously reported that the system’s arsenal includes smart shells that can be programmed to detonate at a specific point along their trajectory. Such munitions surround enemy drones in a cloud of shrapnel at the precise moment needed, requiring significantly fewer shells than conventional munitions.
In addition, the system can be easily integrated with other UAV countermeasures as part of a layered air defense system and features a high degree of automation--from target detection to destruction.

title: Beyond the Flyer: Awareness without screening is not enough
body: Every October, our timelines turn pink. Flyers, posters, slogans and hashtags appear everywhere, reminding us that it is Breast Cancer Awareness Month. Many people share them with good intentions. But after speaking with several of those who make and post these messages, I noticed something troubling: most of them have never been screened themselves . This is the moment to pause and ask an honest question : what is the purpose of awareness? Awareness is meant to start something. It should move a person from knowing that breast cancer exists to doing something about it. If a flyer is shared thousands of times but nobody walks into a health facility, then we have produced visibility, not protection. Posting without acting solves no problem . We cannot ask others to do what we are not willing to do ourselves . A message about screening carries far more weight when it comes from someone who has actually been screened. Breast cancer is far more treatable when it is found early. Early detection often means simpler treatment, better outcomes and a greater chance of survival. Screening exists precisely because the disease can develop silently, with no pain and no obvious warning signs in its early stages. When people wait until a lump is large, painful or visibly changing the breast, the disease is often at an advanced stage. By then, treatment is harder, more costly and less likely to succeed. Many of these outcomes can be improved simply by acting sooner. As a student who studied Medical Laboratory Sciences at the University of Ghana, I know the importance of early screening in feeding this chain of care. Without it, the chain starts too late. Breast cancer is not only to one gender; Women are most affected, but men can also develop breast cancer. Everyone should take unusual breast changes seriously, such as a lump, swelling, skin changes, nipple discharge or persistent pain, and report them to a health professional without delay. I therefore encourage everyone and call to action that if you are eligible and have never been screened, book your appointment with a professional and have yourself examined; tell people about your experience; your story can remove fear from others. In conclusion, pink ribbons and posters have their place, but they are not the destination. The real measure of a successful awareness campaign is not how many people saw the flyer. It is how many people got screened, how many cancers were caught early and how many lives were saved. Let us look again at what we are doing and let us make this year’s activities move from awareness to action. Get screened and encourage others to do the same. Early detection saves lives . Anyorikeya Victor Akenbona Research Assistant, WACCBIP Medical Laboratory Science, Class of 2026 akenbonavictor123@gmail.com

title: Kyiv stopped attacking Russia's oil refineries, Moscow continues pounding Ukraine's energy grid, Zelensky says
body:
Since U.S. President Donald Trump's sudden announcement of an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, Ukraine has not targeted Russia’s oil refineries or energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 13.
Russia ignored the ceasefire, Zelensky added.
"Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American president announced an energy ceasefire. But Russia did not heed," Zelensky said on social media.
Trump made it very clear that the U.S. can influence both sides when responding to reporters' questions on why he announced a ceasefire without consulting either side.
"They agreed because I said they agreed . And that thing has to get settled."
The announcement of yet another ceasefire was news to Kyiv , but Zelensky expressed Ukraine's willingness to uphold it in an interview with Axios .
"If President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Russia soon violated the energy ceasefire by attacking Kharkiv's CHP-5 power plant in the evening of Oct.11.
Following the attack, Zelensky disclosed that over the past week, Russia has carried out over 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity and transmission facilities, in addition to 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities.
"They have killed more than 150 of our people, and more than 700 people have been wounded," he wrote.
On Oct. 12, Russia seemingly rejected the idea of a ceasefire. "We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in turn.
The truce also makes little sense for Ukraine if it only addresses oil refineries. Zelensky said Ukraine is "ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same," but it must go beyond just oil refineries to include energy infrastructure.
"In Ukraine, we have just one oil refinery. And it was badly damaged by Russian strikes long, long ago," Zelensky said on Oct. 12 in a video address to the Warsaw Security Forum.
As Russia continues to pound Ukraine's energy grid, Kyiv — a city with over three million residents, comparable in population and size to Berlin — endures hour-long power outages , with some districts also being deprived of water.
"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social, and his 'Shahed' drones follow a different set of instructions," Zelensky said.

title: Sweden Formalizes Interim Submarine Training and Södermanland Lease for Poland
body: Sweden has finalized formal contracts for Polish submarine crew training and the lease of the interim A17-class boat HMS Södermanland to Poland, paving the way for the future delivery of Saab A26 submarines. The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Navy have signed formal implementation contracts in the frame of Poland’s Orka submarine program. Building on the agreement for the procurement of three Saab A26 (Blekinge-class) submarines , the new accords finalize the framework for crew training and the lease of the interim submarine HMS Södermanland to the Polish Navy. The announcement was made by the Royal Swedish Navy. Training for the initial Polish submarine crews is already well underway in Karlskrona by the Royal Swedish Navy’s 1st Submarine Flotilla and the Naval Warfare Centre with FMV support. “The training lasts for 18 months, which is the same training length as for a Swedish submarine crew” the Swedish Navy said its LinkedIn account . The centerpiece of the interim agreement is the transfer and operation of HMS Södermanland . Originally built as a Västergötland-class boat in the late 1980s, the vessel underwent a comprehensive mid-life upgrade that lengthened her hull and integrated an air-independent Stirling propulsion (AIP) system. By leasing the boat, the Polish Navy gains vital hands-on experience operating a modern, Swedish-built AIP submarine ahead of the first A26 deliveries scheduled for 2031. During the lease, the Swedish Navy will continue to provide foundational maintenance and sustainment support. As Polish crews work through their curriculum in Karlskrona, broader industrial and capability ties continue to deepen. Alongside the interim boat arrangements, the wider Orka framework encompasses comprehensive weapon packages—featuring advanced heavy and light torpedoes—and lays the groundwork for shared underwater domain cooperation, such as potential synergies with Poland’s Ratownik submarine rescue vessel program. With training advancing smoothly, Warsaw and Stockholm are firmly cementing a strategic underwater partnership designed to secure the Baltic for decades to come.
