title: 2027: INEC Launches QR Codes To Assist Voters Locate PVC Collection Centres In Lagos
body: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in Lagos has introduced QR codes to help eligible voters locate designated Permanent Voter Card (PVC) collection centres ahead of the 2027 general elections. The QR codes will be available for scanning across the Commission’s social media handles and website. Speaking at a press conference at the Commission’s headquarters in Lagos on Tuesday, the Resident Electoral Commissioner, Professor Ayobami Salami, urged voters to collect their cards, verify their registration details and rely on official information as INEC intensifies preparations for the polls. Beyond voter services, the Commission said preparations for the 2027 general elections are in top gear in Lagos State, with ongoing efforts to procure and test voter accreditation devices, improve election-result transmission systems, strengthen logistics, and recruit and train election personnel. In preparation for the poll, INEC had approved and issued a revised timetable and schedule of activities for the general election. The Commission had earlier fixed Saturday, 20th February 2027 for the Presidential and National Assembly Elections and Saturday, 6th March 2027 for the Governorship and State Houses of Assembly Elections pursuant to the Electoral Act, 2022. However, following the repeal of the Electoral Act, 2022 and the enactment of the Electoral Act, 2026, which introduced adjustments to statutory timelines governing pre-election and electoral activities, the Commission has now reviewed and realigned the schedule to ensure full compliance with the new legal framework. Accordingly, the Commission noted that the Presidential and National Assembly Elections will now be held on Saturday, 16th January 2027, while the Governorship and State Houses of Assembly Elections will be held on Saturday, 6th February 2027. The post 2027: INEC Launches QR Codes To Assist Voters Locate PVC Collection Centres In Lagos appeared first on Channels Television .

title: FIFA/ FIBA agency Pep Sports moves to admit Ghana’s 7-Foot Basketball talent to its Ultra-Modern Sports campus after MyJoyOnline report
body: What started as a community profile on MyJoyOnline.com has turned into a life-changing breakthrough for Ngleshie Amanfro’s tallest young basketball hopeful. Pep Sports Limited, a FIFA and FIBA-accredited Player Agency in Ghana, after a few hours of reading the publication, moved swiftly to officially express interest in building the basketball career of the young Ephraim Zinser Mac-Saawa, the 7-foot giant of Ngleshie Amanfro who dreams of winning an international trophy for Ghana. The company made contact just hours after MyJoyOnline published the story , which highlighted Mac-Saawa’s daily struggles, his training with Magic Basketball Academy at Tudu in Accra, and his audacious ambition to play for Ghana’s national team one day. According to the company, the story struck a chord with its management, which immediately saw the raw potential that needs to be groomed into a professional career. Following the swift intervention, Master Ephraim Zinser Mac-Saawa, together with his father, was invited to meet the Chairman of Pep Sports Limited, Dr Martin Ofori, at his office in Dzorwulu, Accra. Present at the meeting was Miss Lucille D. Amoako, a legal consultant to the company, who is expected to handle the legal formalities surrounding the youngster’s career development. Mr Amatus Mac-Saawa, speaking after the meeting, expressed sincere gratitude to MyJoyOnline for the community service it continues to render through spotlighting hidden talents in local communities. “ MyJoyOnline has done what many have not been able to do. We are grateful for bringing our son’s story to the world,” the father said. As part of the plan, Pep Sports Limited has outlined a clear roadmap to transform the lanky teenager from a street sensation into a professional prospect. After the planned initial registration and onboarding, Ephraim will be sent to the company’s state-of-the-art sports facility at Asamankese in the Eastern Region to undergo an intensive three-month training programme designed to groom him for his professional career, which could lead to an international contract. The programme will focus on comprehensive basketball fundamentals, strength and conditioning, footwork, shooting mechanics, defensive positioning, and game intelligence. Before full training commences, the player will be taken through the facility in the coming days to undergo mandatory fitness tests and thorough medical examinations to assess his physical readiness and tailor a specialised development plan for him. In a brief remark, Dr Ofori noted that Pep Sports Limited is known for its success in both football and basketball training prowess. It has a joint FIFA and FIBA accreditation as an agency and is expanding its scope to develop talents in other sporting disciplines, including boxing, Golf and Swimming, where Ghana has huge untapped potential. He explained that Mac-Saawa’s height, combined with his age, discipline, and hunger to learn, makes him a rare asset who, with the right guidance and exposure, could compete at the highest level. The development has sparked excitement in Ngleshie Amanfro, where residents who have watched Ephraim struggle for legroom in trotros and endure stares and photo requests now see him on the verge of a professional career. For Ephraim, who idolises NBA star Victor Wembanyama and currently juggles training with work at a printing press in Ngleshie Amanfro while preparing to study Computer Science, this could be the stepping stone to his twin dreams of playing professional basketball and becoming a software engineer. If all goes according to plan, the boy who once trained on borrowed courts because his school at Abakrampa SHS had no basketball facilities could soon be on his way to a professional contract abroad — carrying not just his own dream, but the hopes of Ngleshie Amanfro and Ghana basketball.

title: UN, IGAD warn hate speech could threaten South Sudan elections
body: As the December elections approach, the United Nations and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) have called on South Sudan to strengthen coordination and early response mechanisms to counter hate speech and disinformation, warning that harmful narratives could threaten peace, social cohesion and preparations for elections. The call was made on Tuesday during the launch of a three-day workshop to establish a national multi-agency coordination platform to address hate speech and disinformation in the country. Beleteze Foretia, representative of the United Nations Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Horn of Africa, said inflammatory rhetoric, rumors and deliberately misleading information could undermine trust between communities and contribute to political and security instability. “Countering hate speech and disinformation is, therefore, not simply about regulating information, but it is fundamentally about preventing conflict, protecting civilians, strengthening social cohesion and sustainable peace,” he said. “Political uncertainty, limited access to credible information and declining public trust can create conditions in which harmful narratives flourish, potentially undermining confidence in political and electoral processes.” “At the same time, efforts to counter hate speech and disinformation must safeguard freedom of expression, independent journalism and legitimate political participation,” Foretia added. He called for stronger cooperation among government institutions, independent media, civil society organizations, faith-based groups, traditional leaders, women, youth and academic institutions to address the problem. He said the proposed platform should prioritize early identification of harmful narratives, coordinated preventive action and stronger links with existing early warning and response mechanisms. Foretia added that cooperation with regional bodies, particularly the African Union and IGAD, would help improve information sharing, coordinated analysis and timely responses to emerging threats. Meanwhile, Victoria Anib Majur, IGAD Head of Mission for South Sudan and Social Development, said the changing information environment required stronger cooperation among national, regional and continental institutions. She said digital platforms had created new opportunities for communication and civic participation but had also increased the speed at which misinformation, disinformation and harmful narratives spread. “Their purpose is not to replace existing mandates, but to strengthen cooperation, information sharing and coordinated responses to emerging challenges,” Anib said, referring to the proposed national multi-agency coordination platform. She added that the initiative was part of IGAD’s broader commitment to conflict prevention and peacebuilding through effective early warning and early response mechanisms. Anib urged participants to use the three-day workshop to develop a shared understanding of the challenges, clarify responsibilities among stakeholders, strengthen the link between early warning and preventive action, and ensure national ownership and sustainability of the platform. The IGAD official said the initiative was timely as South Sudan advances its peace process, prepares for elections and pursues constitution-making and other peacebuilding efforts. The workshop is expected to examine South Sudan’s hate speech and disinformation landscape, review proposed governance arrangements for the platform and identify measures to strengthen coordination. Foretia said the success of the initiative would ultimately depend on its contribution to preventing violence, strengthening public trust and promoting a peaceful and cohesive society. Organized by the African Union and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the training brought together participants from various institutions, including representatives from the president’s office, foreign ministry, media, civil society and members of the faith-based groups, among others. title: How far can $1k take you when training an agentic LLM from scratch?
body:
Over the past three years, SWE-bench has served as a north star for the development of coding agents. With ever larger training budgets, frontier models now essentially solve the benchmark. 1 We instead ask: how far can we go with just $1000 of train compute?
Our starting point is Andrej Karpathy's nanochat . We add support for long-context training, and swap the train data for Qwen Coder trajectories from existing post-training datasets. 2 No train data comes from any of the SWE-bench codebases; they are strictly held out. We then train models from randomly initialized weights , with train compute ranging from $10 to $1000. Dollar figures throughout refer to train compute only. 3
Surprisingly, even the $10 model 4 achieves non-zero pass@1 (0.53%) 5 . Our $60 speedrun 6 achieves 5.0% pass@1 7 , matching Claude 2 (4.4%), the state of the art at SWE-bench's release. Solve rate continues to improve roughly log-linearly with train compute (Figure 1 ), reaching 11.0% at $1000 8 , landing between Claude 3 Haiku (7.2%) and Claude 3 Opus (15.8%). All from randomly initialized weights!
Is it fair to compare our speedruns against Claude 2 and Claude 3? No, for two reasons. First, our speedruns train on hundreds of thousands of bug-fixing trajectories, whereas the Claude models likely did not target SWE-bench as much. 9 Second, the Claude models use orders of magnitude more training compute than we do, with our $60 speedrun likely using 1000x fewer training FLOPs than Claude 2. 10 Thus, the comparisons are unfair along two dimensions: test-task training and scale [ 4 ] . That our tiny speedruns can compete with Claude 3 is striking, and speaks to the power of targeting specific capabilities at train time. 11
That power is precisely what we set out to study: how far can $1000 of train compute ultimately take us when aimed solely at SWE-bench?
In a speedrun, participants compete (or collaborate) to maximize performance within a fixed budget [ 6 – 9 ] . 12 Speedruns give researchers a shared experimental setup in which to compete, with the current record serving as a strong baseline. Because the training budget is fixed, simply out-scaling the competition isn’t an option; any advantage has to come from somewhere else.
Though training compute is capped at $1000, we deliberately impose no other budget constraints. This leaves several promising avenues for improvement. One is data, specifically, synthesizing trajectories that best elicit SWE-bench capability. Such synthesis should likely be student-aware [ 13 , 14 ] , since our student is maximally weak. Another axis of improvement is inference-time compute. Finally, we place no cap on experimentation itself: researchers can test as many ideas as they can afford. This makes autoresearch agents particularly compelling, as they can massively scale the experimentation loop.
We expect nanoswe to be a challenging setting for autoresearch. At $1000 per run, blindly trying ideas and keeping what sticks quickly becomes unaffordable. A successful agent must instead create faithful smaller-scale setups that support inexpensive iteration. This is substantially harder for SWE-bench than for perplexity-based environments. Scores on the Verified test set sit near zero. Worse, extrapolating solve rate from smaller-scale experiments is notoriously challenging. Data remains the most promising axis for improvement, but synthesizing tens of billions of tokens is itself too expensive to iterate on carelessly. These challenges make nanoswe a natural testbed for evaluating how efficiently autoresearch systems convert experimentation budget into performance gains.
Does SWE-bench speedrunning boil down to picking the strongest model available and simply distilling from it? Not necessarily. We show as much by swapping our teacher model, Qwen Coder 30B A3B (29% pass@1 13 ), for the much stronger Qwen 3.6 35B A3B (58% pass@1).
We use Qwen 3.6 to synthesize about 1.3B tokens, in identical fashion to our Qwen Coder pipeline. As expected, the new dataset contains a much greater share of correct trajectories: 49%, versus 22% for our Qwen Coder dataset. We then re-train the 12 B200-hour speedrun, replacing mini-coder-trajs with the newly generated Qwen 3.6 dataset. 14 Performance drops sharply, from 5.0% to 2.1% pass@1 (Figure 2 ). We speculate that performance drops due to Qwen 3.6's more complex solve strategies, which weaker students find much harder to reproduce.
Qwen Coder tends to apply a patch without writing any tests. In contrast, Qwen 3.6's typical workflow is to create test files that reproduce the issue before applying a patch. Trained on Qwen 3.6's trajectories, our speedrun model attempts to write long test files and inevitably makes mistakes. Stuck in this test-reproduction phase, it often never reaches the patching stage. The effect is stark. The student distilled from Qwen 3.6 fails to produce any patch in 74% of its attempts, compared to just 8% for the student distilled from Qwen Coder. 15
While training data is a key axis for improving the speedrun, better data will likely require more ingenuity than simply distilling from stronger teachers.
Our speedruns target a particular class of task: given a codebase and an issue description, produce a relatively small, self-contained fix. We refer to these as “SWE-bench-like” problems. To probe generalization beyond Verified, we construct four additional test sets by taking the outer product of two dimensions: bug source (LM-introduced synthetic bugs or issues derived from recent GitHub pull requests) and codebase (SWE-bench codebases or other codebases).
We obtain synthetic instances by prompting Opus 4.8 to inject a relatively small, self-contained bug into the target codebase. 16 Pull-request instances are derived from merged GitHub pull requests, restricted to those created in 2026—well after the release of our teacher model (July 2025). 17 The two bug sources have complementary strengths: synthetic bugs do not appear anywhere on the internet, but are inherently artificial; pull-request bugs are more realistic, but are publicly available on GitHub.
For the “other codebases” sets, we source 28 repositories from GitHub, roughly matching the star distribution of the SWE-bench repositories (median ≈15k stars). 18 19 Both SWE-bench and the “other” codebases are strictly held out from training: our speedruns never train on either set.
We evaluate our speedruns on each of the four test sets (Figure 3 ). Across all four, we observe similar trends: our smallest speedrun solves almost none of the problems, while increasing the training budget yields monotonic improvements that are roughly log-linear in training compute. Performance is not directly comparable across test sets, however, since they are not difficulty-matched. 20 On the natural pull-request-derived problems, our $1000 speedrun achieves solve rates in the same ballpark as on SWE-bench Verified, at around 10%.
The surprising effectiveness of speedrunning thus extends well beyond SWE-bench Verified: our speedruns solve synthetic bugs that exist nowhere on the internet, bugs derived from real pull requests created after our teacher model’s knowledge cutoff, and bugs in codebases outside SWE-bench.
We now ask whether we can elicit from our speedruns other capabilities beyond software issue fixing. We consider three benchmarks: MMLU [ 15 ] for world knowledge, GSM8K [ 16 ] for mathematical reasoning, and HumanEval [ 17 ] for non-agentic code generation. We use nanochat's evaluation harness throughout.
To elicit these capabilities, we curate a small fine-tuning dataset totaling 270M tokens 21 . As a baseline, we repeat our speedrun scaling sweep but swapping the train data to FineWeb-Edu [ 21 ] , a high-quality web corpus.
Before fine-tuning, we compare the speedrun and web models on DCLM CORE [ 9 ] , a suite of 22 pre-training benchmarks (Figure 4 , left). The web models improve with training compute, whereas the speedruns do not. We then SFT every model on our elicitation dataset and evaluate them on MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval (remaining panels of Figure 4 ). For each model, we use five different data seeds and report the resulting inter-run variation.
On both MMLU and GSM8K, the web models improve monotonically with training compute, whereas the speedrun models do not. The MMLU result is expected: models cannot recall facts they never saw. The GSM8K result is much more surprising: GSM8K benefits from multi-step reasoning, which is abundant in our training trajectories. HumanEval (code generation) is the only benchmark of the three where the speedrun models improve with training compute. Even there, however, the web model catches up to the speedrun at our largest compute budget.
Thus, our speedruns seem to buy coding performance, and little else. Conversely, little else appears necessary to reach a 10% SWE-bench solve rate.
Training exclusively on agentic trajectories could bias which problems our speedruns can solve. Intuitively, some problems may be very hard without the latent knowledge of web pre-training (e.g., the documentation, StackExchange discussions, and issue threads of the SWE-bench libraries themselves). This matters especially for RL post-training: if the speedruns' problem coverage is fundamentally limited, they make for worse base models for RL.
To determine whether such blind spots exist, we compare our nanoswe speedruns against fine-tunes of SmolLM3 3B, a model comparable in size to our speedruns but pre-trained on over 10T tokens. We take checkpoints from across SmolLM3 pre-training and fine-tune each on a subset of the Qwen Coder trajectories used for our speedruns. We fine-tune a total of 69 SmolLM3 fine-tunes, which we compare against 21 speedrun models. 22 We evaluate each model on SWE-bench Verified with up to k =90 attempts per problem, so that even problems a model solves only occasionally register in our coverage estimates.
We thus have two cohorts of models: those trained from scratch on Qwen Coder trajectories, and those first pre-trained on the web and then fine-tuned on Qwen Coder trajectories. We ask whether these two cohorts, A and B , agree on which SWE-bench problems are easy. 23 To answer this, we borrow a standard methodology from psychometrics: differential item functioning [ 22 ] (DIF). We fit a single Rasch model with DIF to all outcomes,
where p i j is the probability that model i solves problem j on a single attempt, θ i is the ability of model i , z j the easiness of problem j , and c i indicates membership in cohort A . Our object of study is z j diff : how much easier problem j is for cohort A than for cohort B , at matched model ability. 24 We estimate and plot the distribution over z diff , with each problem contributing one unit of probability mass, spread according to its own measurement uncertainty. 25
Since z diff is measured in logits, a shift of Δ multiplies a cohort's odds of solving the problem by e Δ . A shift of 2 is thus a e 2 ≈ 7 x change in those odds. 26 This is the scale at which we take the two cohorts to genuinely disagree about a problem's difficulty 27 , and we mark ± 2 on each panel.
Figure 5 left shows the distribution of difficulty differences z diff between the speedruns and the SmolLM3 fine-tunes. The two overwhelmingly agree: the distribution is unimodal, with most of its mass close to 0. That is, we observe little detectable reranking among the measurable SWE-bench items: web pre-training barely changes which problems are easy and which are hard. The exception is a small negative tail: whatever latent knowledge web pre-training supplies seems to surface in at most a handful of problems.
In our setting, skipping web pre-training leaves no detectable blind spots among the problems within either cohort's reach: at matched ability (i.e., pass@1), the speedruns solve essentially the same problems as the SmolLM3 fine-tunes.
We speedrun SWE-bench Verified by training from scratch on agentic trajectories. Speedrunning is strikingly effective: our $60 run achieves 5.0% pass@1, matching Claude 2, the SOTA at SWE-bench's release. With $1000 of train compute, our speedrun reaches 11.0% pass@1, outperforming Claude 3 Haiku (7.2%).
Our speedruns demonstrate genuine issue-fixing ability: they solve both synthetic bugs that never appeared on the internet and natural issues derived from recent GitHub pull requests. 28 At matched model ability, and among the problems either cohort can solve, our speedruns and models pre-trained on 10T web tokens and then specialized agree closely on which problems are hard. The catch is that our speedruns can do little beyond code. Even when we explicitly fine-tune them to elicit MMLU and GSM8K performance, accuracy on these benchmarks does not improve with additional speedrun compute.
We release nanoswe as a community speedrun project, forked from nanochat. Beyond adhering to the prescribed training budget, the only rule is not to train on the SWE-bench repositories. We are especially keen to see how well autoresearch systems fare: without carefully designed experimentation strategies, such systems could easily burn through compute with little to show for it.

title: Attacks: Catholic Church shuts schools, hospitals in Benue community
body: By Peter Duru, Makurdi The Catholic Diocese of Gboko, Benue State, has ordered the suspension of church institutions, including schools and hospitals, in Ihugh, Vandeikya Local Government Area, LGA, over repeated attacks, arson, burglary and alleged harassment of its personnel. The affected institutions are St Winifred Secondary School, St Winifred Nursery and Primary School, St Thomas Hospital, including Salus Mind Care Center and its chaplaincy, and St Winifred Parish. The Diocese also ordered the withdrawal of priests, Reverend Sisters, teachers, medical personnel and other workers from the institutions, effective October 12, 2026, until further notice. Ihugh is the hometown of Governor Hyacinth Alia. The decision was contained in a pastoral letter and decree signed by the Bishop, Most Rev. William Avenya, and the Diocesan Chancellor, Rev. Fr. Marcellinus Wende. The Diocese said the decision followed repeated attacks, including the burning of St Winifred Secondary School students’ hostels on October 28, 2025; May 10; May 15; and October 11, 2026. In the letter, it stated: “Over a considerable period, the Catholic institutions in Ihugh have suffered repeated disturbances, attacks and acts of destruction. “Among these were the recent burning down of the students’ hostels of St Winifred Secondary School, Hugh, on October 28th, 2025; May 10th, 2026; May 15th, 2026; and October 11th, 2026, acts that have destroyed the shelter of young people entrusted to our care, wiped out the labour and sacrifices of many years, and placed the lives and safety of students, teachers, and staff in grave danger.” It also cited persistent burglaries at St Winifred Parish and criminal incidents at St Thomas Hospital. The Diocese recalled that during the hospital’s reopening on June 21, 2024, some residents allegedly displayed placards and chanted slogans demanding the withdrawal of the Reverend Sisters. “The persistent burning down of St Winifred Secondary School students’ hostels was not an isolated event. The consistent burglary issues in St Winifred Parish, Ihugh, the repeated criminal incidents at St Thomas Hospital, Ihugh, and the hooliganism witnessed during the time of the reopening of St Thomas’ Hospital, Ihugh, on 21st June, 2024, wherein the people of Ihugh openly projected placards and chanting slogans that ‘They no longer want the Reverend Sisters to work in Ihugh’,” the letter stated. It described the incidents as “a systemic pattern of hostility and destruction directed at church-owned properties, alongside arson and harassment.” Each incident has left behind fear, loss and uncertainty among those who serve and are served by the Church.” Lamenting that its institutions, established to serve the public, had repeatedly been targeted, it said, “The Church exists to bring life. Our schools, hospital and parish in Ihugh were established for the good of all, irrespective of creed or origin. It is therefore a source of profound grief that works meant for the common good have repeatedly become targets.” The Diocese said it had engaged the host community, traditional rulers, elders and security authorities in efforts to resolve the crisis. “The Church does not take the path of withdrawal lightly, nor in haste. The Lord instructs us to be peacemakers, and we have laboured to be so. At every stage we sought dialogue rather than confrontation and reconciliation rather than recrimination. “The Diocese has met with the host community, engaged the traditional rulers and elders of the land, and brought these grievances before the relevant civil and security authorities, all in the hope of finding a just and lasting peace. “We have listened, we have appealed, and we have waited patiently. Sadly, these sincere efforts have not yielded the peace, security and guarantees that the continued presence of our institutions requires.” Explaining the closure, the Diocese declared, “The Church is a partner in development, not a victim to be repeatedly wounded. A partnership requires mutual respect, protection and good faith. When the very institutions that serve a community are burnt and their workers threatened, such a partnership cannot be sustained. “The Church cannot, in conscience, continue to expose her priests, consecrated persons, teachers, medical personnel, students and patients to danger, nor continue to invest the resources of God’s people where they are not safe and are not valued.” The Diocese stressed that the decision was not motivated by vengeance, saying, “We do so not in anger, nor in bitterness, nor in vengeance, but in sorrow, with prayer, and with the door of reconciliation left open.” The Diocese directed the withdrawal of all pastoral and other personnel from the institutions and warned that nobody could resume duties in its name in Ihugh without the Bishop’s written authorisation. It said students would be assisted to continue their education in other Catholic schools, while patients at St Thomas Hospital would be referred to other health facilities. Expressing appreciation to its workers, the Diocese stated, “We express our deepest gratitude to our priests, consecrated persons, teachers, nurses, doctors, catechists and staff who have served in Ihugh with courage and fidelity, often at great personal cost. You have been faithful servants, and the Lord who sees in secret will reward you.” While assuring employees affected by the decision, the Diocese said, “staff affected by this decision will be treated with justice and charity, in accordance with Church teaching on the dignity of labour.” It appealed to community leaders, traditional rulers, youths and government authorities to restore peace, stressing that it did not blame innocent residents. “To the entire people of Ihugh, to its leaders and to its youth, we make no accusation against the innocent, and we hold no hatred in our hearts. We bear no ill will toward our brothers and sisters, many of whom have known only the good that these institutions brought,” it stated. However, it condemned the attacks, saying, “We say plainly that violence, arson and destruction are contrary to the Gospel, contrary to the dignity of the human person, and contrary to the good of the community itself. They impoverish the very people they claim to defend, depriving children of education, the sick of healing, and the faithful of worship.” It urged security agencies and governments at all levels to protect lives and property and prosecute those responsible. Declaring that the closure was not a final departure, the Diocese said, “This decision is a painful one, but it is not a final farewell. The Church leaves in sorrow, not in contempt.” It said it would consider returning if there was “genuine repentance, restitution, a firm commitment to peace, and credible lasting assurances of safety” for its personnel and property. The Diocese also declared Friday, October 23, 2026, a day of prayer and fasting for reconciliation. “We invite all the faithful of the Diocese to a season of earnest prayer and penance for the restoration of peace in Ihugh and in all our communities,” the letter stated. Contacted Bishop Avenya, who confirmed the resolve of the Diocese, saying, “It is the suspension of activities over the things that happened.” The post Attacks: Catholic Church shuts schools, hospitals in Benue community appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: GAUA strike disrupts academic plans at University of Ghana as students, parents express frustration
body: The ongoing strike by the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) is disrupting academic activities at the University of Ghana, with students and parents expressing frustration over the uncertainty surrounding the start of the new academic year. The university has postponed the reopening date for fresh students, leaving prospective students and their families uncertain about when academic activities will officially begin. Some students who spoke to Joy News on October 12 said the industrial action has disrupted their plans for the academic year, leaving them uncertain about when normal academic activities will resume. For fresh students, the postponement has created additional uncertainty as they wait to begin their university education. Continuing students are also concerned about the possible implications of the industrial action for academic activities and the university’s schedule. Parents have also expressed frustration over the situation, particularly those who have already made financial and logistical arrangements for their wards to begin school. They are calling on the government to urgently intervene and engage the relevant stakeholders to resolve the dispute and restore normal operations at the university. The disruption comes at a critical time for students preparing to begin or continue their academic journey, with the uncertainty adding to the pressure on families who have invested in their wards’ education.

title: 18th Headies Awards postponed to April 2027 in Toronto
body: Organisers of The Headies Awards have postponed the 18th edition of the ceremony to April 10 and 11, 2027, in Toronto, Canada. The event was initially scheduled to be held on October 23, 2026, before the organisers announced the revised dates in a statement published on their official Instagram page. According to the organisers, the change is intended to create more opportunities for engagement across the music and creative industries. They added that activities under the “Road to the Headies” initiative would continue during the period originally scheduled for the main ceremony. The initiative is expected to feature workshops, seminars and other industry engagements ahead of the awards ceremony. The organisers also apologised to guests who had already made travel plans and other arrangements for the October event, acknowledging the inconvenience caused by the rescheduling. The Headies is one of Nigeria’s major music awards platforms, recognising outstanding achievements in the Nigerian music industry and celebrating artists and other professionals in the entertainment sector. The 18th edition will now take place in Toronto over two days in April 2027. The post 18th Headies Awards postponed to April 2027 in Toronto appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Robotic freight transportation prices to lose 8% by 2035 — Russian Transport Ministry
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The cost of driverless freight carriage will drop by 85 by 2035, the Russian Ministry of Transport said.
About 100 driverless trucks are already operating on the M-12 East highway in the Moscow Region, the ministry noted. "The freight transportation cost will be lowered by 8% at the least by 2035; savings for shippers will be 108 bln rubles ($1.3 bln)," it added.
The driverless truck fleet may amount to dozens of thousands of units by 2035, making it possible to make up to 25% of country’s logistics robotic, Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said earlier.

title: EBRD increases guarantee fund for insuring Ukraine's war risks to EUR 150 million
body:
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Aon, a leading global professional services firm, are expanding the size and capabilities of the Ukraine Recovery and Reconstruction Guarantee Fund (URGF) for war risk insurance from EUR 110 million to EUR 150 million.
"As the existing capacity of EUR 110 million is now fully used by Ukrainian insurers and their clients, the bank is increasing the scheme to EUR 150 million so that more companies in Ukraine can obtain war risk insurance and address the current problems caused by the war," the EBRD said on its website.
It is noted that the scope of such insurance has also been broadened. The coverage will now also include transportation and storage of gas-related assets, as well as goods temporarily stored in warehouses, in addition to domestic cargo, damage to vehicles and railway rolling stock, which are already covered by the existing scheme.
The additional capacity is backed by donor coverage from the European Union under its Ukraine Investment Framework. This will allow insurance companies INGO, Colonnade and UNIQA, as well as two new Ukrainian insurers, USG (owned by Vienna Insurance Group) and Universalna (owned by Fairfax Financial Group, Canada), to offer more war risk coverage.
Through the URGF, which is managed by Aon, the EBRD guarantees to global reinsurer MS Amlin coverage of losses from war-related risks that are reinsured from participating Ukrainian insurers.
"The initial guarantee of EUR 110 million, backed by donor coverage from France, Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the TaiwanBusiness-EBRD Technical Cooperation Fund, remains fully in force and supports reinsurance coverage of more than EUR 500 million for goods and vehicles under almost 10,000 policies. Premiums received under these policies currently exceed the amount of insured events, and MS Amlin has not had to call on the EBRD guarantee, which shows that the war risk insurance and reinsurance markets in Ukraine can operate commercially," the EBRD said.
It is also reported that the URGF expansion comes amid intensified Russian attacks on energy, transport, logistics and civilian infrastructure, as well as the renewed blockade of Black Sea ports.
The EBRD is Ukraine's largest institutional investor. The bank has significantly increased its investment in the country since Russia's full-scale invasion, placing EUR 11 billion there since 2022, including a record EUR 2.9 billion in 2025.

title: UAE food aid reaches Gaza through Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge
body: Food aid from the UAE has entered the Gaza Strip through the Rafah crossing under a plan to deliver more than 10 million meals to Gazans in need. The delivery was made as part of the Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge initiative, named after Sheikh Ahmed, brother of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, who died on September 21. The initiative was launched to recognise Sheikh Ahmed's generosity and philanthropic work. The aid was transported from Al Maktoum International Airport to the Gallant Knight 3 team, operating from the UAE Humanitarian Aid Logistics Centre in the Egyptian city of Al Arish. The team prepared, loaded and transported the supplies to the Rafah crossing before they were moved into Gaza. The operation is part of broader, sustained efforts to support Palestinian civilians and alleviate the humanitarian crisis in the territory. The 10 million-meal target reflects the scale of need and the UAE's continued commitment to addressing it through organised, large-scale relief operations. Continuing relief The Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge is one of several continuing UAE-led initiatives directly assisting Gaza residents. Since the launch of Operation Gallant Knight 3, the UAE has provided more than $4 billion in humanitarian assistance to Gaza, accounting for 46 per cent of global humanitarian aid directed to the enclave since 2023. That assistance has included 130,708 tonnes of relief, medical and food supplies delivered by 796 aircraft, 25 ships and 14,483 lorries. By channelling aid through established logistics networks and co-ordinating with Egyptian authorities at the Rafah crossing, the operation aims to ensure supplies reach those most in need in a structured and efficient manner. Meanwhile, Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, the region's largest humanitarian and community development foundation, recorded expenditure of more than Dh2.3 billion in 2025, positively impacting approximately 165 million beneficiaries across 122 countries. Its humanitarian aid and relief programmes alone exceeded Dh625 million in expenditure, benefiting more than 53 million people worldwide.

title: Rada summons Kyiv Mayor Klitschko on Wednesday to report on affairs in city
body:
The Verkhovna Rada has supported summoning Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.

According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, the proposal was submitted by Mariana Bezuhla. It was backed by 151 MPs at Tuesday's session, with eight voting against.

An earlier attempt to summon the Kyiv mayor was proposed by Bezuhla on Monday, but it did not gather the necessary number of votes. She then proposed summoning him for 12:00 on Tuesday, October 13.

When calling for Klitschko to be summoned, the MP did not name a specific time or date.

However, First Deputy Speaker Oleksandr Kornienko later clarified that Klitschko has been summoned for 12:00 on October 14.

title: Lotus Improv on the NeXT
body:
"Cult classic" isn't a term typically applied to software, but if it were, this would be its poster child.
It is spoken of in reverent tones, invoked like a magic spell, whispered about as one of the mythical "roads not taken" in computing history. Its proponents write glowing reports and fawning YouTube reviews, lamenting its failure in the historical marketplace, each offering some justification for it not having set the world ablaze. It is safe to say, the legend of Lotus Improv persists to this day.
If we put ourselves in Steve Jobs's shoes circa 1988, it's easy to see why he would have been smitten by an early preview of what we now call a "pivot table." NeXT was struggling to find its market, and exclusives which justified a system purchase were sorely needed. "Maybe Improv can do for NeXT what VisiCalc did for the Apple II," must surely have crossed Jobs's mind. In making it a NeXT exclusive, Improv seemed to be a clear-eyed, forward-looking answer to the question dogging the company, posed by the inaugural issue of NeXTWORLD Magazine , "Why NeXT?"
Both NeXT and Improv brought innovative solutions to their respective computing questions of the day. NeXT made UNIX palatable to those scared of the terminal, debuted Display Postscript on a mega-pixel display, and made development for the system a snap. Improv rethought multi-dimensional data modeling, offered English-like formulas, and made it easy to rearrange data views on a whim.
The bones of both remain to this day. NeXT's operating system, NeXTSTEP / OPENSTEP, morphed into macOS, and by extension iOS. Lotus abandoned Improv fairly quickly, but a quick survey of today's spreadsheets shows a universal embrace of pivot tables.
Even today, it feels like nothing else, and still does data tricks no other spreadsheet can do as elegantly. Given its mythos, I feel a kind of nerd obligation to love it.
Events have converged to make this the right time to finally talk about Lotus Improv . First, it is time once again for "International Spreadsheet Day." Second, as Improv was initially a NeXT exclusive, it seems only appropriate to take a look at that machine here on the 15th (!) anniversary of the passing of Steve Jobs. Third, and not to toot my own horn too loudly, it is the 1st anniversary of this very blog.
Lotus Improv was one of four pieces of software I had in mind when deciding to start Stone Tools. In fact, it was quite literally the software that first triggered the thought, "I wish I had a place to talk about stuff like this." Deluxe Paint , the first post, was also one of those four. There are two yet to go; place your bets.
The trouble was, while I knew Deluxe Paint intimately and could jump right in, I simply had no real experience with other categories of productivity software. It would have been impossible to judge Improv fairly without first getting better acquainted with the landscape into which it was born. So, I bided my time.
Boy, howdy, do I want to impress upon you the superhuman restraint I've exhibited in waiting a full year to examine Improv .
I think we all understand Improv, being a spreadsheet , knows how to calculate sums and transcendentals and other mathematical goodness. "It does math!" is not a particularly compelling justification for its existence, nor to support its claim as the "NeXT generation of spreadsheets." Instead, let's get to know it by studying examples which show off its unique strengths, and with the suggestion of the book Improv 2.1 Revealed! we'll model up some good ole' American baseball, a game I love and understand completely.
Industry historians are far more capable of discussing the exile and homecoming of one Mr. Steven Paul Jobs back to Apple. I touched on the TL;DR of it in the timeline, and if you're really clamoring for juicy tidbits, a book was published this very year that delivers on that front.
While NeXT hardware was well regarded, it never really caught on. In the long run, the better result of NeXT engineering was NeXTSTEP and how neatly it wrapped UNIX in a clean, user-friendly, graphical interface. It's quite an accomplishment.
For me, it was the technology behind NeXTSTEP/OPENSTEP developer tools, Objective-C and Interface Builder, that kickstarted my programming career when those became the OS X development environment (hat tip to Aaron Hillegass's Cocoa Bootcamp at the Big Nerd Ranch). Even today, years after the advent of iOS and Swift, NeXT technology remains in the Foundation layer of Apple software, as denoted by NS -prefixed classes (a name-spacing trick from the Objective-C days).
For this investigation, I'm using NeXTSTEP 3.3, the last version before transitioning to OPENSTEP. NeXTSTEP looks and feels like a modern system, with some choice differences. Familiarity with any modern operating system, especially macOS, will inoculate you from breaking out into hives using it.
Considering the eye-candy Jobs seemed excited to add to OS X after the Apple merger, NeXTSTEP is positively staid; nothing here screams " lickable ." If you've ever wondered what Susan Kare could have achieved if she'd had a larger canvas and palette (NeXTSTEP is 2-bit) than the original Mac, look no further. I like it.
The dock is present, though more rigid than the playful fluidity it acquired when transitioning to OS X. No "genie effects" nor dynamic magnification; it is ever-present and doesn't hide itself when not in use. Some applications change the dock icon when running (like Mail ), while other applications do not (like Edit ). One odd quirk is how the dock indicates running apps, by the absence of three dots on an icon tile. That's a strange choice, decorating the inactive icons.
File browsing adds a little complexity to system usage. The file browser contains its own mini-dock for favorites, the path to the currently selected item rendered as giant icons, and the file browser proper. Dragging files and folders around can only be done with an item's full-size icon. If you're browsing in list view, you can't drag list items into a folder or the dock, for example. Bit of a head-scratcher, that one.
Menuing for all applications is handled via a user-positionable, vertical menu. Sticking the menu somewhere sets its position for the active application, and every application can have its own position. You could theoretically have the menu jumping around all over the place as you hop between apps. Thankfully, it can also be called up at the current mouse position with a right-click; shades of RISC OS.
Also, good news for those who love the spinning beach ball on macOS! You'll feel that little ASMR tingle when it appears, especially if you run a color workstation. It's funny the things that can make something feel like "home."
Honestly, my biggest issue in adjusting to NeXTSTEP is the mouse. By default, it feels weird to use, with a dual-level acceleration curve, one for slow movement, one for fast. Crossing the threshold between "slow" and "fast" jumps the cursor across the screen when the alternate acceleration curve kicks in. I could never find my cursor except when moving the mouse verrrryyyy slooowwllllyyyy. Luckily, the emulator Previous has tools to help compensate ( check "Sharpening the Stone" ).
Overall, you'll only need to adjust your thinking a little here and there, forget some modern habits, and you should be comfortable with NeXTSTEP in short order. 35 years later, it still looks and feels much like any modern operating system.
Almost depressingly so? Maybe that's a topic for another day.
Question: what is interesting about the following screenshot from Improv ?
Answer: it contains all information necessary to build a copy for yourself. All data, formulas, dimensions, and relationships are exposed and visible. I note this not to suggest that screenshots are a great way to share Improv worksheets with others, though you could; the sheet above was rebuilt from a screenshot, in fact. Rather, I want to illustrate how "graspable" data can be in Improv's environment. Its formulas read naturally, and value references match the item names in the table. The work does what it claims.
Let's interrogate that a little more thoroughly.
To understand Improv is to forget what we know about spreadsheets. Slash commands? Never heard of him. B1? J93? K12 = int(A14 * lookup(B2..B7))? The ramblings of a madman. Rather than generic alphanumeric column/row identifiers, we define our rows and columns with "categories of items" specific to our domain.
Put another way, instead of asserting, "Columns A to L represent the months, and rows 1 through 31 represent the days," we will create a category called "months" and define twelve items for it named "January," "February," etc. and we will create a category called "days" and define 31 of those.
Take a look at these comparative videos which illustrate the difference. First, I'll use LibreOffice Calc to create a months/days grid, apply a value to January 1, and calculate December 31 as a multiple of January 1.
Here's how that same table is created in Improv . There are three things to note: how sequential items are generated, how categories are named (not strictly necessary for this simple example), and how formulas are created/applied.
There's a lot to absorb, I know, starting with how a new, blank worksheet consists of a single cell, not an infinite table of empty cells. Improv works with only and precisely the data we define. Where in the LibreOffice example we attached meaning to the columns by adding labels to the top of each column, that was for our benefit not Calc's .
I could, just to feel the warm, snuggly blanket of classic column/row naming, make an Improv category called "columns" and name my items A, B, C, etc. and a category called rows, with names 1, 2, 3, etc. Were we to take such a pedestrian approach to categories and items, we would diminish the magic of Improv's formula builder.
The bottom panel holds all formulas, which are applied at the granularity defined, in the order shown. In the example, I specified December:1 = but could just as easily have targeted all of December by specifying December = . That single formula would apply to every list item in December without needing to copy formulas through to each cell, nor set absolute/relative markers for cell references.
Here's a simple expansion of the previous table. Every day in January increases by 10%, and its corresponding day in December doubles the January value.
The two formulas shown are the only two formulas for the entire worksheet. I want to stress this; there are no other formulas lurking inside cells, hidden from view, waiting to be revealed by a selection or editing process. There are no duplicated formulas per cell, each increasing a relative cell reference by * 1.1 . We simply refer to categories (in this case "months" or "days"), items (as "January" or "27"), or specific intersections (as "April:19"), including relativity signifiers [THIS] , [PREV] , and [NEXT] .
You might be thinking of ways to trick the system; to confuse and befuddle it. Why would you want to bully an old app like that? What did Improv do to deserve such shabby treatment? "What if two items have the same name? What if two formulas target the same cell?" Fret not, all shall be revealed and you will feel proper shame at trying to confuse this old program.
In the above example I have renamed one of the Days as "March," to create ambiguity when referencing "March." Does "March" mean the Day or the Month now? We can be explicit, referring to Months:March . Note though that if we aren't explicit, Improv will be on to our tricks and call us out, as in formula 5.
In formula 2, I set December:15 to the static value 1000 . In formula 3, I also set it to be calculated as "double its corresponding January value." Note the "overlap" icon (two intersecting squares) on those formulas and the Overlap text in the cell. Clicking the overlap icon gives us an opportunity to resolve ambiguity by explicitly selecting which formula should win for that cell.
Cleanly handling formula ambiguity was originally seen by the prototype team as an intractable engineering problem. From "Improv: The Inside Story", by Simson L. Garfinkel, NeXTWORLD , Fall 1991:
Personally, I like Improv's solution. I honestly think more software should be very dumb, and not try to intuit or guess what I want. Tell me the problem in clear language, and provide the simplest tool that gives me the most control over problem resolution. Be smart about helping me, don't try to help me by being smart.
Before we get in too deep, I want to make sure I note Improv's beautiful help system, replete with index and search. Considering the difficulty in tracking down a manual for the NeXT release , having this available during my exploration proved invaluable. It's neatly illustrated, with terse (sometimes overly terse) descriptions of the tools, hyperlinked to other pages of the documentation, as warranted. Improv felt it could do even better than that and made its help contextual .
The Help system, when invoked, defaults to displaying documentation for whatever is currently selected in the user interface. That's very useful, but becomes supercharged with "Point for Help," as demonstrated in the video above. This turns the cursor into a ? symbol, and whatever we click will be revealed in the Help window.
This is a great idea, because I don't always know what Lotus wants to call some little interface doohickey, so I don't know what to search for. Now I know: the "Calc" button is a "Status Indicator" and the triangle icon that sometimes shows up is the "Formula Error Indicator." Pork chop sandwiches.
Looking through Usenet archives, I saw this called "toilet paper" by at least one person. Lotus called it the "item dispenser." It's an interesting first attempt to do something we take for granted today and only exists in the NeXT version of Improv . It's cute, but smacks of someone being overly excited with new development toys.
If we need to generate a list of items to populate an axis of your data, this tool generates sequential list items for you. It does its best to kind of "guess" our intentions, so if we type in "Sunday," then pull down on the dispenser, days of the week will be auto-generated in a list. We then "tear off" the list, which loads the cursor with the items, which we attach to an existing item, appending that category with the loaded list items.
That means we need to have at least one item in a category onto which the list can be attached. This is annoying, because the existing item likely has no relationship to the generated list. I'm always having to make a list, attach it to an existing item, then delete the original, unrelated item. These days, we can type directly into a cell and extend that cell intelligently across adjacent cells. In fact, Lotus would switch to that methodology when migrating Improv over to Windows for version 2. Hold ALT and drag an existing item to get the same effect.
The original dispenser truly is a feature that could only have been thought up within the NeXT environment. I don't hold it against the devs for getting excited by the GUI flexibility Interface Builder afforded. I, too, did the same back in the early OS X 10.2 days. It practically begged us to play around with GUI ideas, remixing elements into new configurations. "First Responder" and "bindings" stans, represent!
One of the great features of that development environment was how easy it was to “say ‘No’ a thousand times” while trying ideas. Lotus embraced that, achieving quickly on NeXT what had blocked their progress on OS/2 and Microsoft's Presentation Manager.
The "item dispenser" was singled out as a specific tool that benefitted from Interface Builder; there really wasn't anything similar to its rapid, iterative, GUI development at the time. In fact, I might go so far as to say there's nothing quite like it today, even from Apple .
Joel Spolsky, in editing The Best Software Writing I , added a personal aside on Lotus Improv , blaming its failure thusly, " Improv required you to define strict n-dimensional hypercubes for your data. There was none of the flexibility of traditional spreadsheets."
I suppose if one wanted to paint Improv in the most inhospitable light, Spolsky is correct. In practice, it doesn't feel as impenetrable as his description. However, I do think he's on to something that gets at the heart of why Improv never gained traction.
For now, let's hold our collective nose and dive into the scary, foreboding waters of "n-dimensional hypercubes" and model up some baseball. Our first dimension will be Year .
Next, we'll get more granular and add Division . Internally, Improv separates our work into three parts: data, views, and formulas. What we see on screen is just Improv's best-effort to represent our three-dimensional data flattened out into a two-dimensional view. Improv adds extra columns to the view, as necessary, to ensure we always see the full extent of our data relationships.
Now, we'll add some win/loss data and the next thing you know we’ve built a 4-dimensional hypercube. Are we scared yet?
Since I've only modeled at the "Division" level, I'll add together divisional wins inline to calculate the totals and... hmmm... "No dice," as they say in baseball (Presumably. Are dice involved in baseball?)
Alas and alack, we can only enter concrete numbers, dates, or text into cells; any formula, no matter how trivial, must go into the Formula Panel (bottom). In this case, I could add a formula that targets a specific cell, as American:East:2020:Win = 40 + 33 + 32 + 25 + 24 , but the whole point of a spreadsheet is to automate that kind of junk for me. I suppose the path of least resistance is to add a Teams category to add up all team wins and, wait a second...
Dang it, that petard I confidently told myself wouldn't hoist me has come around to do precisely that. Here we see the downside of dimensional modeling, at least for the layperson, and arguably for most typical spreadsheet users. It all looks like a neat little chart, but that word "dimension" describes and reveals the problem. To add a category, its items necessarily apply to all other categories. Teams don't do that; they are unique to each League and Division.
Lotus engineers clearly understood that categories alone weren't going to cut it. Categories impose rigidity to our data that does not always accommodate the messiness of real data. We need another way to organize our data.
Groups are intra-category, named collections of sequential items. Make a category and add a bunch of individual items. Select a sequential group of some subset of items and group them, giving that group a unique name. Once everything is grouped, groups of groups can be grouped to group a group of ... wait, I got myself confused. Groups can be grouped, 'nuff said.
With "Teams," we quickly run into a side-effect of groups, and how it can necessitate a cascade effect across multiple categories. I want to add teams and group them by "Division," but that forces me to also make "League" a group as well. What was three categories have now collapsed into one: "Teams"
Here's what that looks like in practice.
We still gain the benefit of name references in formulas, as in the above untethered-to-reality example. A reference to East would apply to both American and National, unless we specify by . as in National.East and American.East
Groups can be subtotaled, using the groupsum() function, as you can see in this more data-rich chart of the MLB stats from 2022 to 2026. Notice, however, we risk a conflict for Percent in our Total field, where there are two formulas battling it out for dominance over the same cell calculation. The handy SKIP keyword will skip (i.e. "won't apply this formula to") groups, cells, items, and categories as designated.
Groups helped bring granularity and specificity to our data structure, but the more categories we remove, the more we remove access to the very feature that has kept Improv in the back of nerd minds for decades. You know what I'm talking about.
FINALLY we get to the point those in the know have been anxious to talk about, " Lotus Improv invented pivot tables. It says so right there in Wikipedia."
At this stage of my knowledge of all things retro productivity, I think the most I'm willing to concede right now is that Lotus Improv likely invented pivot tables as we understand them today. But, like Yoda coyly teasing the existence of Luke's sister to a guy who should have already known about her, there is another program, a future Stone Tools subject, that may lay claim to the title of "first pivot table." I exercise my right, as "guy who runs the blog," to reserve final judgement on this point until then.
For our purposes today, it's a true enough statement and the inventor even has a nice video on YouTube in which he shows it off to Lotus staff for the first time. Meet Pito Salas, inventor of the pivot table.
Mike Wells (shown in the thumbnail) takes a question at 28:40 and reveals that NeXT has "Objective Fortran" and "Objective Lisp" ?!?!
Salas, now retired , developed the idea while working for Lotus Development's Advanced Technology Group. He put together a fakey version of his vision, a kind of slideshow, showing off the things he wanted to be able to do: English-like formulas, multi-dimensional data, and rearrangeable views into the data. He was given the greenlight to proceed, "All those [ideas] I had described with hand waving,'' recalls Pito. "I had no clue how to build it." A year of nose-to-the-grindstone later, and a prototype dubbed "Back Bay" went on US tour, wowing financial modelers. Everyone who saw it, wanted it.
Let's take a look at how Improv handles pivoting. To start, I'm leaving it empty of data, so we can focus on the dynamic view structure more easily. Then, I'll move categories around to show how the view flexes to present the data. Next, I'll put categories into the third axis, called a "Page Category," allowing us to paginate our data. Finally, I'll enter a formula and a little data to show off a trick pivot table contemporaries cannot perform.
Now I'm going to try and replicate this in LibreOffice Calc v26.8. There are a few things to note, but let's first point and laugh at the fumbling attempts of a LibreOffice newbie (me).
A few things jumped out at me while comparing these approaches. First, modeling up a relatively complex data set in Improv is as easy as thinking about it, and the presentation of the data matches my mental model. LibreOffice requires me to bridge a fairly wide conceptual gap between what I want and how I model it, due to the amount of redundant data I have to enter for every line item.
Some items, like "League," translate cleanly, while "Record" does not. In fact, I'm still unclear what the best approach would be to convert my Improv computed item "Win Ratio." LibreOffice has the concept of a "computed field" inside pivot tables, but reaching across columns to pluck out related data to perform computations is complicated.
In Apple Numbers, Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, and LibreOffice , pivot table data is splintered off into a separate snapshot of the data, dedicated to the pivot table view. Pivot table data can typically be lightly manipulated, but does not affect the original data. The reverse can be done, but only after asking for an explicit update of the pivot table to reflect changes to the primary data table. This is a huge drop-off in ease-of-use from the Improv way of things where every view of the data directly manipulates the base data.
Dragging around categories is just as easy in either approach, though Improv gives immediate drag-and-drop access to what LibreOffice calls a "Filter," i.e. a paged view, and generally "feel better," IMHO. LibreOffice requires us to open up a separate panel and drag things around in there. I will say, however, that being able to filter the filters (i.e. exclude/include specific subsets of data) is handy.
Sheets , Numbers , and Excel (online version) are all strictly panel-based pivoting. Interestingly enough, the panel approach is precisely the interface Lotus rejected , at the behest of Steve Jobs. Once more, from the Garfinkel article.
Having now directly compared Improv's approach to dynamic views against modern pivot tables, it is safe to say they are the same only so much as wagyu beef with gruyere cheese prepared by Gordon Ramsay and the sawdust at the bottom of a Happy Meal are both "cheeseburgers." Improv tastes much better.
A Lotus invention which debuted in Lotus 1-2-3 , "named ranges" have attempted to bring order to the chaos of cell identifiers. In 1-2-3, Range > Name > Create will apply a name of choice to a defined cell range, after which that range can be referenced in formulas by that name. So, in 1-2-3 or any modern spreadsheet we can name range F1..F23 as Sales and sum(Sales) will work.
Superficially, this looks similar to how Improv works with categories and items for multi-dimensional data. However, named ranges are for convenience only, and do not establish relationships between data values. In Improv , Sales would represent a fundamental aspect of a piece of data. Getting the sum of all sales is the same, sum(Sales) , but it being a dimension on the data gives us deeper options. For a specific year, sum(2020:Sales) will match against two axes at once. sum(2020:Arkansas:Sales) could further pinpoint our summation.
Let's see how this would be done with modern spreadsheets and named ranges. If we want to mimic Improv's dimensional relationships, we must define relationships of interest within each formula, (and those formulas have to be copied over to every related cell) such that:
Meaning "sum items in the named range called "Value" only if the Year is 2020, and the League is "American," and the Record is "Win," and the Division is "East")
Of course we could substitute hardcoded filter criteria with values pulled from a lookup, or perhaps extract equated values via a LET statement. Maybe even set up a little sub-table to hold calculated values. Quickly this gets way more complicated than I'd have hoped for, so personally I'd resort to doing it the old-fashioned way and just hardcode in a bunch of cell references. To reiterate, the complete solution for an entire sheet in Improv , where win/loss information is its own dimension, is the single formula:
The last of the big features, which takes advantage of NeXT's graphics prowess, is the charting functionality. Creating a chart launches an entirely separate application, Presentation Builder , which has grand plans on becoming PageMaker when it grows up.
Generating a chart generates a full, blank page onto which a chart is placed. A suite of palettes complements the charting workflow, allowing for precision edits of the chart, its titles, colors, positioning, and more within the full page. Multiple charts can be generated and placed on the same page. Arbitrary text and shapes, lines pointing at interesting bits, and even sound annotations (a system-wide NeXT tool, called "Lip Service") can be placed at will.
So it goes that while we have the tools to place arbitrary text on the page, yet lack tools to center that text, the sense that Lotus has overextended itself is strong. Sometimes it's enough to just generate the output a program excels at, and leave "page composition" to the professionals. Again, I need software to be more dumb . That's without even mentioning the plethora of formatting tools scattered amongst an unreasonable number of palettes, panels, and "inspectors."
A benefit of these tools on the NeXT is that everything we do is Postscript by default, thanks to NeXT's Display Postscript screen rendering engine. "Print" a document as PostScript, and we can render the resultant .ps file on any modern system. I opened it directly in Affinity and received precisely what I saw in Improv , chopped off text and all, but like, high-quality chopped off text.
Look, I try my best to craft a compelling narrative, moving from topic to topic, stitching together callbacks and observations to lead you, my dear reader, on a carefully considered ride. It's just you and me, side by side at the keyboard, chatting about software and learning together. But, sometimes there's junk I need to squeeze in that I can't find a natural segue for discussing. Here, then, is a brain dump of other things I want you to know about Improv .
In 1993, NeXT abandoned its hardware initiative and moved over to Intel, rebranding as NeXT Software, releasing OPENSTEP soon after. At the same time, Improv also moved over to Intel, but parted ways with NeXT. With version 2, Lotus developers achieved the success that eluded them on OS/2, porting Improv over to Windows 3.1.
The feature set for version 2 is disappointingly similar to version 1, and by this time competing software was starting to embrace some of Improv's unique qualities. We do finally get undo, so thank Kapor for small favors. Scripting arrives in the form of LotusScript. A new Windows UI adds a bunch of buttons to the interface, and flushes the toilet paper dispenser for a more sensible list generator.
That's basically it for the new stuff, but at least they kept the old problems as well.
Cell reference relativity is still locked to a single dimension. Formulas cannot be freely rearranged, only cut-and-pasted into position. No 3D worksheets. Then, to throw a little extra wrinkle into the mix, there was Lotus's product strategy on the PC. If Improv wasn't your thing, maybe their other Windows spreadsheet, 1-2-3/Windows , would feel more comfortable. Or their other-other option, Lotus Symphony . Or their other-other-other option, Lotus Works . Or their other-other-other-other option, Lotus 1-2-3 for DOS Release 4 , which went on sale in 1994.
Regardless, it was well-liked by the press, even if reviewers didn't seem comfortable giving full-throated endorsements. Take this Compute , July 1994, review for example.
Or this PC World , February 1994, review.
It would be hard to intuit, based on that review, that PC World had declared Improv the "Winner" in the Applications category for their 10th Annual Awards for Technical Excellence just a few months prior.
3 in spirit, if not in flesh; let's take a quick look at Quantrix , the product I clumsily foreshadowed earlier.
From ex-Lighthouse CEO (also ex-Sun CEO) Jonathan Schwartz's blog , "In 1989, a few friends and I started a software company, Lighthouse Design, that devoted itself to the NeXT platform. Whether any of us admitted it at the time, Lighthouse was built by a group of people for whom Steve Jobs was the gravitational center of the universe."
Their devotion to Jobs was returned in favor, by way of advice for their products to flourish on NeXT. Ultimately, according to Schwartz, the problem was less about finding a way for Lighthouse to flourish on NeXT than it was about getting NeXT to flourish in the first place. When looking for a buyout in Lighthouse's waning days, they had fingers crossed to be acquired by NeXT but Jobs didn't bite. They were bought by Sun, their products shoved in a vault never to see the light of day.
With Microsoft unwilling to support the platform, Lighthouse made the closest thing to an Office suite for NeXT. They built programming tools, project management software, a presentation tool called Concurrence ( that Jobs used and which "inspired" Keynote ), and two spreadsheet programs: ParaSheet and Quantrix .
ParaSheet took the more traditional approach, while Quantrix was just a flat-out clone of Improv , I don't know how else to say it. It has the same split screen worksheet/formulas, the same THIS NEXT PREV formula tools, the same draggable categories, it imports Improv documents, and more. According to one Hacker News reader , "The manuals were interchangeable."
Lighthouse took the ideas behind Improv and ran with them, envisioning what a possible v3 could have been. Put simply, everything I've expressed frustration with in Improv is addressed in Quantrix .
It has undo. It has drag-and-drop, reorderable formulas. It has scripting. It has cross-worksheet category synchronization. The "Item Dispenser" is replaced with an in-line widget; pull to expand like any modern spreadsheet does today. It has multi-dimensional cell relativity. It runs on OPENSTEP for Intel, as well as NeXTSTEP on Motorola 68K . It has color. It loses contextual help (can't win 'em all). And that morass of panels and palettes for editing the charts I showed earlier? Those are collapsed into a single, tidy "Inspector."
Long story short? If you want to experience the best version of Lotus Improv today, use Lighthouse Quantrix v2.3. You'll get all of the original, cool tools built better, with a more sensible interface. Plus, Lighthouse gave away their NeXT applications, with license code, for free. How neat is that?
The big twist, for those affording me a generous definition of "twist," is that Quantrix still exists . It is alive and being sold for "ask for quote," so I think I'll just put this credit card back in my wallet at this time. Today, it very explicitly targets the professional, high-end, financial modeling crowd, and not the general-purpose masses. You know, the crowd that Lotus first showed their Back Bay prototypes to back in the day (see timeline). Its self-introductory video pivots (get it?) many of its 35-year-old features as revolutionary. A back-handed indictment of the stagnation of an industry, or a product finally finding its niche? You be the judge!
It's hard to suss out precisely what happened, but I found a little information floating around the Quantrix forums . If that is to be trusted, Lighthouse's Quantrix chief engineer, Pete Murray, founded the company Subx and rebuilt Quantrix as a Java application in 2003. Quantrix's website says it was acquired by IDBS in 2010. I'm still completely in the dark how Quantrix escaped Sun's containment field, as Sun had refused to sell off the Lighthouse apps to hungry buyers; that stuff could have been converted into OS X apps in the early days.
At any rate, it is one of the more handsome JRE applications, while suffering from telltale Java rendering issues, especially with regard to text positioning and scaling. Otherwise it is clean and inoffensive. Sterile? Boring. That's the word I was looking for: boring. "It knows its target audience," is perhaps more charitable.
So where does this leave my relationship with Lotus Improv ? Why did I dangle that "And yet..." at the start of the post? If I'm completely honest with myself, there is a vibrating tension between "wanting to love it" and "actually loving it."
After all of these weeks, I think I'm in a pretty good position to suggest why it didn't take the world by storm: it's not a great spreadsheet program. Let me qualify that statement lest r/Improv4Life roasts me alive; the roasting can wait a moment.
For what it does, it is amazing and even fun to use. What it doesn't do is provide a good, general purpose spreadsheet experience to the masses. It claimed to do that, positioning itself as the "NeXT generation of spreadsheets." Whatever Lotus Improv did or did not accomplish for the spreadsheet genre, one thing is for certain: it makes a fantastic tech demo.
Seen in that light, I'd have been as sold on it as Jobs was, excitedly showing it to NeXT non-believers, "Look what MY computer can do!" Those moments of smug technological superiority amongst friends are fun, aren't they? Once you played with it for a week or two, and the initial excitement of pivoting dulled, you may have ashamedly harbored a bit of buyer's remorse.
Adam Bosworth, in an article contemplating a talk he gave at ICSOC '04, was thinking about software complexity vs. simplicity, and posited:
Paradoxically, Improv's promise to improve data comprehensibility wound up narrowing its general appeal. Want to quickly throw down a few lines of data, like a makeshift phone directory? You're gonna have to rethink your data as a matrix of abstract qualities about your friends. Despite its friendly English-like formulas and delightful GUI for pivoting data, Improv is in actuality purpose-built for far more rigorous data modeling than its playful tools suggest.
It's the next generation of spreadsheets for a thin slice of the market.
That said, there is a non-zero set of readers for whom their hardcore number crunching needs perfectly align with Improv's promises. If that's you, you're absolutely going to fall in love...
Ways to improve the experience, notable deficiencies, workarounds, and notes about incorporating the software into modern workflows (if possible).
Improv does export to Lotus 1-2-3 , but you'll likely be disappointed with the results. Consider a table with formulas and calculated values in the cells. Everything you see in the cells will be exported, but there will be no formulas or relationships between anything. You will receive a snapshot of all current values, arranged to visually match the table structure you had when exporting. Improv's approach to shared formulas and multi-dimensional data simply don't have an elegant export solution to traditional spreadsheets.
If you have Improv documents you want to import into Quantrix , two criteria must be met. Save your Improv project as an .imx file (not the default .imp ), and make sure you have the Lighthouse FilterServicer.service (available at the same site offering the Quantrix software link I mentioned under "Version 3") installed at ~/Library/Services .
Exporting charts is simplicity, thanks to Display Postscript. The Postscript files NeXTSTEP generates open and render just fine on modern machines, using Ghostscript or other graphics programs.
As mentioned previously, I actually recommend using Lighthouse Quantrix v2.3 instead of Lotus Improv , on the NeXT. The substantial features Improv lacks are numerous:
In general, it's lacking the clay-like malleability of a traditional spreadsheet. If you're doing what a lot of us do, using spreadsheets like a kind of mini-database, you'll probably get frustrated.
Here's the main event. Compare and contrast with his OS X announcement at MacWorld 2000 for bonus points.

title: Russia to cooperate with ASEAN on marine security — Lavrov
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia is going to further promote its strategic partnership with ASEAN and cooperate in the field of marine security and within the framework of Eurasian integration, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the opening of talks with ASEAN Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn.
"We are in the midst of a substantive dialogue on launching new areas of our cooperation, including maritime security, combating pandemics, and dialogue on youth and customs issues," Lavrov said. "I would also like to ask you to share your assessments of the prospects for Eurasian integration, taking into account the contacts you had within the framework of the Kazan summit with the heads of the executive authorities of the Eurasian Economic Union and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization," he noted.
"Promoting the strategic partnership with ASEAN is one of our permanent priorities in the Asian and Eurasian directions," the top Russian diplomat said. "We see the association as a reliable partner with whom we share both long years of work on the international arena and an increasing number of practical projects being implemented and rolled out in practice," Lavrov stressed.
Russia and ASEAN are united by the desire to form a more just and multipolar world order, including in the space of Greater Eurasia, he added.
