title: What ice cream has to do with this year's Nobel Prize in economics
body:
This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here .
On Monday morning, the world's econ nerds tuned in to an announcement from Sweden to learn who won this year's Nobel Prize in economics. And we got a lesson involving … ice cream.
The winners were Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University. The prize committee honored them "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
To explain what the heck that means — as we will try to do in this newsletter — Timo Boppart, an economist at Stockholm University and member of the prize committee, stood up and walked around like he was giving a TED Talk. At one point, he brought up an image on the screen behind him: an ice cream menu.
Boppart used the ice cream menu to serve up a sweet lesson in economics.
"How do firms actually set prices?" Boppart asked. " This is illustrated here with this ice cream menu. Prices do not adjust [on] a continuous basis. Firms instead set the price of this ice cream for a whole season."
Ice cream was a poetic example. Because prices, like ice cream, can get sticky. In fact, economists use the term "sticky prices" to describe how prices can stubbornly stay put even as economic conditions change.
That seemingly minor detail can have huge consequences for the entire economy. Sticky prices are a cornerstone of what's known as "New Keynesian economics" — a framework that has helped reshape macroeconomic theory and how policymakers think about fighting recessions and controlling inflation.
This year's prize honored work that helped lay the foundations for New Keynesian economics. In the process, Hall, Woodford, and other scholars helped breathe new life into the ideas of economics giant John Maynard Keynes, whose intellectual legacy, for a time, seemed in danger of melting away.
To understand why, we need to go back to the 1970s, when the economy experienced something that, for some, seemed to invalidate Keynesian economics.
John Maynard Keynes is basically the father of macroeconomics, the study of how the entire economy works, including what the government can do to fight recessions, boost employment, and control inflation.
Keynes' breakthrough came in the depths of the Great Depression, when he published The General Theory of Employment, Interest, and Money . He articulated an idea that may seem obvious today but challenged the economic orthodoxy of his time: an economy can get stuck in a prolonged slump, and the free market won't necessarily get everyone back to work on its own. Instead, Keynes wrote, we needed the government to help boost spending, put people back to work, and return the economy to health.
If you've ever taken an Econ 101 class, you've probably heard about the "invisible hand" of the free market. It's the idea that people and businesses pursuing their own interests in competitive markets can help the economy reach its full potential without the government having to step in. Keynes basically argued we couldn't count on the invisible hand to pull the economy out of a slump. We needed the visible hand of the government.
Keynes influenced an entire generation of economists and policymakers. Even Milton Friedman, a strong advocate for the free market, was quoted in 1965 as saying, "We are all Keynesians now." (He later said the quote was taken out of context.)
In the 1970s, however, the dominant Keynesian models — and the policies they helped guide — ran into trouble. Inflation and unemployment rose together — a painful combination known as "stagflation." The existing Keynesian models struggled to explain it.
"For a long time, the recipes of Keynes seemed to work, but they then failed during the oil crisis in the 1970s when high unemployment and high inflation took over simultaneously," said John Hassler, the chair of the Nobel committee, when they announced the prize.
When the old-school models faltered, some economists wanted to reject Keynes wholesale. Economists like Robert Lucas and Edward Prescott — who each won Nobel Prizes — challenged Keynesian economics and its confidence that government policy could effectively smooth out the economy's ups and downs. Call it the revenge of the invisible hand.
A central criticism: The Keynesian models relied too heavily on patterns found in past economic data without adequately explaining the individual decisions behind them. Addressing that criticism meant giving models "microfoundations": starting with the decisions of individual people and businesses to explain how the whole economy works. The economy is made of people, and people think ahead. They anticipate what policymakers will do, and those expectations shape how they spend, save, and invest. If policymakers change direction, people's behavior might too — making old patterns an unreliable guide to whether a new policy will work.
One influential alternative to Keynesianism, developed by Prescott and other economists, became known as "real business cycle" theory. These models assumed that prices and wages were completely flexible, adjusting freely as economic conditions changed. If demand for workers fell, wages could fall too, making workers cheaper to hire and allowing the labor market to balance supply and demand. That left little room for a familiar feature of recessions: people who want to work but can't find jobs.
Gregory Mankiw, now an economist at Harvard University, entered graduate school at MIT alongside Michael Woodford in 1980. They were learning macroeconomics just as economists were fighting over how to rebuild it.
"Lucas and Prescott were ascendant, but a lot of us were skeptical of their conclusions," Mankiw tells Planet Money . " And that's when people like Woodford and Hall sort of entered the stage. The sense was that the people who were rejecting the Keynesian model were throwing out the baby with the bathwater. And so rather than throwing it out, they wanted to sort of fix the problems."
Hall and Woodford helped rebuild macroeconomics around the decisions of individual people and businesses. Hall broke new ground in understanding how people's expectations about the future shape their spending today. Woodford built on that work, developing a framework that combined forward-looking spending decisions with sticky prices.
To see why sticky prices matter, let's return to the ice cream example. Say there's a recession and demand for ice cream plummets. Shops might not quickly reduce ice cream prices to entice customers back. Maybe changing menus and signs costs time and money. Or maybe shops aren't yet sure whether the drop in demand is temporary or here to stay. Instead, they keep prices frozen, sell fewer scoops, and ultimately may end up having to cut worker hours or lay people off. When prices don't adjust, jobs and businesses take a hit.
The same story goes for wages, which we guess are a bigger factor in the economy than ice cream prices.
" When economists talk about sticky prices, they're also including sticky wages — the price of labor," Mankiw says. "Most people don't get their wages adjusted every month."
Across the economy, that stickiness or "price rigidity" can have big consequences. When spending drops, prices and wages don't quickly and flexibly adjust to keep people buying and businesses hiring. Instead of prices falling to bring supply and demand together, in these models, price stickiness causes production and employment to fall. It helps explain why, during recessions, people who want to work can remain out of a job for long stretches.
" Bringing in those price rigidities into the framework was absolutely key because this is the reason why the invisible hand cannot do its magic and there is room for policy intervention," said Boppart at the Nobel Prize announcement.
In other words, even when people and businesses think ahead and act in their own interests, sticky prices can keep the economy stuck in a slump. Call it Keynes' comeback. In these models, governments and central banks still have a role to play in getting the economy back on track.
This was the promise of New Keynesian economics: take the criticisms of the old models seriously, rebuild models around individual decisions, and preserve Keynes' central insight that the free market won't always bounce back on its own.
"One thing that clearly differentiates Keynesian models from Real Business Cycle models was the flexibility or stickiness of prices," Mankiw says. "Most economists today — not all — but I think most economists today buy into the sticky price assumption."
These New Keynesian models became integral to how governments and central banks think about fighting recessions and controlling inflation.
Woodford's work, for example, helped lay the theoretical groundwork for "forward guidance," a strategy the Federal Reserve used during the Great Recession. The Fed slashed its benchmark interest rate to near zero, but the economy still needed stimulus. So under then-chair Ben Bernanke, the Fed signaled that it expected to keep interest rates low for an extended period. By shaping expectations about future rates, the Fed tried to help lower longer-term borrowing costs and encourage spending today.
Keynes' ideas survived with new foundations. And Mankiw offers an update to Milton Friedman's famous line: "We're all New Keynesians now," he says.
P.S. Throughout this piece, we've called this award the "Nobel Prize in economics." But calling it that is surprisingly controversial. Technically, it has a much clunkier name. Economics wasn't one of the prizes Alfred Nobel created. So how did it join the club? Ricky and I tell that story in the latest episode of The Indicator from Planet Money. Check it out when it's released Tuesday.

title: Russia to continue selling energy resources on global markets — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia is selling and will continue selling energy resources, its competitive commodity, in international markets, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
"Russia in this aspect is a country presenting its competitive commodity to global markets. We will continue doing that," Peskov said.
European countries are active buyers of Russian crude oil and petroleum products themselves, he noted.

title: GoldBod must be more accountable to Ghanaians – Haruna Iddrisu
body: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has called for stronger accountability at the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), citing the scale of funds involved in its operations and the need to address reported losses. He said attention should focus on improving the institution’s performance and ensuring that its operations, as well as those of the Bank of Ghana, do not generate avoidable losses. “You see, today, you ought to have improved the Gold Board legislation in a manner that it can become more accountable to the Ghanaian people, because the amount of money involved is huge,” he said. Mr Iddrisu acknowledged reports of losses and urged a collective response to the concerns. “So we have a gold board today. There have been reported cases of losses. Let’s not run,” he said. He questioned whether GoldBod and the Bank of Ghana could operate without occasioning such losses, adding: “And I’m saying that is what we must seek to respond to as a country.” The Tamale South MP also criticised the opposition’s decision to walk out of Parliament during the passage of the GoldBod bill. He argued that remaining in the chamber would have provided an opportunity to strengthen accountability provisions in the legislation. “And remember, even when the Goldbod bill was passed, they walked out of Parliament,” he said, describing the action as “Immaturity on their part.” Asked whether he would support changes to the current system to prevent future losses, Mr Iddrisu responded positively. “Why not? President Mahama will accommodate any objective suggestion from any Ghanaian who thinks that this is the way to improve the Goldbod performance.” While calling for improvements, he also defended the economic contribution of the government’s gold interventions, saying they had helped strengthen Ghana’s gold reserves and supported the currency. He maintained that a more stable exchange rate helped businesses plan and reduced pressures on the cost of doing business.

title: Whitaker Says ‘No Change’ to Arms Flows to Kyiv via PURL
body:
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said, to his knowledge, US weapon flows to Kyiv via NATO continue as of Monday.
Speaking to AFP on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Whitaker said he was unaware of any changes to the existing supply structure.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“The United States continues to sell our equipment and munitions to our European and Canadian allies that then provide it to Ukraine,” Whitaker said.
Whitaker referred to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, where alliance members bankroll US weaponry for Kyiv.
The comments followed a Financial Times (FT) report on Sunday, citing unnamed European officials, that Washington is considering cutting arms flows via PURL over US President Donald Trump’s Friday diesel deal with Moscow .
The rumors stem from Kyiv’s hinted refusal to halt attacks on Russian refineries unless Washington secures a bilateral ceasefire that protects Ukraine’s energy grid, with the current terms, after Trump announced an energy truce , rumored to overwhelmingly favor Moscow by including only refineries.
Whitaker’s comments also echoed those of US Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich at the same event, who called for Europe to bolster arms supplies to Kyiv via PURL in response to Russia’s hybrid threats.
However, Whitaker also told AFP he did not wish to comment on “unconfirmed reports” without referencing the FT report.
Whitaker also acknowledged the challenges Ukraine faces this winter, as Russia targets the country’s energy grid while Kyiv’s air defenses remain in short supply.
“Ukraine is facing a winter where, if there is not an energy ceasefire,... their electricity and heating infrastructure could be under a lot of pressure,” he said.
“Air defense largely is in high demand, and the availability is probably not as good as we would like,” he added.
Blackouts have already begun in Kyiv and other cities as the energy grid comes under attack. Strikes on Monday , one day after Trump boasted of an energy truce, also affected water supplies in Kyiv, less than two months before the arrival of subzero winter temperatures.
But Whitaker called it a “short-term challenge” as he said companies are coming up with alternatives to traditional air defense.
“You’re seeing a lot of companies try to come up with new and innovative ways to knock projectiles out of the air,” he said.
“Ultimately, we’re going to solve this problem… I think it’s a short-term challenge,” he added.
As Russia uses more jet-powered drones against Ukraine – with numbers spiking 10-fold from 350 in June to nearly 3,500 in September – Kyiv has also ostensibly explored more cost-effective ways to shoot down the drones.
Apart from using onboard 20mm autocannons from F-16 fighter jets, Ukraine also announced new models of faster interceptors to counter the jet-powered drones.
In Kyiv, automatic machine gun turrets are also being erected around the city after Russia began hitting the city’s bridges in October, with the Ukrainian Air Force hailing their successes in downing jet-powered drones.
But the quantity remains limited for now, and it’s unclear whether Kyiv can scale production enough to cope with the upcoming Russian onslaught this winter.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Drone attack targets two merchant ships off Bulgaria's coast, with Ukrainians among casualties
body:
This was stated by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, according to Novinite , as reported by Ukrinform.
Radev also announced plans to hold talks with Russian Ambassador to Bulgaria Eleonora Mitrofanova and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
During an emergency meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers, Radev reported that the Maltese-flagged cargo ship CHELSEA 3 was struck by three drones approximately 18 nautical miles east of the city of Byala. A second vessel, identified as the Azov Concord, sank approximately 17 nautical miles east of the village of Krapets after being struck by a drone.
A distress signal from the CHELSEA 3 was received at 1:30 a.m. According to the crew, the drones struck the deck and side of the vessel. The Maritime Rescue Center in Varna immediately launched a rescue operation, and a border police unit evacuated all 15 people on board: seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijani citizens.
The vessel, owned by a Ukrainian company and registered in Odesa, sails under the Maltese flag. The crew was taken to the port of Varna, where, according to preliminary reports, five sailors received medical treatment for minor injuries.
The second vessel sank approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. One crew member was rescued, but the available information does not allow for determining the full composition of the vessel’s crew or the fate of other people who may have been on board.
“Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgaria’s territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable,” Radev said.
He added that Bulgaria will seek international assistance to investigate these attacks and determine the origin of the drones. He emphasized that the available evidence is insufficient to pin the blame on a specific country, although, in his words, the outcome of these attacks appears to benefit Russia.
“The logic of what is happening suggests that the outcome of these attacks benefits the Russian Federation,” Radev said, explaining his intention to hold talks with Mytrofanova.
Bulgaria’s permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union have been informed of these incidents.
As Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stated on social media platform X , Ukrainian citizens were injured during Russia’s latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria’s territorial waters.
“Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea,” the foreign minister noted.
Sybiha called on partners to intensify pressure and sanctions against Russia and to take decisive measures to hold it accountable and protect freedom of navigation.
“The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponize hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength,” emphasized the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry.
As reported by Ukrinform, Bulgaria is calling for the creation of a new EU mechanism to ensure free and safe navigation in the Black Sea amid recent attacks on civilian vessels.

title: Diesel agreements meet interest of Russia, United States — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Diesel fuel supply agreements correspond to interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"This corresponds to interests of the United States, this corresponds to interests of international energy markets, and is in line with interests of the Russian Federation, and so it takes place," he said.
Diesel fuel agreements are a highly beneficial item of Russian-American cooperation, the Kremlin Spokesman added.

title: Christian tourists buy West Bank settlement goods in protest of European trade restrictions
body: “This piece of legislation written by the Irish parliament shall not stand,” said Paul Coulter, national director of the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ) in Ireland, as he held up a copy of Ireland's new law restricting imports from Israeli settlements. Then he tore the document apart in front of the camera. The gesture came during an ICEJ visit to Israeli communities in the West Bank, also known as Judea and Samaria, where Christian visitors traveled through Samaria, Gush Etzion and Efrat and were encouraged to shop at local businesses. The tour, organized during ICEJ's annual Feast of Tabernacles gathering in Jerusalem, was intended as a direct response to a growing set of European measures restricting trade in products from Israeli settlements. Some of those measures are already in force; others remain proposed legislation.Ireland's ban took effect on Sept. 15. The Netherlands followed with a broader restriction on Sept. 22 that reaches even goods carried in personal luggage. Norway, meanwhile, is considering legislation that would prohibit imports from and exports to Israeli settlements, along with certain property transactions and services. The Norwegian proposal remains under consideration after a public consultation that closed Sept. 19.David Parsons, ICEJ senior vice president and spokesman, said the organization brought Christians attending the Feast of Tabernacles into the area specifically to support businesses affected by the measures.“In recent weeks, several European countries and even Canada and others have announced that they're going to pass sanctions against the Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria,” Parsons told The Media Line. “We brought them here to the Shomron, to Samaria, also down to Gush Etzion, Efrat, to go and show support by buying goods here.”Christians protest European settlement boycottsThe governments imposing or considering the restrictions present them as measures directed at settlements they consider illegal under international law, rather than at Israel as a whole. Ireland says its law is part of an effort to comply with international legal obligations identified in the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion. The Irish government argues that Israeli settlements in what it refers to as occupied Palestinian territory are unlawful and undermine prospects for a two-state solution. Its law prohibits imports originating in designated settlement postal codes and makes violations subject to existing customs law, including search, seizure and forfeiture powers.Parsons rejected that reasoning and argued that the economic effect was precisely the point. “The real intent of these European countries is to dry up the settlements and their livelihoods, the way of life, so they'd have to leave here,” he said. That characterization is disputed by the governments behind the measures, which describe them as a legal and political distinction between Israel and territory captured in 1967.The Irish measure, however, stops short of restricting what tourists bring home for themselves. Noncommercial goods in personal baggage are exempt when intended for the traveler's own consumption or use. That distinction became part of Coulter's message during the trip.“Come and buy Israeli wine. It's some of the best wine in the world,” he said. Later, addressing Irish visitors specifically, he added: “Break the boycott. If you can buy Israeli wine, buy it.” Coulter noted that Irish law does not prevent tourists from returning with those products for private consumption.Coulter said opposition to ICEJ's position has also followed the organization at home. He described venues receiving calls demanding that ICEJ events be canceled and demonstrations outside meetings that went ahead.“We have our own hashtag, #BoycottApartheidICEJ,” he said. “Our venues are lobbied and phoned to cancel our meetings, and when the venues won't cancel, we actually have protest mobs screaming and shouting at the gates of our meetings.”Norway has not yet enacted its proposed trade ban. Its Foreign Ministry opened the proposal for public consultation in June, saying Norwegian citizens and companies should not contribute economically to maintaining settlements that the government considers unlawful. The proposal would prohibit importing goods from Israeli settlements and exporting goods to them. It would also restrict certain real estate purchases, construction and property-related services, and acquisitions of businesses based in the settlements. Violations would carry criminal liability.Dag Øyvind Juliussen, national director of ICEJ Norway, said the prospect of criminal penalties has sharpened opposition among supporters of Israel in his country. “They want to pass a bill that would make it a crime to trade with the Jewish inhabitants in Judea and Samaria, the so-called settlements,” he told The Media Line, adding that the legislation must still go through the Norwegian parliament.For Juliussen, joining the shopping tour was a way to turn that opposition into a physical act. “This is what we need to do,” he said. “This area has been the heartland of the Jewish people for 3,000 years.” He said Christians who share that view should make their position visible by supporting the people and businesses living there.Christian groups challenge European trade bans on Israeli settlementsThe Netherlands has taken a different approach. Since Sept. 22, travelers entering the country have also been barred from bringing in products that Dutch authorities identify as coming from Israeli settlements covered by the measure. That includes items bought for personal use, such as gifts or souvenirs.Dutch customs officers can check luggage and ask where an item was made or purchased. Products found to fall under the ban may need to be surrendered or seized. The measure does not apply to Israeli goods generally, but specifically to products linked to the settlements covered by the Dutch restrictions. Customs authorities say inspections are selected on the basis of risk assessments and objective information rather than a traveler's nationality, religion, ethnicity or appearance.Parsons said the possible long-term consequences went beyond lost sales. He accused European governments of pursuing policies that could eventually pressure Jews to leave the communities. “Are you really willing to support ethnic cleansing of that nature through these sanctions and criminal laws against buying goods from this area?” he asked. His language went far beyond the stated position of the governments involved, which say their measures are aimed at settlements and at preserving the possibility of a negotiated two-state outcome.ICEJ's response during the tour was deliberately practical. “We've done that now by bringing dozens of Christians on several buses to these areas to shop,” Parsons said. His instruction to participants was straightforward: “Take out your plastic, take out your dollars, your shekels and buy goods from Judea and Samaria.”That leaves people traveling together on the same ICEJ tour subject to different rules once they return home. An Irish visitor can bring a bottle of locally produced wine back for personal consumption under Ireland's exemption. A Dutch traveler carrying the same bottle from a location covered by the Netherlands' restrictions may have to surrender it at customs. title: Russian forces fighting for three communities in pocket of encirclement in Kharkov area
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Battlegroup North forces are fighting for the liberation of three communities in the Kharkov Region and tightening the ring of encirclement of Ukrainian troops in that area, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units are tightening the ring of encirclement in the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. In the pocket of encirclement, they are fighting for the liberation of the communities of Nikolayevka, Varvarovka and Nefyodovka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army lost roughly 60 troops, a motor vehicle and five ground robotic platforms in the pocket of encirclement, it specified.
Battlegroup North forces are expanding the outer area of control and continue battles for taking control of the settlements of Prikolotnoye, Kotovka and Gogino in the Kharkov Region, the ministry said.

title: One Drug Has No Antidote, Anaesthetist Says in Mazonakis Case
body: There is no propofol antidote, so the only response when the sedative stops a patient breathing is immediate breathing support, an anaesthetist said, as authorities examine drugs found in singer Giorgos Mazonakis’ blood. Investigators are looking at three substances found in the singer’s blood: midazolam, flumazenil and propofol. Experts are examining the order, the doses and the conditions in which Dr Ioanna Gaka, 56, one of two doctors accused in the case, gave them. Gaka and her husband, Dr Ilias Theodoropoulos, 58, ran the practice on Karneadou Street, in central Athens, where Mazonakis died. Both are in pre-trial detention and deny wrongdoing. Anaesthetist Dimitris Manikis spoke about the drugs in a television interview. He said that midazolam and propofol can both cause apnoea, which means breathing stops, as their main side effect. No propofol antidote While midazolam has an antidote, there is no propofol antidote, Manikis said. As a result, he said, the only option in a case of apnoea is to support the patient’s breathing at once with specialist equipment. Manikis said that when he sees the risk of breathing stopping, he does “two things” . He gives the antidote, when one exists, and replaces the patient’s breathing. Without a propofol antidote, he said, that second step depends on the skills of an anaesthetist. “I give you air with positive pressure from outside,” he said. He also said there is no propofol antidote for a drug whose effect lasts five to 10 minutes. Combined sedatives When midazolam and propofol are combined, the effect becomes much stronger, Manikis said. “It doesn’t just add up, it multiplies,” he said. In that case, he said, apnoea is a given. According to Manikis, giving such drugs outside a hospital, or without an anaesthetist present, is extremely dangerous. Propofol is an intravenous anaesthetic used for sedation and to start general anaesthesia, according to the US National Library of Medicine’s StatPearls reference . Greek City Times reported on 5 October that toxicology tests had found propofol in the singer’s system. Later, on 9 October, authorities froze the assets of doctors held over his death. The couple face charges of homicide with possible intent by omission. No court has ruled on the case, and the investigation is continuing. Source: Ta Nea The post One Drug Has No Antidote, Anaesthetist Says in Mazonakis Case appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Underwater Altercation Between Dive Guides at Siaes Corner Sparks International Investigation
body: By: Eoghan Olkeriil Ngirudelsang Koror, Palau (Oct.12, 2026) — An underwater altercation on Friday at Siaes Corner, a popular dive site north-northwest of Ulong Rock Island in Koror, involving two dive guides — a Korean national and a Bangladeshi national — has drawn international media attention to Palau. On the night of Friday, October 9, Bangladeshi national Sobuj Patwary identified himself on social media as a PADI Divemaster and wrote that he had been diving with four Taiwanese guests at about 10 a.m. that day when another divemaster, whom he identified as Romeo, a Korean national working for Seaworld, had an underwater altercation with one of his guests. Sobuj said that when he swam over to Romeo to stop the incident, Romeo “then attacked me, damaged my mask and removed my fins” while they were several meters underwater. Patwary wrote on social media, “We work in the same tourism industry, in the same beautiful country, Palau”. He also said their responsibility is to “ensure that every diver returns safely to the surface” and that “underwater aggression is not a small matter”. A video of the underwater confrontation was later posted online. The video and reports of the incident appeared in international media, including Taiwan’s TTV News and Moscow News on Threads, where they drew thousands of views and reactions. The incident received international attention after one of the divers, a popular Taiwanese singer Song Jian-Zhang, known to many Taiwanese by his stage name Dan Tou, gave an interview to a Taiwanese news outlet. According to Moscow News, Song Jian-Zhang accused Romeo of having “struck his mask with fist and attempted to rip it off his face. As the Song tried to defend himself and break away, his dive computer fell off during the struggle”. He also said he had given footage of the incident to Palau police and credited “thanks to his 25 years of diving experience that he survived this attempted killing”. Over the weekend, Sobuj’s post went viral, drawing widespread public attention and being shared numerous times. The posts prompted passionate reactions, with commenters supporting both divers. Another diver, Korean national Haeng Suk Yeom, who also identified himself as a PADI Divemaster and diving instructor, posted on social media criticizing Sobuj, saying he had not followed safe diving procedures. Yeom said he had also been diving at the site and witnessed the incident. He accused Sobuj of “treating guests carelessly” and not briefing them adequately, and said Romeo had been cautioning Patwary and his guests. Yeom also alleged that after the dive, Sobuj and “the boat you were on approached us dangerously close and threatened us”. He said, “You are telling lies and have even omitted certain facts” Other social media users supporting Romeo accused Sobuj of posting a one-sided video that did not show the earlier events. One supporter alleged that Sobuj and his guests had endangered Romeo’s guests, prompting Romeo to intervene. Others accused Sobuj of repeatedly violating dive-site etiquette, claiming that “at German Channel, he and guests harass manta rays and break corals”. They also told Sobuj that “as diving professionals, our guests look up to us for safety and a memorable experience”. Another social media user, Ms. Ngirmeriil, posted in support of Romeo, saying Romeo’s guest from that day had signed a document before a notary public supporting his account of the incident. While some members of the community expressed support for one side or the other, others used social media comments to renew calls for dive-guide jobs in Palau to be reserved for Palauan nationals. Some commenters questioned how foreign nationals could put tourists at risk and damage Palau’s reputation as a tourism destination. Yesterday October 12, Bureau of Tourism Director Jenin Tewid and Koror State Government Director of Conservation and Law Enforcement Hope Rekisiwang issued a joint statement saying that “BOT and KSG are aware of the diving-related incident that occurred on October 09, 2026 and are coordinating with the relevant authorities as the investigation continues.” The Ministry of Justice had not issued a statement about the incident at the time of publication. However, the joint BOT-KSG statement said an investigation was ongoing and added, “As the investigation remains ongoing, no determination of responsibility or fault has been made.” The post Underwater Altercation Between Dive Guides at Siaes Corner Sparks International Investigation appeared first on Island Times News .

title: The Acropolis Now Welcomes a Small Town Every Day
body: Acropolis visitor numbers reached a record 4,609,113 in 2025, an average of about 12,600 people a day, according to data from the Hellenic Statistical Authority. The total rose from about 4.55 million in 2024, according to the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT) data. Traffic now stays above 4.5 million a year. To protect the monument, authorities set a strict limit of 20,000 visitors a day. Acropolis visitor numbers consistently make up 35 per cent of all visits to Greece’s archaeological sites. Before the pandemic, in 2019, the site drew about 3.5 million people. As a result, the 2025 total was 32 per cent higher, with 1,109,113 more visitors than six years earlier. Tickets and time slots for the site are sold through the Culture Ministry’s official Hellenic Heritage ticketing site . Earlier, Greek City Times reported on the upgrade of the nearby Kerameikos site in Athens. Source: Kathimerini The post The Acropolis Now Welcomes a Small Town Every Day appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Hong Kong Electronics Fairs Showcase AI, Robotics and Industrial Innovation
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. HONG KONG – Hong Kong is seeking to strengthen its position in advanced manufacturing and emerging technologies as growing demand for artificial intelligence and electronic components drives exports, officials said on Oct. 13 at the opening of two major technology fairs bringing together more than 3,200 exhibitors from 15 countries and regions. Hong Kong-based accessories brand Momax. Photo credit: Assel Satubaldina/ The Astana Times The Hong Kong Electronics Fair (Autumn Edition) and electronicAsia, running through Oct. 16 at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Center and hosted by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC), are showcasing developments in robotics, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, smart manufacturing and consumer electronics. Electronic products accounted for nearly 80% of Hong Kong’s total exports in the first eight months of 2026, highlighting the industry’s importance to the city’s economy, said Kevin Choi, permanent secretary for innovation, technology and industry of the government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Kevin Choi. Photo credit: Assel Satubaldina/ The Astana Times “The significance of the industry does go beyond trade figures. Electronics is the foundation of artificial intelligence, advanced computing, smart manufacturing and healthcare technologies and many other industries that will shape our future,” he said. According to the HKTDC, electronics exports increased 52.8% year-on-year during the period, supported by demand for semiconductors, computer components and other advanced technologies. However, officials said the city’s ambitions go beyond its established role as an international trading hub. It is increasingly focusing on turning scientific research into commercially viable products and strengthening connections between technology developers, manufacturers and investors. “The challenge is no longer confined to making a scientific discovery. We must also turn the discovery into a product, validate it in a real setting, establish a viable production process and bring it to the market,” said Choi. “This is the essence of new industrialization and a practical way to develop new quality productive forces. It connects technology innovation with industry innovation so that research can create real economic value,” he added. The first day also saw the launch of the Future Industries Zone, a new exhibition platform bringing together more than 100 exhibitors across five areas: advanced computing, manufacturing, microelectronics, marine and quantum technologies, and wellness. The zone is organized by the HKTDC and the Hong Kong Electronic Industries Association, and supported by the Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau (ITIB) of the Hong Kong SAR Government. The fairs will run through Oct. 16. Photo credit: HKTDC The zone is designed to connect research institutions, universities, startups, manufacturers and potential investors, creating opportunities for technology commercialization and industrial partnerships. Choi said Hong Kong was developing an industrial ecosystem built around three major innovation and technology parks and five research and development institutions, drawing on the manufacturing capabilities and supply chains of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. One initiative involves the Hong Kong Microelectronics Research and Development Institute. “They will now support research, proof-of-concept fabrication, pilot production and low-volume production too. The Institute will also take the lead in piloting and operating the first national manufacturing production center to be established in Hong Kong, bringing together resources from Hong Kong, the Chinese mainland and overseas, including local enterprises and startups participating in the zone today, to strengthen our microelectronics ecosystem and accelerate commercialization,” Choi explained. Sophia Chong. Photo credit: Assel Satubaldina/ The Astana Times Sophia Chong, executive director of the HKTDC, said the electronics industry had undergone a significant transformation, moving from traditional consumer products toward AI-enabled devices and smart technologies. “Indeed, the Future Industries Zone is only one of the many highlights of this year’s Hong Kong Electronics Fair Autumn Edition and electronicAsia, which brings together over 3,200 exhibitors coming from 15 countries and regions,” she said. “Another key highlight is the RoboPark. (…) Across the fair, we feature more than 120 robots, including some of the market’s best-selling models,” she said. Among the exhibitors demonstrating practical applications of artificial intelligence is Xeroptix, which develops vision-based AI systems designed to monitor industrial processes. Ken Hon, representing the company, told The Astana Times that its technology is primarily used on factory production lines, where cameras and AI systems monitor tasks that still require manual labor. Ken Hon. Photo credit: Assel Satubaldina/ The Astana Times When a worker skips a step or fails to include a component, the system can issue an immediate alert, allowing the problem to be corrected before the product reaches the end of the production line. Hon said the technology operates independently of an internet connection, processing visual data locally rather than sending entire images to cloud servers. Such devices have less computing power than cloud-based systems, he said, but local processing can offer advantages in reliability and data privacy. Consumer electronics companies are also introducing connected features intended to improve product safety and convenience. Hong Kong-based accessories brand Momax demonstrated a power bank that allows users to monitor battery performance through a smartphone application connected via Bluetooth. The application displays battery capacity, temperature, charging cycles and charging speeds, allowing users to check the device’s condition without physically accessing it. A company representative described the feature as “visible safety,” saying it was designed to give consumers greater awareness of their devices’ performance and potential overheating risks. Next-generation full-sized humanoid robot Walker. Photo credit: Assel Satubaldina/ The Astana Times Alongside the technology displays, the fairs are also placing greater emphasis on international market access. A GoGlobal Connect Zone brings together professional service providers offering advice and support to companies seeking to expand overseas. Hong Kong’s efforts to help companies expand into international markets also follow a push to strengthen economic ties with Central Asia. In June, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee led a business delegation to Kazakhstan, where he identified the country as a potential gateway to the broader Central Asian market and highlighted opportunities for cooperation in trade, finance, logistics and innovation. The delegation, organized by the HKTDC, brought together around 70 business leaders. The visit also highlighted growing interest in the region’s digital economy and technology sectors, areas that also feature prominently at this week’s electronics exhibitions. The Hong Kong Electronics Fair, now in its 46th edition, focuses on consumer electronics and emerging technologies, while electronicAsia brings together suppliers of electronic components, parts and related manufacturing solutions. Together, the exhibitions offer a platform for companies to explore how advances in artificial intelligence and industrial technologies can translate into new products, manufacturing capabilities and international business opportunities. The post Hong Kong Electronics Fairs Showcase AI, Robotics and Industrial Innovation appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Ballistic missile attack warnings could be compromised without US intelligence – head of cybersecurity subcommittee Fedienko
body:
Oleksandr Fedienko (Servant of the People faction), head of the cybersecurity subcommittee of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on National Security, Defense, and Intelligence, doubts the USA will stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine, but notes that if this were to happen, the civilian population could suffer.

"I don't think that will happen. But if it does, it could affect ballistic missile attack warnings because, unfortunately, our partners detect them faster thanks to certain technologies. In all other respects, I think our intelligence services are doing a good job," Fedienko told Interfax-Ukraine on Tuesday.

He emphasized that more data is currently being gathered in cyberspace, "and that involves the UK and partner countries that have not let us down so far."

"It could affect the civilian population... Will it affect the front line? Most likely not," Fedienko stressed.

title: Phone Scammers Target Children and the Elderly
body: Police in north-western Athens have broken up a phone scam gang that allegedly took cash and valuables worth €800,000 from elderly people and children in a few weeks. Officers arrested eight people on Friday in a raid on a call centre in the suburb of Ano Liosia, police said. They believe the gang phoned its victims from there. Scams like these remain common and effective, despite hundreds of arrests and repeated public warnings. As a result, authorities plan new, tougher laws aimed at this kind of crime. The suspects posed as accountants or as staff from electricity and phone companies, police said. They then made up stories, telling victims they had faulty wiring or needed to file extra tax returns. How the phone scam gang worked Once victims believed the story, the callers talked them into packing up cash and valuables kept at home. Some left the packages outside, while others left them inside and kept the front door open. Other gang members then drove by and collected the packages, according to police. In one case, gang members got a ten-year-old boy in the suburb of Petroupoli to hand over jewellery worth €10,000. Officers recovered the jewellery during the raid. Family members among suspects Police said many members of the phone scam gang belong to the same family. They believe the group carried out at least 22 scams since 1 September. During that time, the gang regularly changed both its phone numbers and the places it called from, police said. The phone scam gang case follows other recent arrests. In September, police broke up a voice-cloning scam ring accused of a €1 million fraud. Police advise people to report suspicious calls through the Hellenic Police and to the Cyber Crime Division. Source: Kathimerini The post Phone Scammers Target Children and the Elderly appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: 6 Iranians from Royan Inst. earn places in world top 2% list
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Six Iranian scientists affiliated with the Royan Institute made it into the latest world’s top 2% scientists list, which evaluates researchers worldwide based on citation data and indicators of scientific impact.
The researchers are affiliated with the Academic Center for Education, Culture and Research Activities (ACECR), and their inclusion marks an increase from five Royan Institute researchers recognized in the previous edition, according to the Institute’s Public Relations and International Affairs Office.
The six researchers are Dr. Hossein Baharvand, Dr. Mohammad Hossein Nasr-Esfahani, Dr. Mohammad Reza Baghban Islami, Dr. Reza Omrani-Samani, Dr. Masoud Vosough, and Dr. Ashraf Moini.
The World’s Top 2% Scientists list assesses researchers across scientific disciplines and subfields using citation-based indicators and other measures of research performance, including citation counts, the Hirsch index (h-index), and the composite C-score.
Compiled using data from the Scopus citation database in collaboration with Stanford University and published by Elsevier, the assessment is widely used to evaluate the scientific impact of researchers and their contributions to their respective fields.
Royan Institute’s representation on the list has remained consistent in recent years, with five researchers recognized in 2023, four in 2024, and five in 2025. The latest assessment raises that number to six, highlighting the Institute’s continued presence in international scientific rankings.

title: The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A drone strike on 10 October put more than half of the large fuel tanks out of action at an oil-loading terminal in Russia’s Rostov-on-Don, Russian news Telegram channel Astra found . The terminal loads fuel onto river and sea tankers for export, and it burned for two days while a local channel wrote that reeds might be on fire. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow has officially acknowledged the hit. It came hours after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Russia has spent the autumn hammering Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter. Ukraine’s long-range drones keep hitting the refineries, depots, and terminals that fuel Russia’s army and earn it export revenue. Every burned tank turns that revenue into repair bills, while Moscow is already subsidizing its own fuel pumps. A refinery-only truce of the kind the White House described a day after the strike would shield the Russian plants that feed terminals like this one. Seven of 12 tanks out of action Astra’s analysts concluded from eyewitness footage that at least seven of the terminal’s 12 large tanks had been knocked out. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ counted seven burned-out tanks and one more scorched by the fire. The fire was still burning in the early hours of 12 October. Local channel Rostov Glavny posted video of the burning tank farm, passing on rumors that reeds were on fire and noting the city’s second day under smoke, The Moscow Times reported . Footage filmed in the daytime on 12 October showed no more open flames, only gray smoke, according to Astra. Satellite image of the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk refinery in Rostov-on-Don, Russia, during the fire, 10 October 2026. Satellite image: Radio Liberty A terminal that loads fuel for export The site is the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant, formerly known as Yug Rusi, in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny District. It receives, stores, and transships fuel onto river and sea tankers, including for export, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said . The terminal also supplies fuel to the Russian army and earns Moscow hard currency, ZN reported . The Moscow Times put its loading capacity at 3.5 million tons a year and its tank farm at about 60,000 cubic meters, roughly 16 million gallons. Explore further Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say The refinery itself stands in the town of Novoshakhtinsk near the border with Russian-occupied Luhansk Oblast. The terminal sits on the Don River with access to the Sea of Azov, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi noted . Ukraine hit the refinery in June, and Ukraine’s General Staff reported striking the Yug Rusi terminal on 9 July, placing it in Bataysk. A night of drones over the region Exilenova+ posted images of the burning terminal in the early hours of 10 October. It presented them as the site after Trump’s phone call with Putin. The channel later shared NASA satellite fire data showing the blaze. Rostov Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar claimed the attack injured six people. Slyusar further stated air defenses downed more than 100 drones over the region. Radio Liberty’s Russian Service noted that neither side had officially confirmed the hit on the terminal. Aerial view of the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk refinery in Rostov-on-Don, Russia, with the tanks Astra assessed as hit marked in red and orange, 12 October 2026. Map: Astra Hours after the US-Russia diesel deal The strike came hours after Trump announced on 9 October that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to US and global markets. The US Treasury then cleared the trade with a sanctions license. On 11 October, Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Under it, he expects Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, a White House official told Axios. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that evening that Ukraine’s armed forces had received all relevant orders. Neither Ukrainian monitoring channels nor Russian officials have reported a new strike on a Russian oil facility since. On 13 October, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to guarantee an energy ceasefire if Russia took matching steps. title: Sixteen Years Later, Marfin Suspects Face Tougher Charges
body: ATHENS, October 2026 — The three Marfin arson suspects will answer upgraded charges of murder as part of a terrorist act on 21 and 23 October, over the 2010 firebombing of an Athens bank. Two of the accused will appear again at the courts in the former Evelpidon military academy on Wednesday 21 October. The third will appear on Friday 23 October. All three asked for, and received, extra time to study the case file with their lawyers before making supplementary statements. They are already in pre-trial detention. The added charges also include the attempted murder of 24 employees. At the time of the attack, they were working in the Marfin Bank branch on Stadiou Street. Charges against Marfin arson suspects No new evidence linked to the added charges appears in the case file, according to reports. Similarly, it holds nothing on the origin of the anonymous email that led to the arrests. Minor scuffles broke out outside the courts on Tuesday 13 October, during the latest stage of the legal process. Two of the Marfin arson suspects, both 42-year-old men, went into custody in July. The third, a 46-year-old woman, was extradited from the United Kingdom and remanded a month later. British police first arrested the woman in July , before her transfer to Athens in August. The 2010 attack Three people died in the attack on 5 May 2010, including a pregnant employee. Attackers threw firebombs into the bank during a mass protest against Greece’s austerity measures, held on a day of general strike. Greek City Times reported in July how authorities identified the three, 16 years after the fire. Once the investigation ends, a judicial council will decide whether the Marfin arson suspects should stand trial. Source: Ta Nea, Kathimerini The post Sixteen Years Later, Marfin Suspects Face Tougher Charges appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Fixing the Army’s MDMP Fixation
body:
General George S. Patton reminds us that a good plan, violently executed today is better than a perfect plan next week. Doctrine agrees. Field Manual 5-0, Planning and Orders Production clearly states that “planning and preparation accomplish nothing if the command does not execute effectively.”
The curious question then is why the Army remains so fixated on the military decision-making process (MDMP) and the laborious and still imperfect plans it produces—especially when there’s another choice at hand. The rapid decision-making and synchronization Process (RDSP) is the Army’s methodology for rapidly revising plans today.
Unfortunately, RDSP is not well known. The last six CTC Trends documents mention MDMP 436 times compared to just 17 for RDSP. In doctrine, FM 5-0 gives MDMP a careful step-by-step description over 56 pages compared to just 7 for RDSP. As of 2020 , students at the Command and General Staff College received 30 hours of instruction on MDMP and just 2 on RDSP. The situation is not much better in our Army’s journals. Back issues of Military Review mention MDMP in 37 issues, while RDSP appears in just one. Here at the Modern War Institute, 28 articles mention MDMP while just 3 mention RDSP. Sadly, when RDSP is known , it sometimes gets the bad rap of “two majors in a room, making decisions.”
Assuming lack of attention reveals a lack of awareness, this is a problem. Units should know RDSP, as it provides a timely complement to MDMP. Other writers have noted that RDSP allows well-trained teams to deliver a wargamed course of action that integrates recognized variance in four to six hours, and my own experience as a battalion commander confirms this. Fortunately, this is exactly in line with historically available time for brigade and battalion planning in battle. Where MDMP’s thorough analysis yields plans that are often stale, RDSP by a well-trained staff is both fast and considered.
To win our battles, the Army should rebalance training away from MDMP toward RDSP.
RDSP is one of six doctrinal planning methods laid out in FM 5-0. Derived from earlier thinking , the goal of RDSP is an acceptable course of action. Notably, RDSP differs from MDMP in that it generally produces one satisfactory plan, and so omits the course of action comparison, analysis, and selection steps from MDMP. Current and future operations cells drive RDSP by combining “their experiences and intuition to quickly understand the situation and develop a course of action.” However, FM 5-0 is also clear that skill with RDSP does not just appear. Instead, “commanders and staffs develop this capability through training.”
RDSP follows completion of MDMP. MDMP produces the commander’s intent, base plan, and key warfighting products like the commander’s critical information requirements, execution matrix, and decision-support matrix. These tools help account for anticipated variance and decisions. Then, RDSP helps commanders resynchronize operations to stay on track as un anticipated variances from the base plan present themselves.
Variance is the key insight of RDSP. FM 5-0 defines a variance as the “difference between the actual situation and what the plan forecasted the situation would be at that time or event.” After recognizing variance, the commander and staff decide whether minor changes within the commander’s intent are sufficient to address the new opportunities and threats. Faced with substantial variance, the staff might significantly modify the plan or initiate MDMP.
Broadly, RDSP determines how variances impact the planned course of action and then revises the course of action to fit the new conditions over five steps. The first two steps of RDSP assess the situation, determine whether the variance requires minor or significant changes to the existing plan, and outline the unit’s options. The latter three steps develop, refine and validate, and then implement the course of action.
Perhaps because hardly anyone uses RDSP, doctrine better describes what RDSP is than how to do it. There’s a small amount of writing on how to apply RDSP at the division level , but almost nothing for brigades and battalions. These units with smaller staffs are less likely to have fully developed branches and sequels coming out of MDMP, are more taxed by on-call planning, and have the smallest future plans cells. While doctrine emphasizes the continuous nature of the assessment steps of RDSP, pulling small staffs together to focus on RDSP’s assessment steps can come at the cost of other critical staff functions during operations.
In my battalion, RDSP is the battle rhythm event that starts the daily planning effort. Validated through a Warfighter exercise and National Training Center rotation, we found several benefits to giving RDSP a central role in our planning. First, setting a daily planning period allowed us to also create a small future plans cell that complemented the staff during one twelve-hour shift each day. Second, the battle rhythm event guarded against gradual drift in staff estimates or cross-cutting issues that a single staff section might not catch. Routinely gathering an outside team under the supervision of a more experienced leader increases the likelihood that substantial variances are recognized and addressed.
The key question during the assessment is whether the variances can be handled within the commander’s intent. If it cannot, we begin MDMP. If it can be addressed within the commander’s intent, the staff then generates options to address the variance.
We developed a table to walk our plans cell through RDSP’s assessment steps (an example of the table can be found here ). In the first step, the staff compares their updated running estimates against where they expected to be, filling out the “expected situation” and “actual situation” columns of the table below. They are alert for the presence of exceptional information that would trigger an anticipated decision. If no anticipated decision criteria is met, the staff notes the significant variances from the plan in the third column. Finally, the staff generates options the battalion could take to address the variance before moving into course of action development.
Let’s work an example. As Task Force Green’s RDSP meeting convened, the staff gathered key tools: the commander’s intent, the operation order, the commander’s critical information requirements, updated running estimates, a map with enemy and friendly dispositions, the execution matrix, and the decision support matrix. Reviewing their plan, Task Force Green expected both Attack and Battle Companies to be on line at Phase Line ALPHA with fire support, obstacles emplaced, effective communication, and sufficient supplies at a specified time, H+6. Instead, Attack Company had found limited enemy resistance and pushed forward to Phase Line BRAVO. This unanticipated opportunity came with costs: exposed flanks, expended fuel, no fire support, weak communications, and no clear picture of the enemy’s location. With variance across the warfighting functions, the staff completed the assessment table and Task Force Green’s executive officer determined that the situation required significant modification of the existing plan. After an hour of analysis, the staff carried options into course of action development.
In the two hours after the assessment, the planning team developed, refined and validated, and implemented an updated course of action. As they started, the planners incorporated proposed actions from the RDSP table into a single course of action that reinforced Attack Company with proposed changes to the three key warfighting products: commander’s critical information requirements, decision support matrix, and synchronization matrix. The planning team then wargamed this course of action with the box method on the decisive point, updated the warfighting products, and briefed the wargamed course of action to the commander. Upon approval, the assistant operations officer took another hour to turn the approved course of action into a fragmentary order for dissemination, completing RDSP.
In just four hours, Task Force Green’s staff rapidly developed, validated, and implemented a well-synchronized plan that accounted for unexpected variance. Directed courses of action are also quick, but tired commanders are unlikely to identify and address variances as well as a fresh staff.
Fixing the Army’s MDMP fixation is an imperative. MDMP is well understood thanks to significant investment in the Army’s schools and units. Students in every course from Battle Staff to the Special Forces Qualification Course invest hundreds of hours learning to develop time-consuming, optimal solutions. Almost none is spent learning how to rapidly revise plans while in contact through RDSP. Each of us has a role in rebalancing away from MDMP.
Units can start today with RDSP. Training and evaluation outline reports 71-BN-5002 and 71-BDE-5002 available on the Army Training Network offer checklists for units that want to effectively adjust their plans and win in combat. Our initial staff training for RDSP leveraged the tools described in this article, a simple tactical scenario, and large language models to build the necessary inputs. With these training inputs in hand, a one- or two-hour class is enough to establish a baseline for how RDSP will work for you. I have also found RDSP a useful framework for tactical exercises and garrison planning. Try it out.
But the Combined Arms Center at Fort Leavenworth could really drive broader change in how the Army decides and synchronizes during operations. The Combined Arms Doctrine Directorate could shift RDSP’s description from what to how by incorporating the table our unit employed. With updated doctrine, both the Command and General Staff Officer Course and the Battle Staff course should shift some hours spent on MDMP toward RDSP, ensuring that graduates return to the field able to both develop ideal plans and adjust them during the battle. Finally, leader training programs for both Warfighter exercises and combat training centers should introduce RDSP as an essential component of their staff education. Together, these reforms will develop leaders who can not only build optimal plans but also adjust them under fire.
MDMP is not enough. Lethal units must rapidly revise plans to seize opportunities and squash threats. Together, let’s push the Army away from exclusive focus on the time-consuming and still imperfect MDMP toward making better decisions in contact with RDSP.
Lt. Col. Zachary Griffiths commands 4th Battalion, 10th Special Forces Group (Airborne).
