title: Maritime exercise Ibsamar IX gets under way in Simon’s Town
body:
South Africa, India and Brazil have begun the ninth edition of multinational maritime Exercise Ibsamar, with an expanded programme of air defence, weapons firing and cross-deck helicopter operations aimed at strengthening cooperation against shared maritime threats.
The opening ceremony was held at Naval Base Simon’s Town, Cape Town, on Monday 12 October, bringing together the navies of South Africa, India and Brazil for a week of joint training and professional exchanges. The 2026 iteration is led by India.
Running from 12 to 20 October, the biennial trilateral exercise aims to improve interoperability, strengthen maritime security partnerships and enhance the participating forces’ ability to operate together in an increasingly complex maritime environment.
The theme for this edition, “Stronger Together Towards a Shared Future in the Maritime Domain,” reflects the three countries’ commitment to cooperation, freedom of navigation and the security of vital international shipping routes.
Captain Rohit Mishra of the Indian Navy, Exercise Joint Task Force Commander, said Ibsamar had developed into an important platform for professional interaction, operational coordination and the exchange of best practices since its inception in 2008.
“Ibsamar is a powerful expression of our collective resolve to work together towards a secure, stable and peaceful maritime environment,” Mishra said at the opening ceremony.
He highlighted the growing range of challenges confronting maritime forces, including piracy, maritime crime, threats to shipping, human trafficking and illegal fishing.
“No single maritime nation alone can respond to the challenges,” he said, noting the need for coordinated responses, professional competence and effective cooperation between like-minded navies.
The exercise comprises a harbour phase from 12 to 14 October, followed by a sea phase scheduled for 15 to 19 October.
During the harbour phase at Simon’s Town, personnel will undertake joint operational planning, professional lectures, subject-matter expert exchanges, communication training and cross-deck familiarisation. Sports activities will also provide opportunities for interaction between the participating contingents.
Sea phase activities include surface warfare, air defence, anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction, visit, board, search and seizure operations, anti-piracy drills, search and rescue, damage control, firefighting and helicopter operations.
The Exercise Director, Rear Admiral (JG) Jabulani Mbotho of the South African Navy, said this year’s edition would build on previous iterations by increasing the complexity and scope of the training.
“This time, we are introducing new air defence exercises. We are increasing the scope of VBSS (visit, board, search and seizure). We are increasing the scope of firing exercises at sea,” he said.
Cross-deck helicopter operations will also form part of the programme, providing opportunities for crews to familiarise themselves with different aircraft, platforms and operating procedures.
The participating forces include the Indian Navy’s guided-missile frigate INS Tarkash, the Brazilian Navy corvette BNS Barroso, and South African frigate SAS Amatola, Multi-Purpose Inshore Patrol Vessels SAS King Sekhukhune I and SAS Adam Kok III, together with the submarine SAS Manthatisi. Special forces from all three countries and embarked helicopters will also contribute to the exercise.
The Indian contingent includes a Chetak (Indian-built Alouette III) helicopter, while the Brazilian ship is equipped with a Super Lynx helicopter.
South Africa will additionally commit Super Lynx and Oryx helicopters, as well as the Gripen fighter. Other South African National Defence Force elements include maritime task force personnel, military police and defence intelligence in support of the joint exercise.
A key focus of Ibsamar IX will be the development of a shared operational picture and the ability to communicate securely and effectively during combined operations.
Mishra said the Indian Navy had deployed NISHAR MITRA terminals, an internet-enabled secure command, control and communications system, for the exercise. The laptop-based system will be provided to each participating ship, with an additional node available at the Joint Task Force Commander’s headquarters ashore.
Training and familiarisation with the system during the harbour phase are intended to support coordinated communications and improve maritime domain awareness during the sea phase.
Mbotho said the exercise would focus on identifying activity at sea, including piracy and other illegal activities, while making use of maritime domain awareness centres to build a recognised maritime picture.
He said the participating navies faced common threats, ranging from piracy and the trafficking of arms, drugs and people to illegal fishing.
“We feel that no single Navy can actually counter all these threats all alone,” Mbotho said. “The way forward is to join our hands together, build a stronger cooperation, and operate together in the maritime domain so that we are able to counter these threats.”
For Brazil, Ibsamar also reinforces its commitment to peace and cooperation in the South Atlantic.
Captain (BN) Angelo Chambarelli of the Brazilian Navy welcomed the opportunity to train alongside South African and Indian counterparts, describing the exercise as an important means of strengthening combined maritime security capabilities.
He also highlighted the importance of maintaining safety and freedom of navigation across the maritime routes connecting the South Atlantic and Indian Ocean regions.
Brazil’s participation, he said, reflected its commitment to the South Atlantic Peace and Cooperation Zone, known by its Portuguese acronym ZOPACAS, established in 1986.
Mishra said India’s participation reflected its commitment to a cooperative and inclusive maritime order, respect for international law, freedom of navigation and the peaceful use of the seas.
“Our role in this exercise is not merely to demonstrate operational proficiency, but also to build enduring professional and personal relationships and contribute to collective maritime security,” he said.
For the three navies, the value of Ibsamar extends beyond the individual training serials. By sharing expertise, comparing procedures and operating together, participating personnel will develop a better understanding of one another’s capabilities and improve their ability to respond to maritime emergencies and security threats in the future.
Prior to the Opening Ceremony, the three countries signed the Implementing Arrangement for support during Exercise Ibsamar IX.
The sea phase will take place along the Cape West coast and is scheduled to conclude on 20 October.

title: USA and Europe drafting peace plan for Ukraine and Russia involving security guarantees and territorial compromise – media
body:
The USA and European countries are developing a peace initiative to end Russia's war against Ukraine; the plan entails funding for Ukraine's reconstruction, security guarantees, economic cooperation with Russia, and a ceasefire along the current front line, The Washington Post reports, citing a US official familiar with the negotiations.
According to the ezine, the diplomatic push came during a six-hour meeting last Friday in Florida hosted by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The meeting, which included Ukrainian officials and representatives of Britain, France and Germany, was held at the Shell Bay Golf Club, a development owned by Witkoff in Hallandale Beach.
According to the Washington Post, U.S. negotiators are trying to frame a package that addresses Ukraine’s and Russia’s postwar needs in a way that ends the bloodbath and leaves both countries better off — as a sweetener for a territorial compromise neither side will like.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be — and then make concessions,” the publication quoted an American official as saying.
The peace plan comprises four main components. Ukraine’s reconstruction would be the first pillar. The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock want to create a framework for meeting Zelensky’s myriad cash needs — for rebuilding the devastated areas of the country, providing benefits to families of dead and wounded soldiers, and restoring a shattered economy.
Security guarantees would be the second essential component. Ukraine would get a pledge from the United States and European nations that they would respond militarily if Russia attacked again, which the U.S. official described as equivalent to NATO’s Article 5. The official said Russia would also negotiate agreements with Europe that would address its security concerns, though it’s not clear what this would involve.
A third pillar would be economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy deal. One aspect might be a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia splitting the profits. Such a pipeline could sharply reduce European energy costs, the official said. In addition to providing Russia with “long-term access to the European energy market,” a peace deal would specify how and when existing economic sanctions would be removed. The final, the fourth, piece of the deal would be the most unpalatable. Russia, which began the war hoping to conquer all of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the existing front line, or “line of control,” as negotiators describe it. For Ukraine, that would mean allowing Russia to control the territory it occupies — including the bitterly contested area known as Donbas. One hurdle is that the line of control is fuzzy, given small shifts in the front almost every day.
According to a European diplomat, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries are affecting Russia's economy and strengthening Ukraine's negotiating position.
“Clearly, the Ukrainians’ ability to strike refineries is having impact on Russia’s economy. It has increased Zelenskyy’s leverage,” the European diplomat is quoted by the publication as saying.

title: Press review: Russia-US gas deal riles Europe as Putin says no bombs on Ukraine vote day
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Europe seeks to derail the Russia-US diesel deal; Moscow is ready to halt strikes on Ukraine on its election day; and the US and Iran can't seem to agree on de-escalation at sea. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
The European Union will try to disrupt Russian fuel supplies to the United States and step up pressure on Moscow, experts interviewed by Izvestia said. Foreign ministers of EU member states have approved the bloc’s 22nd package of sanctions on Russia. However, the EU remains divided, with some countries planning to promote a pragmatic approach to relations with Russia.
The EU isn't happy about the Russia-US fuel agreement and will try to disrupt supplies, political scientist Denis Denisov said. One thing it could do is send its leaders on a series of visits to US President Donald Trump in a bid to persuade him to abandon the deal, the way they did following the Russia-US talks in Alaska. Besides, Europe has high hopes for the Democratic Party’s potential victory in the upcoming US midterm congressional elections.
Still, the EU is divided over how to approach Russia as some member states call for dialogue with Moscow. Bulgaria and Slovakia seek to maintain Russian energy supplies, which the EU intends to stop as early as next year, St. Petersburg State University professor Natalya Yeryomina stressed. However, as Brussels will work to derail the Russia-US deal, it won’t allow EU members to reach similar agreements with Moscow, the political scientist pointed out.
Meanwhile, the Russia-US diesel deal has caused a stir not only in Europe and Ukraine but also in the US Congress, Vedomosti notes. A bipartisan group of seven senators has called on Trump to drop Russian diesel imports.
If Democrats win the midterm elections, the deal could be scrapped through a bill fully banning the import of Russian petroleum products, provided it is backed by some Republicans, said Vadim Kozlov, head of the Internal Policy Department at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for US and Canadian Studies. "A move to reverse course on the deal is unlikely to gain support from enough lawmakers at this point because Trump is sure to portray it as Congress obstructing efforts to lower US diesel prices," the expert concluded.
Russia is not prepared to accept the 60-day ceasefire proposed by Vladimir Zelensky, who has claimed that this would allow presidential elections to be held in Ukraine. However, Russian President Vladimir Putin has indicated that what he is willing to do is halt strikes on Ukraine on the day of the vote, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. In the meantime, Moscow remains open to talks, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told Izvestia.
Some are clamoring for elections to be held in Ukraine, said Igor Markov, a former member of the country’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada. And the reasons go beyond simply changing the government. According to Markov, some of the country’s elite already expect the domestic political struggle to intensify once hostilities are over. That's when people will be blamed for decisions made over the past several years, including major corruption crimes, he explained.
Dmitry Solonnikov, director of the Institute of Contemporary State Development, believes that elections in Ukraine could facilitate negotiations on resolving the crisis.
Still, settlement efforts are being hampered by the position taken by the majority of European Union countries, which continue to supply Kiev with weapons and actually encourage it to prolong the conflict. By contrast, the United States under Donald Trump is seeking to find a diplomatic way out of the crisis, even though Washington has not completely halted its support for Kiev.
A change of president in Kiev would not guarantee a shift in Ukraine’s approach to the conflict. Whoever succeeds Zelensky would have to take Brussels’ position into account, while the European Union appears to believe that continued confrontation serves its interests. Notably, European leaders choose to ignore Moscow’s direct statements that Russia has neither plans nor reasons to engage in an armed conflict with the EU. Within this framework, Ukraine’s leader remains merely a variable in someone else’s strategic equation.
A brief lull in strikes in the Persian Gulf was once again disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. With talks stalled, the United States and Iran could engage in another round of active hostilities after the US midterm elections, Vedomosti writes.
Alexey Yurk, a researcher at the Center for Middle East Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, doubts that the election outcome will significantly affect the US president’s position. "Congressional resolutions calling for an end to military operations are advisory in nature and can in no way stop the White House," the expert said.
After the elections, Trump will no longer be so worried about how the American public views his foreign policy actions in the Middle East, Ilya Vaskin, junior researcher at the Higher School of Economics’ Center for the Study of the Middle East, Caucasus and Central Asia, pointed out. On the other hand, the expert did not rule out the possibility that the Democrats could take control of Congress following the vote, making it much harder for the White House to conduct combat operations.
In terms of prospects for an agreement, Washington and Tehran and pretty far apart in their positions on most issues, including the status of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions on Iran, Yurk noted. The sides have also lost all trust in each other, making it all but impossible for either party to concede anything, as the United States has repeatedly launched military operations against Iran in the midst of negotiations, the political scientist added.
In the event of an escalation, hostilities are likely to enter a more destructive phase, Yury Lyamin, senior researcher at the Center for Strategies and Technologies, warned. The US military could launch massive strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure, while Tehran could retaliate by targeting oil and gas facilities and other critical economic sectors of US regional allies, the analyst said.
Saudi Arabia has found itself in a difficult position amid its conflict with the Houthis. A coalition led by Riyadh previously announced a large-scale military operation against the movement, but Saudi Arabia has so far limited its involvement to targeted airstrikes, while it is Yemeni government forces that have engaged in combat, Izvestia notes.
Middle East expert Kirill Semyonov believes that Saudi Arabia has no other option but to launch a ground operation because the Houthis are pursuing a policy of maximum pressure on Riyadh.
The Ansar Allah Houthi movement openly describes itself as Tehran’s main ally in the fight against the United States and Israel. In order to end the conflict, Riyadh will have to enter direct talks with Iran on dividing spheres of influence in the region, Danila Krylov, a researcher with the Department of the Middle and Post-Soviet East at the Institute of Scientific Information on Social Sciences of the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.
Successful Houthi attacks on airports have prompted media reports highlighting the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia’s air defenses. In 2017, Riyadh signed a memorandum on purchasing Russia’s S-400 air defense systems but later abandoned the plan under pressure from the United States. Saudi Arabia eventually yielded to Washington’s demands and signed a separate contract to buy US-made THAAD missile defense systems.
Now, the US has in fact left its once-strategic ally to its own devices, as Americans are unable to supply Riyadh with enough interceptors, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes. That said, Saudi Arabia has turned to France, Britain, Egypt and Pakistan for additional weapons. With the Strait of Hormuz remaining a dangerous route and US President Donald Trump with his hands full on the eve of the November midterm elections, Saudi Arabia is hastily seeking to form a regional coalition willing to fight the Houthis in Yemen without Washington’s support. However, Riyadh will be the one to bear the costs of the war, which could turn out to be the fatal straw breaking the back of the Saudi economy, which is already hemorrhaging money amid the US-Iran conflict.
Russian and foreign analysts have lowered their forecasts for Russian grain exports. Disruptions to shipments through Black Sea ports, the main channel for agricultural exports, is being cited as the main reason, Nezavisimaya Gazeta reports.
Exporters are exploring alternative shipping options though ports in the Far East. Chinese ports could become transit hubs for supplies to various countries, said Ksenia Bolomatova, executive director of the Russian Grain Association. The Baltic Sea route serves traditional destinations of Russian grain exports such as the Middle East, Turkey and North Africa. However, shipping grain to Southeast Asian countries via this route is more difficult, so developing Far Eastern terminals is necessary, the expert stressed.
The Russian Grain Association believes that other exporters will not be able to fully compensate for the shortfall in Russian grain supplies. "Moreover, customers will have to pay more for what they receive, as we have already seen a price rise of 30%," Bolomatova warned.
Amid the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine, Russian grain exports along traditional routes remain largely constrained, Finam analyst Alexander Potavin agrees. "The main grain export route used to run through Russia’s southern ports on the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. Now, it has been disrupted. There are some alternatives but those routes are longer and more expensive, nor can they ensure the same volumes of supplies at this point. Agricultural products can be shipped via Baltic ports, including Ust Luga, which is well suited for exports to Turkey, North Africa and the Middle East, but it now takes much longer to deliver grain from southern Russia to these ports, and it also costs more," the expert added.
"Grain exports through the Far East are more convenient for Asian customers, but they require additional rail and port infrastructure. As a result, it turns out that disruptions affecting Azov and Black Sea ports, as well as risks associated with shipments across the Black Sea, are complicating Russian grain exports this year," Potavin concluded.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

title: The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Has Poured Millions Into Nevada Shell Companies
body:
The problem is that the company—Lantern Production Consultants LLC—doesn’t seem to exist anywhere beyond a post office box in the Spanish Springs shopping complex.
Lantern Production Consultants has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, part of a network of pro-AI super PACs funded by the Leading the Future PAC, for a wide array of services, including polling, digital advertising, research, and strategy, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by WIRED. Backed by major AI investors, Leading the Future has taken a main role in supporting candidates who back what it calls “an AI innovation policy agenda.”
It is just one of four mysterious LLCs based out of Nevada that have received payments from super PACs in the Leading the Future PAC network, including Think Big and American Mission. The network, which is also based in Nevada, has raised over $140 million to influence political campaigns that align with AI-industry priorities in the midterms.
Summit Ridge Media Group LLC, which received around $13 million between December 2025 and September 2026 from American Mission, lists an address at a mail center in a Reno strip mall. Blue Horizon Compliance Consultants, which also appears in the filings, has its address listed as a Staples location in Reno. And Prusik Partners LLC’s listed address is at a strip mall in Henderson, Nevada, sharing a building with a chiropractor and a beauty salon.
Nevada’s secretary of state told WIRED that they were unable to locate any records for the businesses.



Got a Tip?




Do you know about what’s happening here? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at tessowen.77.



Election watchdogs argue that these LLCs are shell companies, designed to mask the identities of strategists, consultants, and production companies who are working with Leading the Future. “This is about hiding where the money is going,” claims Shanna Ports, senior legal counsel at the Campaign Legal Center.
In May, the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC, which enforces campaign finance laws, alleging that Think Big and American Mission had broken federal law by using shell companies in this way. Specifically, lawyers with the Campaign Legal Center alleged that super PACs in the Leading the Future network had violated the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) by failing to disclose the actual recipients of their payments. The LLCs, they wrote in their complaint, “function as mere extensions of the super PACs they serve.”
In an emailed statement to WIRED, Leading the Future spokesperson Jesse Hunt wrote, “We comply with all applicable laws and this is merely a desperate ploy for attention from Public First, Anthropic, and the groups aligned with their outside organizations who see our message resonating with the public and policymakers.”
WIRED reached out to Anthropic and Public First—a pro-AI super PAC focused on transparency and safeguards that has significant backing from Anthropic leadership—to ask about Leading the Future’s charge. “I have no idea what they’re talking about,” said Public First spokesperson Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez. “We unequivocally had nothing to do with this complaint.” Anthropic did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The Campaign Legal Center said in a statement to WIRED that the suggestion they “filed this complaint at the direction of, on behalf of, or in consultation with any outside entity is absolutely false.”
The Campaign Legal Center doesn’t expect its case to be heard by the FEC anytime soon, given that the FEC is essentially toothless at the moment. The FEC has six commissioner seats, all presidential appointees. To make a decision on a legal complaint, the FEC needs a quorum of four commissioners, which it hasn’t had since May 2025. Meanwhile, Think Big and American Mission have continued to pour millions of dollars into the Nevada LLCs.
Leading the Future has piqued a lot of public interest, not just because it has the most cash of any pro-AI group—thanks to Silicon Valley bankrollers like billionaire Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman—but also because it funnels money into super PACs that support both Republicans and Democrats. Think Big overwhelmingly funds Democrats, and American Mission funds Republicans.
The fact that the Leading the Future network is playing both sides of the aisle, supporting AI-friendly Democrats and Republicans, has generated speculation from experts as to why it’s spending so much on shielded vendors. Typically, political strategists and consultants cater to Democrats or Republicans, not both. “If you’re running in a Democrat primary and Think Big comes to spend in your race, and they drop half a million on your congressional district doing positive ads while using Republican vendors and strategists—that’s news,” speculates Kyle Morse, deputy executive director of Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit advocacy group that’s critical of big tech.
There are plenty of reasons why a super PAC may want to hide its vendors, ranging from benign to nefarious. In this instance, it's possible businesses don’t want to be publicly associated with a pro-AI campaign. But with the FEC lacking a quorum for the foreseeable future, “We are not fundamentally equipped to figure out what’s happening here,” says Morse.
Leading the Future isn’t the only PAC accused of shielding vendors by using shell companies. Earlier this year, Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC against pro-gun YouTuber Brandon Herrera, who is running for Congress in Texas District 23, alleging that more than 99 percent of his campaign’s disbursements were funneled through Texas Strategy Group, which was, the complaint claimed, “being used as a shell entity.” When reached for comment, Herrera’s campaign directed WIRED to conservative personality Matt Braynard, who runs Texas Strategy Group. Braynard strongly denied the Campaign Legal Center’s accusations, calling the complaint “meritless” and “little more than a recycled legal theory from a partisan advocacy group.”
Campaign Legal Center also filed a complaint with the FEC against Lead Left PAC, a pop-up super PAC that was funded by Republican operatives while posing as a Democratic entity with the presumed goal of meddling in Democratic primaries. Campaign Legal Center accused it of paying shell companies to avoid being linked to Republican strategists.
Ports says that this marks a disturbing trend in campaign finance, at a time when dark money in politics already reigns. “There’s no way of tracing the source behind the money, and that’s bad enough on its own,” says Ports. “Now there’s this new component, where groups are playing games to hide where the money is being spent. As a result, voters really lack fundamental information about where the money is coming from and where it’s going.”
Updated 2:15 pm ET, 10/13/2026: This story has been updated with further comment from Nevada's secretary of state and the Campaign Legal Center.

title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
body: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available. Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla . And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure. But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it. Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience. But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones? The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic , several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude. So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model. There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid. Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands. But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them). In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code. Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves. Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters. Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from. The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models. Can we make open models safer—and more open? A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models. Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge. Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a recent preprint . But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says. If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information. Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says. Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured. Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.

title: [Kasalikasan] A visit to the homes at Smokey Mountain
body: I first heard of the issue at Smokey Mountain in 2024, when some Tondo residents trooped outside Manila City Hall. It was a protest against relocation and a proposed waste-to-energy facility. Before that, I only knew of Smokey Mountain because of the pop group’s hit Paraiso and from a cursory knowledge of a violent demolition at the mountain of trash years ago. Last May, I started arranging for a visit. On a Thursday in early July, we hiked what is left of Smokey Mountain for a few minutes, and at the top, saw shelters, families, and dogs. There were trees and patches of land where people farm. The smell of garbage permeated the air. From the top, I saw the roofs of the housing tenements. I talked to the residents on top of the mountain — one of them was a young girl named Jenny. She struck me because her voice was clear and she offered to read me a poem she wrote. It mattered that I saw her home and heard of her dreams. A few days later, I attended a consultation for the Smokey Mountain rehabilitation and talked with an elderly woman seated next to me. She lives in one of the tenements and was among those dispersed in 1995. She had a story to tell. So we went back to Tondo to talk to her again, this time recorded on camera. Then I wondered if the relocation site in Cavite would be convincing enough for informal settlers to uproot themselves. We visited the site to see the housing units for ourselves. In late July, we spoke with Phil Ecology Systems Corporation. In August, we then spoke with the court-receiver managing the assets related to the Smokey Mountain development. I understood that the company is set on making profits, as is its nature, and the government has yet to settle obligations under this partnership to develop the area. I began to see my visits to Smokey Mountain as a continuation of an exploration of the theme of home. Before I went to Tondo, my last fieldwork was in South Upi in Maguindanao del Sur, and in Marawi City. There are indigenous peoples struggling to protect their ancestral land in the Bangsamoro. There are people in Marawi City still calling for a safe and dignified return to their homes nine years after the siege . And at Smokey Mountain, despite its past and ongoing threat of relocation, people have made farms and communities. What makes struggling for a disputed environment worthwhile is a home. This documentary, which took months of fieldwork, reporting, writing, and editing, can be watched here . You can support our independent journalism by being a Rappler+ member . Food supply sufficient for Super El Niño, P45-B aid coming for farmers – DA The role of the news media in fighting the climate crisis MovePH welcomes new Movers for community action, local storytelling Amid rising school violence, citizens pitch solutions to keep children safe – Rappler.com Kasalikasan is a bimonthly newsletter featuring environmental and science issues, delivered straight to your inbox every other Tuesday. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to subscribe.

title: URCS joins relief efforts following Russian strikes on Mykolaiv
body:
The Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) rapid response team was working throughout Monday at the sites of Russian attacks in Mykolaiv, assisting with the aftermath.

“Throughout the day, volunteers joined other emergency services at the impact sites, searching for people affected by the attacks and remaining on standby to provide first aid if needed,” URCS said on Facebook Tuesday.

According to the State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Mykolaiv region, a drone attack caused a fire at a cargo terminal, which firefighters extinguished. Later that evening, Russian drones attacked a vehicle service station in Mykolaiv district, sparking a fire at the station and in the surrounding open area where car tyres were stored. Due to the ongoing threat of further attacks, emergency responders and volunteers repeatedly withdrew to a safe distance before returning to continue their work.

title: Impeachment court lifts sub judice rule on withdrawn charges vs Sara Duterte
body: MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday, October 13, lifted the sub judice rule on three withdrawn impeachment articles against Vice President Sara Duterte, allowing the parties to publicly discuss the dropped charges . The decision drew objections from lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, who warned that abandoning Rule 18 midway through the trial could undermine the integrity of the proceedings. The three withdrawn articles cover the alleged misuse of confidential funds (Article I), bribery (Article III), and grave threats (Article IV). The court earlier granted the House prosecution panel’s request to withdraw these charges, leaving only Article II, which involves Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth. “We actually object to the abandonment of Rule 18 if we are to be true and faithful to the rationale and wisdom of the sub judice rule that not only permeates this court, it permeates the entire judicial system,” Sison said. “It is needed to maintain the integrity of the proceedings. There should not be any single instance or occasion that this should be abandoned in the middle of trial and right before the defense or respondent presents her case,” she added. Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero explained that relaxing Rule 18 was intended to allow Duterte to respond to the withdrawn articles both inside and outside the courtroom. “The reason behind the relaxing of Rule 18 was more to afford, actually, the respondent to respond in the manner she may deem fit both in this courtroom, subject to the objections and ruling of the court, and outside,” Escudero said. Amid the defense’s objections, Senator-judge Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan moved to reconsider the ruling and maintain the enforcement of Rule 18 pending a possible motion for reconsideration from the defense. “If the court agrees, pending a possible motion for reconsideration when we resume, then Rule 18 should continue to be enforced and not abandoned,” Pangilinan said. Pangilinan also moved to authorize Escudero to issue a resolution on the matter during the trial break. Senator-judge Joel Villanueva seconded the motion. Defense lawyer Michael Poa cited a gag order issued by a Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) in connection with the separate grave threats case against Duterte. “We just wanted the court to know that the difficulty we’re facing with this, well, lifting of Rule 18 as regards to those articles,” Poa said. “For example, for grave threat, we have a gag order from the RTC, Your Honor, trying that case on speaking on it. So in a way, the prosecution can discuss it but we cannot,” he added. Escudero said his earlier ruling would remain in effect unless the defense indicated otherwise. He added that Pangilinan’s motion for reconsideration would be taken up, with the court deciding whether to reconsider the ruling in whole or in part. “After which, the motion for reconsideration of Senator-judge Francis Pangilinan will come into operation as it will be recorded by the clerk and the reconsideration of that rule shall be made either in whole or in part,” Escudero said. Rule 18 of the Senate impeachment rules bars the presiding officer, senator-judges, prosecutors, the respondent, their counsel, and witnesses from publicly commenting on or disclosing the merits of an ongoing impeachment trial, including through online platforms. In August , Escudero ordered the strict enforcement of the sub judice rule. – Rappler.com

title: F1 announces 10-year deal for African Grand Prix in Rwanda from 'early 2030s'
body: Formula One has announced a 10-year agreement to bring the sport back to Africa, with Rwanda set to host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s. The agreement sees the sport head back to the continent for the first time since 1993, when the South African Grand Prix left the calendar. Racing will take place at a new circuit in Bugesera, which is expected to be completed early in the next decade. The circuit will be located approximately 40 kilometres south of the capital, Kigali. The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board. “Today is a landmark moment for Formula One ,” said Stefano Domenicali, president and chief executive of F1. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe. “Africa has always been part of Formula One’s future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.” Africa, we’re back. 🌍 From the early 2030s, the African Grand Prix will join the calendar and take place in Bugesera, Rwanda 🇷🇼 #F1 pic.twitter.com/c5gSRl7FNt — Formula 1 (@F1) October 13, 2026 The announcement is expected to be well received by Ferrari star Lewis Hamilton , who has long been an advocate of the sport returning to Africa. Hamilton reaffirmed his stance on the need for an African F1 race in Singapore at the weekend. “I’ve always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa. It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, and the most beautiful continent,” said Hamilton. Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: “Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world’s premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement. Rwanda is proud to host the Formula One African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa.” Mohammed ben Sulayem, FIA president, said: “The return of the FIA Formula One World Championship to Africa is a historic moment for our sport and an important step in the continued global growth of motorsport.”

title: Beyond money: Designing a more capable SANDF
body:
The recent parliamentary scrutiny of the South African National Defence Force’s (SANDF) Journey to Greatness (JTG) should be welcomed. A long-term defence strategy involving significant public resources must withstand rigorous scrutiny of its strategic logic, affordability, force design and implementation.
The concerns raised by Parliament’s Research Unit are therefore important. They question the relationship between the different JTG milestones, the assumptions underpinning its long-term financial model, the costing of the proposed force, and whether the information available to Parliament is sufficient to determine what South Africa will actually receive in return for increased defence expenditure.
But there is a danger that the debate becomes trapped in the question of whether South Africa can afford JTG , rather than confronting the more important strategic question:
What kind of defence capability does South Africa need, and how should it generate that capability from the resources it can realistically sustain?
That is a different debate. And it is one South Africa urgently needs to have.
The discussion around JTG has increasingly centred on percentages of GDP. The Research Unit has questioned the various funding trajectories, including references to 1.5%, 2.4% and ultimately 4.6% of GDP. It has also questioned whether these represent successive additions to the force or different force designs at different stages.
Those questions need answers. But a percentage of GDP is not a defence strategy. Nor is a defence budget a defence capability.
Money is an input. Capability is an output. Strategic effect is the outcome.
Two defence forces can consume the same financial resources and produce very different levels of military capability. The difference lies in how those resources are converted into people, organisation, structure, training, equipment, doctrine, technology, infrastructure, information (POSTEDFIT), including maintenance, logistics, industrial capacity and ultimately operational effect.
This suggests a more useful analytical chain:
National interest → National security → Critical capability → Force design → Human capital, technology, infrastructure and industry → Resources → Operational effect.
Only after this chain has been established should the country ask what it costs. The question is therefore not simply:
How much should South Africa spend on defence?
How much credible defence capability can South Africa generate from every rand it spends?
That is the conversation missing from much of the current debate.
The funding problem is real, but it is not the whole problem
There is little doubt that the SANDF has suffered from prolonged resource constraints, ageing platforms, declining readiness and inadequate capability development. The temptation, understandably, is therefore to frame the solution as a funding problem.
But the Parliamentary Research Unit has highlighted a particularly uncomfortable fact: approximately 70% of the defence budget is consumed by personnel expenditure. It consequently questions whether simply increasing the defence allocation will translate into improved capability without accompanying structural reform.
This point deserves far greater attention.
It is not an argument that the SANDF has “too many people” or that personnel are merely an expense to be cut.
People are the principal source of military capability.
The issue is whether South Africa has the right human-capital configuration for the military capability it needs in the future.
That is a much more sophisticated question than headcount.
Human capital must become a force-design variable
The military of 2035 will not require exactly the same skills, organisational structures or workforce composition as the military of 1995.
The growth of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, cyber operations, electronic warfare, advanced sensors, data analytics, digital command and control, simulation and software-defined systems is changing the economics of military capability.
A future SANDF will need highly specialised expertise in areas such as systems engineering, software, artificial intelligence, cyber, data, intelligence, electronic warfare, autonomous systems, advanced maintenance and systems integration.
Some functions may require fewer people because technology increases productivity. Other functions will require more specialised and more expensive skills because technology increases complexity.
The strategic question should therefore be:
What human-capital architecture will generate the greatest operational effect for the SANDF?
This reframes personnel expenditure from an accounting problem into a capability-engineering problem.
And that distinction matters enormously. A military can reduce its personnel bill and become weaker. It can also increase personnel expenditure and become more capable.
The variable that matters is what capability the human capital generates.
This leads to an uncomfortable question that needs to be asked directly:
If South Africa were designing its defence force today for the security environment of 2035–2045, would it design the same force it has today?
If the answer is NO , then simply providing more money to restore the existing structure risks reproducing the problem JTG is supposed to solve.
There is an important distinction between rebuilding the SANDF and transforming the SANDF.
Rebuilding requires restoring basic readiness:
But transformation asks different questions:
South Africa cannot afford to confuse restoring yesterday’s capability with designing tomorrow’s capability.
Technology should change force design and not simply add another procurement category
This is where the JTG discussion can become genuinely progressive. Technology is often treated in defence planning as another line item: aircraft, vehicles, ships, radios, drones, software and so forth.
Technology should be a force-design variable.
Artificial intelligence, for example, is not merely an information-technology acquisition. It can alter intelligence processing, decision support, headquarters structures, training and operational tempo. Autonomous systems can change the relationship between surveillance, manpower, risk and persistence. Digital command systems can change how information flows through the force. Simulation can change the economics of training. Predictive maintenance can change equipment availability and logistics. Cyber and electronic warfare can create strategic effects without requiring the acquisition of traditional platforms.
“How much AI, autonomy or digital technology should the SANDF buy?”
“How should emerging technology change the way the SANDF is organised, staffed, trained and equipped?”
That is a force-design question. And it is precisely why defence modernisation cannot be separated from innovation.
From procurement to capability engineering
South Africa has traditionally approached defence acquisition through a familiar sequence:
Requirement → specification → tender → acquisition → deployment.
That model remains necessary for some capabilities, but it is increasingly inadequate for an environment in which technology is changing faster than traditional acquisition cycles. A more adaptive model would be:
Operational problem → experimentation → research and development → prototype → testing → operational evaluation → adaptation → capability → acquisition and industrialisation.
This is not an argument for abandoning disciplined procurement.
It is an argument for introducing experimentation and technology maturation before procurement becomes irreversible. The building blocks are there through the Defence Research and Development Board, and must be reviewed, strengthened and implemented.
For a resource-constrained country, this could be one of the most important sources of competitive advantage. South Africa cannot realistically outspend major military powers.
It can, however, seek to out-design some of the problems.
The objective should be to generate disproportionate military effect through intelligent combinations of people, technology, doctrine, industry and systems integration.
The defence industry must become part of capability generation
This also changes how the defence industry should be understood.
The industry should not be treated merely as a supplier that receives requirements from Defence and competes to deliver equipment. It should become part of a national capability-development ecosystem.
The SANDF should identify operational problems. Industry, universities and research institutions should help develop solutions. Those solutions should be experimented with, tested, matured and evaluated. Successful technologies should then move into acquisition, industrialisation and sustainment. This creates a much stronger relationship between:
Defence → RDI → Industry → Skills → Technology → Capability.
The opportunity is to make that relationship operational rather than rhetorical.
Capability-based costing is necessary; but capability-based design is better
The Parliamentary Research Unit is right to insist that GDP percentages should not substitute for detailed capability-based costing. But we should go one step further.
Capability-based costing tells us what a force costs while capability-based force design asks whether it is the right force in the first place.
That distinction should shape the next stage of JTG.
For every major capability, South Africa should be able to establish:
What capability is necessary to generate that effect?
What combination of people, technology, infrastructure and equipment provides that capability?
What sovereign dependencies does it create?
What operational effect will it produce?
That would give Parliament something much more useful than a percentage of GDP. It would give the country a capability-to-cost relationship.
Ultimately, Parliament should be able to ask:
This capability, at this readiness level, producing this operational effect, at this life-cycle cost.
That is meaningful defence accountability.
Parliament should scrutinise, but scrutiny is not strategy-making
There is also an institutional dimension to the current debate. The concerns about parliamentary access to information and effective oversight should not be dismissed. Parliament has a constitutional responsibility to hold the Executive accountable and maintain oversight over national executive authority.
At the same time, South Africa’s constitutional architecture gives the Executive responsibility for developing and implementing national policy, while the President holds constitutional authority over the employment and command of the Defence Force, subject to the relevant provisions of the Constitution.
Parliament should scrutinise the strategy. It should not become the co-author of military strategy.
The Executive must formulate policy and strategic direction. The military must provide professional military advice and translate that direction into force development. Parliament must interrogate the assumptions, costs, risks, performance and outcomes, and provide the legislative and budgetary authority that falls within its constitutional role.
That is not a turf war. It is a system of checks and balances.
The danger comes when oversight becomes operational direction, or when Executive authority becomes an excuse for avoiding substantive scrutiny.
The country needs neither. It needs institutional clarity and better strategic management.
Another criticism worth reconsidering is the 30-year horizon. Nobody can accurately predict what warfare, technology, geopolitics or South Africa’s economy will look like in 2055.
But that does not make a 30-year strategic horizon inherently irrational. A long-term strategy should not be judged by its ability to predict the future. It should be judged by its ability to adapt to an uncertain future.
JTG should therefore be understood as a trajectory rather than a fixed shopping list. I however think a useful architecture could be as depicted below:
The strategy should then be periodically tested against changes in the strategic environment, technology, fiscal conditions and national priorities. The value of a 30-year strategy lies not in predicting 2055 with precision, but in creating a mechanism through which the SANDF can continuously adapt towards a desired future capability.
This is where I believe the national conversation needs to change. We should stop measuring defence transformation predominantly through percentage of GDP; number of personnel; number of platforms; and size of the acquisition budget.
These are inputs and indicators. They are not the ultimate measure of military effectiveness.
We should instead be asking about deployability; readiness; equipment availability; response time; endurance; training effectiveness; information superiority; command-and-control resilience; technology maturity; sovereign sustainment; critical skills; industrial capacity; and operational effect.
What capability is being generated per rand?
That should become one of the central performance questions of South African defence.
The journey should be about transformation, not simply recovery
The debate surrounding JTG should not become a choice between its advocates and its critics. The critics are right to demand evidence. The Executive is right to seek a sustainable future for a Defence Force that has endured prolonged resource constraints. Parliament is right to demand accountability. But South Africa needs to move beyond all three positions.
The country needs a capability-generation model that connects national strategy to military effect and connects military effect to the resources available to the state.
strategy, force design, human capital, technology, innovation, infrastructure, industry, RDI and finance.
This is not simply a defence-budget problem. It is a systems-engineering and strategic-management problem. And this is perhaps the most important opportunity presented by the current debate. The question is not whether South Africa should spend more on defence. Given the condition of the SANDF and the security environment, that question deserves serious consideration.
The question is whether additional money will be converted into additional capability.
If the answer is uncertain, simply increasing the budget is not enough. If the answer is yes, government should be able to demonstrate exactly how.
South Africa should not have to choose between an underfunded SANDF and an unaffordable SANDF.
A deliberately designed, appropriately sized, technologically enabled, human-capital intensive where it matters, industrially sustainable and continuously adapting SANDF; one capable of generating greater operational effect from every person, every technology and every rand invested in defence.
That is the standard against which Journey to Greatness should ultimately be judged.
“Is this the smartest way South Africa can generate that capability?”
That is the conversation we should now be having.
And it is a conversation that should extend well beyond Defence and Parliament, to Treasury, the defence industry, academia, engineering and technology communities, organised labour, and the broader national-security community.
Because the future of the SANDF will ultimately depend not only on how much South Africa is prepared to spend on defence, but on how intelligently it chooses to generate defence capability.

title: Education is critical to Ghana’s future and development – Haruna Iddrisu
body: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has underscored the importance of education to Ghana’s development, describing a child’s entry into school as a defining moment in securing their future. Speaking on Joy FM on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, the Tamale South MP said his role as Education Minister offered an opportunity to contribute to the country’s long-term progress. “I believe that the education portfolio is a very important portfolio for the development and the future of the country,” he said. Mr Iddrisu was responding to a question about whether he missed the day-to-day parliamentary politics associated with his previous leadership role. “Oh, not really,” he responded, before explaining the significance he attached to education. “And my honest belief is that the most important single event in life is for a child to step into school, to get educated. And that is where life, in my view, begins. And that’s where, in my view, the future begins to be secured.” He said missing that opportunity could affect an individual’s personal development and ability to contribute to national progress. “If you miss that opportunity, you probably may not get it right, for the most part, even if you want to contribute to your own self-development and the development of the country.” Mr Iddrisu also noted that his ministerial responsibilities had not ended his participation in parliamentary work. “But I’m still a Member of Parliament. I still have an opportunity to be in Parliament to answer questions as a Minister for Education, subject area-specific questions that come up.”

title: France Boards Russian ‘Shadow Fleet’ Tanker Near Reunion Island
body:
The French Navy intercepted and boarded the sanctioned oil tanker DF Peak in the Indian Ocean over suspected false-flag registration and illegal fuel transportation, French President Emmanuel Macron said.
The operation took place on Monday morning, Oct. 12, more than 450 nautical miles (approximately 830 kilometers) south of Réunion, a French island east of Madagascar.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“France is determined to fight the shadow fleet, everywhere in the world,” Macron wrote on X .
“Our French Navy boarded the oil tanker DF Peak, suspected of sailing under a false flag and being involved in illegal fuel transport activities,” he added.
Macron said the operation followed international maritime law and showed France’s determination to combat illegal trafficking.
French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said the Navy was escorting the tanker for further inspections under the prefect of Réunion’s authority.
French authorities have not yet announced whether they will confiscate the vessel or its cargo. The boarding and escort therefore do not by themselves constitute a final seizure or establish criminal liability.
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) lists the DF Peak, IMO number 9341067, in its War & Sanctions database as a vessel involved in ferrying Russian crude oil and petroleum products.
The tanker previously operated under the names NS Captain and Kaliningrad and has sailed under several flags. It currently claims registration in Benin, although French authorities suspect that the flag may be invalid or improperly used.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the vessel is associated with Russia’s state-controlled shipping company Sovcomflot, which has been sanctioned for helping Moscow export energy products and generate revenue during the war.
The US sanctioned the vessel in February 2024 as part of measures targeting ships affiliated with Sovcomflot. The EU added it to its sanctions list in June 2024, followed by Switzerland, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and Japan.
The Ukrainian database also records cases in which the tanker switched off its automatic identification system (AIS) and lists previous calls at Russian oil ports, including Primorsk and Ust-Luga near the Baltics.
Russia’s “shadow fleet” consists largely of aging tankers with opaque ownership structures, frequently changing flags and limited access to reputable Western insurance.
The vessels allow Moscow to continue exporting oil while evading or reducing the effect of Western sanctions, including the G7 price cap and EU restrictions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
France has intensified operations against suspected shadow-fleet tankers in 2026.
In June, French forces and their partners intercepted the Russia-linked tanker Tagor in the Atlantic after authorities raised doubts about its claimed Cameroonian registration.
Later that month, France boarded the tanker Deliver near Sicily , also on suspicion of violating international maritime rules.
Shadow-fleet ships frequently operate under questionable registrations, use complex corporate structures to conceal their owners and sometimes disable tracking equipment. European officials have also warned that poorly maintained tankers carrying large quantities of oil create serious environmental risks.

title: Russian drone strikes university building in Rivne, injures 25
body:
A Russian drone struck a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, injuring 25 people, Rivne's National Police branch said on Oct. 13.
Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said .
Ukraine's Education and Science Minister Andrii Butenko said that a fire broke out in a building of Rivne State Humanitarian University as a result of the Russian drone strike. The Faculty of Music building was almost completely gutted by the fire, while neighboring teaching facilities had windows smashed, he added.
Oleksandr Koval, head of Rivne Oblast Military Administration, said on Oct. 13 that the drone strike damaged the second floor of the building. The fire in the building had been contained, and emergency services were on site.
"All victims are receiving medical assistance. Rescuers, police, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and municipal services are working at the scene," Koval said .
According to the university, all students were in shelters at the moment of the attack. There were casualties amongst the university's administrative staff.
At around 10:35 a.m., Ukraine's air force had reported a jet-powered drone flying over Rivne. The air alert was issued in the city at 10:10 a.m.
On Oct. 12, the air alert was issued several times in Rivne Oblast .
The city of Rivne came under Russian drone attack at around 9 p.m. local time, Koval said. A non-residential building was damaged, while no one was injured. Later, at 11 p.m., air defenses were active in the city.
Separately, the Sarny District of Rivne Oblast came under attack late in the evening of October 12, Koval added. Сivilian infrastructure, non-operational facilities, dormitories, and residential buildings were damaged as a result of the attack.
Overall, Russian attacks across Ukraine killed 10 people and injured 80 over the past day, regional authorities said on Oct. 13.
Overnight on Oct. 13, Russian forces launched five ballistic missiles, 108 Shahed-type attack drones, including 74 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, and nine Banderol missiles, Ukraine's Air Force said .
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 88 drones, while strikes were recorded at 17 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at seven locations, the Air Force said.

title: RAM launches leadership programme for Majlis Ash’shura
body:
MUSCAT: The Royal Academy of Management launched a Leadership Programme for members of the Majlis Ash’shura to strengthen their leadership capabilities and support the objectives of Oman Vision 2040. The programme focuses on four key areas: leadership; strategic planning and integrated work; policies, legislation and decision-making; protocol, foreign policy and diplomacy; and public communication and media appearances. These areas aim to help Majlis Ash’shura members examine issues from multiple perspectives and apply modern tools and methodologies in their work and committee activities, in line with development priorities and citizens’ aspirations. Dr Ali bin Qasim al Lawati, President of the Royal Academy of Management, said the programme reflects the Academy’s commitment to supporting national institutions in developing leadership capabilities and improving performance efficiency. He highlighted the Majlis Ash’shura’s role in national development through its legislative and oversight responsibilities, as well as its members’ understanding of societal issues and citizens’ aspirations. The nine-day executive learning programme is divided into two units and covers four main tracks, with the diplomacy component delivered in cooperation with the Diplomatic Academy. Its practical modules include modern leadership in Shura councils, strategic performance indicators for Oman Vision 2040, legislative analysis, evidence-based policymaking, economic security, sustainable economic diversification, Oman's foreign policy and international relations, and strategic communication with the media. The programme reflects the Academy’s broader approach to developing national leaders through modern management practices, with the aim of enhancing efficiency, productivity and innovation and preparing leaders to contribute to the country’s future development. - ONA
