title: Ukraine Holds Off Refinery Attacks for Second Day After Trump Ceasefire Claim
body:
Ukrainian forces appeared to refrain from targeting Russian oil refineries during an overnight drone attack Tuesday, the second day since U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire.”
Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries, or the energy sector in general, for the two days since the American President announced an energy ceasefire, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
However, Zelensky said, “Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine.”
The Kremlin said Monday that talks regarding a potential energy ceasefire were continuing.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 604 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “a majority” of the 417 Ukrainian drones launched toward the capital region had been “neutralized,” 65 of them directly on approach to the capital.
The air raid alerts caused flight delays and cancellations for around 150 flights at four Moscow airports, including around 100 at Vnukovo airport.
Ukrainian drones damaged industrial zones at the chemical hub of Nevinnomysk in the Stavropol region, according to the regional governor.
Belgorod region Governor Alexander Shuvayev said two men were killed in Ukrainian drone attacks over the past 24 hours.
A school building was damaged in the Kaluga region.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it carried out strikes against a Ukrainian missile and drone production workshop in Kyiv, a logistics center in Ternivka and other non-refinery targets.

title: SOF cut off Russian infiltration route in Donetsk sector
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Special Operations Forces (SOF) reported this on Facebook .
"Special Operations Forces operators raided a hideout that the Russians were using as a rest and staging area. From a captured radio, the special forces learned that several more enemy groups would be moving along this route. The operators remained in position and set up an ambush: three Russian servicemen were killed , and one was taken prisoner," the statement reads.
The prisoner had a radio and a phone with waypoints and other routes for advancing into the area. He provided the call signs of commanders and other valuable information.
The captive also described the Russian Federation’s army tactics of “human wave assaults,” as well as class divisions and inhumane treatment of ethnic minorities, the prohibition on providing aid to the wounded, and the killing of their own troops if they refuse orders.
As noted by the Special Operations Forces, they have observed all of this firsthand from the enemy’s side.
“We mainly encounter Yakuts, Buryats, Tajiks, and Uzbeks here. They are sent to the front as ‘cannon fodder,’ and then their other units, such as the 74th Brigade, move in and secure strategic lines,” explained the commander of the 3rd Special Operations Regiment.
As reported by Ukrinform, pilots from the 237th Separate Unmanned Systems Battalion of the 7th Corps of the Ukrainian Armed Forces ’ Airborne Assault Troops, in coordination with other units, destroyed a workshop and warehouse containing Russian drones and electronic warfare equipment in the Donetsk region.

title: Chanting Festival kicks off in Nizwa on Oct 18
body:

It presses ahead with steps to furnish an artistic landscape that shows significant evolution in performance styles, production techniques and audience engagement. - ONA

title: Arise News Bars Anthony Kila From Network Following Academic Credentials Allegations
body: Arise News Channel has announced that Anthony Kila, who has appeared several times on the network as a freelance political analyst, will no longer appear on the channel following allegations that he falsified his academic credentials. In a disclaimer by the Editorial Board titled “Investigation: Anthony Kila’s ‘Degrees’”, Arise News Channel said the allegations followed a damning investigative report by Premium Times Newspapers. The network said it contacted Kila on October 3, 2026, with the allegations, but he asked for more time to respond. “He has not responded 10 days after,” the disclaimer stated, adding that “the allegations have gotten worse.” “In the circumstances we find that his contributions to The Arise News Channel is no longer tenable,” the network said. Arise News said it was unaware of the allegations when Kila appeared on its platform, stressing that it takes matters of credibility and integrity extremely seriously. title: What Happened to the Desktop Metaphor?
body:
For a long time, personal computers tried very hard to explain themselves.
You had a desktop. On that desktop were files and folders. Programs opened in windows. Commands were grouped into menus. If you wanted to move something, you dragged it somewhere else. If you wanted to throw it away, there was usually a trash can or recycle bin waiting for it.
None of that was accidental. Early graphical interfaces borrowed heavily from the physical office because computers were unfamiliar and needed a way to make abstract operations understandable. A folder on a screen was not really a folder, of course, but the metaphor gave users a mental model for what the computer was doing.
That model was never perfect, but it was remarkably successful. What interests me now is how much of it modern software has gradually hidden.
The traditional desktop interface exposed a great deal of the computer’s structure.
Files existed in particular places. Folders contained other folders. Applications were separate things that you launched. A window usually belonged to a particular program, and menu bars showed you what commands were available. Even if you did not understand the technical details underneath, the interface gave you a reasonably coherent picture.
That mattered more than it might appear. Once someone understood the basic hierarchy of drives, directories, folders, and files, that knowledge transferred from one program to another. Saving a document in a word processor was conceptually related to moving a photograph or copying a spreadsheet. The details differed, but the structure remained familiar.
The desktop metaphor taught users enough about the machine to navigate it.
It is easy to get nostalgic about files and folders, but the old desktop was not some pure or natural way to use a computer. It was an abstraction built on top of a much more complicated system.
A directory is not literally a manila folder. A file is not a sheet of paper. A desktop on a computer can contain thousands of items in ways that would make a real desk unusable. Software designers stretched and broke the metaphor whenever it was convenient.
The traditional desktop also had plenty of weaknesses. Users lost files because they forgot where they saved them. Deep folder hierarchies became difficult to manage. Applications created their own strange directory structures. Different programs used inconsistent menus and terminology.
Search improved partly because browsing through directories was not always the best way to find information. Cloud synchronization became popular partly because manually moving files among several computers was inconvenient. Mobile interfaces changed things because a desktop metaphor designed around a large monitor, keyboard, and mouse did not translate cleanly to a small touchscreen.
The old model was useful, but it was never perfect.
One of the biggest changes has been the gradual separation between users and the files they create.
On a traditional desktop system, creating a document usually involved choosing a filename and deciding where to put it. The user participated directly in organizing the information.
Many modern applications do something different. You create a note, photograph, document, project, or message inside the application, and the application decides where the underlying data lives. It may be stored in a database, a private application directory, a cloud service, or some combination of the three.
From the user’s perspective, there may be no file at all. There is simply “my note” or “my document” inside a particular application.
That can be convenient. Most people do not want to spend their time thinking about file paths, storage formats, or synchronization directories. An application can take care of all of that and present the user with the thing they actually care about.
The tradeoff is that the application becomes the map.
Another change is the move from knowing where something is to asking the computer to find it.
Older desktop systems encouraged hierarchical organization. If you wanted a document, you navigated through something like Documents > Work > Projects > 2026 > Reports .
Modern interfaces increasingly assume that searching is easier. Instead of remembering the path, you type a few words into a search box and let the system locate what you need.
In many cases, that is genuinely better. I use search constantly, and I would not want to give it up. Large collections of email, documents, photographs, and notes are difficult to manage using folder hierarchies alone.
But search changes the relationship between the user and the information. A folder hierarchy gives you a visible structure. Search gives you results.
When search works well, the difference barely matters. When it fails, or when you cannot remember enough about what you are looking for to formulate the right query, the underlying organization suddenly becomes important again.
Menus have gone through a similar change.
Traditional desktop applications often had a visible menu bar containing categories such as File, Edit, View, Tools, and Help. The menus were sometimes cluttered, and poorly designed applications could produce absurdly long lists of commands. Still, they served an important purpose: they exposed what the software could do.
Modern interfaces often prefer simplified toolbars, unlabeled icons, context-sensitive controls, hidden panels, and menus tucked behind symbols such as three dots or three horizontal lines. The theory is understandable. Screens are cleaner, touch interfaces have limited space, and showing every command all the time can overwhelm users.
A menu saying “Export” tells me that exporting exists. An icon that changes depending on what I have selected may be elegant once I understand it, but it does not necessarily teach me anything. When controls are hidden until the system thinks they are relevant, users have fewer opportunities to discover capabilities by looking around.
Software becomes easier to approach at first, but sometimes harder to learn deeply.
Traditional desktop operating systems were built around the idea that multiple applications could be visible at once. Windows overlapped, resized, minimized, and moved around a larger workspace. The user managed the arrangement.
Mobile operating systems largely abandoned that model. Applications generally occupy the entire screen, and switching between them becomes an operating-system function rather than a spatial one.
That makes sense on a phone. There is not much value in putting six tiny overlapping windows on a five- or six-inch display.
What is more interesting is how some of that design thinking has moved back onto desktop systems. Full-screen applications, simplified interfaces, web applications, hidden chrome, and single-purpose views are now common even on large displays.
The computer is increasingly treated less like a workspace containing several visible objects and more like a sequence of activities.
You are not necessarily looking at files and applications anymore. You are “checking mail,” “editing a document,” “viewing photos,” or “working in Slack.”
The web probably deserves some of the credit or blame for this shift.
A website does not normally expose its internal file structure to the visitor. Users do not navigate through the server’s directories looking for pages. They follow links, use menus, search, or interact with whatever interface the site provides.
As more software moved into the browser, that model became normal.
A web application often presents information as records, projects, conversations, cards, posts, dashboards, or workspaces. The underlying storage is intentionally invisible because there is no reason for most users to care whether a particular item lives in a database table, object store, or file.
Cloud applications extended the idea further. A document can simply exist “in Google Docs” or “in Microsoft 365” without the user thinking much about what machine actually holds it.
From a usability standpoint, this can be a major improvement. From the standpoint of understanding and controlling your own data, it is more complicated.
There are good reasons interfaces have moved in this direction.
Computers have become far more complicated, and many users have no interest in learning the machinery underneath. A phone that requires someone to understand directories, processes, mount points, and file permissions before taking a picture would not be a triumph of user empowerment.
Abstraction is one of the things computers are supposed to do.
A well-designed application should remove unnecessary work. Automatic saving is usually better than losing an hour of writing because someone forgot to press Save. Synchronizing a document automatically across several devices is useful. Searching thousands of photographs by date, location, or subject can be far more practical than manually maintaining hundreds of directories.
I am not interested in making computers deliberately harder to use just so users are forced to understand them.
The problem appears when abstraction turns into concealment.
There is a difference between not requiring users to manage something and preventing them from seeing or controlling it at all.
If an application stores my information internally but also lets me export it in a useful format, that is one thing. If the only practical way to reach that information is through the application itself, the situation is different.
The same applies to synchronization. Hiding the mechanics of syncing files is convenient. Making it impossible to determine whether a file is actually local, remote, cached, or available offline can become a problem.
Modern systems sometimes blur those distinctions so thoroughly that even experienced users have to stop and figure out where something really is.
Is the document on the computer? Is it in the cloud? Is there a local copy? If I delete it here, does it disappear everywhere? If I cancel the service, what remains?
Those are questions the traditional desktop generally made easier to answer because storage was more visible.
One consequence of hiding structure is that users may become very good at particular applications without developing a broader model of how computers organize information.
That is not necessarily their fault. The software has stopped teaching them.
If an application handles filenames, locations, extensions, synchronization, and storage automatically, there is little reason for a new user to learn those concepts until something goes wrong.
Then they become important very quickly.
Anyone who has provided technical support has probably encountered variations of the same problem: someone knows a document exists but has no idea where it is. It may be in Downloads, Documents, a browser’s temporary storage, OneDrive, Google Drive, an email attachment, or an application’s private storage.
The computer has made the structure invisible right up until the moment the user needs to understand it.
Despite all this, the desktop metaphor has not disappeared.
Windows, macOS, Linux desktops, and traditional file managers still use files, folders, windows, and hierarchical storage. Professional work in programming, media production, system administration, research, and many other areas still depends heavily on visible files and directories.
Even newer interfaces frequently fall back on desktop concepts when users need more control. Export a project, upload an attachment, choose a backup location, organize source code, or manage photographs outside an application, and files and folders quickly return.
The metaphor survives because the underlying concepts remain useful.
What has changed is that they are no longer the first thing many users see.
I do not think the answer is to return every computer to the interface conventions of 1995. Modern interfaces have solved real problems, and many of the changes that weakened the traditional desktop metaphor also made computers easier to use.
Still, I think something was lost when software stopped showing as much of its structure.
Files and folders gave users a mental map. Menus exposed capabilities. Windows made applications visible as separate things sharing a workspace. None of those ideas perfectly represented what the computer was actually doing, but they made important parts of the system understandable.
Modern interfaces often provide more convenience while asking users to understand less. Most of the time, that works because the software handles the hidden details successfully.
A good abstraction should save us from unnecessary complexity without making the underlying system incomprehensible. The desktop metaphor was clumsy in places, but one of its strengths was that it gave users enough of the structure to make sense of their own computers.
I am not convinced that hiding more of that structure is always progress.

title: Storm Alert Turns Red for One Greek Island
body: ATHENS, October 2026 — Greece’s national weather service issued an Evia red alert for storms and heavy rain on Tuesday and Wednesday, and placed Attica, the region around Athens, on orange alert. The Hellenic National Meteorological Service (EMY) upgraded its emergency bulletin to a dangerous weather warning on Monday 12 October. It said heavy rain, storms and local hail will hit most of the country, especially coastal and island areas. As a result, the General Secretariat for Civil Protection put state agencies, regions and councils on high alert. It wants them ready to respond quickly to any damage. Unlike the Evia red alert, the orange warning for Attica sits one level lower. Even so, forecasters said the Athens area should still expect strong storms and heavy rain. Evia red alert forecast Strong north-easterly winds will also build in the northern Aegean from Tuesday evening, according to the bulletin. By Wednesday 14 October, winds in the Aegean will reach 8 and locally 9 on the Beaufort scale. The meteo unit of the National Observatory of Athens ranked the rain as Category 3, or “significant”, on its scale. Temperatures will also drop gradually, forecasters said. Tuesday’s highs will not pass 22–23°C on the mainland and 25–27°C on the islands, before falling to 20–22°C on Wednesday. On Wednesday, the rain will mainly affect the Aegean and the eastern mainland, although it should ease significantly from midday. Civil protection advice Civil protection officials urged people to take extra care during the Evia red alert. They also asked people across the country to take steps to protect themselves. Lightning brings its own risks. Anyone caught on open, flat ground who feels their hair stand on end should crouch low, head between the knees, and drop any metal objects, officials said. Residents can check flooded roads on the Hellenic Police website . Safety advice is on the site of the Ministry for Climate Crisis and Civil Protection . The Evia red alert comes after autumn storms cut temperatures by up to 7°C earlier, in September. Source: Ta Nea The post Storm Alert Turns Red for One Greek Island appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Zelensky Says Ukraine Received No Warning From Partners Before Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine received no warning from its international partners before Russia launched five ballistic missiles at civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, calling advance intelligence on such attacks critical to saving lives.
“There was also a particularly cowardly ballistic missile strike on Kyiv – five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Intelligence data on the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. Having a warning about ballistic missiles is precisely what helps prevent killings,” he added.
Zelensky did not specify which partners Ukraine expected to provide the warning or explain why the information was not received.
Notably, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said at the Warsaw Security Forum that Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the US.
“You are likely asking whether we receive intelligence from the American side. Yes, we are continuing this cooperation,” he said Tuesday.
According to Sybiha, the air raid alert issued late on Monday, Oct. 12, was delayed due to the specific type of weaponry Russia used.
However, in his statement, Zelensky referred to a failure to receive a warning about only one attack on Kyiv.
Meanwhile, the Financial Times (FT) previously reported, citing sources, that US officials had threatened to halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Kyiv continued to strike oil refineries inside Russia.
Zelensky said Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles.
In Kharkiv, a Russian strike destroyed a residential building, killing four people. Rescue workers searched the rubble through much of the night, while 41 people were wounded in the city over the course of the evening, Zelensky said.
He added that a significant number of the incoming weapons had been intercepted, but not all.
Zelensky also accused Russia of ignoring US President Donald Trump’s call for a ceasefire covering energy facilities.
He said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian oil-refining and energy infrastructure for two days after Trump’s announcement, but Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure.
Over the same two-day period, 19 Ukrainian regions came under attack, Zelensky said.
“Ukraine is ready for reciprocal de-escalation steps, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to bring about that de-escalation,” he wrote.
Zelensky argued that international pressure was necessary to bring the war closer to an end, warning that support for Russia, delays in aid to Ukraine and obstacles to defending against ballistic missiles undermined efforts to achieve peace.
He called for continued support from the United States, Europe and other partners.
In an explainer published on Monday, the Kyiv Post reported that, according to the FT, Reuters, and Axios, US officials had reportedly threatened to suspend arms deliveries and intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Kyiv continued striking Russian oil refineries.
The warnings were allegedly delivered during talks between US and Ukrainian delegations in Miami, as well as in calls involving Ukrainian and European officials.
Such a move could significantly weaken Ukraine’s defense capabilities, particularly by limiting early warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches and access to intelligence on Russian military movements, weapons systems, and targets.
A cutoff of US arms supplies could also affect Ukraine’s ability to operate Patriot air defense systems, F-16 fighter jets, HIMARS launchers, and other American-made equipment that relies on US ammunition, spare parts, or technical support.
However, Ukraine has alternative sources of intelligence and military assistance. Its own intelligence services and electronic surveillance networks, alongside support from European partners such as France, the UK, and Nordic and Baltic states, help monitor Russian military activity. Commercial satellite imagery also helps fill potential gaps in US intelligence.
Ukraine has also expanded domestic arms production, particularly of drones and interceptor drones, while European partners have strengthened its air defenses with systems such as Germany’s IRIS-T and Gepard.
Nevertheless, replacing US capabilities would be particularly difficult in two areas: early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches and the supply of Patriot interceptors, which remain critical to protecting Ukrainian cities from such attacks.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Tompolo Donates 25 Vehicles, Seeks Votes for Tinubu in Kogi
body: Voters in Kogi State have been urged to mobilise and re-elect President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in the 2027 election to sustain ongoing reforms. The call was made by High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, when he donated 25 vehicles to the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement in Kogi State for grassroots mobilisation. Tompolo, the Grand Patron of the Movement, announced the donation through the Managing Director of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, Kestin Pondi, at the inauguration of the movement’s Kogi State structure in Lokoja yesterday. The Niger Delta high chief said the vehicles would support the movement’s campaign to mobilise voters for Tinubu’s second term, urging Nigerians to re-elect the president. He argued that the president had demonstrated courage by removing the petrol subsidy, supporting direct allocation of funds to local government areas and allowing states to regulate electricity within their jurisdictions. According to him, the reforms have increased resources available to state governments to pay salaries, pensions and execute projects. “If somebody has done so much for you, what do you do for the person? You give him more,” he said. He urged members of the movement to take the president’s message to homes, workplaces, churches, markets and communities, adding that Nigerians needed to give Tinubu another four years to consolidate his reforms. Tompolo acknowledged that the reforms had brought challenges but maintained that the country would eventually benefit from them if citizens remained patient. king at the event, Kogi State Governor Ahmed Usman Ododo commended the movement for providing vehicles to facilitate its grassroots mobilisation, urging its members to use them to reach every street, village, market, and household. He, however, stressed that vehicles alone could not guarantee electoral success, noting that effective organisation and engagement with voters would be crucial. “Vehicles do not win elections, but people do; conventions win elections, and organisations also win elections,” the governor said. Ododo called on the movement’s coordinators to explain the administration’s policies and projects to Nigerians, listen to their concerns, and answer questions with facts rather than insults. He explained that President Tinubu inherited serious economic challenges and had chosen to confront them through reforms, adding that the country needs continuity to consolidate ongoing development efforts. The governor also listed infrastructure and development projects in Kogi State which he said had received the president’s support, including the proposed Economic City and Free Trade Zone, as well as the Kogi International Airport project. He further cited renewed attention to the Abuja-Lokoja-Benin expressway, the development of universities and primary healthcare centres, road construction, support for farmers and youths, and women empowerment initiatives. Ododo said improved infrastructure, security and an enabling business environment are necessary to attract investment, create jobs, and raise living standards. He also thanked Tinubu for supporting security operations against criminality and backing efforts to establish state police, saying improved security would enable farmers to return to their farms and businesses to operate without fear. The governor pledged to lead the mobilisation efforts in Kogi State, declaring his support for the movement’s campaign ahead of the 2027 presidential election. He urged its members to engage communities peacefully and persuade voters through their messages and conduct. Earlier, the National Coordinator of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Mr. Sunday Asuku, called on residents, youths, students, and farmers to mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election. Asuku described the president’s reforms as necessary for the country’s development, and urged Nigerians to support the continuation of the administration’s policies. He also cited the administration’s engagement with organised labour and efforts to prevent strikes by the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) as reasons for supporting Tinubu.

title: 11 Sailors Missing After Black Sea Drone Strikes
body: Eleven sailors are missing after drone strikes hit two cargo vessels in the Black Sea near Bulgaria, leaving one ship sunk and several crew members injured. The Turkish-owned Azov Concord sank after the attack, with five crew members rescued and 11 reported missing. A second vessel, the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, was struck by three drones while travelling from Turkey towards Moldova. Several crew members were reportedly wounded in the explosions. The attacks occurred approximately 18 nautical miles off the Bulgarian coast, raising fresh concerns about the widening security risks facing commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid Russia’s war against Ukraine. Bulgaria has moved to summon the Russian ambassador over the incident. The circumstances surrounding the strikes, including responsibility for the attacks, remain subject to confirmation. The post 11 Sailors Missing After Black Sea Drone Strikes appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Aktau Port Dredging Project Aims to Cut Shipping Costs and Boost Cargo Capacity
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Dredging works at the Port of Aktau on the Caspian Sea are expected to increase cargo volumes along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) by up to 30% and reduce maritime shipping costs by 10-15%, according to the port administration. Photo credit: Ministry of Transport. The main phase of the project began in October, with completion scheduled for the end of 2026. The project is valued at 20.6 billion tenge (US$45.6 million) and is financed by the Kazakh government and the Ministry of Transport, partly through loans, administration told the Kazinform news agency. The work is being carried out by China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), which serves as the general contractor. According to Aktau International Sea Trade Port, the company is responsible for the entire process, from geodetic surveys to removing sediment from the seabed. The port administration also clarified that reports of a French company’s involvement in the project were incorrect. Dredging to address falling water levels The project covers 77.1 hectares of the port’s waters, including approach channels and areas near berths. The port administration said declining water levels in the Caspian Sea have prevented vessels from entering the port at full capacity. Depths near the berths currently range from 4.5 to five meters. Following dredging, they are expected to reach six to seven meters. Approximately 1.3 million cubic meters of seabed material will be removed. The extracted material will be transported to designated sites, with some of it intended for use in creating artificial land for the construction of new berths. Higher cargo capacity and lower shipping costs The port administration expects the deeper waterways to allow vessels to carry larger loads, increasing cargo transportation along the TITR by up to 30% after the work is completed. By 2028, the route’s annual capacity is planned to increase from six million to 10 million tons. “Thanks to the possibility of fully loading vessels, the cost of maritime cargo transportation is expected to decrease by approximately 10-15%,” the port administration said. The improvements are intended to strengthen Aktau’s role in the Trans-Caspian corridor, which connects transport networks across Central Asia and the Caspian Sea. Greater vessel loading capacity could help reduce the need for partially loaded voyages and improve the economics of maritime freight. Part of broader efforts to address Caspian challenges The project comes amid growing concern over the Caspian Sea’s declining water levels and their effects on navigation, port operations and regional connectivity. Earlier, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed establishing a pool of international projects to help protect the Caspian Sea. He has also called for a shared digital platform to collect and analyze data on water resources, shoreline changes, biodiversity, pollution and river flows. The post Aktau Port Dredging Project Aims to Cut Shipping Costs and Boost Cargo Capacity appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Senate calls for $30M Compact Trust Fund injection into NDBP
body: By: Eoghan Olkeriil Ngirudelsang Ngerulmud, Palau — A Senate joint resolution is urging President Whipps to inject US$30 million from the Compact Trust Fund into the National Development Bank of Palau (NDBP) to boost lending for agriculture, fisheries, housing, infrastructure and small business. Resolution aims to unlock long-stalled development Senate Joint Resolution No. 12-22 seeks to capitalize NDBP so the bank can expand its lending capacity and stimulate investment in priority sectors. The resolution argues that while a significant portion of Compact assistance “is held in a trust fund intended for long-term development goals”, development in key sectors such as agriculture, fishing, housing and infrastructure “has remained stagnant for the past thirty years, hindering economic growth and perpetuating reliance on foreign aid.” It says NDBP is “positioned to address these challenges by providing accessible and affordable loans to Palauan’s seeking to invest in these critical sector.” Lawmakers weigh trade-offs: trust fund earnings vs. domestic investment During Monday’s Senate session, Senator Mason Whipps said he supports moves to inject more capital into NDBP but raised concerns about the opportunity cost of pulling money out of the trust fund’s overseas investments. He stated that, “We get earnings of our trust fund funding while it’s being invested in the U.S. Stock market. The challenge we face is, if we are to give that money to NDBP, can it afford to pay those earnings that we currently realize, or do we decide to forgo those earnings because instead of our money invested in the U.S., it will instead be invested in Palau?” Senator Mariur raised concern that, “We should review the bank’s purpose and its services; does the bank have the capacity to receive such funding? Should we just hand them this funding or give it to the bank as a loan?” Mariur further said that, “While our trust fund is required to be invested in the United States, we must find ways to invest in Palau, and possibly hand such funding to the development bank but require the bank to pay it back including interests.” Recent $15M housing loan, Temenos rollout and CEO vacancy fuel capacity questions NDBP recently received a US$15 million loan from the national government at a fixed 2.5% interest rate for a 20-year term, channeled through the bank for housing development. The infusion came amid staff complaints about management and reports that the bank lacks sufficient capacity to operate its newly procured core banking and digital transformation system, Temenos. NDBP also currently has no CEO, raising concerns among lawmakers and the public about whether the bank has the capacity to absorb another large funding injection. President Whipps: ‘There is no reason why it’s been left… for a year and a half’ At a press conference yesterday, President Whipps highlighted the need for additional funding to NDBP and criticized the slow progress of related legislation. He said, “A request to the Senate to consider a commemorative coin is additional funding to NDBP to help NDBP. There is no reason why it’s been left in Senator Mariur’s committee in the Olbiil er a Kelulau for a year and a half.” NDBP was established in February 1982 during the first constitutional government to promote economic development through targeted lending. The Senate resolution frames the proposed $30 million capital injection as a way to finally leverage the Compact Trust Fund for on-the-ground investment in Palau, even as lawmakers debate the funding structure and the bank’s readiness to deploy it. The post Senate calls for $30M Compact Trust Fund injection into NDBP appeared first on Island Times News .

title: 2027: Wike, Adeleke, Soludo make revised APC presidential campaign council
body: The All Progressives Congress (APC) has officially released its revised Presidential Campaign Council list ahead of the 2027 presidential election, featuring high-profile additions from opposition figures, serving governors, and key legislative leaders. In a notable cross-party alignment, the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has been appointed as the Campaign Coordinator for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in both Rivers State and the FCT. The revised list also incorporates Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, as the Osun State Campaign Coordinator, while former Gombe State Governor and serving PDP Senator, Ibrahim Dankwambo, has been appointed as an Adviser to the Campaign Council alongside Obafemi George, who will also advise on media strategy. Key leadership positions within the campaign hierarchy were also confirmed in the updated release. FG files fresh charges against ‘phantom’ council’s DG 150 girls benefit from menstrual health outreach in Abuja Senator Abdulaziz Yari retained his position as Director-General of the re-election campaign. Former Edo State Governor, Senator Adams Oshiomhole, serves as Deputy Director-General for Mobilization, while Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, takes on the role of Deputy Director-General for Administration. Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, was named Deputy DG South II, while the Speaker of the Rivers State House of Assembly, Martin Amaewhule, will serve as South-South Deputy Coordinator for State Assemblies Mobilization. Minister of Works, David Umahi, was appointed Deputy DG for Infrastructure and Sensitization. Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, has been named Director of Finance, while Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, and Chairman of the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS), Zacch Adedeji, will jointly coordinate fundraising operations. Former Kano State Governor, Abdullahi Ganduje, was named Director for Stakeholder Mobilization, while former Lagos State Governor, Babatunde Fashola, serves as the South-West Zonal Coordinator for Stakeholders’ Mobilization. Chief Ayiri Emami was named Director for Special Duties, while former Super Eagles captain Joseph Yobo was appointed Deputy Director for Sports Sector Mobilization. Minister of Solid Minerals, Dele Alake, continues his role as Official Spokesman for the Campaign Council. Joining the media communications team are Minister of Aviation Festus Keyamo, Abdulmumin Jibrin, Lere Olayinka (media aide to FCT Minister Wike), and Segun Sowunmi. In administrative and operational roles, Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, continues as Secretary of the Campaign Council, supported by APC National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Bashiru, and Hadiza Bala-Usman as Deputy and Assistant Secretaries, respectively. Representative James Faleke will serve as Deputy Director-General for Election Planning, Coordination, and Monitoring. The expansion of the campaign structure underlines the ruling party’s strategy to build a broad-based political coalition as momentum builds toward the 2027 general elections. A statement by the APC National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Bashiru, said the campaign council would be nominated on Wednesday .

title: Friendship Pickleball Tournament Draws Taiwan and Palau Players Together
body: By: Laurel Marewibuel KOROR, Palau – The Taiwan-Palau Friendship Pickleball Tournament brought participants from both sides together through energetic competition and continued play, according to Elaine of the Taiwan Embassy. The event drew an enthusiastic response, with President Surangel Whipps Jr. wanting the games to continue and players staying on the court after the tournament ended. “The game went really well!” Elaine said. “President Whipps even wanted to keep it going longer, and a lot of people stayed to play after the tournament ended!” That response offered a clear sign of how much participants enjoyed the gathering. Rather than wrapping up when the tournament concluded, many continued playing, extending the opportunity to compete and spend time together. For Elaine, the most memorable part was the intensity of the matches. She said Ambassador Chen, the Taiwan Coast Guard Administration team and participants from Palau all played with strong commitment, competing for each point. “I think the highlight was seeing how competitive and exciting the games were,” she said. “Ambassador Chen, the Coast Guard Administration team, and everyone from the Palauan side were really into it, giving their best and fighting for every point!” The tournament gave players from Taiwan and Palau a shared activity centered on friendly competition. Both groups took part with enthusiasm, and the close attention to each point helped create an atmosphere that Elaine described as exciting. The enjoyment continued beyond the scheduled tournament, as participants chose to stay and play more. “Seeing everyone having such a great time and enjoying themselves really made me happy,” Elaine said. She said the turnout and participation left her pleased with how the event went. While she did not provide a participant count, her account of President Whipps wanting to continue and players remaining after the tournament indicates that interest extended beyond the formal competition. The event also prompted thoughts about future opportunities. Elaine said she would welcome the chance to work with other organizations to arrange more tournaments and invite additional people to take part. “It also made me think that, if we have the opportunity, I’d definitely love to work with other organizations to arrange more tournaments in the future and invite even more people to join!” she said. Her remarks point to a tournament that was not only competitive but enjoyable for those involved. The enthusiasm from players on both sides, along with the willingness to keep playing after the event ended, made the gathering a positive experience and left open the possibility of similar events in the future. The post Friendship Pickleball Tournament Draws Taiwan and Palau Players Together appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Zelenskyy: No partner warning on Kyiv ballistic strike
body:
Ukraine received no warning from partners about the Russian ballistic strike on Kyiv, in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

"There was also a rather vile ballistic strike on Kyiv, five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from partners about this strike. Intelligence on the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save people's lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. It is exactly this that helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistics," he said on Telegram on Tuesday.

title: US, Europe drafting four-point plan to settle Ukraine conflict — newspaper
body:
WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. The United States and Europe are working on a four-point proposal to settle the Ukraine conflict, The Washington Post columnist David Ignatius reported, citing sources.
According to the sources, Washington and Brussels are moving toward a joint peace proposal that would deliver financial and security benefits to both Ukraine and Russia as a baseline for a territorial settlement. A US official said the package would have four basic components, including a proposal for Russia to reach an economic and security deal with Europe that would restore stability to the region.
"Ukraine’s reconstruction would be the first pillar," Ignatius said, adding that the negotiators had asked Kiev for detailed cost estimates.
Security guarantees for both Ukraine and Russia would constitute the second essential component. However, it remains unclear what security arrangements are expected to be offered to Moscow.
"A third pillar would be economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy deal. One aspect might be a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia splitting the profits," the columnist noted. The proposal would also provide Russia with long-term access to the European energy market and specify when economic sanctions would be removed.
The fourth and final piece of the deal would be a ceasefire along the existing front line.
According to The Washington Post, "the diplomatic push" for the plan came at a recent meeting in Florida involving US, European and Ukrainian negotiators.

title: HMS Queen Elizabeth aircraft carrier prepares for NATO role and resumes air operations
body: The ship holds NATO command ship duties until mid-2027 and would lead a multinational naval force during a global crisis. A command staff has spent several weeks aboard, familiarising itself with the carrier and establishing how it would operate if called upon. Training this autumn is split between UK waters and the eastern Atlantic. It will prepare Queen Elizabeth for more complex exercises in 2027, including NATO’s Steadfast Defender, as the carrier works towards taking over flagship duties from HMS Prince of Wales. Before flying resumed, the crew had to demonstrate its ability to handle emergencies both on the flight deck and below decks. Drills included responding to an aircraft crash, recovering a pilot and tackling an engine-room fire with casualties. A Commando Wildcat from 847 Naval Air Squadron at Yeovilton became the first aircraft back aboard following the dry-dock re-certification period. Maritime Wildcats from 815 Naval Air Squadron, maritime Merlins from 814 Naval Air Squadron and Commando Merlins from 845 Naval Air Squadron subsequently joined the flying programme. The helicopters practised launches, recoveries and refuelling with engines running, putting the aircraft handlers, flying control teams and bridge personnel through their paces. Three pilots earned deck landing qualifications during the training. Daytime helicopter certification is the first major step towards embarking an air wing of F-35B Lightning II stealth fighters, helicopters and drones. Gunnery crews also practised machine-gun firing to test their accuracy, reactions and night-vision skills. Queen Elizabeth was commissioned into the Royal Navy on 7 December 2017, following a construction contract signed in May 2008, keel laying in July 2009 and launch in July 2014. Sections were built at six UK shipyards before final assembly at Rosyth Dockyard on the Firth of Forth. The Queen Elizabeth class displaces 70,600 tonnes and has flight decks measuring 280 metres by 73 metres, with an air group of 40 aircraft including F-35B fighters and helicopters. The Royal Navy operates two carriers of the class: Queen Elizabeth and Prince of Wales. The carrier recently paused training to visit Belfast, becoming the first Royal Navy aircraft carrier to call at the city since HMS Centaur in 1965. It welcomed cadets, Royal Navy Association members and families from the Army’s Northern Ireland-based 38th Brigade. “It has been a huge honour for us to be the first Queen Elizabeth-class carrier to visit Belfast and is a real proof of concept for future visits,” said Captain Claire Thompson, the ship’s commanding officer. “We will definitely strive to get back within a shorter timeframe than the previous 61-year gap between aircraft carriers.”

title: MARSS to provide counter-drone defense systems, hard-kill interceptors to Kuwait
body: MARSS has signed a £370 million ($489 million) contract with Kuwait to provide a nationwide counter-drone defense system that includes hard-kill interceptors. On October 12, 2026, MARSS said the defense system will cover threats from both the air and the sea through the installation of electro-optical, radar and sonar sensors across a network of sites to feed central command centers. MARSS will deploy a cellular system built around NiDAR, the UK firm’s AI-enabled command and control (C2) system, designed for multi domain surveillance and counter-drone defense. According to MARSS, NiDAR will “fuse the data into actionable threat assessments, providing hemispherical coverage against airborne and coastal seaborne drones”. MARSS “Recent conflicts in the Middle East have shown the damage drone attacks can inflict, and the limits of air defences that rely on expensive interceptor missiles,” MARSS said. “With soft-kill and hard-kill effectors integrated into and controlled through NiDAR, operators have layered defeat options and can select the most appropriate response for each situation.” The company added: “NiDAR dramatically shortens the decision cycle from detection to defeat, using AI to classify threats automatically, recommend engagement and reduce the cognitive burden on operators.” The UK has already supported Kuwait with Rapid Sentry, a ground-based air defense missile system. The RAF’s ORCUS system is also operating in the country, helping personnel detect drones early and take decisive action. AeroTime The MARSS agreement with Kuwait forms part of the UK government’s Taskforce Sabre, which brings together government and industry to help Gulf states rapidly secure the systems they need. “Countering drones and aerial threats is not about any single system. It is about an intelligent, layered architecture that detects, decides and defeats within seconds, and MARSS has built exactly that,” Johannes Pinl, CEO of MARSS, said. “Over the coming 24 months, MARSS will integrate the sensors and effectors that protect Kuwait’s people, critical infrastructure and national assets, backed by British engineering and new skilled jobs here in the UK.” RELATED MARSS Interceptor: the designer behind the drone hunter built for modern warfare The post MARSS to provide counter-drone defense systems, hard-kill interceptors to Kuwait appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Charting a Drug-Free Course: Young Sailors Converge in Palau
body: KOROR, Palau — A fleet of 17 young sailors, parents and coaches from Taitung, Taiwan, joined local mariners in Palauan waters from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5 for a five-day sailing exchange highlighted by the Palau-Taiwan Friendship Race on Oct. 3. The athletic exchange brought together young sailors maneuvering Optimist (OP) dinghies, ILCA 4 (Lasers) and traditional sailing canoes. The event gave the visiting crew an opportunity to test their nautical skills in local waters while building camaraderie with Palauan youth. Pictures by Palau Sailing Association and Taitung Sailing School The Friendship Race proved to be a demanding test on the water. Unstable weather patterns tied to a passing typhoon produced heavy squalls, gusty winds and severe sailing conditions. Despite the rough seas, athletes, coaches, parents and shore crew coordinated seamlessly to ensure every vessel and sailor returned safely to port. For the young athletes from Taitung, the voyage carried meaning far beyond competitive scoring. Sailors learned that maintaining course requires a clear mind, physical strength, sound judgment, focus and stamina. The program emphasized how alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, amphetamines and other illicit substances impair performance, encouraging participants to “Take the Helm – Don’t let Drugs Steer Your Course.” Representing a milestone for the Taitung Sailing School, traveling beyond local waters to Palau marked a major step forward for athletes whose prior experience was limited to sailing around Taiwan’s offshore havens of Green Island and Lanyu. Language differences presented no barrier as participants bonded through rigging, tactical play and shared seamanship both on and off the water. Taitung coaches emphasized that victory was measured in character rather than finish line order. “They helped each other and came back stronger and more united,” the coaching staff reflected following the exchange, describing the journey as a lesson in courage, teamwork and cross-cultural understanding. The event was organized through cooperation among the Palau Sailing Association, the Taitung Sailing School, parents, coaches and the local sailing community. Additional support was provided by the crew of the Alingano Maisu , the Micronesian Voyaging Society and the Taiwan Embassy. Funding was granted by the 2026 Palau Taiwan small grants program, reinforcing the message of personal responsibility and healthy, substance-free choices. Organizers aim to establish the five-day exchange as an annual fixture. Continued maritime exchanges with athletes from Taiwan and other nations will provide young Palauan sailors with broader opportunities to compete, sharpen their seamanship and build international friendships. title: Chasing a -O2 pessimization in antcc
body:
2026 Oct 12 â c compilers optimization antcc
Recently I was benchmarking the generated code efficiency for my C compiler antcc , and I noticed something concerning in a simple Lua benchmark:
The "optimized" builds were actually slower. Now, my compiler doesn't implement many optimizations at the moment so I wouldn't expect a huge improvement, but being 1.4x slower should definitely not happen. [1] One of the optimizations that antcc does have is inlining, which generally speaking is one of the most impactful compiler optimizations and it usually improves benchmarks all around.
So my first thought was, okay my inlining heuristics and thresholds are very simple and not really tuned, so perhaps it's being too aggressive and blowing up the code size, leading to very bad instruction cache thrashing. If I disabled inlining, the pessimization seemed to go away, which could support that theory. That's not a very satisfactory explanation though, and I would like to fix it, so I looked into it more.
The main culprit was in the function luaV_execute , whose code blew up to ~43KB with -O2, ~2.4x bigger than the -O1 build. Now, this function is the main bytecode interpreter loop for the Lua VM, and these are one of the worst kinds of functions for a compiler to deal with: it's a huge function with a hot loop, many cases/control flow branches, distinct hot/cold paths nested in the graph where a wrong optimizer or register-allocation decision can pessimize the whole loop, etc... [2] So the baseline function is a tricky one, but it doesn't explain this.
Tweaking the inlining thresholds didn't seem to help: either few things got inlined (like -O1) and binary size & performance stayed roughly the same, or small functions start getting inlined and the pessimization happens. In particular, these functions were getting inlined (some in multiple instances): floatforloop , lessequalothers , lessthanothers , luaV_idiv , luaV_mod , luaV_modf , luaV_shiftl , luaV_tointegerns , plus some of their respective callees. In the Lua source code link above you can see those are all pretty small simple functions.
Looking at the final codegen is not that helpful, but examining the IR [3] revealed something interesting: after all optimizations, the -O2 IR was only 11% bigger than -O1. How could that be amplified to a 2.4x difference in the binary?
The final passes that run after optimizations and before code generation are instruction selection and register allocation . Instruction selection mostly concerns itself with ensuring instruction operands are ready to be lowered into machine code, but keeps temporaries as virtual registers. For example, for x86-64, it models memory operands and will turn a sequence of IR instructions like:
It does other things like introducing register constraints for certain operations, but anyway because it only expands into small sequences of instructions like this, it couldn't be the cause.
Register allocation is the process of mapping virtual temporaries to the target architecture's physical registers. For the previous snippet, that might result in
which is compiled to the x86 instruction mov eax, DWORD PTR [rsi + rdx * 4] .
The problem is that there are infinite virtual temporaries but a small number of registers, so you have to choose which variables get which registers and when there are not enough registers for all of them, some of them have to go on the stack, which is called spilling .
Most operations require values to be in registers, so spilled variables often have to be moved back and forth between registers. Or even worse, they might have to be moved between two different stack slots in some situations.
antcc has a basic implementation of linear scan regalloc . If there is a lot of register pressure and many temporaries get spilled, potentially a lot of instructions can be created just to shuffle values between stack and registers.
And indeed, comparing relative IR size increase before and after regalloc at -O2, the +11% difference was turning into +70% blowup after regalloc... looking at the disassembly, >40% of instructions in luaV_execute were just stackâregister mov s. That's really bad, something being inlined must be resulting in this dreadful register pressure and spilling, but it's not obvious what.
My compiler like most modern backends uses a Static Single-Assignment representation. In this form, straight-line code such as (I'm using C-like pseudocode to simplify):
That is, there are no variable mutation instructions. The reason this representation is great for compilers is that it simplifies all kinds of data-flow analysis and permits some more powerful optimizations than the non-SSA counterpart.
With control flow, data flow merges are explicit in the IR:
This magic "phi" instruction [4] has as its result the value of x1 or x2 depending on which control flow branch was taken. Same approach can be applied for variables modified in loops:
Textually, it looks like the phi function references i_n before its definition, but importantly that value is only taken in the loop back-edge ( LoopEnd -> LoopBegin ), and at that point the value of i_n is available.
A key thing to realize here is that this i_l temporary, being a loop phi, is live across the whole loop, since its value is used to compute the next iteration.
Ignore the undefs for now, and notice the ; preds line indicating the predecessors of that block: @1 , the beginning of the function, and @892 , hundreds of blocks later: the end of the main interpreter loop. Meaning, we have 16 phis that are live across the whole loop. This is what is creating a lot of register pressure, wrecking register allocation and resulting in that big code size blowup from stack spilling traffic. So, what are these phis, where do they come from, and why the undef s...
C programs don't start in SSA form, so they have to go through a transformation pass. I borrowed the terminology and design from clang/LLVM in my compiler:
Initially generates an IR that looks like:
I'm glossing over the trickiest part of this, which is knowing when and where to insert these phi instructions in the general case. There's basically two algorithms to do it, and the one I'm using is from the paper "Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form (Braun et al, 2013)" . The gist of it is: walk the control-flow graph (CFG) in reverse post-order (RPO); when you see a write, memoize the current definition keyed by the block; when you see a read, look for that definition or query the predecessors' definitions recursively and insert phis when that lookup finds distinct definitions. Loops are trickier: because the back-edge predecessors haven't been visited yet, you have to insert a provisional phi and resolve it later.
Something about C that almost every language that came after it removed as a Bad Idea is the ability to leave variables uninitialized. For example:
After the control flow merge, x is phi(uninitialized, y) . That is what the undef in my IR is. The way it's introduced in my mem2reg is that if the recursive "read current definition" function reaches all the way to the beginning of the function without finding a definition, it gives it undef . (Later on, moves and operations on undef can be effectively optimized away.)
So was the Lua interpreter reading uninitialized variables? Well, no. Look at some of the affected code from the interpreter function:
The key is the tointegerns macro, which in turn calls the function luaV_tointegerns :
In -O2, this function and luaV_flttointeger get inlined, resulting in an expansion like this (simplified):
mem2reg is always ran after every inlining pass. The undef in question comes from the variable ib which I've marked. You can see that the local variable is initialized in every path where the inlined function returns 1 , but mem2reg cannot correlate that with the later if (tointegerns_ret) guard, so it sees a possibly uninitialized read.
But that does not tell the whole story! It explains the undef , but not why the phi is live across the whole loop. After all, this local is scoped to a block inside a branch of the loop, it does not live across loop iterations...
Eventually I figured out the root cause: I was treating the idea of "variables start as uninitialized" too literally in mem2reg. When it encountered an alloca , it didn't give it a definition for the current block. This sounds correct, and the recursive lookup in the algorithm terminates at the function entry with an undef . But recall the catch with loops being that when you encounter a backedge, you don't know if there's a later definition, because you haven't visited the whole loop yet, so you insert a provisional phi...
In essence, my mem2reg was behaving as if code like:
In the 2nd function, the value of x is kept across iterations, whereas in the 1st, the value of x is a 'fresh' uninitialized every time the if branch is not taken... This is not a miscompilation: as far as C is concerned, this is fine because uninitialized variables' values are not legally usable anyway. And if you frame it in terms of stack-allocated variables, it's a sensible approach: the slot for x is fixed for the whole function and doesn't get reset between loop iterations, so it keeps the previous iteration's whatever it was and it doesn't matter. But the problem is that in the context of SSA form, this generates something like:
And it is these loop phis that result in the pathological register allocation. The fix was one line:
Initializing the var as undefined (a nice oxymoron) at the place of the alloca ensures that the recursive lookup doesn't cross loop backedges and insert phis in the loop header. This is enough to fix this case, and that change made the mysterious pessimization disappear.
This problem can still bite for C code that is old-style declaring all variables at the top of the function. It's possible to fix this general case by using Tarjan's algorithm to find the graph SCCs of the phi data-flow to detect cycles, and making use of these undef semantics when classifying phis as redundant; but I haven't implemented that yet.
Jump threading an inlined function used directly as a branch condition, or more generally SSA-aware phi jump threading, could've also fixed the branch correlation issue that led to mem2reg not seeing the dominating write of those variables and introducing undefs.
I made use of AI agents to help debug this issue. It saved me a lot of time in investigating, filtering through disassemblies and IR dumps, running the compiler with different inlining thresholds and measuring, etc; but it was not good at trying to find the root cause. It proposed probably around 10 convoluted "fixes" before I eventually arrived at the conclusion myself. Still <$1 well spent for the sake of reducing tedium.
Lua 5.4.7, bench.lua , AMD Ryzen 5 5600G. Take these with a grain of salt.
antcc was worse than even tcc, but that's mainly because my frontend was lowering switch statements to linear if-else chains. I implemented a simple binary search codegen, which was one of those things that I just hadn't gotten around to yet; and a few other minor optimizations; after this fix.
Do note that antcc performs mem2reg by default when passed no optimization flags, unlike gcc. It might seem counterintuitive, but from my testing, running mem2reg improves compile times too; presumably due to the reduced number of stack store/load instructions for the backend to churn through.
I omitted the bars for clang because they are all very similar to gcc.
The only difference between -O1 and -O2 is in inlining thresholds and -O2 running some optimization passes more than once. â©
This is why LuaJIT's interpreter in hand-written assembly beats almost every other bytecode interpreter, and it's not just about the while-switch loop â©
variously known as phi function, Ï, /faÉª/, /fi/, phony instruction â©
Not to be confused with the dynamic alloca() function. â©
The register storage class exists, but it doesn't really matter in modern architectures so you (almost) never see it used. â©

title: Trump says US may have gone 'too far' in killing Iranian leaders, complicating talks
body: US President Donald Trump suggested on Monday that Washington may have gone “too far” in targeting Iran's leadership, acknowledging that killing senior Iranian officials had complicated efforts to identify figures with whom the United States could negotiate.Speaking at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio, Trump addressed the difficulties facing Washington as it seeks a diplomatic resolution to the conflict with Tehran.“We might have gone too far with the leaders because we don't know who the hell we're dealing with anymore,” Trump told supporters.“Nobody wants to be the president of Iran,” he added, noting that potential candidates were unwilling to assume the position.At the rally, Trump also affirmed that as “the No. 1 state sponsor of terror,” Iran would not be allowed to obtain nuclear weapons.Trump reiterates claims Iranian navy 'at the bottom of the sea'Despite acknowledging the difficulties created by the campaign against Iran's leadership, the president reiterated his claims that US military operations had effectively destroyed the regime's air force and navy.Trump maintained that Iran had lost all 159 of its naval vessels, describing them as “resting beautifully in the bottom of the sea.”The comments echoed concerns raised by US Vice President JD Vance, who said in an interview with Reuters earlier this month that Washington remained uncertain about how decisions were being made within Iran's leadership.Vance stressed that any agreement ending the conflict would require Tehran to make meaningful reductions to its nuclear enrichment capacity.

title: Supreme Court Establishes Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure
body: The Supreme Court has established a Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure to support the continued review and improvement of the rules governing judicial proceedings. Clear and effective rules are essential to the fair and efficient administration of justice. To help ensure that the Judiciary’s rules continue to meet those objectives, the Rules Committee will provide a formal process for reviewing existing rules and considering recommendations for change. The Rules Committee will review rules of practice and procedure governing civil and criminal matters, evaluate proposals for amendments, conduct research and analysis, and prepare proposed rule changes for consideration by the Supreme Court. The Committee may also recommend new rules for judicial proceedings where rules do not currently exist. Certain matters fall outside the Committee’s responsibilities, including the Palau Bar Admission Committee’s Rules, rules governing Continuing Legal Education, the Disciplinary Rules, and rules involving administrative or other matters. All proposed amendments and new rules developed by the Committee will be submitted to the Supreme Court through the Chief Justice for review and final approval. The Rules Committee welcomes proposals from the justices and judges, members of the Palau Bar Association, and members of the publi c . Proposals to amend an existing rule or create a new rule may be submitted to the Rules Committee at JRC.Submissions@palausupremecourt.net . The post Supreme Court Establishes Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure appeared first on Island Times News .
