title: ideaForge Secures Orders from Survey of India for Q6 V2 UAVs to Support Mapping and Geospatial Applications
body:
Bengaluru, Oct 13, 2026. ideaForge Technology Limited has received an order from the Survey of India (SOI) for its Q6 V2 UAVs, further expanding the use of its indigenous UAV technology across specialised government applications. The UAVs will support SOI’s surveying and mapping requirements, enabling the collection of high-quality aerial and geospatial data across diverse terrains and project environments. The growing use of UAVs is transforming how geospatial data is collected, processed, and used for planning and decision-making. By enabling aerial data collection across large and difficult-to-access areas, UAVs can complement conventional survey methods while improving the speed, coverage, and frequency of data collection and processing. This is particularly relevant for applications where current and accurate geospatial information is critical to planning, infrastructure development, land administration and public programmes.



The Q6 V2 is a survey-grade UAV designed to provide high-area coverage, enabling large-scale mapping projects to be completed faster and more efficiently. A high-endurance, lightweight, and VTOL-capable platform, the Q6 V2 is designed and developed entirely in India. Equipped with advanced Mapping payloads, autonomous navigation, and encrypted communications systems, it has rapid deployment capability in under 10 minutes. The quadcopter designed UAV has an endurance of 60 minutes, having an operational range of 5 km and a maximum takeoff weight of 6kg. The platform supports daylight, thermal, mapping, and multispectral payloads, offering flexibility across various kinds of survey requirements. Q6 V2 is field-proven across varied terrains, from high-altitude zones to flood-affected areas.

Speaking on the development, Mr. Somil Gautam, Associate Director – Enterprise Business, ideaForge Technology Ltd., said,“The adoption of UAVs in geospatial applications is creating a more efficient way to collect the aerial data that informs how we plan, develop, and manage our physical environment. Our engagement with the Survey of India reflects the growing relevance of indigenous UAV technology in specialised applications where reliable and timely data is important. At ideaForge, we are focused on building platforms that can deliver dependable performance across real-world operating environments, and we see significant potential for UAV-enabled mapping and geospatial intelligence across government and enterprise applications.” 

The order adds to the use of ideaForge's UAV technology in mapping and geospatial applications, in a field where aerial data collection is becoming a regular part of how surveys are planned and carried out. The company’s UAVs have already demonstrated their capabilities across a range of government and enterprise survey requirements, including large-scale deployments under the Government of India’s SVAMITVA Yojana and large-scale mapping. ideaForge looks forward to supporting Survey of India as it applies drone technology to its surveying and mapping needs, and to working with its teams as they put the platform to use.

title: We checked 495 AI product photos against the originals; 35% of errors were text
body:
Since late September, every image a ProductAI subscriber generates in the studio gets a second look. A vision model is shown the photo the seller uploaded next to the finished render and asked one question: is this still the same product? The scene, the light and the angle are supposed to change. The product is not.
In the first 18 days that check looked at 495 renders and flagged 111 of them , about one in five. We read every one of those 111 notes by hand. This is what they say about where AI product photos go wrong, and what you can do before you press Generate.
One problem is bigger than the next two combined: text .
More than a third of all flags were about writing on the product. The failures came in three kinds.
The first kind is the dangerous one. A garbled word looks wrong at a glance. "110 mL" looks perfectly fine, and it is a false statement about your product on your own listing.
What helps: keep the product large in the frame. Many of the cases we opened were products shown small, in a hand or in a wide lifestyle scene, where the label is a few dozen pixels tall. If the label has to be readable, shoot it close.
Nineteen flags were colour or finish. Navy was rendered purple on two different models, for the same product. Silver jewellery came back gold on one run and rose gold on another. A burgundy bag turned black. A white bottle became transparent.
What helps: say the colour and the finish in the prompt. "Navy blue, matte" or "polished silver" costs four words and gives the model something to hold on to.
Nine flags were a missing part, and the parts were consistent: the chain of a necklace, the battery pack of a power tool, a lid, a charm on a keyring. Sixteen more were shape changes, where an unusual outline was "corrected" into a familiar one. A teardrop-shaped compact came back round. A cropped sweatshirt came back as a bodysuit.
What helps: upload a photo that shows the whole product with every part attached. If the chain is out of frame in your reference, expect it to be out of the render too.
Eleven flags were the wrong product altogether. In about half, the product was simply absent: the render showed an empty pedestal, or only the gift box the product comes in. Four more had one cause: several different products uploaded as references for one image. The model picked the sibling product from the same brand, or added an extra one that was never asked for.
What helps: one product per generation, unless a group shot is really what you want.
About one flag in seven was a false alarm, and they were not random. Our own instructions to the checker had asked for most of them.
The most instructive one was a pill bottle flagged because its label had changed to a different medication. That looked like the most serious catch in the whole set, until we read the prompt: the seller had asked for exactly that label swap. The checker never saw the prompt, because of how the studio stores it. A checker that does not know what was asked for cannot tell a mistake from a request.
We are testing a revised checker now. It ignores a product being open, held, tilted or styled, it reads the prompt, and it names the kind of change it found instead of raising a generic warning.
In this sample, yes, with a large caveat.
GPT Image 2 was flagged about half as often as the others. That fits what we saw in two client catalogues , where it was the model that kept label text correct. The caveat: all of this comes from 13 accounts , and different sellers used different models for different products. Treat it as a direction, not a ranking.
A flag after the fact is useful. Not needing one is better. So the three most common mistakes now show up as a one-line tip above the prompt box, and only when your prompt touches that subject:
One tip at a time, and you can dismiss each one for good.

title: Voters here will decide whether to force cities to build cheaper, smaller homes
body:
In North Braintree, Mass., larger lot sizes imposed decades ago have meant fewer homes, and bigger more expensive ones. Voters will decide whether to force cities to allow smaller homes on smaller lots. Jennifer Ludden/NPR hide caption
LEXINGTON, Mass. — Massachusetts is one of the most expensive states in the country, and it's easy to find people frustrated with high home prices.
"It's really hard to find housing, it's extremely expensive, and I can't afford to live alone," said renter Jamie Sharken, 34, as she walks her dog in Lexington, north of Boston and near where she shares a home with three others. "There's four of us in two bathrooms, definitely a run-down old house."
A massive housing shortage has pushed up prices. Sharken grew up in the state and would love to buy a home, but finds it hard to see how she could afford it. She's not alone. "Most of my friends have so much debt from education," she said. "Just being able to save money to put a down payment on a house feels impossible these days."
She's heard about the ballot measure that aims to make housing more affordable by creating more starter homes on smaller lots.
Jamie Sharken, 34, grew up in Massachusetts but doubts she'll ever be able to afford a house there. She supports a ballot measure that aims to create smaller starter homes. Jennifer Ludden/NPR hide caption
Cities and towns here and across the U.S. have set minimum lot sizes for single-family homes, many of them quite large. The measure would require them to allow homes on lots as small as 5,000 square feet, about the size of a basketball court . If it passes, Massachusetts would become the latest in a growing number of states to mandate such a zoning change amid a nationwide housing crunch.
The idea is to boost overall supply and override persistent, local "not in my backyard" opposition to new development. Critics bristle at the loss of local control and say the measure may not really help struggling first-time buyers.
But Sharken said encouraging smaller homes makes sense to her.
"There's so many homes that are empty with five, six, 10 bedrooms and one couple living there," she said. "I think it's time to share the wealth in terms of the space that we have and to have more housing for people."
To understand what's driving the zoning measure and how it would work, it helps to go back in time. Andrew Mikula, a housing economist leading the push for the ballot measure , takes me to a quiet street in North Braintree, about 10 miles south of Boston.
The block we stand on was built a century ago. Colonial and Cape Cod-style clapboard homes, with shutters and dormer windows, sit fairly close together. Some are about 1,000 square feet, with three bedrooms and 1.5 bathrooms. But this is a snapshot in time.
"With modern zoning, these homes are illegal to build today," Mikula said.
That's because after World War II, as suburbs exploded, cities across the country mandated bigger and bigger lot sizes for single-family homes only. The trend effectively banned apartments , duplexes or townhomes on large swaths of residential land and locked in economic and racial segregation. We see the change as we walk a couple of blocks down the street.
Andrew Mikula is a housing economist leading the push for smaller lot sizes. He stands on an older block in North Braintree, Mass., with smaller lots that would be illegal for new homes today. Jennifer Ludden/NPR hide caption
Suddenly, the yards are a lot bigger and so are the houses, with stylish arched windows and two-car garages. "You need to build a large McMansion just to justify the cost of assembling so much land," said Mikula. "So this is what you get."
In fact, most single-family zoning in the state requires at least an acre of land — about 40,000 square feet, or nearly the size of a football field without the end zones. That also means fewer homes get built. The ballot measure does not apply to Boston, which has its own zoning rules.
By the state's own data, expensive housing is fueling an exodus of working-age people . "And when we lose young workers and family members of people who already live here," Mikula said, "that not only separates extended families but also hurts our economy."
Retail, service, and healthcare workers who stay "just can't afford to live in the communities that they serve," said Jesse Kanson-Benanav, executive director at Abundant Housing Massachusetts .
He called the state's housing shortage "an existential crisis" that hits all generations. An estimated 400,000 young adults still live with their parents. Meanwhile, he said seniors struggle to maintain aging homes, "because we haven't built … moderate-sized and reasonably priced homes for them to downsize in their own community."
In recent years, Massachusetts lawmakers have forced cities to allow multifamily housing near transit stations and accessory dwelling units wherever single-family homes are allowed, and committed billions toward public and lower-income housing. Kanson-Benanav called the starter home ballot measure "one strategy among many" and hopes that if it passes, it will inspire lawmakers to do even more. Polling suggests broad support.
Critics resent the prospect of a blanket state mandate and question whether it will produce truly affordable housing. To illustrate that concern, Lexington Select Board member Jill Hai took me to the backyard of a yellow clapboard two-story home with windows trimmed in red.
"We're looking at a beautiful home, I have to say," she said. "It's got beautiful hydrangeas."
This smallish lot is exactly what the ballot measure would allow, because the house was built in 1900. But it's been gut-renovated and expanded, and was on the market for nearly $1.3 million. "By the way, that is less than the median home value in Lexington, so it's a great deal!" Hai said with a laugh.
But it's hardly what most would consider a starter home. Just up the street, an even bigger new house on a small lot sold last year for more than $2 million.
Adam Chapdelaine, with the Massachusetts Municipal Association, and Lexington Select Board member Jill Hai question how affordable smaller-lot homes would be and worry that a surge in new homes could strain local infrastructure. Jennifer Ludden/NPR hide caption
In the current market, at least in this affluent town, Hai didn't think the zoning change would be nearly as effective as other things Lexington has done, like creating rentals tied to people's income and using town-owned land to build affordable housing. She said local leaders know better what's needed — and she understands the housing crisis.
"My kids are 28 and 30, and they can't afford to come back to Lexington," she said.
Critics also worried that an unplanned surge in housing could strain schools, roads and other infrastructure.
The ballot measure only applies to places with water and sewer access, but "it doesn't speak to the water or sewer system capacity," said Adam Chapdelaine, executive director of the Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposes the measure. Some already feel the need to expand capacity or are in the middle of planning for that.
"They are terrified that if this passes, that will completely upend those plans, or make it far more expensive and have to see those costs passed on to existing ratepayers," he said.
This year alone , lawmakers in Kansas, Maine and Idaho imposed smaller minimum lots to tackle housing costs. Texas did so last year. Most mandated even smaller sizes than Massachusetts' 5,000-square-foot ballot measure.
"Five thousand is a good start, and in our opinion it should be lower," said Tobias Peter, who tracks such policies at the conservative-leaning American Enterprise Institute.
He noted that zoning power has long been delegated to cities, but for years they've failed to produce enough housing to meet the need. Now, a growing number of states are taking back a power they've always had under the U.S. Constitution.
AEI has researched the impact of smaller lots on housing prices and supply, and found builders do produce more starter homes "if you allow them to build on smaller lots in areas that have lower land prices," said Peter.
But finding that cheaper land is hard near major cities like Boston. It's more likely in new developments farther out, Peter said, and the smaller the lots, the more affordable the price of the homes will be.
A century-old home in Lexington, Mass., sits on a smaller lot that's since been outlawed. But after a gut renovation and expansion, it was listed for more than $1 million. Jennifer Ludden/NPR hide caption
So how much should a starter home cost? AEI defines it as less than four times a county's median household income. For the national median, which reached a record high in 2025 at $87,460 , that would mean a starter home should cost less than $350,000.
But Massachusetts' housing shortage is so severe, Peter thought five or even six times the income made more sense. Given Massachusetts' high average income , that could mean $500,000 or more.
Is that really a starter home? "In Massachusetts it is!" he said.
On a recent evening, about 30 people in a library conference room pledged allegiance to an American flag on a large screen. It was the start of a meeting of the Weymouth Democratic Town Committee to discuss this year's election ballot measures. The organizer noted he'd heard a lot of interest in the one on zoning.
The crowd was mostly older, with many homeowners, but opinions were mixed.
"I understand the problem. But I think they need to work a little harder to find a better solution," said Kathy Swain, who's lived in Weymouth all of her 70-plus years. She's very involved with local politics and does not like the idea of a state mandate.
"I just think that people in local communities need to have local authority, otherwise they're going to become more disengaged than they already are," she said.
A few feet away, Susan Donovan said she might be in favor of the measure, "because I wouldn't mind downsizing myself." Expensive housing makes that hard, too.
Donovan has been thinking about building a smaller place on her property and having the children move into the big house. "We don't need all the big land anymore," she said. "We don't want to mow it anymore, right? Small sounds good to me."

title: One way to protect coral reefs? Bring back seabirds
body:
At Palmyra Atoll in the remote Pacific Ocean, wildlife refuge manager Paige Mino observes red-footed boobies. Scientists have found a surprising link between the seabirds and the health of the surrounding ocean. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
The remote Pacific Ocean has some of the most pristine coral reefs in the world. The corals themselves are bigger than cars, their delicate arms creating a dense underwater maze. Above them, the skies are filled with seabirds like red-footed boobies and white terns, searching for fish.
These species, separated by land and sea, are far more intertwined than once thought. Their relationship is the backbone of an entire ecosystem — a hidden connection that's changing the way scientists think about conservation.
That connection: bird poop. Coral reefs near seabird colonies are generally healthier, thanks to the nutrients that birds deposit in their guano. It's one reason tropical islands and atolls are biodiversity hot spots in the vast Pacific Ocean.
Joe Pollock of The Nature Conservancy photographs the reefs of Palmyra Atoll, known for being some of the most pristine coral reefs in the world. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
On some islands, this close-knit partnership has broken down. Seabird colonies have declined because of habitat loss and invasive species like rats. With fewer birds, fewer nutrients reach the ocean ecosystem.
Now, as coral restoration projects work to bring back reefs, they're also focusing on bringing back seabird colonies, reestablishing a connection that helps both species. Coral reefs are increasingly vulnerable to rising ocean temperatures, and biologists say they need every advantage in a hotter world.
"If we can figure out ways to just stop the local threats to ecosystems, they will, in a lot of cases, find ways to repair themselves," says Alex Wegmann, lead scientist for The Nature Conservancy's island resilience strategy. "They can reestablish their natural functions that will then allow them to adapt to the climate impacts that are coming."
A white tern takes flight among native trees on Palmyra Atoll. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
More than a thousand miles south of Hawaii, there's a tiny group of islands known as Palmyra Atoll. In the rainforest there, a tiny chick the size of a fuzzy, white golf ball perches on a tree limb. The parents hover nearby, chattering rhythmically.
"That's a white tern chick, and a young one at that," Paige Mino, manager of the Palmyra Atoll National Wildlife Refuge with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, says as she looks up at the birds. "I think that their call sounds like an electric rubber band snapping," she adds with a smile.
The forest echoes with the calls of seabirds, like red-footed boobies, large birds with bright blue beaks and signature red feet. Almost all of the birds on Palmyra Atoll rely on the ocean, flying out to sea daily to feed on fish or squid, bringing some back for their young.
White tern chicks (left) and red-footed boobies (right) depend on the ocean for food. Tens of thousands of birds nest on Palmyra Atoll. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
The abundance is thanks in large part to Palmyra Atoll's remote location. While it was likely visited by Polynesians who crossed the Pacific on seafaring voyages, the atoll wasn't permanently inhabited. In the 1800s, coconut plantations were developed. The U.S. military turned the atoll into a logistical station during World War II, building bunkers and roads.
In 2000, The Nature Conservancy bought Palmyra Atoll from private owners and transferred the majority of it to the federal government. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service manages it as a national wildlife refuge.
"There's no human impact of pollution or overcapacity, so I think it really gives the wildlife and vegetation the space to thrive," Mino says. "It gives the wildlife a chance to do what they naturally do."
During World War II, the U.S. military built bunkers, supply buildings and a runway on Palmyra Atoll, the remnants of which are still visible today. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Palmyra Atoll's thriving ecosystem has given scientists a window into the hidden processes that make it work, including some mysteries.
More than a decade ago, a team of scientists noticed something at Palmyra Atoll: Manta rays were more commonly seen in waters near seabird colonies. The massive mantas, some with a 9-foot wingspan, slowly glide through the water as they feed on tiny plankton.
That led them to uncover an efficient system of nutrient recycling that starts with the birds.
Roughly 100,000 sooty terns nest on Palmyra Atoll. The birds spend years at sea before returning to land to breed. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
When seabirds return to land after eating fish at sea, they roost in the trees. There, they deposit a lot of nutrients in their guano. One study of almost 200 atolls estimated that seabirds brought more than 100,000 pounds of nitrogen back to land. That acts as a fertilizer, nourishing the trees and plants.
Those nutrients spread with Palmyra Atoll's frequent, heavy rains. They get washed into the ocean, where they help the entire marine food web. Tiny, microscopic plankton grow, feeding larger plankton that are eaten by many species, including fish and manta rays. Though it's not their primary food source, even corals eat plankton.
Reef manta rays (left) are known to feed in waters near seabird colonies, where there's more abundant food, thanks to nutrients from birds. Coconut crabs (right) are scavengers that break down organic matter in Palmyra's forests, helping support the nutrient cycle. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
"Studies show that those marine nutrients from seabird guano are really valuable and important for the whole reef ecosystem," says Katie Franklin, who works on Palmyra Atoll conservation strategy for The Nature Conservancy. "Guano will help nourish the ecosystem from the rainforest to the reef, so we really just want to bring on more guano."
The Nature Conservancy's Alexandra Corti searches the forest with binoculars. At most, only a few dozen people stay on Palmyra Atoll at a time, living temporarily at the small research station. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Scientists figured out the seabirds' role because there are places on Palmyra Atoll where birds are hard to find. Some forests are eerily quiet.
"We're standing in a dense monoculture of coconut palms," Franklin says, pushing past large palm fronds. "It is literally just coconut palms growing. There are way fewer birds in this type of forest."
A juvenile red-footed booby sits on a nest. Palmyra Atoll has one of the largest red-footed booby populations in the world. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
The palm trunks are densely packed together, letting in very little sunlight. The trees are the legacy of coconut plantations established more than a century ago.
"None of these attempts at farming coconut palms ended up being very successful or profitable and were all abandoned," Franklin says. "But the impact that these coconut palm plantations made has lasted."
In 2000, almost half of Palmyra Atoll was covered in coconut palms, where few seabirds nest. It's why the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and The Nature Conservancy have started a decade-long project to bring the native forest back.
Katie Baur, a conservation science volunteer on Palmyra Atoll, saws down invasive coconut palms. More than a million palm trees and sprouts have been removed from the atoll. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
In blazing midday tropical heat, Katie Baur saws the trunk of a young coconut palm. The beach is covered in coconuts, all sprouting young trees. She's a conservation science volunteer with The Nature Conservancy who lives on the atoll for six months.
"It's hard — it's definitely not glamorous," she says with a laugh.
Since the project started in 2019, more than a million coconut palm trees and sprouts have been removed. Baur says once the palms are gone, the native forest returns rapidly.
"I get to go around the atoll and see places where new native flora is starting to reestablish," Baur says. "So it's exciting for me because I know that the work I'm doing now, in six months, in a year, is going to look like those places."
Katie Franklin of The Nature Conservancy says Palmyra Atoll's thriving ecosystem makes it a "natural laboratory, where we can really understand how an ecosystem like this works and what can we take away from Palmyra that can be useful for islands elsewhere." Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Even as native forest has returned to Palmyra Atoll, the ecosystem's recovery has also depended on tackling another tricky invader: rats.
Rats were likely brought to Palmyra during World War II accidentally, but they quickly made themselves at home.
"They probably thought they had gone to heaven," says Wegmann of The Nature Conservancy's island resilience strategy. "Palmyra is so productive as an ecosystem. There are invertebrates everywhere, land crabs, insects, cockroaches, lots of yummy things for them to eat, and there are no predators."
With unlimited food and warm weather year-round, rat populations boomed, topping an estimated 30,000 rats. As a result, seabird populations declined, particularly birds that build their nests on the ground. It's a pattern that's been seen on hundreds of other islands. One study found that 41% of highly threatened mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians are found on islands, where invasive species have been a major driver of extinctions.
Ground-nesting birds, like the sooty tern, are highly vulnerable to invasive rat populations. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
In 2011, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, along with nonprofit partners, led a campaign to eradicate rats from Palmyra Atoll. Wegmann says when the rats were successfully removed, the ecosystem rebounded quickly .
"Land crab populations exploded and the forest exploded," Wegmann says. "We saw new crab species emerge. We saw more and more seabirds nesting in trees throughout the entire atoll. And we started to see the native forest trees that had not been reproducing with rats here start to reproduce."
Researchers are now hoping to see the return of other seabirds that seem to have disappeared from Palmyra Atoll. Eight species are thought to have once nested there, but are no longer found. One, the gray-backed tern, recently reappeared and has nested on the atoll for four consecutive years.
Fake decoy birds on Palmyra Atoll are used to attract seabirds that were once thought to nest there but are no longer found. The hope is to reestablish the populations. One species, the gray-backed tern, recently reappeared and has nested there for four years in a row. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Even with its remote Pacific location, Palmyra Atoll is still threatened by global changes. In 2013, a marine heat wave elevated ocean temperatures for months, causing the corals to bleach and turn white. Many of the atoll's reefs have since recovered, but some didn't bounce back as readily.
As the climate gets hotter, the future for coral reefs globally is dire. Studies show that if humans continue burning fossil fuels, the planet will heat up more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), compared to preindustrial temperatures. At that level, between 70%-90% of coral reefs worldwide won't survive , according to a report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
Even in remote places like Palmyra Atoll, coral reefs are threatened by rising ocean temperatures from climate change. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
With marine heat waves getting more frequent and intense, research shows it's vital that reefs recover as quickly as possible between bleaching events.
"We want to give them the best chance possible to do that," Wegmann says. "And we believe that by creating the habitat for the seabirds and maximizing that seabird nutrient benefit, we will give the reef its best chance of enduring whatever climate future comes."
Wegmann says the conservation lessons learned at Palmyra are being applied at other islands and atolls, like the Chagos Archipelago in the Indian Ocean.
Coconut palms have taken over half of the forested land at more than 200 atolls around the Pacific. Roughly a quarter of all tropical seabirds in the world also rely on atolls for nesting. While atolls seem small, the linkages between land and sea mean they play an outsized role in global biodiversity.
"They create this halo of influence on the ocean around them," Wegmann says. "If you add up all of the area of ocean for all the atolls just in the Pacific, it's about the same size as South America. So, protecting atolls is important for the individual atoll, but also for a huge amount of ocean surrounding it."
Alex Wegmann, Dana Sabine and Katie Franklin of The Nature Conservancy head to a seabird colony. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption

title: Polls are a snapshot, and other helpful things to remember during the midterm elections
body:
Residents line up to cast their early-voting ballots in Arlington, Va., on Sept. 18, the first day of early voting in the state. Tom Brenner/Getty Images hide caption
This is about the time of year when the country engages in the Great American Biennial Polling Freakout.
A few weeks before an election, lots of people start to really engage. They read headlines showing this candidate or that candidate leading a race. People wonder who's going to win and whether the polls are right or wrong. And it all often leads to a blend of anticipation mixed with confusion and anxiety.
Stop and breathe. All that needs to be known from the polls at this point is that over the last several months, the compass needle has moved more in Democrats' direction. That's it. They are the favorites to win the House and are within striking distance of winning the Senate, something that was seen as a long shot when this election cycle began.
That's based not just on the polls but on conversations with campaigns and on-the-ground reporting. But here are some tips and things to remember as the deluge of polls comes your way:
They are snapshots in time of when those surveys were conducted.
They're more like fuzzy targets. Remember: Polls have margins of error. So when someone has a 2-point lead, that's not a lead at all. If a poll has a 3 percentage-point margin of error, this means that candidate could have a 5-point lead or be losing by a point.
There has been a proliferation of not-so-great polls this cycle, some driven by AI, others without long track records and even a pollster exposed to be fake . Good pollsters show their work with detailed methodology pages. If you can't find a methodology, that's a red flag.
With the decline of local journalism, there has been a decline in well-conducted, rigorous and frequent state polls. There is less money for those local outlets to pay for polling, which can be very expensive. So take those state poll averages with a grain of salt.
Horse-race polling isn't the best use of polls. Polls are best when measuring attitudes over time to help inform us of how Americans are feeling and thinking about key issues. There is so much more underneath those top-line numbers, from job approval ratings and who is most motivated to vote, to which party is more trusted to handle the issues people care about most — and so much more.
The fact is that many of these races are expected to be close. Millions of votes are not yet cast, and anyone professing to know exactly what's going to happen is lying.
When you're looking at who's up and who's down, just remember that horse-race polling is like sprinkles on top of a bowl of ice cream. Lots of people like sprinkles, but if all you eat is the sprinkles, you just wind up with a mouth full of wax without ever getting to the good stuff.

title: Win or lose, independent candidates want to meet voters in the middle
body:
Alaska U.S. House candidate Bill Hill, an independent, poses in a park in downtown Juneau, Alaska, on June 4, 2026. Becky Bohrer/AP hide caption
These days, Seth Haskin often puts on a puff-sleeved linen shirt under an 18th century waistcoat, breeches fastened just below the knee, long socks and buckle shoes that make a distinctive clip-clop when he walks.
The outfit is meant to remind people of the Founding Fathers and evoke their idea of limited government, which the 26-year-old supports.
Haskin's day job is managing his family's coffee shop business but this year he's been vying for another position: independent congressional representative for Southwest Florida. While campaigning, Haskin also carries an old-school bell.
"Getting their [people's] attention is the biggest battle that most candidates have," Haskin said. "But especially independent or no party candidates."
Independent congressional candidate Seth Haskin in Naples, Fla., posing for his campaign on Sept. 3 in his typical outfit of a puff-sleeved linen shirt under an 18th century waistcoat. Tyler Haskin/Seth Haskin for Congress hide caption
Some could dismiss Haskin's attire as a stunt, and they may write off other independent candidates the same way. Sarah Zabel, 61, an independent candidate for Idaho's western district, said that view is outdated.
"Independents used to be a curiosity or a protest or a single issue," said Zabel. "Now, with the parties having gone to such extremes, independents are the necessary relief for the American voter."
At a time when 45 percent of adults identify as political independents — a record high — and just a handful of tight races will decide control of Congress, the 173 independents running for the House this fall will test how big the political middle really is, and whether people who identify as independents will vote for one.
Despite the significant chunk of Americans identifying as independents, right now just one independent serves in the House: Kevin Kiley. The congressman whose newly redrawn California district leans Democratic, switched from Republican to independent while in Congress and continues to caucus with Republicans, reported Politico .
Some candidates said they were always independent, others said their political beliefs didn't change, but their parties did. While some are confident about winning, others said even a double-digit share of the vote will show both parties that it's time for change.
Zabel, who is running in a deep-red district in Idaho, describes herself as a "heritage Republican," or someone who used to be a Republican and adheres to conservative values. But since 2018, during the first Trump administration, she stopped feeling in line with the Republican party and the "MAGA program."
The retired Air Force major general said she didn't feel represented by either party, and she soon learned that many of her neighbors felt the same way.
"That's why I decided that I would step forward and be a candidate from the center," Zabel said. "Idaho is more Republican than Democrat, it is more conservative than not. But the extremes you see, they are a minority."
The Cook Political Report rates the district, which voted for Trump by a 45-point landslide in 2024, as solid Republican for the incumbent, Rep. Russ Fulcher.
Zabel, who noted that she would not caucus with either party if in Congress, recognizes that the Democratic nominee narrows her path to victory, but Zabel sees value "in showing Idaho and showing the country that we aren't the MAGA stronghold."
In Colorado, Shimon Blau, a lifelong independent, did not intend to run for Congress. Until Melat Kiros, 29, won the Democratic nomination for the state's 1st Congressional District, which encompasses the solidly Democratic city of Denver.
"I was deeply disturbed by the results of the primaries in which our 30-year incumbent, Diana DeGette, was beat by a member of the Democratic Socialists of America," he said. "I was offended and bothered by [Kiros'] past antisemitic rhetoric, as well as a lot of her socialist beliefs."
Kiros faced wide criticism in June for declining to describe a 2025 fatal firebombing attack on Jewish activists in Boulder, Colo., as antisemitic. Blau, the Denver-based physician, received an endorsement from The Denver Gazette on Oct. 6; it described him as the "candidate of conscience."
Kiros' upset of DeGette propelled Blau to swiftly gather the 1,500 signatures he needed to be eligible to run as an independent. Blau believes that in a city as blue as Denver, Republicans are "more of the message candidate than independents," with the latter having a real chance at winning.
"I think there's a lot of disillusionment right now with both parties," he said. "It seems like both of our traditional parties are leaning more and more towards the extremes."
Seth Haskin from Florida is also running in a district where one party has dominated for years. Trump won at least 60 percent of the vote in the past two presidential elections in Haskin's district, and local media mogul Jim Schwartzel won a tight and crowded Republican primary in August with almost 30 percent of the vote.
A "strict constitutionalist," Haskin, who previously also ran for governor of Wisconsin as a write-in candidate, said he could've seen himself in either party before the Covid-19 pandemic, before he believed that both parties had been "captured by the same industry leaders and PAC money and foreign lobbies and everything else."
Now, he's running as an independent because he thinks voters are ready for a change.
"Even if I don't win, if I can get double-digit percentage points as an independent candidate, I will get a lot of phone calls from both parties," he said. "It's going to threaten the duopoly that they have, right?"
In this undated photo from the campaign, independent congressional candidate Sarah Zabel campaigns with community members in Grangeville, Idaho. Shireene Hale/Zabel for Congress hide caption
In competitive swing districts like Iowa's 1st and states with ranked-choice voting like Alaska, independents aren't campaigning on the idea that both parties have gone too far, but that neither is delivering.
Businessman Michael Bridgford is running as an independent against Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Christina Bohannan, the Democratic nominee and former state representative.
The Cook Political Report, which long had the race as a toss-up, recently rated the district as lean Democratic.
Bridgford said people are tired of the "dysfunction" from both parties and by watching Miller-Meeks and Bohannan compete, and they believe that independents can provide the stable center that will let the government solve problems.
Running in a swing district has some advantages for independents.
"People are more independent minded. It's not gerrymandered to one side," Bridgford said. "People are more middle of the road and so there's naturally more attraction to this type of campaign."
The challenge is competing against the money that parties typically pour into a competitive district, he said.
In Alaska, even though voters have almost always picked the Republican presidential nominee, their streak of independence has allowed independents and Democratic nominees to win statewide races.
Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman who said he registered as an independent when he was 18, has decided to take his chances in Alaska's at-large congressional race, rated as a likely Republican win. Hill said, like many other Alaskans, he doesn't fit into a political box.
"People who are registered Republicans often have some progressive viewpoints and people registered as Democrats may have more conservative viewpoints as well," he said. "Alaskans just don't toe a political line with every vote."
Like other independents, Hill lauds that independents can work for their constituents without worrying about leadership in Washington. He's competing against the Republican incumbent Nick Begich, the Democratic nominee Eric Hafner and Jim McDermott, a Libertarian.
Hill, who was about 12 points behind Begich in the primary, also has an offer of support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, according to Anchorage Daily News .
Independent candidates throughout the country are running for a variety of reasons and facing challenges including fundraising and finding debate platforms with party candidates, but what unites them and keeps them going is their belief in the power of the moderate middle.
"When you talk to enough people and they're all moderate and everybody they know is moderate, but they believe everybody they don't know must be right wing," said Sarah Zabel, the independent candidate from Idaho. "You see that it's just an illusion. And we can bust that illusion."

title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
body: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left. Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

title: FACT CHECK: Quezon City disputes claims of DILG fire truck, ambulance turnover
body: Claim : The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) turned over fire trucks and ambulances to Quezon City under the government’s “Bawat Buhay Mahalaga” campaign. Rating: FALSE Why we fact-checked this : The claim was posted by the Facebook page Quezon City Updates on October 7. As of writing, it has accumulated over 315,000 reactions, 24,000 comments, and 21,000 shares. The post shows photos of the vehicles allegedly set to be delivered to the city, meant to help provide faster government services. “ Layunin nitong palakasin ang kakayahan ng mga lokal na pamahalaan sa pagtugon sa sunog, aksidente at iba pang emergency, upang mas mabilis na marespondehan ang bawat insidente at mas maprotektahan ang buhay ng mga mamamayan ,” the post reads. (It aims to strengthen the local government’s capability to respond to fires, accidents, and other emergencies, enabling faster incident response and better protection of citizens’ lives.) The facts : The Quezon City government clarified in a Facebook post on October 8 that no fire trucks or ambulances from the DILG were turned over to the city. It also clarified that it has no affiliation with the page that posted the claim, advising the public to refer to its official social media accounts for verified information. “ Walang katotohanan ang kumakalat na post sa social media tungkol sa umano’y pamamahagi ng ‘fire truck’ at ‘ambulance’ sa Quezon City mula sa Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG). Base sa inilabas na press release ng DILG, ang turnover ay isinagawa sa ‘QUEZON PROVINCE’ at hindi sa Quezon City, ” the post read. (There is no truth to the post circulating on social media about the alleged distribution of ‘fire trucks’ and ‘ambulances’ in Quezon City from the Department of the Interior and Local Government. Based on the press release issued by the DILG, the turnover was conducted in ‘Quezon Province’ and not in Quezon City.) On October 7 , Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla led the turnover of 30 Unified 911 emergency response motorcycles to the Quezon Police Provincial Office. During the event, Remulla also announced that the department is set to procure new fire trucks as part of a major push to modernize the Bureau of Fire Protection’s fleet. Viral ‘fire trike’ claims: A similar claim circulated on social media around the same time alleging that the DILG bought fire trikes priced at P10 million each, to be distributed to different local government units. Remulla clarified in an interview that the agency did not buy the small fire tricycles shown in the viral posts. He said the Nueva Ecija local government bought those vehicles back in July. The interior secretary made the clarification as the photos of the small fire tricycles were linked to the DILG’s plan to buy 1,500 fire trucks next year . The planned purchase aims to address the country’s fire truck shortage and replace aging equipment. According to the DILG, the procurement is expected to save the government P9 billion, with each unit priced at P10 million, down from the previous P16 million price tag. The agency added that its representatives went to Korea to establish a government-to-government agreement for the purchase. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

title: Russia’s Battlegroup West destroys 105 Ukrainian heavy multicopters over past day
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Over the past 24 hours, the Ukrainian armed forces lost 105 heavy combat multicopters, four Starlink satellite communication stations, and 42 robotic systems as a result of operations by Russia’s Battlegroup West, the battlegroup’s spokesman Ivan Bigma reported.
"Air defense teams and mobile armed units shot down 178 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), four loitering munitions, and 105 enemy heavy combat multicopters," Bigma said.
In addition, according to him, 56 UAV control centers, four Starlink satellite communication stations, 42 robotic systems, and five enemy field ammunition depots were located and destroyed.

title: Russia’s Diana Shnaider advances to second round of Wuhan tennis tournament
body:
BEIJING, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Diana Shnaider has defeated Britain’s Katie Boulter in the first round of a Women's Tennis Association (WTA) tournament in Wuhan, China.
The 11th-seeded Shnaider won 6-3, 6-1. In the next round, she will face the winner of the match between Yulia Putintseva of Kazakhstan and Zeynep Sonmez of Turkey, both of whom made the main draw through qualification.
Shnaider, 22, is currently 13th in the WTA rankings. She has won five WTA singles titles, with her semifinal appearance at the 2026 French Open being her best result to date at majors.
The Wuhan Open, part of the WTA 1000 series of tournaments, is played on hard courts and offers a total purse of $4 mln. Coco Gauff of the United States won the tournament last year.

title: Dubai inflation eases even as fuel costs rise
body: Dubai's inflation rate eased slightly in September from the previous month, even as rising oil prices pushed up the cost of petrol. Inflation on an annual basis stood at 5.03 per cent, down from the 5.54 per cent recorded in August and the 5.7 per cent peak for this year reached in June. . The figures were released by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Dubai’s General Monthly Consumer Price Index decreased by 0.05 per cent month-on-month in September on falling airfares and cheaper holiday packages. Airfares on a monthly basis fell by 23.44 per cent and holiday packages dropped 12.47 per cent from the August level. However, on an annual basis, the transport division was the biggest contributor to the rise in consumer prices in September, climbing 14.7 per cent. The increase in transport charges was driven by a 37.52 per cent rise in the cost of fuels and lubricants for personal transport, as well as a 13.48 per cent rise in passenger transport by air, according to the latest government data. Biggest contributor The transport segment, which accounts for 9 per cent of Dubai’s Consumer Price Index basket, has been the main driver of inflation in the emirate over the past several months amid a rise in prices petrol prices . The UAE lifted fuel subsidies in 2015 and prices are evaluated on a monthly basis, based on movements in global markets. Petrol prices in the Emirates rose for a third consecutive month for October as prices in global oil markets remain elevated amid escalating geopolitical concerns in the Middle East. Global crude prices, which surged by nearly 109 per cent during the peak of the war, now in its eighth month, are still more than 70 per cent higher on concerns of a possible resumption in fighting between the US and Iran . Brent crude, which hovered around the $110 per barrel mark in September, has largely remained above $100 over the past few weeks. The West Texas Intermediate benchmark passed $105 a barrel in September as the Strait of Hormuz remained a flashpoint. Increasing attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the Red Sea by the Houthi rebels in Yemen have added another layer of risk to energy supplies from the region. Rebound Despite economic headwinds, Dubai's economy has largely skirted the deeper slump experienced by some neighbours. Non-oil private sector business activity in the emirate, which is one of the largest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Purchasing Managers' Index stood at 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, indicating a “solid improvement” in Dubai, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026, S&P Global Markets Intelligence said earlier this month. The boost to the emirate’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven by a “sharp and accelerated increase in output” as new orders also rose markedly and employment in the emirate rose, according to the PMI survey data. The tourism and retail sectors in the emirate have also bounced back from the initial shock of the war. Property, among the top contributors to the emirate’s economy, has also held up relatively well. The food and drinks category increased by an annualised 8.05 per cent last month, while housing, water, electricity, gas and domestic fuel rose by almost 6.23 per cent, “as a result of the growth of the average residential rental prices in most areas of the emirate during September”, the latest government data shows.

title: Spox Ihnat explains why explosions sometimes occur before air raid sirens sound
body:
Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, made this statement during a television broadcast, according to Ukrinform.
“There’s no denying that such situations do occur—not only in the Kyiv region, but also in frontline regions—where an explosion is heard first, followed by the air raid siren. Unfortunately, such incidents do happen. Here, the enemy wants to inflict as much damage on us as possible, so it uses various opportunities to launch a surprise strike,” Ihnat noted.
According to him, during the attack on Kyiv, Russian troops fired five missiles that followed a ballistic trajectory, but the type of these missiles still needs to be determined.
He noted that Ukraine receives intelligence from its partners, specifically regarding the activity of strategic aviation and ships in the Black and Caspian Seas, as well as ballistic missile launches from northern regions and the temporarily occupied Crimea.
“There are times when this information doesn’t reach us. And this isn’t the first such instance. There are also certain technical issues,” the spokesperson noted.
He added that if technical problems are identified, specialists will work with partners to resolve them.
As reported, a series of explosions rocked Kyiv on the evening of October 12, and only afterward was a missile alert issued.
The Ukrainian Air Force is investigating why there was no information about the launches.

title: FSB detains Russian woman over Ukraine-backed plot to attack military airfield
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained a Russian woman suspected of preparing a drone attack on a military airfield on orders from the Security Service of Ukraine, the FSB said in a statement.
"The Federal Security Service in the Voronezh Region has foiled a large-scale act of sabotage and terrorism orchestrated by the Security Service of Ukraine, which planned to attack the Russian Defense Ministry’s Baltimor military airfield with short-range drones," the statement reads.
Law enforcement operations made it possible to expose and disrupt the illegal activities of a Russian woman who had been recruited by a Ukrainian intelligence officer during a trip to Ukraine in 2022. "Acting on instructions from her handler, she traveled to Voronezh and rented a garage, where she planned to assemble and launch drones meant to be used to destroy infrastructure and aircraft, as well as kill military airfield staff," the FSB said. The drones were supposed to be operated remotely by personnel based in Ukraine.
According to the FSB, the woman retrieved nine drones equipped with explosive devices, along with drone control equipment, from previously established caches and took them to the garage. Each drone carried 500 grams of foreign-made explosives.
"FSB officers responded immediately after receiving intel, promptly detaining the accomplice of Ukrainian intelligence agencies and preventing the act of sabotage before it was carried out, thus containing the potential consequences of the Kiev regime’s actions against the military facility," the agency stressed.
The suspect has been taken into custody. "Efforts are ongoing to establish all circumstances of the crime and identify all those involved," the FSB added.

title: Palestinian West Bank resident arrested for filming Bnei Brak light rail, posing as Israeli
body: A 32-year-old Palestinian who allegedly participated in past terrorist attacks against Israeli targets was arrested on Monday after being caught filming inside the underground Aharonovich light rail station in Bnei Brak, Israel Police announced on Tuesday.According to police, security guards at the station noticed a suspicious individual taking photographs and recording videos in the underground section of the station on Monday morning.Officers from the Tel Aviv District Police's light rail unit arrived at the scene and began questioning the suspect.During the initial questioning, the man provided an Israeli identity number and claimed to be a resident of the Israeli Arab city of Tayibe.However, a more thorough examination revealed that the suspect was a 32-year-old West Bank resident staying in Israel illegally, who had allegedly provided false identification details.Police said the suspect had previously been involved in security-related incidents and was suspected of participating in terrorist attacks targeting Israelis.Suspect transferred to Bnei Brak police station for questioningThe suspect was arrested and taken to the Bnei Brak police station for further questioning.He is expected to appear before the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court on Tuesday for a hearing on extending his detention.

title: Where Are Our Leaders of the Bai?
body: Dear Editor: In the book, “Leadership in the Pacific islands: tradition and the future” Edited by Donald R. Shuster, Peter Larmour and Karin von Strokirch, Ngiraked Roman Tmetuchel shares that the traditional bai of Palau was more than a meeting house. It was the heart of leadership, a place where chiefs gathered to deliberate, debate, and reach consensus. Every symbol carved into its beams carried meaning: the rooster reminding chiefs to rise early and hear the cries of the poor, the bat teaching humility, the clam warning of the consequences of harm to a village, and the school of fish showing the importance of unity under a leader. Chiefs were not paid salaries. They carried burdens, fed the hungry, and sacrificed for their clans. Leadership was service, not privilege. Today, our leaders in the Olbiil Era Kelulau and the Executive Branch seem far removed from this tradition. Where are the leaders who wake early to hear the cries of the poor? Where are the leaders who stoop in humility, who act carefully knowing their decisions carry consequences, who guide sthe people in unity rather than scatter them in division? The bai demanded consensus. Chiefs sat on the stone platform under the sun and rain until agreement was reached. Compare that to today’s politics, where majority votes replace consensus, leaving division and unrest. The bai reminded leaders that they had one voice, one mind, one united front. Yet our modern leaders often speak with many voices, each serving personal gain or corporate interest rather than the people. Ngiraked Tmetuchl reminded us that chiefs were chosen carefully, prepared through upbringing, and ratified by the community. Leadership was feared because it meant sacrifice. Today, leadership is sought for prestige, salary, and influence. The Constitution even provides for chiefs to advise the president on matters of tradition, but that advisory role has weakened, overshadowed by imported systems that prize individual ambition over collective responsibility. So we must ask: where are our leaders of the bai? Where are the lawmakers who will stop sitting on their hands while families struggle under taxes? Where is the executive branch who will sacrifice privilege to lift burdens? Where are the leaders who understand that governance is uplifting the people not just padding your wallet? Palau’s future demands leaders who embody the bai’s lessons: humility, responsibility, unity, and sacrifice. Not leaders who preach slogans while ignoring the cries of the people. Everything for Everyone and Nothing for Ourselves. That is the leadership Palau needs, not status, not self-interest, but service. Your Humble Servant Dudalm Kelulau The Silent Majority The post Where Are Our Leaders of the Bai? appeared first on Island Times News .

title: More ships were attacked near the Bulgarian coast. What about the crew?
body:
On the night of 12-13 October 2026, further drone attacks were carried out against civilian merchant vessels in the Black Sea near the Bulgarian coast. According to official reports, one ship was damaged, and another – according to information provided by Prime Minister Rumen Radev – sank.
The main confirmed incident involved the Maltese freighter Chelsea 3. The vessel was en route from the Turkish port of Giresun to Giurgiulesti in Moldova. The ship is owned and managed by Ukrainian companies (Black Sea Shipping Management from Odesa). Between approximately 01:30 and 02:00 local time, the vessel was attacked by three aerial drones, which struck the deck and the hull. The ship remained afloat, albeit with a slight list. The crew of 15 – consisting of seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijani citizens – was fully evacuated by units of the Bulgarian Border Guard and transported to Varna.
BREAKING: 2 commercial ships have been targeted in drone attacks just outside Bulgarian territorial waters in the Black Sea, resulting in one vessel sinking and another damaged, according to the Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev. AZOV CONCORD sank 17 nautical miles east of Krapets following a drone strike, with a civilian ship assisting rescue operations. CHELSEA 3 was struck by three drones 18 nautical miles off Byala, where Border Police rescued all 15 crew members. The Prime Minister has summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova and requested urgent NATO surveillance assistance in the region. None of the ships came from Ukrainian ports.
During an extraordinary meeting of the Security Council at the Council of Ministers, Prime Minister Rumen Radev reported on the second incident . Another vessel was hit approximately 17 nautical miles east of the town of Krapets (north-eastern Bulgaria). According to currently available data, the ship sank. At least one person from the crew has been rescued. Details regarding the vessel’s name, flag, cargo, and full crew complement have not yet been officially released.
A similar attack occurred on 6 October, when two merchant ships were hit by drones in the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone in the Black Sea.
This is no longer a problem limited to the Ukrainian coast. If further attacks on merchant vessels occur within a week in the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone and right next to the territorial waters of a NATO member state, the Black Sea is increasingly becoming a space where civilian shipping will be exposed to the consequences of hostilities far from the front line. Earlier, vessels were fired upon near Romania and Turkey.
This will have more than just military consequences. The importance of reconnaissance, the protection of ports and shipping routes will increase, as will the pressure on NATO to enhance the monitoring of the airspace and maritime areas over the western part of the Black Sea. But which NATO members will support Bulgaria?
If similar incidents continue to recur, the risk to commercial shipping will become a permanent threat to the security of Romania and Bulgaria, rather than just a problem for Ukraine and Poland. At this point, the entire eastern flank must be protected.

title: Haruna Iddrisu calls for limits on annual university accommodation fee increases
body: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has proposed a framework to regulate annual increases in accommodation charges at public universities, suggesting that adjustments could be guided by inflation and set within a range of five to 10 per cent. He called for a committee to examine accommodation costs and recommend permissible annual increases to Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson under the Fees and Charges Act. Speaking in a media interview, Mr Iddrisu expressed concern about high rents and said a defined adjustment mechanism could help make university accommodation costs more predictable. “We do not support exorbitant rent prices being charged across the country,” he said. “It is my view that we should constitute a committee to advise the Minister of Finance before he proceeds with the Fees and Charges Act on what percentage increase is permissible each year.” The Minister suggested that prevailing economic conditions should inform any recommended adjustment. “We can say, for instance, take inflation as a guide, 5 to 10 per cent increase annually,” he added. The proposed committee would assess an appropriate benchmark for increases, with the aim of limiting arbitrary or disproportionate adjustments to accommodation charges. The five to 10 per cent range remains a suggestion by the minister, rather than an approved cap.

title: Finnish foreign minister calls on EU to ban Russian tourist visas, slams Trump lifting sanctions on diesel from Russia
body:
"Issuing visas to Russians for non-essential travel was banned by government resolution in Finland already in 2022... The same must finally happen at the EU level," Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) said.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) has called for a complete EU ban on issuing tourist visas for Russians until Russia ends its war in Ukraine.
"As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is now in its fifth year. It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians," Valtonen said in the release.
In recent years, Schengen countries have been issuing more tourist visas to Russian citizens. Last year, nearly 500,000 tourist visas were granted to Russians across the Schengen area.
"Issuing visas to Russians for non-essential travel was banned by government resolution in Finland already in 2022," Valtonen pointed out. "The same must finally happen at the EU level."
Valtonen has invited other EU states to sign a joint letter to the European Commission.
"In addition to the complete ban on tourist visas, the letter proposes a ban on Schengen visas to [Russian] President Vladimir Putin 's inner circle, visa restrictions for Russian athletes, and the effective implementation of the visa ban on Russian (ex)combatants agreed by the EU Member States this summer," the ministry explained in the release.
Valtonen has also sharply criticised a deal between US President Donald Trump and Putin.
Aiming to lower diesel pump prices in the US, Trump has decided to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
In an interview with news agency Reuters, the Finnish foreign minister said that as the leader of the free world, the US should stand with Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression.
"The rest of the world should be on the side of the victim and certainly those countries ​who want to still be strong ​for the concept of freedom," she told Reuters.
Valtonen also commented on her proposal to other EU member states to restrict tourist visas for Russians.
"I hear ​from all ​of my ⁠colleagues in the European Union an agreement to the principle and ​I am so sure that ​all ⁠of the European Union countries will start restricting tourist visas to Russians even more strongly ⁠now, ​especially because Russia is ​also waging a hybrid war against Europe," she said, according to Reuters .
