title: APC Appoints Wike, Adeleke, Soludo Campaign Coordinators, As Party Rejigs PCC List
body: Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja The All Progressives Congress (APC) has appointed the Minister of Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, and the Governor of Osun State, Senator Ademola Adeleke, as state campaign coordinators for FCT and Osun in the revised Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) list. The inauguration of the council is scheduled for Wednesday at the Banquet Hall, Presidential Villa, Abuja by 11:00 a.m, according to a notice signed by the National Secretary of the party, Senator Ajibola Basiru. Vice-President Kashim Shettima will serve as Vice-Chairman I, while the National Chairman of the APC, Prof. Nentawe Goshwe Yilwatda, is Vice-Chairman II. Senate President Godswill Akpabio, House Speaker Tajudeen Abbas and Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq are Deputy Vice-Chairmen. Former Zamfara State Governor, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, remains the Director General of the Campaign Council. The Deputy Director-Generals of the PCC are: Yobe State Governor, Mai Mala Buni (North I), Senator Opeyemi Bamidele (South I), Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin (North II), Deputy Speaker Benjamin Kalu (South II), while Senator Adams Oshiomhole will head mobilization. Also on the list is the Chief of Staff to the President, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, who will serve as the Head of Administration; Hon. James Faleke is Deputy Director General in charge of Election Planning; Hon. Ibrahim Masari is in charge of Logistics and Operations; Hon. Aminu Masari heads Parliamentary Mobilisation, and Minister of Works, David Umahi, heads Infrastructure Mobilization and Sensitization. Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, is the Secretary of the council, while Basiru is Deputy Secretary and Hadiza Bala Usman is Assistant Secretary. The Zonal Campaign Coordinators include Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for South-west, Governor Peter Mbah for South-east, Senator Bassey Otu for South-south, Governor Umar Bago for North-central, Governor Uba Sani for North-west and Senator Ali Modu Sheriff for North-east. The list also showed state coordinators comprising serving APC governors, past governors, National and State Assembly members and other critical stakeholders. Key directorates in the council are: Finance/Treasury to be led by Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori; Fund Raising by Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun; Policy and Manifesto by Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Atiku Bagudu; and Legal Directorate by Muiz Banire (SAN). The Directorate of Media and Strategic Communications has Minister of Information, Idris Malagi as Coordinating Director I, while Dele Alake is Presidential Campaign Spokesperson I. Other spokespersons include: Bayo Onanuga, Lere Olayinka, Ajuri Ngelale, Ayobami Oyalowo, Kemi Asekun-Shitu, Bala Ibrahim, Hon. Adamu Fanda and Mohammed Garba. The Directorate of Security and Intelligence would be headed by Gen. Sarki Yaki, Data Management by Dr. Bisoye Coker, while the Directorate of Support Groups is headed by Silas Agara. The party said all members are expected to be present at the inauguration.

title: The Island That Disappeared From the Map — and the One That Never Appeared
body: By: Jack Huang On October 6, fourteen heads of government flew to Funafuti to look at the ocean. Not to negotiate with it, not to issue a joint statement about it. Just to look. Tuvalu’s runway sits two meters above sea level. At high tide, the Pacific doesn’t knock on the door. It simply arrives. The optics were, by any measure, extraordinary. World leaders standing on an airstrip that is also, depending on the calendar and the weather, a beach. Tuvalu’s Prime Minister Feleti Teo didn’t need a speech. He had the tide. This was Pre-COP31: four days of ministerial meetings in Nadi, Fiji, bookended by that leaders’ trip to Funafuti, all of it designed to do what decades of conference room negotiation hasn’t quite managed, which is to make the climate crisis feel real to people who have the power to do something about it. More than fifty countries showed up. Fiji pledged US10 million toward the Pacific Resilience Facility.Denmark committed another US2.2 million. The Taku Pakasoa Declaration, adopted in Funafuti and eventually backed by around thirty countries, called for stronger ambition and faster access to climate finance. Thirty countries. A declaration. Ten million dollars from Fiji. The Pacific Resilience Facility, the one mechanism specifically designed to bypass the notorious bureaucratic bottlenecks of existing multilateral funds and get money directly to communities for sea walls and water security and climate-resilient fishing, has a target of US$500 million. After four days of Pacific solidarity, it remains mostly a target. This is the central absurdity of international climate politics. The countries that did the least to cause the problem are the most effective at dramatizing its consequences, and the least effective at extracting commensurate action from the countries that actually caused it. Tuvalu has mastered the art of moral clarity. What it cannot conjure is the political will of others. Australia is the interesting case here. Canberra holds the presidency of COP31 negotiations, a co-hosting arrangement with Turkey, which runs the formal conference in Antalya in November, and spent considerable diplomatic capital positioning Pre-COP as proof that Pacific voices would shape global climate outcomes. Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen flew to Funafuti. The photographs were striking. The coal and gas export data, which Australia did not fly to Funafuti, tells a somewhat different story. Australia remains among the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters. It is simultaneously the Pacific’s most vocal climate champion and one of the structural contributors to the problem the Pacific is drowning in. The Pacific knows this. The Pacific is also heavily dependent on Australian aid. This is a relationship with a lot of unsaid things in it. For Teo, the week was about more than climate. The Falepili Union Treaty with Australia grants Tuvaluan citizens a pathway to Australian residency and commits Canberra to security cooperation, but it has always carried an uncomfortable subtext about sovereignty. Teo used his address at the Pre-COP Leaders’ Plenary to make this point plainly: the Pacific has its own knowledge, its own expertise, its own accountability structures, and what it needs from international partners is finance without conditions that undermine local agency. This was a message directed partly at Australia, delivered on a stage Australia helped build. Diplomacy is rarely simple. Now here is where the story gets genuinely strange. Among Tuvalu’s twelve remaining diplomatic allies, the small club of states that recognize Taipei rather than Beijing, Taiwan is arguably the most consequential partner Tuvalu has on the ground. And Taiwan was nowhere near Pre-COP31. Because it cannot be. Taiwan is not a UN member. It cannot sign the Paris Agreement. It has no seat in the UNFCCC process. When fourteen world leaders flew to Funafuti to bear witness to climate frontline reality, Taiwan’s contribution to keeping that frontline functional was, officially, not part of the story. Unofficially, it very much is. Billion Electric Group, a Taiwan-listed company, has deployed solar and battery storage systems across Tuvalu, Palau, and the Marshall Islands: 495 kilowatts of generation capacity, nearly 2,000 kilowatt-hours of storage, cutting roughly 800 tonnes of annual emissions and providing renewable energy coverage for agricultural and fishery facilities. Taiwan’s International Cooperation and Development Fund has been operating in Funafuti for years, running agricultural technology transfer, vocational training, and community resilience programs. The unglamorous, granular, actually-useful kind of development assistance that multilateral institutions spend decades trying to replicate at scale. The desalination capacity, the distributed energy systems, the agricultural plots that visiting delegations pointed to as evidence of what adaptation looks like in practice: Taiwan built a lot of that. Taiwan’s name appears in none of the formal documentation. There is something almost philosophical about this situation. Taiwan is a democracy of 23 million people, home to the semiconductor supply chains that make the clean energy transition physically possible, operating one of the more sophisticated carbon pricing experiments in Asia, and running technical assistance programs across the Pacific that the international climate system is now trying to institutionalize at a fraction of the effectiveness through mechanisms like the Pacific Resilience Facility. And it does all of this from outside every formal framework, without a nameplate at any conference table, in a kind of perpetual diplomatic parenthesis. The conventional framing is that this is Taiwan’s tragedy, the talented outsider pressing its face against the window of multilateral governance. That framing is not wrong. But it misses something. Taiwan’s model of climate cooperation, precisely because it is unburdened by the institutional politics of formal membership, has developed qualities that the multilateral system is only now learning to value: speed, community embeddedness, technical specificity, no-conditions delivery. The Pacific Resilience Facility was designed specifically because existing multilateral mechanisms are too slow, too bureaucratic, and too conditional. Taiwan has been running the Pacific Resilience Facility’s operating model, informally and bilaterally, for twenty years. The question worth taking to Antalya in November is not whether Taiwan deserves a seat at the table. That is a geopolitical question that COP31 cannot solve. The more interesting question is whether a climate governance system that is genuinely serious about results can afford to keep treating effective contributors as non-entities because of their political status. The Pacific is running out of time. The ocean does not check membership credentials before it comes in. Somewhere between the declaration and the tide, there is a more honest accounting to be done about who is doing the work, who is getting the credit, and whether those two things have any relationship to each other. In Tuvalu, they mostly don’t. That is not only a problem for Taiwan. It is a problem for the system that decided to hold its meetings there. The post The Island That Disappeared From the Map — and the One That Never Appeared appeared first on Island Times News .

title: HM issues two Royal Decrees
body:
Muscat: His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik on Tuesday issued two Royal decrees, reading as follows: Royal decree No (90/2026) on the ratification of the technical cooperation agreement between the Government of the Sultanate of Oman and the Government of the Republic of Angola, signed in Luanda on September 18, 2026. title: Tiny dragons of Darjeeling: How a small community became the last hope for the Himalayan salamander
body: Towards the end of summer in the emerald-green tea estate of Margaret's Hope, the weather cannot make up its mind. One moment, drizzle comes soft and steady through the tall pine trees. Next, mist rolls in and swallows everything as the hills play hide-and-seek with the sky. A steep tarmac road drops from the main hill cart path through rows of tea bushes. At the bottom, about 11 kilometres north of Kurseong town, a pond sits hidden in the mist. Sedge, a dense waterside plant common to Himalayan wetlands, stands along its edges like a barricade. In the hill villages of Darjeeling, India , these ponds have long been more than bodies of water. “Local communities have been protecting this species long before any funding or international recognition,” says Barkha Subba, a Darjeeling conservation biologist. “These wetlands are deeply intertwined with local culture and religious beliefs.” What they have been protecting is one of India's last remaining breeding grounds for the Himalayan salamander, known locally as gora or pani chepara in Nepali . They are sometimes described as a tiny dragon that swims quietly in mountain ponds. Growing up to 20 centimetres long, they are also called crocodile newts, for the ridges along their dark bodies. Scientifically known as Tylototriton himalayanus, it is listed as vulnerable on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List of Threatened Species , with a declining population trend. The munshi at the water's edge Ramesh Rai, 55, moves around the pond in a white cotton T-shirt and rubber gumboots, parting the sedge and scanning the water. He is searching for eggs tucked into submerged vegetation. Ramesh is the munshi of Margaret's Hope tea estate, head of the workforce that keeps the 160-year-old site running. His grandfather and father worked this land. He was born and grew up here and has known the gora since childhood. “There is a place called Gorabari not far from here,” he says, pointing at the tea bushes above the pond. “In the past the gora used to be found throughout the garden fields up there. The place was named after them. That is how many there once were.” Gorabari translates as the garden of the salamander. In 1993, Ramesh noticed the gora losing ground. While planting tea, he saw ponds shrinking, eggs dying and habitat being consumed by human activity and a shifting climate. He began protecting the salamanders without formal conservation training. In 2005, he wrote about the vanishing creature in the first issue of Sahityashri , a Nepali literary journal printed within the estate. MK Rai, 52, farms land around the estate. “In June, July, August, you would see them on the road,” he says. “We called them baby dragons then. We did not know their value.” Now tourists arrive with cameras and picnics, often leaving plastic on the bank. The two men have helped build the nursery pond with estate management and join clean-up campaigns run with Subba's organisation, the Federation of Societies for Environmental Protection, or Fosep. “Saving the salamander,” MK says, “means saving our culture, too.” Subba grew up in these hills, hearing stories of tigers, forests and mountain spirits from her grandmother. She studied biological sciences, completed a doctorate on high-elevation amphibians and returned to Darjeeling to work on conservation. In 2014, researcher Kartik Vasudevan of CCMB Hyderabad mapped 38 salamander habitats across Darjeeling. When Subba returned to check them, most were gone or severely degraded. Wetlands had dried up and invasive species had moved in. A life cycle tied to the monsoon “Climate change is no longer a myth or a mystery,” she tells The National . “It is a fact we are seeing in everyday life. And the salamander is one of the clearest signs of what is being lost.” A peer-reviewed study published in Atmosphere in December 2024, analysing Darjeeling's temperature and rainfall records between 1991 and 2023, found that total rainfall has increased while maximum temperatures have also risen significantly. The rains are coming harder and shorter, not steadier. The salamander's entire life cycle is tied to the monsoon. With the first rain, it emerges from hibernation and returns to the same pond in which it was born; behaviour scientists call this site fidelity. Destroy that wetland and the species has nowhere else to go. At Margaret's Hope, 1,500 metres above sea level, salamanders mate and lay 60 to 90 eggs in submerged vegetation. But if the rain stops after two days, the shallow pool dries quickly and the clutch desiccates before hatching. “They lay eggs thinking there will be rain for another month,” Subba says. “Then suddenly the rain stops, the sun comes out, the pool dries up. The whole generation dies off.” The threat to the species doesn't stop there. Carp and guppies, which have been released into the main pond by local religious communities, eat eggs and larvae. Invasive phragmites grass has choked the banks. But, above all, it is climate change. In a bid to help the species, Ramesh, with members of the community and estate management, built a 1.8m-by-3m nursery pond with a vegetated island close to the main pond. Every March and April, he searches for clutches and moves them away from fish, herons and snakes, monitoring them for 12 to 15 days until they hatch. He is not paid for this work. The scientist who came home Subba grew up in these hills and has been coming to Margaret's Hope since childhood. However, 2020 was the first time she came as a scientist, specifically to map the district's salamander habitats. What she found when she arrived surprised her. The community had already been doing the work without her. Around 2015, when the pond had nearly dried up and invasive grass had taken over, residents and estate management cleared it by hand. The salamanders returned. When Subba met Ramesh, she found something harder to teach than biology: decades of watching. “For him,” she says, “the salamanders are like his children.” Their collaboration now has formal backing. This year Subba received the 2026 Whitley Award, a prestigious British conservation prize, presented by Princess Anne at London's Royal Geographical Society. She was recognised for protecting seven critical breeding sites across Darjeeling. Margaret's Hope is one of them. Subba plans to extend the work to Nepal and Bhutan, creating a transboundary framework for a species that knows no borders. An estimated 5,000 individuals survive in the wild, with about 80 per cent living outside protected areas on tea garden land and private holdings. As the mist thickens again, Ramesh moves on, steady and unhurried. What began in 1993 as one man's effort to protect a disappearing species has grown into a wider conservation movement, bringing together local knowledge, community action and scientific expertise. But at the water's edge, his work remains much the same: watching, waiting and protecting what is left.

title: Ukraine’s swimming robot can tow 10 tons, its maker says. Hook up a gun, and the shells ride aboard
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s amphibious ground robot UNEX UGV can tow artillery guns, its project lead said in a video interview, Militarnyi reported on 13 October. The electric platform from ABRIS Design Group (ABRIS DG) also swims, climbs, and hauls cargo on its own deck. The Defense Ministry’s robot tally, kept in its DELTA system, counts supply and evacuation runs. It logged 25,143 of them in August, a monthly figure that has climbed all year. In April, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the goal was for robots to handle all frontline logistics. A robot that brings a gun and its shells to a position adds artillery moves to that workload. A gun behind, shells aboard The robot can pull a gun or another wheeled vehicle of up to 10 metric tons (about 22,000 lb), the project lead said. Ammunition can ride aboard, so the gun and its rounds reach the position together. No crew has to go with them, he said, and the team has already demonstrated the setup. On its own deck, ABRIS DG says, the robot carries up to 1.7 tons (3,750 lb) on land and 1.25 tons (2,760 lb) on water. UNEX UGV ground robotic system. Screenshot: Militarnyi ABRIS DG said US Army testers ran UNEX through scenarios that included towing Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTVs), which are armored US military trucks. The trials took place at the Army’s XTech competition in Vilseck, Germany, in March 2026. UNEX was picked as one of five winners, the company said . Swims, climbs, backtracks The robot can float for more than an hour. The team has already crossed the Desna River and narrow stretches of the Dnipro with it, the project lead said. Ultra-low-pressure tires spread its weight over soft ground and swamps. ABRIS DG says it climbs obstacles up to one meter (3.3 ft) high and drives out of water onto ice. Explore further Ukraine turned ground robots into a frontline workhorse. Its first competitive tender may reward cheap copies over proven machines, an officer warns Operators steer it via Starlink or radio. An escort drone can add an overhead view to the robot’s own cameras. If the link drops, the robot retraces its route to where the signal last held. It runs on a Ukrainian-made 78 kWh battery. The project lead puts its work time at up to six hours and its range at up to 120 km (75 miles), with a top speed of 20 km/h (12 mph). Load and terrain cut into those figures, he added. With a generator now in development, a mission should stretch to about 12–14 hours, he said. The robot is not built for the zero line, the project lead said. It works 20–30 km behind the front, at night, where armor would add little. Developers also plan demining and air defense versions. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry codified the robot and cleared it for use in its forces in April 2025. Read also Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. It just ran its first supply mission, 40 kilometers to positions others can’t reach Robots won’t replace armored vehicles, says Ukrainian company that builds both. title: Flaming Saganaki: The Fiery Greek Cheese You Can Make in 15 Minutes
body: Flaming saganaki, the fried Greek cheese set alight with brandy at the table, takes just 15 minutes to make at home with Chef John’s Allrecipes method, which home cooks rate 4.8 out of 5. Flaming saganaki made with kasseri cheese. Photo: Allrecipes Flaming saganaki starts with a firm cheese Saganaki takes its name from the sagani, the small two-handled frying pan used to cook it in Greece. In its simplest form, it is a thick slice of cheese dusted in flour and fried until the outside turns golden while the middle softens. The fire came later. According to Allrecipes, restaurateurs in Chicago started the habit of pouring brandy over the hot cheese and lighting it, while diners shouted “Opa!” as the flames rose. As a result, flaming saganaki became a fixture of Greek restaurants in the United States, and the dish now turns up on taverna menus around the world. Greek City Times has previously reported on saganaki’s place among the world’s best dishes . Still, few people try it in their own kitchens, even though the method needs only one pan and a handful of ingredients. Chef John Mitzewich, who wrote the recipe, uses kasseri , a semi-hard Greek cheese made mainly from sheep’s milk. It holds its shape in the pan but melts in the centre, which is what gives flaming saganaki its stretch. In addition, he says Graviera, Kefalograviera, Kefalotyri or even a firm feta also work. Halloumi is another option, although he points out that it barely melts, so the soft centre is lost. Readers who want to compare those cheeses can start with Greek City Times’ guide to Greek cheeses worth trying . Ingredients for kasseri cheese saganaki The Allrecipes version serves two as a starter. Overall, the shopping list for flaming saganaki is short, and most of it is probably already in the pantry. 1 packet (about 115 g, or 4 oz) kasseri cheese 1 tablespoon water, plus extra if needed 1/4 cup plain flour, plus extra if needed 1 tablespoon olive oil 2 tablespoons brandy, at room temperature Half a lemon, or more to taste 1 tablespoon chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley Chef John adds that any high-proof spirit can replace the brandy, and dried oregano can stand in for the parsley. Each serve comes to about 391 calories, according to the Allrecipes nutrition panel. How to fry and light it The flaming saganaki recipe needs about 10 minutes of preparation and 5 minutes of cooking. Because the cooking moves fast, measure everything out before the pan goes on the stove. Brush both sides of the cheese with water, then press each side into the flour until it is fully coated. Heat a well-seasoned cast iron pan over medium-high heat until it just starts to smoke, then add the olive oil. Lay the cheese in the hot oil and fry for about two minutes, until a golden crust forms and the cheese begins to ooze. Turn it quickly with a spatula and fry the second side for about 30 seconds. Take the pan off the heat and set it on a heatproof board or plate. Pour the brandy over the cheese and light it with a long fireplace lighter. Squeeze lemon juice over the top to put out the last flames, then scatter over the parsley. Allrecipes suggests serving flaming saganaki with sliced fresh or grilled bread. The lemon does two jobs at once, since it cuts through the rich cheese while it puts out the fire. Tips from home cooks More than 20 home cooks have rated this flaming saganaki on Allrecipes. One member, elwain, wrote: “The flaming brandy went well without setting my kitchen on fire!!” Reviewers also shared practical advice. In particular, one warned that a pan that is too hot will burn the cheese and fill the kitchen with smoke, so the oil should only just start to smoke. Another suggested soaking the cheese in brandy for an hour before frying it. Safety came up as well. One reviewer noted that the napkin under the pan, which the original method mentions, should be removed before the brandy goes in, given that loose paper near an open flame is a fire risk. That is why this version calls for a heatproof board instead. Similarly, keep long hair, sleeves and tea towels well away from the pan when lighting flaming saganaki, and never pour brandy straight from the bottle into a hot pan. Lighting it at the table also gives guests the full taverna moment, which is half the fun of the dish. For a seafood take on the same pan, Greek City Times also has a traditional prawn saganaki recipe . The original Saganaki (Flaming Greek Cheese) recipe is on Allrecipes, along with Chef John’s video. Source: Allrecipes The post Flaming Saganaki: The Fiery Greek Cheese You Can Make in 15 Minutes appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: ‘Niger Delta Cannot Afford Another Cycle of Instability’
body: Okon Bassey in Uyo The Akwa Ibom Ex-Militants Forum has expressed support for the Special Adviser to the President on Niger Delta Affairs, Dr. Dennis Brutu Otuaro, strongly condemning recent calls by individuals and groups for his removal from office. “As stakeholders and beneficiaries of the Niger Delta peace process, we recognise the critical role of Presidential Amnesty Programme (PAP) in sustaining peace, rehabilitation, reintegration, human- empowerment across the region.” The forum in a statement issued in Uyo noted that Dr.Otuaro demonstrated a growing emphasis on education, vocational training, skills acquisition, empowerment and sustainable reintegration, beyond the traditional focus on monthly stipends. “We particularly commend the reported expansion of PAP’s Postgraduate Scholarship Programme. In 2026 alone, 243 Niger Delta youths have reportedly been deployed for postgraduate studies abroad, including 150 recently deployed to Universities in the United Kingdom to study various disciplines. “These investments represent opportunities for young people to acquire knowledge and skills that can contribute meaningfully to the development of the Niger Delta and Nigeria. “The Forum rejects attempt to create the impression that Dr. Otuaro has lost the confidence of Niger Delta stakeholders. We are particularly concerned that some of the campaigns against him appear to be driven by ethnic, sectional, personal or political interests rather than an objective assessment of the Programme’s performance and mandate. “Our position should not be misconstrued as opposition to the Ijaw ethnic nationality. We respect the Ijaw people and acknowledge their historic contributions to the Niger Delta struggle. “However, no ethnic group owns the programme. PAP is a federal government intervention established for the peace, stability, rehabilitation and development of the Niger Delta and must therefore serve the collective interest of the region and Nigeria. “We support legitimate accountability. Where genuine allegations exist, they should be submitted to the appropriate authorities and subjected to transparent, impartial and evidence-based investigation. “Accountability, however, must not be confused with politically motivated campaigns or attempts to destabilise a critical national peace-building,” it stated. “Besides the monthly stipend the long-term objective must remain education, skills acquisition, rehabilitation, reintegration and sustainable livelihoods. “Issues concerning PAP’s policy framework, beneficiary structure, budgetary provisions and government funding operate within the federal government decisions, approvals and directives,” it added. The Akwa Ibom Ex-Militants Forum reaffirmed its support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, and his Renewed Hope Agenda, saying: “We believe the Niger Delta requires stability, responsible leadership, sustained investment in human capital and continued Federal Government engagement.” The forum said: “The success of the PAP should be measured by the peace it preserves, lives it transforms, young people it educates, skills it develops and the sustainable future it creates for the Niger Delta.” The body called on stakeholders to place peace above politics, development above personal interests and the collective future of the Niger Delta above ethnic and sectional considerations; as the Niger Delta cannot afford another cycle of instability.

title: Belgian Royal Visit Signals Central Asia’s Growing Importance to Europe, Expert Says
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – The first state visit of King Philippe and Queen Mathilde to Kazakhstan reflects growing European interest in Central Asia, where expanding transport links, critical minerals and new economic opportunities are drawing greater diplomatic attention. President Tokayev, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde visit the National Museum of Kazakhstan on Oct. 13. Photo credit: Belgian Royal Palace Fabienne Bossuyt, an associate professor at Ghent University specializing in EU relations with Central Asia, said the visit carries significance beyond bilateral diplomacy. Dr. Fabienne Bossuyt. Photo credit: ughent.be “This visit should be seen as an endorsement of Central Asia’s growing importance for European countries. As the region’s most advanced economy, Kazakhstan stands out as the country with the most opportunities for Belgium,” she told The Astana Times in a written comment. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde are visiting Kazakhstan from Oct. 11 to Oct. 14, accompanied by a 110-member delegation of government officials, business leaders and academics. The visit is the first by a Belgian monarch to Kazakhstan, although King Philippe previously traveled to the country as crown prince. During talks in Astana on Oct. 12, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Philippe discussed expanding cooperation in transport and logistics, critical minerals, energy and digital technologies, among other sectors. The two leaders also adopted a joint statement emphasizing the strategic importance of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, known as the Middle Corridor, which connects Asia and Europe. Tokayev described Belgium as a reliable and time-tested partner for Kazakhstan in Europe. He also said this visit ushers in a “golden chapter in the history” of the two nations. “It truly honors the friendship between our peoples. Belgium is a brilliant and time-tested partner of Kazakhstan in Europe. We deeply admire your beautiful country, its distinguished history and its enduring traditions,” Tokayev said. Economic ties have provided a foundation for broader engagement. Belgium has invested more than $15 billion in Kazakhstan since 2005, making it one of the country’s leading investment partners. More than 100 Belgian companies currently operate in Kazakhstan. Bilateral trade reached $582.4 million in 2025, up nearly 28% from the previous year, according to the Kazakh government. Kazakhstan exported $311.5 million in goods to Belgium and imported $270.9 million. Beyond bilateral relations While the visit primarily serves Belgium’s national interests, Bossuyt said it also reflects the EU’s broader effort to deepen its engagement with Central Asia. “This is first and foremost a bilateral initiative, but Belgium highly values its membership of the EU and it always tries to align its diplomatic activities and initiatives with the broader EU agenda,” she explained. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde visit the National Children’s Rehabilitation Center in Astana on Oct. 12. Photo credit: Belgian Royal Palace “The EU has been upscaling its strategic agenda for Central Asia in recent years by prioritizing its Global Gateway initiative for the region, which focuses heavily on critical raw materials and increased connectivity,” said Bossuyt. The broader European push gained momentum at the first EU-Central Asia Summit in Samarkand in April 2025, where the two regions elevated their relations to a strategic partnership. At the summit, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a 12 billion euro (US$13.4 billion) Global Gateway investment package targeting transport connectivity, critical raw materials, digital infrastructure, and water, energy and climate initiatives across Central Asia. Those priorities were also reflected in the discussions between President Tokayev and King Philippe, who identified critical minerals, renewable energy, industrial cooperation and transport connectivity as areas for closer partnership. The two countries also expressed interest in expanding cooperation in artificial intelligence, cloud technologies, data centers and supercomputing infrastructure. Belgium also has solid industrial expertise, including in the processing and recycling of critical raw materials, while Kazakhstan is seeking foreign investment and technology to develop more of its mineral resources domestically. Kazakhstan has the capacity to supply 21 of the 34 critical raw materials identified by the EU, Deputy Industry and Construction Minister Olzhas Saparbekov said at a Kazakhstan-Belgium seminar in Astana on Oct. 12. Saparbekov said Kazakhstan was seeking to expand domestic processing and develop higher-value products, including battery materials, specialty alloys and semiconductor materials. “We are ready to discuss phased models under which processing gradually moves to Kazakhstan, along with technology and expertise,” Saparbekov said. Contributing to the Middle Corridor Transport connectivity is another area where Belgium could play an important role, particularly through the Port of Antwerp-Bruges, one of Europe’s major maritime and logistics hubs. Bossuyt said Belgium’s infrastructure and strategic position could support Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop alternative trade routes connecting Central Asia with European markets. “In terms of the Middle Corridor, Belgium can offer added value by capitalizing on the strategic location and multi-modal infrastructure capacities of the Antwerp-Bruges logistical hubs,” she said. Kazakhstan and Belgium have earlier explored closer cooperation between Antwerp-Bruges and Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk, including potential collaboration on port management, digitalization and multimodal logistics. In September, Kazakh and Belgian representatives discussed the possibility of a framework cooperation agreement between the ports, as well as training opportunities for Kazakh logistics specialists. Such initiatives could help connect infrastructure development along the Middle Corridor with established European logistics networks. Bossuyt also pointed to the diplomatic presence of Central Asian countries in Brussels, where their embassies engage with both Belgian authorities and EU institutions, as an advantage for strengthening ties. Beyond trade and infrastructure, the royal visit includes academic, scientific and cultural exchanges, reflecting another dimension of the bilateral relationship. “Belgian royal visits typically have an economic agenda, although they also serve to stimulate further cultural and people-to-people cooperation, including concerning higher education and science,” Bossuyt said. The combination of economic diplomacy, infrastructure cooperation and academic exchanges illustrates how Belgium’s bilateral engagement with Kazakhstan increasingly intersects with the EU’s broader strategic priorities in Central Asia. What the visit has delivered so far The visit has also produced a roadmap between the foreign ministries of Kazakhstan and Belgium for 2027-2029, signed on Oct. 12. The document provides for regular political consultations, closer contacts between the two ministries and joint initiatives in priority areas of bilateral cooperation, according to the Kazakh Foreign Ministry. Tokayev and King Philippe also adopted a joint statement outlining cooperation priorities, including transport connectivity, critical minerals, digital technologies, education and health care. Further agreements are expected during the fourth meeting of the Kazakh-Belgian Business Council and the Rectors’ Forum on Oct. 13. Kazakh Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek said 12 agreements were planned in higher education, covering joint master’s and doctoral programs, academic exchanges and research internships. The post Belgian Royal Visit Signals Central Asia’s Growing Importance to Europe, Expert Says appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Inside Syros’ 162-Year-Old Apollo Theatre, Inspired by La Scala
body: SYROS, October 2026 — The Apollo Theatre in Ermoupoli, a 162-year-old landmark inspired by Milan’s La Scala, still plays a leading role in the cultural life of Syros. From Vardakas Square, known locally as Theatre Square, its plain facade gives little hint of the lavish hall inside. Its architecture and decoration reveal a long history, while comforts and technology added in the recent restoration keep it in modern use. One regular user is Animasyros , the international animation festival that Syros hosts every autumn. Organisers set the 2026 festival’s official opening at the Apollo Theatre for 23 September, Greek City Times reported. The festival also screened Ermoupoli , a short animated documentary it co-produced with MagentaTV for the series Places of Hellenism . Part of a “200 Years of Ermoupoli” tribute, the film gives the theatre a starring role. Inside the Apollo Theatre In the foyer, marble and brightly coloured ceiling paintings set the tone. However, they are only a prelude to the main hall. There, a painted ceiling honours great figures of art and thought, while boxes rise in several tiers. The hall seats only 350 people. Even so, it carries a real sense of grandeur. Italian architect Pietro Sampo drew up the original design, and the Apollo Theatre keeps elements of it. His models included La Scala in Milan and the San Carlo in Naples. He also drew on the academic theatre in Castelfranco and Florence’s Teatro della Pergola . Greek City Times’ weekend guide to the town highlights this Italian pedigree too. A town built by refugees The Apollo Theatre’s story begins in the early 19th century, when Ermoupoli grew fast as a home for refugees. Following the Greek Revolution of 1821, they came from Chios, Psara and Kasos, as well as Smyrna and Ayvalik. As the economy boomed in the first half of that century, so did a thirst for art. Syros, long a pioneer of women’s rights, even had a local theatre troupe founded by a woman. Writer Evanthia Kairi, sister of Enlightenment scholar Theophilos Kairis, set it up. Thomai Mendrinou, Deputy Mayor for Culture at the Syros municipality , described how the town and its theatre came about. “Ermoupoli was born in very difficult historical circumstances, but the refugees created, within a few decades, a city with commercial, maritime and, above all, cultural radiance. The Apollo Theatre is perhaps its most characteristic symbol. It is the first theatre of free Greece, built in a newly founded city with European ambitions.” Thomai Mendrinou, Deputy Mayor for Culture, Syros-Ermoupoli Verdi, stars and wartime The Apollo Theatre opened on 20 April 1864 with Verdi’s Rigoletto . Mikes Salvagos, the man who conceived the project, attended the premiere. Its opening program also included Donizetti’s La Favorita and Verdi’s La Traviata and Un Ballo in Maschera . The theatre gave local artists a proper home. Until then, they had performed in shacks, warehouses, clubs and coffee houses. Builders finished the work in a record two years. But weaknesses soon appeared, and repairs began after only a decade. Despite this, the stage in Ermoupoli never fell silent until the Second World War. Operas, plays, operettas and revues followed, with stars such as Mitsos Myrat, Manos Katrakis, Attik, Kyveli, Vasilis Argyropoulos and Marika Kotopouli. Kotopouli also gave the final performance of her life there, in Dario Niccodemi’s The Shadow in 1953. “During the Occupation, the Apollo Theatre was used by the Italian and then the German garrison for film screenings,” Mendrinou said of a dark chapter in its history. After liberation, it carried on as a cinema while still hosting some plays, she added. Mendrinou said those hard years belong to the building’s story too. “This is a period that reminds us that the theatre did not only live through times of prosperity. It lived through wars, the Occupation, economic decline, abandonment and dangers. And perhaps that makes it even more moving that today it is, once again, a space of freedom, creation and culture.” Thomai Mendrinou, Deputy Mayor for Culture, Syros-Ermoupoli Restoring the Apollo Theatre After the war, as Greece struggled to recover, the Apollo Theatre faltered. It shut soon after Kotopouli’s farewell, once the building was declared unfit for use. A renovation effort began in 1970, but it dragged on for decades because of a lack of funds. Locals still longed to see it revived. In one old black-and-white photograph, a banner on the facade asks, “Why have you abandoned me?” Even so, amateur troupes kept performing in the unfinished building from the 1970s to 2000. An architectural team led by Petros Pikionis began restoring the Apollo Theatre in the 1990s. The European Union and Greece’s Ministry of Culture funded the work. It finally reopened on 17 July 2000 with Theofrastos Sakellaridis’s O Vaftistikos , staged by the Athens Chamber Opera. “What we see today is an effort to restore its historical character, and not a simple ‘renovation’ in the modern sense,” Mendrinou said. Painter Dimitris Fortsas created the ceiling paintings, a key part of its look today, she added. In 2026, the Syros-Ermoupoli municipality also replaced the facade’s window frames, “because a monument of such value needs constant care,” she said. For visitors, Mendrinou has simple advice. “If you have the chance, watch a performance at the Apollo Theatre,” she said. “Because then you truly understand what it means for a historic theatre to keep breathing.” Source: travel.gr The post Inside Syros’ 162-Year-Old Apollo Theatre, Inspired by La Scala appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Bandits Kill Immigration Officer In Niger, Injure Another
body: Laleye Dipo in Minna An Assistant Superintendent of Immigration Ibrahim Usman Babagiwa has been killed by suspected bandits in Woko village in Borgu Local Government Area of Niger state. An Inspector of Immigration, whose identity has not been disclosed, was also seriously injured during the attack by the bandits. Babagiwa and the Inspector were said to have gone on surveillance operation along the Tungan Taya–Woko axis of the local government when they came under attack by the bandits at Woko Village. It was learnt that Babagiwa after being killed by the bandits was set on fire and left in the bush, while the Inspector escaped with several matchete injuries inflicted on him by the attackers. The remains of the Immigration Officer was discovered in the forests two days after the attack and was taken for burial according to Islamic rites. The Public Relations Officer of the Immigration Service, Niger State Command, Deputy Superintendent Mohammed Abubakar, confirmed the incident in Minna on Monday. Abubakar said the unnamed Inspector of Immigration is currently receiving treatment at an unnamed hospital. “The Niger State Command reiterates its unwavering commitment to combating irregular migration and addressing other security challenges along the international border,” Abubakar said He added that the command “remains resolute in discharging its statutory responsibilities despite the prevailing security challenges”. The Niger State Police Command Public Relations Officer, Superintendent of Police Wasiu Abiodun, also confirmed the incident.

title: The carnage and consequences of rising extremism in Asia
body: Warning: this story contains descriptions of violent events that may be confronting. (ABC-Australia) Fourteen-year-old Bryan Pamonag is passing the time, working on a project with his schoolfriends. It’s lunchtime but they’re staying inside a classroom, avoiding the oppressive September humidity in the southern Philippines town of Banga. Suddenly they’re interrupted by loud bangs. Two at first but more quickly follow. With his ears still ringing, he realises what the noise is and where it has come from. “I looked out the window, and I saw a student carrying a gun,” Bryan told 7.30. “I looked over at my classmates, and my best friend Chaldean had been shot. “We panicked. We dropped to the floor and started crawling.” The young gunman was now walking towards the classroom, carrying his father’s 9mm pistol, and Bryan inched closer to the line of fire. “I saw him approaching the door while still firing. I crawled toward it to close it,” Bryan said. “I kicked him in the stomach and shut our classroom door … blocking it because he was trying to force it open. “Even though I was scared, I had to stop him from entering our classroom. “He moved to the window … he shot at me. I tried to dodge but I was hit in the hand. “I saw one of my classmates run out of the room. He was shot three times.” Video posted to social media showed chaotic scenes of children desperately fleeing out of the school gates as the shooting unfolded. The young gunman then died by suicide. Bryan witnessed it. Across town, 14-year-old Chaldean’s mother, Catherine Lubaton, heard about the shooting on a community group chat. “I got on a motorbike and called Chaldean on her cell phone … she wasn’t answering,” she said. “I entered the school. I went to Chaldean’s classroom, but she was no longer there. I saw traces of blood. “I thought maybe she had only suffered minor injuries. “I immediately went to the hospital. In the emergency room my child was already gone. There was no doubt. My child was dead.” Earlier this month, the devastated community came together for Chaldean’s funeral. A white coffin adorned with purple butterflies passed through the streets of Banga in an ornate golden carriage, Catherine only a few steps behind the procession. Experiencing a pain no parent should, she was surrounded by the smiling face of her child in uniform, taken too soon. Banga’s residents woke early to watch the procession pass and reflect on the unimaginable tragedy. Bells tolled as family and young friends sombrely filled the local church. Extended family, classmates and friends watched on as Chaldean was laid to rest, often leaning on each other for support during the emotional ceremony. Family and friends gathered in the small church for the funeral service. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones) Catherine said she would miss the quiet moments she shared with her daughter. “Sometimes she would sleep next to me. When we watched TV, she would rest her head on my lap … she was very affectionate,” she said. “She wanted to become a teacher. She was like a big sister to her cousins.” The shooting at Banga National High School killed two students and the gunman, and injured eight others in just two minutes. It was the third school shooting in the Philippines in just four months. The True Crime Community The Philippines has rarely seen this type of violence at schools in quick succession. In June, two students opened fire at a school in Tacloban, killing three people and injuring 20. Two months later, a high school shooter in Zamboanga City live-streamed an attack, killing a student, injuring dozens and fatally shooting himself. Officials are examining why this wave of violence has swept through schools across the country. Analysts and cybersecurity experts are investigating the cases as possible acts of nihilistic violent extremism, or NVE. NVE is a term used by law enforcement officials to refer to acts of violence motivated by a misanthropic worldview, or a general hatred for society, rather than for a social, political or religious cause. Philippines officials have honed in on a specific online subculture tied to NVE, known as the True Crime Community (TCC), where members of its extremist fringe may become obsessed with mass killers. Philippine National Police has confirmed it is investigating the link between the Banga shooting and the TCC. “The suspect … posted his manifesto, stating that he is a member of the True Crime Community,” Brigadier General Alan Bolongon Manibog told 7.30. “Everything is under consideration. “The forensic digital examinations of the cell phones that we have recovered from the shooter and also from his classmates is still undergoing.” “Right now, we have our experts coming from the anti-cybercrime unit and other law enforcement agencies looking into [nihilistic violent extremism].” ‘Manipulating, influencing and radicalising’ Analysts at the International Centre for Political Violence and Terrorism Research are examining at least nine youth-perpetrated school attacks likely linked to NVE in South-East Asia over the past year. Among them is a shooting at a Thailand school in Nonthaburi this year, in which a young gunman killed seven people, including his two grandparents, before fatally shooting himself. Another is a bombing at the SMAN 72 school and mosque in North Jakarta which injured 99 people. Philippine National Police said the Jakarta school bombing was referenced in the Banga shooter’s manifesto. In the wake of the shooting in Tacloban, in July the Philippines Senate convened hearings into the incident and to work on an institutional response. The Senate heard allegations the shooting in Tacloban might have been influenced by 764, a decentralised online extremist and child sextortion network. Although researchers disagree about how 764 and the TCC overlap, both are considered major, growing, global threats that use online pathways to groom or radicalise children. Angel Redoble from the Philippine Society of Cyber Security Professionals said young Filipinos were typically targeted on social media apps like Discord, or on gaming platforms like Roblox, before contact moved to encrypted messaging apps. “These shootings are connected very closely, if not directly connected, to what’s going on in the online gaming platforms, content platforms, chat platforms and social media,” Mr Redoble told 7.30. “Platforms where a group of individuals, we call the groomers, are manipulating, influencing and radicalising vulnerable Filipino minors into committing real life violence, such as shootings.” Analysts say the grooming or recruiting of minors can be done either by adults or other young people. Mr Redoble said in all three shootings in the Philippines, the TCC had celebrated the acts of violence. “After every shooting, there is strong support and glorification in content platforms like TikTok where there is the True Crime Community,” he said. The shootings have prompted a national discussion over firearm safety in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia. The father of the school shooter in Banga, who worked for the Department of Education, is under investigation for firearm safety offences due to his son’s ability to access his handgun, which police say the boy took from a vault. Taking protective measures At a high school in Koronadal, the administrative centre of South Cotabato province near Banga, 7.30 viewed enhanced security measures being used to protect students. Students were being funnelled into lines at the school gates, where security officers were scanning students and their possessions with metal detectors while rummaging through their bags. “We are very worried that what happened to Banga could happen here,” assistant principal Sanny Pama said. He said parents should more closely monitor what students were doing on their smartphones and laptops, including who they were talking to. “There is no communication between the parents and the students and they are using their cell phones up to late at night,” he said. “We encourage the parents to check the phones, the apps and the lines of communication, who they are engaging with.” It’s a sentiment echoed by Philippine National Police. “We remind parents to look into the activities of their children online, including [on] social media,” Brigadier General Manibog said. “The safety and security of these children starts at home.” Brigadier General Manibog said there had been an increased number of online threats to cause violence in the community since the Banga shooting. “Most of these threats are made by minors … They don’t have the capabilities or access to firearms,” he said. Philippine National Police told a Senate inquiry earlier this year they had “rescued” 24 minors, who were identifying themselves as members of the TCC or 764, by connecting the children with social workers. In October, Philippines media reported the country’s national interior secretary revealed authorities had foiled more than 50 planned school shootings in South Cotabato following the shooting in Banga. Fifty-three people allegedly involved in online threats and grooming were arrested. “The cases involved different individuals and were not part of a single coordinated group,” Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said. Turning point? Recent shootings have prompted a nationwide school safety and security audit, while Philippine politicians look to expand laws to fight online abuse, grooming and radicalisation. In August, the Philippine government said it had secured commitments from Roblox aimed at strengthening child safety online, including enhanced age verification, faster cooperation with law enforcement and improved detection of harmful content. Roblox has also implemented additional safeguards to detect early signs of potential child endangerment. In a statement, a spokesperson for Discord said the platform used safety teams to prevent the spread of content that violated policy. “We maintain strong systems intended to prevent the spread of violent extremism, sexual exploitation and grooming on our platform and also work with other technology companies and safety organisations to improve online safety across the internet,” the statement read. Philippines authorities are also considering a social media ban for teenagers. South Cotabato Vice-Governor Arthur Pingoy said more work needed to be done. “After what happened in Tacloban and Zamboanga, the question is, was anything done to address similar incidents and problems?” he said. “Looking at what happened, we still need a lot of things to do to address incidents like this.” Catherine Lubaton just hopes the death of her daughter isn’t in vain. The post The carnage and consequences of rising extremism in Asia appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Ibrahim Kareem Makes Prestigious List of 63 Artists Selected for 2026 Abuja Photo Festival
body: Beating thousands of entries, the Nigerian photographer earns a place among a select group of artists set to exhibit at the festival’s landmark 10th edition. In a remarkable achievement that underscores the competitive nature of contemporary photography, Nigerian photographer Ibrahim Kareem has secured a place among the 63 artists selected to exhibit at the 2026 Abuja Photo Festival. His selection comes after thousands of applications were submitted for the festival’s 10th edition, making his inclusion a noteworthy moment in his creative career. The festival, scheduled for October 27–30, 2026, will celebrate a decade of photographic expression with the theme ‘Convergence: The Future of Imaging.’ For Kareem, the recognition goes beyond earning a place on an exhibition list. It presents an opportunity to share his creative vision on a platform that brings together different perspectives, experiences and approaches to visual storytelling. At a time when photography is constantly being redefined by technology, culture and new forms of artistic expression, the Abuja Photo Festival offers an important meeting point for artists exploring what images can communicate and how they shape our understanding of the world. With thousands of photographers seeking the opportunity to participate, the selection process has produced a final list of just 63 exhibiting artists. Kareem’s emergence from this highly competitive field is a significant accomplishment, reflecting the recognition his work has received through the festival’s selection process. His inclusion is also a meaningful moment for a photographer whose identity bridges Nigeria and the United Kingdom, two environments with distinct cultural experiences and rich traditions of visual expression. Beyond the prestige of being selected, the exhibition offers Kareem an opportunity to introduce his work to new audiences, engage with fellow creatives and participate in conversations about the direction of photography in an increasingly image-driven world. This year’s festival carries additional significance as the Abuja Photo Festival celebrates its 10th edition. Under the theme ‘Convergence: The Future of Imaging,’ the event will explore the meeting points between artistic imagination, evolving technologies and the changing role of photography in society. For the selected artists, the festival represents more than an exhibition. It is a space for creative exchange, professional connections and the presentation of photographic ideas that may influence how audiences experience visual art. Kareem’s place in this year’s lineup puts him among the photographers contributing to that conversation. His selection is particularly encouraging in an era when emerging and established African creative voices are increasingly seeking opportunities to reach audiences beyond geographical boundaries. As the countdown to the festival begins, Kareem will be looking ahead to an occasion that marks an important chapter in his artistic development. For a photographer chosen from thousands of hopeful applicants, being counted among just 63 exhibiting artists is already an achievement worth celebrating. The 10th Abuja Photo Festival will take place from October 27 to 30, 2026, under the theme ‘Convergence: The Future of Imaging.’

title: United Capital Investment Banking Named Most Prolific Investment Banking Company in Nigeria
body: United Capital Investment Banking has been recognised as the Most Prolific Investment Banking Company in Nigeria at the Association of Issuing Houses of Nigeria (AIHN) 30th Anniversary Awards and Dinner, held in Lagos. The award, a new category introduced at this year’s anniversary edition, was presented for the first time to recognise the investment banking company with the highest number of successfully closed transactions in 2025, making United Capital Investment Banking its inaugural recipient. The introduction of the category comes at an important point in the evolution of Nigeria’s investment banking industry. As the market expands in scale and sophistication, the role of investment banks continues to extend across capital raising, financial advisory, mergers and acquisitions, debt and equity transactions, and increasingly complex financing solutions for businesses, institutions and governments. For United Capital, becoming the first recipient of this recognition reflects the breadth of the team’s transaction activity and its ability to consistently originate, structure and execute transactions across an increasingly dynamic market. The recognition also coincides with a significant milestone for AIHN as the association celebrates 30 years of contributing to the development of Nigeria’s capital market. Over the past three decades, AIHN and its member institutions have played an important role in strengthening the issuing house profession and supporting the mobilisation of capital for businesses, governments and other institutions. Its 30th anniversary provides an opportunity to reflect not only on the progress of the industry, but also on the increasing depth, diversity and sophistication of Nigeria’s capital markets. The anniversary, themed ‘Three Decades of Catalysing Capital, Pioneering the Future and Enabling Wealth,’ brought together industry stakeholders to celebrate the institutions and transactions contributing to this progress and to consider the opportunities shaping the next phase of the market. Against this backdrop, United Capital’s recognition as the Most Prolific Investment Banking Company in Nigeria reinforces the team’s position at the forefront of this evolution. Commenting on the recognition, the Managing Director, Investment Banking, United Capital Group, Dr Gbadebo Adenrele, said: “We are honoured to be the first recipient of this recognition from the Association of Issuing Houses of Nigeria. It is particularly meaningful to receive this award as AIHN celebrates 30 years of advancing Nigeria’s investment banking and capital markets industry. This achievement reflects the expertise, commitment and execution capabilities of our team, as well as the trust our clients continue to place in us. As the market evolves, we remain committed to delivering transactions that create value for our clients and contribute meaningfully to the growth of Nigeria’s capital markets.” The latest recognition builds on United Capital Investment Banking’s strong track record within the industry. At the previous AIHN Awards, the firm received the Innovative Issuance of the Year Award for its role as Lead Issuing House and Coordinator of the landmark Inaugural FGN Domestic Dollar Bond, Nigeria’s first US dollar denominated bond issued in the domestic market. From being recognised for an innovative landmark transaction to becoming the inaugural recipient of an award recognising transaction volume, the consecutive honours demonstrate the breadth of United Capital Investment Banking’s capabilities and its continued contribution to the development of Nigeria’s capital markets. As the industry enters its next phase, United Capital Investment Banking remains focused on helping businesses, institutions and governments access capital, execute strategic transactions and unlock opportunities for sustainable growth. At the Group level, United Capital Plc is a leading African financial services group providing investment banking, asset management, wealth management, securities, trusteeship and other financial solutions. Through its businesses, the Group continues to connect individuals, businesses and institutions with capital and investment opportunities while contributing to the development of Africa’s financial markets.

title: Russia’s RTS Index tops 900 points for first time since early August
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The dollar-denominated RTS Index crossed the 900-point threshold on Tuesday for the first time since August 6, 2026, according to Moscow Exchange data.
At 10:49 a.m. Moscow time, the benchmark index gained 0.82% to reach 906.04 points.
By 10:59 a.m. Moscow time, the RTS pared gains slightly to stand at 903.58 points (+0.55%).
Meanwhile, the ruble-based MOEX Index climbed to 2,406.95 points, also up 0.55% from the previous close.

title: Fertility Treatment in Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – This article explores why Iran has become an option for international patients seeking fertility treatment.
This article explores why Iran has become an option for international patients seeking fertility treatment. It covers the global prevalence of infertility, Iran’s position in reproductive medicine, and factors such as specialized treatments, accessibility, and comparatively lower costs. The article also introduces VitaLife Fertility Center and its support for international patients seeking IVF, egg donation, surrogacy, and other fertility services in Iran.
Infertility is no longer a health challenge limited to a small group of couples. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately one in six people of reproductive age experience infertility during their lifetime, making access to effective and affordable fertility care a growing global health priority.
As demand for assisted reproductive technologies continues to grow, patients are increasingly looking beyond their home countries for fertility treatment. Cost, access to advanced reproductive technologies, legal restrictions, waiting times, and the availability of specialized services can all influence where international patients seek care.
Among the destinations receiving increasing attention is Iran, where assisted reproductive medicine has developed substantially over the past several decades.
Infertility can result from male factors, female factors, a combination of both, or unexplained causes. Treatment may involve medication, surgery, intrauterine insemination (IUI), in vitro fertilization (IVF), egg donation, embryo-related genetic testing, or other assisted reproductive technologies.
The challenge, however, is not simply whether treatment exists. Access matters.
WHO notes that fertility treatments remain inaccessible or unaffordable for many people, with the high cost of assisted reproduction creating a significant barrier in numerous countries.
This has contributed to the growth of cross-border reproductive care, in which patients travel to another country to obtain fertility services that may be more accessible, affordable, or legally available there.
Research examining international reproductive care has found that cost and the legal availability of assisted reproductive technologies are among the most frequently reported reasons patients seek treatment abroad, alongside cultural and practical considerations.
Where Does Iran Stand in Fertility Treatment?
Iran has developed a substantial medical infrastructure for assisted reproduction. Assisted reproductive technologies have been used in the country since the 1980s, and a national report published on Iranian ART centers documented tens of thousands of IVF/ICSI cycles across dozens of centers. Researchers concluded that Iran has considerable potential to provide IVF services not only to Iranian patients but also to patients from other countries in the region.
Iran's position has also been highlighted by Iranian medical authorities. In a report published by Mehr News, Hamid Choubineh, head of the Iranian Scientific Association of Infertility and Reproductive Health, described Iran as being among the top 10 countries in the world for infertility treatment, while emphasizing the country's access to modern assisted reproductive techniques.
The country's reproductive medicine sector includes IVF, ICSI, genetic testing, donor programs, and gestational surrogacy. Iranian research has also documented the use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis for conditions such as beta-thalassemia, aneuploidy screening, and sex selection.
For international patients, this combination of medical expertise and comparatively lower treatment costs can make Iran an option worth investigating.
Why Do International Patients Consider Iran?
The reasons vary from patient to patient, but several factors frequently influence the decision.
Access to Specialized Fertility Services
Some reproductive treatments are heavily restricted in certain countries. Regulations concerning donor eggs, donor embryos, gestational surrogacy, and embryo testing vary significantly around the world.
Iran occupies a distinctive position within the Muslim world in this regard. Islamic bioethics literature notes that the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a fatwa permitting certain third-party reproductive arrangements, including egg donation and surrogacy, and that these practices subsequently became incorporated into Iran's reproductive medicine framework.
This religious and legal context differs from the position adopted by many Sunni authorities regarding third-party gamete donation. For international patients, therefore, Iran can provide an alternative where certain fertility treatments are available within a Shia Islamic legal and medical framework.
At the same time, eligibility is not unlimited. Iranian fertility programs operate within local medical and legal requirements, and international patients should confirm their eligibility before traveling. For example, VitaLife's current program information specifies eligibility requirements for international intended parents and states that its surrogacy pathway is designed for legally married heterosexual couples.
Surrogacy, Egg Donation and Gender Selection
For patients who cannot safely carry a pregnancy, surrogacy in Iran can provide another reproductive pathway. In gestational surrogacy, an embryo created through IVF is transferred to a gestational carrier.
Egg donation is another important option for patients whose own eggs may not be suitable for treatment. Iran has developed clinical experience with donor-assisted reproduction, making it an area of interest for some international patients.
Another service sought by some international couples is gender selection through IVF and preimplantation genetic testing. Iranian medical research has documented PGD-based sex selection in clinical settings, although the medical, ethical, and legal circumstances surrounding its use should always be discussed with a qualified fertility specialist.
The important point is that international fertility care should not be viewed simply as a search for the cheapest treatment. Patients need to consider medical suitability, legal requirements, laboratory standards, documentation, and the process for returning home with a child born through assisted reproduction.
How VitaLife Supports International Patients
For someone traveling abroad for fertility treatment, the medical procedure is only one part of the journey.
International patients may also need help with medical records, treatment planning, translation, travel arrangements, legal documentation, surrogate coordination, and communication with clinics.
This is where an international surrogacy agency and fertility coordinator can play an important role.
VitaLife Fertility Center in Iran works with international intended parents seeking coordinated fertility and reproductive services. Its programs include IVF, egg donation, gestational surrogacy, embryo-related genetic services, and support with the practical aspects of treatment in Iran.
The center's international support model is designed to coordinate different stages of treatment rather than leaving patients to manage each component independently. According to VitaLife's published program information, this includes medical coordination, surrogate matching, legal documentation support, international patient coordination, and assistance throughout the treatment process.
For intended parents considering treatment abroad, this type of coordinated approach can make an otherwise complicated process easier to navigate.
Choosing fertility treatment abroad involves more than cost. International patients should consider the medical team, clinic facilities, legal requirements, treatment eligibility, timeline, total costs, and support throughout the journey.
Fertility treatment cannot guarantee pregnancy or live birth, as outcomes depend on individual medical factors such as age, reproductive history, and embryo quality.
At VitaLife Fertility Center, international patients are supported throughout their treatment journey in Iran, from the initial consultation to delivery. Mobina Hosseini, a midwifery specialist with a master’s degree in midwifery, serves as the dedicated patient coordinator, helping international intended parents navigate their treatment from A to Z.
Medical care is provided under the supervision of Dr. Farah Ghasemi, the treating physician, with IVF procedures carried out at Baharan Negar Infertility Treatment Center. For patients undergoing surrogacy, delivery takes place at Nikan Aghdasieh Hospital, providing a coordinated pathway from fertility treatment through pregnancy and birth.
This integrated approach allows international patients to have one coordinated team supporting their medical, communication, and practical needs throughout the process.
A Growing Role for Iran in International Fertility Care
Iran’s experience in assisted reproduction, specialized fertility services, and comparatively accessible treatment costs has made it an option for international patients. For intended parents, choosing the right pathway means finding medically appropriate, legally compliant, and well-coordinated care. VitaLife Fertility Center supports international patients throughout their fertility journey in Iran.

title: LIVESTREAM: ICC’s 4th status conference on Rodrigo Duterte’s case
body: MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) will hold its fourth status conference on former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes against humanity case on Tuesday, October 13. A status conference is where parties discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial. So far, the court has had three conferences: on May 27, when it announced that the trial will begin on November 30 ; on June 23 , when the chamber cautioned lawyers against granting media interviews; and the third one, on September 16, when the former president made an appearance. Duterte is again expected to appear during Tuesday’s hearing. For the fourth status conference, the Trial Chamber III and the parties will discuss the following: Daily sitting schedule: For the trial’s opening statements For the first evidentiary block in December 2026 Prosecution’s List of Witnesses and number of hours to present the case ⁠Defense and Common Legal Representatives of victims’ estimates ⁠Defense’s responses to Rule 68 applications and requests for in-court protective measures ⁠Disclosure/Prosecution’s List of Evidence ⁠Further observations on recent filings Registry’s capacity to assist the process Registry’s update on interpretation for the start of trial Defense’s submissions on readiness for the trial Watch the livestream starting at 4:30 pm (Manila time). Download the Rappler app and join the Justice and Crime chat room to get live updates from Rappler’s justice reporter Jairo Bolledo. – Rappler.com

body:

title: Rin Tueny appoints Lakes State caretaker executive
body: The caretaker governor of Lakes State, Gen. Rin Tueny Mabor, on Monday issued gubernatorial decrees for the appointment of officials to the executive, including advisors, ministers, and commissioners, among others. The governor’s decree stated that all appointees are directed by President Salva Kiir to act impartially and not use public resources for electoral leverage. The decree also directed appointees to cooperate with the state leadership to deliver peaceful campaigns, ensure candidate protection, and ensure free and fair elections.
