title: Zelensky’s behavior angers Trump amid refinery strikes — media
body:
WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky's refusal to heed Washington’s calls to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries is angering US President Donald Trump, The Atlantic magazine reported, citing a White House official.
"Zelensky is overplaying his hand and pissing the president off," the White House official said, as cited by The Atlantic. "The president is asking for one thing: stop hitting the refineries. Give him that," the official added.
According to the magazine, after a heated confrontation with the US leader at the White House in February 2025, Zelensky "spent more than a year trying to repair his relationship with Trump," while Ukrainian officials hoped that Trump "would not actively hurt their cause." "That hope may be fading," The Atlantic wrote.
The US president said on October 10 that the US had repeatedly urged Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries but Zelensky had ignored the calls.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a phone call on October 9, particularly discussing petroleum product supplies. The Russian leader said that Moscow had reiterated its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the United States and global markets. According to Novak, Russia is lifting its ban on diesel exports ahead of schedule and is ready to supply 300,000 tons of diesel in October, increasing the volume to 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December. Monthly supplies could subsequently reach 3 million tons. The US administration, in turn, issued a general license authorizing Russian diesel supplies to the global market until April 7, 2027.

title: Creusot 0.14.0 release - Contracts for Rust, formally proved
body:
We are pleased to announce the release of version 0.14.0 of Creusot , our formal verification tool for Rust.
In this post, we highlight a small selection of new features. See the full changelog for the rest.
Previously, Creusot restricted its specification of PartialOrd to total orders. Since version 0.13.0, we have relaxed it to allow partial orders. (We skipped a devlog entry for 0.13.0 so let's talk about this here.)
Our previous definition of total order ( OrdLogic ) relied on the comparison function cmp_log (the logic counterpart to cmp ), which returns an Ordering .
That had the benefit of making totality an implicit consequence of the type of the function: any two elements must compare either Less , Equal , or Greater .
With the switch to partial orders, a traditional formulation based on a boolean comparison function (" < ", aka. lt_log ) becomes more natural. A strict partial order ( PartialOrdLogic ) consists of a comparison function lt_log which is irreflexive and transitive. Totality becomes another law: for all x , y , the trijunction x < y || x == y || y < x must hold.
Interestingly, none of our existing proofs were affected by this change. Our automated provers just took it in stride.
Creusot now generates verification conditions (VCs) for snapshots, which are logic expressions embedded in Rust programs. In particular, this enhances the use of "lemma functions", a common idiom in verification tools similar to Creusot.
For example, you can encode a lemma as a logic function such as this, which logically amounts to the proposition forall<x> hyp(x) -> concl(x) :
Then, inside a program function you can call lemma inside a snapshot! :
Creusot now translates this call to an assertion that hyp(n) (the precondition of lemma ) is true and an assumption that concl(n) (its postcondition) is true. Notably, these statements are specialized to n , the argument of lemma , so we avoid relying on provers to instantiate the universal quantifier in forall<x> hyp(x) -> concl(x) .
It should be said that this new feature specifically enables logic functions to be used as lemma functions. Before, you could already do something similar with program functions:
The difference is that (1) this version introduces a Rust function call, however trivial it may be, and (2) it must pass the borrow checker, which may require boilerplate to work around when all you wanted is to state some facts. In contrast, snapshots are entirely erased, so it is clear that they are there only for the sake of formal proof. Thus, these newly generated VCs for snapshots let us draw clearer boundaries between the worlds of programs and proofs.
It may seem surprising that Creusot did not already do this. This comes down to the fact that programs and specifications are written in two separate languages, with their own semantics, and thus with different mechanisms and motivations for generating VCs. Without going into too much details, VCs were originally not generated for snapshot! because it isn't necessary for soundness, but it turns out to help catch mistakes in specifications quicker (such as out-of-bounds indexing), on top of enabling new techniques such as that described above.
It is finally possible to use Go-to-definition in Pearlite specifications.
To start, we needed to make rust-analyzer expand the code of specifications. In normal compilation, specification macros ( #[requires] , #[ensures] , proof_assert! , snapshot! , etc.) erase themselves, discarding their contents. We just needed to pass options to rust-analyzer for it to expand those macros the same way Creusot does (see our guide for the relevant rust-analyzer settings ).
One worry we had was that Pearlite macros expand to not quite valid Rust code, not meant to be compiled by rustc: it passes the type checker, but not the borrow checker. Luckily for us, rust-analyzer does not do borrow checking, so it doesn't see any problem with the expanded code.
With that done, Go-to-definition did start to work, but it returned numerous irrelevant results. The problem was that the tokens produced by Pearlite macros carried spans that were too coarse-grained.
To explain it very roughly, when you activate Go-to-definition, rust-analyzer looks for identifiers in the final AST whose span ranges over your cursor. For example, a + b in Pearlite expands to a method call ::creusot_std::logic::ops::AddLogic::add_logic(a, b) , where every generated token carries the span of the whole expression a + b . Hence, Go-to-definition from anywhere in that expression ends up looking up the definitions of all of creusot_std , logic , ops , AddLogic , and add_logic .
In this case, we'd like to only look up add_logic , and only when the cursor is right next to + . The fix is to make the token add_logic have the span of + , and to make the other identifiers have a zero-width span, which seems to be enough for rust-analyzer to ignore them.
Many thanks to Sarah Quiñones for figuring all this out. This fix makes navigating specifications in Creusot much more pleasant.
Thanks for tuning in. If you have any questions about Creusot, you are welcome to join our Zulip channel , or to open a discussion or an issue on the Creusot repository.

title: Egypt and Sudan investigate after two Egyptians shot dead in Khartoum
body: Egypt and Sudan say they are investigating the deadly shooting of two Egyptians in Khartoum, an attack that followed the weekend death of scores of Sudanese goldminers in an air strike near the Egyptian border. Police in Sudan said they have apprehended the gunman whom they identified as Ibrahim Abdullah Adam, 23. They say he has admitted carrying out the attack, in which a third Egyptian was wounded, to avenge the death of his brother in Saturday's air strike. They said all three Egyptians were lorry drivers. A Sudanese police officer was also wounded in an exchange of fire before the gunman's arrest. “The investigation is continuing to establish the circumstances of the incident and its motives,” police said late on Monday night. “We will firmly deal with the matter under the law.” Neither Egypt nor Sudan publicly have said who was behind the air strike. The Egyptian military issued a statement saying troops and police were continuing to counter “illegal” gold prospecting in the country's Eastern Desert. It said it had dropped flyers on what it called criminal elements, warning them they must stop illegal mining “so that full sovereignty is safeguarded inside the Egyptian state's borders”. Egypt's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, said it was closely following the “regrettable” shooting in Khartoum. It said Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and his Sudanese counterpart in the military-backed government, Mohieldin Salem, spoke on the phone on Monday evening. It added that the ministers “emphasised the mutual respect that binds the two nations, including respect for each other's sovereignty, and the safety and integrity of their territories and borders”. The air strike near the border was initially reported by human rights and watchdog groups in Sudan, including the Emergency Lawyers, the civilian-led Somoud alliance and the Sudan Doctors' Network. They gave widely varying death toll figures, from 13 to 72. Some media reports in Sudan put the figure as high as 200. “We reject the targeting of civilians and putting their lives at risk, which cannot be justified on security grounds,” Somoud said. “The leadership of the relevant authorities appointed by the armed forces bears the responsibility for what happens in areas under their control.” Sudan's military-led Sovereign Council said the air strike took place in the border region with Egypt. “The leadership in the two brotherly nations have been in contact since immediately after the incident took place to guarantee the protection of lives and safeguarding relations between the two peoples, find out the circumstances of the incident and give public opinion ownership of the facts,” it said. Images ​and video shared online, which The National has been unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn across rubble, others wrapped in green sheets and angry survivors, mostly men in their 20s or 30s. There has been an influx of gold prospectors in northern Sudan in recent years as the civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has hit the economy hard, driving hundreds of thousands to seek alternative sources of income. Egypt 's military said in June it was engaged in a large-scale operation in the south of the country to tackle gangs involved in drugs and arms trafficking, as well as illegal gold prospecting. It said 87 Egyptians and 136 foreigners had been arrested. Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign parties seeking quick profit. In several ways, the current gold rush is a by-product of most of the country’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011. The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold in Sudan. Some estimates put the number of artisanal miners involved at about two million. Official figures place Sudanese government revenue from gold exports at about $2 billion but experts say smuggling and the use of gold outside official channels account for far more. Last year, Sudan’s gold production was about 70 tonnes but only 20 tonnes were exported, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated primitive localised refineries. Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda

title: US evaluates Bath Iron Works’ capacity for additional destroyer
body:
The US Department of War has certified Bath Iron Works (BIW) as capable of building an additional destroyer for the US Navy, following a review of the shipyard’s production capacity and ongoing workload.
The decision follows assessments and visits to the Maine-based shipyard to verify that it can take on another ship while continuing work on its existing orders, according to Senator Susan Collins , who advocated for funding for a second destroyer in this year’s budget.
BIW, a General Dynamics shipyard, builds Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyers for the US Navy. BIW President Charles F. Krugh welcomed the announcement and said the assessment recognizes improvements in the shipyard’s construction processes, production schedules and workforce stability. He added that these changes are helping the company accelerate ship deliveries to the navy.
“This announcement recognizes BIW’s unprecedented improvements in our build process, our production schedule and the stability and skill of our shipbuilders,” said Krugh.
The certification comes as the US Navy seeks to expand its fleet of surface combatants amid China’s continued naval expansion. The U.S. has also considered using overseas shipyards to help address its shipbuilding capacity requirements.
Collins said she would continue advocating for resources to support the shipyard and meet the navy’s requirements.
“At a time when our nation urgently needs more surface combatants and is even looking to shipyards overseas, this American shipyard is answering that call, delivering each destroyer to the Navy faster than the last. The announcement makes it clear that we are succeeding in our efforts to improve shipbuilding and that is leading to more work – which is good for the business and good for each and every one of us who works here,” Krugh added.
The shipyard is investing in its facilities. According to BIW, projects include a new Kitting Terminal, a Pier Support Center, a Trades Storage Building, security facilities and pier reconstruction. Its modernization efforts are intended to improve material preparation and delivery processes and working conditions for shipbuilders.
Meanwhile, BIW received a US Navy contract in August 2023 for the design and construction of three Arleigh Burke-class destroyers under the fiscal year 2023–2027 multiyear procurement program. The contract also included options for additional ships, subject to authorization and appropriations, giving the navy flexibility to increase production. This year, BIW also secured a contract to build another Arleigh Burke-class destroyer for the US Navy, which will be named after retired Navy Hospital Corpsman Third Class Robert R. Ingram .

title: Russian strike collapses a Kharkiv apartment stairwell and kills three, days after the US waived sanctions on Russia’s diesel
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian munitions brought down a stairwell of an apartment building in Kharkiv on the evening of 12 October, and rescuers recovered three bodies from the rubble overnight, local authorities reported. Survivors described fire, falling glass, and pets left behind. The strike came days after Washington waived sanctions on Russian diesel, as it expects Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries. Russia hits Ukraine’s cities every day as it readies a winter campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, and its oil exports keep bringing in the money that pays for the drones and missiles. A halt to Ukraine’s refinery strikes with no matching halt to Russia’s strikes would leave Moscow’s fuel income intact while Kharkiv digs through rubble. Estonia’s prime minister has already urged Europe to help Ukraine destroy those refineries instead. A stairwell gone in Kholodnohirskyi district Russian munitions hit Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district repeatedly from around 21:17, and Mayor Ihor Terekhov preliminarily identified them as Banderols. At 22:21, he said one strike had hit a residential building, possibly trapping people. He then added in a follow-up post: “Very serious destruction—an entire stairwell has collapsed.” The strike destroyed an entrance of the four-story building, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) said . It counted 11 injured across the city’s evening strikes, and a rescuer was hospitalized, while Terekhov put the number at 10. By 06:56 on 13 October, rescuers had found a third body. Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov confirmed three dead and said the search continued. Experts will check whether the building is still fit to live in, he added . A rescuer at the collapsed stairwell of an apartment building hit by a Russian strike in Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district, Ukraine, 12 October 2026. Photo: Oleksandr Manchenko/Suspilne Kharkiv Over 24 hours, Russian attacks killed three people in Kharkiv and injured 37, including two children treated for acute stress, Syniehubov reported . “I realize I’m on fire”: two residents recall the strike Larysa Maksimenko had just put her bedridden husband to sleep when the strike hit, she told Suspilne Kharkiv. She suffered a head wound and burns. “I went to the kitchen to switch on the kettle for myself, to have some coffee. I realize I’m on fire. Then glass fell on me. I came to, and I’m buried under everything. All covered in blood,” she said. Larysa Maksimenko, a resident injured in the Russian strike on her apartment building in Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district, Ukraine, 13 October 2026. Photo: Valeriia Yemets/Suspilne Kharkiv The window bars were broken, and medics carried her husband out through the window. Rescuers later found a woman under the rubble in her apartment, likely a neighbor, Maksimenko said. All she wants now, she said, is to get to her husband in hospital. Viacheslav Chibitko, a resident of the apartment building hit by a Russian strike in Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district, Ukraine, with one of his dogs, 12 October 2026. Photo: Valeriia Yemets/Suspilne Kharkiv Viacheslav Chibitko, who lives on the second floor next to the collapsed entrance, saw a flash, and then everything blew out. He got his three dogs out, but five cats are still inside. During the clearing, a concrete slab fell on a rescuer, Suspilne’s correspondent reported. Crews pulled him out and handed him to medics. Cars burning outside a 25-story apartment building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district after a Russian drone strike, Kyiv, Ukraine, 12 October 2026. Photo: Office of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine Kyiv’s toll rises, and strikes hit other cities overnight The evening drone strike on a 25-story building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district killed two people, Kyiv prosecutors reported . The second victim was found dead in a car near the building. Prosecutors counted at least seven injured, including a 17-year-old girl, while Mayor Vitali Klitschko counted 11 in the capital. Explore further Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches From 18:00 on 12 October, Russia launched five ballistic missiles, nine loitering munitions, and 108 attack drones, Ukraine’s Air Force reported . Air defenses downed or suppressed 88 drones. A Russian drone attack injured four patients at a medical facility in Khmelnytskyi Oblast, oblast head Serhii Tiurin said . In Dnipro, a Russian attack injured a 64-year-old man, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported . A downed Russian drone set two houses on fire in Murovane near Lviv, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said . On 12 October, a Russian Smerch rocket with a cluster warhead hit a house in Cherkaske, Donetsk Oblast, killing three people, including a 13-year-old girl, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported . Russian attacks killed more than 150 people in the week to 11 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . Russian bombs killed at least 20 people in Zaporizhzhia on 10 October, by the oblast’s count . On 9 October, the US waived its sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. The White House expects Kyiv to halt refinery strikes under its proposed energy ceasefire. title: Almaty Expands International Air Links With New Routes to Dubai, Hanoi and Prague
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Flydubai has launched regular cargo flights between Dubai and Almaty, establishing a direct air freight connection between two major logistics hubs in the Middle East and Central Asia, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport reported on Oct. 12. Photo credit: Ministry of Transport. Almaty International Airport welcomed the airline’s first cargo flight from Dubai on Oct. 12. The arrival was marked by a welcoming ceremony, including a traditional water-arch salute for the aircraft. Flights on the Dubai–Almaty–Dubai route will operate once a week using Boeing 737 aircraft, according to the ministry. The new route is expected to expand cargo transport options between the two cities and strengthen Almaty’s role as an aviation and logistics hub in Central Asia. Almaty International Airport continues to develop freight connections with major logistics centers worldwide, the ministry said. The cargo service follows the launch of a new passenger route connecting Hanoi, Almaty and Prague on Oct. 10. VietJet Air operates the route twice a week using Airbus A330 aircraft. Under fifth-freedom traffic rights, passengers can travel along the full Hanoi–Almaty–Prague route or book flights separately between Almaty and Prague, according to Almaty’s tourism department. The route is expected to improve the city’s accessibility for travelers from Europe and Southeast Asia while creating additional opportunities for inbound tourism. The number of tourists from Vietnam visiting Almaty increased 20% in 2025 compared with the previous year. The new service is expected to further strengthen tourism ties between Kazakhstan and Vietnam and make Almaty more accessible to Vietnamese travelers. The post Almaty Expands International Air Links With New Routes to Dubai, Hanoi and Prague appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Kyiv has learned to live between air raid alerts. After two months of relentless Russian attacks, there’s barely any time between them.
body: Kyiv residents in a pedestrian underpass during an air raid alert. October 4, 2026 Kyiv residents have lived under Russian drone and missile attacks since the start of the war, but this summer the attacks became a daily occurrence. Since late August, Russian forces have been attacking the city day and night, and air raid alerts constantly disrupt residents’ plans. Dozens of civilians have been killed in the capital over these months, and hundreds have been injured. As winter approaches, residents are preparing for power outages and heating problems. Meduza spoke with Ukrainian journalist Denys Trubetskyi, who writes for Die Zeit and other European outlets, about how doctors, business owners, and other Kyiv residents live and work under relentless attacks, and whether the coming winter could be much harder than previous ones. Denys Trubetskyi ‘ Since last winter, Russia has focused on Kyiv. It’s the number one target behind the front lines ’ — You were born in Sevastopol, but now you live in Kyiv and cover Ukraine for German-language outlets. When did you move? — My career in German media came about pretty much by chance. I’ve never lived permanently in Germany or another German-speaking country, but at some point I started learning the language because I was interested in German sports and politics. I got into journalism 14 or 15 years ago as a sportswriter, working for fairly big Ukrainian outlets like Football.ua . In 2012, Ukraine and Poland hosted the European soccer championship, and I met German colleagues while covering the German national team’s matches. Then Ukraine entered a very interesting period politically: Maidan, the annexation of Crimea, which affected me directly because of where I’m from, and so on. I’d always thought about moving to Kyiv, and I’ve lived here since 2015. That’s also when I started working as a political correspondent for major German outlets — Die Zeit and Table.Media — as well as Swiss and Austrian publications. — In late August, Russia began attacking Kyiv and the Kyiv region almost nonstop — at night and during the day. How is the city coping? — To understand that, you have to look at Russia’s whole strategy of total war against Ukraine. I should explain why I call it total war. You can debate whether Russia is using all its resources for mobilization. When it comes to the war economy, it isn’t using all its resources yet. But in the air war, Russia has been using every resource available since the fall of 2022. It’s sending pretty much everything it produces at Ukraine, including Kyiv. The jet-powered drones that have been pounding Kyiv since August are so new that some were built just two weeks ago. They sometimes stockpile ballistic missiles, but overall, attacks on the current scale wouldn’t be possible without using missiles fresh off the production line. On September 11, 2022, Russia launched the first wave of attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The strategy was meant to put as much pressure as possible on civilians. Since then, Russia has tried all kinds of ways to pressure Ukrainians — trying to knock out the country’s energy system, for example. But it’s come to realize that plunging half the country into a total blackout for a couple of weeks is very difficult. So since last winter, Russia has focused on Kyiv. It’s the number one target for attacks behind the front lines. Kyiv and its metropolitan area account for roughly 15% of the population currently living in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Last winter was the harshest in 20 years. Temperatures sometimes dropped to minus 25 degrees Celsius (minus 13 degrees Fahrenheit). Entire districts of Kyiv, especially on the left bank of the Dnipro, went weeks without electricity or heating. But this summer also turned out to be the hardest in the city’s history. — What made it so hard? — Two things coincided. First, [in winter] the genius U.S. president launched his “very successful” Operation Epic Fury, which caused a major weapons shortage. That had a serious impact on air defense. The PAC-3 MSE missile used in Patriot systems is the most effective against ballistic weapons. In July, Ukraine was receiving small batches of 15 to 20 missiles. We don’t know how things stand now, but those July figures are unlikely to have changed much. Second, Russia increased production of its ballistic missiles. It used to produce up to about 60 standard ballistic missiles a month; now it’s up to 75 . There are also missiles that follow a quasi-ballistic trajectory, like the Zircon. Roughly speaking, we’re talking about production of around 80 to 100 ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles a month. Ukraine has almost nothing to shoot them down with. And several Patriot systems are stationed in Kyiv — that’s an open secret. Obviously, once shortages developed here [in air defense], Russia started firing at Kyiv, because a new opportunity had opened up for its military. Then there’s the situation with jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5. Ukraine had more or less been mentally prepared for attacks like these since the beginning of the year. Technically, there are ways to shoot them down , but it’s extremely difficult to find a solution that can be used on a large scale against drones flying at up to 650 kilometers per hour (about 400 miles per hour). And to make sure that solution doesn’t cost one and a half to two times as much as the Gerans themselves. ‘ With everything flying so fast, you don’t even have time to do anything ’ — How has this crisis affected everyday life in Kyiv? — From May through the end of summer, ballistic missile strikes happened every third night on average. That’s really hard on your mental health and your day-to-day life. Quite often, the strikes came before an air raid alert was even issued. But ballistic missiles fly so fast that many people barely have time to get down to a shelter, even after hearing the alert: A missile can hit one or two minutes after the alert. And if you’re outside at that moment, say, on your way to a shelter, that can be more dangerous than staying in the hallway. You go to bed and you don’t know which night it’ll happen. In practice, a strike can come at any moment. When it happens every day, it’s hard to describe it without swearing. — After the attacks intensified, The Guardian and The Washington Post described Kyiv as a frontline city. Do you agree? — Things are different here. Kyiv is still a city behind the front lines, even if it’s the “number one target” behind them. FPV drones , artillery shells, and so on don’t reach us here. I wouldn’t use that particular term [“a frontline city”], although I understand it from a journalist’s perspective, and the situation [in Kyiv] is very difficult. The problem with the endless launches of jet-powered drones is that it’s basically one endless attack that’s been going on since August. Without exaggeration, several people are killed and dozens are wounded every day. Of course, the chance of you personally getting hit is still small. But it’s increased considerably. There was a time when your risk of dying in a car crash in Kyiv was much higher than in an air attack. Now it’s the other way around. I’m noticing that a lot of people around me are at their limit. They’re thinking about the coming winter. People who have the option of leaving for the winter are looking into whether they can afford it. I can’t do that: You can’t work as a Kyiv correspondent without being in Kyiv. My friends were looking at apartments in Ivano-Frankivsk and Chernivtsi. Prices have naturally gone through the roof . You can describe Ukraine’s economic situation in one sentence: People have become much poorer . And we can say with certainty that food, internet, phone service, and so on will inevitably get much more expensive. Finding the money for an incredibly expensive apartment somewhere in western Ukraine is very difficult. The economic side of this is very important right now. Many employers are suffering from the attacks — almost every industry has been affected. People’s wages are being cut while everything is getting more expensive. It leaves people feeling paralyzed. Some people cope better than others in stressful situations like these. Among the people I know, the number taking sedatives or seeing a psychologist or psychiatrist has multiplied several times over. — If you walk around Kyiv on a weekday now, what’s changed since the summer? What’s the first thing you notice? — There’s a lot more destruction. Kyiv has 1,200 high-rise buildings , and I think about a third of them have been damaged over these four and a half years. Not always anything hugely dramatic, but at least a window blown out here or there. There are fewer people in the city, though you might not notice it. The thing about Kyiv is that as some people leave, new people arrive — from Sumy or other cities [near the front lines]. There aren’t any official figures yet, but I’ve noticed it’s easier to park and fewer people are going to cafés and restaurants. You see fewer people on the streets, too, though that may be because so many are being switched to remote work. And another thing you notice is that people are much more on edge. — More and more people are working remotely? — Yes, wherever that’s possible. Universities have been switching to remote learning on a fairly large scale. Schools haven’t been able to resume regular in-person teaching since September 1 — that’s very difficult with so many hours of air raid alerts every day. — Which parts of the city are suffering the most from the attacks? — Right now, all districts are suffering about equally. For example, Russia has recently been specifically targeting Kyiv’s gas stations. Literally any gas station could become a target, and you could happen to be nearby — stuck in traffic, for instance. Jet-powered drones can reach Kyiv from Russia’s Bryansk region in half an hour, depending on the model, and can fly around the entire city in three or four minutes. In that situation, there’s nothing you can do. Russia has also been attacking Ukrainian data centers recently. Take the strike on the National Academy of Sciences [on September 28]: One of the offices of Ukrtelecom, a Ukrainian internet provider, is in the building next door . That same day, there was a strike on another Ukrtelecom office, which shares a building with the private clinic Dobrobut. Another strike [on September 25] hit a data center in Shuliavka, in an office building. There were terrible scenes there, too — bodies were literally lying in the street. Russia isn’t holding back — I’m saying that without exaggeration. It’s not necessarily setting out to strike civilian facilities in these particular cases, but this is no longer collateral damage. It’s part of the military strategy. Russia can strike a gas station or a large office complex during the workday. It apparently intends to stick with this tactic. And with everything flying so fast, you don’t even have time to do anything. A Russian missile’s trail in the sky over Kyiv. October 10, 2026 The aftermath of a Russian missile strike at a garage complex in Kyiv. October 7, 2026 Kyiv residents take shelter in the metro. October 10, 2026 The National Academy of Sciences building in Kyiv after an attack. October 5, 2026 — You’ve already said that internet and communications services in general could soon get more expensive in Ukraine. Are people already feeling the effects of attacks on data centers? Has internet service in Kyiv gotten worse? — There are local disruptions, yes. At one point, roughly 100,000 subscribers in Kyiv and the Kyiv region lost internet access . But I still find it hard to understand exactly what this campaign is meant to achieve. The military’s internet infrastructure isn’t entirely independent of these data centers, but they [the Ukrainian armed forces] have their own infrastructure and networks, plus Starlink. These attacks seem more aimed at the civilian economy. Ukraine relies heavily on digital services. How effective are they really? You might find yourself unable to pay for something by card, but there won’t be a total catastrophe. Ukraine may have one of the most decentralized networks of internet providers in Europe, or even the world — there are about a thousand operators in the country. Of course, there are big companies, but overall it’s a very extensive network. ‘ We’ve been through all sorts of things in four and a half years. But never this level of anxiety. Now it’s constant ’ — Are businesses managing to adapt to round-the-clock attacks and the changed conditions? — It varies a lot. I’ve spoken with people running many large restaurants and food-service chains. They all have different views of the future, but they agree that restaurants in shopping malls won’t survive this winter: It’s dangerous to have employees come to work there during an air raid alert, even a yellow-level one . There are reasons to believe Russia will strike shopping malls. So not only restaurants but probably all retail businesses in those malls will close down . And shopping malls are an important part of Ukraine’s economy. Kyiv has Respublika and Blockbuster Mall — they’re among the largest shopping malls in Ukraine and [Eastern] Europe. Business owners — whether they sell clothing, run restaurants, or do something else — are trying to find solutions. But nobody can predict with complete certainty what things will look like in winter, so everyone’s improvising. More generally, businesses are trying to adapt: A red alert means we don’t work; a yellow alert means we try to work somehow, because otherwise you could go crazy. — Can a red alert last for hours? — No, actually. That’s more likely with yellow alerts. This is a deliberate Russian tactic: launching small groups of jet-powered drones one after another. One arrives, gets shot down, then another is launched. It’s all done either to keep a yellow alert going almost indefinitely or to have another yellow alert issued 20 minutes later. A red alert means either a truly massive drone attack or a specific missile threat. — How much have Kyiv residents’ daily routines changed since attacks started happening during working hours? — There is no routine — everyone’s improvising. Meetings are constantly being rescheduled and canceled, but businesses somehow manage to keep working. I’m amazed myself at how the cafés on my street manage to open on time. If you want to get a coffee at a café that opens at 8 a.m., somehow you can. We’ve been through all sorts of things in four and a half years. But never this level of anxiety. Now it’s constant. People see it all happening. Very often, jet-powered Gerans fly right overhead. This will sound surprising, but that’s a good thing, because it means you won’t be directly hit. Most likely. I’ve seen a lot over these years, but when this superfast thing that sounds like a quiet jet aircraft races over your head, it really gets to you. — How has life changed for families with children? — Everything’s become harder for them, because the children are effectively learning remotely all the time. Officially, it’s hybrid or in person, but the reality this school year is distance learning. And this is another area where the internet situation matters. Because if attacks on energy infrastructure intensify, cell service and internet access could go down. But the city has been through that before. — The daily attacks must also have affected hospitals. How are they operating now? — As a rule, surgery doesn’t stop during an alert — it all depends on the specific situation. During a red alert, hospitals try to move anyone they can to a shelter. During a yellow alert, they’re more likely to keep patients where they are, and 80% of Kyiv’s air raid alerts are yellow. Nobody moves intensive care patients anywhere. Ambulances and intensive care units keep working all the time. As for strikes on hospitals, I wouldn’t say hospitals are being deliberately targeted at this point. But honestly, with the current strategy of terror — let’s call it that — we can’t rule out Russia moving on to that. Take the strike on the private clinic Dobrobut: The clinic wasn’t the specific target. Though perhaps Russia didn’t mind it getting hit, either. There could be serious problems with medicines in the future. Some medications could be in short supply: There have been strikes on a facility in Kyiv belonging to Darnytsia, a major pharmaceutical company. This is primarily part of the economic war, but attacks like these show that Russia doesn’t care much about civilian lives. I don’t think that needs explaining anymore in 2026. There’s also collateral damage. When warehouses are attacked, absolutely everyone gets hit — book publishers, manufacturers of all kinds of things. Quite a few warehouses storing medicines have also been destroyed. That doesn’t mean there’ll be a catastrophe, but shortages of certain medicines could develop. You can support Ukrainian civilians facing these difficult conditions through Davayte, a project launched by Meduza, Helpdesk, and TV Rain in February 2024. We collect donations and work with our partners to help Ukrainians repair their homes and recover from injuries caused by Russian attacks, provide shelter for people who have lost their homes, and much more. Please follow this link to find out how to donate quickly and securely. ‘ Shortages and major price increases are almost inevitable ’ — You mentioned that Russia is heavily attacking warehouses in Ukraine. In late August, Agriculture and Food Minister Taras Vysotskyi said that about 90% of the country’s grocery-chain warehouses had been destroyed. Can you see that in the selection of products in stores? — Yes, it’s changing. That’s especially true of perishables, because there are virtually no refrigerated warehouses left in the Kyiv region [because of Russian attacks]. I can’t say we’re facing an across-the-board shortage of fish, meat, or milk. But the selection has shrunk, and exactly what’s missing from stores depends directly on what was damaged two, three, or four days earlier. For example, right now you can barely find cola in Kyiv supermarkets, because the Coca-Cola plant in Brovary was hit very recently. I don’t think there’s a risk of famine. Ukraine’s agricultural sector has enormous capacity, despite all the problems of 2022. But shortages and major price increases are almost inevitable. We can’t yet tell how severe they’ll be. But you’ll certainly be able to get through the winter eating, say, buckwheat. There’s an effort now to reorganize logistics so that more goods go straight from suppliers to supermarkets. But the vehicle fleets that retail chains and suppliers needed and maintained in the 2000s no longer exist. There’s still the option of importing food from the EU. We saw a similar situation in 2022 with gasoline and food. Back then, Russia was destroying Ukraine’s few oil refineries, and now Ukraine depends almost entirely on gasoline from Europe . — In August, Ukrainian media reported that air raid alerts were bringing Kyiv’s transportation system to a standstill . The metro had effectively stopped carrying passengers, and buses and trolleybuses were overcrowded. Kyiv residents were flagging down cars in the street and asking drivers to give them a ride to the other bank. How is public transportation working now? — That was actually one of the reasons for dividing alerts into yellow and red levels. All city-run surface transportation keeps operating during yellow alerts. That’s dangerous, of course, but otherwise the city simply can’t function. Previously, though, large numbers of passengers on buses and trolleybuses would be made to get off at the nearest stop. If you can’t get to a shelter, that’s hardly safe, either. The metro is a little different. Kyiv has three lines, two of which connect the left and right banks. During yellow alerts, one of those stops running, and the other becomes severely overcrowded. — Has planning a route become harder? — I’d strongly recommend avoiding trips from one bank to the other whenever possible. Especially from the left bank to the right. The city center is on the right bank, so large numbers of people travel there for work in the morning and return in the evening. That’s another reason so many people are being switched to remote work. There’s the general safety concern, but also a very specific everyday problem: With constant traffic jams, people can easily be an hour late. There’s no point sitting in traffic. October 7, 2026 October 8, 2026 October 8, 2026 October 7, 2026 A traffic jam on the left bank of the Dnipro in Kyiv. October 2, 2026 — Since the beginning of October, the Russian military has struck bridges over the Dnipro several times, particularly the Northern and Southern bridges . What consequences could those attacks have for the city? — Completely destroying bridges over the Dnipro is virtually impossible — we can see that from many other bridges in Ukraine. Despite continuing attacks and damage, the bridge over the Dniester estuary in Zatoka [in the Odesa region], the bridge over the Dnipro in Zaporizhzhia , and the Antonivskyi Bridge in Kherson are all still standing. Ukrainian forces struck the Antonivskyi Bridge during their counteroffensive in the fall of 2022, when Kherson was still occupied. We’re talking about strategically important bridges, not small structures somewhere on the Siverskyi Donets , which really can be destroyed. Still, if intensive attacks on Kyiv’s bridges continue, serious logistical problems will naturally develop. According to Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry, roughly 600,000 vehicles cross Kyiv’s main bridges every day. The city is now considering setting up pontoon crossings and ferries, but as I understand it, the infrastructure needed for that isn’t ready yet. And it would be hard to replace the Southern Bridge fully that way, for example. It’s particularly important for transportation and logistics: A significant share of freight passing through the capital crosses it , and it also carries a metro line. ‘ A friend of mine says she’s learned to fall asleep in the metro without worrying about what might happen ’ — You regularly see headlines about air raid alerts lasting for hours. According to Ukrainska Pravda, Kyiv had one of its longest air raid alerts on September 28: It lasted more than nine hours. How does the city change during an air attack? — It depends. If you walk around Kyiv during an ordinary attack, when there aren’t explosions right around you — whether you’re downtown or elsewhere — the city won’t look much different from normal. Life doesn’t stop. It’s an ordinary workday: People go about their business, drink coffee, and go places. When there’s a confirmed threat of ballistic missile strikes, things are a little different. You can see people trying either to take cover with two walls between them and the outside or to get to a shelter. Again, it varies from person to person and depends on where you are. What has really changed is that quite a few people, including people I know, are choosing to spend every night in a shelter — in the metro or an underground parking garage, for example. For many, that’s hard mentally, but a friend of mine, for instance, says she’s learned to fall asleep without worrying about what might happen. Signs of a massive combined strike — an attack involving cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, and drones — usually appear several hours [before the strike itself]. You can tell whether an attack is coming from the movements of strategic bombers inside Russia. At times like that, Kyiv’s metro is packed. The record for the number of people spending the night in the metro has been broken many times. The current record is 56,000 . Realistically, that’s the maximum the metro can accommodate. Experts give higher figures , but after this summer’s combined attacks, you get the impression those are only possible on paper. — Does Kyiv have enough shelters? Are they equipped for attacks lasting hours? — The situation is pretty bad. Kyiv has about 4,500 shelters. It’s hard to say whether that’s a lot or a little. Not all of them are in good condition, and, let’s put it this way, not all of them are actually accessible . During a jet-powered drone attack, conventional shelters — the metro, basements in schools and government buildings, and so on — aren’t all that helpful. They’re important, but Kyiv has almost none of what you see in Kharkiv and Odesa, for example. There, you can see portable concrete shelters on the streets that provide decent protection from drones. Why are there almost none in Kyiv? That’s partly down to domestic politics. I don’t want to get too deep into it, but President Zelensky and Mayor Klitschko have been at odds for a long time. Different authorities block each other’s decisions to some extent. I don’t want to take anyone’s side. But why almost nothing has been done about portable shelters in four years remains an open question. Kyiv’s mayor bears a great deal of responsibility here. — What’s happening in Kyiv’s shelters during these hours-long alerts? — Sometimes in the evenings, people try to get [into the stations] before the metro closes so they can lay out their mattresses and other things. Sometimes there’s a fight for spots. Apart from these rather comical situations, I don’t think the atmosphere is that bad. It probably doesn’t compare anymore with the start of the war, when people held impromptu concerts in the stations. But even though everyone’s on edge, you can still feel people supporting each other. They share coffee and sandwiches, get to know each other, and so on. Several times, I’ve gone down into the metro specifically as a journalist, to see how it all works and how people behave. And you really can still see some of that unity. — In September, the Kyiv Post reported that Kyiv residents were increasingly ignoring air raid warnings. What do you think about that? — You have to understand that it’s impossible to respond to every air raid alert for four and a half years. At some point, you could just go crazy. During yellow alerts, you could theoretically spend 18 hours in a shelter, but, as you can imagine, almost nobody does that. But at night, when the chance of a ballistic missile strike is fairly high, people do go to shelters. I’d say that since May 2026, there’s actually been a noticeable increase in the number of Kyiv residents who don’t ignore air raid alerts. ‘ People who wanted to prepare for winter have mostly been ready for a long time ’ — You’ve already mentioned attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Last year, some districts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks at a time, and temperatures often dropped below minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit). What’s the outlook for this winter? — It’s obvious there’ll be problems with energy supplies. Russia is trying to cut Kyiv off from the country’s power grid by striking both thermal power plants and power lines . Frequent repeat attacks make it harder to repair the damage. Kyiv could end up spending a week or two either with no electricity at all or with power for just a few hours a day. Hospitals, public and private, have long been ready for this. They largely prepared during the first winter of the war: They have generators and fuel reserves, so things are more or less okay on that front. Air defense is also in worse shape now, for the reasons I mentioned at the beginning. But the weather is expected to be better this winter. Electricity consumption has also fallen. I think this winter will be more or less like the last one. It won’t be good, but I’m not expecting an outright apocalypse. There could be problems with the sewer system — that’s very dangerous, and you can’t really prepare for it. If that happens, it’ll be a new experience for Kyiv residents. — Last year, 600,000 people left Kyiv because of power and heating outages. Should we expect a similar mass exodus this winter? — First, I want to point out that Klitschko’s figure of 600,000 was pulled out of thin air. People did leave, but there wasn’t a noticeable exodus. This winter will probably be different, since a whole range of factors will come into play. Obviously, for people who have relatives [in other cities] or a house in some village where they can at least heat with firewood, that’s an option. But many people’s ability to travel is limited — primarily, I’m talking about military mobilization. There are checkpoints outside Kyiv, and if your paperwork isn’t all in order, you won’t get very far by car. So some people effectively won’t be able to leave Kyiv. And their girlfriends, wives, and children often stay with them. And as I’ve already said, prices have risen so much that many people can’t afford to rent an apartment somewhere in western Ukraine. — Can those who stay in the city prepare for winter? — There’s nothing new here. Obviously, you can’t put a gasoline generator on the balcony of an apartment building, because your whole apartment could burn down. But people generally already have their power banks, EcoFlow portable power stations , and all that equipment ready. I’m not saying everyone does, because there are people who don’t put much effort into it and just take things as they come. But people who wanted to prepare for winter have mostly been ready for a long time. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter . Interview by Kira Kiseleva

title: Dubai plans new underground transport network
body: Plans have been unveiled for an underground transport network in Dubai. The proposed integrated underground system is part of wider efforts to reshape mobility above and below ground, said Mattar Al Tayer, director general of Dubai’s Roads and Transport Authority. At the Mohammed bin Rashid Leadership Forum on Tuesday, Mr Al Tayer said an RTA team was examining the proposed network, which could form part of a broader transformation of the city’s transport infrastructure. He described a future in which mobility extends beyond conventional roads and public transport to encompass three dimensions: the ground, the sky and underground. The proposal aims to create a more integrated and innovative transport system, while freeing up surface space for wider green areas, pedestrian movement and social interaction. “Through this transformation, we are redefining how space is used, opening up new opportunities for investment and prosperity, while enabling mobility that is more efficient and sustainable,” Mr Al Tayer said. A video included with Mr Al Tayer's presentation depicted a Dubai Metro Station on the ground, before panning out and showing tunnels with buses travelling on a road network underneath the station, while drones fly overhead. The footage shows metro trains and buses travelling underground past a number of key Dubai locations, including the emirate's port network. Mr Al Tayer said Dubai records more than 11 million journeys on its roads each day, equal to more than 7,000 a minute. More than six million people move around the city during daylight hours, a figure he said is expected to double by 2040. He said the emirate’s approach to transport planning was shaped by a principle instilled by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai: rather than wait for the future, Dubai should create it. The RTA also has a goal for one in every four journeys in Dubai to be autonomous by 2030. Driverless taxis have travelled more than four million kilometres in the past year, Mr Al Tayer said. Dubai is moving towards commercial urban air mobility, with the opening of its first air-taxi station planned for this year. He said the emirate’s infrastructure investments had delivered savings exceeding Dh319 billion ($86.8 billion) and added Dh156 billion to its economy. Going underground Tuesday's announcement was the latest in a line of recently unveiled transport projects focusing on the city's underground. Earlier this year, The National reported how construction was under way on the Dubai Loop , a high-speed underground transport network led by the government in partnership with Elon Musk's Boring Company, aimed at cutting congestion in the city. The RTA said in February that the first phase of the underground project would cost Dh565 million and connect DIFC with Dubai Mall as using autonomous Tesla cars. The first four stations are to be in Burj Khalifa, DIFC 2, Zabeel Dubai Mall Parking and ICD Brookfield Place. The network will eventually cover 22km and consist of 19 stations. The final cost is estimated at about Dh2 billion. The emirate's transport chief is exploring options to meet the demand created by Dubai's increasing population, which had crossed 4.5 million by the end of last year. The emirate's population reached 4.58 million, representing an increase of 7.5 per cent year-on-year, government statistics revealed. Last month, The National reported how the Boring Company was planning to build 150km of tunnels in the Emirates after it raised $3 billion in a funding round, led by the UAE. This was followed by last week's announcement that Elon Musk's firm had signed an agreement to explore underground transport, utility tunnels and related infrastructure opportunities in Abu Dhabi .

title: The need for military museums explained
body:
With over 10 years of formal research into South African military history, Vaal University of Technology academic Dewald Venter is adamant the country’s military museums preserve more than just obsolete aircraft, armoured vehicles, uniforms and medals.
With the country’s second military heritage symposium set down for month-end at Cape Town’s Castle of Good Hope under the leadership of the Department of Defence (DoD) Logistics Division, headed by Vice Admiral David Mkhonto, an exclusive scene set for DefenceWeb by Professor Venter shows SA National Defence Force (SANDF) and other military museums are more than repositories for old machines.
There are three SANDF museums – the SA Air Force (SAAF) Museum headquartered at the Mobile Deployment Wing in Centurion with branches in Cape Town at Air Force Base (AFB) Ysterplaat and Air Force Station Port Elizabeth; the Armour Museum in Tempe, Bloemfontein, and the SA Naval Museum at Naval Base (NB) Simon’s Town. Others include the Ditsong National Museum of Military History in Johannesburg as the best known while the Springs Military Museum on Gauteng’s East Rand is becoming a must-see for aficionados.
At the outset Venter has it military museums preserve the physical evidence of the country’s defence history, the technical knowledge associated with it and the personal memories of the men and women who served. This, according to him, is important when taking into account military equipment is not generally considered as heritage while in service/active use. He refers to the SAAF Museum, established in 1973, which lost aircraft of historical significance because they were disposed of or sold as scrap. “By the time it became apparent their value as heritage items was important, they were already lost.”
What is widely known as the “Swartkop museum” in line with the oldest – and still operational SAAF base housing 17 Squadron – shows what can be achieved by “careful preservation”.
“As South Africa’s largest military aviation museum, it houses aircraft, missiles, uniforms, logbooks, photographs, technical documents and a considerable research library. Even more important is the work carried out over many generations by museum staff, technicians, volunteers and enthusiasts who realised preserving an aircraft involves more than simply keeping the airframe.
“In the case of aircraft restored to flying condition, the experience takes on even greater significance, since an aircraft in flight can convey sound, movement and technology in ways a static display cannot reproduce,” Venter said.
Going some 1 500 km south to the SA Navy (SAN) fleet home base Simon’s Town as well as the SA Naval Museum, Venter notes it, under Officer in Charge and Curator, Commander Leon Steyn, displays SAN history by means of exhibits on submarines, diving, weapons, hydrography, training and personnel who served. “That it is situated in Simon’s Town is integral to the museum’s story; Simon’s Town is not just the site of the museum, as the dockyard and the surrounding naval area provide important historical context for the collection” added to by its location in the historic combined mast house and sail loft built by the Royal Navy in 1815.
More value comes in the preserved Daphne Class submarine – SAS Assegaai (S99) previously SAS Johanna van der Merwe. Venter said the challenge of extensive engineering work, financial backing and co-operation was shouldered by the SA Naval Heritage Trust to move the 58 metre, 700 ton submarine to its Cole Point display site.
In Bloemfontein’s Tempe the SA Armour Museum is also a specialist one. As its name implies its collection of vehicles show the evolution of South African armour. On display are, among others, the locally built reconnaissance Eland car, the Centurion tank and its successor, the Olifant, as well as Rooikat and others including Ratel, the world’s first wheeled infantry fighting vehicle (IFV). Additionally, the Armour Museum has a number of foreign military vehicles – used for comparison and training – in its collection. “They are not just impressive pieces of machinery,” Venter said adding “they serve as tangible evidence of changes in military policy, operational needs, local engineering and the growth of South Africa’s defence industry”.
At national level he points to the National Museum of Military History, on the northern side of the Johannesburg Zoo as linking the specialised histories of the SANDF museums.
The War Museum, as it is popularly known, started as preservation point for South Africa’s wartime records and memorabilia during World War II and now features in its collection weapons, vehicles, aircraft, uniforms, medals, documents and photographs. It, Venter said, remains a meeting place for military history and veterans’ organisations.
The biggest danger he sees confronting military museums is not in objects rusting away – an artefact can survive even if the knowledge needed to interpret it is lost. “Often, veterans, aircrew, sailors, soldiers, engineers and technicians have information which has never been included in official manuals or archives and it is their memories that explain how the equipment was used, modified and experienced. It is just as important to record these memories as it is to restore a vehicle or aircraft”.
“Military museums should also attract those with no personal ties to the armed forces; younger people nowadays encounter the Border War, national service, earlier conflicts and Cold War defence technology only as part of their history, not as direct personal experiences. It is possible to eliminate this gap without turning museums into places of entertainment by using effective interpretation alongside digital media, oral histories and interactive exhibits,” he said adding “the museums’ objective is not to glorify conflict but to preserve and explain it”.
“South Africa possesses a remarkable network of military heritage sites and the current task is to preserve and connect them as well improve accessibility. The museums named should not be regarded as separate collections of old military equipment; rather, together with other museums, memorials, battlefields and private collections, they form part of the country’s historical resources and represent a potentially more attractive option for military heritage tourism.
“Once an aircraft has been scrapped, a vehicle consigned to rust, or a veteran’s memories fall silent that history is lost. Military museums stand against that loss, preserving the machines, memories and meaning before they disappear,” is his over-arching input on the necessity of keeping military museums alive.
The second military heritage symposium takes place on 27/28 October at the Castle of Good Hope, itself both a military and cultural heritage site.

title: ‘My mum is my fire’: UAE Olympic sprinter Maryam Al Farsi’s mission to give back
body: On the mirror in Maryam Al Farsi’s bathroom are coloured Post-it notes carrying the promises she makes herself every morning. “I will provide for my mum. I am strong. I will do this.” On the days she doubts herself, she reads them, walks out of her room and sees her mother working on her laptop, a reminder of why she must continue pursuing her dreams. Al Farsi is now 18, but two years ago in Paris, at just 16, she became the first Emirati sprinter to compete at the Olympic Games . One would presume her pursuit is for herself, but it’s not. “It’s my lifelong mission to provide for my family,” she told The National . Al Farsi was a speaker at Middlesex University Dubai’s Women in Sport series, launched through its London Sport Institute. The series brought together Emirati women to speak about identity, heritage and the next generation. And while she hopes to pave the way for the younger generation, her main purpose in life is to provide for the women who made her. The women behind the woman Her inspirations are her mother, Leila, and Leila’s twin sister, Elham. “They’re both like my mothers. They are the strongest pillars in my life and they are my why. They’re the reason I chose track in the first place. They’re the reason why I didn’t give up,” she said. Then Maryam catches herself. “Actually, I did give up.” At around age 14, the pressure she piled on herself became too much, and Al Farsi walked away from athletics for almost a year. She kept much of what she was feeling to herself, but Leila and Elham sensed it anyway. “My mum said, 'Just give it one more try ... just for me.' And I was like, ‘Only because it’s you.' And that was the best decision I made because if I didn’t do that, I wouldn’t have gone to the Paris Olympics.” View this post on Instagram Al Farsi’s parents are divorced. Her father is Emirati and her mother is Iranian. Leila raised Maryam and her brother as a single mother, with her twin sister, Elham, and the rest of the family close beside her. “She has six sisters and they’re all so amazing. It’s like basically a family full of women, which I love, a house full of women,” Al Farsi said. 'My mum is my fire' Her appreciation and gratitude to her mum and her aunt are so profound they almost lendthemselves to guilt. She watched as her mother toiled and laboured to ensure Maryam could make her Olympic dreams come true. Leila paid for school, training, physiotherapy and everyday costs that came with raising two children. “She financed my whole life; no one else was helping. Her and my aunties were the only people there.” I don't want her to ever worry about money. I never want her to worry about her job. I want to retire her. When I say her, I mean both of them, like the twins – one person. I just want to make them happy. Maryam Al Farsi She recalls one memory that left her in tears after she dropped her mum off at work one day. “I just started sobbing after, and I was like, 'I want to provide for my mum. I don’t want her to work a nine-to-five. I want to pay for her house, I want to pay for her bills.' “I don't want her to ever worry about money. I never want her to worry about her job. I want to retire her. When I say her, I mean both of them, like the twins – one person. I just want to make them happy,” Al Farsi explains tearfully. She admires her mother’s character and her disinterest in all things material. “She doesn’t care about money. My mum does not care. She cares about health, she cares about happiness, about love.” What the mother sacrificed, the daughter wants to repay. Leila fought for her daughter’s right to compete when others questioned whether she should continue pursuing sport. “My mum is my fire.” Maryam continues, “My whole essay for university was that my mum was a fire in my life. Because she said no to someone. Because they didn't want me to compete in sport and she said no, she is competing and the second I saw her say that it felt like because she was able to do that, I'm able to do anything.” Success on and off track Success always comes at a cost, and Al Farsi remembers all the weekends and birthday parties she had to miss. “I lost a lot of friends,” she added. Education remains a priority. Al Farsi put athletics “a little to the side” while completing A-levels in economics, business and maths. “I love track, and I really want a future in it. But I also need to prioritise my education. And for my mum, it's education, education, education. But thank God I graduated with a great grade.” Attending Harvard Business School is the ultimate goal. “I really want that picture in front of the banner of me posing in front of Harvard Business School.” Al Farsi is also an aspiring entrepreneur. She has launched a company that focuses on parent engagement for schools and aims to bring all the information needed into one place. The idea was inspired by watching her mother’s struggles with her own children’s education. Mo Farah and Maryam Al Farsi at RunYas - in pictures “I saw my mum struggling with trying to even paint a picture for me and my brother’s education. Even though she has so much information, it’s just fragmented.” Athletics remains part of her future. She admits that she "kind of thought I was fast but I wasn’t naturally fast.” Then her competitive nature came into play. “I need to get better at this. I will die if I don’t become the best.” Al Farsi has her sights set on qualifying for the LA2028 Olympics and competing in as many Diamond League meetings as possible. She’s proud to represent the UAE. “I get to represent such an amazing country and amazing people, so I definitely won’t stop with that.” Advice Dr James Doty, a Stanford neurosurgeon and neuroscientist, says manifestation is most effective when it’s driven by compassion and the wish to improve other people’s lives. Al Farsi's instinct to look after people extends beyond just her own family. “I just love it, seeing the happiness in someone else’s eyes, just taking the pressure off of them. I’ll do it, even if that puts pressure on me.” Her advice to young girls is to find their niche, their fire that will spur them to succeed. “It could be something like I want to prove this person wrong, or I want to make this person happy, and if I can make this person happy, that will make me happy. That's really it.” Asked to choose among another Olympic opportunity, attending Harvard or owning a successful company, Maryam doesn’t hesitate. “I would choose whichever provides for my family.”

title: Reuters: Witkoff and Kushner told Kyiv that a diesel deal with Russia would help bring the Kremlin back to the negotiating table
body: U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner tried to convince the Ukrainian delegation at a meeting in Miami that a diesel deal with Russia could help bring the Kremlin back to the negotiating table, three sources told Reuters. At the meeting, Kushner also relayed Donald Trump’s demand that Kyiv stop striking Russian oil refineries. “The idea was that the US could go back to Russia and say ‘See, the Ukrainians stopped striking and we gave you ​this deal. Now it’s your turn to do something,” one of the sources said. Witkoff and Kushner told Ukrainian representatives at the meeting that Vladimir Putin is not willing to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, two sources told Reuters. A source close to the Kremlin said Putin will return to the negotiating table only once he “gets ⁠the remaining 11% of Donbas, which he can present domestically as victory.” Part of the meeting between Witkoff, Kushner, and the Ukrainian delegation focused on Ukraine’s reconstruction funds and the need for Kyiv to formally draft plans for attracting investment in the country. Ukrainian representatives “were skeptical” of the U.S. approach, the sources said. The Ukrainian side left the meeting without formally agreeing to anything but signaled it was prepared to accept an energy truce if Russia observed it as well. On October 9, Trump spoke by phone with Putin and afterward announced a “diesel deal” under which Russia would supply diesel fuel to American and global markets. Ukrainian representatives met with Witkoff and Kushner in Miami that same day. The talks had been scheduled to run October 9 and 10 but ended after just one day. title: Ukraine’s Air Force confirms lack of timely data on missile launches
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Ukraine’s Air Force has confirmed that the country’s air defenses failed to get timely data on Russian ballistic missile launches amid speculation of the suspension of US intelligence sharing.
"Radar systems detected ballistic targets already during an attack on Kiev. There was no data on launches from the enemy’s territory. The causes are being established," Ukraine’s Air Force said on its Telegram channel.
In turn, the so-called Center for Countering Disinformation under the Ukrainian National Security and Defense Council also reported on its Telegram channel that it was specifying information on the causes of a failure in receiving intelligence data on Russian ballistic missile launches amid various versions on this score in the Internet.
"In particular, it could be presumed that there has been a halt to intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Official information is being specified so far," the Center reported.
On the evening of October 12, Ukrainian media reported that explosions rocked Kiev before an air raid siren went off. Verkhovna Rada lawmaker Galina Yanchenko said earlier that the Ukrainian authorities would be unable to promptly receive data on Russian ballistic missile launches, if the United States stopped sharing intelligence with Kiev.
The Financial Times reported, citing unnamed European sources that the US administration was threatening to block arms for Ukraine and cut off intelligence sharing with Kiev. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian media outlet Strana reported that there was no official information that the United States could have halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

title: Iran’s control over Hormuz represents enormous natl. wealth
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – The secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) has said that the country’s control over the Strait of Hormuz represents the enormous national wealth.
Speaking in an interview late on Monday, Major General Mohsen Rezaei stated that Iran’s interests go far beyond closing the strait and collecting transit fees, emphasizing, “Its real value lies in our ability to ensure security.”
Earlier, General Rezaei had described Washington's response to Iran's seven conditions as insufficient, saying the United States has accepted some of the conditions but has yet to clarify others.
In a post on social media, Rezaei stressed that Iran's diplomatic approach has changed and that the country would not return to its previous position.
In a separate post, Rezaei had said that US President Donald Trump is resorting to smuggling after the failure of the US fleet to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Ukraine’s largest steelworks begins cold shutdown after extensive damage from Russian strikes, saying safe operation is impossible while war continues
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih has begun the process of placing its plant in cold shutdown following four Russian missile attacks, the company said on 10 October. The attacks killed six workers, injured more than 18 others, and forced the suspension of primary steel production. ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih is Ukraine’s largest steelworks, so its shutdown adds to the pressure on an industry already hit by Russian attacks and disrupted exports. ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo said the company’s priority was to protect workers and industrial assets. He said the ArcelorMittal Group would remain in Ukraine, but that its assessment was that safe operation was impossible while the war continued. Workers and the city As of July, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and its subsidiaries employed about 17,000 people, local outlet Pershyi Kryvorizkyi reported . On 29 September, the outlet reported that the company had not said how many workers could lose their jobs and was assessing its staffing needs after production stopped. It also said municipal water and heating utilities had about 1,000 vacancies and had been instructed to help ArcelorMittal workers find jobs. The outlet noted that it was unclear whether the vacancies were new and that the announcement did not specify the roles or salaries. In late September, Kryvyi Rih defense council head Oleksandr Vilkul wrote on Telegram that the city would cut spending and stop a number of projects as tax revenues fell. He attributed the pressure to Russian attacks and the inability to export through seaports, and said several major industrial facilities were idle, including ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and three mining and ore-processing plants. September steel output down 4.7-fold Ukraine’s steel production fell 4.7-fold year on year in September, to 131,000 tons, the steelmakers’ association Ukrmetalurhprom said, NV reported . Metinvest chief operating officer Oleksandr Myronenko told Forbes Ukraine on 15 September that the group would declare force majeure on some contracts after Zaporizhstal and Kametstal halted operations. An expected $1 billion impairment The ArcelorMittal Group said on 25 September that it expected to record a non-cash impairment of about $1 billion, mostly related to property, plant, and equipment. It also said it had provided more than $700 million in financial support to its Ukrainian business. Read also Ukraine’s steel output fell 57% and may hit zero next month.
