title: IMF sticks to 3.5% Ukraine growth in 2027 after 1% in 2026
body:
The International Monetary Fund has kept its estimate of Ukraine's real gross domestic product growth at 1% for 2026, compared with 1.8% last year, in its October World Economic Outlook, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reported from the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
The forecast for growth to accelerate to 3.5% next year is also unchanged, as is the estimate of 3.6% growth in 2031, according to the report published on Tuesday morning.
In June, the IMF cut its 2026 growth forecast for Ukraine to 1-1.6%, compared with 2% in the April World Economic Outlook and 1.8-2.5% when the new four-year Extended Fund Facility program was approved in late February.
For next year, the fund forecast acceleration of GDP growth to 3.5% during the second review of the program in June-July, although most other analysts have cut their forecasts since then.
The IMF also confirmed its July forecast for the other main indicators. It expects inflation to rise from 8.0% last year to 10.5% this year and return to 8.0% next year, and the current account deficit to narrow from 16% of GDP last year to 11% of GDP this year and 4.7% next year.
The fund expects unemployment to fall to 10.2% this year from 11.6% last year and to rise again to 11.3% next year.
The World Bank cut its forecast for Ukraine's 2027 economic growth last week from 4% to 1.5%, but kept its estimate of 1.2% growth this year. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development cut its forecast for Ukraine's GDP growth in late September to 1.5% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027.
Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said in late September that he is considering cutting the 2027 GDP growth forecast by 0.3-0.5 percentage points from the already built-in pessimistic plan, from 1.3% to 0.8-1%, and the 2026 forecast to 0.5% from the current 1.6%.
The National Bank of Ukraine lowered its estimate of real GDP growth this year to 1.1-1.2%, compared with 1.8% in late July.
Leading Ukrainian investment company Dragon Capital also cut its macro forecast significantly last week. It now expects GDP to fall 0.5% this year and 1.0% next year. Before the escalation of the war in July, it estimated possible growth of 1.5% this year and 0.5% next year.

title: Opinion| South Sudan needs bold and fearless leadership: The Kalisto Lado example
body: South Sudan needs leaders who are not afraid to stand up for what is right, confront injustice and speak for ordinary citizens, even when doing so comes at a personal cost. After years of insecurity, corruption, land-grabbing, weak institutions and unfulfilled promises, the country urgently needs a style of leadership built on courage, conviction and a genuine commitment to public service. Kalisto Lado Faustino Nyigilo, the caretaker commissioner of Juba County, embodies these qualities. His public life reflects a determination to confront difficult issues, challenge practices that undermine people’s livelihoods, and put the concerns of ordinary citizens at the centre of public debate. At a time when South Sudan desperately needs courageous leadership, Kalisto stands out as an example of a leader willing to speak boldly and act decisively in the public interest. What distinguishes bold leadership is the courage to confront problems that others would rather avoid. It means speaking openly about injustice, standing firm in the face of intimidation, and refusing to remain silent when people’s rights and livelihoods are threatened. For South Sudan, where land disputes, corruption and insecurity continue to affect communities, such leadership is not simply desirable; it is essential. Kalisto’s public career demonstrates the importance of confronting difficult questions directly and placing the interests of citizens at the heart of governance. Kalisto’s experience in public administration began well before his current appointment. In March 2021, he became Mayor of Juba, taking responsibility for a capital city facing serious challenges in urban planning, sanitation, infrastructure and the management of public spaces. During his approximately eight-month tenure, his administration pursued efforts to reorganise the city, improve its appearance and address longstanding urban management problems. His time as mayor attracted considerable public attention, and his dismissal in November 2021 prompted petitions and calls from sections of the community for his reinstatement. These events reflected the strong public interest surrounding his leadership and his approach to the challenges facing the capital. For Kalisto, public service has also meant being willing to address uncomfortable truths. One of the most significant episodes in his public life came in March 2024, when he was reportedly arrested after delivering a speech condemning land-grabbing practices and urging Equatorians to speak out against injustice. Security personnel reportedly took him from his home on 30 March. His family reported his arrest, while police indicated that he might have been in the custody of the National Security Service. The circumstances of his detention raised serious concerns about the treatment of people who speak publicly about land-related injustice. His detention became a matter of concern for human rights organisations and those committed to the rule of law. Amnesty International called on the authorities to disclose his whereabouts and the reasons for his detention, and to release him unless a lawful basis for continued detention could be demonstrated. Human Rights Watch also raised concerns about his disappearance and the need for judicial safeguards. In August 2024, Vice President James Wani Igga publicly acknowledged that the government was holding Kalisto and said he faced criminal charges. Kalisto was released on 6 September 2024, after approximately five months in detention. Human Rights Watch subsequently reported that he had been held incommunicado and released without being presented in court. This episode forms an important part of Kalisto’s public story because it highlights the personal cost that can accompany speaking out on issues affecting the public interest. His experience brought renewed attention to land governance, the protection of citizens’ rights, and the importance of due process. It also underscored a principle that South Sudan must embrace: people who raise concerns about injustice deserve lawful treatment, and public institutions must be accountable to the citizens they serve. Kalisto’s willingness to speak about land-related grievances has kept these concerns firmly within the national conversation. Land is among the most sensitive and consequential issues facing South Sudanese communities. It is not merely a source of economic value; it is connected to identity, family heritage, agriculture, housing, and the security of future generations. When land is taken unlawfully, or disputes are handled unfairly, families can lose their livelihoods, communities can become divided, and public confidence in institutions can erode. Addressing these challenges requires leaders who are prepared to speak openly, insist on fair procedures and ensure that the rights of ordinary citizens are not overshadowed by the influence of powerful individuals. Kalisto’s public stance on land-related injustice reflects the importance of placing these concerns at the centre of governance. His return to public administration as Caretaker Commissioner of Juba County, following his swearing-in on 2 October 2026, offers an important opportunity to bring this bold leadership approach directly to the communities he serves. On 5 October, he visited the busy Kuburi Haboba access road in Gudele West and engaged business people on road access, organization, cleanliness and hygiene. He has also emphasized unity, peaceful coexistence and development, pledged to visit communities across the county, and promised to address the destruction of farmers’ crops by cattle. These priorities speak directly to the daily realities of ordinary people. For a farmer, the destruction of crops can mean losing months of hard work and the food or income needed to support a family. For a small business owner, poor road access and an unclean trading environment can make it harder to earn a living. For families living in insecure neighbourhoods, peaceful coexistence and effective local administration are essential to their sense of safety. Leadership becomes meaningful when it recognises these struggles and responds with practical action. Kalisto’s focus on community engagement, agricultural protection, sanitation and local development reflects an understanding that government must be felt in people’s everyday lives. His commitment to addressing corruption and the misuse of public resources is equally important. Corruption deprives communities of services, weakens public institutions and undermines citizens’ confidence in government. A bold approach to governance means confronting the practices that divert public resources away from their intended purpose and ensuring that public money serves the common good. Transparent revenue collection, accountable financial management, fair procurement, and responsible administration are essential to ensuring that resources reach the communities that need them. South Sudan needs leaders prepared to place public interest above personal or political advantage, and Kalisto’s stated commitment to tackling corruption speaks to that national need. Kalisto has also proposed using revenue from locally available natural resources, including gold, sand and murram, to support development across Juba County’s payams and bomas. The proposal reflects an ambition to connect local resources with the needs of local communities. Properly managed, such resources could contribute to road construction, sanitation, agricultural support, and other essential services. For communities that have long waited for improvements in their living conditions, the prospect of locally generated revenue supporting local development is significant. Transparent management and fair distribution would help ensure that the benefits reach residents across the county and contribute to lasting improvements in their lives. The challenges facing Juba County are considerable, but they are also closely connected to the broader question of leadership in South Sudan. Insecurity, communal tensions, land disputes and cattle-related destruction of crops require firm, fair and accessible administration. These problems cannot be resolved by government declarations alone. They require leaders who listen to residents, engage communities, respond to grievances and work with relevant authorities to find lasting solutions. Kalisto’s pledge to visit communities across the county creates an opportunity to bring government closer to the people and ensure that the concerns of residents beyond the county headquarters receive attention. His caretaker position also provides an opportunity to demonstrate that bold leadership and fairness can go hand in hand. Every community deserves equal protection under the law, and every resident should be able to approach public institutions with confidence that their concerns will be heard. Political differences, social background, or personal influence should not determine who receives government attention. A strong public administrator serves the entire community, protects public resources, and applies the law fairly. These principles are essential to building trust between citizens and the institutions responsible for their welfare. Kalisto’s leadership also speaks to a wider need in South Sudanese politics: the need to move beyond leadership defined by titles and promises towards leadership demonstrated through courage, service and action. Citizens want leaders who can speak honestly about difficult problems, defend their interests and respond to their concerns. They want roads that are accessible, markets that are clean, farms that are protected, neighbourhoods that are safe and public resources that support development. These are not unreasonable demands. They are the basic expectations of people who deserve a government that works for them. No single commissioner can resolve every challenge facing South Sudan. Many problems require cooperation among county, state, and national authorities, as well as the active participation of communities. Yet strong local leadership can make a meaningful difference by showing citizens that public administration can be responsive, accessible and committed to results. Kalisto’s experience as Mayor of Juba, his public stance on land-related injustice, and his return to local administration place him in a position to contribute to that effort. His leadership offers an example of why courage and conviction matter when public institutions must confront longstanding problems. South Sudan stands at a critical point in its search for better governance. The country needs leaders who are bold enough to confront corruption, fearless enough to speak against injustice, determined enough to protect ordinary citizens and committed enough to turn public promises into meaningful improvements. Kalisto Lado represents this kind of leadership. His public journey reflects the importance of standing firm on difficult issues and keeping the concerns of ordinary people at the centre of public life. Ultimately, the importance of Kalisto’s leadership lies in the example it offers to a country hungry for courage, accountability and genuine public service. His challenge as Caretaker Commissioner is to bring that boldness to bear on the everyday problems affecting Juba County: protecting farmers, improving local infrastructure, strengthening community safety, promoting peaceful coexistence and ensuring that public resources contribute to development. These are the issues through which leadership becomes real in the lives of citizens. South Sudan does not need leaders who retreat when problems become difficult. It needs leaders who confront those problems with courage, conviction, and a clear sense of responsibility to the people. Kalisto Lado’s bold and fearless leadership offers a compelling example of the qualities the country needs. At its best, such leadership gives ordinary citizens a voice, brings neglected problems into the open, and reminds those in public office that their ultimate responsibility is to serve the people. South Sudan needs more of that courage, more of that determination, and more leaders willing to put the public interest first. title: Abu Dhabi court sentences teacher to two years in prison for assaulting pupils
body: A male teacher has been sentenced to two years in prison for assaulting four pupils, the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department said on Tuesday. He was found to have assaulted the four pupils in a classroom at a private school in Abu Dhabi, according to a statement by the ADJD on Tuesday. The assault resulted in the pupils suffering injuries that left them unable to attend school. The teacher admitted the charges during the investigation and in court, the ADJD added. He admitted to “assaulting the students, claiming he did so to prevent them from causing chaos and disruption during the lesson, and in an attempt to discipline their behaviour”. CCTV footage corroborated the confession, capturing the violence inflicted on the pupils without justification, the ADJD said. Committing the offence inside a school during lessons meant the teacher was guilty of a breach of public security and order. Protecting public order aims to safeguard the fundamental values of society, ensure the safety of its members and maintain respect for the law – principles that directly apply to the case at hand, the court heard. The teacher will be deported after serving his sentence and will have to cover all the legal costs of the case, Abu Dhabi Criminal Court ruled. The court was told the defendant’s behaviour represented a blatant breach of existing laws and regulations, underlining the necessity of firm legal enforcement to protect public safety, uphold individual rights and deter violations that subject people to harm or undermine their security and stability.

title: Russian stock indices decline as main trading session opens on Moscow Exchange
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The Russian stock market opened lower on Tuesday during the main trading session, according to Moscow Exchange (MOEX) data. The Chinese yuan also weakened against the ruble.
At the opening of the main session, the benchmark MOEX and RTS indices both shed 0.13%, easing to 2,390.78 and 897.51 points, respectively, as of 09:00 a.m. Moscow time. The yuan-ruble exchange rate dipped by 0.6 kopecks from the previous close to trade at 12.5065 rubles.
By 09:15 a.m. Moscow time, the decline in the MOEX index pared losses to 2,393 points (-0.03%), while the RTS index stood at 898.34 points (-0.03%). Meanwhile, the yuan recovered slightly but remained down 0.2 kopecks at 12.51 rubles.
Earlier, at the start of the early morning session, the MOEX index had dropped by 0.52% to 2,381.49 points, according to trading data as of 07:00 Moscow time.

title: More than 400 Ukrainian drones flew toward Moscow, school building damaged in Russia’s Kaluga region
body: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 417 Ukrainian drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight on October 13. Most of the drones were “neutralized by air defense forces on distant approaches,” he said. Another 65 drones were destroyed as they approached Moscow. No casualties from the drone attack have been reported. The Russian state news agency TASS reported that the attempted attack on Moscow was one of the largest since the start of the year. Temporary flight restrictions were imposed overnight at three Moscow airports (Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky). Kaluga Governor Vladislav Shapsha said 73 drones were destroyed in the region. The attack damaged a school building, two private homes, and one vehicle in the Mosalsky district. There were no casualties. title: France’s angry youth are demanding a future – not just better schools
body: Last week, on my way through the Latin Quarter, a neighbourhood in Paris, I passed the gates of Lycee Henri-IV. It is one of the most elite schools in France, the kind of place that produces philosophers, scientists and presidents – the equivalent of getting into Harvard or Yale universities, but for high-school students. A cluster of teenagers in hoodies stood outside holding signs. They were very young and very annoyed. Today, near Boulevard Raspail, I came across more students. “If we are old enough for you to use violence against us, we’re old enough for you to listen to us,” said a 17-year-old marching through the leafy district of the French capital. Violence has not reached this wealthy neighbourhood bordering the Jardin du Luxembourg. But students at the Institut Catholique, which Pope Leo XIV visited two weeks ago , are joining in solidarity and resistance against President Emmanuel Macron’s government, calling for change . The protests began on September 21 at Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil, a suburb in the Val-de-Marne, south-east of Paris. Many other schools in the Ile-de-France region quickly joined, followed by Marseille, Lille, Rennes and Strasbourg. As the days pass, the students’ demands have grown. At first, the protests were about the lack of resources in public schools: teacher shortages, classes of 35 or more, leaking buildings and long days that start at 8am and run into the evening. Now the rallying cry is about a generation that feels unheard and is inheriting a dysfunctional world it did not create. I have spent three decades watching young people take to the streets: in Cairo, in Aleppo, in Belgrade, in Ramallah, in Kyiv. Some, like in Belgrade, were successful – the students overthrew Slobodan Milosevic. My first year as a new mother in France, 2005, brought the riots triggered by the electrocution of two teenagers. They later spread across the country’s suburbs, with burning cars and real violence . The deaths of the teenagers were the trigger, but the real causes were unemployment, discrimination and broken relations with the police. The first thing I learnt about the protests in France is that the stated grievance is rarely the whole story. What is happening now is no exception. The French are exceptional at protesting. Their protests are effective, and the protesters know they work. The country has a culture of dissent that goes back to the French Revolution, and taking to the streets is seen as a civic duty rather than a disruption. That legacy runs through May 1968, when a general strike drew in between seven and 10 million workers. It all began with a handful of students at Nanterre, whose early grievances included dormitory rules. The grievances behind this latest movement should embarrass the government. On October 1, according to the Interior Ministry, 1,027 of France’s roughly 3,700 lycees were affected, 222 of them blockaded. Bins burned in Toulouse and Rennes. There was tear gas in Strasbourg and Lille, and a school in Nantes was firebombed. The Justice Minister, Gerald Darmanin, says about 2,000 people have been arrested since the movement began, the majority of them minors. More than 400 schools were closed the following day. The student who lives with me and studies at Institut Catholique just came home disgruntled because protesters were blocking the streets. The government’s response is predictable: condemnation, a crisis meeting, protest bans outside closed schools. Next come the endless TV and radio shows looking for a scapegoat. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ’s office called it a manoeuvre organised by La France Insoumise, the hard-left party. LFI’s Manuel Bompard replied that the government was sliding into conspiracy theory. Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis and France’s answer to New York City’s Zohran Mamdani, put himself between riot police and students and was tear-gassed for it, an amazing moment caught on camera and widely shared this week. Remember that all this is happening in the run-up to a presidential election that fills most of us with dread. Mr Macron, whom I voted for, is on his way out. He is barred from running again next May, because Article 6 of the Constitution limits a president to two consecutive terms. Personally, I like Mr Macron, but I’m in a minority. He is credited with being strong on foreign policy, less so on domestic issues. Meanwhile, the National Rally, the far-right party founded by the late Jean-Marie Le Pen in 1972, is on the rise. With Mr Macron close to the end of his term next year, the RN believes the Elysee is finally within reach. Jordan Bardella , its 31-year-old president, has spent years cultivating young voters even as he faces allegations, which he strongly denies, of anti-Semitic messages from the 2010s. LFI is finding a niche, particularly among the young. It’s no coincidence that the protests came to a head in the same week the government unveiled a budget built on spending cuts and tax rises to bring down France’s deficit. The teenagers did not miss the timing, and neither should we. “Most of all, we’re fed up with the high cost of living,” an 18-year-old political science student told me. She ran through the cost of food, cell phones, metro transport and drinks in a cafe. It’s not Manhattan or London, but salaries in France are lower. I expect the protests to be put down fairly soon, but it will be telling to see who benefits most. Marine Le Pen , daughter of Jean-Marie, blamed LFI for stoking the unrest, and her officials have demanded damage reports and crisis meetings. RN supporters aren’t on the streets, and they don’t need to be. They are content to watch France lose control of its schools and its young. This plays nicely into the party’s education platform, which promises a “big bang of authority”: phone bans, uniforms and sanctions that reach families’ benefits. They are standing back, watching the left fall on its face. It remains to be seen whether the RN will win young supporters once the protests actually end. But the real story here is generational, and it began long before the protests. In 2023, Mr Macron forced through pension reform raising the retirement age from 62 to 64. Millions marched against it, many of them young people who saw that the changes meant they would have to work longer. I remember watching French TV and being amazed how many young people were protesting against pensions . But they saw it as their future being crushed. France’s wealth sits disproportionately with older owners of property and savings. Its debt, and now its austerity, will fall on the young. Whether French teenagers are reading budget tables and spread sheets, or not, they do understand that their classrooms are cold because a radiator has not been fixed for a year. They do understand that their teachers are exhausted and cannot give them the time or attention they need. They do understand that they are being handed a world threatened by war in Eastern Europe, with Russia’s latest hybrid war, a mounting national debt and high unemployment for recent graduates. Mr Macron came to power in 2017 as the young man who would modernise France. It was his youth that attracted so many of us: youth and energy which the older politicians lack. But he is leaving office a middle-aged weary man with teenagers in the streets demanding a better world. At the very least, he has to listen to them before deciding who to blame.

title: Woman kills mother-in-law in Aweil East County
body: A 22-year-old woman has been arrested after stabbing her mother-in-law to death on Sunday morning in Aweil East County in Northern Bahr El Ghazal State, local authorities and witnesses confirmed. Ajou Mawein Yuot, the Director for Gender, Child and Social Welfare in the county, announced that the murder occurred during an argument when the suspect’s mother-in-law, Abuk Mawein, 47, was under the influence of alcohol. “A lady called Adhel Majak Ngor, 22, killed her mother-in-law, Abuk Mawein, 47, in Madhol Payam’s Abu area,” he said. “The deceased, who was under the influence of alcohol, fought the suspected killer for two consecutive days and on the third day, she was killed.” Pual Kuch, Director for Information and Communication in Aweil East County, said the suspect was apprehended by the South Sudan National Police Service (SSNPS) and taken to Wanyjok Central Prison. “The murder happened in a place called Abu Boma under Madhol Payam in Aweil East County, and the accused woman is currently detained at the Wanyjok Central Prison,” he stated. Meanwhile, Peter Diing, Executive Director for Wider Aid and Development Agency (WADA), attributed the case to hardships and poverty. “Such incidents are happening because people have been cultivating their crops, but the drought and long dry spell have limited food production this agricultural season,” he said. “The people are developing stress, and family members fight each other as a result of insufficient food.” According to Diing, insufficient resources have increased stress and domestic violence among family members. The post Woman kills mother-in-law in Aweil East County appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Traffic resumes along Juba-Mundri Road after ambushes
body: Movement of people and vehicles along the Juba-Mundri Road in Western Equatoria State has reportedly returned to normal following the release of civilians who were abducted while travelling along the route. Benson George Papa, Executive Director of Mundri East County, told Radio Tamazuj on Sunday that vehicles and passengers continue to travel in both directions between Mundri and Juba despite lingering security concerns. “As I am speaking now, vehicles are coming from Mundri, and others are travelling from Juba to Mundri,” he stated. “People are moving in both directions.” His remarks come after more than 78 civilians who were abducted along the Juba-Mundri Road on 26 September were released on 1 October 2026 after spending up to four days in captivity. Papa previously said the abductees included men, women and children. Eight people had reportedly been released earlier as efforts continued to secure the freedom of those remaining in captivity. Meanwhile, Isaac Fora, Director General of the Western Equatoria State Ministry of Information and Communication, has urged travelers and residents to remain vigilant despite reports of improved movement along the road. He cautioned that the absence of newly reported incidents did not mean the area was completely safe, noting that armed criminals were still believed to be operating in the bush. “People have to be cautious because you never know,” he cautioned. “There are still armed criminals in the bush, so you cannot guarantee security 100 percent.” Asked whether authorities had received reports of other criminal incidents apart from cases involving people who were reportedly taken into the bush and later released, Fora said he was not aware of additional incidents but acknowledged that some cases might not yet have been reported. A boda-boda rider who preferred anonymity said he travelled from Mundri on Thursday and arrived in Juba on Saturday told this publication that he completed his journey safely without incident. “I was fearing to travel, but thank God I went, and nobody stopped me on the road apart from checkpoints, and I arrived safely in Juba,” he said. The developments suggest that civilian movement along the important transport corridor is continuing, although officials have warned travelers against becoming complacent about security risks. Authorities have urged road users to remain alert, exercise caution while travelling and promptly report suspicious activities to the relevant security agencies. The Juba-Mundri Road is an important route connecting communities in Western Equatoria State with Juba, supporting passenger transport, trade and other daily activities. title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
body:
Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 13.
The number includes 1,390 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,412 tanks, 25,534 armored combat vehicles, 162,418 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,141 artillery systems, 2,211 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,704 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,942 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Russia s UVZ Reports 300 Armoured Vehicle Upgrades Eyes India s T-90 Fleet
body:
Russia’s Uralvagonzavod (UVZ), part of state-owned Rostec, says it has introduced more than 300 modifications to its armoured vehicles since the start of the war in Ukraine, focusing on combat performance, protection, survivability, crew situational awareness and command-and-control capabilities.
Ahead of its 90th anniversary on October 11, the company said military equipment production had increased severalfold. Current production includes the T-72B3M and T-90M Proryv tanks, BMPT tank-support fighting vehicles, and specialised engineering vehicles. UVZ is also developing next-generation tanks and combat vehicles while integrating new technologies into existing models.
UVZ chief executive Alexander Potapov claimed India was interested in modernising its T-90 fleet using lessons from the Ukraine conflict. The company is ready to assist, but formal requests have yet to be received, and government-level decisions are required. India operates substantial fleets of Russian-origin T-72 and T-90 tanks and has licensed production capabilities at Avadi, Chennai. Any upgrade programme would need to align with India’s Make in India policy, domestic manufacturing requirements and technology-transfer priorities.
Potapov highlighted export prospects for the T-90MS, Russia’s export-oriented T-90 variant, an updated version of which UVZ showcased at the IDEX 2025 defence exhibition in Abu Dhabi. “The T-90 of 2022 and the T-90 of 2026 are different machines,” he said, referring to modifications based on operational experience. Despite sanctions and other obstacles to defence cooperation, UVZ is working with Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, to expand exports and develop customers, including across South Asia.
According to Potapov, the Ukraine conflict has accelerated modifications to Russia’s T-72, T-80 and T-90 tank families. UVZ is also developing unmanned combat systems and integrating them with armoured vehicles to improve protection and automate control systems.
Potapov said tanks remain relevant despite growing threats from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), electronic warfare and precision weapons. Future platforms will require enhanced protection, automation and closer integration with drones, potentially serving as drone command centres. Adapting to evolving battlefield threats, he stressed, is an ongoing process.

title: Iran among one of world’s top four powers: Gen. Hassanzadeh
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Emphasizing that Iran is one of the world’s top four powers, the IRGC commander in Greater Tehran says not only were enemy's sinister goals not achieved in recent war, but also Iran stood firm and powerful against aggression.
Speaking in a local ceremony, Brigadier General Hassan Hassanzadeh commemorated the name and memory of martyrs during the eight years of the Sacred Defense and also the recent wars imposed by the United States and Israel against Iran, noting, “If Iranian nation maintains its faith and readiness, the enemy will continue to fail in its calculations.”
Referring to the enemy's complicated and complex plots during the two wars [12-, and 40-day wars] imposed against the country, aimed at toppling the Islamic Establishment and assassination of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei and high-ranking military commanders, destroying missiles, air defenses, nuclear sites, and infrastructures, he maintained, “Relying upon the assistance of the God Almighty, not only did the enemy fail to achieve its sinister objectives, but also Islamic Iran stood firm with authority, and gave a crushing and panful response to the enemy.”
Elsewhere in his remarks, Brigadier General Hassanzadeh pointed to the salient achievements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) during the war, appreciating the vast production of missiles, drones and also the initiatives taken by the combatants of Islam in the battle against the "Great Satan” the United States of America.
He called upon everyone to maintain unity, amity, faith and readiness in the face of enemies.

title: ‘You’re Not Winning This Fight’: Kellogg Says Putin Shows Weakness as War Drags On
body:
Keith Kellogg , former US envoy and general, said Ukraine should determine how it fights Russia, including whether to strike Russian refineries, while dismissing public tensions between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as rhetoric that should not be overinterpreted.
Speaking to Bloomberg Television on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum, Kellogg argued that Ukraine’s military decisions should be left to Kyiv and that Russia should not be allowed to treat its fuel infrastructure as a sanctuary from attack.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We should all need to step back and let Ukraine make determinations of what it’s going to do, how it’s going to attack,” Kellogg said.
He also pushed back against concerns that recent exchanges between Trump and Zelensky could signal a return to the tensions that culminated in their contentious Oval Office meeting in early 2025.
Kellogg described the two presidents as stubborn leaders who speak their minds, adding that differences in language and the nuances of translation could contribute to misunderstandings.
“I think people ought to take a step back and just assume it’s noise level, even from the President of the United States,” he said.
Kellogg said decisions about holding elections in Ukraine should rest with Ukrainians, not Washington or other foreign governments.
He acknowledged that democratic legitimacy was an important concern, noting that Ukraine’s presidential term is five years and that Zelensky has remained in office beyond that period. However, he also pointed out that Ukraine is under martial law, during which national elections are not held.
“It’s up to the Ukrainian people, not the United States, nor is it for anybody else,” Kellogg said.
Kellogg argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin is trying to outlast Ukraine and its international supporters, betting that public fatigue after years of war will eventually weaken their resolve.
He said continued pressure on Moscow was necessary because Russia had not achieved its strategic objectives despite the territory it had seized.
Kellogg also cited estimates of between 1.2 million and 1.5 million Russian military casualties and said Russia was losing around 30,000 troops a month.
To illustrate the scale of Russia’s losses, he compared them with the Soviet Union’s experience in Afghanistan, saying the Soviet military lost around 18,000 people during that war before withdrawing.
Kellogg described Putin’s current approach as a sign of weakness rather than strength and said Western countries should continue supporting Ukraine for as long as necessary.
“We just need to keep pressure on him [Putin] and the constancy of saying, ‘You’re not winning this fight.’ We’re going to be here as long as it takes to do so and keep putting the pressure on him. I think his response right now is a response of weakness, not of strength.”
Kellogg also criticized Putin’s approach to a diesel deal with the US.
“And what he’s trying to say with the diesel deal with the United States – that’s not really a good deal. It’s not really all-encompassing out there, and it shows me his weakness, not his strength,” Kellogg said.
He added that Putin was trying to capitalize on the upcoming US elections and Trump’s presidency:
“He’s trying to capitalize on elections coming up in the United States. He’s trying to capitalize on President Trump right now, and most people see through it.”
Kellogg once again defended Ukraine’s attacks on Russian military targets and fuel infrastructure, rejecting the idea that such facilities should be off-limits.
He argued that allowing an adversary to maintain sanctuaries during a war could be a strategic mistake, pointing to fuel production and refineries as examples.
Kellogg said the impact on the global diesel market had been limited, adding that Ukraine had demonstrated an ability to strike targets inside Russia while Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian cities and civilian areas.
Julia is a Deputy Head of News and correspondent for Kyiv Post who has previously worked as a parliamentary editor, journalist, and news editor. She has specialized in covering the work of the Ukrainian parliament, government, and law enforcement agencies.

title: Video: Why does Finland celebrate failure?
body:
October 13 is 'International Day for Failure', a now-global initiative that has its origins on a Finnish university campus.
Back in 2010, a student group at Aalto University in Helsinki came up with an idea: what if failure was something to be celebrated, instead of lamented?
Their initiative became 'Epäonnistumisen päivä', or 'Failure Day', and it was marked for the first time on 13 October that year.
Since then, the concept has been picked up by organisations and businesses in dozens of countries around the world — from 'failure panels' in the US to 'failure meetups' in Japan.
October 13 has now become the 'International Day for Failure', and it seeks to remove the social stigma around making mistakes as a means of encouraging open discussions about setbacks, reframing failure as a normal aspect of every day, and to encourage people to create and innovate.

title: Kazakhstan’s Business Tourism Market Expands: Which Region Attracts Most Visitors?
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s resort areas received 510,800 visitors traveling for business and professional purposes in the first half of 2026, with the Almaty Mountain Cluster accounting for 77.3% of the total, according to an analysis by Ranking.kz. The figures highlight the growing role of business tourism in the country’s tourism industry, as companies increasingly combine professional events with leisure and wellness activities. Photo credit: gov.kz. Business tourism, also known as MICE tourism, encompasses meetings, incentive trips, conferences and exhibitions. In Kazakhstan, the sector is developing along two main directions: hosting international events in major cities and organizing business gatherings directly at resort destinations. International events generate revenue The first direction has significant export potential. According to the Ministry of Tourism and Sports, Kazakhstan hosted 13 major MICE events in 2025, generating nearly $18 million in revenue, up 20% from 2024. Almaty plays a key role in this segment. International events held in the city contributed nearly $3 million to its budget in 2025. The second direction involves organizing business events outside major cities, including off-site conferences, national and international exhibitions, industry forums, seminars and corporate incentive programs at resort destinations. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, business tourism at Kazakhstan’s resort areas has grown in recent years. In 2024 and 2025, the number of visitors staying at accommodation facilities in these areas for business and professional purposes reached record levels, exceeding 1.1 million. Nearly one in four guests staying at hotels and recreation facilities in resort areas traveled for business purposes. Almaty Mountain Cluster leads resort destinations In January-June 2026, resort areas welcomed 510,800 business and professional visitors. Kazakhstanis accounted for 64% of the total, while foreign visitors made up 36%. The Almaty Mountain Cluster was the leading destination, attracting nearly 395,000 business travelers, equivalent to 77.3% of all visitors traveling to resort areas for professional purposes. The cluster has increasingly become a destination not only for holidaymakers but also for visitors combining work and leisure. Between 2020 and 2025, the number of business and professional travelers staying at hotels in the area increased 2.5 times. In 2025, hotels in the Almaty Mountain Cluster accommodated 925,700 business and professional visitors, up 7.1% from 2024. Business travelers contribute to tourism revenue According to the Bureau of National Statistics, accommodation facilities in Kazakhstan’s resort areas provided services worth 91.2 billion tenge (US$202.1 million) in the first half of 2026. Spending by foreign visitors traveling to Kazakhstan for business purposes also increased. According to the Bureau of National Statistics’ visitor expenditure surveys, their total spending in the first half of 2026 rose 5.4% compared with the same period in 2025. Expenditure on accommodation increased 9.7%, while spending on food rose 7.7%. The strongest growth was recorded in culture-related spending, up 24.1%, followed by recreational and sporting activities, up 22.2%, and medical and wellness services, up 13%. According to Ranking.kz analysts, the spending patterns may indicate that business trips to Kazakhstan are increasingly combined with leisure, cultural experiences and wellness activities. The growth of MICE tourism in major cities and resort destinations offers Kazakhstan an opportunity to broaden its tourism market, generating additional revenue for hospitality and related services. The post Kazakhstan’s Business Tourism Market Expands: Which Region Attracts Most Visitors? appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Child dies from injuries sustained in Gaza attack last month
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – A four-year-old boy has died from injuries sustained in an Palestinian Israeli attack last month.
A four-year-old boy has died from injuries sustained in an Israeli attack in the town of az-Zawayda in central Gaza three weeks ago, according to Wafa news agency.
The death of Osama Ahmed Abed raised the number of people killed in Gaza since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on October 7, 2023, to 74,382.

title: Sage Technologies Leads Industry in Digitization of Military Night Vision Goggles
body:
WASHINGTON, D.C., OCTOBER 12, 2026 — Sage Technologies, an innovator in low-latency digital data processing and defense electronics, announced today the release of its DPVS military-grade digital night vision goggles. DPVS is designed to address the Department of War’s (DOW) current requirements around soldier-borne digital vision and soldier connectivity. Leveraging expertise gained from the IVAS program, the new product leads the industry in quality of low-light performance, matching current analog NVG systems in the market today. Unlike analog systems, Sage’s digital version allows for the benefits of advanced technology, including real-time command and control data sharing as well as the integration of AI. Utilizing commercially available components and the Army’s MOSA strategy (Modular Open Systems Approach), Sage’s night vision technology is designed to deliver real-time situational awareness for military personnel, civil agencies, and first responders. “Our mission at Sage Technologies has always been to solve complex, real-world problems on the front line leveraging the latest technologies available,” said Steve Cantrell, CEO and President of Sage Technologies. “By fusing advanced digital sensors with real-time data processing, this system provides operators with situational awareness in the modern connected battlefield.” Building on Sage’s legacy as a trusted supplier to the DOW for over 30 years, the DPVS goggles integrate low-light sensors and real-time computing to ensure 24/7 operational capability where traditional analog night vision systems fall short. Key features of the new digital night vision platform include: Advanced Sensor Integration: Offers the best low-light visible (LLVis) sensor on the market for high-resolution optical imaging in degraded visual environments. Ability to integrate AI: Enables state-of-the-art image enhancement software onboard the platform. Ultra-Low Latency Processing: Leverages Sage’s proprietary embedded processing to provide ultra-fast digital data processing, eliminating display lag for high-tempo operations. Tactical Network Compatibility: Integrates seamlessly with tactical Android systems (such as ATAK) to display real-world situational awareness data directly to the operator’s display. Helmet-Mounted Design: Engineered specifically for dynamic tactical environments, with a fit for all common helmets . Source: Sage Technologies Click here to read the latest issue of ESD.

title: Russian attacks damage cargo terminal and warehouses in Mykolaiv region
body:
According to Ukrinform, Heorhii Reshetilov, acting head of the Mykolaiv Regional Military Administration, reported this on Telegram .
He said Russian forces attacked the region with Shahed drones on October 12 and overnight into October 13.
In Mykolaiv, a cargo terminal was damaged. Warehouses were damaged in the village of Balovne, within the Kostiantynivka community, and in the village of Novofedorivka, within the Kobleve community.
In the Mishkovo-Pohorilove community, a vehicle service station and a private house in the village of Zaichivske were damaged.
In Mykolaiv district, Russian forces attacked the Halytsynivka community with an FPV drone. In the village of Lymany, a freight truck was damaged.
Russian forces also shelled the Kutsurub community three times using multiple-launch rocket systems and carried out additional FPV drone attacks. In the village of Dmytrivka, two private residential properties were damaged.
In addition, Russian forces shelled the coastline of the Ochakiv community with multiple-launch rocket systems.
As Ukrinform previously reported, a 54-year-old woman was injured in Ochakiv in a Russian attack involving a Banderol-type weapon.

title: Philippines introduces e-visa system for Omani travellers
body:
MUSCAT: Oman’s Foreign Ministry has informed citizens travelling to the Philippines that the country introduced an electronic visa system on October 5, 2026, allowing holders of approved e-visas to present them digitally or as printed copies upon arrival. In a consular notice issued on October 13, the ministry said applications can be made through [https://evisa.gov.ph](https://evisa.gov.ph). No visa sticker will be placed in the passport for an electronic visa. The e-visa is valid alongside the machine-readable visa (MRV) sticker system for individual visas under the temporary visitor category, 9(a), and other applicable Philippine visa categories. The ministry said electronic visas cannot be converted into other types of Philippine visas, and the period of stay granted under an e-visa cannot be extended. Omani citizens planning to visit the Philippines must ensure their passports are valid for at least six months from the date of entry. The ministry also urged travellers to have health insurance covering their entire stay.
