title: Standards are not Seasonal: What the EC appointments teach both sides
body: On Monday, 12 October 2026, President Mahama swore in two new Deputy Chairpersons of the Electoral Commission, Emelia Afi Agbenyo and Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah. They fill the vacancies left by Dr Bossman Eric Asare, who resigned with effect from 31 July, and Samuel Tettey, who retired. At the ceremony, the President told them he expected “no preferential treatment” from the Commission for himself, his party or his government. Within hours, the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) was on the attack. Its Director of Communications, Dennis Miracles Aboagye, described one of the appointees as an openly partisan operative, a campaign team member of a political party, and said the appointment undermines the independence of the Commission’s leadership. The presidency has answered that she is not, and has never been, a card-bearing member of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), and that her involvement in campaign activities came from her advocacy for gender inclusion. I have not been able to verify either side’s claim independently. Party membership is a matter of record, and the public deserves a clear answer. I do not write this article to settle that dispute. I write because what we are watching is older than this appointment, and it will keep happening until we decide that politics needs standards that do not change with the seat a party occupies. The same argument, in different mouths Ghanaians have heard this argument before, with the speakers reversed. In April 2023, the NDC, then in opposition, wrote to the Council of State asking it to reconsider its advice on two appointees to the Electoral Commission under President Akufo-Addo, Hajia Salima Ahmed Tijani and Dr Peter Appiahene. The party described one of them as a card-bearing NPP member and warned that the Commission’s reputation would suffer unless the appointments were reconsidered. The NPP government of the day defended its choices. In 2019, the NDC’s General Secretary went further and accused the then Deputy Chairman, Dr Bossman Asare, of acting as an NPP sympathiser after he spoke publicly in favour of the referendum on the election of district chief executives. The argument then was that a deputy commissioner must act as a neutral referee. Read those statements today and the roles have simply been exchanged. The NDC now defends an appointee against the charge of partisanship, and the NPP now delivers the speech the NDC once gave. The Director of Communications says an appointment like this has never happened before in our democratic history. The record suggests that both parties have been accused of it, and that both parties have defended it when the accusation was aimed at them. That pattern should trouble every citizen, whichever party they support. Why the opposition’s voice changes There is a simple human explanation. In opposition, a party sees power from the outside. It sees the abuse of appointments, the sidelining of institutions and the quiet rewarding of loyalists, and it speaks about these things with real conviction. Then it wins, and the view changes. The loyalists are now friends who are qualified, the appointments are now reasonable judgement calls, and the critics are now people who are just playing politics. The reverse is just as common. A party that spent eight years defending its own appointments leaves office and suddenly discovers the virtue of neutrality, independence and clean process. Its principles seem to arrive on the day it loses the keys. I am not saying politicians are insincere. Many are sincere in both positions, which is exactly the problem. When a principle is held only by those who lack power, it was never a principle. It was a tactic. Why the Electoral Commission is different Some will say that all governments appoint people they trust, and that is true. Presidents appoint ministers, ambassadors and board chairs who share their outlook, and nobody is surprised. The Electoral Commission is a different kind of institution, and Article 46 of the Constitution explains why: it states that the Commission shall not be subject to the direction or control of any person or authority in the performance of its functions. The Commission is the referee of the contest in which the President’s own party competes. A referee does not have to be a person without opinions, but must be someone whom both teams can trust, and the perception of fairness matters almost as much as fairness itself. A losing candidate who believes the referee was on the other side will not accept the result. Ghana has already seen how heated the arguments about electoral credibility can become. We do not need more suspicion built into the system before the next election cycle begins. This is why the question to ask about any appointment to the Commission is not only whether the person is qualified. It is also whether a reasonable citizen from the other side could look at that person and believe the contest will be fair. If the answer is no, the government has chosen the narrow route when a wider one was available. Dr Asamoah, for example, comes with more than seventeen years of experience across electoral administration, public service, law, accountancy and teaching, including earlier service within the Commission itself. That kind of record is what makes an appointment easier to defend. What each side owes the country To the government, I say this: the President’s own words at the swearing-in set the bar. He asked the deputies to be impartial and to protect the right of Ghanaians to choose their leaders freely. That standard applies first to the person who made the appointments. If there is a real doubt about an appointee’s independence, the answer is not to attack the critics. It is to answer the specific allegations openly, publish the evidence of the person’s record, and let the public judge. A government that once complained loudly about partisan appointments to the Commission has more reason than most to hold itself to the standard it demanded. To the opposition, I say this: your criticism will be taken more seriously if it is consistent. If you believe partisan appointments to the Commission are wrong, then say so about your own past appointments as well. Acknowledge what was said about the appointees under your government and explain what you would do differently. Otherwise, your complaint, however valid in substance, will be dismissed as the temporary anger of those out of office. And let the allegations be accurate. Where a claim is disputed, say what you know, say what you do not, and allow the person concerned to be judged by what she actually does in office. To both, I say that the accusation “your appointee is a partisan” should never again be a statement whose truth depends on who is speaking. What would real standards look like? Standards need to be written down, because memory is too short and convenience too strong. Parliament and the political parties could agree on a plain code for appointments to constitutional bodies such as the Electoral Commission: a stated cooling-off period for people who have held party office or played prominent campaign roles, public disclosure of any party membership or campaign involvement, and a transparent vetting process in which the Council of State publishes its reasoning. None of this requires a constitutional amendment to begin, and all of it can be proposed by a party that is in opposition today and might be in government tomorrow, which is precisely why both parties should want it. The test is easy to state. Before criticising an appointment, ask what you said when your own side made a similar one. Before defending an appointment, ask what you said when the other side made it. If your answers differ, you do not have a position. You have an interest. The country that outlasts its parties Governments change in Ghana, and that is something to be proud of. The NDC and the NPP have each held power and each lost it, and one day each will again. The institutions they pass between are the only things that remain constant, and they stay trusted only if each side leaves them in better shape than it found them. We should therefore judge the new deputies by what they do. If they act fairly, show restraint and treat every party alike, the doubts will fade. If they do not, the opposition will have been right and the government will have wasted public trust it could ill afford to spend. Either way, the larger lesson stands. Standards are not seasonal. They do not belong to the party in power or the party in opposition. They belong to the people, and the people are watching who keeps them when keeping them is costly.

title: King Mohammed VI urges private sector to create youth jobs and spread benefits of growth
body: Morocco’s King Mohammed VI has urged businesses to increase investment and create more jobs for young people, while calling for the benefits of economic growth to be shared more fairly across the country. Addressing Parliament at the opening of the 12th legislature, the King outlined a new phase of development aimed at strengthening Morocco’s economy, reducing regional inequalities and improving citizens’ living conditions. He called on the private sector to play a greater role through productive investment, innovation, exports and sustainable job creation. Economic transformation, he stressed, requires businesses to complement state policies and reforms by expanding productive activities. Youth employment was a prominent development priority. The King advocated an integrated approach linking education, skills development and access to economic opportunities, with training better aligned to labour-market needs. The aim is to give young people clearer prospects, support social mobility and ensure equal opportunities, while responding to their aspirations for freedom, dignity and stability. The King also emphasised that sustained growth should translate into better public services and tangible improvements in everyday life. Reducing disparities between regions and distributing economic gains more equitably would be central to that effort. To support Morocco’s competitiveness and resilience, he called for new national strategies covering water, energy and food security, industrial development, the digital economy and artificial intelligence. He also urged faster action to establish strategic reserves and secure supplies of essential goods, helping the country reduce external dependence and withstand crises. On territorial reform, the King called for an end to delays in implementing advanced regionalisation and administrative deconcentration. He urged the transfer of powers, staff and financial resources to regions and provinces so that policies could better reflect local needs and stimulate investment. Turning to migration, he announced that Morocco would present its partners with a new strategic vision based on co-development, economic competitiveness and regional stability. He said international commitments should rest on reciprocity and respect for Morocco’s sovereignty. The King reminded parliamentarians that their mandate carried both political responsibility and a moral commitment to citizens, urging them to fulfil their legislative and oversight duties and help turn national ambitions into concrete results.

title: KGL U17 Colts 2026: Greater Accra win title after penalties win over Western Region
body: Greater Accra Region were crowned champions of the 2026 KGL Foundation Inter-Regional U17 Colts Championship after defeating Western Region 5-4 on penalties following a goalless draw in Sunday’s final at the Ghanaman Soccer Centre of Excellence in Prampram. In a tense and closely contested encounter, neither side could find the breakthrough during regulation time, forcing the final to be decided from the penalty spot. Greater Accra held their nerve in the shootout to secure their maiden title and bring an eight-day championship to a memorable conclusion. The triumph marks a significant milestone for the capital region, which joins an illustrious list of past winners of the youth competition. Desmond Asare, who played a key role in Greater Accra’s campaign, was named Most Valuable Player of the final. For Western Region, however, the defeat extended a painful run of near misses on the tournament’s biggest stage. Having reached the final for the third consecutive edition since 2024, they have now suffered back-to-back final defeats, following their loss to Ashanti Region in 2025. Western Region lifted the trophy in 2024 but were unable to reclaim it, with Greater Accra ending their latest title challenge in dramatic fashion. Prempeh Academy claim bronze Earlier, Prempeh Elite Academy secured third place with a deserved 3-0 victory over Brong Ahafo in the third-place playoff at the GFA technical centre. Thomas Asante delivered an outstanding performance, scoring twice, while Dennis Duah added the other goal to give the Kumasi-based academy a comfortable win. Asante opened the scoring in the 20th minute before Duah doubled the advantage five minutes into the second half. Asante then completed his brace in the 74th minute to seal the emphatic victory and ensure Prempeh Elite Academy finished the tournament on a high. Greater Accra join the Championship’s roll of honour The 2026 edition marked the sixth staging of the Inter-Regional U17 Colts Championship, which continues to provide a competitive platform for emerging football talent across Ghana. MAL FC won the inaugural edition in 2021, followed by Great Corinthians in 2022. Ashanti Region claimed the title in 2023, before Western Region triumphed in 2024 and Ashanti Region returned to the summit in 2025. Greater Accra’s victory adds a new name to the roll of honour and underlines the growing competitiveness of the tournament. Sponsored by the KGL Foundation, the championship forms part of the Ghana Football Association’s Talent Development Scheme (TDS), which is designed to identify, develop and nurture the next generation of Ghanaian footballers. The competition gives promising under-17 players the opportunity to demonstrate their technical ability, tactical understanding and potential while testing themselves against some of the country’s finest emerging talents. As the curtain falls on the 2026 edition, Greater Accra celebrate a historic first title, while Western Region are left to reflect on another painful final defeat after three consecutive appearances on the championship’s biggest stage.

title: Saudi Arabia vows to remain strong after deadly Houthi attacks
body: Saudi Arabia has vowed to remain strong in the face of repeated attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels on its civilian infrastructure. Speaking at a government press conference in Riyadh on Monday, Minister of Media Salman Al Dosary praised the Saudi security forces and military, saying the kingdom would “remain strong and united” behind its leadership and continue its development efforts despite the attacks. “We strongly condemn the Houthi terrorist attacks targeting civilians and civilian facilities in the kingdom,” Mr Al Dosary said. The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's government said it intercepted a Houthi missile launched at Riyadh on Monday night, while the rebels claimed to have achieved a “direct hit” on the capital's King Khalid International Airport. The airport's operations have been suspended until midnight on October 17 after Houthi missile strikes on Saturday and Sunday killed 14 people and injured more than 300. On Tuesday, the coalition intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched towards Khamis Mushait in the south-west of the kingdom. A brief statement issued by spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki did not say where the missiles were launched from or whether the incident had caused any casualties or damage. The Iran -backed group's military spokesman, Yahya Saree, repeated its warning “to all international airlines, experts, employees, workers and passengers from all countries of the world against flights to Saudi airports, as they are unsafe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah”. He also claimed a drone launched at the Khamis Mushait airbase resulted in a “direct hit”. Later on Tuesday, the coalition urged civilians in Yemen's rebel-held capital Sanaa to evacuate the area around the Yemen Oil Company’s Al Sabahah central station ahead of a “special operation”. The Houthis warned any attack on Sanaa would be met with a harsh and painful response. Fighting in Yemen Meanwhile, pro-government forces and the Houthis are battling for control of the key city of Taiz. Human rights groups have raised the alarm on the humanitarian situation inside the city, where people are cut off from food, water, medical and energy supplies amid what some organisations described as a “siege”. “Within five days, the city lost its main supply route for goods and commodities: Taiz-Al-Turbah-Lahj-Aden, following the Houthi group’s takeover of areas west and south of Taiz,” the Studies and Economic Media Centre in Yemen said in a report this week. The government also closed the eastern route used by civilians for security reasons, it added. The International Organisation for Migration estimates that more than 216,000 people have been displaced since the escalations in Yemen began in August. At least 172,000 of them are from Taiz. The UN said it was providing assistance to those in need but that reaching them was proving difficult, especially with key roads closed. That has disrupted “civilian movement, commercial supplies and humanitarian access”, the UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in a briefing on Monday. At least 54 civilians have been killed, half of them children, the agency said. “A further 171 civilians have been injured, including 107 women and children,” it added.

title: Strait of Hormuz attacks surge as Iran steps up campaign against US-backed oil shipping
body: At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, maritime agency reports show, as Iran increases its campaign to halt US-backed efforts to move oil through the vital waterway. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency issued delayed reports yesterday covering six vessels struck on Sunday – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage. The UKMTO reclassified the Sohar incident from suspicious activity to an attack after confirming a tanker had been struck by a drone. Local authorities assisted in evacuating the crew. In a separate incident, an outbound tanker was damaged when it was hit on its port side, although all crew members were reported safe. The incidents follow a sustained increase in attacks, attempted attacks and the harassment of commercial vessels. The US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Centre said that showed Iran’s “intent to assert [its] presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels”. The centre's assessment followed reports of at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait between September 28 and October 5, Reuters reported, quoting maritime security sources. The International Maritime Organisation recorded nine vessel-related incidents in the same period, reflecting differences in verification and reporting. UKMTO WARNING 169-26 Click here to view the full warning⤵️ https://t.co/RPA5f2EHIf #MaritimeSecurity #MarSec pic.twitter.com/D28qf30tRn — UKMTO Operations Centre (@UK_MTO) October 12, 2026 Iran has accompanied the pressure on shipping with increasingly explicit warnings to vessels attempting to transit the strait. On Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a crude oil supertanker had struck a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route with its navigation systems switched off. Shipping analyst Sal Mercogliano said video circulating with the claim did not appear to show a mine strike, as the vessel was stationary and there was no underwater explosion. The IRGC claimed any tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait would face a similar fate. Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint co-ordinator of Iran’s army, issued a further warning on Sunday. “We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” he said. On Monday, the IRGC said it had struck a supertanker attempting to transit the strait with its transponders switched off. Seatrade reported a separate Iranian claim that a supertanker had been hit. The incident not been confirmed. Earlier this month, a crude tanker was struck while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, but the threat to commercial shipping has also extended beyond the waterway. A vessel reported being hit by projectiles about 95km north of Madinat Ash Shamal in Qatar, with casualties reported. The Panama-flagged crude carrier Gem No 2 was struck by a drone, with reports placing the vessel about 25km west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. The resulting fire was extinguished and Indian officials said the vessel’s 22 crew members were safe. The attacks and warnings have sharpened the divide between Tehran’s claims of control over the waterway and Washington’s assessment of shipping conditions. Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the IRGC's commander, said Iran would close routes it considered to be illegal, including passages along Oman’s coast. “The Strait of Hormuz is closed and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mr Naqdi was quoted as saying by the Fars news agency. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected that assessment last week, saying commercial oil flows had largely recovered despite Iran’s efforts to disrupt shipping. “The Strait of Hormuz is open. There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he said. “So they’ve lost complete control of the strait.”

title: Moscow repels one of this year’s largest drone attacks, calculations show
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Last night’s drone attack on Moscow became one of the largest this year, according to calculations by TASS based on official data from the mayor of the Russian capital, Sergey Sobyanin.
According to the official, between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on October 12 and 7:00 a.m. Moscow time (4:00 a.m. GMT) on Tuesday, 417 UAVs flew toward the Moscow Region. "Air defenses neutralized most of those on the distant approaches," Sobyanin wrote on his Max channel.
The largest ever enemy drone attack was repelled on the night of September 19 when air defenses downed more than 1,600 UAVs, of them 450 targeting Moscow, Sobyanin said.

title: A slightly faster slimmer curl
body:
Back in August I mentioned the new curl performance tests we have running. I figured it could be apt to return to this topic just to mention some of the initial outcomes.
When the team gets a new set of charts, graphs and plots that visualize something, like performance, they offer an excellent opportunity for us to try to make them look better. This new setup is no exception.
The performance tests have only been running for just a little over two months but they have already made us improve curl performance in several areas. Of course, for most transfers these changes won’t make many visible differences to users. This is more in the vein that every little bit counts and that nothing should run slower than it has to.
This is a list of some improvements that are included in the curl 8.23.0 release, to be shipped tomorrow on October 14.
With a few different changes, the internal base64 encoding function is more than twice as fast, while base64 decoding is 40% faster.
Meaning percent encoding the octets that are not safe to use in URLs. The decoding function now runs more than twice as fast compare to before, while the encoding function is around four times as fast.
Converting a date provided in plain ASCII text, as is used in for example cookie headers, to the epoch – number of seconds since Jan 1st 1970, is now more than twice as fast as before. Mostly thanks to completely replaced functions for week day, month name and time zone name lookups.
Parsing a full URL to split it up into separate components as well as confirming its validity is a core component of curl, and libcurl exposes this functionality in its API.
In a test with several hundred different URLs, the new version executes 20-30% faster than before – with an improved ability to return precisely what the problem was when the URL is considered invalid.
For portability and now historical reasons, libcurl has its own printf() implementation. This ensures that it always works identically on all platforms but it also makes it our job to make sure it executes as fast as possible.
Most printf() calls now run slightly faster (5-15%) because it handles “chunks” instead of single byte-by-byte at a time.
We have a generic internal function in curl that converts a number provided in ascii to its binary version (for decimal, hexadecimal and octal). It handles 64 bit values, has overflow detection and supports a maximum. This parser now runs almost twice as fast as before thanks to a simple trick to avoid the boundary check for most loops.
The easy handle was 4256 bytes large two months ago, it is now 3064 bytes. About 28% trimmed off. One of these structs is allocated for every concurrent transfer done with libcurl.
There is also one multi handle allocated for each set of transfer. This struct shrunk from 900 bytes to 656: 27%.
The connectdata struct that is allocated once per connection libcurl handles, went down from 824 to 656 bytes: slightly over 20%.
For the test case where we count all allocations necessary for the curl tool to download a single 512MB file over clear text HTTP://, it went down from 100 to 96 used allocations. Not too exciting perhaps but it is now really hard to squeeze this further!
Mostly thanks to the decreased struct sizes mentioned above, this use case of a single HTTP download now only use 126,875 bytes allocated at peak. Down from 130,622 bytes two months ago. Also quite difficult to trim further.
It should be noted that the download buffer is 102,400 bytes of this amount. If we exclude that buffer from the count, curl is using 15% less memory.
If you think you can speed up any of these functions, it is now very easy to check: the tests are there in the git repository, ready to be invoked by anyone!

title: SANDF soldiers in Durban are not deployed against the people
body:
On 8 and 9 October, violence swept through Durban’s city centre, and 14 vehicles were torched, shops looted and buildings damaged. The violence followed protests against illegal immigration. KwaZulu-Natal Premier Thami Ntuli asked national government for help, and soldiers were sent to support the police. Only the President can authorise such a deployment, under Section 201 of the Constitution, and Parliament must be informed. The SANDF says the soldiers will remain until 31 October 2026.
Social media users have since claimed that the SANDF has been sent to crush protesters or to silence the March and March movement. That claim is false and should be firmly rejected.
The soldiers are deployed in Durban to support the police, who are charged under Section 205 of the Constitution with preventing crime and keeping public order. The soldiers are deployed to help secure key areas so that police officers can make arrests and open cases.
Section 17 of the Constitution protects the right to protest peacefully and unarmed. No soldier or police officer may stop a lawful, peaceful march because of what it stands for. However, burning vehicles and looting shops is not protest; it is crime, whoever commits it and whatever flag they carry. Concerns about illegal immigration are a legitimate subject of public debate, and the authorities responsible must answer them. But those concerns can be raised without violence, and nothing in this deployment prevents that. A march that stays peaceful has nothing to fear from the soldiers. The deployment targets violence and destruction, not any group, party or movement.
South Africans should have learnt from recent history. In July 2021, more than 300 people died in unrest across KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng, and the economic damage was severe. The state was widely criticised for being slow and unprepared. The lesson of that episode is that hesitation costs lives.
It must also be understood that the men and women in camouflage patrolling Che Guevara Road and other streets of Durban are South Africans who come from communities (townships, villages and towns) like those they patrol and serve under the Constitution, which obliges them to protect the people. Our job as citizens is to hold them to that obligation, not to cast them as the enemy.
The apartheid-era SADF served a government that denied most South Africans the vote. During the states of emergency, it was sent into Black townships to defend that system. The SANDF, by contrast, was created under our democratic Constitution and brought together members of the former SADF, Umkhonto weSizwe, APLA and the former homeland armies into one force for all South Africans. It is guided by Section 200, which gives it a clear purpose which is to defend the Republic and its people. It is bound by the Bill of Rights and represents the interests of every South African.
Citizens are right to watch the SANDF closely. They should ask the governance and accountability questions such as whether the President has reported the deployment to Parliament, what rules soldiers must follow, and where complaints about soldiers’ misconduct can be lodged. That is how a democracy keeps its institutions honest.
But scrutiny is not the same as hostility. The task of soldiers on Durban’s streets is to help restore order so that businesses can reopen, workers can reach their jobs and families can feel safe again. They are sworn to uphold the Constitution and serve all of us. Everyone with a stake in a peaceful Durban, KwaZulu-Natal and South Africa has every reason to let our soldiers do their job.
Lt Col (Rtd) Baliwinile Kwankwa (SA Army Int C) writes in his personal capacity on South African defence, military veterans, intelligence and security governance.

title: War update: 202 combat engagements on front line over past day
body:
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine stated this on Facebook in an update on the battlefield situation as of 08:00 on Tuesday, October 13.
Russian forces carried out 90 airstrikes, dropping 301 guided aerial bombs. In addition, Russian troops deployed 9,516 kamikaze drones and conducted 2,619 attacks on settlements and Ukrainian military positions, including 31 strikes using multiple-launch rocket systems.
Russian attacks targeted Pavlivka, Vilna Sloboda, Vasylivske, Zarichchia, Koreniok, Korchakivka, Nova Sich, Khrapivshchyna, Sopych, Ulanove, Rohizne, Mala Rybytsia, Potapivka, and Iskryskivshchyna in Sumy region, as well as Khrinivka in Chernihiv region.
Ukraine's Air Force, missile forces, and artillery struck a Russian troop concentration area and a drone command post.
In the N orthern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk directions, Russian forces carried out 49 attacks.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna direction, Ukrainian units repelled 20 Russian attacks. Russian troops attempted to advance near Starytsia, Izbytske, Vovchanski Khutory, and Zybyne, as well as toward Zakharivka, Varvarivka, Radkivka, and Doroshivka.
In the Kupiansk direction, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
In the Lyman direction, Russian troops launched six attacks near Kolodiazi and Lyman.
In the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk directions, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
In the Kostiantynivka direction, 15 Russian attacks were recorded. Russian troops launched offensive operations near Kostiantynivka, Sofiivka, and Dovha Balka, as well as toward Mykolaipillia.
In the Pokrovsk direction, 29 Russian attacks were recorded. Russian forces attempted to advance toward Hruzke, Toretske, Vilne, Kucheriv Yar, Dobropillia, Svitlе, Myrne, and Serhiivka, as well as near Molodetske.
In the Oleksandrivka direction, Russian forces launched one attack toward Ternove.
In the Huliaipole direction, Russian troops made 12 attempts to advance near Rizdvianka and Ternove, and toward Nove Zaporizhzhia, Kosivtseve, Hіrke, Vozdvyzhivka, and Prydorozhnie.
In the Orikhiv and Dnipro River directions, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
In the Volyn and Polissia directions, no signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russia's total combat losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, through October 13, 2026, are estimated at approximately 1,555,700 personnel, including 1,390 over the previous 24 hours.

title: UK Investment Roadshow opens in London to advance UK-Ghana growth partnership
body: The UK Investment Roadshow 2026 opens in London today, bringing together investors, businesses and key stakeholders to unlock investment opportunities under the UK-Ghana Growth Partnership. Held under the theme, “From Confidence to Capital: Unlocking the Next Wave of Growth through Strategic Investment,” the roadshow aims to turn commitments under the partnership into concrete trade, investment and commercial outcomes. It builds on the GhanaUK Investment Summit held in London in June, featuring a programme of investor meetings, business showcases, and networking sessions focused on sectors critical to economic growth, industrialisation, and regional trade. Connecting investors with opportunities Participants will hear from Claire Innes, Deputy Director of the Growth Directorate at the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO); Sabah Zita Benson, Ghana’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom; and Augustus Goosie Tanoh, Presidential Adviser on the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme. Business leaders, project sponsors and investment partners will also take part, giving investors direct access to decision-makers and insights into Ghana’s industrial transformation agenda. The roadshow follows the UK-Ghana Trade and Investment Summit organised by the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce in September. Its Deal Room and Investment Matchmaking Session generated investor interest in opportunities worth more than £250 million, drawn from a broader pipeline exceeding £1.4 billion. These opportunities span agribusiness, pharmaceuticals and health technology, financial services, infrastructure and the circular economy. Many are now being discussed with prospective investors and strategic partners. “The UK Investment Roadshow is the Growth Partnership in action, connecting UK investors with credible opportunities in Ghana and building on our strong momentum to unlock investment, create jobs and turn shared ambition into practical economic opportunities for both countries,” said Dr Christian Rogg, British High Commissioner to Ghana. Turning interest into action The roadshow is taking place alongside AFSIC – Investing in Africa, which organisers describe as the largest annual Africa-focused investment event held outside the continent. It will give Ghanaian businesses, project sponsors and government partners access to a global investor audience to showcase investment-ready opportunities. “This strategic event represents an important next step in converting interest into action. Building on the relationships and opportunities created during the Summit, it provides a platform to showcase Ghana’s investment potential, facilitate business-to-business connections and advance commercially viable discussions with investors seeking opportunities in Africa,” said Adjoba Kyiamah, Executive Director of the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce. Roundtable and deal room engagements The programme includes an Investment Opportunities Roundtable hosted by British Expertise International and a dedicated Ghana Country Investment Session at the AFSIC Summit. It will culminate in a Ghana Investor Deal Room Day, where investors will engage directly with businesses, project sponsors and government partners on investment-ready opportunities. Activities will take place at several locations in London, including the Park Plaza Westminster Bridge. The programme is being delivered by the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce and the UK Government’s flagship Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) programme in Ghana, as part of efforts to accelerate bilateral trade and investment. By helping investor interest develop into commercial partnerships, the roadshow seeks to deepen economic ties between the UK and Ghana and deliver lasting value for both countries.

title: Assemblies of God requires pastors to resign before entering partisan politics – Rev. Wengam
body: The Assemblies of God, Ghana, requires pastors seeking to pursue active partisan politics to step down from their ministerial positions, citing provisions in the church’s constitution and code of conduct designed to protect its unity. The church’s General Superintendent, Rev. Stephen Yenusom Wengam, explained that the rule applies to pastors who intend to contest political party primaries or otherwise pursue active partisan political roles. He said the policy allows worshippers with different political affiliations to remain united in their faith without their political differences creating divisions within congregations. Speaking on Channel One TV on Monday, October 12, Rev. Wengam said the requirement was consistent with the church’s global practice, although other denominations might permit their ministers to engage in partisan politics. “Assemblies of God, it can’t happen. You must resign as the pastor of the church,” he said, adding that the rule was enforced during the 2024 election period when two pastors under his leadership resigned after contesting party primaries. He maintained that the restriction did not prevent individuals from pursuing political ambitions but required them to relinquish their pastoral responsibilities before doing so. “It’s a calling, but we are saying that lay down your tools as a pastor. And then pursue your calling,” he added. Rev. Wengam’s comments come ahead of the 2026 World Assemblies of God Congress, scheduled to take place in Ghana from October 14 to 16. The gathering is expected to bring together church leaders from across the world and will be the first time the congress is held on the African continent.

title: Ghana targets 20% annual reduction in maternal deaths – Health Minister
body: The Minister of Health, Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, says Ghana is targeting a 20 per cent annual reduction in maternal deaths as part of renewed efforts to improve maternal healthcare and prevent avoidable deaths among pregnant women and new mothers. He said the target reflects the government’s commitment to strengthening maternal health services and ensuring women have access to timely, quality and effective medical care throughout pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period. Mr Akandoh made the disclosure while addressing global health leaders at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany, where he outlined Ghana’s interventions to improve maternal health outcomes. He explained that the government’s commitment to reducing maternal mortality had informed the launch of the Presidential Initiative on Maternal Health Emergency Response (PRIMER), which seeks to strengthen the country’s response to emergencies threatening the lives of pregnant women and mothers. “We recognise that financing alone will not save mothers. It takes political leadership, it takes functioning health systems and it takes accountability for results. That is why under President John Dramani Mahama, we have launched the Presidential Initiative on Maternal Health Emergency Response. Our ambition is clear: to reduce maternal deaths by 20 percent annually,” he said. Mr Akandoh stressed that reducing maternal mortality required more than financial investment, emphasising the need for strong political leadership, functional healthcare systems and accountability for results. The Presidential Initiative on Maternal Health Emergency Response was officially launched on September 16, 2026, by Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang. The initiative is expected to support Ghana’s efforts to improve maternal health outcomes by strengthening emergency responses and ensuring pregnant women and mothers receive timely and appropriate medical care. The 20 per cent annual reduction target forms part of the government’s broader efforts to improve maternal healthcare and prevent deaths that could be avoided through effective interventions and access to quality health services.

title: Al Ahli coach Marino Pusic calls for action after 'dangerous' bottle throwing at Al Wasl
body: Marino Pusic said something needs to be done to stop fans throwing bottles at players, terming it “dangerous”. The Al Ahli Saudi coach was speaking after his side’s 3-1 win over Al Wasl in Dubai on Monday night. The AFC Champions League Elite group match was played in an electric atmosphere created by 4,500 supporters at the Zabeel Stadium. Emotions boiled over at points, though, with many plastic bottles and cups being thrown onto the pitch. In particular, Saleh Abu Al Shamat, the Ahli forward, became a target after irritating supporters with his antics. First, he invoked ire after being perceived to feign injury in an altercation with Adryelson, the Wasl defender. When he was playing on the wing near Wasl’s diehard supporters in the second half, he was pelted with bottles. He responded by gesturing to them to throw more. Later in the game he was stretchered off on a medical buggy with a shoulder injury. The injury did not stop him from goading the home supporters, and celebrating when he went past the away section. That led to more aggravation, with even a couple of bottles being lobbed his way from the Wasl bench – leading to a confrontation between the opposing sets of substitutes. The issue of bottle throwing is not unique to Wasl. Most high profile fixtures in the region see instances of projectiles being thrown at moments of tension in the game. With matches played in high temperatures, clubs make water readily available to supporters. At Al Ain , for example, that now takes the form of paper cups alongside large water coolers at the back of stands. Other clubs provide small bottles or plastic cups of water. Sometimes these are thrown by irate fans, targeting players, coaching staff, or match officials. It happened at the AFC Champions League Elite final last season, which Ahli themselves ended up winning. High profile international fixtures between Qatar and the UAE have also been notable for it happening. Pusic joined Ahli, the two-time Asian champions, ahead of this season after leaving Abu Dhabi club Al Jazira. He said he does not want the passion of supporters to be diluted, and pointed out that the fixture against Wasl ended with cordial relations between the two sides. Saudi football pushes on despite security threat But the Croatian-Dutch coach said players and officials should not have projectiles thrown at them. “It could be a problem with people throwing very dangerous things on the pitch, because players and staff members [could] be hurt by these kind of things,” Pusic said. “I feel always pity about things when that happens. The passion and the support must be always there, and that's good. I like that part as well. “But as you can see, after the game, it was everything was nice, fine, like it should be. “In the heat of the moment, things can happen. But it's dangerous when you throw too much. It shouldn't happen, of course. But we are professionals; we are used to a lot of things.” The result leaves Wasl without a point after two matches in the Champions League, with many supporters voicing their frustration with coach Rui Vitoria. Roger Ibanez, who scored the first goal for Ahli, said his side were glad to get out of Dubai with the three points. “We knew it would be a tough game,” said the Brazil centre back, who was the player of the match. “We played here two years ago when we also got the result, and today was again a really tough match but we got the result. “We did a good job. Inside of the pitch, the players who started and the players who came in helped a lot. “Now let's go home and recover because we have a tough match [in the Saudi Pro League against Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr on Thursday].” Al Ain maintained their sparkling start to the Champions League and they sit at the top of the 16-team table. The UAE double winners followed up their opening day thrashing of Al Nassr with a 4-1 win over Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basra.

title: Cyber attacks in Africa grow faster than global rate, report finds
body: Nearly 70,000 cyber events were recorded across the continent in 2025, with financial services, technology and public institutions among the main targets. Cyber attacks in Africa increased by 421.4% between 2016 and 2025, outpacing the global increase of 307.3%, according to a new report examining the security risks facing the continent’s expanding digital economy. The figures indicate that if Africa recorded 100 cyberattacks in 2016, the equivalent figure would have risen to about 521 by 2025. Globally, an equivalent starting figure of 100 would have increased to about 407. In other words, the African figure grew to more than five times its 2016 level over nine years, while the global figure rose to just over four times its starting level. The comparison illustrates the faster growth in observed cyber activity in Africa, although the figures do not establish that every African country experienced the same increase or that attacks rose at a constant rate throughout the period. The Africa Cybersecurity Whitepaper: Africa’s Digital Defense Race says 69,236 cyber events targeting African organisations were observed in 2025, equivalent to approximately one recorded event every eight minutes. The report draws on Mastercard Cyber Insights, industry research, law-enforcement intelligence and interviews with cybersecurity experts to examine the threats confronting Africa’s digital infrastructure and the measures needed to strengthen its defences. It focuses on South Africa, Nigeria, Morocco and Kenya, which together accounted for 54.7% of the cyber events observed across Africa in 2025. The findings come as digital payments, financial technology, e-commerce, mobile connectivity and online public services continue to expand, increasing the importance of securing the systems that support businesses, governments and consumers. Financial services and public institutions among key targets Technology companies, public-sector institutions and financial services organisations accounted for 44% of observed cyber threat activity across Africa, the report says. These sectors support essential digital services, including financial transactions, business operations and government services, making their systems important targets for cybercriminals. The report also points to the increasingly organised nature of cybercrime. More than 60% of attributed cyber events were linked to black-hat hackers and organised cybercriminal groups. Black-hat hackers are individuals or groups who use their technical skills to gain unauthorised access to computer systems, steal information, disrupt services or make money illegally. The report examines the methods used by cyber attackers, the industries and digital assets they target, and the state of cybersecurity regulation, governance and national preparedness. Africa’s expanding digital economy is creating new opportunities for businesses and consumers, but it is also increasing the need to protect online transactions, personal information and critical infrastructure. The report projects that the continent’s digital payments market could reach $1.5 trillion by 2030, while its artificial intelligence economy could grow to $16.5 billion by the end of the decade. As more economic activity moves online, weaknesses in digital security can expose organisations to fraud, service disruptions and unauthorised access to sensitive information. The report warns that cybercrime can undermine public confidence in digital services, increase operating costs and slow innovation. Small and medium-sized enterprises may also face risks as they adopt digital tools but lack the resources or specialist personnel available to larger organisations. Governments and financial institutions face similar challenges in protecting the systems on which public services and financial transactions depend. Shortage of cybersecurity professionals A shortage of skilled cybersecurity workers is another challenge identified by the report. Africa has approximately 200,000 unfilled cybersecurity positions, representing a 23% workforce gap, according to the findings. The shortage raises concerns about whether organisations have enough trained personnel to identify vulnerabilities, monitor suspicious activity, investigate incidents and respond to attacks. Strengthening the workforce will require investment in cybersecurity education, professional training and the development of skills needed to protect increasingly complex digital systems. The report also examines cybersecurity regulation and governance, as well as differences in national readiness across the four countries studied. The whitepaper identifies four priority actions to improve cyber resilience across the continent, although the provided summary does not specify them individually. Its broader findings point to the need for stronger protection of critical digital infrastructure, improved preparedness for cyber incidents, effective governance and investment in cybersecurity skills. The report argues that cybersecurity must remain a strategic concern as African economies become more dependent on digital services. The scale of observed cyber activity, the concentration of threats in key economic sectors and the shortage of skilled professionals highlight the challenges facing organisations seeking to protect their systems. For African countries expanding digital payments, online public services and technology-driven businesses, the task is to ensure that security measures keep pace with the growth of the digital economy.

title: Dubai Design Week 2026 announces programme spanning architecture and craft
body: Dubai Design Week has unveiled its 2026 programme, with installations drawing on Emirati palm craft, traditional Japanese woodwork and the reuse of concrete rubble. The event will be held at Dubai Design District from November 3 to 8, bringing together exhibitions, public installations, talks and workshops. Downtown Design, its contemporary design fair, will take place from November 4 to 8. Abwab, the event's commissioning programme, will move from individual pavilions to a group exhibition. Called In Other Words, it will bring several practitioners together to explore how people communicate through gestures, signage, symbols, oral histories, and spoken and written language. Gardens and outdoor installations Dubai-based practice Nao Architects, founded by architect Reem Nassour, has won this year’s Urban Commissions competition with Three Gardens and a Room . The annual competition focuses on design for public spaces. Responding to this year’s theme, Atmospheres, Nassour’s proposal uses vegetation, colour, shade and filtered light to create three distinct gardens around a shared central space. The arrangement forms a room between the gardens where visitors can gather. Elsewhere, Emirati architect Rasha Saffarini’s Taqleem will draw on the traditional practice of palm-tree trimming to create a communal space. Palestinian-Turkish practice aestudio will use reclaimed concrete rubble to make new architectural forms in InBetween What Was and What Will Be . Japanese firms Nikken Sekkei and Sobokuya will return with Chatai 2.0 , an expanded timber structure combining traditional craftsmanship with spaces for gathering and collaborative craft. Their Japanese teahouse was among last year’s installations. Other installations will draw on games and domestic life. Indian practice Alter’s Playing Field will turn Ludo into a space for shared play, while Bahrain’s Palm and Palazzo will explore the balance between privacy and social connection in the traditional Bahraini home through Bayn . UAE designers and craft The UAE Designer Exhibition will return under the theme Inherited Futures, with architect and designer AlZaina Lootah as this year’s design collaborator. Supported by Dubai Culture, it will bring together UAE-based designers exploring how inherited materials, rituals and technologies can inform contemporary design. Craft will also feature in an exhibition by L’Ecole, School of Jewelry Arts, supported by Van Cleef & Arpels, presenting experimental archaeological research into lost goldsmithing techniques from the Second Iron Age. Al Jalila Cultural Centre for Children will return with an exhibition of ceramics by young practitioners. Downtown Design and public programme Downtown Design will showcase work developed through UAE training and mentorship programmes, including Tashkeel’s Tanween Design Programme and Abu Dhabi’s Athath Fellowship. The latter’s 2026 cohort will present furniture prototypes developed for the market. Carpet and textile specialist Iwan Maktabi will present new work by UAE-based designers Nadine Kanso and Omar Al Gurg. Kanso’s designs draw on Arabic calligraphy and symbols of the UAE, while Al Gurg’s reflect memories of the traditional majlis. An exhibition dedicated to Memphis Milano will explore the design movement’s graphic patterns, unconventional forms and continuing influence. British-Nigerian artist and designer Yinka Ilori will create the fair’s Veuve Clicquot lounge. Alongside the displays, interior architect and designer Tristan Auer will be a keynote speaker at the fair’s Forum in a space designed by architecture and interiors studio Bone. The wider festival’s workshops will take place at a dedicated Maker Space, with sessions led by practitioners from institutions including the University of the Arts London and SAE University College. The programme is open to participants of all ages and experience levels. The outdoor Marketplace will be held on November 7 and 8, bringing together independent makers selling homeware, jewellery, fashion and handcrafted goods, alongside children’s activities and live performances.

title: Jabal Shams records highest hourly rainfall of 42.8mm
body:
Muscat: Jabal Shams recorded 42.8mm of rainfall in a single hour on August 20, the highest hourly rainfall figure among the locations listed in an infographic issued by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) for the period from June to September 2026. Wilayat of Nakhal recorded 30.2mm of rain in one hour on the same day, while Wilayat Buhla received 27.8mm on July 4. Other locations also recorded significant hourly rainfall during the period. Wilayat of Dhank registered 20.4mm on August 21, followed by Wilayat of Mahdah with 19.2mm on August 26 and Wilayat of Samail with 16.8mm on July 27. The figures also showed 13.8mm of rainfall in Ibri on September 9, 13.2mm in Saiq on August 20 and 12.2mm in Al Hamra on September 8. Saiq Airport recorded 12mm on June 26, while Wilayat of Izki received 11.6mm on August 8.

title: ADF neutralizes 88 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram .
Beginning at 16:00 on Monday, October 12, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles launched from Russia's Bryansk region, nine Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and 108 attack drones, including Shahed drones (74 of which were jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody decoy drones. The attacks came from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The aerial assault was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Tuesday, October 13, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 88 drones.
Impacts were recorded at 17 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at seven locations.
In addition, impacts by loitering munitions were recorded in Kharkiv, although some of the weapons failed to reach their targets.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian forces attacked Kyiv on the evening of October 12, reportedly using six ballistic missiles, according to preliminary information.
In Kharkiv's Kholodnohirskyi district, the bodies of three people were found beneath the rubble of a residential building hit by a Russian missi le strike.

title: Ghana signs UAE deal to create 5,000 overseas jobs
body: The government has signed an agreement with a United Arab Emirates (UAE) company to facilitate the recruitment of up to 5,000 Ghanaian workers for construction, building maintenance and facilities management jobs in Dubai. The Minister responsible for Labour, Jobs and Employment, Emmanuel Kwadwo Agyekum, signed the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Masa Depan Building Maintenance L.L.C., represented by its Managing Director, Junhong Deng. Recruitment will be carried out in phases, beginning with an initial batch of 500 workers, based on the company’s employment requirements. Under the agreement, the Ministry will coordinate recruitment in Ghana, verify job demands and employment contracts, facilitate skills testing and certification, and provide pre-departure orientation on UAE labour laws, workplace safety and workers’ rights. The arrangement is also intended to reduce irregular recruitment, prevent abuses involving recruitment fees and promote safe and orderly labour migration. Masa Depan Building Maintenance L.L.C. will directly employ the recruited workers and take responsibility for their wages, accommodation, insurance and other employer obligations. The company will also cover specified costs in the UAE, including visa and work permit fees, medical examinations, health insurance and air tickets from Ghana to the UAE. To safeguard the welfare of the workers, the agreement provides for occupational safety training, protective equipment, a worker welfare officer and a mechanism for submitting complaints without charge or retaliation. A Joint Working Committee will also monitor recruitment, employment conditions and the implementation of the agreement. The government says the partnership will expand access to international employment while strengthening protections against exploitation and unfair recruitment practices. It is also expected to support skills transfer and help returning workers reintegrate into Ghana’s labour market, with recruitment and deployment conducted in phases under the applicable labour laws of both countries.

title: One Million Coders Programme targets 100,000 digital jobs in two years – Sam George
body: The government is targeting the creation of 100,000 digitally enabled jobs within the next two years under its flagship One Million Coders Programme, as it shifts its focus from digital skills training to employment opportunities. Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, said the new emphasis followed a directive from President John Dramani Mahama to ensure that beneficiaries of the programme could secure jobs after completing their training. Speaking during a monitoring visit to the Ashanti Region, he explained that while the National Democratic Congress’ manifesto committed to training one million Ghanaians in digital skills over four years, the government was also working to connect trained participants to businesses that need digital expertise. Mr George said the Ministry had presented the President with progress reports and remained confident of meeting the one-million training target within the administration’s four-year term. He said Ghana was seeking to build a large pool of skilled digital workers to meet growing demand for digital services, particularly from international companies looking to outsource work to the country. “We have shown His Excellency the trajectory the programme is on; we will cross a million in the four years. We are pivoting now away from the training into the job creation,” he said, expressing confidence in the employment target. He disclosed that the programme had already developed a pool of 10,000 data annotators whose skills could be presented to businesses seeking workers for specific digital assignments. The Minister’s visit to the Ashanti Region formed part of efforts to assess the programme’s progress and implementation at various training centres. He toured training centres and artificial intelligence laboratories at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology before visiting other facilities at Kwadaso, Asawase and Nkwantakese.

title: John Jinapor, Italian Ambassador explore opportunities for energy sector investment
body: Minister for Energy and Green Transition, Dr John Abdulai Jinapor, has held talks with Italy’s Ambassador to Ghana, Laura Ranalli, on strengthening bilateral cooperation and attracting investment into Ghana’s energy sector. In a Facebook post on Monday, October 12, Dr Jinapor said he hosted the Italian envoy for what he described as a productive and constructive engagement, with discussions focusing on deepening cooperation between the two countries. The Minister said the meeting explored opportunities to partner with Italian companies to unlock investment and support the development of Ghana’s energy sector. The proposed collaboration is expected to align with Ghana’s energy priorities while creating avenues for stronger business partnerships between the two countries. Dr Jinapor expressed optimism about the prospects for closer Ghana–Italy relations, saying he looked forward to deepening the strategic partnership to support the country’s energy objectives and sustainable economic growth.

title: Merchant ship comes under drone attack in Black Sea off Bulgaria — news website
body:
SOFIA, October 13. /TASS/. Two sailors were injured as unidentified drones attacked the Maltese-flagged merchant vessel Chelsea 3. The attack with three drones occurred roughly 14 nautical miles off the Bulgarian coast in the country’s exclusive economic zone, maritime.bg reported.
The crew of the 136-meter-long vessel sent a distress signal on Monday night, as the ship stayed afloat, while the injured sailors and the other crew members were evacuated to Varna on board border patrol boats.
The news portal did not provide more details.

title: Bekwai MP inspects KNUST Medical School project, engages hospital management
body: The Member of Parliament for Bekwai, Ralph Poku-Adusei, has inspected progress on the KNUST Medical School project at the Bekwai Municipal Hospital as part of efforts to strengthen healthcare delivery and expand access to specialist services in the municipality. The visit, on Monday, October 12, 2026, also provided an opportunity for the MP to engage hospital management and staff on the facility’s achievements, ongoing projects and operational challenges following its accreditation by the Health Facilities Regulatory Agency (HeFRA) as a secondary-level health facility. Hospital management briefed Mr Poku-Adusei on the medical school project, which has received support from VALCO and is expected to position the facility as a teaching and training centre for future doctors. The project is also expected to improve access to specialist consultants for residents of Bekwai and surrounding communities. Addressing health professionals during the visit, Mr Poku-Adusei commended their dedication and sacrifices in advancing the hospital’s development. “Life is precious and good health is fundamental to everything we do. My commitment to supporting the welfare of my constituents transcends political differences,” he said. Medical Superintendent Dr Serebour and the management team outlined challenges confronting the hospital, including limited emergency unit capacity, the absence of a dedicated isolation unit, inadequate accommodation for critical health personnel, the lack of a CT scan facility and delays associated with laboratory equipment. Management also identified the need for infrastructure expansion and expressed interest in exploring public-private partnerships to establish a CT scan and advanced diagnostic centre. The MP pledged to provide free airtime on his FM platform to educate residents on hospital procedures, patient rights and health protocols. Management also briefed him on plans to introduce a queue management system to improve patient flow and reduce congestion and misunderstandings between patients and staff. Both parties agreed to maintain regular engagement towards developing the facility into a centre of excellence in the Ashanti Region.

title: Iran endures relying on people, ancient culture
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani marked Hafez Day by saying Iran will always endure through its people and ancient culture, citing his message that hardship does not extinguish hope.
Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani marked Hafez Day in a post on her social media account, saying Hafez is the collective memory of Iranians and the voice of love and hope that has remained alive in their homes for centuries.
She recalled his teaching that the difficulty of the path does not extinguish the joy of achievement, adding that with reliance on the people and the long-standing culture of this land, Iran will always endure.

title: The More Putin Escalates Attacks on Europe, the more Europe Should Support Ukraine
body:
Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own.
While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.
In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology.
He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said, “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”.
In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology.
West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (e.g. something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.
Schulze Wessel makes another simple but very pertinent point: Russia’s expansion was always facilitated by cooperation with other great powers and arrested when it faced equal and opposing powers. Since Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year, the United States has ceased to be the latter and has at times looked like the former.
So now it’s Europe that is shouldering the burden of being the equal and opposing power. Europe (including the UK) has now given more aid to Ukraine than the US. Its combined economies are 10 times larger than Russia’s; Germany’s economy alone is twice the size.
So now it’s Europe that is shouldering the burden of being the equal and opposing power. Europe (including the UK) has now given more aid to Ukraine than the US.
And it’s Germany that’s now central to this European effort. Cumulatively, since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, Germany has been the biggest individual country donor apart from the US. According to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine support tracker, it has given twice as much as Britain or France.
As people in Kyiv and Odesa are daily pounded by Putin’s ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, it’s worth looking at the Kiel tracker’s figures for air defense systems. Germany has so far donated 19 of them, including five of the vital US-built Patriot air defense batteries – two more than the US itself has given.
In the first year of this war, I argued that Germany “has a unique historical responsibility to help defend a free and sovereign Ukraine”. At that time, I felt strongly that Germany was not yet doing what it should. Now, in the fifth year of a conflict that has already lasted longer than the first world war and shows no sign of ending, I can say without hesitation that it is.
This is not just a matter of the numerical scale of its support for Ukraine and its own increased defense spending, which, on the latest projections from the German finance ministry, will reach €154bn (£130bn) in 2028 (Roughly the same as Russia’s total estimated military expenditure for this year).
It’s also a matter of political will. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shown that will, and courage, by taking the train from Germany to Ukraine on the evening of Oct. 3, the 36th anniversary of German unification, with a strong delegation including defense industry leaders.
The Russian bombardment of civilian targets in central Kyiv, including Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and bridges across the Dnipro River, did not stop even though – or perhaps exactly because – Moscow knew the German leader would be there.
For a historian, there’s something very familiar here. Oh no, it’s Germany and Russia again! Yet each time is different. Historically, Germany is one of the powers that has done most to facilitate Russian expansion (just think of the 1939 Hitler-Stalin pact) but also most to threaten it.
In the first world war, and even at the margins in the second, some Ukrainian nationalists saw in a conflict between Germany and Russia a chance for their independence. Instead, they got imperial Germany’s colonialism (and then German defeat) in the first case and Hitler’s genocidal fascism (and then German defeat) in the second.
Another kind of German-Russian relationship. Has the former German Chancellor no shame? (Answer: no.) Gerhard Schröder and Vladimir Putin (from an official Kremlin social media post, 8 October)
Now, at last, Germany is genuinely engaged, at some cost and risk to itself, for the sovereignty of Ukraine. To anyone who knows this tangled history, there is something not just redemptive, but frankly inspiring in this sight: a democratic Germany playing a leading role in supporting an independent Ukraine’s bid to assume its proper place in a wider European community of free countries.
Now, at last, Germany is genuinely engaged, at some cost and risk to itself, for the sovereignty of Ukraine.
But for how long? And with how much support elsewhere in Europe? Precisely because Putin sees Germany’s centrality, it’s one of the main targets of his hybrid war, from explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport that the German government has firmly attributed to Russia and assassination threats against defense industry bosses, all the way to covert political interference and disinformation.
While Ukraine faces its most difficult winter yet, three closely connected things will be put to the test: Germany’s will to stay committed on the right side of history; the capacity of democracies to sustain the fight against a dictatorship (a perennial concern); and Europe’s ability to remain united in this cause.
A sceptic can point to many grounds for pessimism. Merz is unpopular at home. Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the party currently making the running in German politics, would abandon Ukraine to Russia. In France, the National Rally’s presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, says her country can’t afford to go on giving so much to Ukraine.
Solidarity with Ukraine is also crumbling on the right in Poland, with two smaller parties sounding frankly anti-Ukrainian. In one Italian opinion poll last month, more than half those asked were opposed to continued weapons deliveries to Kyiv.
In Brussels recently, I found a large audience seemingly stalwart in support of Ukraine – until, right at the end, our discussion turned to the issue of using the Russian frozen assets held in Belgium. Ah now, that’s a different matter …
Yet with the terrible damage being inflicted on the Ukrainian economy, including its grain exports via the Black Sea, experts estimate that as much as €100bn of additional support for Kyiv may be needed in 2027 alone – and hard-pressed European taxpayers are in no mood to cough that up.
Putin believes that decadent European democracies will crumble before the iron determination of an imperialist strongman. Our job is to prove him wrong.
This op-ed, reprinted from the author’s blog History of the Present, first appeared in the Guardian. See the original here.
