title: NHIA seeks legal reforms to support Free Primary Healthcare
body: The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) is calling for amendments to the National Health Insurance Act, 2012 (Act 852), to accommodate the government’s Free Primary Healthcare initiative and population-based payment systems. Deputy Chief Executive Officer of the NHIA, Dr Kwesi Djokoto, told Parliament’s Health Committee that the existing legal framework needed to be updated to support the new healthcare financing arrangements and strengthen efforts to eliminate claims fraud, leakage and unauthorised charges imposed on patients. “The legal framework is something that has to be modified to accommodate the free primary healthcare and the population-based payment methods,” he said. Dr Djokoto said the Authority was pursuing tariff adjustments and deploying artificial intelligence (AI) and other digital tools to improve claims verification, identify fraudulent practices and address discrepancies between service tariffs and available funding for the National Health Insurance Scheme. He also highlighted plans to establish an anti-fraud and illegal payments directory to help prevent and detect unauthorised charges, including illegal co-payments, and ensure appropriate sanctions for offenders. He urged the committee to support the proposed legal changes, strengthen penalties for fraud and illegal co-payments, and help prioritise capital budget allocations for 2027. Dr Djokoto said the NHIA had already introduced electronic claims processing to improve efficiency and accelerate reimbursements to healthcare providers. “In summary, claims are fully electronic with 20 days turnaround time. We are paying monthly; we have digital interventions to enhance the work of the National Health Insurance Authority,” he said. President John Dramani Mahama launched the Free Primary Healthcare initiative on April 15, 2026, to provide essential first-contact medical services without charge at the point of use. Services are expected to be delivered through CHPS compounds, health centres, polyclinics, public health units, health posts, community pharmacies and mobile or container-based health kiosks in busy locations such as markets and lorry parks.

title: Kazakh Foreign Ministry Condemns Attacks in Saudi Arabia, Issues Advisory for Kazakh Citizens
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has urged citizens in Saudi Arabia to exercise heightened caution following attacks on the country’s civilian infrastructure that caused casualties, according to the ministry’s spokesperson Zhanbolat Ussenov. The ministry advised Kazakh citizens to follow instructions from local authorities, avoid airports unless necessary and check flight statuses with airlines before traveling to terminals. It also recommended avoiding crowded places and high-risk facilities, and postponing non-essential trips where possible. Ussenov also noted that citizens facing emergencies can contact Kazakhstan’s Embassy in Riyadh or its Consulate General in Jeddah through the following emergency numbers. The ministry urged citizens to follow official updates from Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry and the relevant Saudi authorities. Earlier, the ministry strongly condemned attacks by Houthi militants on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, which resulted in casualties. It described the attacks as violations of international law and humanitarian principles. Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry called for an immediate halt to the attacks and urged the parties to resolve the crisis exclusively through political and diplomatic means. Kazakhstan also expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed its right to protect its sovereignty and security in accordance with the United Nations Charter. The post Kazakh Foreign Ministry Condemns Attacks in Saudi Arabia, Issues Advisory for Kazakh Citizens appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Can Agricultural Growth Make Kazakhstan Regional Food Security Hub?
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – The global food system is facing several pressures at once. Population growth and rising incomes, particularly in middle-income countries, are changing consumption patterns. Demand for meat, dairy products, and other protein sources is increasing. Photo credit: Shutterstock At the same time, agriculture faces growing climate risks. Water scarcity, higher input costs and supply chain disruptions linked to geopolitical tensions are adding to the pressure. Against this backdrop, Kazakhstan is seeking to strengthen its role in regional food security. The country is increasing agricultural production and expanding exports. It is also investing in irrigation, processing, logistics and agricultural technologies. Agriculture gains momentum Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector continues to show growth. Gross agricultural output increased 4.4% in the first six months of 2026 to 2.2 trillion tenge (US$4.9 billion), according to the government. Investment has been a major driver. Investment in agriculture increased 36.4% in the first five months of 2026, while investment in food production grew 2.7 times to 207.3 billion tenge (US$464 million). At a Sept. 18 operational headquarters meeting in Astana, Vice Minister of Agriculture Nazgul Khatepova said Kazakhstan’s total sown area this year stands at 24.2 million hectares. Photo credit: primeminister.kz The country is also progressing with its harvest campaign. At a Sept. 18 operational headquarters meeting, Vice Minister of Agriculture Nazgul Khatepova reported that Kazakhstan’s total sown area reached 24.2 million hectares, including 15.6 million hectares planted with grain and leguminous crops. As of the meeting, farmers had harvested 11.3 million hectares, with an average yield of 14.2 centners per hectare. Grain harvesting had covered 72.5% of the total grain area. Farmers had harvested 16.2 million tons of grain. Around 74% of the soft wheat delivered for storage was classified as third-grade wheat. The livestock sector is also expanding. Cattle numbers increased by 5.8% to 9.3 million head, while horse numbers rose by 7.4% to 5 million and camel numbers increased by 3.6% to 312,000. Meat production in slaughter weight rose by 5.5% to 559,000 tons. Milk production increased by 2.4% to 1.9 million tons, while egg production grew by 7.9% to 2.4 billion eggs. In addition, Kazakhstan is preparing for the 2027 harvest as the current harvesting campaign continues, Deputy Agriculture Minister Azat Sultanov said at a government meeting Sept. 29. According to Sultanov, the country has stored 2 million tons of seeds, or 90% of the 2.3 million tons required for next year’s harvest. Winter plowing is also under way, with 2.1 million tons of fertilizer applied so far, or 66% of the scientifically recommended amount, compared with 58% last year. Kazakhstan has also completed the digitization of all agricultural land to support soil-quality monitoring and crop-yield forecasting. Logistics strengthen export potential Growing agricultural output is driving higher grain transportation and export volumes. Kazakhstan’s strategic location between major consumer markets across Eurasia further strengthens its position as an agricultural exporter. For the agrifood sector, this provides access to markets in Central Asia, China, the Caucasus, the Middle East and beyond. According to Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the country transported 9.3 million tons of grain during the first eight months of the year. This was 13% more than in the same period in 2025. Domestic transportation accounted for 2.1 million tons, an increase of 8%. August saw a record monthly volume of grain transportation following the start of the new harvest. The figure reached 1.157 million tons, up 35%. Kazakhstan exported 7.1 million tons of grain from January through August. Of this amount, 4.8 million tons went to Central Asian countries, an increase of 37%. Uzbekistan received 3.6 million tons, up 50%. Exports to Tajikistan reached 998,000 tons, up 17%. Another 562,000 tons were transported to China, an increase of 34%. According to the Ministry of Agriculture, agricultural exports reached $3 billion in January-April 2026, up 36% from $2.2 billion a year earlier, and are expected to reach $7.2 billion by the end of 2026. Grain market faces price pressure Strong production and export capacity, however, do not eliminate market risks. Kazakhstan’s grain market entered the autumn season under pressure from growing supplies of the new harvest and cheaper Russian wheat, according to Yevgeny Karabanov, head of the Analytics Committee of the Grain Union of Kazakhstan. Yevgeny Karabanov, head of the Analytics Committee of the Grain Union of Kazakhstan. Photo credit: Karabanov’s Telegram channel “The supply of grain and oilseeds on the domestic market is increasing. Prices for grain and oilseeds from the new harvest are continuing to form on both domestic and foreign markets,” Karabanov said in his Telegram channel . He noted that prices for some wheat grades on the domestic market fell by 1,000-3,000 tenge (US$2.2-US$7) per ton over one week, while export prices declined by up to $5 per ton. Karabanov identified two main factors affecting the market. One is the growing supply of Kazakhstan’s new harvest. The other is the availability of Russian wheat at lower prices. Export shipments are beginning to increase, but logistics costs have also risen. Karabanov said transportation costs increased 10%-15% over the week, or about $3.50-$5.50 per ton. He emphasized that buyers also remain cautious about purchasing large grain volumes. Importers are expecting further price declines and are looking for cheaper Russian wheat. “Amid restrictions on wheat exports in Russia, due to the effective blocking of Black Sea and Azov Sea ports, wheat prices in Russia continue to decline. Proposals to supply Russian wheat to Kazakhstan and Central Asian countries were increasing, while the weakening ruble was making Russian wheat more attractive to regional importers,” Karabanov said. He warned that increasing supplies of cheaper Russian grain could intensify competition in Central Asian markets for grain, flour and vegetable oils. According to Karabanov, tighter restrictions on Russian wheat imports into Kazakhstan could temporarily support domestic prices, but competition from Russian agricultural products in Central Asia would remain. From grain exporter to food security hub Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector faces challenges amid a broader shift in how food security is understood. In a written response to The Astana Times, the Islamic Organisation for Food Security (IOFS) said food security is no longer measured solely by the volume of food produced. It increasingly depends on the resilience of the entire food system, from genetic resources and agricultural production to storage, transportation, trade and access to food. “Whoever controls the seeds controls the food,” the organization said, highlighting the importance of conserving genetic resources and developing crop varieties that can withstand changing climate conditions. Agriculture faces growing pressure from climate change, water scarcity, land degradation, pests and diseases. According to IOFS, countries need to invest in agricultural research, plant breeding, biotechnology, innovation and resilient seed systems. Production must also be supported by reliable supply chains, adequate storage, food processing, transport and open trade. IOFS noted that effective governance, early-warning systems, and coordination across agriculture, water, trade, transport, energy, and finance are also important. “Ultimately, food security is not simply about producing more food. It is about building resilient food systems capable of withstanding shocks, adapting to changing conditions, and ensuring that safe, nutritious, and affordable food remains accessible to all, even in times of uncertainty,” the IOFS said. Kazakhstan’s strategic assets and remaining gaps IOFS identifies several advantages that could strengthen Kazakhstan’s role in regional food security. These include extensive land resources, a developed grain sector, strong livestock production and an established scientific and research base. The country also has plant genetic resources and experience in crop breeding, seed production and agricultural research. Some crop varieties have been adapted to harsh continental and water-scarce conditions. “This makes them increasingly relevant as countries seek to adapt their agricultural systems to climate change,” IOFS said. The organization identified several areas where Kazakhstan could contribute to regional and international food security, including agricultural science and innovation, climate-resilient seed systems, technology transfer, logistics and trade connectivity, and the exchange of agricultural expertise. For Kazakhstan to become a regional food security hub, several challenges still need to be addressed, particularly water management, technology, processing and logistics. Agriculture will increasingly depend on efficient water use as climate pressures intensify. Kazakhstan is modernizing irrigation and introducing digital solutions, while IOFS recommends more precise water management through better measurement, digital allocation, satellite monitoring, telemetry, and data-based decision-making. Technology also needs to reach farmers faster, including digital agriculture, precision farming, modern breeding and climate-adaptation solutions. At the same time, Kazakhstan could strengthen its position by expanding food processing and exporting higher-value products rather than raw commodities. “Storage and logistics remain important because Kazakhstan is landlocked,” IOFS said, adding that long-term competitiveness will depend on integrating water management, science, technology, processing and logistics. The post Can Agricultural Growth Make Kazakhstan Regional Food Security Hub? appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Kingfish fishing ban ends on October 15 in Oman
body:
MUSCAT: Kingfish fishing will resume along all Oman’s coasts on Friday, October 16, 2026, following the end of the seasonal ban on Thursday, October 15, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources announced. From October 16, catching, possessing, transporting, buying, selling, trading and exporting kingfish will be permitted under the Executive Regulation of the Living Aquatic Resources Law, issued through Ministerial Decision 70/2026. The ministry reminded fishermen and those involved in trading and marketing kingfish to comply with the regulations governing the species. These include a minimum fish length of 65 centimetres, as stipulated in Article 179 of the executive regulation. It thanked fishermen and fisheries sector workers for their cooperation during the ban and urged continued compliance with fishing legislation and requirements to protect fish stocks and ensure the sustainability of Oman’s kingfish fisheries. Separately, the Directorate General of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources in Dhofar Governorate announced a campaign to remove unauthorised materials and equipment from fishing ports, beginning on October 15, 2026. Fishermen and port users have been asked to remove items marked with warning stickers within a maximum of two weeks of the stickers being placed. The campaign covers abandoned or unlicensed boats; boat trailers, vehicles and associated equipment in breach of regulations; nets, fishing equipment and fish storage boxes left outside designated areas; and unlicensed or prohibited fishing gear. The directorate urged compliance to avoid legal or administrative action, saying cooperation would improve safety, port organisation and the efficient use of facilities.

title: Iran envoy to Vatican denounces Rubio remarks on civilization
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Iran’s ambassador to has strongly condemned US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s remarks in Athens about Iranian civilization, terming the remarks raised by Rubio as deep rooted in ignorance and prejudice.
Mohammad Hossein Mokhtari called Rubio’s recent comments at the Acropolis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, an “unethical and provocative act,” saying the US official had used the occasion to justify hawkish positions and threats against Iran out of desperation.
Human civilization’s history is not a field for political fantasies or judgments born of ignorance and prejudice, Mokhtari said. Civilizations were built over thousands of years through human thought, culture, knowledge and effort, and their legacy could not be dismissed through superficial claims or distorted accounts, he added.
Mokhtari highlighted Iran’s historical and spiritual standing, citing references to the country in religious texts. In the Old Testament, he said, Cyrus the Great is presented as the Lord’s anointed and chosen instrument for fulfilling divine will. The books of Ezra, Daniel, and Esther also refer to Persian kings, the grandeur of the Persian Empire, and their role in the fate of nations.

title: Beatrice Annan defends Afi Agbenyo’s EC appointment, cites record of gender advocacy
body: Presidential staffer Beatrice Annan has defended the appointment of Emelia Afi Agbenyo as Deputy Chairperson of the Electoral Commission (EC), arguing that her participation in political campaigns should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of partisan allegiance or a threat to electoral neutrality. Agbenyo’s appointment, alongside that of Dr Joseph Kweku Asamoah as another Deputy Chairperson, has drawn criticism from the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP). The party has questioned her suitability for the position, pointing to her involvement in the National Democratic Congress (NDC)’s campaign activities and her role as a spokesperson for its manifesto committee on governance. Her defenders, however, point to her professional experience in gender advocacy and policy work, including serving as a technical adviser and gender analyst with GIZ Ghana. Her involvement in the NDC’s 2020 and 2024 election campaigns has been explained as an effort to advance women’s representation in leadership rather than evidence of formal membership of the governing party. The defence also draws on her reported criticism of the NDC in 2016 over governance concerns and her warning before the 2024 elections that gender advocates could campaign against the party if it failed to retain a female running mate. These positions, her supporters argue, demonstrate that her engagement with political parties has been shaped by specific policy and gender-related issues. Speaking on Citi FM on Monday, October 12, 2026, Ms Annan insisted that Agbenyo had never been a card-bearing NDC member and had not demonstrated any conduct suggesting she would be biased in the performance of her duties. “She has not done anything to demonstrate any potential bias or imminent bias,” she said. She also maintained that the presidency followed the constitutional procedure for the appointments, explaining that the nominees were presented to the Council of State more than a month before their swearing-in and that the council undertook consultations with relevant stakeholders.

title: DNA and vehicle-tracking help French investigators recover stolen Renoirs
body:
Recovered paintings "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano", right, and "Young Woman at the Well," stolen from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer are on display at the Interdisciplinary Centre for the Conservation and Restoration of Heritage in Marseille, France, Monday Oct. 12, 2026. Philippe Magoni/AP hide caption
NANTERRE, France — DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said Monday.
Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera. The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said.
One painting, "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano," suffered a tear. The other, "Young Woman at the Well," had slight damage to its frame, Bessone said. He estimated their combined value at 4.2 million euros ($4.7 million).
The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that "apparently caused the perpetrators to panic," Bessone said.
"As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve," he said.
The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said.
Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said.
Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection.
The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003.
Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent."
The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of "theft committed by an organized gang" and "criminal association," among other counts. They were sent to prison pending further investigation. The have denied wrongdoing, Bessone said.
Recovered paintings "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano" right, and "Young Woman at the Well," stolen from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer are on display at the Interdisciplinary Centre for the Conservation and Restoration of Heritage in Marseille, France, Monday Oct. 12, 2026. Philippe Magoni/AP hide caption
The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft. Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said.
The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings but said he did not immediately recognize them. Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of "concealment" of stolen paintings. They were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France.
Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge.
The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice.
The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France.
Christian Sainte, national director of judicial police, said Monday that the country "is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage" in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries.
French museums recorded 23 cases in 2025 and about 10 this year, he said.

title: Ghana seeks investment deals in Bangkok amid global economic crises
body: Ghana is seeking investment and financing deals to advance its New Economy agenda at the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) in Bangkok, Thailand. The delegation, led by Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Baah Forson and supported by Bank of Ghana Governor Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, is engaging international investors, financial institutions and development partners on the sidelines of the meetings. The meetings, taking place from October 12 to 18 at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Centre, bring together representatives of the IMF’s 191 member countries and the WBG’s 189 members to deliberate global challenges involving debt, energy security, climate change among others. The rapid expansion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the economic impact of the US-Iran war are also on the agenda. For Ghana, the gathering offers an opportunity to mobilise investment ahead of the 2027 Budget, in which Dr Forson is expected to outline the Government’s New Economy agenda, its blueprint for the next phase of economic development. The agenda seeks to translate recent economic stabilisation into sustained transformation through value addition, industrialisation and improved global competitiveness, while creating jobs. Following the September IMF staff-level engagement in Ghana and the country’s exit from the US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility (ECF) programme, the Bangkok meetings are expected to advance discussions on benchmarks and reforms under the new Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI). Dr Forson is expected to engage IMF leadership, senior World Bank officials, finance ministers, representatives of international financial institutions and other development partners. He mentioned the shift towards the New Economy during the presentation of the 2026 Mid-Year Fiscal Policy Review. The 2027 Budget is expected to provide further details on how the Government intends to translate its development ambitions into policies and action. “Stabilisation was never the destination. It was the price of entry,” he stated. “Ghana has paid that price. What comes next is the work that changes lives at scale – the work of transformation.” At the 132 nd Monetary Policy Committee press briefing in Accra last month, Dr Asiama said Ghana would use the meetings to engage investors and development partners and secure beneficial agreements for the country. Responding to a question from the Ghana News Agency, he described the gathering as an important platform for bilateral engagements, allowing Ghana to present its economic programme directly to investors and development partners. “The annual meetings is where we get to meet our counterparts from the other side and to discuss Ghana’s economic programme… it is really an important meeting that all countries and officials do attend,” he said. Dr Asiama said the Ministry of Finance team would intensify investor outreach in Thailand to reassure markets and attract investment into key sectors of the economy. He expressed optimism that the engagements would yield positive results for Ghana. Globally, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva has warned of opposing forces shaping the economic outlook, with energy supply disruptions weighing on growth while AI-related investment supports demand. In her address ahead of the meetings, she said the IMF’s World Economic Outlook projected global growth at three per cent, with conflict-affected economies and vulnerable energy-importing countries facing significant pressures. She cited the continuing Russia-Ukraine war and the conflict in the Gulf as sources of uncertainty for the global economy. “Putting all of it together, my message to the world’s economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said. World Bank Group President Ajay Banga has said the global economy had remained resilient, supported by substantial AI investment and adjustments in oil supply. However, developing countries faced sharp increases in diesel and fertiliser costs, alongside risks associated with the El Niño weather phenomenon. He said the Bank was in active discussions with between 30 and 40 countries on possible crisis assistance to help them manage energy shocks, rising prices and the effects of the conflict in the Middle East. Mr Banga also said the Bank was advancing 14 to 15 debt-for-development swaps and guarantee projects designed to convert high-cost legacy debt into lower-cost financing linked to health, education and water programmes. Previous efforts has involved countries including Angola, Côte d’Ivoire and Argentina. Thailand is hosting the meetings for the second time, having previously hosted them in 1991. The return highlights the region’s growing role in discussions on global economic and financial stability. The Annual Meetings bring together central bank governors, finance and development ministers, private sector executives, civil society representatives, academics and the media for a common agenda. They discuss the global economy, financial stability, poverty reduction, inclusive growth, employment, climate change, among others pertinent global issues. . Key activities include the plenary session, meetings of the Development Committee and the International Monetary and Financial Committee. There will be regional briefings, press conferences and specialised forums.

title: Russian drone attack at medical facility in Khmelnytskyi region leaves four patients injured
body:
According to Ukrinform, Serhii Tiurin, head of the Khmelnytskyi Regional Military Administration, reported the incident on Telegram .
He said Russian forces had repeatedly attacked Khmelnytskyi region with attack drones over the course of the day. Air defense forces were active and intercepted some of the drones.
"During one of the attacks, windows and the entrance area of a medical facility in the region were damaged, as were vehicles parked nearby. Four patients receiving treatment at the facility sustained minor injuries. They were provided with the necessary medical assistance," Tiurin said.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, three residential buildings caught fire after a Russian drone crashed in the village of Murovane in Lviv district.

title: Policy reforms aim for single-digit inflation – Minister
body: The Federal Government has stated that its ultimate economic target remains achieving single-digit inflation, assuring citizens that ongoing structural reforms under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu are designed to strengthen the nation’s economy while prioritising public welfare. Speaking during a media briefing and subsequent interactive session with senior editors in Abuja, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Alhaji Mohammed Idris, said Nigeria remains on track to achieve an economic growth rate of over four per cent in 2026. Idris disclosed that inflation had dropped significantly from approximately 27 per cent in January 2025 to around 15 per cent, adding that government policies are aimed at driving down price levels further into single digits. Highlighting macroeconomic performance, the minister revealed that Nigeria’s external reserves exceeded $54 billion in September, reaching their highest level in nearly two decades. He said Nigeria recorded a current account surplus of $12 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $8.6 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. The minister said that domestic crude oil production had expanded following a reduction in oil theft, while non-oil exports generated over $6 billion in 2025, marking the highest yield in the country’s history. However, the minister acknowledged that the administration must ensure these macroeconomic gains translate into direct benefits for citizens, particularly regarding food prices, transportation costs, and general household expenditure. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu remains firmly committed to the economic reforms that are strengthening our country, while ensuring that the welfare of Nigerians remains paramount,” Idris said. He acknowledged the pressure of higher energy costs on households and businesses, adding that the government is determined to translate economic recovery into improved purchasing power and better living conditions by expanding affordable energy alternatives and boosting domestic production. Idris clarified that the recent decision of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) to absorb part of its profit margin to cushion pump prices does not signal a return to the petrol subsidy regime. Dismissing assertions that the government adopted a “knee-jerk” approach or acted in response to attacks from opposition parties, the Minister maintained that extensive consultations involving economic experts and top NNPC leadership preceded the intervention. He explained that rather than reversing the administration’s core policy on subsidy removal, NNPCL acted strictly within its corporate mandate as a limited liability company to forego a fraction of its operational profits.

title: IMF raises Ghana’s 2026 growth forecast to 5.7%, sees inflation falling to 4.8%
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised Ghana’s economic growth forecast for 2026 to 5.7% and projected year-end inflation at 4.8%, despite global economic pressures and uncertainty. The growth forecast represents an increase of 1.1 percentage points from the 4.6% projected in April. The projections are contained in the IMF’s latest economic outlook report, released on the sidelines of the Annual IMF/World Bank Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. Joy Business understands that the upward revision reflects Ghana’s commitment to fiscal discipline, spending targeted at stimulating growth, and strong commodity export earnings, particularly from gold. Higher gold export earnings have supported the country’s trade balance and helped build economic buffers. Ghana’s commitment to targets under the Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) programme also contributed to the revised outlook, according to information available to Joy Business. However, sources close to the Fund have expressed concern about Ghana’s reliance on gold exports and urged the government to diversify its export earnings. The IMF expects growth to moderate to 5.2% in 2027. Its 2026 forecast exceeds the government’s estimate of 4.8% outlined in the 2026 Budget, indicating a more optimistic assessment of Ghana’s growth prospects. According to the Ghana Statistical Service, the economy expanded by 6.0% in the second quarter of 2026, bringing the first-half growth to 6.2%. Inflation outlook The IMF projects that Ghana will end 2026 with inflation of 4.8%, down from its April forecast of 7.9%. The revised projection is also below the government’s and the Bank of Ghana’s target band of 8% ± 2 percentage points. That band ranges from 6% to 10%. With September inflation at 5.2%, the IMF’s forecast suggests a further easing in price pressures by the end of the year. Bank of Ghana internal projections cited by Joy Business had anticipated an increase in inflation in September, while expecting the year-end rate to remain within the target band. If the IMF’s forecast materialises, Ghana would record single-digit year-end inflation for a second consecutive year, following a similar outcome in 2025. World Bank on Ghana’s growth and inflation estimates The World Bank, in its Africa economic update released in October 2026, maintained its growth forecast of 4.8% for Ghana, unchanged from April. It projects 4.9% growth in 2027. The Bank expects growth to be supported by the services sector, a recovery in oil and gas activity, and continued progress with structural and fiscal reforms under national programmes. It described economic activity in the second quarter of 2026 as robust, although growth moderated slightly, with real GDP expanding by 6.0% year-on-year. On the expenditure side, the Bank said growth was supported by strong domestic demand. Investment increased by 53.0%, while domestic demand rose by 11.2%, reflecting continued strength in private and public spending. Impact The IMF’s improved outlook could strengthen investor confidence in Ghana’s economy and support efforts to attract foreign direct investment and additional assistance from development partners. For investors, stronger growth and lower inflation could improve perceptions of economic stability and the prospects for returns. Ghana’s participation in the PCI programme could also provide further reassurance to development partners about the government’s commitment to fiscal discipline. The outlook comes alongside recent upgrades to Ghana’s credit ratings by Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. Together, these developments could improve Ghana’s borrowing conditions and potentially lower the cost of future financing, including any eventual return to the international capital market. Global economic outlook The IMF said global economic activity had remained resilient, with the technology upturn, existing buffers and economic adjustments helping to cushion the effects of geopolitical disruptions. Nevertheless, it projects global growth to slow to 3.1% in 2026, then recover to 3.4% in 2027. Global headline inflation is expected to rise to 4.7% in 2026, then ease to 4.1% in 2027. Energy-importing economies outside the technology value chain face the most challenging outlook. The Fund warned that the factors supporting resilience have limits, with growth risks tilted to the downside. Further escalation of conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence, renewed trade tensions and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken economic activity. Conversely, stronger investment in artificial intelligence, associated productivity gains, and a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions could support faster growth. The IMF also called for stronger fiscal frameworks to respond to disruptive shocks and rebuild room for policy action through revenue measures.

title: Trump says 'would love' to serve third term as US president
body:
WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said he would like to run for a third term as US president if he had the opportunity.
"I would love to do that," the Associated Press quoted him as saying while addressing Republican Party supporters in Ohio ahead of the November US congressional elections as the crown broke into chants of "four more years."
By law, Trump’s second term as president is set to end in January 2029. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, which was adopted in 1951, limits a president’s tenure to two terms. Nevertheless, the current US leader has repeatedly indicated the possibility of seeking re-election for a third term. Steve Bannon, the president’s former key political strategist, also insisted last fall that Trump be president again.
Trump won the election for the second time in November 2024. He defeated Democratic Party candidate Kamala Harris. He previously headed the US administration from 2017 to 2021.

title: FG pays N1.23trn power debt, targets full settlement next year
body: The Federal Government has paid N1.23 trillion of its legacy debts to power generation companies (Gencos) through bonds, with the outstanding balance expected to be cleared next year. The Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, disclosed this at the Harvard Business School Association of Nigeria (HBSAN) Energy Conference in Lagos. He said the government was committed to settling the outstanding obligations to Gencos while preventing fresh arrears from accumulating in the power sector. Tegbe said clearing the debts was part of efforts to attract investment into the sector and improve electricity supply to homes and businesses across the country. He reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to providing reliable electricity to Nigerians while ensuring that vulnerable groups were adequately protected. He said by clearing its obligations to Gencos and making full use of available generation capacity, the Federal Government is building a stronger, more investment-ready power sector in line with the Renewed Hope Agenda, so that homes, businesses and industries can count on steady power to drive growth and prosperity.

title: Over 100 Women Raise Funds to Digitise Melbourne’s Greek Archives
body: More than 100 women gathered at The Hotel Windsor on 9 October for a High Tea supporting the Greek Community of Melbourne’s Archives Digitisation Project. More than 100 women gathered at The Hotel Windsor for a High Tea supporting the Greek Community of Melbourne’s Archives Digitisation Project The event raised funds to digitise the first five of 30 hard-copy volumes held in the GCM archives, marking the start of a longer effort to make the records publicly accessible. Archivist Dr Juliana Charpantidou Organised by a volunteer committee including Paula Konidaris, Maria Pirpiris, Spiz Demetriou and Simela Stamatopoulos, the afternoon featured a raffle with prizes from sponsors such as the Hellenic Museum, Mary Di Carlo and local businesses. Archivist Dr Juliana Charpantidou spoke about the fragility of key records, including the community’s first Minute Book from 1898 and early registers from Evangelismos church. “We are preserving the handwriting, the names, the decisions and the family stories of those who came before us,” she said. Consul General Dimitra Georgantzoglou and guest speaker Helen Mantzis also addressed the gathering. GCM Board Member Simela Stamatopoulos described the turnout as a strong start for the project. Donations remain open via the Antipodes Centre Trust (tax-deductible over $2): https://donate.greekcommunity.com.au/archivesproject The post Over 100 Women Raise Funds to Digitise Melbourne’s Greek Archives appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Ablakwa urges Africans not to view immigrants as threat to national progress
body: The Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, has urged African countries to view immigrants as contributors to national development rather than threats to economic progress. He said African countries could manage migration through effective regulation while respecting free movement protocols and protecting the rights of travellers. Mr Ablakwa made the remarks during an interview on TV3 on Saturday, October 10, 2026, while reacting to renewed tensions in South Africa following developments surrounding an apex court decision on the rights of asylum seekers. “We should not see immigrants and people who travel using our free movement protocols as people who are detrimental to our national progress. They are not parasites,” he said. He argued that countries could establish arrangements that regulate migration without violating the rights of people who travel across borders. “We can have an arrangement where we have regulated migration, where the free movement protocols are respected, where the rights of all persons are not violated just because they are travellers,” he added. Describing himself as a perpetual optimist about Africa’s future, the Foreign Affairs Minister said he remained confident in the continent’s integration agenda. He reaffirmed his belief in the vision of Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, that African countries could unite politically to achieve economic emancipation. According to him, although the continent has overcome significant challenges associated with colonialism, imperialism and political subjugation, it must now intensify efforts to tackle poverty and economic underdevelopment. “We have won the battle against political subjugation, colonialism, imperialism. We now must win the war against poverty, the war against economic underdevelopment. And I believe that can be achieved,” he said.

title: Mahama Cares must fund treatment, not looting – Asogli chiefs
body: The Asogli State has welcomed the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF), popularly known as Mahama Cares, while calling for transparent and responsible management of its resources. Togbe Kasa III, speaking on behalf of the Agbogbomefia of the Asogli State, described the Fund as a laudable initiative that could bridge gaps in the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and improve access to specialised healthcare. He said the initiative offered hope to people struggling to afford essential medical treatment but cautioned against the misuse of its resources. “The Fund should not be created for people to go and loot and share, but to take care of the healthcare needs of the population,” he said. He made the remarks when the GMTF Administrator, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, paid a courtesy call on the chiefs of the Asogli State as part of the Fund’s Volta Regional sensitisation tour. Togbe Kasa III commended the Administrator and her team for involving traditional authorities in public education on the Fund’s mandate, describing the engagements as essential to building awareness and support. He expressed optimism that the Fund would complement the NHIS by improving access to specialised medical services, particularly for patients unable to afford treatment. He said its success should be measured by how effectively it improved access to care and eased the financial burden on families facing serious medical conditions. Ms Darko-Opoku thanked the chiefs for receiving the delegation and stressed the need to extend public education on the Fund to communities across the country. She explained that the sensitisation exercise sought to help Ghanaians understand the Fund’s purpose, the support it offered and how eligible patients could access its interventions. She said the Fund needed to take its message beyond institutions and directly into communities, particularly to people unaware of the specialised healthcare support available to them. Ms Darko-Opoku added that collaboration with traditional authorities and other community leaders was essential to reaching more people with accurate information. The courtesy call formed part of the GMTF’s Volta Regional sensitisation tour, which aims to strengthen stakeholder collaboration and raise awareness of its interventions. The Fund was established to support the prevention and treatment of non-communicable diseases, improve access to specialised medical care and strengthen the training of specialist health professionals.

title: NATO will cut Russia off from the Baltic. We are talking about hours
body:
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated that, in the event of a Russian attack on a NATO member state, the Alliance could close Russia’s exit to the Baltic Sea through the Gulf of Finland within a few hours. This is not just a political declaration, but another element of a scenario in which the Baltic Sea becomes one of the first areas of confrontation between NATO and the Russian Federation.
In European defence planning, the Baltic Sea is increasingly treated not as a rear area, but as a battlefield. This is determined by the short distances between NATO states and Russia, the presence of the Kaliningrad Oblast, the military importance of St Petersburg, the proximity of Finland and Estonia and the concentration of critical infrastructure. In the event of war, Russia would not have to begin with a classic land attack against the Baltic states. A more likely scenario would involve hybrid operations, sabotage, cyberattacks, attempts to disrupt shipping, pressure on ports, missile strikes and actions using the maritime component.
This is precisely why such statements by allies are so important. The Estonian minister says directly that if Russia attacked NATO and Article 5 were triggered — here the Nordic states, the Baltic states and Poland would react immediately — the Alliance would have the ability to close the exit from the Gulf of Finland within a few hours. This would mean cutting off one of Russia’s most important maritime arteries. Russian vessels leave St Petersburg through this route, the Baltic Sea maintains the connection with the Kaliningrad Oblast, and the route itself also matters for Russian exports of raw materials. For Moscow, this is a first-order theatre of war and, at the same time, an area important for the economy, logistics and demonstration of force.
It must be stressed, however, that this is not a declaration of a pre-emptive blockade. We are referring to a situation in which Russia begins military action against NATO. This is very important, because Moscow has for years portrayed the Alliance as an offensive structure, while the logic of this declaration is exactly the opposite. If Russia strikes, it will lose freedom of action in the Baltic Sea . In practice, NATO is telling Russia that the war will not be fought only where the Kremlin chooses the point of attack. Interestingly, Western countries — with France at the forefront — see the Baltic Sea precisely as the region of the first clash.
Closing the Gulf of Finland would have significance beyond the military dimension. The Baltic Sea is one of Russia’s last exits to the West. The Black Sea has already been largely constrained by the war against Ukraine, including Kyiv’s actions and Turkish control over the straits. If, in conditions of war with NATO, Russia also lost freedom of exit from St Petersburg to the Baltic Sea, it would lose its connection with the Kaliningrad Oblast, which would in any case be eliminated within several dozen minutes by strikes from Poland.
The whole discussion fits into a broader scenario that has been appearing in European military analyses for months. Russia would begin the conflict below the threshold of full-scale war, striking critical infrastructure, ports, energy systems, communications, undersea cables, civilian vessels and selected military targets precisely in the Baltic Sea.
The aim would be to paralyse the reaction of the Baltic and Nordic states, as well as to create political pressure on Western countries before the open phase of the conflict. That is why it is increasingly assumed that the fight for the Baltic cannot be based only on defending one’s own coastline. It must include the rapid limitation of Russian freedom of action at sea.
In such a scenario, frontline states would be of key importance. Estonia, Finland, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Sweden, Denmark and Norway would have to maintain infrastructure, ports, logistics, coastal defence and freedom of military movement. Support from the largest European states, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, would be necessary, but the first hours of the conflict would belong to the countries of the region. They would have to delay Russian actions, secure routes and maintain the ability to receive allied support.
The use of very large forces is assumed. In the European variant, this means around 12 divisions, or 40–50 brigades, with a total of around 200,000 soldiers. This would require at least 1,500 tanks, more than 3,500 infantry fighting vehicles, around 1,000 pieces of tube artillery and nearly 400 rocket launchers. In the air, 300–350 combat aircraft would have to be committed, together with early warning, refuelling and reconnaissance aircraft, as well as several thousand medium-range precision strike assets.
The maritime component would be one of the main elements of the response. Surface ship groups, air defence of critical infrastructure, anti-submarine warfare and the maintenance of freedom of navigation would be needed. Russia could attempt to block ports, attack the coast and slow down the reaction. NATO’s response would therefore have to include both defence and offence. NATO significantly surpasses Russia in military power.
The most important point, however, is that the Estonian declaration changes the way the Baltic is viewed. It is no longer only a question of how NATO will defend the Baltic states against a Russian strike. The more important question is how quickly the Alliance will be able to take away Russia’s ability to operate at sea. If Moscow started the conflict, closing the Gulf of Finland could become one of the first steps towards limiting the Russian fleet, exports and connection with Kaliningrad.
This is also a significant political signal. Frontline states do not want to wait passively for Russian escalation . In their thinking, defence is no longer only about absorbing a strike and waiting for support. Defence also means an immediate strike against Russia’s ability to wage war. Closing Russia’s exit to the Baltic Sea would be exactly such an action: not symbolic, but directly military.
For Poland, this discussion has direct significance. The Baltic Sea is one of the most important areas of our security, and Russian activity in the region is not limited to the Kaliningrad Oblast. If the Baltic and Nordic states openly speak about closing Russia’s access to the Baltic Sea in the event of war, Warsaw should treat this not as rhetoric, but as an element of operational planning. First, the elimination of the Kaliningrad Oblast; then blocking an attack from Belarus , as well as support for the Baltic states in the context of the Baltic Sea.
Russia may want to start a confrontation in the Baltic, but it has no guarantee that it will control its course. After Finland and Sweden joined NATO, the balance of power in the region changed significantly in favour of the Alliance. The Gulf of Finland is no longer a safe corridor for Russia, but a place that, in wartime conditions, can be quickly closed by NATO states. This is one of the most important changes on NATO’s north-eastern flank. Russia must take into account that it will meet resistance .

title: Ghana’s economic salvation lies not in shifting geo-political allegiances – Dr Atuahene
body: Ghana’s ultimate economic salvation lies not in shifting geopolitical allegiances, but in a radical domestic structural transformation, Dr Richmond Akwasi Atuahene, a Financial Analyst, has asserted. “Joining a new economic bloc will not cure the systemic vulnerabilities of the Ghanaian economy,” he explained, in an exclusive interview with Ghana News Agency (GNA). The Cabinet of Ghana is taking steps toward a BRICS application, reflecting a desire to escape Western-dominated institutional conditionalities. The BRICS is an international organisation currently comprising ten countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. The Foreign Minister, Samuel Okudzeto-Ablakwa, recently, during a joint press briefing with Indian External Affairs Minister, Dr Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, announced a Cabinet decision for Ghana to formally apply for membership of BRICS, which had generated discussions across academia, economists, civil society organisations and the public. Re-orienting Ghana’s economic destiny must be the topmost priority, Dr Atuahene, argues, rather than relying on external bodies – whether the IMF or BRICS. Ghana must dismantle the colonial-era, affectionately primed “Guggisberg economy” and replace it with a modern, self-sustaining, value-added model, the analyst said. The term “Guggisberg Economy”—coined from the legacy of colonial Governor Gordon Guggisberg—defines an economic structure optimized strictly to extract and export raw materials, while relying heavily on imported finished goods. To dismantle this century-old architecture, the corporate governance and financial performance expert alluded, Ghana must focus inward on the following structural pillars by pursuing aggressive value addition by transitioning from exporting raw cocoa beans, unrefined gold, and crude oil to processing these resources locally. Dr Atuahene noted that true resource sovereignty requires manufacturing domestic chocolate, refining gold, and expanding petrochemical industries and undertake industrialization and import substitution by prioritizing domestic production over imports—through targeted support for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and specialized industrial zones—is essential to retaining wealth within the borders. Ghana’s justification and expected benefits for joining the BRICS bloc centres, according to Dr Atuahene on diversifying its economic partnerships, resource sovereignty and industrialisation, expanding development financing and bilateral trade and adding value to its natural resources as well as global south cooperation, giving stronger voice in shaping multipolar global governance, trade policies and collective stance on climate change and food security. He said justifications why Ghana should not join the BRICS now, could be attributable to Ghana’s economic structure, which remains fundamentally deformed by a colonial-style model that relies on exporting raw materials, while importing finished goods, creating deep, recurring cycles of debt, inflation, and currency depreciation. “BRICS membership is not a magic fix for Ghana’s structural and macroeconomic problems.” The Financial Analyst underscored that Ghana’s economy remains undiversified and vulnerable to external shocks, arguably the most significant underlying cause of bad economic management and chronic instability in Ghana, in addition to revenue volatility, lack of value addition, core structural failures – raw commodity export dependence, chronic weak currency, underdeveloped manufacturing, agric-business and industrialization and the galamsey menace. Dr Atuahene recounted that Ghana sought its 17th financial assistance programme from the International Monetary Fund in 2022 (approved in May 2023) due to an overwhelming debt burden, severe macroeconomic instability, and the loss of access to international capital markets, loss of international market access, dwindling foreign reserves, weak fiscal fundamentals and overspending. He said the country is likely to offer endemic corruption to the BRICS drive over financial irregularities stemming from the loss of over GHS18 billion by 2024, prompting the launch of the National Ethics and Anti-Corruption Action Plan (2026–2030). Again, Civil society groups, including the Centre for Democratic Development (CDD), estimate that Ghana loses close to GHS 10 billion (nearly $3 billion) to corruption over multi-year cycles, with Corruption Watch tracking about GHS 9.6 billion stolen from the public purse since late 2017. Also, cash bribes according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) reported that an estimated GHS 5 billion ($320 million) was paid in cash bribes in a single year, which equals roughly one-third of the Ministry of Education’s annual budget with Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, Ghana scored 42 out of 100 (ranking 80th out of 180 countries), performing slightly better than the Sub-Saharan African average of 33, though marking a downward trend in public sector perception. He said from the above discussions the negatives outweigh the positives, which demands thoughtfulness and forthrightness. And avoid premature Dr Atuahene suggested an aggressive domestic resource mobilization by leveraging domestic financing mechanisms to fund infrastructure, agriculture, and technological upgrades, thereby reducing the fiscal exposure to foreign debt and exchange rate volatility. He postulated that external economic alliances could be tools, and not cures, indicating that “Whether aligned with the global West or the global South, Ghana will remain economically fragile as long as its core economic structure remains colonial.” Dr Atuahene, also Director of Salman Partners and Financial Consult Ltd insisted that true economic independence requires a bold domestic blueprint that transforms Ghana from a passive, rent-seeking supplier of primary commodities into a competitive producer of high-value goods, which should shape the economic imperative. “The priority must be domestic reconstruction first, and international multi-alignment second.” He said Ghana cannot negotiate its way to prosperity from foreign capitals while its Rivers run toxic, farms are destroyed and its prime human resource, the youth wander in desperation.

title: Sports events in Saudi Arabia to go ahead despite Houthi attacks
body: The situation in Saudi Arabia has been tense for many weeks, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensifying their attacks on the kingdom. Over the past week, attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports in Riyadh, Abha, Jazan and Najran caused multiple deaths and major destruction. As the kingdom faces a major security challenge, the crisis is casting a shadow over live sports. Here we take a look at where things stand in Saudi Arabia. Football (Saudi Pro League) The Saudi Pro League continued on Sunday even as Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport endured deadly attacks over the weekend, leaving 13 dead and hundreds injured. Al Shabab’s match against Al Taawoun in Riyadh went ahead, with Shabab completing a comfortable 3-0 win. Al Fayha and Al Riyadh played out a draw, but the game between Abha and Al Faisaly was postponed until later in the month. The SPL continues this Thursday. Football (Asian Champions League) Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr hosted Uzbek side Neftchi in their AFC Champions League Elite match in Riyadh on Monday. There was uncertainty surrounding the match , especially after training for the game at Al Awwal Park was called off. Kick-off was delayed due to a security alert issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence, but the match went ahead and Nassr eased to a 3-1 win . Fellow SPL heavyweights Al Ittihad are all set to take on Shabab Al Ahli in Jeddah on Tuesday. Tennis (Six Kings Slam) The world's top men’s tennis players are scheduled to compete in the third edition of the Six Kings Slam, to be shown on Netflix from October 21-24. Carlos Alcaraz , Alexander Zverev, Novak Djokovic, Alex de Minaur and Taylor Fritz are set to compete at the ANB Arena. However, defending champion Jannik Sinner has been replaced by Learner Tien in the line-up. Tickets for the tournament have gone on sale, with no changes announced so far. Earlier in the year, it was announced that the 2026 WTA Finals had been relocated from Riyadh to Indian Wells, California, after Saudi Arabia relinquished the right to host the tournament. Boxing (Alvarez v Mbilli) Boxing great Saul "Canelo" Alvarez is scheduled to take on Christian Mbilli for the WBC super middleweight title in Riyadh on October 31. There was uncertainty over the bout after several days of deadly strikes on the city. However, organiser Turki Alalshikh said Canelo would fulfil his commitment and compete in the Saudi capital. “Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Alalshikh posted on X. “He fears nothing.” Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens. He fears nothing. My country is home to the two Holy Mosques, land of peace, safety, rich civilization, deep history, and kind-hearted people. Thank you to everyone who checked in… — TURKI ALALSHIKH (@Turki_alalshikh) October 11, 2026 WWE Crown Jewel World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE)'s Crown Jewel event is set to take place on November 7 at Riyadh Season Stadium. It is the 16th event that WWE will hold in Saudi Arabia under a 10-year partnership. At the event, Roman Reigns will face Sami Zayn, while in the women’s category, Liv Morgan is scheduled to fight Chelsea Green. Riyadh Racing Season The 2026/27 racing season in Riyadh is scheduled to start on Friday and end April 17 next year. As things stand, the season is set to last six months and include 69 races. The total prize pool on offer is 197.8 million Saudi riyals. Golf (Saudi International) ⁠Golf's Asian Tour said on Tuesday that it is monitoring the ⁠security situation ahead of the Saudi International ​in Riyadh. The PIF ​Saudi ⁠International, which serves as the Asian Tour's ‌season-closer, is scheduled to take place at the Riyadh Golf Club from November 18 to 21. "Any changes to the schedule will be announced as soon as we have determined the right course of action for our players, fans and partners," the Asian Tour told Reuters in a statement. "The PIF Saudi International is incredibly important to the Asian Tour as our season finale, however the safety of our players, staff and service teams is always our number one priority."

title: BoG proposes tougher rules on loan repayment assessment‎
body: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has proposed rules requiring lenders to assess borrowers’ ability to repay loans from income and cash flows, rather than rely on collateral. ‎The proposal forms part of the draft Credit Risk Management Directive, 2026, which seeks to strengthen credit assessment, loan monitoring and the early identification of problem loans. ‎Paragraph 53 of the draft states that “collateral shall not be used as a substitute for a comprehensive assessment of repayment capacity.” ‎The proposed directive covers banks, specialised deposit-taking institutions, non-bank financial institutions and financial holding companies regulated under the relevant laws. ‎Under the rules, lenders would have to verify borrowers’ income and cash flows, assess repayment history and expenses, and determine their ability to service loans under adverse economic conditions, including rising interest rates and reduced income. ‎For businesses, assessments would cover historical financial performance, projected cash flows, management expertise, industry conditions, equity contributions and capacity to share risk. Lenders could also use alternative data and analytical tools, provided they were reliable, explainable and proportionate. ‎The draft retains collateral requirements but mandates prudent policies for its acceptance, valuation and enforceability. Lenders would also have to reassess collateral values regularly and ensure that valuations were independent of credit origination, assessment and approval. ‎“The valuation of collateral shall reflect fair values, accounting for market liquidity and realisation timeframe” the draft states. ‎Paragraph 189 further provides that collateral must not determine whether a loan is classified as non-performing ‎An exposure meeting the relevant criteria must be classified as non-performing even if the value of pledged assets exceeds the overdue amount.‎ ‎“Collateral and other mitigants may be considered in assessing unlikeliness-to-pay but shall not affect past-due counting or the determination of non-performance,” the document states. ‎The exposure draft invites stakeholder comments by November 30, 2026. ‎Regulated institutions would have until June 30, 2027, to align their governance arrangements, policies and processes with the directive, which is scheduled to take effect on July 1, 2027.

title: Saudi Arabia: Etihad and Qatar Airways Cancel Flights
body: Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways suspended flights to and from Saudi Arabian airports on Monday amid rising regional tensions. Etihad canceled services between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Dammam, and Jeddah, citing “regional unrest.” Flights to Riyadh are halted until October 19. Qatar Airways temporarily suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam “due to the current situation,” as Yemen’s Houthi rebels escalate attacks on Saudi Arabia. title: Iran Army Navy built new weapons to target US vulnerabilities
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Deputy Commander of the Iranian Army Navy Admiral Bamani has said Iran has developed new weapons designed to target America's vulnerabilities and is responding to enemy tactics with its own new approaches.
Speaking in an interview, he stated that the powerful Armed Forces of the country have learned from the experience of recent wars, and the Army Navy has proceeded to produce new weaponry in compatible with the vulnerabilities and weaknesses of the enemy.
Enemies’ threats are nothing new, he said, adding, “Islamic Republic of Iran has consistently faced threats since the beginning of the Islamic Revolution, the threats that have been voiced sometimes covertly and at other times openly.”
He claimed that following Iranian retaliatory strikes, adversaries have withdrawn significantly from Iran's maritime borders, now positioned at their greatest distance since the Iran-Iraq War.
Referring to the two wars imposed against Iran [June 13 and February 28], Rear Admiral Bamani added that the Army Navy, alongside the Navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), has at times dealt heavy blows to the American enemy, have occasionally been acknowledged by the opposing side as well.
Following these blows, US forces have moved away from Iran's maritime borders and are now positioned at the greatest distance from them compared to previous periods, he stipulated.
The deputy commander of the Army Navy also addressed the issue of the naval blockade, stating that the government is pursuing strategies to counter this situation in the political and economic spheres.

title: Ship Attacked Off Bulgaria: Second Strike Near Byala Hits Ukrainian-Managed Cargo Vessel
body: A cargo ship was struck about 15 miles off the Black Sea town of Byala, Bulgaria—the second such incident in a week. The previous attack occurred 70 km east of Byala. The vessel, the Malta-flagged Chelsea 3, is managed by Black Sea Shipping, based in Odesa, Ukraine. Twelve crew members were injured. Bulgarian authorities have not attributed the strikes to Russia. The attacks on a Ukrainian-managed ship are expected to draw close scrutiny. title: Government plans mandatory drug tests for public service jobs — Muntaka
body: The government is preparing a Cabinet memorandum to introduce mandatory drug testing for applicants seeking employment in the public service, Interior Minister Mohammed Mubarak Muntaka has announced. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Monday, October 12, 2026, Mr Muntaka said the proposed policy would initially target public service recruitment, with plans to extend it to the private sector if Cabinet approves. He said the measure could serve as a deterrent to substance abuse and discourage prospective employees from using illicit drugs. The Minister cited the recent security services recruitment exercise, during which he said more than 6,000 applicants were disqualified after failing drug tests. “We were alarmed during the security services recruitment about the number of persons we had to disqualify because they failed the drug test. We disqualified over 6,000 people due to drugs,” he said. He added that concerns about substance abuse among serving security personnel had also prompted the introduction of drug and mental health screening into recruitment procedures. Mr Muntaka expressed further concern about reports of students smuggling drugs into senior high schools to sell to their colleagues, as well as alleged illegal cannabis cultivation and the use of ambulances and bullion vans to transport the substance. He said the government was intensifying enforcement, including the destruction of illicit cannabis farms and the arrest of suspected offenders, while expanding public education in schools, churches, mosques and organised groups. He also announced plans to establish a state-owned narcotics rehabilitation centre to complement existing private facilities. Mr Muntaka urged interested persons to apply for licences to cultivate and trade in industrial cannabis, saying regulated production could strengthen oversight and help curb illegal activities. Ghana’s existing framework, comprising the Narcotics Control Commission (Amendment) Act, 2023 (Act 1100), and the Narcotics Control Commission Regulations, 2023 (L.I. 2475), provides for licensed cannabis cultivation with THC content not exceeding 0.3 per cent for industrial and medicinal purposes.

title: Finland mostly sunny on Tuesday — ahead of rain on Wednesday
body:
On Tuesday night, temperatures across many parts of the country will dip below zero degrees.
Much of Finland will see mostly sunny conditions on Tuesday, but the weather will take a rainy turn on Wednesday, with slightly milder temperatures.
Some areas will be partly cloudy on Tuesday, particularly Lapland.
Daytime high temperatures in southern areas will rise to around +8 degrees Celsius, while in central parts of the country it will be around +5 degrees. Temperatures in some northern areas will remain below the freezing point.
Then on Tuesday night, temperatures across many parts of the country will dip below zero degrees.
Milder conditions will return on Wednesday, raising the temperature by a few degrees.
But precipitation will accompany those slightly warmer temperatures, bringing rain to nearly all of Finland on Wednesday. Up in Lapland the precipitation may arrive in the form of snow.
Driving conditions in Lapland may be poor due to the anticipated snow and sleet.

title: Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Porfirije Visits Australia
body: Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Porfirije visits Australia for the first time in his role as patriarch, with Senator Alex Antic welcoming His Holiness to Parliament House. Antic shared details of the visit in a statement on X, saying he had the honour of speaking at Parliament House to mark the patriarch’s first pastoral visit to Australia. The South Australian senator highlighted the significant presence of Orthodox Christians across the country, noting that Australia is home to almost 95,000 Serbian Orthodox Christians and more than 535,000 Orthodox Christians overall. “Many Orthodox believers here in Australia take great courage and hope from the Serbian Orthodox Church’s profound witness throughout history of faithfulness in the midst of hardship,” Antic wrote. He also thanked Patriarch Porfirije for visiting Parliament that morning. Serbian Orthodox Community in Australia The visit recognises the Serbian Orthodox Church’s longstanding religious and cultural presence in Australia, where Serbian communities have established parishes and institutions across multiple states. For Serbian Orthodox Christians, a patriarchal pastoral visit provides an opportunity to gather with their spiritual leader, strengthen ties with the Church and celebrate their faith and traditions. Patriarch Porfirije leads the Serbian Orthodox Church, which has a long history in the Balkans and among Serbian communities around the world. His visit to Australia brings that connection into focus for the country’s Serbian Orthodox faithful and the wider Orthodox Christian community. Source: Senator Alex Antic, X. The post Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Porfirije Visits Australia appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Media urged to intensify awareness campaigns on breast cancer
body: The media has been urged to strengthen advocacy and partnerships aimed at creating awareness on breast cancer to help reduce its impact on individuals, families and communities. Mrs Beatrice Wiafe Addai, President of Breast Care International (BCI), who made the call, said sustained public education remained the most effective way of encouraging women to undertake regular breast self-examinations and seek early detection and treatment. She said this would help reduce the number of deaths associated with the disease in the country. Speaking at the 2026 Annual Walk for the Cure organised by BCI at Asante Mampong, Mrs Wiafe Addai stressed that breast cancer was not a death sentence and should not be associated with spiritual causes. She said increased collaboration among stakeholders would promote early detection and treatment while giving greater visibility to breast cancer survivors whose experiences continued to inspire patients and strengthen awareness campaigns. This year’s walk, which began from St Monica’s Schools, was held on the theme: “Our Walk, Our Fight, Our Future.” The event, described as one of the country’s largest breast cancer awareness campaigns, attracted schoolchildren, health professionals, security personnel, representatives of institutions and members of the public. It was sponsored by the Kempinski Hotel, Delta Airlines, and other partners. Mrs Wiafe Addai noted that survivors of breast cancer served as a source of hope to patients and urged women to seek early medical attention whenever they noticed unusual changes in their breasts. She also called for the elimination of myths and misconceptions surrounding the disease and encouraged men to actively support the fight against breast cancer, noting that its effects extended beyond women alone. Madam Roslaine Hakiki, General Manager of Kempinski, Nairobi, Kenya, said the company would continue to partner BCI in promoting breast cancer awareness and supporting treatment initiatives in Ghana. She said breast cancer awareness and treatment remained among the company’s priority social interventions and pledged continued support for oncology training in the country. Daasebre Osei Bonsu II, Paramount Chief of Asante-Mampong, called on men to support women in the fight against breast cancer. He urged BCI to extend its awareness campaigns to more communities to promote early detection and treatment of the disease. The Paramount Chief also pledged his support for the campaign and encouraged other traditional leaders to contribute to efforts aimed at saving lives through breast cancer education. Mrs Vivian Gyasi Sarfo, a 21-year-old breast cancer survivor, advised women to seek prompt medical attention whenever they experienced abnormalities or discomfort in their breasts. She identified stigmatisation as one of the challenges faced by breast cancer patients and appealed to the media to help address the problem through public education. Mrs Sarfo also urged husbands and family members not to abandon women diagnosed with breast cancer but to provide the support needed for their recovery.

title: Oman to open duty-free shops at land border crossings
body:

Lieutenant General Hassan bin Mohsin al Shraiqi, Inspector General of Police and Customs, has issued Decision 145/2026 regarding the establishment of duty-free shops at the Al-Wajajah, Khatmat Malaha, and Rub' al-Khali (Empty Quarters) border crossings.
The decision is aimed at stimulating economic and commercial activity at these land crossings by offering products and goods at competitive prices, exempt from customs duties and taxes in accordance with approved regulations.
