title: Meet the US generals and admirals advancing Israeli policy
body:
JINSA and its American 'people' have taken credit for a number of recent legislative efforts, including the controversial NDAA Section 219
In August, the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) publicly took credit for shaping “multiple provisions” now in this year’s defense policy bill, stating that many were “impacted by prior JINSA policy recommendations,” including “proposals to strengthen U.S.-Israel defense industrial base integration” and “renew pre-existing joint U.S.-Israel programs.”
Among the provisions JINSA takes credit for is the controversial Section 219 . In the House version of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), this section mandates the creation of a single executive agent tasked with “synchronizing cooperative efforts” between the U.S. and Israel across nine basket categories, including AI, quantum technology, biotechnology, and virtually every category of weapons.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has argued that such provisions would transition the U.S.-Israel security relationship from aid to partnership. But pro-Israel advocates have emphasized the leverage it would provide over Washington’s military policy.
Mark Dubowitz, the CEO of the pro-Israel Foundation for Defense of Democracies, appeared to reference this provision in an article arguing that the U.S. and Israel must “deepen their military, technological, intelligence and economic integration to such an extent that inflicting financial harm on Israel would also carry a significant cost for Washington.”
Other initiatives JINSA has advocated for likewise read like an Israeli government wishlist. They include a pending provision to “extend the existing War Reserve Stockpile Authority for Israel,” which provides a secretive and high-speed pathway for funneling weapons to Israel, as well as Abraham Accords provisions including “Improvements to Air and Missile Defense Acquisition” and a “United States-Abraham Accords Defense Cooperation Initiative.”
The policy wins JINSA is trumpeting are a result of its strong foothold within the military-industrial complex, and are perhaps one of the most overlooked aspects of the pro-Israel lobby. The group says it achieves these goals “by conducting both educational programs that build ties among American, Israeli and other Middle Eastern partner military leaders, along with in-depth research and actionable recommendations to influence U.S. policy.” JINSA’s “Our People” webpage includes a long roster of retired U.S. military officials.
One of JINSA’s most important programs, which has existed for more than four decades, is its “Generals and Admirals Program.” The initiative involves flying recently retired U.S. military officials to Israel. Many of the trip’s participants were already sitting on defense-industry boards when they went, while others joined soon afterward. At least 55 of the 83 alumni from the 2019–2026 G&A program cohorts (about 66%) have held or currently hold positions in the defense industry spanning board seats, executive jobs or advisory roles at defense contractors and defense-tech firms, or posts at defense-focused investment funds, consultancies and lobbying shops.
JINSA hopes that, when these former military officials return from Israel, they will use their credentials and defense industry power to become Israel’s advocates.
JINSA describes the program, founded in 1981, as “designed to ensure that the delegation is well briefed on the security concerns of Israel, as well as the key role Israel plays as a friend and ally of the United States.” The Helmsley Charitable Trust, which provided a 13 month grant for the program in 2017 worth $237,846, similarly says the purpose of the program is in part for participants to “return home to share publicly what they learned.”
The itinerary for the Generals and Admirals program includes meetings with Israel’s prime minister, defense minister, IDF chief of staff and the Director of Mossad. According to JINSA, after completing the program, “participants often engage on important policy initiatives through JINSA’s Gemunder Center for Defense and Strategy that strengthen…the U.S.-Israel security relationship.” JINSA CEO Michael Makovsky highlighted the program’s influence in 2014, calling U.S. generals and admirals “America’s most admired leaders, who remain very influential even after retirement.”
The JINSA program trains retired military leaders, many of whom go on to work in the defense industry, to be advocates for Israeli interests, both in their public writing and in their work behind the scenes.
A 2023 Quincy Institute report found that 80% of four-star officers who retired between June 2018 and July 2023 went on to work for the defense industry. Of the 32 officers tracked in the report, nine appear on JINSA’s participant lists, and seven of those nine retired officers hold industry lobbying or defense-tech roles. Gen. Joseph Dunford, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, joined Lockheed Martin’s board five months after leaving the military and went on JINSA’s Israel junket the following year, 2021. Adm. Michael S. Rogers, the former NSA director and head of U.S. Cyber Command, retired in 2018, became a senior adviser at the lobbying and public relations firm Brunswick Group in 2019 and went on the JINSA trip in 2021.
Gen. Hawk Carlisle participated in the 2019 delegation while serving as president and CEO of the National Defense Industrial Association, the war lobby’s leading trade group, and has served on the board of the U.S. subsidiary of Israel’s largest defense contractor, Elbit Systems of America, which was renamed Twenty-Six Defense in September. Some participants, such as retired Gen. Robert Magnus and Gen. Duncan McNabb , joined the board of Elbit America after their JINSA trips.
Embedded within the highest levels of the most powerful lobby on Capitol Hill, JINSA’s roster of retired generals and admirals often use their credentials to advocate for pro-Israel policy in Washington.
In 2010, when then-head of U.S. Central Command Gen. David Petraeus testified to the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Israel-Palestine conflict “foments anti-American sentiment, due to a perception of U.S. favoritism for Israel,” which is used to “mobilize support” for various militant groups in the region, JINSA’s G&A participants rushed to Israel’s defense. Responding to Petraeus, 30 ex-military leaders associated with the program put out an ad claiming that “a strong, secure Israel is an asset,” labeling the country, which has been deemed an apartheid state by numerous human rights groups , as “a democracy” that “shares our commitment to freedom, personal liberty and rule of law.”
In May 2018, a JINSA task force of retired senior officers chaired by Adm. James Stavridis released “ Atlas Supported ,” urging Washington to elevate Israel to “a top-tier ally” and invest jointly in next-generation military technology — the latter now a central purpose of Section 219. JINSA says the report was also the first to recommend moving Israel from the U.S. European Command to U.S. Central Command, which Trump then ordered on January 15, 2021. JINSA celebrated the fifth anniversary of Israel’s shift into CENTCOM this January by noting that the “Wall Street Journal recognized” it as “the only organization promoting this move,” and by featuring glowing tributes from JINSA G&A participants.
JINSA’s roster of retired military officials was once again mobilized in October 2026 to deny the findings of a trifecta of human rights groups and the U.N. that Israel committed a genocide in Gaza, praising what it called a “pattern of law-abiding IDF conduct in Gaza.”
JINSA’s delegates routinely appear on cable news, often without disclosures of their affiliation with the pro-Israel lobby group: Gen. Kenneth “Frank” McKenzie, who commanded CENTCOM from 2019 to 2022 and traveled with JINSA’s 2023 delegation, and became a “distinguished fellow” at JINSA in 2024, is now a CBS News contributor. In July, McKenzie appeared on Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, who introduced McKenzie as a retired CENTCOM commander but omitted his fellowship with JINSA. In that appearance, McKenzie recommended Washington consider seizing Kharg Island. Ret. Vice Admiral Robert Harward, a member of JINSA’s “Iran Policy Project,” frequently appears on Fox News too, though his affiliation is generally disclosed.
One of the group’s most consequential efforts was to push the Trump administration to start a war with Iran , with a group of JINSA-aligned military leaders writing a March 2025 letter arguing that “U.S. support for Israeli action to prevent a nuclear Iran should be a top priority,” adding that “time is running out to stop its march to the bomb.” Sixty-six of the 79 signers of that letter appear on JINSA’s Generals and Admirals participant lists. Members of JINSA’s roster of retired military officials subsequently wrote open letters of support for the 12-Day War and the current months-long Iran War.

Aviv Kohavi, Israel Defense Forces Chief of General Staff, left, attend a briefing at U.S. Central Command headquarters, June 22, 2021. title: Former UK diplomat: My return from Russia became a nightmare
body:
I was held for hours and forced to submit to a DNA test upon my return to Heathrow from an international conference
Britain is clamping down even harder on critics who consider Western foreign policy to have been a catastrophic failure. We are fast approaching the point where expressing an alternative opinion can land you in jail.
On the night of October 2, while exiting a flight from Moscow via Istanbul, I was detained by UK counter-terrorism police for three hours under the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2026 . I had no right to remain silent, my person and possessions were thoroughly searched, I provided fingerprints and a DNA sample, and was required to give up my electronic devices and provide my passwords or face arrest.
This was a “suspicionless” detention. I was not suspected of anything, yet police officers were empowered to subject me to an intrusive examination to assess whether I was planning a “hostile act” against the United Kingdom.
An officer approached me and immediately took me into custody after I informed him that I had been to a conference in Russia to discuss geopolitics. I was not told why I was being detained, except that he wanted to ask me “a few questions.” Bizarrely, he pointed out that the “counter-terrorism” powers he was using “aren’t as scary as they sound.”
I had attended the International Valdai Discussion Club Conference in Moscow Region from September 27 to October 1, including attending President Vladimir Putin’s keynote address. I participated at the invitation of the Valdai Club, which provided my flight and accommodations, as is standard practice for foreign guest attendees at such international conferences.
The Valdai Club, founded in 2004, is primarily a meeting of academics from all over the world. Before the Russian invasion of Ukraine, it was attended by a former Head of MI6, former British Ambassador to Russia Sir Tony Brenton, and Fiona Hill.
Valdai has found itself in the British government’s crosshairs. Throughout September, a host of journalists and academics have received letters from the UK Home Office inviting them to register with the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme , if they are “being directed to carry out relevant activities in the UK as part of an arrangement with a foreign power.”’ Non-compliance with the scheme is considered a criminal offense.
British journalist Mary Dejevsky, who was The Times Bureau Chief in Moscow in the 1990s, is the latest to receive such a letter as a publicly listed contributor to the Valdai Discussion Club , though she has not attended since the war began. The idea that if you attend an academic conference you are being directed by a foreign power is patently absurd. Nevertheless, and given the obvious risks, I wrestled with the dilemma of whether I should accept the invitation from Valdai and make my first visit to Russia since I drove out of that country in February 2019 at the end of my four-and-a-half year diplomatic posting there.
My primary role then was as the Economic Counsellor responsible among other things for sanctions policy. After my return to the UK, I authorized around 1000 sanctions against Russians, including after the war broke out.
I had some concerns that my role in sanctions may cause me problems once inside Russia (indeed, I was subjected to an extremely stressful four-and-a-half-hour detention and interrogation by the FSB upon arrival in Moscow).
Sir Tony Brenton, with whom I had consulted, suggested that I should attend, saying that Valdai was an “excellent event.” Upon his advice, I notified the UK Foreign Office, underscoring my commitment to abide by my obligations under the Official Secrets Act before I left for Moscow. This included confirmation that while Valdai had paid for my flights, I had not received any payment for my attendance.
I served as a British diplomat for 24 years and I take seriously my ongoing commitments to preserve the secrets that I had access to during that time. The suggestion that I might plan a hostile act against Britain is offensive and wrong. However, since my retirement in 2023, I have been an outspoken critic of the direction of UK foreign policy towards Russia, notably the departure from diplomacy in favor of war.
The important and necessary precautions that I had taken were insufficient to prevent me from being detained with fewer rights than had I been formally arrested and cautioned. I am of the view that security figures in London had authorized the action against me ahead of time. Indeed, Russia commentator Mark Galeotti suggested on his podcast that the system was “making a statement” by acting in this way.
(Editor’s Note: A request by RS to the UK’s Counter Terrorism Policing for comment about the author’s detention — for which he provided RS with documentation – went unanswered as of this writing.)
My detention marks the latest escalation in the British state’s war on free speech. Increasingly, people who speak out publicly against forever wars — not only in Ukraine, but also in the Middle East and elsewhere — are seen as a threat to national security that must be quashed.
Airport detentions are one step short of full-blown imprisonment, of course, but this pattern of intimidation has been spreading over the past four years.
British conservative academic and author John Laughland was detained at an airport for one hour in 2022. The late Robert Skidelsky, a member of the House of Lords and esteemed British economist, and investigative reporter Kit Klarenberg were subject to more lengthy and rigorous detentions in 2023. Klarenberg still has not received back an SD memory card that was confiscated at the time.
Professor Richard Sakwa , Emeritus at Kent University, was detained for three hours at Heathrow in 2025; he has only been able to return to Russia since that time following an intervention by his lawyer. George Szamuely, a Hungarian-born British political analyst, was detained in March 2026.
In 2023, Craig Murray , former British ambassador to Uzbekistan, was detained for an hour at Glasgow Airport under the tougher provisions of the Terrorism Act 2000 , which is concerned with activity related to the commission, preparation and instigation of acts of terrorism. His phone was not returned to him afterwards.
Investigative journalist Richard Medhurst was arrested for making statements in support of a proscribed pro-Palestine organization and held for 24 hours before his release. His home and office in Austria were subsequently raided in February 2025 and he was accused of membership of Hamas. To date, no charges have been laid against him.
More broadly, in Britain, the group Palestine Action has been proscribed as a terrorist organization following widespread protests against the gross violations of international humanitarian law by the Israeli state in Gaza. Elderly people, including Holocaust survivors, have been arrested at Palestine Action protests for the crime of holding cardboard placards.
The practice of suspicionless airport detention is uncommon in European states, although alternative, more insidious forms of repression of free speech are employed. Former Swiss military intelligence officer and author Jacques Baud remains in Brussels, de-banked and unable to travel home, having been sanctioned by the European Union for “pro-Russian propaganda.”
This past week, Russian-born journalist and former BBC reporter Leonid Ragozin was declared persona non grata by Latvia, where he has lived since the onset of the Ukraine crisis. Having criticized the direction of Western foreign policy toward the war in Ukraine, he has also been a regular Putin critic and described the 2022 invasion of Ukraine as “criminal and irrational.”
This pattern of repressing free speech in Britain and more broadly in Europe is growing. I fear that the more obvious it becomes that the war in Ukraine cannot be won by the West and that Israel cannot remain insulated from international censure over its actions in Palestine, actions by the British state may become even harsher.
We are reaching the point where offering an opinion on the perilous state of Western foreign wars can land you in prison.
I thought I had been careful in notifying the British government before my sole visit to Russia since 2019. If the UK is at the point where former diplomats can be detained and have their property temporarily confiscated, then no one is safe from the long arm of lawfare.
Upon my return from Valdai, I wrote again to the Foreign Office, offering to brief them in full on the insights I gained while I was in Russia. To date, they have not replied.

title: 'Major wipeout' of 2006 proportions could force a new GOP reckoning
body:
Crushed by a blue midterm wave, it took years of war for Republicans to start turning against George W. Bush. Trump is way ahead of the game.
Republicans could be looking at a major wipeout in the midterm elections.
Their tiny House majority was always going to be difficult to maintain, but the Senate should not be in play at all. Yet it surely is, with Democrats leading in nearly all the toss-up races , including in the reddest states, and competitive in at least a dozen of the contests that will determine which party controls the upper chamber.
The Iran war is a big reason this has come to pass. It has demoralized the least indefatigably partisan part of President Donald Trump’s coalition by abandoning his promise to avoid new forever wars in the Middle East . The conflict has not only distracted from the affordability focus that many voters were expecting when they threw out the Democrats in 2024, but also directly cuts against it by spiking energy prices and increasing inflation overall at a time when it might have otherwise continued to come down.
Among voters, this war has virtually no Democratic support . It is overwhelmingly opposed by independents. A critical mass of Republicans never were in favor of the war, and many of its GOP supporters wanted it to be over quickly, as Trump repeatedly promised.
Trump himself was seemingly ready to end the war by June, but has been unable to restore the Strait of Hormuz to the pre-war status quo despite attempting a series of escalations, ceasefires, and negotiations, including the failed memorandum of understanding signed by both Iran and the United States on June 17.
Trump never really tried to persuade the general public to support the war, at least not in any sustained way. He ignored Iran in a pre-Christmas primetime address last year that was supposed to represent his pivot to the economy. He barely mentioned the Islamic Republic in his State of the Union address. He delivered his first primetime address on the war more than a month after it started. And he never sought congressional authorization for the use of force, even though Republicans controlled both houses of Congress.
Republicans were probably always going to lose congressional seats this year. History since 1938 favors the party that doesn’t hold the White House in these elections, and elements of Trump’s coalition are low-propensity voters, especially when he isn’t on the ballot himself, while Never Trumpers will turn out to cast anti-Trump protest votes against Republicans no matter what.
Yet before the war there was still a good chance that the actual election-day result for Democrats would be underwhelming, just as it was for Republicans in President Joe Biden’s midterm election in 2022. The blue wave, like the red wave before it, could have been limited to a trickle. Eighty-six percent of House Republicans represent districts that went for Trump by at least 10 points, a structural advantage they sought to buttress through mid-decade redistricting in red states. The path to control of the Senate similarly ran through states Trump had won in 2024, often by double digits.
But thanks to the Iran war and its fallout, there is a potential for a midterm election more like 2006. Twenty years ago, as Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter pointed out earlier this year, we had an unpopular president waging an unpopular war while Republican congressional incumbents were beset by assorted scandals.
Today, the public has even less patience for the current war than in 2006.
Just look how quickly Republicans in tight races have equivocated in their support for the Iran war compared to Iraq 20 years ago. And Iraq had been going on longer with more American casualties by the time of the 2006 midterm elections.
Hawkish Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, the sort of candidate who held onto the fiction that victory was always around the corner in Iraq two decades ago, is already singing a different tune . “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Rogers, who is running in one of the country’s most competitive races, said in an ad back in September. “Michigan families can’t afford to wait.”
The economic costs of the war are undeniable even to its remaining supporters, and are being inflicted on an electorate that has been angry about the high cost of living for at least five years. It took the combination of Iraq and the 2007-08 economic meltdown for Bush’s popularity to finally wane among congressional Republicans late in his second term. Thanks to the preexisting economic conditions, as well as Trump’s fraught relationship with the remnants of the old GOP establishment, we are running ahead of schedule with Iran.
But if the worst happens to Republicans in November, many will be eager to blame the tariffs rather than the war. The tariffs can be more squarely pinned on Trump and MAGA, and the people and policy assumptions behind them can be more easily excised from the party than the long-entrenched interventionism that Trump was supposed to excise and didn’t.
The tariffs, and their haphazard implementation, are surely a big part of the equation. But the war raised prices beyond imported goods, illustrated Trump’s lack of interest in domestic issues during his second term, and made the tariffs’ bite worse.
The war has also complicated things for Vice President JD Vance, who by many accounts was the senior administration official most skeptical of starting the war in the first place. Trump was able to unite Republicans with disparate foreign-policy views because he seemed to appreciate the futility of much of what the U.S. has attempted to accomplish in the Middle East over the past quarter-century without appearing hostile to Israel or fearful of potential adversaries in the region. After Iran, less interventionist Republicans may want to hear Vance make stronger criticisms of neoconservatives or Israel that could divide the party.
Hawks will still take aim at Vance, sensing he is not one of them. Doves may be reluctant to come to his aid, fearing he is not one of them either. There is also an opening for one of two Republican Kentuckians, Sen. Rand Paul or soon-to-be-former Congressman Thomas Massie, to run an antiwar primary campaign, though probably not both.
Paul and Massie both owe their congressional careers to the movement-building GOP presidential candidacies of former Congressman Ron Paul, the senator’s father. Massie in particular would have little chance of winning the nomination for the same reasons he lost his congressional primary earlier this year, but one of them could conceivably help rebuild the libertarian wing of the party, currently in disrepair.
It’s possible that being attacked by neoconservatives as too dovish and by libertarians as too hawkish will help Vance convince ordinary Republicans that he is just right. He has shown great political skill in managing his relationship with Trump. His most touted potential rival, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is just as closely associated with the administration and much more associated with the assumptions behind the Iran war, if not the decision to go to war itself.
There’s a chance that the war will be over by 2028 and seen as a chastening experience by Republicans. They might have reached their limit with the party’s pro-war posture after Trump and George W. Bush threw away their tremendous political opportunities to wage wars in the Middle East that ended up costing the party its congressional majorities. But there is no guarantee on either front. And the Republicans' structural electoral advantages could still mitigate the electoral reckoning that appears to be headed their way this year.

title: China invites Russian Knights to Airshow China in Zhuhai
body:
BEIJING, October 13. /TASS/. China has invited the Russian Knights aerobatic team to the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, known as Airshow China, in Zhuhai in the southern province of Guangdong this December, the city’s mayor Wu Zetong said.
"The Russian Knights aerobatic team will perform at the upcoming airshow again. The team is well known to audiences, having participated in Airshow China seven times since 1998. Its virtuoso performances have left a deep impression on the public and won widespread affection," he said at a news conference in response to a TASS question.
Wu stressed that expanding international participation is "the main direction for Airshow China’s development." He said the flying displays will be "even more spectacular," with pilots from the United Arab Emirates joining the Russian Knights. "For the first time since 2016, two foreign military aerobatic teams will participate in Airshow China together," he added.
The Bayi Aerobatic Team of China’s People’s Liberation Army Air Force will also "perform an aerial ballet" alongside them, the mayor said.
China’s largest aviation and aerospace exhibition takes place in the coastal city of Zhuhai, attracting hundreds of companies from several countries. Russian defense companies regularly participate. The exhibition focuses on military and civilian aircraft, space, navigation and radar equipment, aircraft weapons, rocket engines, fire control systems and air defenses. Its 16th edition will run from December 7 to 13.

title: Massive Russian attack on Kharkiv: Eight injured, entrance section of residential building destroyed
body:
Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
"A 19-year-old man is in the intensive care unit for burn victims, and another man is undergoing surgery," he wrote.
According to preliminary information, Syniehubov said Russian forces used 10 missiles of the Banderol type to attack civilian infrastructure in the city.
In the Kholodnohirskyi district, a four-story residential building was hit, destroying an entire entrance section. At least 10 private houses were also reported damaged.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, Russian forces struck a five-story residential building. A bank office on the ground floor and six cars caught fire. Window glazing in three apartment buildings was also damaged.
"Emergency rescue operations are continuing at the sites of the enemy strikes. People may be trapped under the rubble. State Emergency Service units, emergency medical teams, and the National Police are working at the scene. Law enforcement officers are checking houses and apartments to identify people who may need medical assistance," Syniehubov said.
As previously reported, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russian forces attacked Kharkiv on the evening of October 12 with nine S-8000 Banderol loitering munitions.

title: IRGC chief warns against foreign meddling in Persian Gulf
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – No extra-regional power has the right to threaten the Persian Gulf region, the IRGC chief says.
Major General Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps, said in a social media post that no extra-regional power has the right to threaten, have a domineering presence, or intervene in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf.

title: IMF Warns Europe’s Growth Will Slow as Russia’s War, Middle East Crisis Drive Up Energy Costs
body:
Economic growth in the eurozone is expected to slow to just 1.1% in 2026 as Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine and escalating conflict in the Middle East push energy prices higher, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned in its latest World Economic Outlook.
The forecast, released Tuesday, Oct. 13, represents a modest 0.2-percentage-point upgrade from July but remains below the 1.2% growth recorded in 2025.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The IMF expects the eurozone economy to expand by only 1.2% in 2027, with persistently high energy costs, weak consumer confidence and inflation continuing to constrain economic activity.
The Fund forecasts eurozone inflation at 3.1% this year and 2.8% next year – both significantly above the European Central Bank’s 2% target.
The figures underscore Europe’s vulnerability to energy disruptions as Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine and instability across the Middle East threatens global oil and natural gas supplies.
The IMF warned that elevated energy costs could continue weighing on European households and businesses through next year.
Europe remains particularly vulnerable because many of its economies depend heavily on imported oil and natural gas.
The Fund warned that gas storage levels in parts of Europe remain below normal seasonal levels, potentially exposing consumers to further price increases during the winter heating season.
The combination of higher energy costs and persistent inflation could force the European Central Bank to maintain restrictive interest rates, limiting household spending and business investment.
The IMF expects underlying inflation to return to the ECB’s 2% target only around mid-2028, suggesting that price pressures could persist even if economic growth remains weak.
The latest projections also follow a volatile period for the eurozone economy, which recorded no growth in the first quarter of 2026 before rebounding by 2.6% in the second quarter.
The IMF projects significant differences among Europe’s largest economies.
Germany, the EU’s biggest economy, is expected to grow by 1.3% in 2026, while Spain is forecast to maintain stronger expansion of 2.5%.
France faces a much weaker outlook, with growth projected at just 0.4%, compared with 0.9% in 2025.
French unemployment is expected to rise to 8.4%, up from 7.7% last year.
For Britain, the IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.3%, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from July.
However, UK growth is expected to slow to 1.2% in 2027 as higher energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on consumption and investment.
The diverging forecasts reflect the uneven economic consequences of energy shocks and financial pressures across Europe.
During the World Economic Outlook press briefing , IMF officials said the economic consequences of the Middle East conflict differ sharply between oil-producing and oil-importing countries.
An IMF official said the Fund had revised its forecasts shortly before publication to account for higher oil prices, while warning that further escalation could worsen the outlook.
“We actually revised in the last minute almost our forecast to incorporate the higher oil prices,” the official said.
For Gulf oil exporters, the IMF forecasts a sharp contraction in production and exports, followed by a strong rebound in 2027, assuming conditions develop as projected.
Some of these economies are also experiencing slower growth in non-oil sectors.
Oil-importing countries, however, received modest forecast upgrades in several cases, supported by domestic demand, remittances and tourism.
Egypt was among the countries benefiting from upward revisions for both 2026 and 2027, partly because of a recovery in Suez Canal activity and petroleum-related industries.
But officials warned that renewed Houthi attacks and disruptions around the Bab al-Mandab Strait could jeopardize regional trade, shipping and economic activity.
The IMF also highlighted the growing importance of artificial intelligence in sustaining international trade despite geopolitical instability.
Responding to questions from Bloomberg and Reuters about whether the global economy could face a recession if the AI investment boom collapsed, an IMF official said demand for AI-related products had made a substantial contribution to trade growth.
Global trade expanded by a cumulative 8.3% between 2023 and 2025, while trade in AI-related goods increased by 29%.
Without AI-related products, overall trade growth would have reached just 4.6%, according to the Fund’s calculations.
The IMF outlined several possible scenarios for the technology boom.
In the most favorable case, continued investment in AI would generate genuine productivity improvements, strengthening economic activity without adding to inflation.
A less favorable scenario would see investment and demand remain strong without corresponding productivity gains, producing weaker growth benefits and greater inflationary pressure.
The Fund is also examining the consequences of investors reassessing expected profits from AI, potentially triggering a correction in asset prices.
The IMF’s latest assessment suggests that the technology sector has become an increasingly important source of global economic resilience, even as its future contribution remains uncertain.

title: Bryan Cranston leads tributes to Breaking Bad co-star RJ Mitte: 'I’ll miss you, son'
body: RJ Mitte, best known for playing Walter White Jr in Breaking Bad , has died aged 34. The American actor died on Monday in Brownsville, Texas. "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," a representative for Mitte said. The actor appeared in all five seasons of hit drama Breaking Bad , which ran from 2008 to 2013, playing the teenage son of Bryan Cranston ’s chemistry teacher turned drug dealer. Mitte and his character had cerebral palsy. The role brought him international recognition and provided a platform for his work advocating for people with disabilities, including greater representation in the entertainment industry. Cranston was among those who paid tribute, remembering Mitte’s enthusiasm for acting and the years they spent working together. “I’ll miss you, son,” he wrote on Instagram. View this post on Instagram Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman in the series, also expressed his sadness. “RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed,” he said. Dean Norris, who played Hank Schrader, recalled looking out for Mitte as a young actor on set and said he would be greatly missed. Oh my God! Was working just found out about RJ I am heartbroken Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and… — Dean Norris (@deanjnorris) October 12, 2026 Tributes also came from his co-stars on Switched at Birth , including actress and disability rights advocate Marlee Matlin. “My heart is shattered. There will never be another like RJ Mitte,” she wrote on Instagram. View this post on Instagram Lea Thompson, who also worked with Mitte on the series, remembered him as “joyous, professional and kind”, and said his work had inspired many people. Born and raised in Jackson, Mississippi, Mitte was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at the age of three. He moved to Los Angeles in 2006 and took small television roles before joining Breaking Bad as a teenager. He appeared in 56 episodes and was part of the cast that won the Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding ensemble in a drama series in 2014. His other TV credits include Now Apocalypse and The Guardians of Justice . On film, he appeared in The Recall and The Oak Room , among other projects. In the 2021 drama Triumph , he played a high school student with cerebral palsy determined to become a wrestler, continuing his work portraying characters whose experiences reflected aspects of his own. Away from acting, Mitte served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s, as well as leading the Mitte Foundation and supporting philanthropic and community initiatives. His representatives highlighted his efforts to challenge stereotypes and improve opportunities for people with disabilities.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo's 981st goal helps Al Nassr win as Al Ain go top of AFC Champions League
body: Cristiano Ronaldo was on the scoresheet as Al Nassr got their AFC Champions League Elite campaign back on track with a comfortable win over Neftchi Fergana. Ronaldo scored the second of Nassr's goals just before the break after Angelo Gabriel had given the hosts a 33rd-minute lead. Alishev Odilov had reduced the deficit in the 51st minute before an Anvarjon Gofurov own goal sealed a 3-1 victory for Nassr. Kick-off was delayed at Al Awwal Park due to a security alert issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence. Riyadh has suffered a series of ​deadly ​attacks ‌by the ⁠Iran-aligned Houthis over the past week. Supporters were allowed to remain in their seats as authorities carried out safety protocols before the match kicked off 20 minutes after it was scheduled. Ronaldo, 41, was spotted kissing the badge on his shirt during the warm-up. He was also pictured holding the shirt up to his face to cover his eyes in an emotional moment. The Portuguese superstar scored the 981st goal of his career in the 42nd minute, latching on to a knockdown from Ayman Yahya in the area before firing past Neftchi goalkeeper Botirali Ergashev. ⚽️🔥 كريستيانو رونالدو يواصل هوايته المفضلة ويضيف الهدف الثاني للنصر! #دوري_أبطال_آسيا_للنخبة #ACLElite pic.twitter.com/eF5WyuKIdp — beIN SPORTS (@beINSPORTS) October 12, 2026 "Important win tonight. We keep building," Ronaldo posted in a message on his social media channels after the match. Angelo broke the deadlock in the 33rd minute, meeting a cross inside the box and turning the ball into the net to give Al Nassr the lead. Odilov capitalised on a Nawaf Boushal blunder to spark life back into the Uzbek champions in the 51st minute, but a red card shown to Ali Bayev for violent conduct after he caught Nassr defender Mohamed Simakan swung momentum back in Nassr's favour. @Cristiano 🤍📸 #النصر_نيفيتشي pic.twitter.com/oZ7MbgSqu4 — ALOSAIMI 📸 (@motim_osm) October 12, 2026 Nassr made the extra man count on 78 minutes. Bojan Cecer turned the ball into his own net, handing the Saudi champions all three points and their first win in this season's competition after they were routed 4-0 in their first match at Al Ain . Ange Postecoglou revealed after the match that he had been worried about his players' mental state before the match following the deadly attacks on Riyadh. “I was worried about the players during the match because I care about them, but I was very happy with the professionalism they showed,” the Australian told reporters. Postecoglou said the club will monitor injuries to Kingsley Coman and Mohamed Simakan. French forward Coman was forced off injured after only 13 minutes, while Simakan was withdrawn following the red-card challenge by Bayev. Al Ain go top with big win in Basrah Al Ain maintained their 100 per cent start to the league phase with a thumping win over Iraq's Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basrah. Houssine Rahimi struck twice as Al Ain raced to a 4-0 lead at the break, as the former champions cruised to a second successive win in emphatic fashion. Alejandro Romero had opened the scoring in the 13th minute before Saed Al Rodsan turned into his own net to double Al Ain's advantage. Football at its flowing best 🔥 Houssine Rahimi put the cherry on top to a superb Al Ain team move for their third of the night. #ACLElite | #AFCvAIN pic.twitter.com/dUSCHHveE7 — #ACLElite | #ACLTwo (@TheAFCCL) October 12, 2026 Rahimi, who struck twice for Al Ain in their victory over Nassr in September, grabbed another brace against Al Quwa before half-time to kill the contest. Mohammed Jawad grabbed a consolation goal in the 89th minute. “We know what we can do, and the players did their job excellently until the end. They deserve this victory," Al Ain coach Vladimir Ivic told reporters. “We sent a message to ourselves about what we can do, and that is the most important thing for me.” Victory took Al Ain top of Group B ahead of Esteghlal on goal difference. Tijjani Reijnders was on target as Al Qadsiah were held to a 1-1 draw at Pakhtakor.

title: Trump comments on Russia's violation of energy truce
body:
Ukrinform reports this, citing Suspilne .
"I have to look at it. Because there have been violations on both sides," Trump said.
The US leader was responding to a request from Suspilne to comment on Russia's alleged violation of the so-called energy truce, which he announced after a conversation with Putin about supplies of diesel fuel from Russia.
Regarding the possibility of reaching an agreement to end the war, the US president said that Putin and Zelensky wanted to reach a deal but did not know how, adding that the United States would make them reach an agreement.
He also expressed the view that Putin was more interested in a peace agreement than Zelensky.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Donald Trump said on October 11 that an energy truce in the war between Russia and Ukraine would supposedly take effect on Sunday.
Volodymyr Zelensky said he had not been aware of such an arrangement but confirmed Ukraine's readiness for a truce if Russia also stopped attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky stated that the Ukrainian Armed Forces had received the relevant orders following the US president's announcement.

title: Shettima to North: You Have Nothing to Fear over Tinubu’s Second Term
body: Idris says Tinubu’s reforms yielding results despite high living costs Lists falling inflation, $55bn reserves, student loans as key achievements •Science minister defends reforms, seeks president’s re-election Iyobosa Uwugiaren, Deji Elumoye in Abuja and Emmanuel Ugwu-Nwogo in Enugu Vice President Kashim Shettima yesterday mounted a fresh campaign to win the North over for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid, assuring the region that it had nothing to fear from another four years of the administration and insisting that it stood to benefit even more if the president secured a second term in 2027. With the battle for 2027 gathering momentum, Shettima urged northern political leaders and citizens to close ranks behind Tinubu, arguing that the region had already benefited from the administration’s appointments, agricultural interventions and infrastructure projects. The vice president spoke at the State House, Abuja, when he received a delegation of Arewa for Asiwaju (A4A), a northern-based political group campaigning for Tinubu’s re-election, urging the region not to view another Tinubu presidency with apprehension but as an opportunity to consolidate the gains he said the region had recorded under the administration. Also, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, yesterday said Nigeria’s economic reforms under Tinubu were beginning to produce measurable results, citing declining inflation, rising foreign exchange reserves, improved oil production and increased investment in infrastructure and social programmes. In the same vein, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Udeh (SAN) has defended Tinubu’s quest for a second term in office, maintaining that the president deserves to stay for another four years in Aso Rock to complete his ‘bold’ economic reforms. Shettima urged political leaders and citizens across the region to unite behind the administration, arguing that the North had benefited from its policies, appointments and development projects and stood to gain more if Tinubu secured another term. According to him, the administration’s commitment to the region’s development and the welfare of its people should encourage northern stakeholders to support its continuation beyond 2027. “Let’s unite as a people and work for the development of our region and the progress of our people through the re-election of this administration. We are benefiting and we stand to benefit more from this government in many ways,” the vice president said. He cited the Bank of Agriculture’s disbursement of N450 billion to 700,000 smallholder farmers across the country, saying about 70 per cent of the beneficiaries were from the North. “The Bank of Agriculture has disbursed N450 billion to 700,000 smallholder farmers in Nigeria and about 70 per cent of the beneficiaries are from the North,” he said. Shettima also pointed to major infrastructure projects being undertaken by the administration, assuring the delegation that Tinubu remained committed to the region. “The present administration is working towards completing landmark and groundbreaking projects in parts of the country. I can assure you that the president loves the North and the president will work for the North,” he said. The vice president thanked the organisation for its support for Tinubu and urged its members to intensify mobilisation across wards, communities and local government areas in the region ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Earlier, the Director General of Arewa for Asiwaju and former Jigawa State Governor, Abubakar Badaru, said the group would sustain its mobilisation efforts until Tinubu was re-elected. Badaru disclosed that the organisation planned to engage religious leaders, including Muslim and Christian clerics, as well as other prominent Nigerians, to drum up support for the Tinubu-Shettima ticket. “On discussions with the high profile, we have gone far. We have met them several times and the BoT is meeting them again to consolidate our gains and to tell them why there is a need to support this ticket,” he said. He added that the group was also working with the Presidential Campaign Council (PCC), while concentrating on grassroots mobilisation to complement the council’s broader activities. Also speaking, Chairman of the organisation’s Board of Trustees (BoT) and former Kano State Governor, Ibrahim Shekarau, said the group, which supported Tinubu’s election in 2023, was determined to repeat the feat in 2027. Shekarau said the organisation had been engaging northern governors and other stakeholders to compare notes and identify areas of collaboration towards securing the president’s re-election. He disclosed that the group had concluded plans to establish a fully fledged secretariat to coordinate its activities, with offices for directors and state coordinators who would collate reports, analyse developments and issue directives to members. The former governor also formally invited Shettima to inaugurate the organisation’s office complex on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Among those present at the meeting were former Plateau State governors Joshua Dariye and Simon Lalong; former Taraba State Governor, Jolly Nyame; former Kogi State Governor, Yahaya Bello; former Katsina State Governor Ibrahim Shema; former Bauchi State Governor Isa Yuguda; the President’s Special Adviser on Policy and Coordination, Hadiza Bala Usman; and Chairman of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, Buba Marwa. Idris Lists Tinubu’s Achievements, Says Reforms Yielding Results Also yesterday, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, said Nigeria’s economic reforms under Tinubu were beginning to produce measurable results, citing declining inflation, rising foreign exchange reserves, improved oil production and increased investment in infrastructure and social programmes. However, Idris acknowledged that many Nigerian households continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures, stressing that the federal government’s priority is to ensure that improvements in the country’s economic indicators translate into more affordable essential goods and services, increased purchasing power and better living conditions. Also, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Udeh (SAN) has defended Tinubu’s quest for a second term in office, maintaining that the president deserves to stay for another four years in Aso Rock to complete his ‘bold’ economic reforms. Idris spoke during a media chat with senior editors at Radio House, Abuja, where he outlined the administration’s economic performance, security interventions, social investments and implementation of its Renewed Hope Agenda. He maintained that the government’s economic reforms were strengthening the country’s fundamentals and restoring investor confidence, while conceding that more work was required to ensure that the benefits reached households across the country. “Our task now is to ensure that this clear macroeconomic recovery is felt even more widely in the lives and households of Nigerians,” the minister said. He identified food prices, market transactions, transport and household spending as areas where citizens needed to experience tangible improvements. The minister recalled that the economy is projected to grow above 4 per cent, saying the nation’s economy was on course to grow by more than 4 per cent in 2026, while the country’s external position and foreign exchange market had improved. He reiterated that Nigeria recorded a current account surplus of $12 billion in the first half of 2026, compared with $8.6 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, stressing that inflation declined from approximately 27 per cent in January 2025 to around 15 per cent at the time of the briefing. He described the development as an encouraging sign for household budgets but said the government’s ultimate objective remained to bring inflation into single digits. According to him, external reserves exceeded $54 billion in September, representing their highest level in almost two decades, adding that the foreign exchange market had stabilised sufficiently to enable businesses and investors to make longer-term plans with greater confidence. He explained that recent economic reporting has also documented the increase in Nigeria’s external reserves. Recent reports indicate that reserves stood at approximately $55.07 billion on October 8, citing Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) data. The World Bank, meanwhile, projected average annual economic growth of 4.4 per cent through 2028, subject to continued reforms and improvements in public service delivery. The minister further disclosed that Nigeria earned more than $6 billion from non-oil exports in 2025, describing the figure as the highest in the country’s history. He said the earnings supported businesses and entrepreneurs across agriculture, mining, petrochemicals, manufacturing, processing, transportation and logistics. Idris argued that the combination of stronger external reserves, increased non-oil exports, improved oil production and a more stable foreign exchange market was creating opportunities for domestic investment and economic diversification. Nevertheless, he emphasised that improved macroeconomic indicators must be accompanied by practical benefits for Nigerians, particularly those struggling with food, transportation, energy and other household expenses. The minister identified infrastructure development as one of the principal channels through which the administration intends to translate economic recovery into employment and increased economic activity. He explained that road construction projects generate income for contractors, suppliers, engineers, artisans, transport operators and food vendors, while completed roads improve connectivity, facilitate the movement of agricultural produce and increase access to markets. According to Idris, the administration’s four legacy projects collectively cover approximately 3,000 kilometres across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones. He said the projects formed part of a wider portfolio of road, rail, port, electricity, healthcare and education investments being implemented across the country. The minister also highlighted the recently approved highway project valued at approximately N1.5 trillion in Niger State, describing it as an investment expected to improve connectivity along an important agricultural and commercial corridor. He maintained that the projects were intended not only to improve transportation but also to stimulate economic activity in communities along their routes. The expected benefits, he said, include faster transportation of goods, improved access to commercial centres, increased business opportunities and stronger links between rural producers and urban markets. Speaking on food security in the country, the minister said Tinubu places food security at the centre of national economic policy, with government interventions focused on increasing domestic agricultural production and improving farmers’ incomes. He listed mechanisation, improved access to agricultural inputs, irrigation development and agricultural financing among the measures being pursued to strengthen the sector. According to the minister, these interventions are designed to increase food supplies, improve productivity and make food more affordable for Nigerian households. He argued that higher agricultural output would also strengthen rural economies by supporting farmers, processors, transporters and other businesses involved in the food supply chain. The minister’s remarks come as the administration faces pressure to demonstrate that economic stabilisation is producing meaningful improvements in the affordability of basic commodities. Although Idris described falling inflation as encouraging, he acknowledged that the government still needed to ensure that the improvement was reflected in the daily experiences of ordinary Nigerians. The minister also outlined investments in healthcare and education, describing them as central to the administration’s efforts to improve living standards and expand access to essential services. He disclosed that the federal government had recently commissioned two additional cancer treatment centres, bringing the number commissioned under the initiative to five following the earlier commissioning of three. The administration, he said, was working towards making a total of 10 cancer treatment centres available to Nigerians. Idris added that the government was also pursuing the revitalisation of primary healthcare facilities to expand access to medical services and strengthen the national health system. On education, he said the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) had supported more than 1.6 million students, with over N192 billion paid in institutional fees and approximately N180 billion provided as upkeep allowances. The programme, according to the minister, is intended to reduce the financial burden of tertiary education on students, parents and guardians. Idris said the intervention was part of the government’s broader social investment programme, which seeks to reduce financial barriers to education and support access to higher learning. He also highlighted the Three Million Technical Talent programme, which aims to expand young Nigerians’ access to digital skills in software development, data science, cybersecurity and other emerging technologies. The minister said investment in technical training, innovation and digital capabilities was intended to prepare young people for employment opportunities while supporting the country’s wider economic diversification objectives. He added that renewed attention to domestic refining, solid minerals, industrial production and innovation was expected to support sustainable employment and reduce dependence on traditional sources of foreign exchange. Idris said the Presidential Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and Electric Vehicle Initiative had attracted approximately $2.5 billion in private investment, alongside about N250 billion in government funding and commitments. He disclosed that more than 120,000 vehicles had been converted under the initiative, while the country had established more than 400 certified conversion centres. According to him, Nigeria also had more than 90 refuelling stations, with approximately 180 additional stations under development. Idris said the growing network of conversion centres and refuelling infrastructure was generating business opportunities and employment in host communities. He also linked the programme to the administration’s wider response to rising energy costs, arguing that affordable alternatives and stronger domestic production could contribute to easing pressure on households and businesses. The minister disclosed that the Federal Government had issued a N758 billion bond to settle pension arrears dating back as far as 2007, with almost one million pensioners expected to benefit. He described the intervention as part of the administration’s effort to address inherited financial obligations and improve the welfare of retired workers. Idris also announced that the government had issued N1.2 trillion in bonds to settle inherited debts owed to electricity generation and gas companies. He said clearing these obligations would help lay the foundation for new investments in the power sector, where outstanding payments and financing constraints have remained significant concerns. The minister further disclosed that the National Social Register was directing support to more than 10 million households, while the Consumer Credit Corporation was helping working Nigerians spread the cost of essential purchases. On national security, Idris said the protection of lives and property remained the first responsibility of the government and a central priority He said the federal government had strengthened the operational capabilities of the Armed Forces, intelligence services and other security agencies through improved coordination, equipment, logistics and support for personnel deployed to the frontlines. According to the minister, security operations across several theatres had recorded successes against terrorists, bandits, kidnappers and other criminal groups. He said terrorist commanders and criminal kingpins had been neutralised, insurgent networks disrupted, hostages rescued and criminal enclaves dismantled. Idris also highlighted operations in the Niger Delta targeting crude oil theft, illegal refining and pipeline vandalism, saying the measures had contributed to improved oil production and the protection of national revenue. He said the government was encouraged by efforts to restore access to communities and economic activities in areas affected by insecurity. Addressing fuel prices, the minister acknowledged that rising energy costs were placing pressure on households, businesses and the wider economy. He said governments across the world were adopting different measures to protect their economies and cushion the effects of higher energy costs on citizens. Idris maintained that Tinubu remained committed to the economic reforms introduced by his administration while recognising the need to protect public welfare. According to him, the government’s approach includes expanding affordable energy alternatives, strengthening domestic production and creating conditions for sustainable reductions in the cost of living. Science Minister: President Deserves Second Term Meanwhile, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Udeh, has defended Tinubu’s quest for a second term in office, maintaining that the president deserves to stay for another four years to complete his economic reforms. Udeh, who is a member of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, while appearing on Arise News Prime Time, insisted that Tinubu has the capability to lead Nigeria out of the woods. He backed the position that the presidency remains in the southern part of the country till 203, in line with power rotation arrangement. Alluding to the challenges that Tinubu is getting from fellow southerners who are flying the presidential banners of opposition parties, the minister said that the South-west should retain it given that he is from that zone. Udeh acknowledged that the South-east region has not produced Nigeria’s elected president but stated that he believed that it would eventually happen at a time in the future. However, he added that winning the presidency would ultimately depend on engagements across Nigeria’s regions, and winning votes from across Nigeria. When asked what argument the ruling APC was advancing for Tinubu’s re-election, Udeh said the president, who is still in his first term, had initiated reforms that were beginning to produce positive results. “Well, (the argument) is that Mr. President is in his first term, and has started reforms that are beginning to make a positive impact in the lives of Nigerians. It is not yet fully realised, but you can even tell that we are no longer as bad as we were in 2023, 2024,” he added. To buttress his argument the minister cited statistics on Nigeria’s economic growth, saying the country has moved from about 2 per cent growth in 2023 to about 4 per cent presently. He also argued that increased revenue available to sub-national governments was creating opportunities for states and local governments to undertake development projects. Referencing Enugu State, Udeh stated that developments recorded in the Coal City State so far in infrastructure and transportation have been unprecedented. On the argument that the economic growth that the government is pointing to had not necessarily translated into improved living standards for ordinary Nigerians, Udeh acknowledged that inflation and hardship were yet to abate. “We know that there’s inflation. We know that there’s still hardship. But we also know that Nigeria has been put on the track for development, to come out from economic hardship,” the minister said.

title: Can you drive an EV up Jabal Akhdhar, without a 4WD?
body:
MUSCAT: Visitors to Jabal Akhdhar can now make the mountain journey in electric vehicles without needing a four-wheel-drive (4WD) vehicle, a change that could open up one of Oman’s most popular tourist destinations to more travellers. The update was announced by Shabib al Maamari, Managing Director of Visit Oman, in an interview with the Oman Observer. He said electric vehicles are now legally permitted to travel up the mountain, adding that visitors who do not own one can rent an EV for the trip. Previously, access to Jabal Akhdhar through the checkpoint at Birkat Al Mouz was restricted to 4WD vehicles under safety regulations designed for the mountain’s steep, winding roads. The change comes as the destination prepares for a higher tourism profile after being named the GCC Tourism Capital for 2027. Jabal Akhdhar attracted more than 220,000 visitors in 2025, with around 101,608 visiting in the first half of 2026 alone. Further plans to improve access are also being explored, including proposals for a regional airport and passenger terminal on the mountain, as well as an alternative road linking Jabal Akhdhar directly to South Al Batinah without the need for a 4WD vehicle.
