title: Iran welcomes diplomacy, ready to defend itself
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Iran welcomes all diplomatic processes and is simultaneously prepared to defend itself, a senior Foreign Ministry official said.
Kazem Gharibabadi, deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, said in an interview with Al-Arabi TV that Iran welcomes all diplomatic processes and is prepared to defend itself, adding that Tehran is finalizing its response to American views on the proposal Iran presented in New York.
Gharibabadi said Iran will announce its final position after consultations through mediators, and that Tehran remains ready for diplomacy provided that the matters raised are genuine. He said Iran has consistently welcomed diplomacy and has not fallen short in this regard with any party.
He added that Iran's readiness to defend itself and to fight is no less than its readiness for negotiations.
Gharibabadi said continued participation in talks demonstrates Tehran's political flexibility and commitment to the diplomatic process, and that the United States must return to implementing its obligations. He stressed that Tehran has not violated any of its commitments, while Washington has failed to honor its obligations under the Islamabad MoU and must take compensatory steps.
The deputy foreign minister added that as long as the American side has fully violated all its commitments, Iran cannot be expected to show greater flexibility in this regard.

title: Obi: Fuel Subsidy Removal, Naira Floating, Tax Reforms Reasons for Nation’s Hardship
body: ª Says FG’s petrol discount covers less than 4% of filling stations Chuks Okocha in Abuja Presidential candidate of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, yesterday, blamed President Bola Tinubu’s major reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidy, floating of the naira, and tax reforms for the worsening hardship in the country. Obi said implementation of the different reforms had contributed to rising prices, business closures, unemployment, and declining living standards. He also criticised the federal government’s 30-day petrol discount, stating that the initiative covers less than four per cent of the filling stations nationwide and offered inadequate relief to Nigerians struggling with high living costs. Obi, in a statement, maintained that the government should focus on policies capable of reducing the cost of living rather than introducing short-term measures that would expire without resolving the underlying problems. The former governor of Anambra State also reiterated his position that fuel subsidy should be restored alongside support for agriculture, healthcare, education, and infrastructure. He said such interventions should operate under a transparent and accountable framework to ensure that public resources benefitted Nigerians rather than being diverted through corruption. Obi promised to provide a more detailed policy roadmap on what he described as fair, transparent and affordable petroleum pricing. He stated that Nigeria needed leadership focused on reducing the cost of living through sustainable policies and accountable administration. Obi described the 30-day petrol discount intervention as a political gimmick, questioning why the administration introduced a temporary discount after Nigerians had endured years of economic hardship following the removal of fuel subsidy. He said the policy failed to address the wider consequences of rising petrol prices, including poverty, unemployment, insecurity, and the increasing cost of goods and services. The former governor also faulted the limited reach of the initiative, saying the discount would be available to about 900 Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited retail stations out of an estimated 24,000 filling stations across the country. Obi said that meant fewer than four per cent of filling stations would offer the discount, raising questions about how millions of Nigerians would access the relief. He estimated that, based on a population of about 243 million, each NNPC retail station would serve approximately 243,000 Nigerians if the stations were evenly distributed nationwide. He said the situation could lead to intense competition among motorists seeking a discount of about N66 per litre, particularly in areas with limited access to NNPC outlets. “Imagine 243,000 Nigerians struggling for a N66 per litre discount in each of the NNPC petrol stations. This is certainly not how to govern a richly blessed and endowed nation!” he said. Obi, who questioned the timing of the discount, also queried whether the initiative was designed to test the possibility of restoring fuel subsidy or to influence public opinion ahead of the 2027 general election. He stated, “What really does the President Bola Tinubu-led government want to achieve with a one-month discount of less than five per cent on fuel cost? Will it reduce poverty, unemployment, insecurity, and inequality? Will it increase productivity and exports? “Is it a test to ascertain if subsidy should be restored? Is it another political gambit in the face of threats of electoral loss in the 2027 election? Too many questions, no answer!” The NDC presidential candidate said the government should have conducted a detailed regulatory impact assessment and consulted stakeholders before implementing major economic policies. He insisted that the initiative was too insufficient to address the economic challenges facing Nigerians, describing it as a policy driven by political considerations rather than a lasting solution.

title: Dangote Refinery Extends $1.6 Billion Public Offer By Two Weeks to October 27
body: • Aliko says IPO already four times oversubscribed Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja and Peter Uzoho in Lagos Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has extended the deadline for its initial public offering (IPO) by two weeks to October 27 to give more investors across Africa the opportunity to participate in what is expected to be the continent’s largest share sale. The extension, approved by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), moves the closing date from October 13, following efforts to expand access to the offer through stock exchanges and investment platforms in other African countries. The company said yesterday that the additional time would enable it to broaden distribution channels, facilitate cross-border investments and allow prospective investors to complete account-opening procedures, identity verification and other regulatory requirements. The IPO, which opened on September 14, is part of the plan by Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, to broaden ownership of the 700,000 barrels per day refinery by attracting as many as 10 million retail investors in Nigeria and other African countries. The offering comprises 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 each, with a minimum subscription of 10 shares. It is expected to raise approximately $1.6 billion, although the amount could increase to about $2.1 billion if an over-allotment option is fully exercised. Confirming the extension, the President of the Dangote Group, Aliko Dangote, said the move followed ‘exceptionally strong interest’ from a broad spectrum of eligible investors across Africa and other international markets. Since the launch of the offer, he stated that investor participation has underscored the growing confidence in Dangote Refinery’s long-term growth prospects and its strategic role in transforming Africa’s energy landscape. “The IPO is going very well. We will extend the closing date because we want more of our African brothers and sisters to participate. Following our discussions with the Nairobi Stock Exchange, we have identified what we believe is the best way to facilitate participation. We are now trying to replicate that arrangement with other African exchanges to ensure wider participation… “But when it comes to the amount of money we originally intended to raise, we have already received subscriptions amounting to more than three or four times that figure…So, it is not about the amount of money. “It is about the number of people who will have the opportunity to participate in this offer. That means quite a lot to us,” the statement quoted Dangote as having said in a chat with media men at the facility. The company said the additional two-week period will support ongoing market-access initiatives across African jurisdictions, including the expansion of distribution channels and the rollout of unsponsored depository receipt programmes designed to facilitate seamless cross-border investment. It explained that it will also provide more time for prospective investors to complete account-opening procedures, identity verification processes, and other regulatory requirements necessary for participation in the offer. Also speaking on the extension, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE, David Bird, stated that the additional time will help extend more opportunities to additional investors. He said: “We welcome the SEC’s approval of the extension, which will give more investors across Africa the opportunity to participate in the offer. From the outset, our ambition has been to enable as many people as possible to participate in the IPO and share in DPRP’s future growth. The additional time will help us extend that opportunity to more investors across Africa.” The company noted that it remains highly encouraged by the level of investor engagement received across its target markets and believes the extension will ensure broader participation by retail, institutional and cross-border investors seeking to be part of the refinery’s next phase of growth. THISDAY learnt that the proceeds are intended to support the expansion of the refinery complex in Lagos, which began processing crude oil in early 2024 and has become central to Nigeria’s ambition to reduce dependence on imported refined petroleum products. Exchanges across Africa had been in discussions with the company over arrangements to facilitate participation in the listing, which could value the business at close to $50 billion. Global depositary receipts have already been made available to investors in Kenya and Botswana, according to people familiar with the matter. However, the offering’s prospectus indicates that the share sale is not registered as a public offering outside Nigeria, meaning investors in other countries must rely on applicable local regulations or access the shares through eligible investment platforms. The arrangement highlights the challenges facing efforts to develop a pan-African investor base, as differences in regulations, trading infrastructure and investment procedures continue to complicate cross-border transactions. Although the refinery is seeking to attract investors across the continent, the absence of a uniform framework for public offerings means that access to the shares may vary from one country to another. The IPO is therefore being viewed as a major test of whether African exchanges and regulators can support large-scale equity offerings involving investors from multiple jurisdictions. The listing is also intended to demonstrate the potential of African capital markets to mobilise domestic savings for large-scale industrial development, reducing reliance on foreign financing while expanding public participation in major businesses. Meanwhile, President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, has said Africa needs to measure economic progress by the productive capacity it develops, the employment it generates and the resilience it builds, rather than relying on growth figures alone. Dangote spoke at the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt, where participants urged African governments to move beyond economic growth figures to building productive industries, creating jobs and retaining more value from the continent’s natural resources. The two-day forum, held in New Alamein and officially launched by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, brought together heads of state, investors, financial institutions and private-sector leaders to explore partnerships capable of translating Africa’s economic potential into sustainable prosperity. The meeting was convened by Egypt in collaboration with the African Union (AU), the African Union Development Agency-New Partnership for Africa’s Development (AUDA-NEPAD) and the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank). Dangote argued that developing local industries, processing raw materials within the continent and producing higher-value goods would help African countries reduce their dependence on imported fuel, medicines and technology. “Growth does not tell us enough. We should ask: what are we growing, how many productive jobs does it generate, and how much economic resilience does it leave behind?” Dangote said. Dangote also identified fragmented regulations, inconsistent standards and cumbersome border procedures as major obstacles to businesses seeking to expand across African markets. He stressed that stronger regional integration was necessary to enable African companies to achieve economies of scale, develop competitive industries and participate more effectively in global trade. Other African leaders, financiers and business executives at the event called for increased mobilisation of domestic capital, stronger regional integration and greater investment in local industries to accelerate economic growth and reduce the continent’s dependence on imports. President and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Afreximbank, George Elombi, similarly called for greater African ownership of the continent’s economic future, highlighting the role of homegrown financial institutions in financing development priorities. “Elombi highlighted Afreximbank’s support for African economies during periods of disruption and called for assessments of African financial institutions to reflect their performance, ownership models and development role,” the forum’s statement said. He also commended Egypt’s longstanding support for the bank, describing New Alamein as a place where Africans could come together to determine their economic future. Chief Executive Officer of AUDA-NEPAD, Nardos Bekele-Thomas, called for greater participation by African investors and businesses in financing the continent’s transformation, including through cross-border investments and regional value chains. “We need more Africans investing in Africa. We need more African businesses able to go beyond national markets, build regional value chains and compete globally,” she said. President of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA), Abdullah Almusaibeeh, said stronger coordination among development finance institutions could unlock additional funding for infrastructure and other strategic projects. “When we coordinate with other institutions, we can bring substantially more financing to a project than any one institution could provide alone,” he said, citing opportunities for cooperation with institutions including the Africa Finance Corporation and the Trade and Development Bank. Chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, emphasised the importance of domestic production and value addition in creating jobs and building wealth across the continent. “Domestic transformation creates jobs, value addition and wealth,” he said. Youssouf also called for measures to ensure that small and medium-sized enterprises benefited from regional integration, including improved access to finance, payment systems using local currencies and financing guarantees. The President of Burundi and Chairperson of the African Union, Évariste Ndayishimiye, urged international partners to view Africa as a centre of production, innovation and investment rather than primarily as a market for imported goods. Secretary General of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat, Wamkele Mene, said the forum’s success should ultimately be assessed by the commercial transactions and partnerships generated by its discussions. The programme featured sessions on agriculture and food systems, energy, infrastructure and logistics, trade, digital innovation and healthcare markets, bringing together policymakers, investors and businesses to examine potential areas of collaboration.

title: International Day of the Girl Child: Makinde Pledges Free Education, Healthcare
body: Chuks Okocha in Abuja A Seyi Makinde-led administration would prioritise free education, vocational training, adolescent healthcare and stronger enforcement of child-protection laws to reduce child marriage and keep more Nigerian girls in school, the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation has said. The campaign organisation said the proposed measures would also include legal aid for vulnerable girls, protection for survivors of abuse and community sensitisation programmes to address harmful social norms associated with early marriage. Its Director of National Women Coordination, Hon. Toyin Balogun, disclosed this in a statement on Monday to mark the 2026 International Day of the Girl Child, observed annually on October 11. The 2026 observance is themed, “End Child Marriage, Invest in Girls Rights.” Balogun, a former Oyo State Commissioner for Women Affairs and Social Inclusion, said the proposed administration would replicate the free education policy implemented in Oyo State as part of efforts to reduce Nigeria’s high out-of-school population. She said vocational and artisanal training would complement conventional education, particularly for girls whose schooling had been disrupted by early marriage, enabling them to acquire skills to support themselves and their families. According to her, the administration would also strengthen the implementation of existing child-protection laws and address gaps that leave girls vulnerable to exploitation, abuse and forced or early marriage. She said child-friendly justice mechanisms would be strengthened to enable girls to report violations safely and receive timely support, while legal aid and protection services would be expanded, particularly in poor, rural, remote and underserved communities. Balogun added that survivors would be protected from retaliation, stigma and further harm when seeking justice, with progress assessed by the number of girls protected and supported, as well as those able to remain in or return to school. On healthcare, she said the proposed government would introduce inclusive policies to address gaps in services for child brides and prioritise adolescent-responsive sexual and reproductive healthcare. She also called for community sensitisation programmes to educate families and communities about the consequences of child marriage, including vesicovaginal fistula, maternal deaths and neonatal mortality. Balogun said protecting girls from early marriage required coordinated action by policymakers, families, communities and government institutions, noting that poverty, harmful social norms, discrimination and weak protection systems continued to limit girls’ opportunities. Citing available data, she said 33.4 percent of young women in Nigeria were married before the age of 18, while UNICEF had reported that 7.6 million Nigerian girls were out of school, with significant numbers in both the northern and southern parts of the country. She noted that child marriage went beyond the age at which a girl married, as it could interrupt her education, compromise her health, limit her economic independence and increase her vulnerability to violence and coercion. Balogun urged stakeholders to work together to ensure that every Nigerian girl had access to education, healthcare and protection, enabling her to realise her potential. “Together, all hands must be on deck to support the Nigerian Girl Child to enable her to attain her maximum potentials,” she said.

title: NHRC Raises the Alarm Over Mental Health Abuses, Says Less than 3% Covered by Insurance
body: Michael Olugbode in Abuja The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has raised alarm over the treatment of Nigerians living with mental health conditions, warning that inadequate health insurance, widespread stigma and persistent human rights abuses are denying vulnerable citizens access to care and exposing some to degrading and inhuman treatment. The commission disclosed that fewer than three per cent of people with mental health conditions in Nigeria were covered by health insurance, leaving many individuals and their families struggling to pay for treatment in a country where mental healthcare services and trained professionals remain inadequate. It also revealed cases involving children and adults with psychosocial disabilities who were subjected to solitary confinement in Kano State, as well as a child rescued in the Federal Capital Territory from a woman living in what the commission described as an extremely distressing and inhuman condition linked to her mental state. The Executive Secretary of the NHRC, Chief Tony Ojukwu, raised these concerns in Abuja on Monday while commemorating the 2026 World Mental Health Day, calling on the Federal Government to urgently increase funding for mental healthcare, expand access to treatment and strengthen enforcement of laws protecting the rights of affected persons. Ojukwu warned that Nigeria could not claim to uphold human dignity while people experiencing mental health conditions were abandoned, discriminated against, denied appropriate treatment or subjected to abuse because of their conditions. He said mental health must be recognised not merely as a medical concern but as a fundamental human rights issue requiring urgent and coordinated action by government institutions, healthcare providers, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. “A mental-health condition does not reduce a person’s worth, dignity or human rights,” he said. The NHRC chief stressed that people living with mental health conditions were entitled to equality, respect, appropriate medical care and the opportunity to participate fully in society, adding that their conditions must never become grounds for exclusion, neglect or the denial of personal autonomy. The commission’s warning comes amid continuing concerns about the accessibility and affordability of mental healthcare in Nigeria, where poverty, insecurity, displacement and shortages of specialised services place additional pressure on individuals and families seeking treatment. Citing World Health Organisation estimates, Ojukwu said nearly one in seven people globally lived with a mental disorder, while many requiring care remained unable to access effective treatment. He noted the situation was particularly concerning in communities affected by terrorism, abductions, armed violence and displacement, where survivors often experienced psychological trauma capable of affecting their daily activities, relationships and ability to contribute meaningfully to society. According to him, survivors of gender-based violence, torture, trafficking and other serious human rights violations also require mental health and psychosocial support as part of efforts to restore their dignity and help them recover. He said the government must therefore move beyond general awareness campaigns and make concrete investments in accessible services, trained personnel, health insurance and community-based care. Of particular concern to the commission is the gap between Nigeria’s legal commitments and the actual experiences of people living with mental health conditions. Nigeria enacted the National Mental Health Act in 2021, which received presidential assent in December 2022, establishing a legal framework for mental healthcare and the protection of the rights of affected persons. The country also has a National Mental Health Policy and a National Suicide Prevention Strategic Framework. However, Ojukwu maintained that the existence of laws and policy documents would have limited impact unless they translated into affordable treatment, accessible services and effective mechanisms for holding perpetrators of abuse accountable. He called for the full implementation of the National Mental Health Act and Policy, warning that people experiencing mental health conditions continued to face discrimination in education, employment, housing and community life. Some, he said, were denied the opportunity to make decisions about their own lives or subjected to treatment that undermined their dignity and fundamental rights. The NHRC executive secretary urged the federal government to expand affordable mental health services through primary healthcare centres, strengthen health insurance coverage and recruit, train and deploy more psychiatrists, psychologists, counsellors, psychiatric nurses and social workers. He also called for effective oversight of mental healthcare facilities to prevent neglect, unlawful confinement and other forms of abuse. Highlighting the commission’s interventions, Ojukwu disclosed that the NHRC had handled cases involving children and adults with psychosocial and psychological disabilities in Kano State who had been subjected to solitary confinement before being moved to a welfare facility following the commission’s intervention. He also recounted a recent case in the Federal Capital Territory in which the commission rescued a child from a woman living in what he described as an extremely distressing and inhuman condition linked to her mental state. The cases, he said, demonstrated that mental health challenges could affect entire families and communities, requiring responses based on professional care, protection and support rather than punishment, abandonment or abuse. Ojukwu said the commission had established a Counselling Unit at its headquarters to provide emotional support to victims of human rights violations and traumatic experiences. The unit also supports NHRC personnel who may experience emotional distress from handling cases involving violence, abuse, bereavement and human suffering. He added that the commission’s Human Rights Institute had organised training programmes for investigation officers to help them identify mental health and psychosocial concerns, respond appropriately to vulnerable complainants and recognise cases requiring professional intervention. The establishment of the NHRC’s Vulnerable Group Department had further strengthened its capacity to address the needs of vulnerable populations, including persons experiencing mental health challenges, he said. The commission had also partnered with the Taipei Trade Office and civil society organisations to provide grants and free mental health sessions to some indigent women who were victims of human rights violations. Ojukwu said the NHRC was collaborating with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and other stakeholders to incorporate human rights considerations into the proposed National Mental Health Strategic Plan for 2027–2032. He described the proposed plan as an important step towards establishing a consolidated national direction for mental healthcare, but stressed that its effectiveness would depend on implementation, funding and measurable improvements in access to services. The commission also participated in training organised by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime on drug prevention, treatment and care, with particular attention to the relationship between substance use, mental health and human rights. Ojukwu advocated a rights-based approach to drug-related challenges, including access to treatment, rehabilitation and psychosocial support. The intervention is significant in a country where mental health conditions may intersect with substance use, poverty, violence and social exclusion, making coordinated healthcare and social support essential to recovery. In a goodwill message, the Founder of the Mandate Health Empowerment Initiative, Ameh Zion, also called for stronger implementation of the National Mental Health Act and greater collaboration among government agencies, civil society organisations and development partners. Zion said people experiencing depression, psychosis, trauma and psychosocial disabilities must not lose their dignity or fundamental rights because of their conditions. He expressed concern that stigma, inadequate services and shortages of trained professionals continued to prevent many Nigerians from obtaining the help they needed. According to him, survivors of terrorism, violence, displacement and abuse often carried psychological wounds that affected their functioning and ability to contribute to national development, while their families and caregivers struggled with emotional and financial burdens. He urged stakeholders to ensure that mental health legislation translated into accessible services and enforceable protections across the country, rather than remaining largely a policy commitment. Zion also expressed his organisation’s readiness to work with the NHRC and other African mental health reform stakeholders on public awareness, institutional capacity building, referral systems, psychosocial support for survivors and policy advocacy. Both Ojukwu and Zion called for a broader national response involving schools, workplaces, families, communities, religious institutions and traditional leaders. Ojukwu urged religious and traditional leaders to complement professional mental healthcare rather than substitute spiritual or traditional interventions for clinical treatment when such care was necessary. He also called on the media to report mental health issues accurately and sensitively, warning that sensational or stereotypical portrayals could deepen stigma and discourage affected persons from seeking help. The NHRC executive secretary said the commission would continue to investigate human rights violations, protect vulnerable persons and advocate policies that upheld the rights and dignity of all Nigerians. He called for stronger mental health and psychosocial support for survivors of conflict, terrorism, gender-based violence, displacement, torture and trafficking, stressing that their recovery must be treated as an essential component of protecting human rights. The commission’s position underscores a broader challenge facing Nigeria: ensuring that mental healthcare is treated as an essential public service rather than a privilege available only to those who can afford it. Without sustained funding, trained professionals, insurance protection and effective enforcement of existing laws, millions of Nigerians requiring mental healthcare risk remaining without adequate support, while stigma and discrimination continue to compound their difficulties. For the NHRC, the priority is clear: Nigeria must move from policy commitments to practical protection, ensuring that no citizen is denied dignity, safety or access to care because of a mental health condition.

title: Kalu: South East Devt Commission Must Operate from South-east, Not Abuja
body: Sunday Aborisade in Abuja The Chairman of the Senate Committee on the South East Development Commission (SEDC), Senator Orji Uzor Kalu, has insisted the commission must operate from the South-east, declaring that its presence in Enugu has resolved earlier disagreements over its decision to run its affairs from Abuja. Kalu, who represents Abia North Senatorial District, spoke on Monday during an oversight visit by members of the Senate committee to inspect the commission’s headquarters in Enugu State and assess its operations. The former Abia State governor, according to a statement from his Media Office on Monday, expressed satisfaction with the progress of work on the headquarters, noting that the commission had made significant improvements since the lawmakers’ previous engagements with its management. He however urged the management to sustain the progress and extend the commission’s activities to communities across the South-east, stressing that its impact must be felt beyond its administrative offices. “Well, so far, we are making very good progress, unlike when we started. I’m sure you, both me and my colleagues, are seeing very serious progress. I hope that the commission, especially the management team, sustains this progress,” he said. Kalu disclosed the committee would return to Enugu in December to assess the level of progress and review the commission’s operations. “We will be here in December to see the progress so far. We are happy now that something is going on. We also want them to go to the grassroots to show the South Eastern people that they are on the ground,” he added. The lawmakers inspected two facilities during the visit: the office currently occupied by the commission and another building provided by the Enugu State Government, which is being completed for its use. Kalu described the headquarters project as encouraging, saying the improvements had addressed the committee’s earlier concerns about the commission’s decision to operate from Abuja rather than from the region it was established to develop. “Where we were before and now, we are making progress. We were quarrelling about our office being in Abuja. Today, we have seen two offices, one where they are staying and the one they are completing, which the government of Enugu State gave them,” he said. The senator added: “So, we are very impressed. Once they are back home to do what they are sent to do, nobody has problems with them.” Despite his satisfaction with the progress recorded, Kalu reiterated that the commission must maintain its operational base in the South-east. “The only problem that I said before, and I repeat, is that they cannot operate from Abuja. They must operate from where they are set up. This is where they are located,” he insisted. He said the dispute over the commission’s location had been resolved following the progress made in establishing its presence in Enugu. “Our quarrel before was about being in Abuja and not being in Enugu. So that quarrel is over now,” he said. Kalu also called on the commission’s management to take its activities to communities across the five South-east states, emphasising that its success would depend not only on the establishment of offices but also on its ability to demonstrate tangible development outcomes for the people. He acknowledged that the commission was still relatively new, having been in operation for less than a year, but urged its management to remain focused on delivering on its mandate. “It’s a new commission, less than one year. We are making progress. We are impressed with what we have seen so far. So far, so good,” he said. The Senate committee is expected to return to Enugu in December for another inspection of the headquarters project and an assessment of the commission’s operations.

title: Wike Declares Self Field Commander for Tinubu in 2027, Mobilises APC, PDP in FCT
body: Olawale Ajimotokan in Abuja Minister of the FCT, Nyesom Wike, yesterday, unveiled a cross-party mobilisation strategy involving stakeholders of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election in 2027. Wike declared himself at the stakeholders’ meeting of the Rainbow Coalition in Abuja as the coordinator of the president’s re-election campaign in both FCT and Rivers State. He vowed that political differences would not prevent members of the two parties from working towards a common presidential objective. The minister said for the FCT, the coalition had agreed to support Tinubu’s re-election as well as the APC Senatorial and House of Representatives candidates. “For the presidency, all of us have agreed that it is Bola Ahmed Tinubu. I am going to coordinate the FCT and Rivers State. So you can imagine how important it is. “I am in charge of the FCT election. I am the commander of field operations as far as the FCT election is concerned.” The meeting, which saw the PDP National Assembly candidates openly declaring support for the APC candidates, was a gathering of APC and PDP stakeholders, including party chairmen, serving and former senators, candidates for the National Assembly and leaders from the six area councils of the FCT. The former Rivers State governor explained that the purpose of gathering was to establish a common political front ahead of the 2027 general election and ensure that stakeholders understood the coalition’s objectives, irrespective of the parties they might belong to in the coming months “I want to let all of you know that we are going to work together. Nobody should say, ‘I am PDP’ or ‘I am APC.’ For the purpose of this election, we are together,” he said. He referenced the 2024 Edo State governorship election as proof that political coalitions could determine electoral outcomes, claiming that cooperation between elements of the APC and PDP had helped prevent the incumbent governor from installing a successor. Making a case for Tinubu’s re-election, he challenged political leaders to identify any of the six area councils of the FCT that had not benefited from the administration’s infrastructure projects and institutional reforms. According to him, notable reforms like the creation of the Women Affairs and Youth Development Secretariats had created opportunities for career progression among FCT civil servants and expanded participation in governance.

title: AbdulRazaq Presents 25 More Vehicles to Police in Kwara in Fight Against Insecurity
body: Hammed Shittu in Ilorin Kwara State Governor, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, yesterday, presented additional 25 Toyota Hilux vehicles to the State Command of the Nigeria Police to strengthen their mobility and sustain the success in the fight against crimes. AbdulRazaq, therefore, commended the police and other security agencies for doing yeoman’s jobs to check crimes in the state. Presenting the vehicles to the police command in Ilorin at a brief event at the Government House, Ilorin, the governor said, “You know the yeoman’s jobs the security agencies have been doing to improve the security of the state. “We have made serious progress in the recent months. And to sustain the work they have been doing we have decided to provide mobility vehicles for the police force. “Other agencies will also benefit soon. We are doing this in stages. Altogether we are giving about 100 vehicles. This is the first set of vehicles to be delivered. Others will come soon. We trust they will use them judiciously. “We thank them for their services. As you can see, from all indices, Kwara State is still one of the most peaceful states in Nigeria, by independent observation.” AbdulRazaq enjoined the people of the state to always support the security agencies by giving them useful information that could assist in averting or combating crimes. “My message to Kwarans is to always tell the security agencies anything they see. Active intelligence gathering is the most important thing to nip things in the bud and make sure they don’t degenerate,” he added. Responding, the state Commissioner for Police, Adekimi Ojo, said the governor’s intervention was another in its series, noting that the new vehicles would strengthen their operational capacity. “This is one of the many (good) things the Executive Governor has been doing for the Police, apart from paying special allowance to those on special duties, which is assisting in making our jobs easier.. “This particular gesture will assist in bridging some gaps that we currently have, especially in hard to reach places. So, we thank the Governor for this great job. We are promising the state and the Executive Governor that we are going to make good use of the vehicles. “The security system has improved but we are going to double our efforts to achieve greater success,” he added.

title: NSA Unveils New Security Framework to Tackle Oil Theft, Pipeline Vandalism, Others
body: Linus Aleke in Abuja National Security Adviser (NSA), Malam Nuhu Ribadu, has unveiled a new security framework for Nigeria’s oil and gas industry to combat crude oil theft, pipeline vandalism, illegal refining, and other criminal activities threatening the country’s petroleum assets. The framework, known as the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry-Wide Security Architecture, sought to harmonise security operations, clarify responsibilities, and strengthen collaboration among security agencies, industry operators, regulators, and private surveillance contractors. Speaking at its official unveiling, Ribadu said Nigeria’s hydrocarbon resources remained central to economic stability and national development. But he said persistent oil theft, pipeline vandalism, and illegal refining had undermined production, damaged the environment, and threatened national security. He explained that the SOP was developed through consultations involving the armed forces, security and intelligence agencies, the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC Ltd), regulators, and other industry stakeholders. The framework establishes standard procedures for surveillance, arrest, detention, and the evacuation of recovered petroleum products, while promoting effective command and control, accountability and professionalism. Describing the document as more than an administrative measure, Ribadu said it was “a practical instrument for enhancing synergy, reducing operational friction, promoting accountability and protecting critical national infrastructure”. He stressed that the effectiveness of the new framework would depend on implementation, urging participating institutions to communicate its provisions to their personnel and integrate them into their operational structures. The NSA also called for information sharing, respect for institutional mandates, and strict adherence to existing laws and established procedures, expressing confidence that stronger cooperation would improve the protection of Nigeria’s oil and gas infrastructure. Equally speaking at the occasion, Dahiru Gwarzo, who represented NNPC Ltd’s Group Chief Executive Officer, Bayo Ojulari, endorsed the framework, describing it as essential to safeguarding petroleum assets, boosting government revenue, and restoring investor confidence. Gwarzo said security was fundamental to the industry’s sustainability, as it affected national revenue, operational continuity, environmental protection, and the welfare of host communities. He commended Ribadu and his team for providing the leadership and coordination required to harmonise the operational procedures of security agencies, regulators, operators, and surveillance contractors. Recalling the severity of the challenges, Gwarzo said Nigeria’s crude oil production fell to about 950,000 barrels per day in August 2022, while major pipelines remained unavailable for extended periods, affecting government revenue, industry operations, and communities in the Niger Delta. He also acknowledged the sacrifices of military personnel, police officers, and intelligence operatives protecting critical infrastructure, saying some have paid the ultimate price. Gwarzo said the experience underscored the need for collective responsibility, stressing that “no single institution or operator could secure Nigeria’s oil and gas infrastructure in isolation”.

title: Confusion delays medical help for Christa Pike after failed execution — media
body:
NEW YORK, October 13. /TASS/. Confusion between prison officials and emergency responders delayed medical assistance for Christa Pike after she survived an attempted execution, the Associated Press reported.
According to AP, the first 911 call came about an hour after the lethal injection procedure began. Another half-hour passed before prison officials confirmed that the request for emergency assistance was genuine and allowed responders through the gates.
On September 30, Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug at a prison in Nashville, Tennessee. Her lawyers had previously warned that she had thrombocytosis and that administering the drug could cause blood clots and additional suffering.
Pike was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Following the failed attempt, Governor Bill Lee ordered an investigation and halted another execution scheduled for 2026.

title: Trump says Ukraine, Russia agree to energy strike ceasefire 'because I said they agreed'
body:
Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump once again said that Ukraine and Russia agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, despite the confusion around the alleged ceasefire.
"They agreed," said Trump after a reporter pointed out that neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed they would refrain from strikes on energy sites. "Do you know why? Because I said they agreed. That's why. They agreed because I said they agreed. And that thing has to get settled."
The U.S. president's comments came after he unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, causing confusion in Kyiv. According to a senior Ukrainian official, Ukraine had no prior information about an energy ceasefire.
In a short interview after Trump' s announcement, President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Russia has nothing to say yet about an energy ceasefire with Ukraine announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, the Kremlin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Oct. 12.
When asked by a reporter about his response to Russia continuing to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure after his announcement, Trump said there had been violations by both sides, without pointing to any evidence.
Hours after Trump's announcement on Oct. 11, Russia struck Kharkiv’s CHP-5 power plant . In Overnight attacks on Oct. 11-12, at least 10 people were killed and 69 others injured across Ukraine as Russia continued to target residential buildings and energy infrastructure across the country.
Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery .
Trump's energy ceasefire announcement followed his lifting of sanctions on Russian oil on Oct. 9, a move that could help Moscow earn a substantial boost in its war funding and blindsided Kyiv. By removing the sanctions, Trump could try to reduce high oil prices caused by his war with Iran ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.
On Oct. 12, the Kyiv Independent learned that the Trump administration threatened to cut intel sharing and weapons shipments to Ukraine if more Russian oil refineries were targeted in attacks.
"We're going to see what happens," said Trump to reporters on Oct. 12 about ending the war. "We'll get it done"

title: ‘They Agreed Because I Said They Agreed’ – Trump Insists Ukraine, Russia Accepted Energy Ceasefire Despite Denials
body:
US President Donald Trump insisted Monday, Oct. 12, that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure simply because he told them to, despite neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirming any agreement and Russian strikes continuing against Ukrainian facilities.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for Ohio, Trump was challenged over his announcement of an energy ceasefire the previous day, which appeared to catch both governments by surprise.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“They agreed. You know why? Because I said, ‘You agree’ – that’s why,” Trump replied.
“They agreed because I said they agreed, and that thing has to get settled,” he added.
The exchange followed Trump’s Sunday announcement that the two countries had agreed to stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure immediately, although he provided no details about the arrangement or how it would be enforced.
Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities after his announcement, Trump said he was uncertain whether Moscow had violated the supposed agreement.
“I’m not sure about that,” he said, before urging both leaders to bring the war to an end.
Trump also suggested that violations had occurred on both sides, without providing evidence or identifying specific incidents.
When reporters pressed him on whether Russian President Vladimir Putin had actually accepted the proposal, Trump insisted that both leaders supported the idea.
“I think they both support it. I think they wanna make a deal, but they don’t know how. But we’re gonna get them to make a deal,” he said.
He then suggested Putin was more willing to negotiate than President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky,” Trump said.
Earlier Monday, Zelensky said Russian forces had attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump’s announcement, including a power plant in Kharkiv and a gas-production facility.
Speaking by video link at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelensky said Ukrainian forces had refrained from striking Russian refineries overnight, but Moscow had not reciprocated.
Ukraine was ready to observe an energy ceasefire if Russia did the same, he said, urging Washington to ensure Moscow complied with any agreement.
In his official address , Zelensky said Russian drone attacks continued over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities after Trump’s declaration.
The Kremlin had not confirmed accepting Trump’s proposal, and no jointly agreed ceasefire terms or monitoring arrangements had been announced.
Trump’s insistence that an energy ceasefire was in place came amid growing criticism of his administration’s agreement to allow Russian diesel exports.
Announced after a conversation with Putin on Friday, Oct. 9, the arrangement temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel imports as Washington sought to relieve pressure on fuel prices.
The decision drew objections from Democratic and Republican lawmakers, who warned that additional energy revenues could help finance Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Trump defended the arrangement Monday, arguing that European governments continued purchasing Russian energy while criticizing Washington’s decision.
A bipartisan group of seven US senators had urged the administration to reverse course, warning against providing Moscow with additional financial resources while Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians continued.

title: Pakistan detains Imran Khan ally in stronghold province
body: Pakistan has detained an aide to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and several cabinet members, the government said on Monday, a day after it suspended the provincial government. President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency in the north-western province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Sunday, saying the administration had failed to tackle Islamist militancy. Azam Nazeer Tarar, Minister of Law and Justice, said a governor would take charge. Khan's ​Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) ⁠party rejected the move, saying it was ‌intended to deter his supporters from marching on the capital to demand his release. The detentions took place on Sunday at the chief minister's residence in Peshawar, where police and paramilitary forces sealed off the area using shipping containers, witnesses and officials said. Khan's three sisters and hundreds of supporters were also detained ahead of the planned march. Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, a Khan ally, and several cabinet members were taken into custody, the government said. “Yes, I can confirm that the Chief Minister and some of his cabinet members have been taken into preventive custody,” Junior Interior Minister Talal Chaudhry told Reuters. The imposition of emergency rule and suspension of the provincial government have led to a sharp rise in tension between Khan, 74, a former cricket star, and Pakistan's powerful military. The move came a week after Khan's supporters had rallied for days in the province, preparing to march on Islamabad to demand his release and access to medical treatment. Mr Chaudhry said those facing charges would be prosecuted, while the others would be released. He added that the detentions occurred on Sunday at the provincial chief minister's house in Peshawar, the provincial capital. Khan aide Shaukat Yousafzai demanded the release of all those held. The PTI's last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces. Khan's arrest in 2023 also sparked nationwide riots during which some of his supporters attacked military installations. Pakistan's constitution allows the government to assume control of a provincial administration during an emergency. The government and PTI have held several rounds of talks since the party called for the march on Islamabad last month. The government was ready to accept all the PTI's demands, including permission for the march, Mr Chaudhry said. “We asked for just one thing, that the party should publicly condemn militancy and join us in the fight against militant groups,” he added. The PTI refused and the talks broke down, he said.

title: How the Gulf can turn threats into shared purpose
body: Yesterday’s call for stronger collective defence in the Gulf by Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, comes at a moment when a beleaguered Iran and its remaining armed proxies have decided to escalate and target the Arab world's largest economy. As the Iran-backed Houthis’ repeated strikes on travellers at Riyadh’s King Khalid airport show, the human cost of failing to deter attacks or intercept missiles is steep. Such attacks also strike at the region's prosperity, something that depends on transport networks, energy infrastructure, the environment and the confidence that connect active economies and those who benefit from them. A threat to an airport or a shipping route has consequences well beyond the country directly targeted. Airlines reassess risks to flights and businesses are forced to reconsider other supply chains. Investors also have to debate the costs of operating in a volatile region. Even the mere threat of disruption can come with a heavy price tag. As we have seen since the Iran conflict began in February, aviation is particularly vulnerable. The Gulf’s position as a global hub depends on reliable connections between Europe, Asia and Africa. Attacks, such as those seen in Riyadh, can force airlines to reroute flights, increasing costs and disrupting travel. From this tourism, trade and international connections are imperilled. Environmental security presents another shared challenge. Attacks on oil centres, tankers and other energy infrastructure risk causing pollution that crosses international borders and presents a generational problem. The region's marine environment is already under pressure, while the concentration of energy infrastructure and shipping in a relatively confined Strait of Hormuz makes the consequences of a major spill particularly serious. Economic security is equally inseparable from the wider crisis. Arab states may be competitors in some markets, but their economies are also linked. Disruption in one country can ripple through its neighbours. A beleaguered Iran and its remaining armed proxies have decided to escalate Joint environmental response arrangements and plans to protect critical infrastructure could also improve the region’s joint ability to withstand the kind of shocking events witnessed in recent days in Saudi Arabia . This does not mean individual Gulf countries suddenly dropping their individual national priorities or resolving every difference of opinion. It is more a question of building on the long-standing ties that unite Gulf societies and recognising the that although economic interdependence can create shared prosperity it can also come with common responses to threats. At a time when ideological actors are lashing out at those around them, the eventual outcome may just be a more aligned approach by Arab neighbours to the challenges that face them.

Blenheim student Marcus O’Neill says he’s done plenty of online research about joining the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF), but he jumped at the chance to experience it first-hand.
Marcus, in Year 12 at Marlborough Boys’ College, was one of 39 senior college students who attended the Royal New Zealand Navy’s (RNZN) “School to Seas” programme during September and October at Devonport Naval Base in Auckland.
The separate tane and wāhine four-day camps showcased Navy life and career options across a multitude of marine disciplines.
The students were able to meet sailors, explore career pathways and take part in experiences designed to challenge them and open their eyes to possibilities once they finished school.
Activities included a powhiri at Te Taua Moana marae, ship and base tours, rides on Waitematā Harbour in a Navy rigid-hulled inflatable boat, seeing how recruits lived and worked, and hands-on practical tasks at the Sea Safety Training Squadron – where the students donned firefighting equipment to tackle a set fire, before facing the challenges of the Navy’s flood simulator.
Marcus says he has a legacy of family in the armed forces, including both parents in the NZDF and ancestors who served in both World Wars and Vietnam.
He said it was an eye-opener to appreciate the scale of Navy warships below and above water, and how much infrastructure existed at a single Navy base.
“School to Seas was an unforgettable experience,” he said.
Marlborough Boys’ College student Marcus O’Neill at Devonport Naval Base.
“From speeding down the Waitematā on the RHIBs, touring HMNZS Otago, and experiencing flooding in the damage control simulator."
“That last was the best – we were put into a mock warship and as water flooded in you had to try and slow it down before eventually escaping.”
But it wasn’t just being immersed in water; it was the total immersion of the Navy environment that was his biggest highlight.
“Since I was about 14, I’ve wanted to join the Navy. So being able to talk to people about something I was so interested in was very positive for me.
“The camp was action-packed and it really helped me understand better the structure and standards of the NZDF.
“I can see a career for me in the RNZN, full of positive opportunities, good people and something to look forward to and be excited for every day.”

title: U.S. Army Receives First South Korean Mobile Tactical Cannon to Replace Indigenous M777 Artillery
body: The U.S. Army has received its first prototype of the XM1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon, a South Korean 155mm self-propelled howitzer intended to replace the ageing M777 towed artillery system in selected formations. Developed by Hanwha Defense, the new system is based on the wheeled K9 Mobile Howitzer and is intended to provide greater mobility, a higher rate of fire and improved survivability on increasingly transparent battlefields. The Army accepted the first prototype ahead of a program of testing and soldier experimentation, marking a significant step towards introducing a new generation of mobile artillery into U.S. Army service. The procurement reflects a broader trend towards the United States and NATO members more broadly relying increasingly heavily on South Korean ground forces equipment. The K9 has been particularly popular in Europe, and recently emerged as a frontrunner for the Swedish Defence Ministry’s selection of a new artillery system, while Romania has the systems on order, and Finland, Norway, Poland, Turkey, and Estonia already field them. A Spanish in September followed a followup Finnish order for 112 additional K9s in April. The four-year contract to equip the U.S. Army with the K9’s wheeled derivative has a potential value of approximately $262.9 million and covers six initial prototypes, with options for up to 12 additional systems. Sales of several hundred are expected once the system passes trials. One of the principal advantages over the M777 is the new system’s ability to move under its own power rather than requiring a separate vehicle to tow it between firing positions. The wheeled configuration is intended to provide mobility suited to Stryker Brigade Combat Teams, which require artillery capable of keeping pace with their formations. The Army plans to prioritise these units before considering the system for Mobile and Infantry Brigade Combat Teams. The XM1776 is not intended to replace every M777 across the force, but rather to provide a more mobile alternative in formations where its characteristics offer particular advantages. Like the K9, the XM1776 can fire up to nine rounds per minute, more than twice the approximately four rounds per minute cited for the M777 under comparable reporting conditions. The system’s performance is also expected to exceed that of the M777 in several important areas. The K9 family uses a 155mm, 52-calibre gun, compared with the M777’s 39-calibre barrel, allowing it to exploit the potential of compatible ammunition and propelling charges to achieve greater range. Published figures for the K9 family indicate a maximum range exceeding 60 kilometres with suitable ammunition, although actual performance depends on the projectile and firing conditions. The M777 has a conventional maximum range of less than 24 kilometres, rising to approximately 40 kilometres with extended-range M982 Excalibur precision-guided ammunition. These figures are not directly interchangeable across all ammunition types, but they illustrate the potential reach of the longer-barrelled system.
