title: The Middle East's biggest archaeological discoveries in 2026
body: The Middle East continues to reveal traces of its ancient past, with discoveries offering new insight into how early civilisations lived, worshipped and organised society. Since January, archaeologists have uncovered ancient burial chambers, royal monuments and prehistoric artworks. Some finds may answer long-standing historical questions, while others are challenging what we know about the region's earliest communities. Here are six of the most significant discoveries announced over the year so far. A Bronze Age communal tomb in Al Ain A burial chamber uncovered at the Qattarah Necropolis in Al Ain has revealed evidence of funerary traditions that endured for at least 1,000 years. Announced by the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi in July, the chamber was 11 metres long and 2.5 metres wide. Dating back to the Wadi Suq period, it remained in use into the Iron Age, suggesting successive generations continued to bury their dead at the same site. Archaeologists recovered weapons, vessels and personal ornaments, providing clues about the customs of the communities that inhabited the region. The chamber's entrance faces the East, potentially allowing the rising Sun to illuminate its interior, although whether this carries symbolic significance remains uncertain. The discovery adds to Al Ain's archaeological importance, with its Unesco-listed sites already documenting thousands of years of settlement, burial practices and technological development. The possible discovery of Egypt's lost city of Masn An inscription bearing the name of a long-lost Egyptian city may finally help settle an archaeological mystery dating back almost 140 years. Discovered at Tell Abu Seify, near the Suez Canal, the sandstone lintel bears the royal titles of Ramses II, who ruled Egypt during the 13th century BC. It also records the restoration of a statue of Horus, described as Lord of the City of Masn . Announced in August, the find strengthens the possibility that Tell Abu Seify was the ancient settlement, although further investigation is required to confirm its identity. Excavations have also revealed a temple complex, defensive walls, roads and evidence of Roman military occupation. Establishing the city's whereabouts could help researchers reconstruct Egypt's eastern frontier, particularly the Horus Military Road, which connected the Nile Delta with Sinai and territories farther east. A rare Assyrian royal monument in Nineveh, Iraq More than 2,600 years since the reign of King Ashurbanipal, archaeologists have uncovered a monument documenting the ambitions of one of Assyria's most powerful rulers. The two-metre stone stele was discovered in June at Shamash Gate in Nineveh , once the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. It features cuneiform inscriptions and relief carvings associated with Ashurbanipal's reign from 668BC to 627BC. The inscriptions offer further evidence of how the king developed Nineveh and commemorated his achievements through public monuments. The discovery also carries significance for the city's modern history. Nineveh's archaeological remains suffered extensive destruction during ISIS's occupation of the Mosul area between 2014 and 2017. Recovered by a joint Iraqi-American archaeological mission, the stele contributes to efforts to document and preserve one of the ancient Middle East's most important cities. An image of the lost Lighthouse of Alexandria, Egypt An ancient bronze ring recovered from the Mediterranean Sea bears a rare depiction of one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It was announced last week that the signet ring had been discovered during underwater excavations at Antirhodos, a submerged island that once housed a royal palace in Alexandria's Great Harbour. Its engraving depicts the Lighthouse of Alexandria and resembles representations found on Roman-era coins. Archaeologists have yet to establish the ring's precise date or identify its owner, but it is believed to be the first known depiction of the monument on a signet ring. Constructed during the third century BC, the lighthouse guided ships into Alexandria's harbour for centuries before successive earthquakes brought about its destruction. The discovery adds to the limited surviving visual record of the structure, whose appearance is known largely through ancient descriptions and representations. An 11,000-year-old carved human face in Karahantepe, Turkey A human face carved into a limestone pillar is providing new evidence of artistic expression among some of the world's earliest settled communities. Unveiled in November 2025, the discovery was made at Karahantepe in south-eastern Turkey, a Neolithic site dating back about 11,000 years. The 1.4-metre T-shaped pillar features deep-set eyes and a prominent nose. It is the first known example of a human face represented directly on this type of pillar at the region's prehistoric sites. Similar structures have been found at nearby Gobeklitepe, with archaeologists suggesting their forms may represent stylised human figures. The discovery at Karahantepe lends weight to that interpretation. Alongside other sculptures and monumental structures uncovered at the site, the pillar reveals the sophistication of prehistoric artistic and ceremonial traditions thousands of years before the emergence of writing or cities. Thousands of years of rock art in Sinai, Egypt Paintings, engravings and inscriptions spanning thousands of years have been documented at a previously unknown archaeological site in South Sinai . Announced by Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities in February, the discovery was made on the Umm Iraq Plateau, where researchers identified a natural sandstone rock shelter extending more than 100 metres. Its walls contain prehistoric paintings depicting animals and other figures, alongside later engravings and inscriptions. Archaeologists have also documented pottery fragments and material associated with different periods of human activity. Some of the earliest artwork is believed to predate the emergence of the ancient Egyptian state, although further research is needed to refine its chronology. The site is particularly valuable for its unusually long archaeological record. Its changing imagery and inscriptions suggest communities returned to the same location across vastly different historical periods, leaving evidence of their environments, beliefs and artistic traditions.

title: Airports forced to review security as missile and drone threats rise
body: Airports are being forced to rethink how they protect passengers and keep flights running as missile and drone attacks pose an increasingly serious threat to civilian aviation, industry experts have warned. Repeated attacks by Houthi rebels in Saudi Arabia, alongside months of disruption caused by the war in Iran, have exposed the vulnerability of airports to modern warfare and the difficulty of maintaining operations during prolonged security crises. Industry leaders gathered at the Dubai Airport Show on Monday said airports were investing in new technology and contingency planning to withstand threats from military strikes to cyber attacks, while acknowledging that no facility could ever be completely secure. Tim Walder, chairman of the British Aviation Group, said the changing nature of global conflicts had created unprecedented challenges for airport operators. “What we’re seeing today is a completely different set of challenges being faced geopolitically,” he said. “Resilience isn’t something that’s 100 per cent, it’s always going to fail on occasions, but we learn faster. “The key thing is the airport can be a leader in terms of understanding where the threats can come from, such as cybersecurity and climate change.” Crisis support Mr Walder, whose company offers expertise on meeting the challenges of the global aviation industry, said supporting passengers during a crisis was critical to retaining confidence. “If something goes down, you lose passenger confidence and you can lose that for a long time,” he said. “Cyber-attacks are obviously high up there when talking about risk and we are seeing different levels of that. “A few months ago in the UK and Europe, hackers attacked the software that supports the check-in process and that impacted a number of airports in Europe, including London and Brussels. “These attacks aren't going to be just necessarily hitting an individual airport or airline, they're going to hit a network. The question is how do we make the network more resilient as well.” Critical Gulf transit hubs and other major infrastructure are increasingly connecting site security with dedicated anti-drone and air defence measures to improve protection at airports. International gateways to the region have increased perimeter screening and police patrols near airports, while others have implemented terminal entry checkpoints in response to raised threat levels in the Middle East. Exhibitors at Dubai World Trade Centre displayed the latest countermeasures and showed how drone technology was rapidly advancing to help secure airspace. Udi Lowy, sales director for the Gulf Co-operation Council and India at D-Fend Solutions, said his company’s EnforceAir Plus system was capable of taking over unidentified drones and bringing them under control. “Drones are quite a new threat in the world, so most of the technologies just adopt [existing] air-defence mechanisms for drones,” he said. “We are using cyber systems that detect the communication of the drone and we have the ability to retract the relevant information from the drone itself.” Take control Rather than jamming a drone’s signal to bring it down, potentially causing damage or injuries on the ground, the EnforceAir Plus system takes over its controls and lands it safely nearby. It can then verify from where the drone was deployed and by whom. The system can even be programmed to deal with a swarm attacking airspace simultaneously, Mr Lowy said. “Sometimes, a kid can fly a drone and create mayhem. Rather than jamming all signals, we cherry-pick the signal we want to interfere with and actually take the drone itself. “We don't interfere with any other signal, so there is no interference with airplanes.” The Ministry of Defence has reported a total of 2,265 drone attacks on the country since February 28, when the Iran war broke out, with Dubai International Airport handling 111 aerial threat alerts. Future airport developments, including the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, will feature blast-proof designs and hardened concrete shells to bolster defences against aerial attacks. Speaking on a panel at Dubai Airport Show on operational resilience under pressure, Binu Gopal, chief operating officer at Ras Al Khaimah International Airport, said the priority in a crisis was to maintain operations as safely and efficiently as possible. “We prepare for multiple kinds of disruption which may occur at the airport,” he said. “Resilience is the ability to continue our operations even when we face some kind of disruption, maintain critical activities and respond to the disturbance, and get back to normal safely and efficiently. “This cuts across the entire ecosystem, be it set operations, terminal operations, airlines, ground-handling operations, customs and immigration. However, during a crisis, it becomes more and more interdependent. For us it is not about having a contingency plan, it's about how well we are able to respond as a team.”

title: Hold your horses: Therapeutic riding programme helping people build confidence and skills
body: In Abu Dhabi's city centre, the stables at the Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club are an oasis where time slows down, and the clip-clop of hooves can soothe the effects of even the most stressful day. It is here that horses are being used to help children, people of determination and senior citizens build confidence and improve their well-being through a new therapeutic riding programme. The initiative, launched at Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club at the end of September, has already attracted 45 participants and aims to harness the bond between humans and horses to support some of the community’s most vulnerable members. Funded and supported by Mubadala Investment Company and the Authority of Social Contribution – Ma’an, the programme offers participants the chance to interact with horses in a safe and calm environment, with activities designed to develop confidence and encourage social interaction. “The programme will give people of determination, vulnerable children and elderly citizens the opportunity to learn about horses,” said Dayle Brown, chief sports and equestrian officer of Al Khail Square. “Horses are very intelligent, they're very used to working around people and relating to people where there is a need. It's well known around the world.” Faye Galvin, a therapeutic riding instructor, is in her element at the club. With her horse Ally – one of three she brought over from Ireland this summer – by her side, she said she has witnessed first-hand the difference that working with horses can make. “Horses have been a big part of my life, and working in different elements of care and with children and seeing the difference that horses can make to people’s lives and the connection is beautiful,” Ms Galvin told The National . “To bring the two together is the dream job.” Finding His Voice The National spoke to Faisal Alsuwaidi, who brought his nephew Ghaith, 7, to the stables for his session. The young boy spoke in Arabic and English until he was two years old, when he became non-verbal. “He was talking, playing with us. Sometimes you will see him looking at the sky, looking at things and thinking. We want him to continue this thinking, and say what is inside his mind; we try our hardest to push him to talk,” said Mr AlSuwaidi. The family, who live in Ras Al Khaimah, have tried many things to help Ghaith find his voice again – from playing with animals on their farm to going to the swimming pool to enrolling him in a specialised school. Mr Alsuwaidi said that Ghaith looked forward to the twice-weekly sessions, and had seen some progress, which gave the family hope. It was clear that he felt comfortable on the horse – his mood changed when he mounted Doolin. “We try to let him have lots of contact with the animals, and we try to improve his motivation to talk to anyone. Today he tried with the horse to push him to move forward,” he added. Grassy fields to sandy dunes Ms Galvin's three ponies were brought from Ireland for the therapeutic riding programme and had to acclimatise to the desert conditions. “They've been out in a big field in Ireland, so it's quite a contrast coming to Abu Dhabi,” she said. “We've had to get them desensitised, because when you're working in the therapeutic environment, there's a lot of different variables and different sounds, which takes time.” Each lesson is tailored to the rider, and can involve playing games, working on co-ordination or balance, and doing exercises that engage motor skills. The instructor has seen the impact horses can have on people, and she believes they can connect with anyone. “They are very spiritual, empathetic and sensitive, so they can connect with people in so many ways,” she said. “Their gait mirrors that of a human, so for people with physical disabilities, it can be very good for their whole physical development as well, and it gives them that feeling and experience.” The programme is open for volunteer applications in addition to session applications.

title: IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies due to prolonged Hormuz closure
body: The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz , and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening. In its latest World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year. The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 from to 3.4 per cent. “This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom. The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices. The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly. Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.” The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits Silvana Tenreyro, IMF chief economist The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs. Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada. Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan. Gulf outlook The IMF projects the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The new projections for the Middle East 's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia , but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year. Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year. Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year. Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade. Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon. Conflict and AI boom lift inflation The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures. Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points. Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter. “This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said. Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury , a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs. Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

title: Service Life of SSJ-100 Aircraft with Sanctioned Engine Extended to 20 Years from 15
body:
The Russian SSJ-100 aircraft with SaM146 engines has received a Main Change Approval (MCA) document extending the aircraft's designated service life to 20 years.
Western sanctions imposed in 2022 halted maintenance, technical support, and spare parts supply for the SaM146 turbofan engine developed by PowerJet (a joint venture between France’s Safran and Russia’s NPO Saturn).
The MCA document issued by Russian aviation regulator, Rosaviatsia establishes the following values for the assigned resource and service life of the aircraft: 20,000 flights, 40,000 flight hours, 20 years (previously - 15,000 flights, 25,000 flight hours, 15 years).
SaM146 engine replaced with PD-8 power-plant
Russia has since replaced the SaM146 engine with the PD-8 power-plant developed by Russia’s United Engine Corporation in the SSJ-100 which has been re-Christened as Yakovlev SJ-100.
There are currently 154 SSJ-100 aircraft powered by the SaM146 engines in service in Russia. Moscow intends to sell the aircraft to countries which do not attract Western sanctions. A Russian aviation executive had told Defensemirror.com earlier that if the aircraft were sold to “sanctions-free” countries, Safran would provide engine support and spares.
SSJ-100 is the only Russian airliner to receive European aviation safety certificate
In 2012, the SSJ 100 become the first Russian passenger aircraft to be certified by the European Aviation Safety Administration (EASA) since the Agency's creation in 2003. The EASA certificate is a validation of the certificate issued in January 2011 by the Russian Interstate Aviation Committee Aviation Register (IAC AR).
The EASA Type certification is a prerequisite to the first delivery to international airline customers. It allows the European airlines as well as those airlines operating in countries which use EASA regulations as a reference to operate the SSJ100 aircraft.

title: Russian emergencies minister conveys greetings from president, PM to North Korean premier
body:
PYONGYANG, October 13. /TASS/. Russian Emergencies Minister Alexander Kurenkov met with North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song in Pyongyang and conveyed greetings from Russian President Vladimir Putin and Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
"First of all, I congratulate you on the 81st anniversary of the founding of the Korean Workers’ Party and convey greetings from Russian President Vladimir Putin and Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin," he said.
Kurenkov noted that Russia seeks to strengthen cooperation with its North Korean counterparts under the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership between the two countries. "We also seek to develop cooperation between our emergency response agencies in a spirit of friendship and good neighborliness," he said.
The previous day, Kurenkov met with North Korean Minister of Disaster Management Kim Chol Nam. The two sides discussed priority areas for joint work in detail.

title: Herzog calls Nobel Peace Prize winner choice affront to peace-loving people at Medal of Honor award
body: The awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize to South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay is an "affront to any life-affirming, peace-loving people,” President Isaac Herzog announced during his own awarding of the Presidential Medal of Honor to Israel Bonds on Monday.“Awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to one of the leading proponents of the genocide lie is a cynical decision which celebrates a shameful display of moral erosion," he added.Herzog also marked the explosion of a Hezbollah bomb earlier in the day which had killed one teenager and injured several dozen others.“We gather here today under the heavy shadow of a grave and heartbreaking tragedy unfolding in the north of our country," he began his statement at the award ceremony. "Before all else, I wish to offer our prayers for the swift and full recovery of all those who were injured, and to embrace them and their loved ones on behalf of the entire people of Israel.”While awarding the Medal of Honor to Israel Bonds, Herzog praised the organization for its work in developing Israel's economy after the October 7 massacre, saying that it had raised $1 billion in the first month after October 7, and another $8.5 billion since."Over the past 75 years, more than $58 billion dollars' worth of Israel bonds have been purchased around the world, solidifying Israel's long-term standing in the global market, and demonstrating the trust investors have in Israel," he said. "And we have repaid that trust, never once defaulting, as I am certain we will continue to do.”Israel Bonds leaders thank Herzog for Medal of HonorDani Naveh, Israel Bonds Global President & CEO, said after receiving the award that it was an extraordinary honor, but that it also carried a responsibility."This medal carries with it the weight of generations," he said. "We accept it with humility, knowing that we do so only as representatives of a remarkable organization founded 75 years ago. Our powerful message is that, in times of need, our beloved Jewish homeland will never be alone.”Dr. Andrew M. Hutter, Israel Bonds' US and International Chairman of the Board of Directors, also thanked Herzog for the medal, saying “Mr. President, we accept this medal not for any one person in this room, but on behalf of every single investor who has ever purchased a bond, who has ever believed in the Jewish State, who has ever said, with their own money, I stand with Israel, I believe in its future. This medal belongs to them.”Nobel Peace Prize winner draws international ire from Israel supportersAwarding the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Pillay has drawn sharp criticism from both Israel and the US.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded to the decision by calling Pillay a “bigot” and the prize committee “misguided.”“The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass,” the Prime Minister's Office wrote on X/Twitter. “It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the only Jewish state.”Jerusalem Post Staff and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Merz Calls on Russia to Accept Energy Ceasefire Following Talks With Zelensky
body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire following a phone conversation with President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 12, as Moscow continued striking Ukraine’s civilian and energy infrastructure.
“I spoke with President Zelensky about the Russian airstrikes on civilian targets and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Russia must agree to the ceasefire for the energy infrastructure – an important step toward lasting peace in Ukraine,” Merz wrote on X.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
According to the German government’s official readout , both leaders agreed that it was now up to Russia to accept a ceasefire covering all energy infrastructure.
Merz reaffirmed Germany’s solidarity with Ukraine, while Zelensky thanked Berlin for its military assistance and support for Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of winter.
The conversation followed US President Donald Trump’s announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire, a claim neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed.
Despite the announcement, Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian energy facilities, prompting Zelensky to question Moscow’s commitment to any agreement.
“This is exactly how the Russians behave when pressure eases. It is very important that Europe continue to act on principle,”Zelensky said, according to the Ukrainian presidency .
Earlier Monday, Zelensky said Russian forces had struck six Ukrainian energy facilities in a single day, including a gas-production site and other infrastructure, despite Washington’s declaration.
Ukraine has repeatedly offered to suspend long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and export facilities if Moscow stops attacking Ukraine’s electricity grid and critical infrastructure.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelensky called for stronger European and US pressure on Russia to secure a genuine ceasefire.
He warned that easing pressure on Moscow would only encourage further escalation.
The leaders also discussed diplomatic efforts toward a lasting peace and agreed to maintain close coordination with European and transatlantic partners.
According to the Ukrainian presidency, Merz said Germany was working to organize another meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, which is coordinating support and potential post-war security guarantees for Ukraine.
Merz and Zelensky also agreed to convene a meeting of national security advisers in the E3–Ukraine format, bringing together Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Ukraine.
They discussed Ukraine’s financial resilience as Russian attacks continue threatening electricity and heating supplies ahead of winter.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Russia, Ukraine to reach settlement deal, Trump believes
body:
WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump is convinced that Russia and Ukraine will reach a deal to settle the conflict, he said while addressing Republican Party supporters in Ohio ahead of November’s US congressional elections.
Discussing the war against Iran, Trump expressed confidence that Tehran wants to reach a deal with Washington. "And I'll be honest with Russia and Ukraine. They want to make a deal too. They don't know how to," he said.
Trump pledged that the US will get "that deal done too." He also once again acknowledged that he had underestimated the difficulty of settling the Ukraine conflict: "I thought this would be one of the easier ones, but it's not."

title: French Navy intercepts Russian shadow fleet tanker in Indian Ocean
body:
The French Navy intercepted and boarded a tanker suspected of flying under a false flag as part of Russia's shadow fleet on Oct. 12, French President Emmanuel Macron announced.
The tanker, DF Peak, was allegedly transporting sanctioned Russian fuel and was halted by the French Navy 450 nautical miles (833 kilometers) south of the French territory of Reunion in the Indian Ocean.
"France is determined to combat the ghost fleet, wherever it may be in the world," Macron wrote on X . "This action, carried out in accordance with international maritime law, demonstrates our determination to uphold the rule of law and combat all illicit trafficking, wherever it occurs."
The tanker DF Peak, previously named Kaliningrad, has falsely sailed under the flag of Benin, according to the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence's War and Sanctions portal . The crude oil tanker is sanctioned by the U.S, EU, Switzerland, Canada, and Japan.
The vessel is currently under escort by the French Navy, France's Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said on X .
"International law is not optional," wrote Vautrin. "Our armed forces are fully mobilized to enforce it and combat illicit activities at sea."
Russian state media TASS said the Russian embassy in Paris told them that "France is violating international law by detaining merchant vessels on the high seas and is attempting to cover up piracy by invoking the provisions of the UN Convention."
The DF Peak is just one tanker of Russia's "shadow fleet" — a group of aging, poorly insured tankers used by Moscow to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions. Western governments have also accused Moscow of using the fleet to support its hybrid war against Europe.
Throughout Russia's war on Ukraine, European powers have intercepted shadow fleet vessels in an attempt to stop Moscow from reaping the windfall of illegal fuel sales.
Detentions have helped cut the number of ships in Moscow's shadow fleet flying a false flag to less than half between last October and June 2026, according to a report by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) think tank published on Sept. 25.

title: Air defenses destroy 13 drones heading toward Moscow — mayor
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Air defenses have intercepted 13 drones heading toward Moscow, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
"Another 13 UAVs heading toward Moscow have been destroyed. Emergency responders are working at places where the debris fell," he wrote on his Max channel.
A total of 23 drones approaching the capital have been destroyed since the start of the day, according to TASS calculations based on Sobyanin’s posts.

title: Energy truce must be respected by both sides, says Kallas
body:
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas made the statement at a press conference in Luxembourg following a meeting of the EU Council, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
Kallas said that ministers had expressed support for an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, provided that Moscow also respected it. She stressed that a ceasefire could not work if only one side observed it.
She noted that EU member states clearly understood that it was not the time to ease pressure on Moscow. In this regard, Kallas mentioned that nearly 1,600 new entries had been added to sanctions lists targeting Russia's military-industrial complex.
The EU's chief diplomat said that these measures were making it significantly more difficult, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it used to kill Ukrainians.
According to Kallas, the EU would provide additional funding for Ukraine for drones and missiles that week.
She also welcomed Ukraine's adoption of the necessary legislation ahead of the expected opening of two clusters in its EU accession negotiations tomorrow.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine is ready for an energy ceasefire but will respond if Russia violates it.

title: Trump says he's 'looking at' firing US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle
body:
She allegedly used her position and Trump links to seek money from a donor.
President Donald Trump answered he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle when asked about the embattled U.S. ambassador to Greece on Monday.
Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a campaign rally that his administration is "looking at it" and added that it's "not happy" over reports alleging that she used her official position and links to the Trump family to get money from a donor .
A Trump donor told ABC News last week that Guilfoyle offered access to top Trump officials in exchange for cash.
Eric Deters, a former lawyer, conservative media personality and Trump donor, alleged that Guilfoyle asked him to pay her $100,000 credit card bill in July 2025 -- days before her Senate confirmation hearing.
"It was all quid pro quo," Deters claimed about the request from Guilfoyle, who is the former wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom and ex-fiance of Donald Trump Jr.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on Deters' accusations.
Deters provided messages to ABC News he says he exchanged with Guilfoyle on the subject. In one message from that period, Deters alleges Guilfoyle wrote, "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," which Deters alleged was in reference to the desired credit card payment.
ABC News has reached out to Guilfoyle, her attorney and the U.S. Embassy in Greece for comment and have not heard back.
In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers claimed that the money she was seeking was for appearances and speaking engagements that predate her nomination that have not been paid, according to The Associated Press.
Deters denies he owed Guilfoyle any money. He said he ended up not making the payment because he didn’t have the money.
Deters is considered a controversial character in Kentucky politics. He ran for Kentucky governor in 2023 and to represent Kentucky's 4th Congressional District in the House in 2024; he lost both races in the primaries.
A former lawyer, Deters had his law license suspended in 2012 for actions in multiple cases including comments he made about a judge and improper solicitation of a possible client. In refusing to reinstate Deters' law license in 2021, the Kentucky Supreme Court said he had a "notorious propensity" for filing "malicious or frivolous lawsuits," according to court documents.
In a statement to the Wall Street Journal, the U.S. embassy in Greece said Guilfoyle's "career in and out of public service is guided by deep and abiding values" and "the Ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he wouldn't answer questions about Guilfoyle's alleged conduct last week while departing Athens, Greece.
"I don't even know if it's true or not true," Rubio said. "So it's just not going to work that way, and it will certainly not going to work that way when I'm sitting in another country."
But White House and State Department leadership have held discussions on how to address the allegations against Guilfoyle, including possibly dismissing her, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
Both sources cautioned, however, that no final decision had been made; one source said the the president would have final say over any action.
Several officials close to Rubio have expressed their frustration with Guilfoyle, whose reported misconduct loomed over Rubio’s high-profile visit to Athens last week. Guilfoyle was present throughout the secretary’s program in Greece, even appearing at some events that she had not been invited by the State Department to attend, one U.S. official said.
The official said that the State Department’s inspector general is examining claims of possible misconduct by Guilfoyle, but it is unclear if a formal probe has been launched and the department has declined to publicly comment on any investigation.
ABC News' Jay O'Brien contributed to this report.

title: Russia Uses Massive FAB-3000 Guided Bombs to Take Out Key Ukrainian Mechanised Brigade
body: The Russian Aerospace Forces have used two FAB-3000 bombs equipped with universal gliding and correction modules to strike Ukrainian troop deployment sites near Orekhov in the Zaporozhye Region. The operation was conducted after reconnaissance units identified concentrations of Ukrainian personnel, with Russian aircraft launching their weapons against positions of the Ukrainian Army’s 65th Separate Mechanised Brigade. The Russian military also reported strikes against Ukrainian deployment sites in the Kharkov Region using precision-guided glide bombs, alongside an air-to-ground missile attack against a fortified position in the Zaporozhye Region. The FAB-3000 is one of the largest bombs ever widely used in combat, and is primarily dropped by Su-34M strike fighters which are prized for their very high weapons carrying capacities. The FAB-3000 has a nominal mass of approximately three tonnes. Its large explosive payload gives it substantial destructive potential against buildings, fortified positions and other structures, particularly when detonated close to or within a target. The weapon’s considerable mass, however, also imposes constraints on the aircraft that can carry it and on the conditions under which it can be employed. The addition of universal gliding and correction modules has expanded the range of circumstances in which heavy Soviet-designed bombs can be used. Rather than requiring aircraft to release unguided bombs directly over their targets, the modules provide aerodynamic lift and a guidance system that can correct the weapon’s trajectory after release. This allows the launching aircraft to release the bomb from farther away, reducing its exposure to some ground-based air defence threats. The actual standoff distance and accuracy depend on the release altitude, aircraft speed, bomb configuration and operating environment. The FAB-3000’s size makes it particularly relevant to attacks on substantial defensive positions, where a large explosive charge can damage structures and disrupt personnel occupying nearby areas. The combination of a heavy warhead and a guidance module also allows Russian forces to adapt existing bomb stocks without having to develop an entirely new weapon. Such conversions have become part of a broader effort to increase the utility of legacy munitions through relatively limited modifications. Ukrainian Army frontline personnel speaking to various Western media outlets have widely singled out the effects of large scale glide bomb attacks, stressing that such attacks using bombs with up to 500 kilograms of explosives were obliterating their underground bunkers. One serviceman compared their impact to “hell’s gates,” stressing that the Russian Aerospace Forces “would send them two by two by two, eight in an hour… It sounds like a jet coming down on you.” The impact of a 3,000 kilogram bomb is expected to be very considerably greater, with few militaries in the world having such a strike capability. The 65th Separate Mechanised Brigade comprises mechanised infantry, tank and artillery units, alongside reconnaissance, air defence and combat-support elements. Its equipment has included Soviet-designed T-72 tanks and BMP-1 and BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicles. The formation has also expanded its use of unmanned systems, including the “Ronins” strike-drone company, which operates first-person-view drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles against Russian personnel and equipment, and has gained prominence for its use of robotic systems. Ukrainian sources have widely reported that the country’s tank units are suffering from very low availability of armour, due to both heavy losses that cannot be replenished, and due to difficulties sustaining those vehicles that are in service. According to the Russian Defence Ministry, in parallel to the strikes on the 65th Separate Mechanised Brigade, four high-precision UMPB glide bombs were also used against temporary deployment sites belonging to Ukraine’s 129th Separate Heavy Mechanised Brigade near Prikolotnoye in the Kharkov Region. Separately, an air-to-ground missile strike reportedly destroyed a strongpoint associated with the 128th Separate Heavy Mechanised Brigade near Kushugum in the Zaporozhye Region. The ministry stated that real-time monitoring systems recorded direct hits on the designated targets, although the reported destruction and resulting Ukrainian casualties have not been independently verified. Russian glide bomb strikes are reported to have contributed significantly to the extreme casualty rates suffered by the Ukrainain Army, which had in several cases approached 80-90 percent in frontline units.

title: ‘No More Artificial Delays!’ – Lithuania Urges Faster Ukraine EU Accession
body:
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys called on the European Union to accelerate Ukraine’s membership process and end what he described as artificial delays, saying Kyiv’s accession would strengthen the security of Europe as a whole.
His remarks on Monday, Oct. 12, followed Ukraine’s adoption of legislation expanding educational rights for indigenous peoples and national minorities, a key condition set by Hungary for advancing EU membership negotiations.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Ukraine’s EU accession is a security guarantee for the EU just as for Ukraine, and we shall seek every opportunity to make it a reality, the faster, the better. No more moving targets! No more artificial delays!” Budrys wrote on X.
The Lithuanian diplomat praised Kyiv for fulfilling its commitments through concrete reforms despite Russia’s ongoing full-scale invasion.
“Today, by adopting legislation on the educational rights of indigenous peoples and national minorities, Ukraine has delivered on its part,” Budrys wrote, describing Ukraine as a reliable partner willing to address outstanding issues.
His intervention came as EU member states unanimously agreed to advance two additional accession negotiating clusters for Ukraine and Moldova, following months of delays over Hungary’s demands.
Ukraine’s parliament adopted Bill No. 16119 on Monday, expanding opportunities for children from national minorities and indigenous communities to receive education in their native languages alongside Ukrainian.
The legislation received 273 votes in its first reading and 266 in the final vote.
President Volodymyr Zelensky signed the legislation later the same day.
The changes address long-standing concerns raised by Budapest over education rights for Ukraine’s ethnic Hungarian minority, concentrated mainly in the western Zakarpattia region.
The law allows schools where more than half of pupils study in an eligible minority language to obtain special status, while preserving Ukrainian as the state language of instruction.
Its expanded protections apply to official EU languages and the languages of Ukraine’s indigenous peoples, but not Russian.
All 27 EU member states unanimously agreed on Monday to move forward with the opening of Cluster 2, covering the internal market, and Cluster 3, covering competitiveness and inclusive growth.
The decision clears the way for an intergovernmental conference in Luxembourg on Tuesday, Oct. 13, where the two clusters are expected to be formally opened for Ukraine and Moldova.
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos welcomed the Ukrainian parliament’s vote and praised Kyiv for continuing reforms despite Russia’s attacks.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also welcomed the progress following discussions with Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán in Luxembourg.
Hungary’s previous objections had prevented Kyiv from moving forward with the two negotiating clusters, despite preparations by EU institutions.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Another 11 children return to Ukrainian-controlled territory
body:
According to Ukrinform, Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, announced this on Telegram .
"Another 11 children have been returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory from the temporarily occupied part of the Kherson region. They are seven boys and four girls aged from one year and four months to 17 years," the statement said.
The return was facilitated by the charitable organisation Save Ukraine as part of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's Bring Kids Back UA initiative.
It was emphasised that each child's story involves experiences of fear, pressure and threats. In particular, a 16-year-old boy survived an armed attack by Russian soldiers in his own home. At an occupation-run school, children were forced to learn how to handle weapons and operate combat drones.
Another teenager, aged 17, was forced under threat to attend an occupation-run school and was later forcibly registered for military service. His family also endured regular armed searches.
The family of an eight-year-old girl was threatened with having her taken to an orphanage if she did not attend a Russian school. There, children were involved in propaganda activities, including being forced to draw postcards for Russian soldiers.
According to Prokudin, all these children are now safely back in Ukrainian-controlled territory. They are currently safe and receiving the assistance they need.
He reported that 219 children from the Kherson region had been returned from temporary occupation since the beginning of the year.
As Ukrinform previously reported, as of October 8, Ukraine had verified 20,651 cases of the unlawful deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children by Russia, of whom 2,665 had already been returned home.

title: “Run for Heroes” charity run in Chicago raises $10,000 for wounded Ukrainian soldiers
body:
The organization Revived Soldiers Ukraine reported this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
The 1- and 5-kilometer races were organized by the older youth group of the local branch of the Ukrainian Youth Association. Representatives of the Revived Soldiers Ukraine foundation, led by President Iryna Vashchuk Ditsypio, as well as Ukrainian soldiers undergoing treatment and prosthetic care in the U.S., participated in the event.
Among them were Artem Borysenko of the 151st Separate Mechanized Brigade, Mykola Yukhymenko of the 79th Separate Airborne Assault Brigade, and Serhii Yuriychuk of the 711th Separate Demining Brigade. Colonel Andrii Samoilenko, a surgeon at the Main Military Clinical Hospital in Kyiv, also took part in the event.
Two servicemen who had arrived in the U.S. for prosthetic fitting the day before the event also joined the run: Ihor Marych of the 39th Separate Marine Brigade and Serhii of the 102nd Separate Territorial Defense Brigade. In particular, they met with the Ukrainian community in Chicago.
Also present at the event was Colonel Vitalii Haniuk of the Medical Service, an anesthesiologist at the Kyiv Military Hospital, who accompanied the wounded soldiers during their medical evacuation from Ukraine to the U.S.
According to the organizers, the funds raised will go toward supporting severely wounded Ukrainian soldiers through the Revived Soldiers Ukraine foundation.
“Events like this are about more than just raising funds. For soldiers who are far from home and undergoing a long process of treatment and recovery in the U.S., it’s also an opportunity to feel that a large Ukrainian community—one that remembers and supports them—is right by their side,” the organization noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, a charity run dedicated to Ukrainian defenders was held in the Slovak capital, during which funds were raised to support the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Photo: Revived Soldiers Ukraine / Facebook

title: UK sanctions Dutch businessman exposed by Kyiv Independent for shipping EU machinery to Russian missile suppliers
body:
The U.K. has sanctioned Alexander Tattersall, a Dutch national, and Redwing Metal, the Turkish company he co-owns, nearly four months after a Kyiv Independent investigation revealed the firm had funneled EU-made industrial machinery to Russian metallurgical plants that supply the country's missile and fighter jet manufacturers.
Tattersall and Redwing Metal were blacklisted as part of a package of 38 designations announced by the U.K. Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) on Oct. 8, targeting Russian oil companies, shadow fleet tankers, crypto exchanges, and suppliers of goods critical to Russia's military.
In its announcement , the U.K. government said the package included a European national designated over his association with a third-country entity exporting machine tools to Russia , adding that such trade gives Moscow "material benefits on the battlefield."
U.K. sanctions freeze any assets the designated individuals and companies hold under British jurisdiction and bar British citizens and businesses from dealing with them.
They may also have wider effects, according to Roman Steblivskyi, director of policy and advocacy at the Economic Security Council of Ukraine (ESCU). The designation means that the supply chain through Redwing Metal to Russia has most likely been closed, he told the Kyiv Independent.
Although the EU has yet to sanction Redwing Metal, Steblivskyi said the U.K. sanctions would effectively cut Redwing Metal off from European partners as well.
"I do not think that EU companies or banks would approve transactions with Redwing Metal after the U.K. sanctions were imposed. It is too risky," he said.
The same may apply to Redwing Metal's Turkish counterparts, Steblivskyi added. "This company is sanctioned, so it is already a red flag at least."
The Russian beneficiaries of the supply chain, however, remain partially outside the scope of Western sanctions .
The Kyiv Independent's investigation , published in collaboration with Italy's IrpiMedia and the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), revealed the role of a Turkish company co-owned by Alexander Tattersall in supplying machinery to the Russian defense industry.
Russian customs records showed that Redwing Metal, set up in Turkey shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, shipped $5 million worth of European equipment in 2023 and 2024 to two Russian metallurgical plants: Aluminum Metallurg Rus (AMR) and Stupino Metallurgical Company (SMK).
The shipments included CNC lathes, metal heat-treatment furnaces, hydraulic presses, and other machinery produced by Italian, German, Spanish, and Czech manufacturers — equipment that EU export controls bar from being sold to Russia.
Both plants are controlled by Russian businessman Nikolay Timokhin, the son-in-law of Igor Zavyalov, who has served as deputy head of Russia's state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec since 2007.
The plants use such equipment to produce metal alloys for Russia's defense industry. An analysis of financial documents by the Kyiv Independent showed that AMR and SMK have supplied more than 40 Russian defense manufacturers since the start of the full-scale war, including producers of Kh-101 and Kh-59 missiles, missiles for S-300 and S-400 air defense systems, and fighter jets . Many of these companies are part of Rostec.
Customs data also showed Redwing Metal shipped a further $1.3 million worth of EU-made shipbuilding equipment — including anchors, mooring winches, and ventilation fans — to another company in Timokhin's group, SMS (formerly SMK-Snab), for installation on two Russian Navy ships under construction.
According to Turkish corporate records, Tattersall, who resides in Switzerland, owns 40% of Redwing Metal. The remaining stake is held by a local lawyer, Veysel Cengiz Soylemezoglu.
Tattersall's ties to Timokhin's business predate the full-scale war. For years, he ran a network of AMR trading companies in Switzerland, Germany, and the U.S. that sold AMR's aluminum products on Western markets. In 2019, he was photographed inside the AMR plant in Russia at celebrations marking the factory's 65th anniversary.
When approached by the Kyiv Independent ahead of the investigation's release, Tattersall confirmed he co-owned Redwing Metal but described himself as a part-time consultant with limited knowledge of its operations. He said that, to his knowledge, the company had never been involved in any "schemes" to ship sanctioned goods to Russia.
Soylemezoglu declined to comment on the shipments at the time, citing privacy obligations. Timokhin, AMR, and SMK did not respond to requests for comment.
On July 23, the EU sanctioned AMR , one of the two Russian metallurgical plants that received prohibited EU-made machinery through the Turkish company Redwing Metal.
But the second plant, SMK, and the company that received the shipbuilding equipment, SMS, have not been sanctioned by the EU. Neither has Timokhin, whose business group includes all three companies.
Redwing Metal and Tattersall are also absent from the EU sanctions list.
Sanctions experts interviewed for the investigation said that routing banned EU-made equipment to Russia through Turkey amounts to circumvention of EU sanctions.
EU nationals found to have knowingly helped bypass export restrictions through a third-country intermediary could face both financial penalties and criminal charges under national law, they said.

title: Catholic archbishop in Belarus blesses AI-generated icon of Carlo Acutis, the Italian teenager known as the internet’s patron saint
body: Archbishop Tadeusz Kondrusiewicz, the former head of the Catholic Church in Belarus, blessed an AI-generated icon on October 11, the Belarusian outlet Katolik.life reported . The image is in the Church of St. Mary Magdalene in Novolukoml. It depicts Carlo Acutis, a teenager whom the Vatican canonized a year ago. Katolik.life said believers criticized the blessing on social media, insisting that an AI-generated image cannot be considered an icon. Katolik.life said this was the first time an AI-generated icon had been blessed in Belarus. Meduza was unable to find information about similar images being blessed in other countries, including Russia. Carlo Acutis was an Italian teenager who came to faith as a child. He learned to code and built websites for Catholic organizations. He also created a website documenting miracles around the world. Acutis died of leukemia in 2006 at age 15. The Vatican canonized him in 2025. He has been called the “patron saint of the internet” and the first millennial saint. title: Ukrainian drone strikes have plunged Russia’s internet into crisis. Meduza explains why the damage has been so extensive, and why a full recovery will likely take months.
body: What happened? Overnight on October 11, Ukrainian forces launched a drone strike on a Yandex data center in Russia’s Vladimir region. It was the third attack in a row on the Russian tech giant’s infrastructure: On October 8 and 9, drones targeted facilities in Sasovo , in the Ryazan region, and in Kaluga , respectively. Each strike caused widespread outages across the Russian internet. The disruptions temporarily took down Yandex’s own services, including Yandex Go, Yandex Eats, and Yandex Pay, which vast numbers of Russians rely on. Many other websites and services also went down. The attacks affected major banks, retailers, online marketplaces, classified ad platforms, news websites and apps, and much more. All these companies, including CIAN, Sports.ru, Magnit, and Vkusno i Tochka, used Yandex’s infrastructure to store their data. Russians lost access to a range of everyday services: They couldn’t call a taxi, make payments, order deliveries, check their email, use the Alice voice assistant, and so on. Wow! How did just three strikes bring down the whole Russian internet? Because too much of the data storage market depends on Yandex’s infrastructure. And when the company designed its data centers, it didn’t anticipate drone attacks. That’s apparent from an October 11 update to its user agreement: Yandex classified attacks “using drones, missiles, and other weapons” as force majeure events and disclaimed liability for their consequences. According to BBC News Russian, the company regularly ran drills in which it shut down one of its six data centers and shifted the load to the others. But Ukraine has now attacked three data centers, and two of them — in Sasovo and near Vladimir — were shut down entirely. That makes restoring even some services much harder. For comparison, Iran attacked Amazon data centers in the Middle East in the spring of 2026. On September 15, the company said customer data stored in one particular availability zone in the UAE (mec1-az2) and in all availability zones in Bahrain had been permanently lost. Efforts to recover data in two other UAE zones (mec1-az1 and mec1-az3) were still incomplete at that point — six months after the strikes. Related reading Russia keeps attacking Ukrainian data centers, calling it a ‘mandatory digital detox’ So Ukrainian forces have already knocked out half of Yandex’s data centers? At least. Three of the company’s six major data centers have so far escaped attack : another one in the Vladimir region and one each in Ivanteyevka and Mytishchi, near Moscow. Yandex has acknowledged that its cloud data storage platform, Yandex Cloud, switched to emergency mode after just the third strike on the company’s infrastructure. This means the company has “run out of spare capacity,” and “that’s a very bad sign,” Eldar Murtazin, lead analyst at Mobile Research Group, told Fontanka. Any further strike, whether on data centers already attacked or on those Ukrainian forces have yet to target, would clearly only deepen the crisis. What should customers do? Yandex advised them to arrange backup capacity with other providers: Selectel , K2Cloud , and VK Cloud. That means backing up their data and renting servers in competitors’ data centers. Selectel has its own data centers in Moscow and St. Petersburg, as well as a partner facility in Novosibirsk. K2Cloud lists three availability zones in Moscow and one in St. Petersburg on its website. VK Cloud has four availability zones in Russia and another two in Kazakhstan. Incidentally, Yandex also set up its own server infrastructure in Kazakhstan back in 2024. Actually, wouldn’t it be easier for Russians to send their data somewhere abroad, beyond the reach of Ukrainian drones? In theory, that’s an option. But Russian companies are required to store certain data exclusively within Russia, so they have to choose among Russian data centers. Under the Yarovaya laws, for example, telecom operators must store all user traffic from the past six months and all its metadata from the past three years inside the country. All companies are prohibited from storing customers’ personal data outside Russia. Federal Law “On Communications” Article 64. Obligations of telecom operators and restrictions on the rights of telecom service users during law-enforcement investigative operations, measures to ensure the security of the Russian Federation, investigative procedures, the detention of criminal suspects and defendants, and the enforcement of prison sentences 1. Telecom operators must store the following within the Russian Federation : 1) Information about the receipt, transmission, delivery, and/or processing of telecom service users’ voice communications, text messages, images, sounds, video messages, or other messages — for three years after these activities have concluded; 2) Telecom service users’ text messages, voice communications, images, sounds, video messages, and other messages — for up to six months after their receipt, transmission, delivery, and/or processing has concluded. The Government of the Russian Federation shall establish the procedures, retention periods, and volume of information to be stored under this subparagraph. Federal Law “On Personal Data” Article 18. Obligations of data controllers when collecting personal data 5. When collecting personal data, including through the internet, data controllers are prohibited from using databases located outside the Russian Federation to record, organize, accumulate, store, correct (update or modify), or retrieve personal data belonging to citizens of the Russian Federation, except in the cases specified in paragraphs 2 , 3 , 4 , and 8 of Part 1 of Article 6 of this Federal Law. VK’s and Yandex’s infrastructure in Kazakhstan can only handle data relating to customers in that neighboring country. This restriction doesn’t apply to ordinary users, however. So you could try switching from Yandex Disk to Google Drive. That comes with a different risk, though: Russian authorities could try to block these foreign services at any time, without explanation. Related reading Ukraine strikes Yandex data center housing two of the company’s supercomputers Why didn’t anyone think about the risk of strikes on data centers sooner? Didn’t the attacks on online marketplaces teach them anything? We don’t know why Yandex, specifically, didn’t pay enough attention to protecting its infrastructure. But the data storage industry certainly studied what happened to online marketplaces. First, data centers are just as easy a target for drones as marketplace warehouses: They, too, are poorly protected stationary facilities at known locations, packed with expensive equipment. Attacks on them can cause losses across Russia’s economy and make people more inclined to protest. Second, Russia’s armed forces themselves gave Ukrainian forces a reason to target data centers. The Russian military had been striking the same kinds of facilities in Ukraine over the preceding month, even mockingly calling it a “digital detox” on the Defense Ministry’s Telegram channel. It seems naive to have expected Kyiv to pass up a chance to respond in kind. Third, there is concrete evidence that people were discussing the need to protect Russian data centers. According to BBC News Russian , just a couple of days before the first strike on a Yandex data center, Russian Deputy Digital Development Minister Yevgeny Filatov said these facilities needed to be distributed across locations deeper inside Russia, “somewhere beyond the Urals, where, fortunately, the strikes haven’t reached yet.” Some companies, including VK , MegaFon , and Rosatom , were buying protective frames and netting for data centers, purchasing drone detectors, and designing shelters for employees. On October 12, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said his ministry was “working with the Defense Ministry to arrange protection” for data centers. Great timing! And it’s not just Yandex’s services that are down. What happened to the rest of the Russian internet? As we said above, Yandex’s data centers are very popular. The company uses them for its own services and also actively rents out computing capacity and disk space for data storage. Companies without a backup plan to switch quickly to other servers and recover inaccessible data were unable to operate normally for a time. It’s still hard to predict which companies will be unable to recover from the strikes on Yandex’s infrastructure and whose data will never be restored. Because of this, services many Russians rely on and their favorite websites have been down for four days now. When will everything finally be fixed? We don’t know. A source in the IT industry told Kommersant that much will depend on how quickly Yandex can find equipment to replace its damaged infrastructure. Delivery times for this equipment can currently be as long as six months, the source said. Amazon’s experience in the Middle East, described above, gives little reason for optimism either: A full recovery will probably take months in any event. Further reading Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami And everyone’s losing money in the meantime! That’s right. ComNews Group CEO Leonid Konik told Vedomosti that Yandex’s own losses could be as high as a day’s revenue if all its services were down everywhere at the same time. That would amount to about 4 billion rubles a day. The actual figure is “much lower,” since the outages were only partial. Still, including the losses of dozens of other major companies, the combined damage runs to billions of rubles a day. One last thing: let’s explore what how a real catastrophe might occur As we said above, Ukrainian forces could try to disable Yandex’s remaining major data centers. If that happens, the company may be unable to repair its infrastructure without moving at least some of its capacity to competitors’ facilities. The Ukrainian military could also start destroying other Russian companies’ data centers. We’ve already seen something similar with online marketplaces: Initially, only Wildberries warehouses were targeted, but drones later began striking Ozon logistics centers as well. If events unfold this way, Russia’s IT industry faces a major setback. Rebuilding these data centers is slow and expensive. New facilities will also have to be built with potential drone attacks in mind. That could mean acquiring reliable air defenses, using underground protective structures (bunkers), or building several small data centers in different locations instead of one large one. According to BBC News Russian , manufacturers of mobile data centers the size of a standard shipping container are among the beneficiaries of the Ukrainian attacks. These could be a solution for some organizations, but they are unlikely to replace Yandex’s data centers fully. title: NZDF’s Ex Tropic Twilight concludes on remote Penrhyn
body:
Unfortunately you are viewing this website on an outdated browser which does not support the necessary features for us to provide an adequate experience. Please switch to a modern browser such as latest version of Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari or Microsoft Edge.
After nearly six weeks working alongside Penrhyn locals, around 50 New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) personnel have delivered infrastructure, health, hydrographic support and friendship to one of the most remote communities in the Cook Islands.
Penrhyn, or Tongareva, is nearly 1,400km north of Rarotonga.
The NZDF’s Exercise Tropic Twilight ran from early September to mid-October and involved personnel from 25 Engineer Support Squadron, 2 Engineer Regiment, nine medical and dental personnel and eight Royal New Zealand Navy hydrography personnel. Vanuatu Mobile Force and Les Forces armées en Polynésie française personnel also took part.
NZDF Youth Development Unit personnel also supported a Blue Light youth development programme in Aitutaki.
Tropic Twilight is an annual NZDF-led, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT)-supported series of South Pacific Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief activities. The location and tasks are mutually agreed between the NZDF and MFAT, which provides project funding.
A New Zealand Army vehicle mechanic works on a tractor engine in Te Tautua Village
Detachment Commander, Major Cam Gurney, said the exercise aimed to strengthen the partnership between New Zealand and the Cook Islands and contribute to Pacific resilience.
“Whether working alongside the community or supporting local schools, we had the opportunity to represent New Zealand and the NZDF in a positive way.
“Looking at the friendships that have been formed and the work that we have achieved together, I believe we have succeeded.”
NZ Army engineers completed projects including construction of a laundry at the Omoka Cyclone Centre, a new shelter and water infrastructure at Omoka School, repairs to school stairs and decking, upgrades to toilet block fixtures and fittings, and the fit-out of a new life-skills classroom.
Five solar stills were installed; electrical work was completed at Te Tautua School and water tanks used to increase water collection capacity at community buildings.
Engineers from 25 Engineer Support Squadron construct a solar still at Te Tautua Village
NZDF health personnel worked alongside local providers and almost 60 dental patients received treatment during 17 days of clinics. They also provided checks, medication reviews and follow-ups for residents with ongoing health conditions.
Navy hydrographers surveyed Penrhyn’s navigational approaches, lagoon transit routes and other significant areas, using sonar to build a clearer picture of the seafloor and previously uncharted hazards. The information will be provided to the Cook Islands Government.
Major Gurney said the relationships developed were just as important as the physical work.
Personnel had been welcomed into Penrhyn’s homes, churches, workplaces and community life. The level of hospitality stood out across his operational and exercise experience, he said.
Dental staff deliver a dental health lesson at Omoka School
Penrhyn Mayor Rangi Taia said the community was grateful for both the work completed and the way personnel had become part of life on Penrhyn.
“From the bottom of the hearts of the people of Tongareva, thank you very much for the good job, the kindness and the love you have given to my people,” he said.
Major Gurney acknowledged the contribution locals had made to completing the work, both on the project sites and behind the scenes. Tongarevans had impressed him with their adaptability and hospitality, despite the challenges of such a remote environment.
“We arrived as guests, but we leave as trusted partners and friends, and that is a legacy that will endure long after the exercise has ended.”
The scale of the work required significant preplanning. Construction freight travelled by barge, while specialist tools, personnel and priority equipment were flown in by the Royal New Zealand Air Force.
Logisticians planned for and delivered around 20,000 litres of drinking water, 2,000 ration packs, 10,000 litres of diesel and about 160 cubic metres of freight, as well as thousands of construction items.
After the exercise, tools and construction materials were donated to Penrhyn for further community projects. Surplus ration packs and drinking water were also donated.
