title: The Role of Beneficial Ownership Transparency in the Hard Power Era
body:
Clearly labelled: Companies House Headquarters in Cardiff, UK. Image: ATHENA PICTURE AGENCY ZING LIMITED / Alamy Stock
In the age of hard power, beneficial ownership transparency must shift from an anti-corruption ideal to a national security capability for Britain and its allies.
In the halcyon days of geopolitical stability in 2013, the UK government launched its campaign for raising global standards on beneficial ownership transparency (BOT) during its G8 presidency. One thing that has survived the turmoil in the intervening period is the UK governmentâs continued, cross-party support for this mission. This campaign has certainly achieved a measure of success, especially domestically, with a much-enhanced Companies House register and the novel introduction of the Register of Overseas Entities for improved property transparency , as the two stand-out achievements.
In a political culture of hyperbole, the UK can genuinely see itself as a global leader in championing â and delivering â BOT but as the UK prepares for its presidency of the G20 next year and the now-G7 in 2028, it cannot look at the state of global progress with great satisfaction.
In August this year, the US government defanged its Corporate Transparency Act by announcing the permanent removal of the requirement for US individuals and businesses to register, in a move which made permanent a 2025 suspension celebrated by President Trump as ending the âeconomic menaceâ of BOT. In the EU, the 2022 Court of Justice of the European Union ruling has effectively put an end to public registers, the UKâs policy preference, with focus shifting to a Legitimate Interest Access model. Finally, closer to home for the UK, genuine access to beneficial ownership information in the highest-risk Overseas Territories can be mildly described as suboptimal .
With the tide turning against it, how can the UK find a new argument to support its campaign for BOT to regain its relevance in an era of slipping standards and hard power politics?
The anti-corruption framing which has long accompanied BOT advocacy is technically correct and morally justified. It has proven effective in driving significant progress in the UK, especially when viewed through the prism of Russian kleptocrats. The challenge is not the veracity of these arguments but that the BOT argument is now being made in a world focused on hard security choices over development priorities, while integrity-based politics is suffering at the ballot box. With global norms slipping and the Financial Action Task Force not moving its baseline towards a requirement for public registers, the UK risks continuing to play the old classics to an audience which is not listening anymore.
Much as the security crisis of Russiaâs full-scale invasion of Ukraine proved to be the catalyst for long-overdue illicit finance reforms in the UK, the next salient framing â both rhetorically and substantially â is identifying and articulating the importance of BOT in supporting the UK and its allies in the â space between peace and war â in which they currently operate, rather than proposing transparency as an intrinsic good.
Open economies and societies such as the UK face an asymmetric disadvantage in comparison to more closed adversaries as they present a wider attack surface for these adversaries to exploit. This openness is a key feature and benefit of European countries but also requires greater efforts to protect against those who seek to do harm.
As Russian sabotage attacks spread across Europe, opaque ownership over who owns what should be considered as a national security risk rather than simply a concern of anti-corruption campaigners.
Shoots of this argument already exist across Europe with Nordic and Baltic countries taking measures to restrict the rights of Russian citizens to purchase property near Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) sites, or even across the entire country in some circumstances. This is based on fears that the Russian state will use these properties as âTrojan horsesâ in hybrid or full-scale attacks against Europe. Critically, none of these measures could be successful without understanding who owns what in the first place.
High-quality beneficial ownership information does not just reveal property ownership; it is also crucial for unveiling shell ownership structures of shadow fleet operations, companies linked to the evasion of dual-use controls and even where ownership of CNI itself is at risk.
This is not confined to Russia; clear examples emerge from China too. As detailed by the OCCRP (Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project) and others, Chinaâs authority for foreign exchange reserves (SAFE) was able to acquire equity in a range of European assets from fibre-optic companies, natural gas distributors or renewable infrastructure in the UK through a network of seven shell companies registered in the British Virgin Islands, which in turn controlled 28 registered holding companies in Luxembourg. A lack of transparent corporate ownership represents a clear national security risk.
Help your search results show more from RUSI. Adding RUSI as a preferred source on Google means our analysis appears more prominently.
Beyond Russia and China, the irony should not be lost on the US government that it weakened both its own domestic standards and consequently the international norms on BOT in the same month that it declared an economic D-Day on Iran, itself a frequent abuser of corporate secrecy to evade sanctions and the very pressure the US has unleashed.
So how can BOT improve our national security capabilities? The focus should not merely be on the availability of more data but critically its quality, and the systems built to exploit it. A public register with poor-quality data achieves as little as excellently verified data that is not accessed, analysed and exploited.
Starting at home, the UK government can use the proposed Defence Readiness Bill as the legislative vehicle to plug the remaining gaps in the UKâs beneficial ownership framework such as the role of discretionary trusts. Gaps that are relevant to CNI are especially relevant given its existing prevalence in the Bill. An exercise that separates what legislative gaps exist from the capability gaps in accessing, analysing and exploiting beneficial ownership information from a national security perspective would identify what requires investment rather than statute.
One step removed is the UKâs relationship with its Crown Dependencies (CDs) and Overseas Territories (OTs) that are viewed by many as the soft underbelly of the UKâs BOT campaign. Glacial progress in public registers has resulted in the stop-gap solution, and wonderful acronym, of LIARBOs (Legitimate Interest Access Registers of Beneficial Ownership). LIARBOs are in their infancy but the flaws have already been documented , and after eight years of protracted negotiations since the UK government first pledged public registers in the Overseas Territories, the status quo is likely to be as far as this process will go. This does not mean the UK should reduce its efforts, but with public registers still a mirage, an alternative option â the expansion and more active use of the Exchange of Notes (EoN) concept â that allows for better government-to-government information sharing should be more closely considered.

Get a weekly round-up of the latest commentary and research straight into your inbox.
Ten years on from the original EoN agreement, which allowed for law enforcement agencies in the UK to receive accurate beneficial ownership information on request from their counterparts in the CDs and OTs in a timely and private manner, the 2019 review remains the sole public record of its success. An updated and transparent Exchange of Notes review would provide either the grounds for practical improvements in the arrangements such as direct UK government access to the registers or, in the best-case scenario, a strong footing for the CDs and OTs in the narrative and policy debates they face on BOT. Furthermore, such an intimate government-to-government approach embracing other international financial centre registers that remain closed to public access could be expanded to boost security access to beneficial ownership data and could be integrated into the final leg of the UKâs influence on the international stage via initiatives such as the planned Illicit Finance Summit as well as the upcoming G7 and G20 presidencies.
Given that the UKâs preferred model of public registers is unattainable at present, an EoN model of government-to-government access built on collective security interests may provide a different pathway for continued progress. Expanding the UKâs EoN model with like-minded countries offers the most practical step forward, which might also include creating system-to-system access with the Beneficial Ownership Registers Interconnection System (BORIS), the EUâs interconnected and internal database linking national central beneficial ownership registers.
Whatever the policy direction, recognising that corporate secrecy has become more than a mere criminal threat and is being weaponised would help secure another decade of political support for advancing BOT standards and ensure that access to and analysis and exploitation of accurate beneficial ownership information plays its part in the national security apparatus of the UK and its allies.

title: U.S. Army to stress-test defense production and supply chains in ‘Manufacturing Rodeo’
body: “The U.S. Army is going to do something we’ve never done before: early next year we will conduct what I’m calling a Manufacturing Rodeo—a race between our industrial base partners that strains our organic industrial base, stresses the supply chain, pressures manufacturing processes, and shows us exactly where it breaks,” Telle said. The exercise will test both the Army’s Organic Industrial Base and the wider U.S. manufacturing network. Telle said the Army would learn by doing rather than “sitting around postulating at the Pentagon.” It intends to identify weak links, strengthen them and keep testing improvements to make production more resilient and responsive. The initiative follows the Army’s shift this year from production targets for individual systems toward manufacturing capabilities that can make a wider range of components. The service has established advanced manufacturing hubs at Red River, Anniston and Tobyhanna Army depots and secured public-private partnerships with Hadrian and Siemens. The Army said those investments have expanded its ability to manufacture subcomponents on demand for existing and future weapon systems. Products include complex electric motors and replacement parts such as tank engine transmission belt housings. The service is also seeking to reduce bureaucratic barriers to working with U.S. companies and speed up the acquisition of new capabilities. It said integrating autonomous technologies and expanding production would help provide soldiers with equipment when needed and in sufficient quantities.

title: Russian mines injure 1,739 civilians, including 178 children, since start of full-scale war
body:
This was reported on Telegram by the Main Directorate for Mine Action, Civil Protection, and Environmental Safety, according to Ukrinform.
It is noted that among the victims are, in particular, 306 farmers, 256 unemployed people, 170 retirees, 166 critical infrastructure workers, 112 drivers, and 171 students.
The Main Directorate for Mine Action, Civil Protection, and Environmental Safety, as the secretariat of the National Mine Action Authority, collects, analyzes, verifies, and enters into the mine action information management system data on incidents involving mines and explosive remnants of war, as well as information on civilian casualties resulting from such incidents, which is received from regional military administrations, regional units of the State Emergency Service, and the National Police.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Cabinet of Ministers approved a unified procedure for planning humanitarian demining in Ukraine.

title: Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian forces struck several districts of Kyiv late on 12 October with what the Air Force called, by preliminary data, six ballistic missiles. For once, the air-raid alert reached people only after the attack had begun, Ukraine’s Air Force reported . Reports of Russian ballistic launches are part of the intelligence the US shares with Ukraine, and that data is what lets sirens sound before the missiles arrive, giving civilians a few minutes to hide. Those minutes save lives, which is why the warning gap landed hard amid fears that Washington could cut Ukraine off from such intelligence amid US President Donald Trump's agreement with Russia to let its diesel into the US. The alert came late because Ukraine’s radar detected the ballistic targets only during the attack, with no advance data on launches from Russian territory, according to the Air Force. “No information was received about launches from enemy territory. The causes are being established,” the Air Force said. The stakes are human, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, stressed. “This information is needed first of all by civilians, so that people have time to hide in a shelter,” he said. Beskrestnov says he does not want to believe the US would leave Ukraine without that data because it is a matter of civilian survival. He urged caution on the cause, saying there were nuances and that it was too early to draw conclusions. When the sirens fall behind the missiles However, Ukraine usually sees the launches first. The warning system normally flags Russian ballistic launches before the missiles reach their targets, giving people time to move, but on 12 October, that did not happen, the Air Force noted. Beskrestnov later added a note of doubt about what flew. The suspected S-400 missiles were not being recorded by partners’ intelligence services, he wrote, stopping short of blaming the lapse on a loss of US data. Two cities hit within the same hour The damage in Kyiv was concrete. A missile struck a transport-infrastructure site in the Dniprovskyi district, and another hit a four-story warehouse in the Desnianskyi district, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said . Russia struck Kharkiv at about the same time with nine S-8000 Banderol loitering munitions, Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported . One of the last strikes hit a residential building, where people may be trapped under the rubble and a fire is burning. “Very serious destruction, an entire stairwell collapsed,” Terekhov said. title: Russian missile attack on Kharkiv kills 4, injures at least 41 including rescuer
body:
Russian forces launched a large-scale missile attack on Kharkiv on Oct. 12, killing four and injuring at least 41 people, including an emergency responder, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Hours after the strikes, three bodies were pulled from the rubble, said Ihor Terekhov, the city's mayor . Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov later reported a fourth victim found under the rubble. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that 41 people were injured, while four people were rescued from the rubble.
Three other people trapped beneath the rubble were rescued earlier, UNIAN reported , citing Ukraine's State Emergency Service.
Syniehubov said Russian forces had used 10 Banderol-type missiles in the attack, targeting civilian infrastructure.
"From the evening until now, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different means of attack: jet drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the morning of Oct. 13.
In the city's Kholodnohirskyi district, a strike hit a four-story residential building, destroying an entire section. At least 10 nearby houses were also damaged, Syniehubov said.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, another strike hit a five-story residential building. A bank on the ground floor and six vehicles caught fire, while three nearby apartment buildings sustained window damage.
Among the injured were two people in serious condition, including a 19-year-old man admitted to a burn unit and another man undergoing surgery, according to Syniehubov.
A State Emergency Service rescuer was also injured while responding to the attack and was hospitalized, RBC-Ukraine reported , citing the emergency service. His condition was not immediately confirmed.
Rescue workers from Ukraine's State Emergency Service, emergency medical teams, and the National Police were working at the impact sites. Police officers were also conducting door-to-door checks to identify residents requiring medical assistance.
Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, lies roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the Russian border and has been subjected to repeated Russian attacks throughout the full-scale invasion.
A Russian air strike on Kharkiv on Oct. 11 killed at least one person and injured eight others .

title: The US Army is back in the jungle. Panamanians are showing soldiers the way.
body: Gunshots erupted from solid ground towards a boat that ferried Panamanian soldier Albis Fajardo and his team during a counter-drug mission along the country’s Pacific coastline. The team attempted to return fire as they pulled back from a harrowing effort to target a cartel leader. Fajardo, then early into his military career, felt his adrenaline surge as he realized the team had been unsuccessful: A bullet had torn through the flesh of his friend. Over a decade later, with the early autumn sun sinking over Panamanian base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, the 47-year-old, now a first sergeant, recounted the ordeal. His friend survived, but the horror changed Fajardo’s life. The brush with death, he said, fueled him to learn as much as he could, militarily, and eventually led him to become an instructor at the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama. The class, offered for decades in the Central American nation before it was shuttered in 1999, has resumed in partnership between U.S. and Panamanian forces, with Panamanian service members teaching and attending the 18-day course. As Panama’s troops have trained, lived — and in some cases, fought — in such environments, they are largely seen by U.S. personnel as the ultimate masters of the terrain. Lt. Col. Andrew Eagen, who heads the U.S. Jungle Operations Training Center in Panama, said that as U.S. forces developed the course, they became quickly attuned to the deft tactics their Panamanian counterparts had developed for survival. “They are the experts of this environment. We will never catch up,” he told Military Times in a mosquito-riddled interview at the jungle school. “This does not exist in the continental United States,” he said, gesturing to the lush canopy, which was twinkling with the day’s last glimmers of sun and abuzz with the evening hum of jungle creatures. “We do not have an exposure to it. They do, and they have incredible techniques and an incredible level of comfort that the average American [does not].” Fajardo is one of nine Panamanian instructors — from three branches of the country’s armed forces — who teach at the reestablished school. The instructors assist in some parts of the course, but lead in areas where students learn about jungle survival, Eagen said. In addition to the leading group, more than 10 Panamanian service members attended the course in which Military Times took part, according to Eagen. Throughout each exercise, Panamanian troops sat interspersed with U.S. personnel and were placed in squads with a Spanish-speaking U.S. participant for course assignments. Though the language barrier admittedly made some tactical movements difficult, U.S. personnel seemingly learned just from observing their Panamanian counterparts. During one practical exercise, one squad had to hide in the jungle, cover their tracks to erase any disturbance to the foliage, and position themselves so they would be alerted to any incoming intruders. The other squad’s job was to hunt down the hiding squad using tracking clues, the activity forming a tense game of tactical hide-and-seek. The hunters ultimately won, thanks to one Panamanian squadmate who spotted a tiny vine that appeared slightly too parallel to the ground. One rule of the jungle? Nothing is a straight line. The Panamanian student correctly identified the trailing plant, hovering inches above the muddy ground, as a hasty trip wire. Made using a vine and a piece of trash, it would have alerted the hiding squad to the hunters’ presence. When the two groups gathered to discuss the interaction, the lanewalker found that the Panamanian student in the other squad had set up the tripwire; a particularly impressive development, considering a tripwire class was scheduled for later in the day. During that class, an American instructor showed students how to create different forms of tripwires that could act as early warning systems. Some set off rattling cans. Others used fauna. Before letting students practice, the instructor shared stories from Panamanian cadres who once operated in the Darién Gap, a roadless land bridge of brutally dense, remote jungle that spans 60-plus miles between Panama and Colombia and has been notoriously rife with human and drug trafficking. Trip wires there are not historical relics of warfare from decades ago, the instructor said. Cartel members are using them now. Several instructors, including Fajardo, have attended Panama’s own jungle school, called Panajungla. Fajardo shook his head and shivered as he recounted the intense course in which participants were forced to survive on their own in the Teribe region of Panama’s Bocas del Toro province. Students of the Panamanian course must shop at the “supermarket de la selva” — the jungle supermarket — to eat, using machetes to prepare or kill any nourishment they can find, Fajardo said. Fajardo’s prized jungle delicacy is ñame, a tropical root vegetable similar to a yam. He also appreciates the taste of grubs, he said, which he likens to butter. Tucked neatly into each Panamanian instructor’s backpack, razor-sharp machetes sat nestled in intricately carved leather coverings. The U.S. Army teaches machete training in its jungle school, but some Panamanian instructors have attended a separate, more intensive course on using the long, daunting blade. It can clear brush, help prepare food, carve shelter and even help start a fire. To Fajardo, it is the single most important tool for survival in the jungle. And with a smile, he jokingly referred to the machete as “mi esposa,” or my wife, in English. To date, the U.S. Army is developing the course to dedicate at least 20 of its 120 spots to partner forces and at least 15 to Panamanians. Though no other countries have sent soldiers yet, Eagen is confident that the school is close to having Colombian students join. The U.S. has partnered with Colombia’s Lancero course, which is similar to Ranger School, and all three countries exchange information. Panama supports hosting Colombian forces, Eagen added, as “they have a direct relationship with the country. “They have a lot of shared bilat right there at the Darién,” Eagen said, “so both Panamanian leaders and Colombian leaders want them to be first.” Panama’s expertise in navigating such unforgiving terrain, meanwhile, has also prompted other countries, like Costa Rica and Brazil, to express interest in the course, Eagen said. Other jungle courses worldwide have so far informed the new U.S. Army jungle school’s curriculum, and Eagen said the Army is designing a scenario construct for the school using threat characteristics seen by Panamanian service members. And while Panamanian forces often confront small-team drug trafficking operations attempting to establish supply lines, Eagen was clear that the Army endeavored to replicate a potential combat environment, not the country’s security situation. “That is not the premise of us being in Panama,” he said. “We try to make sure there are clear boundaries of understanding for the students that this is about the skills required of the environment, not about the situation in Panama.” Though public sentiment between the countries has ebbed and flowed in the decades that followed Panama’s 1994 formal abolishment of its standing army — several years after a U.S. military invasion ousted military dictator Manuel Noriega — those tensions were absent from interactions Military Times observed among the service members during the course. Eagen said the U.S. is mindful of the pride Panamanians take in their nation’s sovereignty. The Army, he added, has been purposeful in approaching the course’s renewed partnership with an emphasis on learning from — rather than simply teaching — its Panamanian counterparts.

title: New White House press secretary a 'devoted fan' of Trump and MAGA
body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption
President Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia faced questions about her credentials as an attorney as she took the podium on Tuesday for her first press briefing. Zacharia stepped in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections.
The Trump administration is also engaged in a legal battle with the press corps that work to cover Trump. Last month, the White House restricted access by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, news organizations that Trump views as unfriendly. The Justice Department has since launched an investigation into the five television networks that share pool video coverage of Trump.
In a post on social media, Zacharia, a self-described attorney and a mother of four , offered no hint of the challenges ahead. She described her new job as the "honor of a lifetime" and praised Trump's policies. "His confidence is a true privilege, and his leadership is a blessing to this country," Zacharia wrote on Friday .
But on Tuesday, Zacharia also faced questions about her credentials as an attorney. While standing with Trump, she was asked by reporters where she passed the bar exam.
"When I moved to China," Zacharia answered, an apparent reference to what she has described on her LinkedIn page as a period of time from 2011 through 2013 spent working for a prominent Beijing-based law firm called Zhon Lun.
NPR asked the White House to clarify whether Zacharia is a licensed attorney in the U.S. In a statement provided to NPR, Zacharia said she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
In naming Zacharia, Trump praised her longstanding personal loyalty . "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," Trump said. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!"
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia walks out to speak with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption
Zacharia, 41, a graduate of Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, has also worked for a number of conservative organizations, according to her online resume . She served on the advisory board for an anti-abortion group called The White Rose Resistance that took its name from Christian students who challenged the Nazis. White Rose says it's working to counter "the same evils, the same apathy " faced by opponents of the Nazi regime.
More recently, Zacharia has served as a communications advisor for the Trump Media & Technology Group, the firm that operates Trump's Truth Social platform. She has also been a frequent pro-Trump commentator on conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax.
During an appearance in August on the network Real America's Voice , Zacharia weighed in on the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, arguing that "toxic feminism" had skewed the public's view of the case. Clancy was charged with killing her three children. The five-week trial ended in a mistrial after sparking a national conversation over postpartum depression.
"This started with the advocation of abortion," Zacharia said. "When women are championing the death and murder and the ability to murder their children from conception all the way through, when does humanity begin and end?"
Zacharia has also used her social media posts to amplify right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that Democratic leaders took part in pedophile rings. In one post from 2022, she described former Democratic White House chief of staff John Podesta as "Pedo Podesta." That same year she shared a post from a far-right commentator who claimed Democrats "want to mask and rape your children."
NPR asked the White House for comment on the posts, which were first uncovered by the online progressive media site Popular Information. Administration officials responded in an email by praising Zacharia without addressing her social media comments.
After being named to serve as White House press secretary, Zacharia drew praise from other administration officials. FBI Director Kash Patel described her as "sharp, fearless" and someone who "knows what it means to stand for the American people."
Karoline Leavitt, who held the press secretary post until August before stepping down, also praised Zacharia. "I have no doubt Katie will do great work for President Trump and our country," she said on X .
In an appearance on Fox News on Saturday , Zacharia boosted Trump's controversial plan to import Russian diesel fuel, which has drawn bipartisan criticism . She also praised Trump's efforts to rally GOP support ahead of the November vote, while suggesting congressional Republicans may be to blame for any losses.
"President Trump has made the case and delivered historic results. I would have loved to see more from our congressional Republicans and Senate," she said.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Iran's Araghchi offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks, calls for diplomatic end to hostilities
body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered to help facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi terrorist group amid ongoing hostilities, according to a statement posted on Telegram following his phone call with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan on Sunday.Araghchi expressed concern over escalating tensions, warning that continued reliance on military action while disregarding diplomatic solutions would further complicate the situation, the statement said.He also stressed that the region's ongoing crises could not be resolved militarily and offered Iran's assistance in initiating dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen to help reach a political solution.The phone call came amid several days of Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi airports, which have severely disrupted air travel and prompted international airlines to suspend services. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport is expected to remain closed until October 17, while some airlines have extended flight suspensions into 2027.Authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh's international airport until Saturday, and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia's capital.Riyadh airport closure extended following deadly Houthi attacksOperations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities," the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.A Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) issued later in the day said the airport will remain closed until 2100 GMT on October 17.The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.Houthi attacks disrupt Saudi aviation, raising security concernsThe attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits.They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict."This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented," said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organization that provides aviation safety advice."I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully," he said.Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets crossed Saudi airspace and landed at the country's top hub, Jeddah, on the west coast.Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4%, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.Airlines extend Saudi flight cancellationsLufthansa Group has canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended its suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month, Reuters reported.Etihad Airways canceled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to “regional disruption.” All flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh have been canceled until October 19, the airline said.Qatar Airways said on Monday that it had temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam due to the “current situation.”Delta Air Lines postponed the launch of its Atlanta–Riyadh service, originally scheduled for October 23, until March 2027.

title: Sudanese anti-war forces press for peace roadmap
body: Sudanese civilian and political groups opposed to the war have called for an immediate, unconditional humanitarian truce and a Sudanese-led peace process following talks with the Quintet mediation mechanism in Addis Ababa on Monday. In a statement, the groups said their delegation met the Quintet at the African Union headquarters to discuss ways to end the conflict and establish a peace process owned and led by Sudanese people. “We stressed the priority of reaching an immediate and unconditional humanitarian truce to protect civilians, ensure the delivery of aid and pave the way for a peace process,” the statement said. The delegation included representatives of the Sudanese Declaration of Principles forces, the Popular Congress Party, civil society organisations, women’s and youth networks, and public figures. Former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok also attended the meeting, which brought together international envoys and representatives of regional and international organisations to discuss efforts to end the conflict. Participants included the United Nations personal envoy Ramtane Lamamra, African Union envoy Mohamed Ibn Chambas, representatives of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), European Union special representative Annette Weber, and Western observers. Following engagements in July, the #Quintet continued its consultations with key Sudanese civilian/political blocs today in Addis Ababa. At the @_AfricanUnion premises, we held constructive meetings with the Anti-War Civilian Forces. pic.twitter.com/5NYGHDij81 — Annette Weber (@EUSR_Weber) October 12, 2026 The Sudanese groups proposed a framework built around three interconnected tracks: humanitarian response, a ceasefire and political dialogue to address the root causes of the crisis and lay the foundations for an inclusive peace and a sustainable democratic civilian transition. They called for civilian forces to participate in designing and leading the process under fair criteria that would prevent any one party from dominating it. The statement also called for the exclusion of the National Congress Party, the Islamic Movement and their affiliated organisations. The groups urged regional and international mediators to coordinate their efforts under a unified framework bringing together the Quad, the Quintet and the Troika. They also called for stronger measures to pressure the warring parties and those obstructing peace, including extending the arms embargo to cover all of Sudan, halting external support fuelling the conflict, cutting off funding for the war and holding those responsible for atrocities accountable. Today in Addis Ababa, the Quintet held a productive meeting with the Anti-War Civilian Forces to discuss ways to advance the political process in Sudan pic.twitter.com/F3yzzZk6LJ — OPESG_Sudan (@OPESG_Sudan) October 12, 2026 The statement rejected granting legitimacy to authorities established as a result of the war and stressed the importance of preserving Sudan’s territorial integrity and national unity. The groups said they would continue engaging with the Quintet, the Quad and other actors seeking a peaceful resolution to the conflict. They also pledged to broaden support for an independent civilian anti-war movement that does not align with either side. Their stated goal is to restore Sudanese people’s rights to security, freedom and democratic civilian rule, and to complete the path of the December Revolution, which led to the overthrow of longtime president Omar al-Bashir in April 2019. Sudan’s war began on April 15, 2023, when fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces following a power struggle between their leaders. The conflict has displaced millions and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis. The post Sudanese anti-war forces press for peace roadmap appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Chinese J-16 Fighter Pilot Details First Engagements with French Rafale Jets Over Egypt
body: A Chinese fighter pilot who participated in the Eagles of Civilisation 2026 joint military exercises with the Egyptian Air Force has highlighted Egyptian interest in Chinese combat aircraft, long-range air-to-air missiles, and electronic warfare capabilities, while commenting on the performance of the African service’s Rafale fighters. According to a report by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, the Chinese pilot indicated that Egyptian personnel were especially interested in China’s electronic warfare capabilities, reportedly expressing admiration for the timing and effectiveness of Chinese jamming systems. Electronic warfare has become an increasingly important component of modern air combat, with the ability to disrupt opposing aircraft’s radars, communications, and other electronic systems potentially influencing engagements well before opposing fighters come within visual range. The Chinese pilot also reportedly praised the Rafale’s manoeuvrability during close-range engagements. The Rafale is a considerably smaller aircraft than the J-16, with a much more limited range, weapons carrying capacity, and engagement range and a far weaker radar and electronic warfare suite, with the shortcomings of its size compounded by the limitations of the French electronics industry. The fighter’s agility, while far from exemplary, may well be the area where it sits closest to the J-16 in performance. The Rafale is notably not the most manoeuvrable fighter in Egyptian service, with Egypt’s MiG-29M fighters having far more powerful engines and higher thrust-weight ratios. The Rafale’s M88 engines are currently the weakest in production for fighters anywhere in the world, with only the small size of fighter allowing it to retain respectable manoeuvrability. The limitations of the engines, however, mean that additional fuel or weapons take a much greater toll on the Rafale’s flight performance than they would for larger aircraft like the medium weight MiG-29 or heavyweight J-16. The J-16’s performance record and known capabilities fuelled expectations that it would demonstrate its vast superiority over other participating fighter types during exercises in Egypt. Experience operating against the Rafale provides dissimilar air combat experience, albeit against an adversary far less capable than those which Chinese fighter units face in East Asia, where U.S. and allied forces deploy advanced F-35 and F-15EX fighters. The Rafale not only consistently lost overwhelmingly in tenders against U.S. and Russian fighter types, most notably the F-35 and Su-30, but it has also fared very poorly in simulated combat exercises with U.S. fighters, with French pilots highlighting its inability to engage modern fifth generation fighters. China and the United States are currently the only major producers of fifth generation fighters, while China is leading the world in sixth generation fighter development with an expected service entry date around 2030. The Rafale saw its first high intensity combat test in May 2025, during which between one and four of the aircraft flown by the Indian Air Force were neutralised during engagements with Pakistan Air Force’s Chinese-supplied J-10C ‘4+ generation’ fighters. The J-10C was developed in parallel to the J-16 as a lighter and lower cost counterpart, and has approximately half the engine power and a radar with less than half the power of the larger aircraft. The engagement, and the J-10C’s overwhelming successes against the closely related Eurofighter, which shares common origins with the Rafale, during exercises in Qatar, fuelled expectations that engagements between the J-16 and Rafale would be highly one-sided.

title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1692: Trump suspends Russian diesel sanctions, while EU blacklists record 1,569 arms suppliers
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusive Europe has 11 ways to choke Russia’s war. It doesn’t need Trump’s permission for any of them . Three weeks after signing new Russia sanctions into law, Washington suspended them for Russian diesel, while the levers that would hurt Moscow most sit in European hands. Military Ukrainian drones hit three of Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers in four days. Ukraine’s president says the bots thinned out too . Lithuania’s prime minister wants more such strikes to protect elections. Researchers say the bot data shows Yandex’s web crawlers, not trolls. Ukrainian marines cleared about 6 km² near Pokrovsk without losses. The Russians they faced got a can of meat a week . The deputy commander says the operation also yielded a lot of intelligence—and that more surprises await Russia. Ten casualties to one, by a NATO official’s count: Russia’s September in Ukraine’s kill zones . Russia kept sending troops into drone-packed kill zones in September, and up to 28,000 died, a senior NATO official told Bloomberg. Russia’s supply base in occupied Luhansk Oblast burned overnight—NASA’s fire map caught it . The fires broke out together and grew within the hour, satellite data show, and Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported heavy Ukrainian strikes in the area. Short on interceptors, Ukraine goes after the launchers: eight Russian ballistic systems hit, three destroyed since September, a minister says . Ukraine's Defense Minister says the hits made Moscow rework planned barrages, as he presses partners for anti-ballistic missiles in bulk instead of one-off deliveries. Intelligence and technology Russia’s sabotage of Europe should bring Ukraine more weapons through US purchase scheme, with clear statement of where its red lines lie, NATO’s top European commander says . The PURL program lets allies fund US-made weapons for Ukraine and drew nearly $5.5 billion in pledges before May. Built by Ukraine’s ex-defense minister and unit that wrecked $12 billion of Russian gear, new interceptor downs two jet drones over Kyiv . Mykhailo Fedorov and Lasar’s Group commander Pavlo Yelizarov developed the drone in a month, Fedorov says. Russia is building satellite network that could put all of Europe in reach, defense executive warns . Oleksandr Danyliuk, head of the European defense-tech firm Destinus, called Russia’s Rassvet system an extraordinary threat, first to Ukraine and then to Europe. Russia is hacking cameras across Europe to track arms bound for Ukraine. At home, Ukraine has secured about 40,000 that could guide strikes — WSJ . In 2024, Russian hackers seized residential webcams in Kyiv, according to Ukraine’s Security Service. International “Zelenskyy is helping Democrats”: Trump’s MAGA base accuses Ukraine of trying to swing US midterms, says journalist in US . The narrative runs across all levels of the US information space, from anonymous accounts to national television. Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries . The administration says the deal will lower fuel prices, but lawmakers warn it could help finance Russia's war against Ukraine. Ten years on, Britain’s prime minister says Russia meddled in the Brexit vote—and warns Germany and France . In 2020, London said it saw “no evidence of successful interference.” Now Andy Burnham says Merz told him the AfD is linked to Russia. Political and legal developments For years, Hungary tied Ukraine’s whole EU course to ethnic Hungarians’ language rights. Kyiv has now passed the schooling law meant to lift the block . Hungary had blocked four stages of Ukraine’s membership process over the matter. EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow . Most of the listed firms feed the supply chain behind the ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities, and EU ministers vowed to keep up the pressure despite the US-Russia fuel arrangement. Zelenskyy says Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agrees to 60-day ceasefire. Moscow counters with truce lasting only voting day . Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov says Ukraine needs the 60 days not to hold elections but to heal its wounds and keep fighting. New developments Peacekeepers, riot police, and drone crews: Russia’s bloc rehearses an operation in a Belarusian oblast bordering two NATO states . Police and national guard units train alongside soldiers from five former Soviet states, under priorities Russia set as the bloc’s chair this year. Germany stays in Russia’s sabotage crosshairs, and its industry now braces for the long haul . Companies are no random targets, the country’s main industry lobby warns, a week after the foreign intelligence chief said Germany had become a main obstacle to Russian power in Europe. Read our earlier daily review here .

title: Russian Missile Strike Destroys Kharkiv Apartment Entrance, Killing 4 and Injuring Dozens
body:
Russian missile strikes on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv left four people dead and 41 people injured late Monday, Oct. 12, while emergency crews rescued four people after an attack destroyed part of a residential building, Ukrainian authorities reported Tuesday.
Russia targeted residential neighborhoods and civilian infrastructure in the city’s Kholodnohirskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS).
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
One missile struck a four-story apartment building, completely destroying an entrance section and leaving residents potentially trapped beneath the rubble. Rescuers said the bodies of three people had been recovered from the rubble. Firefighting and search-and-rescue operations are ongoing at the site of the missile strike.
A rescue worker was also injured during the emergency response and hospitalized, the DSNS reported.
Earlier, Kharkiv Regional Military Administration head Oleh Syniehubov said Russian forces had used approximately 10 Banderol-type missiles against civilian infrastructure, according to preliminary information.
Among the wounded was a 19-year-old man admitted to a burns intensive care unit. Another seriously injured man was undergoing surgery, while three additional patients were hospitalized in moderate condition.
In the Kholodnohirskyi district, at least 10 private homes were also damaged.
Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov described severe destruction at the apartment building.
“The destruction is very serious – an entire entrance section has collapsed,” he wrote on Telegram .
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, a separate strike hit a five-story apartment building, igniting a bank premises on the ground floor and several vehicles.
Windows in three nearby residential buildings were also shattered, according to Syniehubov.
Emergency crews continued working at the impact sites into early Tuesday, Oct. 13, with authorities warning that people could still be trapped beneath the collapsed apartment section.
Firefighters, bomb disposal specialists, search dog teams, police, medical workers, volunteers and municipal services were involved in the response.
DSNS psychologists were also providing assistance to residents affected by the strikes.
According to the DSNS report issued at 7:40 a.m., four additional fires in the city’s Kholodnohirskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts have been extinguished.
In a report issued at 12:22 p.m., the State Emergency Service said the death toll from a Russian missile strike on a residential building in the city’s Kholodnohirskyi district had risen to four. Another 41 people were injured.
“Search and rescue operations are ongoing. Information is being updated,” the report added.
Earlier Monday, a separate Russian strike on a residential high-rise in Kharkiv’s Kyivskyi district left 23 people affected, including two children, according to local authorities.
Kharkiv, located close to the Russian border, remains under frequent Russian missile and drone attacks, with residential neighborhoods and civilian infrastructure repeatedly damaged.
Deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: First women on ultra-Orthodox party slate running for Knesset seek change - interview
body: The first two women to run on a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) party's Knesset list have been seeking to address issues facing women in the haredi community, including health, employment conditions, education, and the pressure of raising large families while men study in Yeshiva.Nahumi Yaffe and Zivva Glantz, both running on the recently established Haredi Public party's list, broke down their plans to The Jerusalem Post in a recent interview, voicing existing concerns for women in the haredi community they seek to address."There are issues that were overlooked. Women in the [haredi] community are dying 5% more than the rest of the community from birth, cancer," Yaffe said.Yaffe has been placed third on the party's list and Glantz fourth, meaning both would enter the Knesset if the party passes the required electoral threshold.The Haredi Public Party has sought to enter the Knesset independently of the two major haredi parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ). Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has relied on Shas and UTJ as key coalition partners for years. Neither party has included women on its Knesset list.Unlike the established haredi parties, the Haredi Public party has called for change within the ultra-Orthodox community and encouraged haredi enlistment in the IDF. Though the party has been recently polling below the electoral threshold, Glantz said the Haredi Public party had been gaining momentum despite being new and having limited time to build support."People need this. There have been a lot of individuals waiting for a party like this for a very long time, myself included," she said.Women's health among issues largely unaddressed by haredi communityYaffe said women's health was among the major issues that had received insufficient attention within the haredi community.She added that haredi Knesset representatives had not sufficiently addressed women's issues in the government's past term."I've checked that not even one party member went to one of the Knesset committees dealing with it, for all kinds of various reasons," she said.Yaffe also argued that existing efforts to raise awareness of women's health issues were not adequately reaching the haredi community.Another issue the two candidates spoke on addressing was providing support for the issues of financial pressure on haredi women, many of whom work to support their children and families while their husbands study in yeshivas.Yaffe said women's participation in the workforce had increased significantly over the past two decades.She said that haredi women continued to face lower average incomes than their non-haredi counterparts and that some experienced unfair employment conditions."Their average income is way lower than their secular counterparts, and some of them are being employed in really unfair conditions. There is exploitation. Very simple. And this is something that needs to be addressed," Yaffe said.She added that women supporting large families often had little time or opportunity to advocate for their own rights."Someone has to look at the numbers and ask what's going on. And this is our job as women. These are our sisters and our daughters," she said.Yaffe said she sought to promote haredi women's rights and opportunities, as well as improve access to health and education services.Just being able to make them aware of their legal rights is also important, Yaffe said.Glantz speaks on struggles faced by haredi womenGlantz spoke on the struggle haredi women faced by being required to balance providing for their families in the workforce with raising children. "We have to recognize that there is a limit to every human ability, and we are pushing people to the max," Glantz said."These women are professionals. They have large families. They're hosting and cooking big meals. And we have to make sure that they have the support that they need, because otherwise we're going to deal with families collapsing because people have burnout, and that can't keep on happening," she added.Glantz also spoke on the importance of ensuring that haredi schools teach core curriculum subjects, including math and English, with the state responsible for overseeing their implementation."There needs to be broad educational reform within the [haredi] community and, frankly, within the community at large. I think education reform needs to be a topic of this election, and more people need to be talking about it because it affects everybody," she said."We want to push a core curriculum of math and English so that people should be able to employ themselves and have that opportunity to support themselves in the future, should they choose to. We also think that there need to be other changes in the education system," Glantz said.Regarding military service, Glantz raised concerns about the IDF's readiness to accommodate women. She said she did not believe the military was currently a suitable environment for many women, while adding that further work was also needed to address the challenges facing men who enlist."I do not think that right now the army is a good place for many women in general," Glantz said. "I also think that there's a lot of work that needs to be done for men that are drafting," she added.Yaffe, Glantz as political pioneers in haredi sectorAhead of the approaching October 27 elections, Yaffe said she believed that she and Glantz were pioneers in being the first women to run on a haredi party's Knesset slate."[Haredi] women have been around doing amazing, really incredible jobs, being in key positions and helping and contributing. But politically, we are the pioneers," she said."This is the first time that we are being invited to sit around the table and be part of the major political decisions," Yaffe added.

title: BAE Systems Rolls Out New Autonomous AMPV, Plans For Initial Demo In February
body:
BAE Systems on Monday rolled out its new Autonomous Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle for the first time, with an aim to conduct an initial demonstration of the platform in February.
Bill Sheehy, BAE Systems’ vice president of ground maneuver futures, told Defense Daily the company partnered with Forterra for the autonomy capability and RENK America for the drive-by-wire technology on the project, noting a goal to eventually provide the capability to an Army unit to gather feedback.
“We are on schedule with that. So we aren’t at full autonomy yet, we are still going through and learning. We have the autonomy stack built and we have the drive-by-wire built. That’s all inside the vehicle, and we are working through how it works,” Sheehy said in an interview at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference, where BAE Systems is showcasing the autonomous platform.
BAE Systems’ AMPV is the Army’s replacement for its legacy M113 armored personnel carriers, with the company receiving a full-rate production contract in 2023 ( Defense Daily , Sept. 1, 2023).
Sheehy said work on the Autonomous AMPV began earlier this year at BAE Systems’ Sterling Heights, Michigan facility to get the drive-by-wire tech in place, before shipping the vehicle for continued development at Forterra’s headquarters in Maryland.
“On a wheeled vehicle, when you go to turn your car in a turn, you slow down, you apply some weight. On a heavy track vehicle, you actually apply power because it’s got to turn, and one track goes backwards, so you can pivot. And autonomous software didn’t realize that. So those are the kinds of things we’re learning, right? The blocking and tackling for how an [autonomous] tracked combat vehicle literally moves,” Sheehy said.
“I had envisioned having to designate waypoints and doing this all laborious [work]. [Forterra was] showing me the concept, and they literally just touch the screen, and the vehicle knows it, and then turns it. So it is that quick, and so that’s the intent”
Sheehy detailed the potential benefits an autonomy capability could bring to the Army’s AMPV, with BAE Systems aiming to highlight the solution as a potential future kit to upgrade some of the vehicle fleet.
“When an armored unit moves, it moves from a place of relative security to a last covering concealed spot. If you can do that autonomously and allow your crew to rest, then when you get to that last pitch before they launch into combat, they’re better rested,” Sheehy said. “I think once we get it out there, and the Army starts messing with it and using it and developing it, they’re going to see things that none of us see.”
“If you want to have it on certain vehicles, you install it forward. It doesn’t have to be all or nothing, right? So the ability to [make it] an autonomous vehicle really would rely on the commander’s discretion to make these resupply vehicles autonomous, so [they] can reallocate [their] soldiers to this task over here and allow this vehicle to go back and forth doing resupply,” Sheehy added.
BAE Systems, Forterra and RENK have collectively invested a total of around $8 million into the project so far.
“When the [Secretary of Defense] and [Secretary of the] Army gave us the challenge, us being all of industry, bring me your solutions, self-invest, go fast, that really is the motivation behind any of the capabilities you’re putting on there. So, our ability to come together, self-organize [with industry], look at what we see going on in Ukraine, around the world, in different conflicts. Then, how do we position this vehicle for the Army as an option to what they want to do? So that’s what we really are doing across any of the capabilities,” Sheehy said.
BAE Systems over the last few years has showcased several versions of the AMPV outfitted with different payloads using its new External Mission Equipment Package (ExMEP) top plate designed for rapid integration, to include a turreted mortar capability, an unmanned turret version and a counter-drone platform, with Sheehy adding the autonomous version aligns with the company’s intent to highlight potential options for the Army.
An Army unit also received a pair of AMPVs earlier this year equipped with a remote turret weapon system capable of countering drone threats, called AMPV-30, with BAE Systems previously noting the concept demonstrators were developed in six months with $17 million in internal funding ( Defense Daily , Sept. 22).
Sheehy said the Army unit will retain the AMPV-30s for now, with plans to take them to a National Training Center rotation in March.
“I would love for them to go with AMPV-30. But even if they don’t, I think it’s an inflection point for how the Army develops capability. Getting it to the soldier, let the soldier feedback on it and then have industry move and change,” Sheehy said. “The vehicle is highly lethal. It has brought them capability they haven’t had, like the airburst round. So now they can engage troops in trenches behind walls. They can engage aerial targets, all that.”
Sheehy noted that discussions are still to be had with the Army on potentially bringing in the AMPV-30 capability to the vehicle fleet or cutting the ExMEP into the AMPV production line.
“The AMPV-30 has the capability, because of the [Integrated Combat System], for you to control the turret on another vehicle. So imagine if we had an autonomous vehicle that you could drive out there with the other vehicle. Now, you’ve reduced the exposure of soldiers in a direct kinetic fight, and you keep the same number of turrets in the fight because now your vehicle can control too, right? So there is a natural confluence of all these capabilities coming forward on that piece, and it’s just a matter of time and CONOPS and how you want to run it,” Sheehy said.
BAE Systems is also aiming to get an Autonomous AMPV provided to an Army unit as part of the Transforming in Contact initiative or another experiment opportunity, to gather feedback from soldiers.
“We’ll learn a ton. We learned a ton with the AMPV-30s that have been with soldiers for six months. We’ve learned a ton from them on how they engage. So it’s great,” Sheehy said.

title: Kinzhal is 90% identical to Iskander-M: Ukraine’s intelligence identifies 58 companies in production chain
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) released information on the components of Russia’s Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missile and the companies involved in its production, according to a statement dated 12 October. Russia has used Kinzhal missiles to strike targets across Ukraine since the start of its full-scale invasion. However, 22 of the 58 companies in Russia’s Kinzhal production network are not subject to sanctions, the intelligence agency noted. Kinzhal missile: design, components, and production changes Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has published an interactive 3D model of the Russian Kinzhal missile on its War&Sanctions portal. The 9-S-7760 missile, known as the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal, uses solid fuel and has a single stage. This means the missile does not consist of multiple stages that separate sequentially during flight. About 90% of its components are identical to those used in the 9M723 ballistic missile of the Iskander-M system, HUR noted. The Kinzhal is equipped with a radar homing seeker, an active jamming station, and a decoy deployment system, according to the statement. The homing seeker helps the missile determine the direction to its target, while decoys are designed to make interception by air defense systems more difficult. The missile can carry one of two types of warheads: a penetrating high-explosive warhead or a nuclear warhead. Russia is also developing a version with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead that strikes targets through an explosion and fragments. HUR believes this development may be linked to problems with the missile’s accuracy. In 2026, Russia significantly reduced its state procurement order for Kinzhal missiles and redirected some production resources, components, and raw materials towards manufacturing Iskander-M missiles, HUR noted. Another reason is the limited number of MiG-31I and MiG-31K aircraft used to launch Kinzhal missiles, the intelligence agency reported. Ukraine intercepts Kinzhal missiles, but has limited resources to do so Despite their high speed, Russian Kinzhal missiles can be intercepted using US-made Patriot surface-to-air missile systems. In particular, PAC-3 interceptor missiles are designed to destroy ballistic targets and can be used against threats such as the Kinzhal and Zircon, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported . Ukraine is seeking additional Patriot interceptor missiles to defend against Russian ballistic attacks during the winter. The Patriot PAC-3 surface-to-air missile system. Photo: Swedish Ministry of Defense Most of the approximately 1,000 missiles Kyiv has contracted for are not expected to arrive for several years, prompting Ukraine to ask its allies to supply missiles from their existing stockpiles, Defense News reported on 12 October 2026. Sanctions loopholes allow Russia to obtain foreign components for Kinzhal missiles Russia continues to use foreign components in missile production despite sanctions. For instance, the US-made Texas Instruments processors were found again in a newer version of the Kinzhal missile, Ukrainian presidential commissioner for sanctions policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk said in September, Interfax reported. According to him, foreign electronics continue to reach Russia through various supply channels. Earlier, Ukraine had provided its partners with information on more than 100 Russian companies involved in ballistic missile production and urged them to impose sanctions on those entities, according to the President's Office. On 12 October, the EU Council imposed sanctions on 1,569 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex, including 826 Russian companies and 743 company CEOs.
