title: GM Defense Unveils New UGV, Aims To Have Tech Demonstrator Ready By June 2027
body:
GM Defense [GM] on Monday unveiled its new Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV), based on the commercial Chevrolet Silverado 3500 heavy-duty truck, with plans to have a technology demonstrator ready for use by June 2027.
“What you see here with our Unmanned Ground Vehicle is a direct reflection of how we listen to the Army and how we pay attention to the changing character of warfare. We’re watching closely the developments in Ukraine, the Middle East and how the Army is organizing to campaign in the Indo-Pacific. And all of those observations are pointing to a very clear need: more robotic and autonomous capability to deliver operational effect and to reduce risk for our soldiers. GM Defense is ready to help the Army move in that direction by bringing the speed, scale and innovation of the commercial sector to bear on the defense mission,” Pete Johnson, GM Defense’s vice president of business development for integrated vehicles, told reporters at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference.
GM Defense’s rollout of the UGV comes as the Army is taking a new approach to rapidly prototyping and assessing potential unmanned vehicle requirements, to include a new ground robotics effort focused around three problem statements for autonomous resupply, breaching and multi-mission capabilities, and a recent effort to find platforms for casualty evacuation in the “last tactical mile” of operations ( Defense Daily , Aug. 14).
Johnson said the new UGV is aimed at a capability in the Army’s new Project Sustainment space focused on unmanned ground vehicles for supply distribution, with the service announcing in July it had picked AM General , American Rheinmetall , Carnegie Robotics , HDT Robotics and Stratom for a prototyping effort to inform future requirements ( Defense Daily , July 10).
“There’s a range of autonomous activities [right now] from Last Tactical Mile, Engineering Breaching, and Project Sustainment. [Those] were kind of the three that went out. We thought that we fit very well with the Project Sustainment space, and so that’s kind of where we’ve driven most of our development toward,” Johnson told Defense Daily following the briefing.
“For that first phase, we weren’t ready. There are obviously companies that were much further along. But again, this is where we feel very strongly that one of the things we have in our base DNA on bringing the commerciality and being able to have a path to production and scaling and affordability. We still thought it was very important for us to communicate to the Army to say, ‘We might offer value in this space and we’ll be ready to show you that, but we won’t meet your timelines.’ And so we’re going to be a first follower, for sure,” Johnson added.
Johnson said GM Defense began concept development on the UGV in late spring to early summer, with the company partnering to use Scout AI ’s autonomy stack, and said the base platform brings “a proven and affordable commercial baseline with an open interface and a modularity approach for sensors, autonomy stack, command and control and mission autonomy.”
“There is not a connection tied directly to a program line that you can see, and so there is risk. I think there’s risk for industry. There’s certainly risk that the government is taking, but the need is what’s clear. You can see just looking at the experience in Ukraine and the Middle East and how people are thinking about the kind of threats that they’re going to have to fight through in the Indo-Pacific. You can see the importance of this activity, and so I think it’s worth the risk,” Johnson said.
GM Defense does not currently have a scheduled plan to deliver a platform for testing, while pointing to the June timeframe as communicating when it will have a demonstrator ready for potential use and the company currently assessing opportunities to showcase the platform for the Army.
“We just want to be very transparent with when we think we’re going to be able to deliver real capability,” Johnson told Defense Daily .
The UGV has capability to handle up to 8,000 pounds of payload, supplies 102 kilowatt hours of onboard energy utilizing GM Defense’s Ultium-based battery technology and has silent watch capability to power systems quietly when the vehicle is stopped.
“It’s a very capable platform for hauling supplies. And, certainly, think of all the trucks that are on the road that have to support an Army on the move. This could go a long way to reducing the amount of truck risk that you have out there as well,” Johnson said.
The UGV on the AUSA show floor is integrated with AeroVironment ’s [AVAV] Locust X3 laser weapon system, while Johnson noted the platform is designed to be modular to host a variety of different payloads and effectors.
“It’s a multi-mission platform. It’s a blank slate, whatever you want it to be. There are a lot of different missions that you can be, but one of the really important missions that you can probably sense in the environment right now is counter-UAS.” Johnson said.
Johnson also reiterated affordability as key to meeting potential requirements in the Army’s pursuit of new UGV capabilities.
“Not that it isn’t always, but the pressure to get very, very cheap and more attritable capability is [there]. Because, since you’re unmanned now, you’re going to employ at higher levels of risk potentially, and so you’ve got to be prepared to deal with that,” Johnson said.

title: Ukrainska Pravda demands investigation into Austrian police conduct after journalists' detention
body:
Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda is calling for an independent investigation into the detention of two of its journalists in Vienna, saying Austrian law enforcement officers used excessive force, and questioning the justification for their arrests.
Investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko were arrested on Oct. 8 while carrying out an editorial assignment, and held in custody for 12 and 24 hours, respectively. They described the arrest as "brutal" and said they were treated "like terrorists."
Tkach is known in Ukraine for his investigations of high-level corruption. He alleged that the arrest could have been retaliation from subjects of his investigations, who could have manipulated Austrian authorities by filing a fake report.
In an Oct. 12 statement, editor-in-chief Sevgil Musayeva criticized the Vienna prosecutor's office for defending the actions of officers.
"The right to investigate suspicions does not mean the right to use any means," Musayeva wrote, arguing that the measures taken against the journalists were unjustified and disproportionate.
In an Oct. 12 press release, Vienna prosecutors said that the two journalists were arrested because they were mistakenly deemed conspirators of two different Ukrainian nationals currently in pretrial detention on suspicion of espionage.
The connection was alleged because of "witness statements" that claimed both groups were observed surveilling a certain property, and on the fact that "surveillance was carried out during the same period and in the same manner."
The prosecutor's office maintained that the arrests were justified by the information available at the time and were unrelated to the journalists' professional activities. The prosecutors claimed that at the time of the arrest, "it was not known that the accused were a Ukrainian investigative journalist and a cameraman."
The statement also claimed that the arrest originally targeted only one of the two journalists, and the police arrested the second one "on their own initiative." However, a detailed account of the arrest and questioning, shared by Ukrainska Pravda on Oct. 9, appears to contradict that claim. Both reporters were treated as subjects of an investigation and presented with accusations during their questioning.
Musayeva questioned how investigators had verified the witness accounts, and challenged the prosecutors' explanation that authorities were unaware of the men's profession, saying their identities could have been quickly verified through publicly available information or by contacting Ukrainska Pravda.
Musayeva demanded explanations for the force used during the arrests, the length of the journalists' detention, the seizure of their communications equipment and damage to or loss of their property.
Bondarenko said in an Oct. 10 account that officers smashed the windows of the journalists' vehicle and forced him face down onto broken glass. He said three glass fragments were subsequently removed from beneath his eye during a hospital procedure while he remained handcuffed. Tkach previously described being dragged from the vehicle by armed, masked officers and restrained with a knee against his neck despite repeatedly identifying himself as a journalist.
The journalists had been investigating the whereabouts of former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who is believed to be in Vienna.
Musayeva said the outlet would work with lawyers to seek an independent investigation, establish responsibility for any violations and obtain compensation for damages.
"The release of our colleagues does not close this story," she wrote. The International Press Institute (IPI) has also expressed concern over the journalists' detention and the force reportedly used during their arrests, calling on Austrian authorities to clarify the legal grounds for their detention and investigate the circumstances of the incident.

title: Alibaba Qwen Introduces QwenGyre: Elastic Reinforcement Learning RL for XLong-Horizon Agents
body: Alibaba’s Qwen team has introduced QwenGyre , an elastic reinforcement learning RL framework for extreme-long-horizon agent training. QwenGyre is an online reinforcement learning system from Alibaba that trains coding agents through unmodified, black-box harnesses. It targets rollouts that run for hours and process close to 1M tokens. The QwenGyre elastic RL framework was used on Qwen’s flagship Qwen 3.8 2.4T model. It rests on 2 core ideas. It moves idle GPUs between rollout and training. It also turns branching agent histories into bounded training samples. TL;DR Size: A training framework, not a model. Tested on Qwen 3.6 122B and Qwen 3.8 2.4T ( A95B per Qwen ), with ~700K tokens per rollout. Runs on: Multi-node GPU clusters. The 122B runs used 24 to 32 nodes; the 2.4T run used 192 nodes (4 cells of 48). GPU model not disclosed. Megatron trains, SGLang serves rollouts. Performance: 1.38x to 1.78x faster than Async, 1.21x to 1.85x faster than Colocate, at matched scores. Best: 1.85x end-to-end speedup over Colocate on TerminalBench. Worst: Only 1.21x over Colocate on the 2.4T model, where many queries ran near the timeout. Bottom line: Best: NL2RepoBench rises from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps. Worst: the paper links no public code release. What problem does QwenGyre solve? The research team defines ‘XLong-horizon’ tasks as agent runs spanning hours and hundreds of model and tool interactions. Examples include generating full repositories from specs, as in NL2Repo-Bench . Two problems appear at this scale: First, rollouts have long tails. In a Colocate setup, training waits for the slowest execution while GPUs idle. In an Async setup, fixed GPU pools cannot lend spare capacity to each other. Second, harnesses like Claude Code compact context, spawn sub-agents and retry. One execution becomes a branching tree, not a single trajectory. Expanding every path duplicates shared prefixes and inflates training cost. How does the Elastic Scheduler work? QwenGyre splits GPUs into cells that share a training layout. Each cell can serve rollouts or host a full training replica. A core cell owns the authoritative weights and optimizer state. Satellite cells join training later. The scheduler tracks a rollout waterlevel: queued and running executions. As executions finish, cells switch to training once the remaining cells can still serve all live work. Model calls are rerouted through a proxy, so the harness keeps running. Key mechanics: KV-cache blocks migrate over RDMA during rerouting, reducing prefix recomputation. Satellites pull core weights through Mooncake’s Transfer Engine and join an ongoing batch. Streaming training lets cells claim micro-steps as data becomes ready. Average role switches took 8.52 s (rollout to training) and 3.46 s (training to rollout). How does the Trajectory Processor build training samples? A proxy records exact token IDs and behavior log-probabilities using token-in, token-out (TITO) . Calls are stored as prefix-shared trajectory trees . Partial scoring: Timed-out executions are still scored on their preserved workspace. Evaluator failures are excluded, never treated as a zero reward. Bounded sampling: At most 5 trajectories per execution are kept, ranked main > main-summary > sub-agent > sub-agent-summary. Deduplication: Shared targets count once, and only policy-generated tokens are trained. Fair weighting: Losses average within each execution, so extra branches do not inflate its weight. A cap of 5 matched uncapped training scores while cutting forward-backward time by 25.2%. Training uses an adapted GSPO with 16 rollouts per group. How fast is QwenGyre? Benchmark results All runs used Claude Code 2.1.220 as the harness, with equal GPU budgets and matched staleness. Workload (model) vs Async vs Colocate NL2RepoBench (Qwen 3.6 122B, 48 steps) 1.42x to 1.53x 1.36x to 1.47x DeepSWE (Qwen 3.6 122B, 24 steps) 1.569x to 1.572x 1.610x to 1.824x TerminalBench (Qwen 3.6 122B, 24 steps) 1.383x to 1.430x 1.809x to 1.849x NL2RepoBench (Qwen 3.8 2.4T, 48 steps) 1.78x 1.21x On the 2.4T model, QwenGyre finished 48 steps in 75.42 hours. Async took 134.55 hours and Colocate took 91.47 hours. Evaluation pass rate rose from 52.48% to 58.54%. title: Army To Hold ‘Manufacturing Rodeo’ In Early ‘27 To Find Industrial Base Weak Points
body:
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced Monday the service will hold its first “Manufacturing Rodeo” in early 2027 to identify weak points in its industrial base.
“We’ve invested a lot in our organic industrial base, now we need to strain it and the nation’s larger industrial base. We’re going to stress test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes and see where it breaks,” Telle said during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
“We’re going to learn by doing, not by sitting around postulating at the Pentagon. [We’ll be] finding the weak links, making them stronger and keep iterating,” Telle added.
While few specifics have been confirmed on how the “Manufacturing Rodeo” will be conducted, the Army described the initiative as “competitive stress test for both the Army’s organic industrial base and the nation’s broader manufacturing network.”
The goal for the effort is “identifying weak links, strengthening them and continuously iterating to build a more resilient and responsive industrial base,” according to the Army.
“Take a basic attack drone, we need to be able to make millions of these. It may look simple, but it’s a flying supply chain,” Telle said. “If somebody else controls one part, they can break the whole thing. If we control the parts, we control the pace. That’s why we need to make the things we need here in America and to keep making them when demand surges.”
The Army noted the “Manufacturing Rodeo” will build on current efforts aimed at “scaling flexible ‘advanced manufacturing’ capabilities across the organic industrial base.”
Over the last year, the Army has moved out on the SkyFoundry initiative, which it initially launched as an effort to manufacture its own cheap drones in high numbers but has since shifted toward a focus on using its organic industrial base and advanced manufacturing capabilities to produce key components that support Army and commercial partner requirements ( Defense Daily , June 30).
The SkyFoundry work includes rapidly bolstering capacity in the near future to build around a million circuit cards and hundreds of thousands of brushless motors for small drones at the Tobyhanna Army Depot.
“By establishing advanced manufacturing hubs at key installations—such as Red River Army Depot, Anniston Army Depot, and Tobyhanna Army Depot—and securing critical Public-Private Partnerships (P3) with industry leaders like Hadrian and, the Army has built the production capacity to rapidly manufacture diverse subcomponents on demand,” the Army said.
“This agile infrastructure enables the OIB to sustain both legacy and future weapon systems, producing everything from complex electric motors to critical replacement parts like tank engine transmission belt housings, effectively eliminating supply chain bottlenecks and securing readiness at the speed of war,” the Army added.

title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
body:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.
Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.
One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter.
An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.
Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?
The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.
Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.
What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.
I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.
The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

title: Ukraine budget revenue shortfall reaches UAH 50 bln — Marchenko
body:
Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said this during a government Q&A session in parliament, an Ukrinform correspondent reported.
“Based on nine‑month data, the economy showed almost zero real GDP growth. Over January–September, the general fund of the state budget has already missed nearly UAH 50 billion in planned revenue, including UAH 32 billion in August and September,” Marchenko said.
He said total shortfalls in tax payments could reach about UAH 70 billion by year‑end. Factors include attacks on businesses, destroyed warehouses, blocked sea routes and weaker consumer confidence.
Marchenko added that inflation is accelerating amid rising costs and supply disruptions. Consumer prices rose 2.1% in September, while annual inflation quickened to 10%.
As reported, budget support from partners averaged USD 1.5 billion per month in 2026, while Ukraine had expected USD 4.5 billion.

title: American Army forces in South Korea adapting to new drone threats
body: The U.S. 8th Army deployed in South Korea is incorporating lessons learned from drone warfare in other theaters as it prepares for potential conflicts on the peninsula, officials said Monday at the annual AUSA convention. Drones and missiles have played a major role in the U.S. conflict with Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war. North Korea, an ally of Russia, has also reportedly been conducting exercises to practice “swarm” operations that combine attack drones with missiles and other weapons. During a media roundtable at the AUSA conference, DefenseScoop asked the commanding general of 8th Army about North Korea’s fielding of one-way attack drones and how that’s impacting his force’s modernization plans and operational contingency plans. “I’m going to answer it a little more generally than specific to the DPRK,” Lt. Gen. Joe Hilbert replied, using an acronym to refer to North Korea. “We know that on the battlefield, the one-way attack drones are becoming an ever-present reality, and so … as far as you know, modernizing our air defense systems, but also just looking at our own tactics and how to defend against some of those one-way attack drones, in some ways, you know, there’s a similarity to defending against any other air defense threat, whether it’s a reconnaissance threat or it’s a one-way attack drone. So, we’re incorporating that into our training, we’re incorporating that into our modernization, and we’re incorporating that into the experimentation that we do as we continue to learn those lessons of both [Operation] Epic Fury and Ukraine. And … the same assumption is the DPRK is learning that as well.” Reuters recently reported that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia may have provided its North Korean ally with jet-powered drone technology, which Moscow has been employing against Ukraine. Hilbert declined to say specifically whether Moscow is transferring its attack-drone tech to North Korea. He noted that Pyongyang is sending forces to fight in Ukraine on behalf of Russia. The 8th Army has been learning from what’s happening in Ukraine and the Middle East, and working through changes in its own tactics, techniques and procedures to be able to react to those threats and to be able to defend against them, Hilbert told reporters. “We have the advantage of we live on and we train on the terrain that we defend. So, we’re able to take the things that we observe and apply them to the terrain where we currently defend and fight. And that’ll play itself out in a host of ways, whether it’s looking at that exercise and thinking about how the adversary might use the capability inside that terrain or inside that environment, and then being able to think about ways to counter it and gain an advantage from it,” he said. “We’re certainly watching more than just drones,” he added. “We look at … what strike warfare or fires look like elsewhere. We also look at candidly what a battlefield looks like when you don’t know how to maneuver. And so therefore we see the advantage of operational-level maneuver as we work to train toward operational-level maneuver.” Col. Rosanna “Ro” Clemente, commander of 35th Air Defense Artillery Brigade, said troops are training and preparing for scenarios in which their systems and units would be “hunted” by adversaries. “As we conduct our own internal exercises, all of our air defenders are practicing something as simple as mobility and survivability jumps, which is being able to reposition and displace your systems to different alternative locations based on any type of threat warnings that we receive. So they’re very, very well trained. I think all of our soldiers … know how to move their systems extremely well and move them quickly, and they are able to move them and reposition them into different locations across the peninsula that still maintains that ballistic missile defense coverage,” she told reporters during Monday’s roundtable. “But in addition to that, we also have to rely on the other pillars of integrated air and missile defense, most specifically the passive defensive measures that we also have in place. A little bit more than just hardening, but a couple of other techniques that we’ve learned from the Russia-Ukraine war in terms of deception, how to move things around, create distractions, and make sure that we create different types of dilemmas for the adversary in terms of where our capabilities are and where they’re positioned” to protect and defend assets, she added. U.S. forces in Korea are integrating new tools into their arsenals, such as Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS) technology. “It’s going to be IBCS-enabled Patriot, and then … we will also have Integrated Fire Protection Capability, the IFPC,” Clemente noted. That tech allows air defenders to “pick best sensor and best shooter” and “kind of contain it all into one interface so that we can have a better control of those systems,” she said. “Those concepts, I think, are obviously still being tested, and we’re testing those capabilities as well in Korea.” The post American Army forces in South Korea adapting to new drone threats appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: ARCYBER expanding use of AI agents for network operations
body: Army Cyber Command is upping its use of AI for network operations, according to top service officials, expanding the number of work roles that AI agents are assigned to and teasing upcoming contracts expected to reshape the way service uses the technology in cyberspace. Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank, the head of ARCYBER, said Monday at the annual AUSA conference in Washington, D.C., that a team his command established earlier this year has continued to develop AI cyber agents, giving them additional responsibilities and allowing them to work in the Army’s portion of the Department of Defense Information Network (DODIN). Task Force Lexington, which ARCYBER stood up in April , started developing a handful of cyber work roles that AI agents would tackle, such as exploitation analysts and data engineers. Now, he said, they’ve “mapped out” an entire Cyber Protection Team composed of agents, including for analytic support and network analysts, among other roles. “The task force has built those out. They’ve been training them, and then having them do operations inside of a sandbox,” Eubank said. He added that humans oversee the agents’ actions, retrain them and then have let the agents work inside the Army’s network “over time.” The Army’s development of AI agents for cyber purposes comes amid deep concerns about the technology, especially after high-profile incidents where agents from frontier labs have escaped human oversight and hacked third-party organizations. At the same time, service officials have said that adversaries are wielding the technology against the U.S., and it is too powerful to sideline against those threats. Eubank said none of ARCYBER’s agents “have strayed to this point,” citing the command’s “tight framework” on using them. “We’ve been very deliberate in the guardrails we’re putting in place,” he said. “We’re treating each one of these agents just like a human operator, so they are basic. And so with that mindset, they’re only allowed to do so much.” Eubank described a process in which human operators check agent work in the network and retrain them before the human-machine pair moves on to the next task. At its outset, Task Force Lexington was staffed by nearly a dozen civilians and service members, and headed by a colonel. While the roles are narrow, Eubank alluded to even more expanded use of agents and said that the task force is sharing tools it has built to other cyber-oriented military agencies such as the Defense Cyber Defense Command (DCDC). “As they get trained and learn, we open the framework up,” he said of the AI agents. “The guardrails are really tied to cybersecurity, really based on what humans have learned over the years on what we should do inside of operating and securing the network, defending the network, and attacking a network. We have been very deliberate in kind of ‘okay, what did we learn as humans? How do we write those guardrails, and then how do we incrementally reduce the guardrails over time?’” Meanwhile, the Army is set to announce two awards for its Project Griffin initiative on Friday, according to the service’s principal cyber advisor. Project Griffin, DefenseScoop previously reported , is an effort by the service to build an ecosystem of agents to defend its networks as cyberspace is increasingly defined by how quickly defenders can respond to AI-backed threats. Brandon Pugh, the Army’s top cyber advisor, said the service received over 100 industry submissions to build such an ecosystem, which was narrowed down to ten companies and then two, which he did not disclose the names of but said will be announced this week. That capability will be run by ARCYBER, specifically by Task Force Secure, according to Eubank, who said it is being run by a lieutenant colonel The post ARCYBER expanding use of AI agents for network operations appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?
body:
vfmaddrnd231pd is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like vfmadd231pd , but here rnd means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as: VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control […] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3). Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But vfmaddrnd231pd allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster. Or so it would , if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics _mm_fmaddround_pd and _mm256_fmaddround_pd that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue: VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib VEX is the VEX prefix, but what is DDS ? This opcode is the only mention of DDS in the SDM, and this SO answer says that DDS is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises #UD (“UnDefined instruction”)! I already found it strange that the SDM only lists vfmaddrnd231pd and not other variants like using pd / ps / sd / ss or 132 / 213 / 231 , which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version. I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the vfmaddrnd* set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that. If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer. Update seastarer and 039234562456 gave me enough pointers to crack this. Back in 2023, Intel failed to add AVX-512 support to consumer CPUs due to hardware limitations, but still wanted to add some goodies from AVX-512. That’s how AVX10 was born – a new extension that looked roughly like AVX-512, but had conditional support for 512-bit vector lengths. AVX-512 uses a strange instruction encoding with the EVEX prefix. For compactness, the bits responsible for the static rounding mode are reused for the operation width (128, 256, or 512 bits), so only scalar and 512-bit operations can customize rounding. This was a problem for AVX10, which didn’t support 512-bit operations: if it interpreted the same instruction as operating on 256-bit values instead of 512-bit ones, different CPUs would behave inconsistently. So AVX10 had to use a different encoding for its own custom rounding modes. My theory is that originally, Intel decided that the easiest way to do this was to add an immediate byte that controls the rounding, which is how vfmaddrnd231pd and similar instructions for other arithmetic operations were born. Notice that it uses a VEX prefix, not the AVX-512-specific EVEX prefix – this would allow CPUs without 512-bit vectors to avoid handling the EVEX prefix at all. Since they added an entire byte, they utilized it in full: 2 bits for the rounding mode, 6 bits for everything else they thought might be useful. It seems like by 2024, Intel decided that this approach won’t work. And I get it: it’s odd that vfmaddrnd231pd was more powerful than AVX-512 instructions, but only supported 256-bit vectors. And if it supported 512-bit vectors, the rounding mode control built into AVX-512 would become obsolete for the most part. So Intel bit the bullet, dedicated the last unused bit in the EVEX prefix to enabling rounding modes for 256-bit vectors, and reused the AVX-512 instruction encoding for AVX10. This also allowed them to reuse the AVX-512 assembly syntax and avoid introducing new mnemonics, at which point the vfmaddrnd231pd mnemonic and others became unnecessary. During this process, someone forgot to remove vfmaddrnd231pd specifically from the SDM draft. By 2025, AVX-512 was considered table stakes due to the popularity of Zen 4, and Intel finally decided to make 512-bit support unconditional in AVX10. This made this entire hack unnecessary, so Intel updated the AVX10 whitepaper : Removed references to 256-bit maximum vector register size, enumeration of vector-length support, and 256-bit instructions supporting embedded rounding . …and submitted patches to GCC removing 256-bit rounding support : In this new whitepaper, all the platforms will support 512 bit vector width (previously, E-core is up to 256 bit, leading to hybrid clients and Atom Server 256 bit only). Also, 256 bit rounding is not that useful because we currently have rounding feature directly on E-core now and no need to use 256-bit rounding as somehow a workaround. HW will remove that support. We can partially confirm this theory by inspecting the patches. One of them is named: Revert “AVX10.2 ymm rounding: Support vfmadd{132, 231, 213}p{s, d, h} intrins” …and removes multiple intrinsics, including _mm256_fmadd_round_pd , which is named very similarly to the documented intrinsic for the ghost instruction, _mm256_fmaddround_pd . At a later point, someone at Intel realized that vfmaddrnd231pd was still mentioned in the SDM and removed it. Summing up: I believe that vfmaddrnd231pd is of AVX10 lineage. I think it was added during the prototyping stage of AVX10, then reworked to use a different instruction encoding, until it finally became unnecessary. Market pressures, timing constraints, and weird tech debt affected the design process enough that things had to be reworked on the fly, and at some point someone slipped up and accidentally documented an instruction that has never existed in released hardware.

title: Army turning to AI in its fight against biological threats
body: The Army is moving to combine environmental, clinical, logistics, chemical, biological and intelligence data with artificial intelligence to identify unseen and emerging disease outbreaks before they can spread widely or harm the force. Senior officials who developed the 2026 Army Biodefense Strategy discussed their new approach to operationalizing security measures against biological threats during a media roundtable Monday at the annual AUSA conference . “There’s a lot of data involved in doing bio-surveillance and sort of figuring out when that threat rears its head early enough to do something about it. And so, we are looking very heavily toward how we leverage AI to help us integrate and sort through that data,” Dr. Alison Tamasi told DefenseScoop. Tamasi serves as chief of the Survivability and Effects Analysis Division at the U.S. Army Nuclear and Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction Agency. She noted that, compared to the prior biodefense strategy released in 2021, this new plan marks “a big pivot” for the service in that it transforms biodefense from a more localized medical or chemical specialty into an integrated, “whole-of-Army” operational priority. “We are confronting a volatile technological convergence where advanced biotechnology and artificial intelligence are dramatically lowering the barrier to engineering biological weapons. Our adversaries view these agents as tools to degrade our logistics, paralyze our mobilization and deployment, and erode our combat power. This is a strategic threat to our nation’s ability to respond to a crisis,” former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll wrote in the document’s foreword. At the roundtable, the senior officials emphasized that the Army is taking steps to ensure that its own strategy can be quickly and fully integrated with the overarching approach that the Defense Department is taking towards biological surveillance and defense. They suggested that the Office of the Secretary of Defense has an “imminent biodeterrent posture that will come out” in the future. “The Army is sort of the first service that came out ahead and led the way on having a Biodefense Strategy, but that doesn’t mean that we’re doing anything in a vacuum,” Tamasi said. Lt. Col. David Kingery, who led the strategy’s development as the Army’s senior biodefense advisor, added that coordination with the rest of the services and the department is “extremely important” to ensure that authorities are met and data systems are interoperable. “There is an effort to pull the multiple different data streams and use AI [and machine learning for] predictive analysis to help us speed the early analysis, always using [a human] in the loop,” Kingery told DefenseScoop. Heaps of data sources — from environmental monitoring, compliant medical and clinical information, intelligence resources and more — will be integrated to support biodefense work. “We recognize that all of the wonderful things that are happening in AI to accelerate biomedicine are dual-use problems, and so we are very much doing it from that lens of the fact that the threat could change very rapidly in the biomedicine space,” Tamasi said. She told DefenseScoop that there is not an offensive angle to the Army’s strategy. The post Army turning to AI in its fight against biological threats appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Russian forces strike Kharkiv with Banderol missiles, injuries reported
body:
According to Ukrinform, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported the attack on Telegram .
"A strike has been recorded in the Kholodnohirskyi district. We are clarifying the details," he said.
In a subsequent post, the mayor reported another strike in the district and added that, according to preliminary information, Russia had used 'Banderol'-type loitering munitions in both attacks.
Terekhov later reported a third strike in the Kholodnohirskyi district.
According to the mayor, people were injured in the attacks carried out with Russian 'Banderol' munitions in Kharkiv's Kholodnohirskyi district. The number of injured and their condition are still being clarified.
As Ukrinform previously reported, on the morning of October 12, a Russian attack drone struck a high-rise apartment building in Kharkiv, destroying floors seven through nine in one of the building's stairwells.
Twenty-three people were reported injured, including children.

title: F-47 stealth fighter aims to give U.S. air superiority over China in the Pacific
body: Boeing received the engineering and manufacturing development contract in March 2025 for the fighter, which is intended to replace the F-22. Its first flight is planned for 2028, although the schedule depends on development progress, technological readiness and testing. The F-47 belongs to the Next Generation Air Dominance program, which also includes Collaborative Combat Aircraft drones and advanced electronic warfare systems. The drones are intended to work alongside crewed aircraft. The fighter is expected to exceed Mach 2 and have an operational radius of more than 1,000 nautical miles. That range would be particularly valuable in the Indo-Pacific, where bases can be far from potential combat areas. China’s development of fighters, long-range missiles and integrated air defenses presents additional challenges for U.S. forces in the region. Longer range would give commanders greater flexibility in basing aircraft and could reduce aerial refueling requirements on some missions. Less dependence on refueling would matter when tankers and other support aircraft face the risk of attack. The F-47 is also intended to be more survivable than fifth-generation fighters in heavily defended airspace. Its design combines advanced stealth with sensors, electronic warfare capabilities and integrated mission systems to reduce detection risks and improve threat identification. An open systems architecture is intended to make new software, sensors and other technologies easier to introduce. Upgrading existing fighters has often proved complex and time-consuming. The F-22 has received successive radar, communications and weapons updates, while the F-35A is undergoing modernization through Technology Refresh 3 and Block 4. Boeing will also produce the Navy’s sixth-generation carrier-based fighter under the F/A-XX program, following the Department of War’s September 29 announcement selecting its aircraft. The new fighter will replace F/A-18 Super Hornets operating from U.S. aircraft carriers. Boeing said it had received an initial multibillion-dollar order to produce the first batch of F/A-XX aircraft. The company is therefore responsible for both the Air Force’s F-47 and the Navy’s next-generation carrier fighter. Construction continues on Boeing’s secure manufacturing facility in St. Louis, which it describes as the largest of its kind in the United States. The company says the facility will be part of the world’s most advanced, all-digital aerospace design and manufacturing system. Unofficial reports indicate that the Air Force plans to buy at least 185 F-47s, but the final quantity remains uncertain. Cost is a contentious issue, with estimates putting the price above $300 million per aircraft, compared with approximately $80 million for an F-35A.

title: PAC-3 Edge Will Be The Most Capable Patriot Interceptor Ever
body: Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, a new interceptor that would represent the top tier of the U.S. Army’s Patriot air defense missile family. The missile is being developed to deliver greater performance against advanced threats than the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE), as the Army advances a competition for its next-generation interceptor. The PAC-3 Edge displayed at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention. Howard Altman The company says PAC-3 Edge will offer improved performance against increasingly challenging aerial threats, including advanced ballistic and hypersonic missiles. The design builds on the PAC-3 MSE’s existing technology while incorporating a new seeker, an upgraded control system, and a more advanced solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman. In terms of appearance, PAC-3 Edge differs significantly from the PAC-3 MSE. It does away entirely with the mid-body strakes. The missile body also lacks the distinctive tapered section that separates the narrower forward section from the broader rear section on the MSE version. An overview of the improvements found on the PAC-3 MSE variant over its predecessors. Lockheed Martin Lockheed announced on October 9 that it had been selected to advance to the next phase of the Army’s Future Interceptor program. Company officials said testing is expected to begin in 2027, with initial deployment targeted for 2031. The Army’s selection of Lockheed and another unnamed competitor marks a significant development in the service’s effort to improve the Patriot system’s ability to deal with more sophisticated threats. The Army previously abandoned its Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program in 2024, citing cost concerns, and instead emphasized incremental improvements to the existing PAC-3 MSE. The subsequent emergence of the Future Interceptor competition points to renewed interest in a more substantial leap in capability. A PAC-3 interceptor seen at the moment of launch. U.S. Department of Defense A More Capable Patriot Interceptor PAC-3 Edge is intended to preserve the advantages of the existing PAC-3 family while improving the missile’s ability to engage targets at longer ranges and higher altitudes. One of the central changes is a new seeker being developed by Lockheed Martin’s Strigo Product Center. The company says the technology will improve target detection and tracking, helping the interceptor deal with more demanding threats. The company has not disclosed the seeker’s technical details, but one possibility is a dual-mode or multimode configuration , combining different sensing methods to improve target acquisition and tracking in challenging conditions. Such an approach could help an interceptor maintain a reliable track against maneuvering targets and better distinguish real threats from decoys or other countermeasures. Tim Cahill, president of Missiles and Fire Control (MFC) for Lockheed Martin, told TWZ that the same seeker technology that will be used in PAC-3 Edge will also find its way into future offensive and defensive systems going into the future. “So it isn’t just a one single seeker solution, but it will be a family of seekers that will operate across a number of regimes,” Cahill explained. “Frankly, I’d like to not tell everybody exactly what we’re doing, but it is clearly different from what is out there right now,” Cahill said, adding that hardware assemblies and components are now being tested in the lab, and that seekers have been flown on aircraft testbeds. The missile will also use a three-pulse (as opposed to two-pulse) solid rocket motor designed by Northrop Grumman. Unlike a conventional motor that provides most of its thrust in a single sustained burn, a multi-pulse design can deliver thrust at different points during flight. That can help preserve energy for the terminal engagement, when an interceptor may need to maneuver aggressively to reach a target. Lockheed says the combination of the new seeker, propulsion system, and control system improvements will provide greater maneuverability and improve performance at extended ranges and higher altitudes. To ensure greater agility, Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) at Lockheed Martin, explained that the new missile adds a greater number of more capable attitude control motors (ACMs), compared to the PAC-3 MSE. These small thrusters ring the missile’s forward body. The new characteristics could be particularly important against maneuvering ballistic missile warheads and hypersonic weapons, which can pose difficult interception problems because of their speed, altitude and dynamic flight profiles. However, the company has yet to demonstrate PAC-3 Edge’s performance in flight testing. The extent to which PAC-3 Edge could overlap with, or potentially augment, the capabilities of the Army’s Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system also remains unclear. THAAD is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at higher altitudes and longer ranges than Patriot, where midcourse window bleeds into the terminal intercept window. If PAC-3 Edge delivers a substantial improvement in engagement range and altitude over PAC-3 MSE, it could potentially provide at least some backfill for THAAD. The announcement did not provide detailed performance figures for the new interceptor, including its maximum engagement range, speed, or specific target set. It also did not establish how much better the missile will perform than the PAC-3 MSE in operational conditions. Addressing An Air Defense Force Under Pressure The Army has a pressing need to improve its air and missile defense capabilities while expanding the number of interceptors available to its forces. TWZ has been reporting on the strain facing the Patriot force and its interceptor supply for years. In July 2025, we reported on the Army’s plan to expand its Patriot air defense force by roughly a quarter , adding four battalions as the service sought to meet growing operational demands. More recently, we have detailed the challenges of replenishing interceptors after intensive combat operations, including the scale of U.S. missile and drone engagements in the Middle East , as well as transfers to Ukraine . Related to this, the push for a more capable Patriot interceptor comes as the system faces increasingly sophisticated threats and adversaries that have learned from years of combat. Russia has improved its ballistic missile tactics to pierce the Patriot’s protective umbrella, while Iran has demonstrated ways to exploit gaps in layered missile defenses, including introducing extremely high-speed ballistic missiles and cluster warheads that open at high altitude. A Patriot system received by Ukraine is seen on the Day of Ukrainian Air Force on August 4, 2024, at an unspecified airbase in Ukraine. Photo by Vitalii Nosach/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images VITALII NOSACH PAC-3 MSE is currently the most advanced operational member of the PAC-3 family. It is designed primarily as a hit-to-kill interceptor, destroying targets through the force of direct impact, but it also incorporates a small explosive charge known as a “lethality enhancer,” as TWZ has previously detailed . PAC-3 Edge is intended to push those capabilities further still. Lockheed says the new missile is being designed to work within the Army’s existing and future integrated air and missile defense architecture, including the Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS) and the M903 Patriot launcher. The company has also identified containerized launchers and HIMARS Flex among the systems with which it intends to integrate the interceptor. A graphic showing various load configurations for the M903 launcher, as compared to the previous M901 and M902 launchers. Lockheed Martin Such compatibility could allow the service to retain much of its existing infrastructure while improving the performance of the weapons used within it. The precise extent of that compatibility, however, will depend on development, testing, and integration work that remains ahead. Production And Cost Lockheed is developing PAC-3 Edge as the company and the Pentagon work to expand production of the existing PAC-3 MSE. In January, Lockheed Martin announced a seven-year agreement with the Pentagon to more than triple annual PAC-3 MSE production capacity , initially targeting an increase from roughly 600 interceptors to 2,000 a year. The effort subsequently received a major funding boost in July, when the U.S. government awarded Lockheed a contract modification worth up to $53.86 billion, bringing the total multiyear contract value to $58.62 billion. Lockheed says the effort is intended to more than triple production by the end of 2030, while expanding its workforce and investing in manufacturing infrastructure and its supply chain. Those efforts could provide a foundation for producing PAC-3 Edge if the missile completes development and enters service. Lockheed has said the new interceptor will be manufactured on its existing PAC-3 production line in Camden , Arkansas, with factory modernization expected to support the eventual transition. PAC-3 MSE in production in Camden, Arkansas. Lockheed Martin The company has also highlighted substantial internal investment in the new missile and its seeker technology. That investment could reduce development risk and give Lockheed greater control over critical components, although the program’s final cost and production schedule remain important unknowns. The broader challenge is not simply developing an interceptor with better performance. Advanced missiles can be expensive, and air defense forces must balance the capabilities of individual weapons against the number they can afford to procure and keep available. Sustained combat operations can rapidly consume interceptor inventories, making production rates and replacement costs central considerations. Cahill says the company has also identified the opportunity to mix and match components between PAC-3 Edge and other missile offerings from Lockheed Martin. “We are getting increasingly modular, and increasingly we’re mixing and matching pieces and parts,” he said. Ultimately, if it chooses PAC-3 Edge, the U.S. government will decide exactly how to handle production of the PAC-3 MSE and the new missiles. “We would expect the typical thing is you’ll feather them, so you would expect that over time MSEs would come down,” Cahill continued. “We’re still talking, seven, eight, nine, 10 years away. You would expect that the Edge production would go up, but there’s plenty of capacity in the factory to manage whatever surges are going to be needed there.” At the same time, it should be noted that Lockheed Martin is also working on a lower-cost PAC-3 development, the PAC-3 Adapted Capability Effector (ACE). The company says that this interceptor will cost less than half as much as the PAC-3 MSE, meaning it would have a price tag of around $2.5 million. The company says that the PAC-3 ACE will preserve two-thirds of the capability the PAC-3 MSE had, and it has already generated considerable international interest. A rendering of the PAC-3 Adapted Capability Effector (ACE). Lockheed Martin Future Interceptor Competition Lockheed has confirmed that it is one of two companies selected to continue in the Army’s Future Interceptor competition. The identity of the other competitor has not yet been disclosed, and the Army has not publicly provided a complete account of the competition’s requirements. The effort follows the cancellation of the earlier Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program, which had involved Lockheed Martin and Raytheon. At the time, the Army opted to focus on upgrades to the PAC-3 MSE and on better integration of its existing air and missile defense systems. Gen Lozano, PEO Missiles & Space, tells @JenJudson that they have cancelled the Lower Tier Future Interceptor program, which would have succeeded the PAC-3 MSE. Instead they will upgrade MSE, and want to move forward with THAAD integration into IBCS. #AUSA2024 pic.twitter.com/NZMPgDH4KP — Colby Badhwar (@ColbyBadhwar) October 15, 2024 The renewed competition suggests that incremental upgrades alone may not be sufficient to address the Army’s longer-term requirements. The development of faster, more maneuverable missiles and other advanced aerial threats is driving demand for interceptors capable of operating across a wider engagement envelope. For PAC-3 Edge, which is designed to address emerging threat requirements, the planned 2027 testing start and 2031 deployment target leave substantial development work to complete, including demonstrating the seeker’s performance, validating the propulsion system, and proving the missile’s ability to engage representative targets. For now, the unveiling establishes the direction Lockheed wants to take the Patriot interceptor family. Whether PAC-3 Edge can deliver the promised increase in performance, while meeting the Army’s cost and production requirements, will become clearer as the program progresses. Regardless, from what is being experienced on the battlefield, a more capable, higher-reaching Patriot would be a very welcome addition to the Army’s Patriot family. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post PAC-3 Edge Will Be The Most Capable Patriot Interceptor Ever appeared first on TWZ .

title: Catholics in US Army must not participate in firing squad, prominent archbishop says
body: Catholics serving in the U.S. Army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S. archbishop said on Monday. In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the U.S. armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree. Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan’s victims, and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the U.S. wanted to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries.” “I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said. U.S. Army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the Army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad. Questions about the effect on young viewers U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers. U.S. President Donald Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the livestreaming to proceed. The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the U.S. military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest. Hegseth said last week he wants U.S. soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of Hasan’s shooting spree. Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent. Broglio questioned whether the effect of a livestreamed execution on young viewers had been considered. He said the U.S. military had a good reputation and asked if there was “really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world.” Broglio’s statement was issued shortly after he met on Monday in Rome with Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically. Vice President JD Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get livestreamed, he would not watch it.

title: Lockheed Martin Typhon Passes Two and a Half Years in Philippine Inventory, Army Leaders Say
body:
The Typhon launcher by Lockheed Martin [LMT] for such missiles as the Tomahawk and SM-6 by RTX ‘s [RTX] Raytheon has more than two and a half years of service in the Philippine military, Army leaders said on Monday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) annual convention in Washington, D.C.
“That system was brought over to the Philippines at the request of the armed forces of the Philippines,” said Army Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, the commander of the 7th Infantry Division/Multi-Domain Command-Pacific.
“Based off of our shared interests, that system has maintained forward presence for over 30 consecutive months,” he said. “What that allows us to do is not only train and share lessons on that movement, but also to learn how do you operate and sustain in the environment and how do you protect those types of systems in the environment, how do you connect sensors to shooters persistently forward with our ally.”
The Army and other military services have said that they want to increase their “magazine depth,” their on-hand inventory of munitions and missiles for potential conflicts.
Asked after his AUSA talk what improvements he would like to see with Typhon, Harrington replied, “I don’t think of one particular system.”
“It really is optionality for us,” he said. “We look at the targets in the Pacific and the effect we’re trying to achieve and what’s the right optionality of the things we can integrate–from sensors, to utilizing long range one way attack, USVs [unmanned surface vessels], long-range launched effects, and layering that–whatever the magazine depth is. What can be integrated into this kill web quickest is something I’m interested in. I have the mechanism to be able to integrate it.”
Typhon “has worked out really well as far as you look at their territorial defense, nesting that system,” Harrington said. “I think the indicator is the government of the Philippines, the armed forces of the Philippines asking us to maintain it there now for two and a half years. What that’s allowed us to do is every time the weather, humidity, the road conditions–we’ve had this pretty good feedback loop–things that we would adjust and be able to adjust to.” Harrington said that industry field service representatives for Typhon have been responsive.

title: Russian forces attack Rivne, damage reported
body:
According to Ukrinform, Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne Regional Military Administration, reported the attack on Telegram .
"The regional capital came under attack a few minutes ago. A non-residential building was damaged," Koval said.
According to preliminary information, no one was injured.
As Ukrinform previously reported, three people were injured in one of Russia's attacks on the Rivne region on October 11.

title: French Navy Intercepts and Boards Shadow Fleet Tanker ‘DF Peak’ South of Réunion
body: The French Navy ( Marine Nationale ) has intercepted and boarded the Shadow Fleet oil tanker DF Peak in the Indian Ocean, more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion Island In a major high-seas operation, the French Navy ( Marine Nationale ) has intercepted and boarded the oil tanker DF Peak , a vessel suspected of operating under a false flag and evading international sanctions as part of the broader “shadow fleet” The operation took place more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion Island, highlighting the French military’s far-reaching maritime surveillance and enforcement capabilities in the Indian Ocean. Operators are seen rappelling down from an AS365 Dauphin N3 helicopter on the deck of “DF Peak”. EMA picture. Suspected False Flag and Illegal Transport According to official statements, the vessel is suspected of sailing under a false flag and engaging in the illegal transport of fuels. “This morning, more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion, our French Navy boarded the oil tanker DF Peak, suspected of sailing under a false flag and participating in illegal fuel transport operations,” President Macron stated. “Conducted in strict compliance with the international law of the sea, this operation illustrates our determination to uphold the rule of law and combat all illegal trade, wherever it takes place.” The French Armed Forces General Staff confirmed that the boarding was executed under the framework of Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which grants warships the right of visit on the high seas under suspicion of statelessness or fraudulent flagging. Minister Catherine Vautrin commended the coordination and professionalism of the French Navy elements involved in enforcing maritime law in the region. French military authorities have not released further operational details regarding the specific naval assets deployed or the vessel’s current routing, but images show a French Navy AS365 Dauphin N3 helicopter operated by Flottille 34F, from one of the Floréal-class frigates. The French Navy units based at Port-des-Galets naval base in Réunion under the Armed Forces in the South Indian Ocean Zone (FAZSOI) command consist of: 2x Floréal-class frigates: Floréal (F730) and Nivôse (F732) 3x Offshore Patrol Vessels & Support Ships: Champlain (A623), Le Malin (P701) and Auguste Techer (P781) which was recently delivered. While the AS565 Panther previously served in Réunion for 27 years, the French Navy officially retired the Panther detachment from the island in mid-2025. The Flottille 34F took over permanent embarkation duties on the Floréal-class surveillance frigates with the Dauphin N3. A crew member from what looks like the recently delivered Auguste Techer (P781) offshore patrol vessel keeping a close watch on “DF Peak”. EMA picture. Targeting the ‘Shadow Fleet’ The DF Peak (a 2006-built crude/oil products tanker) has been tracked under various flags and names as part of a global network of aging tankers used to bypass petroleum caps and international trade restrictions. Operating outside standard transparent maritime frameworks, these vessels pose both economic compliance and severe environmental risks due to often opaque insurance and substandard maintenance. Several European navies have conducted operations against Shadow Fleet tankers since January 2026. By executing this seizure far from metropolitan France, the Marine Nationale has demonstrated its unique blue-water reach and its commitment to enforcing maritime law, protecting critical sea lanes, and clamping down on illicit maritime networks operating across the southern hemispheres. Further details regarding the vessel’s ultimate cargo destination and the legal proceedings following the interception are expected to be released by maritime authorities. The post French Navy Intercepts and Boards Shadow Fleet Tanker ‘DF Peak’ South of Réunion appeared first on Naval News .

title: Belgium, Germany, Italy, Seek ‘Emergency Brake’ on New EU Laws
body:
The leaders of Belgium, Germany and Italy called on Monday for a mechanism that would let EU governments halt new legislation from Brussels they perceive as too burdensome for the bloc’s own countries and businesses.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni made the proposal in a letter to European Council President António Costa, according to Politico after reviewing the document. Such an “emergency brake” could be needed to help restore the bloc’s weakening economic competitiveness, they argued.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We call for further ambitious simplification packages to decisively advance the cutting of red tape in the European Union,” the leaders wrote.
Besides the emergency brake, the letter calls on the EU to “significantly accelerate planning and approval procedures.” A new priority rule, as they describe it, is also proposed, under which certain regulatory areas would be suspended “for a specified period.”
The three leaders said the European Commission should ease regulatory pressure on small and medium-sized enterprises.
“More broadly, our common objective should be to prevent unnecessary regulatory burdens and related costs from causing permanent losses of European industrial capacity and further weakening investment and competitiveness,” the letter says, though they did not specify how the proposed emergency brake would work in practice nor which body would trigger it.
The letter comes three days before EU leaders are expected to gather in Brussels for a two-day European Commission summit on Oct. 15-16.
The first item on the provisional agenda is Europe’s economy, including competitiveness and energy prices. The discussions will also include Ukraine’s financing, particularly the EU’s next long term-budget , spanning over the 2027-2034.
According to Politico, the proposal repeats demands first raised in March, after a summit focused on European competitiveness. It also comes amid worsening signs for the EU’s industrial sector.
Under the EU’s ordinary legislative procedure, the European Commission proposes laws, which are then adopted jointly by member state governments in the Council of the EU and by the European Parliament.
A mechanism allowing national governments to stop legislation on cost grounds would add a new check to that process. Because the letter leaves the details open, it remains unclear how far the proposal would shift power toward national capitals.
The proposal also carries political weight. Germany and Italy are two of the EU’s three largest economies. Their joint push makes regulatory simplification a central issue for this week’s summit, alongside the long-term budget and energy prices.
The debate coincides with a step forward in Ukraine’s EU membership bid as well.
Separately on Monday, all 27 member states agreed to open two new accession clusters with Ukraine and Moldova after Kyiv adopted a minority education law that Hungary demanded in exchange for lifting its veto.
Cluster 2, the internal market, and Cluster 3, competitiveness and inclusive growth, are among six thematic clusters that organize the legal and institutional reforms that must be adopted and implemented before being eligible to join the EU.
The process was blocked for both countries by Hungary for several months, as their process remains intertwined.
The letter comes on the same day the EU approved the 22nd sanctions package, covering 1,646 new sanctions targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex , including missile supply chains, drone makers, and submarine shipyards.
Italy has previously objected to several EU sanctions, including a visa ban on Russian combatants that are, in any way, connected to the war in Ukraine.
On Aug. 28, Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov accepted Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto’s invitation to serve as an adviser on defense innovation .
Crosetto previously said Italy would not contribute funds to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), which finances purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Sikorsky unveils four-drone deployment kit in a shipping container
body: Sikorsky has introduced a kit that packs four autonomous aircraft and the equipment needed to operate them into a single 20-foot shipping container. The Nomad 100 Fast Pack, announced on October 12, 2026, is designed to let military crews deploy drones from ships, vehicle staging areas and remote sites without a runway or extensive ground support. Sikorsky said the planned configuration would allow crews to prepare two aircraft for missions in less than 15 minutes. The other two would be ready within four to six hours. Along with the aircraft, the container holds mission-control software, communications equipment, power supplies and equipment to keep the drones operating. After a mission, crews could repack the container and move it to another location by truck. “By packaging aircraft, mission command, communications, power and sustainment into a single containerized system, we are making it easier to move, employ and reposition VTOL UAS capability with urgency and flexibility,” said Rich Benton, Sikorsky’s Vice President and General Manager. The Nomad 100 takes off and lands vertically and can hover like a helicopter, then transition to fixed-wing flight. It uses Sikorsky’s MATRIX autonomy technology. Depending on the equipment selected by a customer, the drones could conduct surveillance and targeting missions, carry out attacks or deliver supplies in areas threatened by enemy forces, the company said. The Fast Pack is a deployment package for the Nomad 100, part of Sikorsky’s family of uncrewed aircraft designed to operate from land or sea. The company says the kit would require few personnel and limited outside support, but did not specify crew numbers in the announcement. Sikorsky developed the Nomad 100 with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency under its Early VTOL Aircraft Demonstration program. The announcement did not provide a price or set a delivery date. The post Sikorsky unveils four-drone deployment kit in a shipping container appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Entire section of Kharkiv apartment building collapses in Russian attack
body: Russian forces attacked Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district with “Banderol” missiles on the evening of October 12, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said . title: One of Latvia’s best-known liquor brands faces an uncertain future as Riga Black Balsam’s producer weighs insolvency
body: The board of Amber Latvijas balzams has called a shareholders’ meeting for November 3 to consider whether the company can continue operating and whether to begin insolvency proceedings. The decision will take shareholders’ proposals into account. In early October, Amber Latvijas balzams asked the Riga City Court to end its legal protection proceedings . The company sought court protection in early 2026 after accumulating more than 28 million euros in unpaid taxes owed to the state. The company attributed its debts to “external problems that have been mounting for years”: the seizure of Amber Beverage Group assets in Russia, a major cyberattack on the company, and “challenges” in global spirits markets. Under the proceedings, Amber Latvijas balzams was required to develop a debt repayment plan and secure approval before October. Among other provisions, the plan called for repaying in full the principal owed to secured creditors, including the State Revenue Service, Latvia’s tax authority, as well as to suppliers. The plan was not approved. Amber Latvijas balzams said MBO Beverages, which had acquired debt owed by the Riga Balsam producer from other major creditors, was among the factors that influenced the decision on the plan. Amber Latvijas balzams said that since the protection proceedings began, it had paid 20.4 million euros in current taxes and had accumulated no new overdue debts. Production in Riga continues. Amber Latvijas balzams produces Riga Black Balsam , one of Latvia’s best-known alcohol brands. The company is part of billionaire Yuri Shefler’s international Amber Beverage Group.
