title: Iran live updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs'
body:
Officials have prepared a range of options for the president to consider.
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.
Despite a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries in June aimed at ending the war, talks broke down and the U.S. and Iran renewed strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint.
Across the region, fighting in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has intensified in recent weeks and the militia group has also launched strikes on Saudi Arabia.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy claims an oil tanker struck a naval mine Friday as it attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz.
A statement from the IRGC Navy claims there was an explosion and fire after the unnamed super oil tanker hit the mine as it attempted to cross through "an unauthorized route."
"The tanker attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz after turning off all positioning and radar systems, with the aim of deception, and with the support of the US military," the IRGC statement claimed.
Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed a container ship sank after it struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz. US Central Command (CENTCOM) later issued a statement disputing those claims saying the container ship, the GFS Pride was hit by an Iranian projectile and sank as it was being towed to shore.
Air defenses destroyed several projectiles in Saudi Arabia, the spokesman for Saudi-led coalition forces said Friday.
Three missiles and three drones targeting different regions were intercepted, Col. Turki Al-Maliki said in a series of posts on X.
Saudi Arabia did not say who launched the projectiles but the Houthi military in Yemen has repeatedly launched projectiles in recent weeks.
A ballistic missile launched in the direction of Yanbu; an important Red Sea port, was intercepted, along with two cruise missiles over the Red Sea. Three drones were also destroyed in the southern and Riyadh regions, Col. Al-Maliki said in a post.
Top administration and defense officials have prepared a range of options for the president to consider as he weighs further military escalation in Iran, sources told ABC News.
The list of options prepared by officials includes the use of the Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb known as the "mother of all bombs," according to sources familiar with the matter.
The president has not made a decision, according to sources. Trump has been meeting with top officials as he considers next steps in the war with Iran and is regularly presented with a range of options.
Trump has said he will not strike Iran before the midterm election. On the campaign trail, he vows the war will end soon but it's unclear how that will happen.
The president used the MOAB during his first administration to attack an Islamic State cave complex in 2017. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon.
A White House official told ABC News, "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."
ABC News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
When asked about the bomb in an interview with Newsmax on Thursday evening, Trump said "it's not nuclear at all. This is just a extremely large bomb. It's like a tiny nuclear bomb, and -- but the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear. I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."
CNN was first to report the options presented to the president.
-ABC News' Rachel Scott and Katherine Faulders
France has started deploying military assets in Saudi Arabia, a spokesperson for the French Foreign Ministry, Pascal Confavreux, confirmed in a press conference Thursday.
"You know that the Houthi attacks in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia threaten not only Saudi Arabia's security and the region's energy security, but you also know that the President announced on September 24th that France would support the defense of Saudi energy infrastructure, particularly the Yanbu East-West Corridor. And this support is currently being deployed," Confavreux said in a news conference.
French President Emmanuel Macron said last month that France would send troops and defense systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, ‌‌a key hub for energy transport.

title: Russians who fled after the 2022 mobilization tell Meduza how they rebuilt their lives abroad — and what they’ve lost along the way
body: View from Belgrade Fortress of a residential and business complex that includes a Yandex office. Belgrade. January 2024 On the fourth anniversary of Russia’s mobilization, we asked you, our readers, about your experiences living abroad. We received many letters from all over the world — thank you so much! While many of you say you’re happy with your lives abroad, almost every story includes struggles with adjusting to a new place or missing Russia. Here are some of the most representative letters. Please note: Our Russian-language newsroom screened every submitted letter for AI-generated text, but even the most thorough checks cannot rule out manipulation entirely. Bear that in mind as you read. Nikolai, Serbia Overall, I’m happy with my life. I wouldn’t say I’ve fallen in love with Serbia, but I like it more every year (despite its obvious drawbacks). The climate is better here [than in Russia], and people are welcoming and friendly. They’ve shown me a lot of kindness. Over these four years, I’ve settled in and found several groups of friends with shared interests. They’re all Russian speakers; I haven’t managed to make friends with locals yet. In Belgrade, whatever your interests, you can find Russian-speaking friends and all kinds of things to do in Russian. And you don’t need a VPN here, either. The hardest part of living abroad was getting through the first three years with undiagnosed depression. And I miss Russia all the time. Our countryside, the air, the feeling of belonging. As [rock musician Yuri] Shevchuk sang, “Somewhere there’s more kindness and freedom, but no homeland.” That’s the whole truth. I’m not coping with that feeling at all. I tell myself I did the right thing. Every time I read the news, I understand why I’m here rather than there. It’s terribly sad, but I try to think about the future and how to survive and thrive in a changing world. The past was beautiful, but it’s not coming back. Let’s thank it and let it live on in our hearts. There are lots of new friends and new roads ahead. Related reading Russian political researcher Alexander Finiarel has lived in Spain without papers for two years. But soon he (and half a million other refugees) will be able to get documents. This is his story. Anya, Spain I’ve managed to get a residence permit I can rely on, rent a decent apartment, get insurance, and open a bank account. Thank you, Spain, for your relatively lenient immigration policy. Even if everything suddenly goes wrong and I can’t renew my residence permit, nobody will deport me. I’ll be able to keep living in this country and eventually get legal status anyway. Knowing that makes life a little less stressful. I should also say that Spain is a fantastically beautiful country. It’s the most beautiful place I’ve ever lived. Everything else is complicated: In more than four years, I haven’t managed to adjust to the pace of life here, make friends with women who share my outlook, or get used to the noise, the cultural differences, and so on. I’m thinking about moving to another country. It’s scary, but staying in Spain is hard for me. Barcelona. 2026 In Spain, I’ve found myself living in two painfully disconnected realities. I work for a nonprofit that helps political prisoners, and every day I read and process all the most horrifying news about political persecution in Russia. Meanwhile, outside my window, life is carefree. People stroll slowly down the streets, many look happy, and families often gather on their little balconies, laughing loudly and talking a lot. Every couple of weeks, there’s some kind of celebration here. Beautiful green mountains rise in the distance, it’s sunny every day, and after school, children happily run around our courtyard while their parents chat over beer or coffee. A couple of kilometers (about a mile) away, you can hear the sea. But on my laptop and in conversations with my husband in the kitchen, it’s arrests, torture, searches, deaths, and war. Sometimes I feel like I’m losing my mind. It can be hard to believe that so much happiness and peace (like we have in the town where I live) can exist in the same world, at the same time, as so much pain, destruction, and suffering (in Russia and because of Russia’s actions). I feel like I’m not coping, and there’s a gaping black hole in my chest. Sometimes I don’t notice it as I go about my daily routine, but that sense of loss is there in the background every day. I desperately miss my family, Moscow as it was in 2018–2019, and my friends, who have either scattered around the world or stayed in Moscow. I often look at old photos. I guess that helps a little. An unplanned call with a friend who now lives in Berlin helped once, too. She’s struggling as well, and she really misses her home in Moscow. Realizing I’m not alone in this pain eases it a little. Max, Israel Overall, I’m happy with my life, but it’s been very hard. On the other hand, you become more resilient as you go through it. The little things that used to seem like insurmountable problems turned out to be just that — little things. I love my new country for its spirit of freedom. You really feel it when you talk to people, and it’s in the air everywhere. The hardest part was the endless waiting and the uncertain future. I was going through the repatriation process, and the wait for consular screening dragged on for two and a half years, which I spent in the mountains in Kyrgyzstan. It felt like time had stopped, like being in prison. Except the prison is in your head. My grandmother died while I was living abroad. We were very close, and I still feel guilty that I couldn’t come to say goodbye. Haifa. 2022 I miss people, I miss the places that gave me strength. I have to find new ones, and that’s turned out to be hard. I miss the conifer forests and the green carpet underfoot in summer (I’m from Novosibirsk). I miss the changing seasons. Luckily, I have a close circle of friends. We message every day and call several times a week. Without that, it would be much harder. When I feel especially sad, I put on music and go for a walk until I’m tired. You can get through anything — the main thing is not to lose yourself. Asya, Vietnam Apart from being here without a visa, which means I can’t get any paperwork sorted out, I really like it. It’s a very beautiful country. Friendly people, delicious food. The language is difficult but interesting. The vibe reminds me of Russia in the 2000s, when the economy was growing and people’s incomes were rising, too. People here are generally optimistic about the future. It was hard to find a job and to cope with being laid off while living abroad, not knowing what would happen and feeling like I could be deported at any moment or refused entry on my next visa run. But that’s all just part of life. The hardest thing was saying goodbye to my grandmother without knowing it was the last time we’d see each other, and that when she died, I wouldn’t be there. Hanoi, Vietnam. 2022 I hardly miss Russia. I miss my relatives and friends, but Russia since the war began feels very bleak and unwelcoming to me. I visited in 2024, and it was terribly depressing to see how everything had changed. Viktor, Kazakhstan I work remotely, so I haven’t lost any income, but the standard of living in Moscow is still miles ahead of Astana’s. It felt like I’d taken a step backward. I haven’t managed to fall in love with my new country. I feel pretty neutral about it. People here are basically the same as in Russia. There’s no difference, and if it weren’t for the different currency and a few other little things, it would feel like I’d just moved to another Russian region. I haven’t had any particular difficulties — I’m an IT professional whose skills are in demand. Surprisingly, Russian bank cards are accepted almost everywhere here. If all else fails, you can withdraw cash from an ATM. I rented an apartment. Then I moved to another one in a more convenient neighborhood. In Russia, I didn’t socialize much in person. And you can talk to people online anywhere. I used to love walking through Moscow’s parks — the climate here and the lack of forests get me down. I’m thinking of moving back to Russia. In the end, I wasn’t mobilized, and I don’t see any signs of another mobilization. But I don’t particularly regret moving. I got to live in another country. That’s a useful experience, too. Related reading Life in exile: Russian singer Monetochka thought Vilnius would be a stopover. Four years later, she says she may stay forever. Yevgenia, Israel I don’t like Israel, and I feel like a stranger in this country. I’m here because it was easiest [here] to get citizenship right away and not have to think about renewing a residence permit and so on. I don’t like the Middle Eastern mentality. I really love Moscow, where I lived my whole life. It was hard to lose all the social capital I’d built up. In Russia, I’m in a good field, I have a job, and I have prospects. Here, I once got turned down for a cashier job in a store. That made the whole situation feel absolutely hopeless. For the first two years, I kept thinking I’d be back soon. That I just had to wait it out, get by here somehow, without intending to stay and put down roots. Now I understand that there’s nowhere to go back to, but I don’t want to be here. Even though I now have a well-paid job in my field here, I still feel like I don’t belong in either place. Dmitry, Serbia In 2022, I had no idea how to go on living. I left for Serbia a couple of months after the war began, taking a week off from my drinking binge. Even through that drunken haze, it was clear that things in the country were going to get worse fast, and if they closed the borders, it would soon be all over. It’s very easy for a country with fresh memories of its totalitarian past to slip right back. We’ll have it all: beatings, handcuffs, and split lips… I left with very little money, about 300 euros. For the first six months in Serbia, I lived in a tent in parks, hitchhiked on visa runs, grabbed whatever odd jobs I could, and bought almost everything I needed at flea markets. Drank rotgut, ate expired food. A kiosk near the border between Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, the most popular destination for Russians making visa runs. Sremska Rača, Serbia I still ended up in debt: I didn’t have a skill suited to the local job market, a remote job, or, most importantly, any foreign language skills. I’ll learn! I thought. Turned out it wasn’t easy. The life I knew was over, and there was no clear future in sight. I could just close my eyes and fall. It turned into the wildest trip of my life. In the late 2000s, I was at a teacher-training college. Our art teacher was a gray-haired old guy; I don’t remember his name. Once, he assigned us a drawing on any subject we liked. I drew a road winding through a field, with people hanging from poles on both sides, and a vehicle heading off into the distance with “NKVD” [the Soviet secret police] written on the back. After class, the teacher returned my drawing with the initials heavily crossed out. I was indignant: What for?! He told me it was dangerous. I remember thinking: You’ve completely lost your marbles, old man… Look around, those days in Russia are long gone, and they’re never coming back. Why the hell did you have to ruin my drawing! Oh, you saw it coming, old man. You were so right. […] Throughout my adult life in Russia, I traveled without a care, loved adventure, worked interesting jobs, and wrote poetry and prose. I stayed out of politics. Yeah… Politics doesn’t affect you until it does… In February 2022, everything fell apart and my plans collapsed. As BG [rock musician Boris Grebenshchikov] sang: “Now our word is a sum of syllables, it’s time to set sail from these shores.” There was no time for homesickness. But things gradually got better. I learned a trade that saved me. I’m still on shaky ground here: no residence permit, no employment contract, no home of my own, and no certainty about tomorrow. But I’ve never regretted leaving: With my anxiety, I wouldn’t have been living in Russia, just suffering. In those first days, weeks, months, years, I’d open the news every morning and feel glad I wasn’t there, wasn’t in Russia, wasn’t part of the shame, wasn’t in a trench. I still do. In Serbia, I started living again in many ways. I went through the 12 steps, discovered sobriety, learned some of the language, and recovered from depression and a host of ailments I’d never paid attention to before. This journey isn’t over yet, and who knows how long recovery will take, but it’s maintenance now, rather than emergency repairs. I’m 39. Life is just beginning. Anonymous reader, Armenia At first [living abroad], things were easier. I had a good job and could afford the very high cost of living abroad. Now the job market is in chaos, there’s no work, and we’re developing our own product, but that’s hard with absolutely no money. There were stretches when one egg and half a potato a day was a pretty normal diet. There simply aren’t any alternatives. We’re not giving up, and we keep working our asses off. I hope that’s light I’m seeing at the end of the tunnel and that I’ll be able to get back to a normal life. But I wouldn’t say no to a little pile of money falling into my lap :)) Yerevan. 2026 There may be a lot of things in Armenia that I can’t accept deep down, but that’s just my view. I’m a guest here, and even when I want to grumble about something, I always remember that at the most terrifying moment of our lives, Armenia simply took us in, sheltered us, and cared for us. That matters more than all the everyday difficulties. I’ve already designed a tattoo I’ll get before I leave, as a reminder of Armenia. When things were going well, I often missed Russia, though I was also glad I’d had the chance to leave. When your daily diet is an egg and half a potato, homesickness is the last thing on your mind. Ksenia, Lithuania I left with four children and my elderly dad. I’m the only adult in the family and the only source of income. First I went to Armenia, then Montenegro. I lived in Montenegro for four years, and this year I moved to Lithuania on a humanitarian visa. Here, my younger children have started school and kindergarten, both free of charge and taught in Lithuanian. I really like the climate (I’m from St. Petersburg). The older two have grown up in that time and now live independently (in Germany and St. Petersburg). I’m a freelancer, but I had savings, and I’m managing to earn a decent living. I work a lot, fortunately. The hardest thing is the uncertainty and not being able to plan anything. Montenegro went and tightened its residency rules, so I had to look for a way to move to the EU on a humanitarian visa. That option was open to me because I’m a journalist at an antiwar publication. Still, it wasn’t easy and took a huge effort. By then, I didn’t know where else to run. Vilnius. 2026 Having to jump through endless bureaucratic hoops is hard for me, too, as are the constant unexpected expenses (Dad’s expensive medical care — he won’t get insurance because he hasn’t paid taxes). But staying in Russia would have been a hundred times scarier, and now going back is no longer an option for me. I’ve always been a patriot of Europe, and I still am. Yes, maybe I’ll never see part of that Europe again (St. Petersburg and Lviv). But I drove all over the Balkans in my own car before I had a Schengen visa. Now I travel all around Lithuania and a little in other countries. Churches, little bridges, new cities, fresh air, Goethe and Mickiewicz — that’s how I keep from missing [Russia]. Anna, Georgia My life has turned out great. I found a job that pays in foreign currency, got married, and got a dog. Georgia has low taxes and beautiful scenery, and it’s not hard to get a residence permit. The hardest thing is knowing that the city I never got to say goodbye to has changed forever, and even when I occasionally visit my family, everything there still feels foreign. It’s hard to realize that I can never get my old life back. It’s difficult to get close to people, because for a couple of years, all my new friends were ready to leave at any moment, and the loneliness was very intense. And it’s frightening to have absolutely no idea what the future holds. Not even my own future — the world’s. In my fourth year away, I don’t miss Russia. I’m just afraid of that country now. I don’t long for Russia, but I do long for my grandparents, whose health keeps them from coming to see me. As for Russia — you start getting used to the idea that it’s no longer part of you. Hi, I’m Katya. I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe. Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza. The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work. Svetlana, Kazakhstan We left as a family: First, in September 2022, my husband and our son, a university student, rushed off to Kazakhstan. Once they’d settled in and my husband had found a job and an apartment, I flew out to join him in February 2023 with our younger son, who was still little. Of course, it wasn’t all easy, especially since we left without preparing, without connections or any support. But we managed, and now, four years later, we’re doing fine. After three years, our older son has resumed studying in his field, now at a local university in Almaty (I really hope he’ll stick with it and get his degree this time). Our younger son goes to kindergarten. My husband works for a Western company and supports us all, and I’ve become a homemaker (I worked as a doctor in Russia). We didn’t manage to get permanent residence permits under the old rules, though, and now that’s become extremely difficult following changes in the law this spring. Oh well, we’re in our fourth year of living here on temporary residence permits — so far, they’re still issued without any problems. We live in Almaty. I like that you really feel a shared background, almost as if you’re not entirely abroad ;) There’s a lot that’s familiar in people’s social lives and everyday routines here. We speak Russian, and people are generally friendly, easygoing, and very good with children. In my view, there’s much less xenophobia than in Moscow (where we came from). Almaty. 2026 The men in our family left almost as if they were fleeing, without preparing, into the unknown, and that put us all under enormous psychological strain: fear, anxiety, exhaustion, depression… But our motivation (saving our son from the war) got us through all that, and we probably had some luck, too. We dealt with all the other questions and problems “as they came up,” including with help from other people who’d relocated — people in the same boat. I should say right away: We had money when we left Russia (we always have a financial cushion). It covered about four months of living expenses — just until my husband’s first paycheck. Of course we miss Russia, because our whole old life is back home, along with our relatives and loved ones and our beloved pets (cats). We go home once a year: my husband for about a week or two to take care of things, and me with our younger son for two months (this year, we were in Moscow in July and August). Our older son last went two years ago — after that, he said he wasn’t going to take the risk anymore. Regular phone calls with loved ones who stayed in Moscow help with the homesickness, as do those occasional trips. It also helps that we’re here together and support each other, and that we’ve more or less settled into life in a new place. Now that I have free time, I try to talk more with local people, make connections, and build friendships so I’m not socially isolated. So far, I consider our move a success (though without permanent residence permits, our long-term future here is pretty uncertain). Alexander, Portugal Right now, everything’s good. We made it. I haven’t been back to Russia in all this time, and honestly, I don’t want to at all. Portugal has its quirks, like anywhere else. But overall, it’s very good here. You feel safe. People are very kind and helpful. Everyone’s upbeat. An anti-Putin demonstration in Lisbon. 2024 The hardest part of living abroad is the uncertainty and fear. We left without jobs, with two small children and the last of our savings. I wasn’t prepared for my parents to betray me. They think I’m a coward and an idiot. And they don’t mince words. I haven’t spoken to my father since September 2022. Or rather, he hasn’t spoken to me. I don’t miss Russia at all. The first two years were hard. I was constantly doubting my decisions and getting no support whatsoever from my parents. At the very moment when you need that support more than ever. I worked with a psychologist. At first, I tried to get through it all on my own. But it’s incredibly hard. In the end, I more or less managed to get through it in the fourth year. Now I’m afraid to go to Russia, and I have no reason [to visit] or need to go. I’m not the same person anymore. Anastasia, Turkey Overall, I’m happy with life abroad. Children and mothers are treated with great care. You see it in people and in the surroundings — flowers everywhere, well-kept parks, lots of greenery, children’s playrooms. I got into one of the country’s best universities, Istanbul University, a public institution, for just 140,000 rubles a year. I changed jobs, and it turns out I’m good at teaching — now I work for myself. [In Russia], I always tried to find beauty around me. Apartment blocks, blizzards, a little river, even trash (I’m serious!). Turns out, when you don’t have to look for beauty because it’s just there, you feel noticeably better. Well-kept houses, landscaped grounds, a tower you can see from anywhere in the city… The hardest things are the language barrier and the culture. It scared me how curious and friendly everyone was. People warned me they were being two-faced. Maybe. I don’t know what’s really going on in people’s heads. Of course I feel nostalgic. I miss familiar things, books from Ozon [a Russian online retailer], the local planetarium, and trips that take no more than 40 minutes. Istanbul University From time to time, I miss Russia. When nothing around you makes sense, you’re drawn to what does. Then my mom tells me how drones thundered overhead all night, how there’s no gas, how they didn’t fall asleep until 5 a.m. and sat in the hallway — and this is central Russia, not far from Moscow. And I realize that books from Ozon and the planetarium aren’t worth it :( When I was in school, I really wanted to move abroad. That was my teenage rebellion. Mom said our local university had an exchange program and that a friend of hers had gone to Canada that way and stayed there. I believed her and came up with a plan. I graduated from school in 2021, and in 2022… they shut everything down, blocked everything, and canceled it all. Sad. I miss what Russia could have been. Alexander, France Our new life is really only just beginning. How could you not love France? My wife and I now have refugee status and 10-year residence permits. Our daughter is 7 months old; she was born here in France. I blog about our new life and am starting to relaunch the small business I had in Russia. I hope someday I’ll also be able to return to journalism at an independent news outlet. We have a future in France. We didn’t have one in Russia. The worst things were the living conditions and the sense of hopelessness during the first months of the asylum process. Before that, it was hard bouncing between countries and being turned down for a Turkish residence permit and a German humanitarian visa. We miss our parents and friends. The country and our hometown, less so. Everything has changed so much. We made a deliberate decision to leave. We knew there was no going back. We need to survive; this isn’t the time for homesickness. We’ve been through a lot. It should get easier from here. Related reading What happened to the Russians Putin mobilized four years ago? Meduza follows two of them — one still at the front, the other now a deserter in Spain. Yekaterina, Peru I should say right away that I haven’t moved abroad for good. I divide my time between two countries and travel to Russia. I left and spent a year away, thinking I’d use that year to figure things out and decide whether to stay. In the end, I settled on living between the two. Overall, I’m happy, but of course there are lots of irritating little things, and I miss home. In Peru, I like the climate, people’s friendliness and openness, and the relaxed atmosphere. And most of all, the feeling of freedom and safety. Lima, Peru. 2024 [What I don’t like is] missing home and not having people around who understand me. The quirks of the local culture — people don’t stick to agreements or keep promises, everything takes a long time and causes a lot of stress. I often miss [Russia], and I deal with it by going back. Konstantin, Georgia Money has been very tight since the first month, and it still is. I left in September 2022 with a salary of around 50,000 rubles, and little has changed since then. I constantly have to look for cheaper housing, put up with the living conditions, cut way back on groceries, and eliminate any nonessential spending. Financially, I feel like I’m constantly sitting on a powder keg. But setting aside my own money problems, I like Georgia, its character and distinctiveness. Sometimes I sense an inner freedom in the people around me — and occasionally even in myself — that I’d never known before. I also regularly think of Lem’s line, “A human being needs another human being.” I think Georgia embodies that idea beautifully. Tbilisi The hardest thing is being completely unable to get legal residency in any country and facing an uncertain future that, in most scenarios, threatens to force me back to Russia. Much as I’d like to, I can neither feel at home nor make plans for the future, because right now, “There’s only a moment between two visa runs, and that moment is called life.” I prepare carefully for each visa run in case it goes wrong, work out where I’ll go next, and take other precautions, but I know things can always get worse, to the point where even precautions won’t help. The list of countries I can afford to live in is pretty short, and many of them are tightening their immigration laws, so being a perpetual tourist is my biggest vulnerability. One small “tectonic shift,” and I’ll either have to literally live out of suitcases or be forced back to the country where I’m a citizen. Those thoughts are depressing. The only Russia I really miss is the Russia of the past — the Russia of my youth, which was already deeply troubling for all sorts of reasons but was still much more carefree. I also miss being able to feel relatively safe and, at the same time, fully part of things — as a member of a team and of society, a citizen, and a native speaker of the language. The list goes on. Sadly, in today’s circumstances, you have to choose. I’m locked in a constant, bitter argument with myself: Who made what mistakes, and when, that led us to where we are now? And what was my own part in it? Thoughts like these help me pass the days — not cheerfully, but that’s how it is. Viktor, Serbia I’m happy with life abroad. In Serbia, I have friends, a relationship, and hobbies. I’ve started earning more. Belgrade is small compared with Moscow, where I lived before I left. I simply have time to do more. The first year to year and a half was emotionally hard, though. But without that crisis, I wouldn’t have gone to therapy, which turned out to be super helpful. I definitely miss Russia at least once a week. I long for the life the war took away from me. But I remind myself that I’ve already built a good life in Serbia. If I have to leave Belgrade, I’ll definitely miss it, too. And reading the news from Russia brings me back to reality and keeps me from sinking into homesickness. title: Death toll rises to two after strike on 25-storey building in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported this on Telegram .
"Two people have been killed and seven others injured in the aftermath of Russia's evening attack on Kyiv," the statement said.
As of 21:00, the death of a 59-year-old woman had been confirmed. The body of another person was found in a car near the building.
At least seven people were injured. They sustained shrapnel wounds, bruises and cuts. A 17-year-old girl was among the injured.
"These are the consequences of a UAV crashing into the courtyard of a 25-storey apartment building in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district. Apartments on the fourth and fifth floors caught fire," the prosecutor's office reported.
The fire destroyed at least 12 cars and two motorcycles.
A pre-trial investigation into a war crime allegedly committed by Russian military personnel has been launched under the procedural supervision of the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office, pursuant to Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko had earlier announced that a Russian drone had struck a high-rise apartment building in the Darnytskyi district. At that time, one person had been reported killed and 11 injured.

title: Joby seeks to overturn $117 million trade secrets verdict
body: Joby Aviation has asked a federal court to overturn a nearly $117 million jury award to Aerosonic, saying it developed its own aircraft sensors without misusing the supplier’s trade secrets. A jury in Tampa, Florida, found on October 2, 2026, that Joby breached a confidentiality agreement and misappropriated Aerosonic’s trade secrets. The verdict is not yet a final judgment. Joby is building a electric air taxi for one pilot and four passengers and aims to begin passenger flights in Dubai before the end of 2026. “We strongly disagree with the jury’s verdict, which we believe is unsupported by the evidence and inconsistent with the law,” Joby said in a statement to media outlets. The electric air taxi developer said it spent years engineering and manufacturing its air data system and would pursue further court challenges, including an appeal if necessary. Aerosonic makes probes that measure air pressure around an aircraft, providing data used to calculate airspeed, altitude and angle of attack. The Clearwater, Florida-based TransDigm subsidiary began supplying probes for Joby’s flight-test aircraft in April 2022, after the companies signed a nondisclosure agreement the previous September. According to Aerosonic’s complaint, Joby asked to buy the intellectual property rights to the probes shortly after receiving its first delivery. Aerosonic declined. The supplier alleged that Joby then began designing its own probes while continuing to ask Aerosonic for confidential engineering information. It sued Joby in March 2025 over the use of its designs and test data. Aerosonic claimed its information allowed Joby to develop the probes in about two years, rather than the decade or more it said the work would otherwise have required. Joby maintains that it developed the system independently. The jury awarded Aerosonic damages for the confidentiality agreement breach and misuse of trade secrets, along with additional punitive damages after finding the misappropriation was “willful and malicious.” Jurors also rejected Joby’s counterclaims that Aerosonic had breached the agreement and sold it defective probes. title: NATO would block, blunt and break an attack, says commander
body: NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe has set out a three-stage approach to defeating an attack on the alliance, which he calls blocking, blunting and breaking. General Alexus Grynkewich described it as a Theory of Victory grounded in the alliance’s agreed strategy for the Deterrence and Defence of the Euro-Atlantic area. “So, while I referred to it as ‘my theory,’ it’s more than that. It is based on a strategy agreed to by all 32 Allies, so it represents and includes all of us. In other words, it is our Theory of Victory,” he said. “In recent days, some have called it a plan, but it’s not, at least not in the military sense of the word,” he said. “Rather, our Theory of Victory provides the Alliance a common vision for how we win in deterrence and defence. It provides my ‘commander’s intent’ to help us focus our militaries on the key tasks we must accomplish in combat.” “I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It isn’t,” he said. “We help avoid conflict by clearly articulating our defensive intentions, and by maintaining open lines of communication to resolve misunderstandings and encourage transparency.” “My Theory of Victory is simple. We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” he said. He described the first stage as falling to land forces at the point of contact, supported from the air and at sea. “To block, our land forces will move to and dominate any enemy assault at the point of contact. Through manoeuvre, we will fix the enemy formations and deny the seizure of Alliance territory. Land-based forces will attack the enemy and destroy his advancing forces, but they won’t be doing this alone. “Our air forces and navies, working in concert with our space and cyber forces, will rapidly gain freedom of manoeuvre. With air and maritime superiority rapidly secured in and over the battlespace, these forces will bring mass and precision to bear, denying the enemy the ability to hold their ground.” “Using advanced sensors, autonomous systems, and multi-domain forces, we will deny the attacker the ability to generate momentum or gain the initiative. Synchronised employment of multi-domain effects down to the tactical level will overwhelm enemy formations in contact, and their advance, if it’s continuing at all at this point, will falter further,” he said. “Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us. This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, or controls that force,” he said. “To do this, we will layer high-end and highly effective precision munitions with an overpowering mass of affordable and scalable systems. We will apply constant and unyielding pressure, both kinetic and non-kinetic, we will do this across and through domains, land, air, sea, space and cyber space. Doing this will break the enemy system and defeat it in detail. Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Any enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. And enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed.” General Grynkewich said the alliance expects warning of any attack, through “a sophisticated layering of intelligence provided by multi-source collection assets” interpreted with advanced algorithms. “This means the Alliance is unlikely to be caught by surprise. We will see if an attack is coming, giving us time to assess intent and rapidly position our forces,” he said. The capabilities he named as priorities for investment were “high-end and affordable long-range precision strike capabilities, sensor networks, and a warfighting cloud” . Forward Land Forces on the eastern flank will exercise to demonstrate the blocking task, and air and maritime forces will demonstrate freedom of manoeuvre and multi-domain effects. “If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent. We will continue to prepare and rehearse each and every day, and will be more ready tomorrow, and even more ready the day after that,” he said, adding that any adversary considering an attack should reach “the only conclusion that matters: Today is not the day.” The post NATO would block, blunt and break an attack, says commander first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Leeds firm offers alternative to AI kill switches
body: A Leeds cybersecurity company has launched a protocol intended to shut down a compromised artificial intelligence agent without pulling the plug on it, aimed at the problem legislators have been circling with proposals for mandatory kill switches, according to Cavero Secure . An autonomous agent executing trades, managing infrastructure or altering databases cannot easily be switched off once it goes wrong. Hard termination in a cloud-native environment risks corrupting state data, severing dependent supply chains and setting off cascading failures, which makes the obvious remedy an expensive one. The company’s approach treats identity as a continuous cryptographic history of an agent’s state transitions from the moment it was created, instead of a static secret such as an API key or session token. Trust is re-evaluated action by action, and keys and authority are derived dynamically across interactions, so there are no stored credentials for an attacker to harvest or clone. An attacker running a stolen or copied agent cannot do so without diverging from the legitimate history, and the contradiction between the two timelines is detected before unauthorised actions clear. Cavero calls this the clone paradox. Halting an agent is handled through what the company calls a history shift, in which modifying the local verification ledger leaves the target unable to prove its continuous historical state, at which point it fails its mathematical challenge and becomes invisible to the network, isolated without crashing host servers or affecting adjacent workloads. Because the suspension is anchored in state continuity instead of process destruction, it can be reversed, and an administrator can roll the agent back to its last known good state. Professor Ben Varcoe, co-founder of Cavero Secure, said: “The industry has spent years trying to govern autonomous AI using 20th-century credential models and blunt emergency stop buttons. Security does not come from building higher walls or pulling physical plugs, it comes from continuous identity verification. By anchoring authority in an unbroken, living state history, CaveroCTX gives enterprises absolute control and surgical precision over their autonomous digital workforce.” The protocol is being deployed with selected enterprise design partners in financial services, cloud infrastructure and defence technology. Cavero Secure describes itself as working on post-quantum key distribution and continuous trust protocols, out of advanced quantum information research. The post Leeds firm offers alternative to AI kill switches first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Twenty-Six Defense unveils new soldier-worn tech
body: The company that previously operated as Elbit Systems’ American subsidiary made its AUSA expo debut this week as Twenty-Six Defense. Under the new brand, the Texas-based defense firm debuted Primex , a lightweight wearable meant to provide soldiers with night-vision capabilities and augmented reality so they can “maintain awareness without distraction or cognitive overload.” For the design, Twenty-Six Defense said it engineered Primex for sustained operational use by equipping it with “the lightest head-borne load and near-neutral center of gravity.” The company explained Primex uses low-light sensors, thermal imagery, and real-time processing to produce an ultra-low-latency digital perception that enables operators to better interpret the surrounding area even amid challenging environmental conditions. What separates Primex from other advanced lightweight heads-up display units for operators, according to Twenty-Six Defense, is that its design was built on mature technologies that have already been fielded. The company said it already produces AN/PSQ-44 Enhanced Night Vision Goggles , which contain features that allow for rapid target acquisition and augment reality to enhance visual clarity. In August, Ernie Basic, Twenty-Six Defense’s senior director of research and development, explained how his company was developing equipment for the Soldier Borne Mission Command , a project to deliver augmented reality wearables to soldiers. He said the technology combines fighter-pilot displays with night-vision systems, so soldiers get “the full operational picture.” “You are not only seeing what is in front of you. You can leverage a feed coming from a drone or from other assets,” he said. “You can start seeing what is going on behind a house or another structure, cue a squad to a different location, and continuously update them.” In addition to Primex, Twenty-Six Defense showcased defensive weapons and equipment like the XM1168 mobile 120mm mortar system, Autonomous Relocatable Surveillance Tower and SkyStriker Block 4E.

title: Telle says Army will ‘find the weak links’ in the industrial supply chain through ‘manufacturing rodeo’
body: The Army will attempt to stress test the industrial base early next year in an initiative meant to help identify weak links in its supply chain and improve them, the acting secretary of the service said Monday, dubbing the effort a “manufacturing rodeo.” Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle provided few details about the initiative at the annual AUSA conference in Washington, D.C., Monday, but said the rodeo constitutes a “race” between companies that support the defense industrial base. “We’ve invested a lot in our organic industrial base,” he said in his opening remarks at AUSA. “Now we need to strain it, and the nation’s larger industrial base.” Over the last two years, Army leaders — initially championed by Telle’s predecessor Dan Driscoll — have endeavored to modernize the service quickly, leaning on commercial companies, new entrants and primes to help the land force keep pace with modern combat. Part of that effort includes shedding the service from unique, lengthy and hard-to-connect projects the Army has embarked on for decades and instead turning toward a more “flexible” industrial base, including through public-private partnerships, according to a press release accompanying Telle’s announcement. Pentagon leaders have frequently touted that these changes will put the industrial base on a “wartime footing.’ Now, “we’re going to stress test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes and see where it breaks,” Telle said. “We’re gonna learn by doing, not by sitting around postulating at the Pentagon.” The Army press release framed the announcement around a service commitment to “American ingenuity,” for the purpose of scaling new technology on demand. “We’re gonna find the weak links, we’re gonna make them stronger and we’re gonna keep iterating,” Telle said.
