title: Sikorsky Plans to Introduce ‘Fast Pack’ Feature for Nomad 100s
body:
Lockheed Martin ‘s [LMT] Sikorsky plans to introduce a “fast pack” feature for its Nomad 100 autonomous drones. The “fast pack” would have a 20-foot container to allow rapid deployment of four Nomad 100s.
Under the concept, a soldier with a tablet would choose a mission, such as reconnaissance, push a button on the tablet with the location of the reconnoiter, press the launch button, and monitor the mission.
“What this allows us to do is move away from that ground control station and pilots flying these aircraft,” Ramsey Bentley, Sikorsky’s advanced concepts director, told reporters last week before this week’s Association of the U.S. Army annual conference in Washington, D.C. “We’ve really put this capability in the hands of the soldier on the forward edge of the battlefield.”
Last October, Sikorsky announced the development of the autonomous, twin prop-rotor Nomad drones, based on the company’s rotor blown wing vertical take-off and landing concept ( Defense Daily, Oct. 6, 2025).
The company said it is developing Nomad 500 and Nomad 1000 drones as well that are larger than the Group 3 sized Nomad 100s.
Group 3 drones have a weight between 56 and 1,320 pounds and speeds below 250 knots.
Sikorsky has a contract for three Nomad 100s under the Defense Advanced Research Project Agency’s (DARPA) Early VTOL Aircraft Demonstration (EVADE) program ( Defense Daily , June 27). In addition, the U.S. Marine Corps is buying two Nomad 100s, Bentley said.
“In its planned configuration, two Nomad 100 aircraft can be mission ready in less than 15 minutes, with two additional aircraft available within four to six hours,” according to Sikorsky. “The containerized system is designed for runway independent launch from locations such as naval vessels, tactical vehicle staging areas and improvised landing zones.”
The Army has said that it wants replacements for Textron ‘s [TXT] RQ-7 Shadow in the Group 3 category and General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. ‘s MQ-1C Gray Eagle drones in Group 4 for Army division and corps-level reconnaissance ( Defense Daily , Aug. 12, 2025).
“The Nomad 100 fast pack is designed to help customers close critical operational gaps where runway-independent launch, limited forward support and rapid relocation are mission priorities,” the company said. “Depending on customer configuration, Nomad 100 fast pack can enable missions including ISR-T [intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting], light attack, and contested logistics, giving operators multi-role capabilities in challenging and dynamic environments.”

title: Faslane submarine base in Scotland to get ballistic shelters
body: Three contracts worth a combined £2.55 million have gone to the Northern Ireland construction firm Henry Brothers for infrastructure work at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, awarded by Babcock International Group, according to the News Letter . The work covers upgrading security fencing around a key support building at Faslane, supplying and installing specialist ballistic security shelters across the base, and refurbishing an existing Pressure Test Building. Work begins immediately. Nick McKeown, regional director for Scotland at Henry Brothers, said in comments reported by the paper: “Being appointed to deliver these new projects at HMNB Clyde reflects the trust Babcock places in Henry Brothers and our capability in delivering complex, secure and highly specialised infrastructure. “Our workforce has extensive experience across the defence sector, and we remain committed to ensuring the Royal Navy’s operational facilities are robust, resilient and fit for purpose. These new appointments strengthen our partnership with Babcock and underline our shared focus on delivering high-quality, dependable facilities for the submarine fleet.” The three projects form part of Babcock’s investment in infrastructure at the base, which supports the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the deterrent and the Astute class attack boats. Ballistic shelters are protective structures intended to shield personnel from blast and fragmentation. The Ministry of Defence has described the work at Clyde as a multi-decade programme, and told Parliament this month that the purchase of the former Finnart Oil Terminal on Loch Long supports the longer-term transformation of the Clyde estate, with mine hunting equipment and autonomous systems relocating there from 2028. The post Faslane submarine base in Scotland to get ballistic shelters first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Heaviside unveils five-pound TYR loitering munition designed to defeat main battle tanks
body: TYR has completed live-fire testing and is under contract with Department of War customers, the company said. Heaviside said it has evaluated the system against operational requirements for range, lethality, portability and performance in contested environments. The munition weighs just over five pounds, with the complete system weighing approximately 15 pounds. The company lists flight time at more than 60 minutes, range at over 25 miles and speed at above 150 mph. Operators can choose from four Nammo warheads: Shaped Charge Anti-Tank, Anti-Structure Munition, Explosively Formed Penetrator and Anti-Personnel Frag. Heaviside said TYR can be used for ground and base defense, counter-drone missions or integration onto larger unmanned systems. The weapon is designed to operate in contested and GPS-denied environments. It also has a low acoustic and visual signature, according to the company. “As peer adversaries increasingly employ autonomous unmanned systems on the battlefield, U.S. and allied forces must adopt technologies that extend our robotic advantage,” said Heaviside President Nils Haagenrud. “TYR does exactly that by enabling widespread fielding of a lightweight loitering munition with the range and lethality necessary to increase standoff distance.” “With a first-of-its-kind combination of size, weight, and performance, TYR packs an outsized punch against armored vehicles, fortified structures, and other enemy targets while keeping warfighters farther from harm’s way,” said Heaviside CEO Phillip Walker. The company said TYR is priced for widespread adoption but did not disclose a price. TYR is the first product in Heaviside’s precision munitions line. Founded in Los Angeles in 2024, the company develops autonomous precision munitions and specialized systems for U.S. and allied special operations and conventional forces.

title: Iran’s Rare F-14 Fighters Take Centre Stage in Live Fire Exercises: Can They Stop U.S. Cruise Missile Strikes?
body: The Iranian Air Force has deployed its rare F-14 Tomcat fourth generation fighter aircraft for joint exercises with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which have involved the firing of multiple ballistic missiles and loitering munitions. Footage from the drills has shown several types of combat aircraft operating in Iranian skies, including older F-4 and F-5 fighters, and Soviet-supplied MiG-29s. The exercises have demonstrated the failure of the U.S. and its strategic partners to significantly erode Iranian air power after over half a year of war, following the United States’ initiation of full scale hostilities on February 28. While the F-4 and F-5 continue to form the backbone of the Iranian fleet, Iran’s more limited number of F-14s provide a unique missile defence capability, with the aircraft having originally been designed to defend U.S. Navy carrier groups from Soviet cruise missile attacks. While the type’s status in service was previously uncertain, footage released in June confirmed that the aircraft were operating as part of Iran’s war effort against the U.S. Although currently obsolete for air-to-air engagements against modern fighter types, the F-14’s combination of the AN/AWG-9 radar and AIM-54 missile to provide a robust capability to engage subsonic cruise missiles like the U.S. Tomahawk, which could be invaluable at a time when the U.S. Navy is facing acute missile shortages. The F-14’s AN/AWG-9 radar was by far the most more powerful radar ever integrated onto a Western fighter during the 20th century, and boasts a detection range exceeding 300 kilometres against large targets and the ability to track up to 24 targets simultaneously while engaging up to six at once. Importantly, its sophisticated look-down/shoot-down capability allowed it to detect and track low-flying cruise missiles against the clutter of the sea surface, overcoming a major limitation that affected many earlier radar systems. With Iran’s ground-based missile defence systems having taken significant losses to U.S. and Israeli air strikes, the fielding of an aircraft capable of contributing to operations may be highly prized. The F-14s are expected to be supplemented, and possibly replaced, with the service entry of Russian Su-30SM and Su-35 fighters, which Iran is confirmed to have ordered in considerable numbers. The F-14’s combat capabilities have long been in serious question, with the aircraft having fired its primary weapon the AIM-54 multiple times in U.S. Navy service during engagements with Iraqi Air Force fighters during the 1990s, while failing to achieve a hit every time. The aircraft itself has exceedingly high maintenance requirements, which combined with the age of the Iranian fleet is expected to limited availability rates. Unlike the F-4 and F-5, which are much smaller and have lower radar cross sections, the F-14 is also expected to be less viable for penetration strikes into hostile airspace. Iran has proven much more capable than analysts expected of sustaining its fighter fleet and even taking to the offensives with strikes deep into well defended hostile airspace.

title: Writing a Demoscene Intro for the ZX Spectrum
body:
A look at the tools, techniques and challenges of creating a retro-style 'crack intro'
Download Now View on pouet.net Discussion on Hacker News
In the late 80s, I spent an embarrassing number of hours hunched over my ZX Spectrum, typing in Sinclair BASIC programs and rudimentary assembler routines copied from magazines, trying to re-create the Amiga crack intros Iâd seen round at a friendâs house. Obviously, they never came even slightly close - but now, many decades later, Iâve finally managed it! Iâm now the proud author of a hand-rolled retro demoscene intro that runs on a stock 128Kb Spectrum. It features all those late 80s tropes: A smooth scrolltext (with âleet custom fonts!), a three-channel AY soundtrack, bouncing VU meters and the essential parallax starfield. Itâs currently 10287 bytes of code, or 19552 bytes as a complete tape image - which, given Iâve been working on this since December 13th last year, means my average rate of code-production is a paltry ~ 455 bytes per week!
This blog post is a technical overview of how I got there, some cool tricks I picked up, and everything I had to learn (and re-learn) about the Speccy and Z80 assembly along the way. It simultaneously rates as one of my favourite side-projects ever, and also the one that most often nearly triggered a foot put through my monitor in frustration. Iâll reflect on all that at the end , but for now if you just want to see the finished product, the download button is at the top of the article and the included .tap cassette tape image should load into any emulator. Thereâs also a YouTube capture , links to the production on pouet.net , and you can run it from within a web browser by visiting my TNFS site portal - check option 4 for recent uploads.
But letâs skip back briefly to the late 80s. Coming from the world of an 8-bit, cassette tape loading computer, seeing an Amiga for the first time was like encountering something from outer space. Like everyone who saw one back in the day, I was blown away by the amazing graphics and sound on display, not to mention the library of ground-breaking games . But I found myself even more captivated by the mysterious (and totally badass) âintrosâ displayed at the beginning of pirated games.
Created by the software piracy groups that had cracked the copy protection and distributed the floppy-disk based games, they were mini works of art in their own right - music, graphics and usually some cool-looking effect to show off the groupâs prowess. Thereâs a great collection of these intros (or âcracktrosâ) archived on YouTube .
Watch a few of those videos and youâll quickly notice the âdesignâ tropes that almost every cracktro shares: a cool, edgy logo at the top of the screen (bonus points if itâs dripping blood or in any way âmetalâ), some boastful text displayed on top of an effect of some sort - usually a scrolling parallax starfield, or rotating 3d object - and a further scroll-text full of shout outs, greetings to fellow pseudonymous crackers and adverts for illegal BBS systems galore. Needless to say, to a kid in the 80s/early 90s this was possibly the coolest thing ever .
I thought this one was the absolute bomb when I first saw it. Sine-scroller, pirate BBS adverts, cool logo with a sword - and of course, a starfield. Thereâs something for everyone here.
The music from this is burned into my brain. I think pretty much everyone of my classmates knew this intro given the popularity of Lemmings in the early 90s. Skid Row as a group are still active to this day and this is probably the quintessential Amiga cracktro of the period.
Endless Piracy. Edgy. Another cool logo, sine-wave scroller, starfield and boasting text. The classics never go out of style.
Another great combination of all the essential ingredients. Cool logo, even cooler text font, scrolling starfield and a scroll-text running along the bottom. Vintage stuff.
Logo. Text. Scroller. But no starfield - otherwise a solid effort from Anthrox here :)
The demoscene grew out of these intros. The cracking eventually faded into the background, and coders, âgraphiciansâ and musicians all contributed to feature-length productions that showcased their abilities, competed with other groups and pushed the machine to its limits. In amazing feats of ingenuity and pure âcode as an art formâ, the scene lives on today, with groups producing breathtaking productions like this and this - bear in mind, both of those are running on a 7Mhz home computer equipped with a floppy disk, 1Mb of memory and a sound chip from 1985.
But much as I admire the sheer skill and dedication that takes, itâs the early âsingle screenâ scrolly-text-and-starfield cracktros Iâve always found captivating. They took on a sort of mystical quality for me, hinting at a scene and a culture I could only ever experience from the outside - which is exactly why I spent all those hours in Sinclair BASIC, trying in vain to re-create them, and dreaming of the day Iâd eventually have an Amiga of my own.
I eventually did trade up to a range of Amiga systems, joined a few âsceneâ groups myself and threw myself into a variety of activities until exams and the end of my teenage years beckoned. I dabbled with Z80 code back then, and at one point knew enough 68k assembly to bluff my way through - partly from the Amigaâs heyday, partly from a few âembedded systemsâ modules at University where I had to program a set of traffic lights or lift-controllers. Given thereâs not much call for that sort of thing at my $DAYJOB, though, it had all pretty much faded from my memory.
I have kept working on a bunch of projects in my spare time, and one of my favourites is my TNFS site - sort of an old-school BBS system or interactive âwebsiteâ for the Spectrum, which grew out of a fun experiment to see how far I could push Sinclair BASIC. It relies on a modern network card fitted to the Spectrum, which is how I came to be chatting to âDesertkunâ, another TNFS-protocol enthusiast. Heâs now producing a great new WiFi network card for the Speccy, and was kind enough to send me a few of the prototypes to test out for him.
I was massively inspired by his hardware and low-level coding chops, and during one of our video calls where weâd been comparing our development setups, he asked why I didnât write any Z80 assembly myself. A throw-away comment, but the challenge was set! Now, I couldnât face re-writing the whole site in asm, but I figured I could produce a self-contained intro to promote it in the style of the early âBBStrosâ, and finally be one of the cool kids with a scene production of my own :)
I mean, how hard could it be ? ( ooooh - foreshadowing! )
My development environment through this was pretty straightforward, and is the same stack I use for developing my TNFS site. I just used a Makefile-driven build system which ran my code through the Pasmo assembler, my fork of zmakebas to build BASIC files, and the FUSE emulator for testing. For final testing on the real hardware, I uploaded my .tap files to my local TNFS server where I could run them on my +3.
A few additional tools I have to call out because they ended up making a big difference - one is the amazing web-based âasm-editorâ I discovered while looking up Z80 instructions. Not only does this site have a great reference of all the Z80 instructions, but it also has an editor where you can run example code and see how the memory and/or various registers change state. Take for example, the djnz instruction - you can build it and step through the example loop construct one instruction at a time. Or try my example of an add instruction in the screenshot to see how the carry flag works when a bit gets shifted out of a register. Although it uses a slightly different syntax to Pasmo (so I couldnât drop my code directly in it), it massively helped when manually stepping through things.
And lastly, probably the most significant debugging tools I used on this project - a notepad and pen, and my two dogs (say âHi!â to Biscuit & Pebbleâ¦) Iâll write some more about this in the wrap-up , but this really was a highly unusual project for me, coming from decades of much higher-level languages and constructs. Most of my z80 code I only ever really understood after drawing out the bytes and bitmasks, keeping a table of register flags and drawing chunks of screen memory out by hand. And I found my evening walks with the two dogs provided ideal rubber duck exercises, although Iâm not sure what they both made of my protracted mutterings about the hl register pair. Either way, debugging-by-dog is highly recommended!
So, letâs get started. I followed a great âHello, world!â example from futurice.com to validate my build environment. Beyond that, the first thing I wanted to do was load in my logo and background image Iâd use as a âstageâ for the remainder of the planned intro. I wasnât really sure what I was going to do at this point, just that I wanted my logo at the top, and a scrolltext along the bottom row of the screen. As my TNFS site header already looked kinda demoscene-y, I made a quick edit putting in place two blue guide-bars inside which Iâd put further content.
Memory map courtesy of breakintoprogram.co.uk
A Spectrum SCREEN$ file (usually displayed as loading screens) is just a dump of screen memory, starting from byte 16384, and running for 6912 bytes. The weird layout of this is very relevant later, but in order to display it all you need to do is load your file into that memory location. After a few hourâs work of reviewing Speccy internals and following various guides, I had a very simple starting point for my demo that served as the basis for everything else that came after.
Not much to look at now, but this simple starting point introduced me to important concepts like interfacing with the Spectrumâs hardware ( ULA chip to start with, and AY sound chip later) via the out instruction, how to pull in binary files using Pasmoâs INCBIN directive, using the Z80âs block copy ldir instruction, the use of register pairs for 16-bit addressing, and simple branching to labels.
The next step was to print something on the screen and explore some of the Speccyâs built-in ROM routines, which are somewhat analagous to syscalls on modern operating systems. There are plenty of disassemblies and guides to the Spectrum ROM available on the internet, one of the best commented and linked one is at https://skoolkid.github.io/rom/ . Using this as a reference alongside the various âHello, world!â tutorials showed me how this sort of thing is built up:
I ended up mostly not using the ROM routines in my code as they dragged in all sorts of things I didnât need, but it was massively useful to understand how they worked as they introduced me to yet more commonly-used constructs. For example, the PR_STRING routine defined here shows how you can build a loop over each character. If youâre just starting out, I highly recommend going over the 8 lines in that routine with a notepad and pen, working out the contents of the registers and following the loop constructs.
I also made a version of it in asm-editor you can try. If you click that link, youâll see a version of the code loaded into the web editor. Click âBuildâ, and then step through the code using the âStepâ button - although no text will be actually displayed (I skipped over the call to the Spectrum ROM ârestartâ vector that does this), youâll see the various states of the registers and for example the BC register counting down as each byte of the string is processed.
Problem is, the Speccyâs built-in font is not exactly dripping with demoscene credibility. I wanted to use some stylish fonts and this turned out to be super easy - a quick search turned up Jim Blimeyâs awesome font collection , which included a ready-to-use set of assembler files and some instructions which soon led me to these additions in my code:
There we go! Now thatâs looking a little more elite. Sorry, I mean 31337 . Strap in folks, weâre leaving lamer cityâ¦ So at this point, a month or so in to my dabblings and Iâd started to get a reasonable understanding of common idioms and was starting to feel like this was a project that might actually go somewhere. The problem started when I moved on to trying to implement actual demo effects: It became very apparent, very quickly, just how much I didnât know about how this all worked. Not to mention the fact that at this level, youâre really closely exposed to the physical hardware intricacies, including the design decisions and trade-offs that the hardware designers had to make when working with the extremely limited specs of the early 1980s.
The first such problem - and the cause of probably 90% of my pain - is the Speccyâs extremely weird screen layout. Rather than standard bitmapped display you might expect on more modern hardware, it is instead split into 3 sections, each with a set of interleaved rows (so if you keep adding 1 to a screen address, eventually instead of reaching the next row, youâll instead end up 8 rows down, and so on until you hit the bottom of the section and then loop back to the row underneath where you started!) followed by a block of âattributeâ bytes which determine the colours of each 8x8 block. The attribute blocks are the reason why each 8x8 character cell can only have two colours (a PAPER and INK attribute) which led to the garish âcolour-clashâ of spectrum games and distinctive style where artists try to keep inside 8x8 blocks as much as possible. But it was the layout of the bitmap portion that is such a mind twister.
You can see this illustrated whenever a game reads in a loading screen from tape. You can see each section built up with the interleaved rows one at a time, and then finally the colour and other attributes (like flashing ). Thereâs a lot of detail at the fantastic Break Into Program site. In the defense of the designers, they were working with extremely limited hardware and I donât think the Speccy was ever imagined as a games machine. When you start shuffling bytes around, you realise that this approach is really optimised for displaying text which is neatly arranged into 8x8 character boundaries. For example, using this âscrambledâ bit order, if you have a screen address in the hl register pair, you can quickly get to the next pixel line of a given address by simply incrementing the âhighâ byte. Thereâs a bunch of other âcheap movesâ you can make by simply shifting bits around:
It was a reasonable choice for a machine that would probably spend a lot of itâs time displaying BASIC program listings - itâs only when you start trying to write demo or sprite routines that it starts to feel really weird. This also means youâll pretty quickly need a routine to convert X,Y addresses to the relevant memory addresses. Again, L Break Into Program has a useful routine and if you disassemble more or less any spectrum game or demo, youâll find a version of this procedure somewhere. And yes, this all became horribly relevant later onâ¦
Admittedly, not the most interesting demonstration - but this was the first time I had made something move on the Spectrumâs screen with assembly! I watched this with pride more times than I care to admit :)
I had a snazzy logo and âHello Worldâ text, but that doesnât make for a very interesting intro! The first effect I wanted was the scrolltext - without that, itâs not really an intro. Now, the Amiga had all kinds of hardware sprites, blitter operations, custom chips but the Spectrum had none of that. I was going to have to work out how to do things the hard way - âbanging on the metalâ, literally by shifting bits around the screen memory by hand and having the CPU do all the work.
This is where understanding the Speccyâs weird screen and character cell layout is so important. It turns out thereâs a neat trick as long as I stay inside one character row - thereâs a RL instruction, which takes a byte and ârotatesâ it left. It inserts whatever is in the carry flag into the rightmost bit, and whatever gets shifted out ends up in the carry bit again. That means if you string a bunch of them together, you can move a set of pixels across the screen - the moment they âfall offâ one character cell, they end up in the carry flag and then the next rl instruction inserts them at the beginning of the next character cell to the left. Repeat 32 times, and youâve just moved a pixel (or set of pixels) across a line of the screen:
Hell yeah. Itâs almost a proper scrolltext now!
Wrapping this in another loop that increments h each time (remember - that gets us moving down a scanline) gets us moving an entire character cell. Here you can see it moving an entire row of my âHello worldâ message. There was however a lot more work needed to make a proper scrolltext, with each letter appearing smoothly. I started off by just printing an entire character at a time on the right-hand edge of the screen - it worked, but was pretty ugly as you saw each new character appear at once in the right-hand side of the screen, scrolling 8 pixels over and then the next character flashed up. Instead, I wanted to make each character appear pixel by pixel and that required a bit more bit juggling. The routine I ended up with effectively streams each character in, line by line, pixel by pixel using the font data directly instead of calling the ROM print character routine.
It does this by looking up the ASCII code for a character, and then fetching the corresponding font representation into a 8-byte buffer, one byte for each line of data. The font data starts with the space character (character code 32), so a lookup is simply font code base address + (ascii code - 32) * 8 to get to the bits for that letter.
Arranged into an 8x8 grid, the bits for the letter H in the font data look like this. For each row of bits, I shift the line left using a neat trick. The byte is loaded into the a register, and then by adding itself to itself - add a,a we shift the value left (in binary, multiplying by 2 moves everything over one bit) so that the pixel I want to draw ends up dropping into the carry flag. This is an idiomatic way of doing it in Z80 code as itâs faster and smaller than the sla instruction. And every cycle quickly adds up when youâre re-drawing 256 bytes every frame!
The character buffer then looks like this, with the top line shifted. Now, with the hl register pair pointing at the correct location on the screen, I can then use the rl trick discussed above. This shifts a scanline from the bottom character row of the screen left by one pixel and draws my pixel in the rightmost position by moving it in from the carry flag. Looping 32 times over this moves the entire row by 1 pixel with my new pixel inserted at the right.
I then repeat this step again using inc h to move down one scan line until the entire character column has been drawn. At this point, the character buffer looks like this, and all 8 lines of the bottom screen row have all been shifted left by one bit by looping over all 32 character columns. The whole thing then repeats another 7 times until the entire character has been smoothly scrolled onto the screen.
So just to re-state this because I think itâs worth the emphasis - just to scroll a message across the bottom of the screen, weâre having to loop over and re-draw 256 pixels every frame! It shows how much faster assembly is than the BASIC interpreter built into the spectrumâs ROM. I found it amazing to see my code finally working and imagining all the bits flying around and registers flapping away. It really makes me appreciate just how much effort went into creating the games I played back then.
The original Amiga module I converted. A proper 1980s ear-worm!
Of course, any good intro needs some music. On the Amiga, the standard was the âtrackerâ module format, which has a long and involved history of different forks, versions and tweaks. A song is built up from a series of patterns, each made up of rows of instructions. Each instruction usually includes note or pitch information, which sample to play and various parameters such as volume, effects - or in the case of some instructions, which position in the song to jump to. In many ways, itâs almost like a programming language for music. Using ProTracker as an example, a typical note cell is 4 bytes, shown on-screen as something like C-2 01 C20 . That breaks down into three fields: the note and octave ( C-2 ), the sample number ( 01 ), and the effect and its parameter ( C20 - in this case, âset the volume to $20 â, which is half of the maximum $40 ).
A close-up of Protracker playing a tune. Note the VUmeters - another classic demo effect I would pinch later on!
For an impressive demonstration of whatâs possible with a tracker and to see what the note data looks like on-screen, check out the work of h0ffman, and in particular his winning â Professional Tracker â entry from the Revision 2014 competition . Heâs an undisputed master of the science (or art!) of tracking, and his â Secrets of Protracker â talk gives a great overview of whatâs possible.
The Amigaâs sound hardware far eclipsed anything else on the market at the time, and the ZX Spectrum is paltry by comparison. The original 48K models only offered a rudimentary âbeeperâ, but the later 128K models included a 3-channel AY-3-8912 sound chip. This was very popular in 8-bit micros of the time, and a more-or-less identical variant was also used in the Atari ST. While it only offers basic waveforms and sound processing, it does enable multi-channel âchip musicâ, and so it became the mainstay of the ZX Spectrum demoscene. It also spawned a variety of SoundTracker clones on the Spectrum itself, although most musicians these days prefer to work in modern tools like Vortex Tracker II, which runs natively under Windows.
Pex looking back on his demos - this starts at the point where he features my letter and plays a bit of my cover version!
For my intro, I wanted to port an Amiga module - and I had the perfect one in mind. One of my favourite Amiga music disks was âSounds Of Gnomeâ, released in 1989 by the Swedish duo âMahoney & Kaktusâ. Mahoney also wrote NoiseTracker, one of the first really widely used trackers on the Amiga, and the program that served as my teenage introduction to making computer music of my own. Back in 2018 I made a rock cover of one of the other tunes on that disk, and wrote to Mahoney (real name â Pex â) about it. He ended up showing my âmusic videoâ at a demo conference, which I am eternally grateful for! So it seemed only fitting that I mangle another song from that collection with a Spectrum conversionâ¦ Sorry, guys! I picked the track âMilkmanâ which was written by âGlue Masterâ, an associate of Mahoneyâs who had a few of his tracks featured on the compilation.
Itâs an ideal track for converting: Itâs short (only 7 patterns in total), most of those patterns share the same chord sequence, and it looked fairly easy to squeeze the original 4 channels down into the Spectrumâs 3. Plus, itâs an incredibly catchy tune and I knew it well - Iâve been listening to it for 35+ years and often jam along to it on guitar or bass. The conversion started off pretty easily: all I really had to do was copy the patterns note-for-note from the Amiga mod, which I had open in OpenMPT as my Windows tracker. Below is a session with both trackers open on the same pattern - the original Amiga mod on the left, and my 3-channel Spectrum conversion on the right.
Note the 11.7 in the 3rd channel of the Spectrum version. This is a âpitch slide downâ effect in Vortex Tracker syntax, which drops the pitch by about a quarter-tone. Itâs repeated on the next line, so the overall effect is a slide down from the A# that leads in to the next bass note. The original Amiga mod does the same thing using its own syntax - those are the 202 s you can see on the same notes, at the bottom of the 4th track.
Using just a single âbeepâ sound for everything was enough to check everything was working, and after a few weeks of hacking on it and re-arranging things in the evenings, I had a basic version which sounded surprisingly good for a first draft:
I have to give a special mention to this forum post which was a massive help getting me started. Itâs probably the best introduction to Vortex Tracker Iâve found - many, many thanks to the original author for taking the time to write it all up!
The real challenge was making it sound as close to the original as possible. That meant building up a library of better-sounding samples for the different parts, and making extensive use of Vortex Trackerâs âornamentsâ. Vortex Tracker comes with a great selection of sounds, and fortunately Iâm also a weirdo who likes to listen to chiptunes in the background while I work! So whenever I found something particularly enticing, I filed it away for later pilfering inspiration. A Vortex Tracker sample isnât really a âsampleâ in the Amiga sense of a recorded sound - itâs a definition of how a note sounds, one line per frame. Each line can mix in a tone or the white noise generator (useful for snare effects and suchlike), along with various other parameters.
Ornaments, on the other hand, give you extra control over what pitch a note plays - and this enables really useful tricks like âarpeggio chordsâ. For example, an ornament of 0,4 makes the channel switch rapidly (25 times a second) between the note being played and the one 4 semitones above it. It happens so quickly that it sounds much like two notes played at the same time, which means you can build up full-sounding triad chords using only two channels. Take the opening chord in my fully converted version, Cm: It plays C in the first channel and the minor 3rd (D#) in the second, then I apply an ornament to the second channel to bring it up 4 semitones to the 5th (G). That gives all three notes of the chord, while keeping the 3rd channel free for other parts.
As well as making much more efficient use of the limited 3 channels, this also gives Spectrum music that characteristic âwarblingâ sound, which I find really appealing in a retro kind of way! Between tricks like this and samples that mix tones with white noise (to make a combined âbass-snareâ sound, for example), I managed to condense the full track down to 3 channels. Many months later, I have to say Iâm really pleased with the final result .
The original site that was home to Vortex Tracker, documentation and other resources appears to be offline at the moment. I managed to grab a copy of everything I needed from archive.org - youâll want the PTxTools.7z file for the playback routines discussed here.
Update - a user on Hacker News added this useful bit of information: âSergey Bulbaâs WWW site is still around and the relevant stuff can be found today at https://ay.strangled.net/progr_e.htm â. Thanks, JdeBP!
The playback was simple in theory: As this overview notes, you basically just pull in the player routine, include your module file and call the playback routine once per frame in your main loop. The catch is, none of the source code versions supplied in the archive worked with my Pasmo assembler. Fortunately, there is a pre-compiled binary object shipped alongside the source ( VTII10bG in the PTxTools/PT3Play directory). This just has to be loaded in at address $C000 - this cannot be changed, as it has lots of absolute addresses baked in.
My code to handle module playback now looks something like this, with the binary module loaded in place:
Well, that didnât work as hoped. TNFStro - tortoise edition.
This brings me to the main event. No self-respecting cracktro is complete without a starfield!
My first, naive approach to the classic starfield effect was to scatter random stars across the screen, then move down each scan-line applying the same rl trick Iâd used for the scroll-text. I figured I could get parallax by shifting each row a different amount: One pixel for the first row, two for the second, three for the third, then back to one again, all the way down the screen to give the impression of several âfieldsâ of stars moving at different speeds.
It turned out there were two major problems with that approach. Firstly, shifting an entire row smeared whatever else was on it along with the stars - which Iâd expected, and had filed away as a problem for future me. The bigger issue was speed: by the time Iâd finished the first three rows Iâd already performed hundreds of shift operations, and it was nowhere near fast enough to fit inside a single frame. Everything crawled across the screen, and the music playback slowed down so much that you could actually hear the arpeggio ornaments warbling away as separate notes.
Clearly I was going to have to keep track of the individual stars instead. I found this routine , which was more-or-less what I had in mind and started me off with the idea of a structure to hold the state of each star. It also uses a screen address lookup much like the one from âBreak Into Programâ.
Dammit. Back with another funeral dirge rendition :(
That got things moving, but the co-ordinate lookup and tracking proved expensive to do (it has to run for every star, every frame as well as keep track of the old position for erasing) and Iâd been ignoring the bigger question how to display stuff on top of the starfield. My original idea was simply to draw the stars and then paint text over them each frame, which blew the frame budget just as comprehensively as my first attempt.
If I wanted something more interesting than an empty starfield, Iâd have to keep track of which cells were occupied by text and avoid drawing stars in them in the first place, rather than over-painting them every time. After lots of scribbling in my notepad and visualising rows of bits, I eventually solved both challenges by âcheatingâ fairly liberally.
So now, I donât generate a random starfield at all. Instead, I built a table of pre-calculated Y and X position pairs:
This saves faffing about with an RNG, and once I have a layout that looks good I know itâll always look good. I can also âfudgeâ things and ensure no two stars share the same y co-ordinate which sidesteps a whole class of problems like stars sharing a scanline, and having to deal with them overtaking each other.
The ârandomâ layout is generated by a simple Ruby script:
When the routine initialises, I convert those co-ordinate pairs into a table that tracks the state of each star. So rather than storing a position and translating it to a screen address every frame, each of my star records now looks like this (offsets from the base address):
The key thing is that there are no X/Y co-ordinates at all. For each star I store the screen byte it sits in and the bit mask within that byte, so itâs already in the form the screen writes need. That means no address conversion per frame, just simple bit shifting and rotation.
Moving a star is then dead simple. I rotate its mask left with rlca , and when the bit rotates out of bit 7, it lands back in bit 0 with the carry flag set. Thatâs the signal I need to move the star one character cell to the left, which is one of the âcheap movesâ from earlier.
Because Iâm tracking which cell each star is in, the collision check comes almost for free. Thatâs what the second pointer is for: STOCC (Star Occupancy) moves in step with STSCR through a table holding one byte per character cell. The âtypewriterâ routine sets a byte to 1 for every cell containing a text character or the cursor, so checking whether a star is hidden behind text is a single or instruction. If the cell is occupied, I skip drawing the star but carry on rotating and stepping it along until it reaches a cell where it can be displayed:
Parallax is still handled by moving each star a different number of pixels per frame, but the cost is a lot lower this time as Iâm only touching the cells the stars actually occupy, rather than every byte of every row.
Thatâs looking more like it! The typewriter routine is a simple copy of the font data from memory, and is very cheap as we can use the âcheap movesâ to quickly fetch the 8x8 block.
I also skip drawing any space character so it leaves the âoccupancy cellâ unmarked. This means the stars keep drifting through the gaps in the text - you can see here the odd star passing in between the words. I switched to ALL CAPS writing for the final version which helps the effect even more as the font is quite blocky, so you donât really notice stars skipping the spaces inside a glyph at all.
A few odds and ends that didnât warrant a section of their ownâ¦
Some sort of graphic display bouncing along with the audio playback was another common early demo trope. I did originally consider a real-time graphic equaliser, but that would have been far too complex, probably in terms of spare cycles per frame, and definitely in terms of my limited mental capacity at this point! So I settled for a simple set of bouncing meter bars instead.
Itâs worth a mention mostly because it gives me an excuse to link to the awesome chibiakumas website! I just love the late 90s web design on display - one can argue that readability and accessibility take a hit, but itâs just so much fun to encounter a site that still looks like this. Itâs a clear labour of love and thereâs a wealth of content there as well, if your eyeballs are up to it.
Their guide on Making Sound with the AY-3-8910 was what showed me how to get the data I needed to draw the meter bars. The examples write a register number to $FFFD to select a register, and I realised that once a register is selected, I could use the in instruction to read its value back out instead of writing a new one. As the page says, R8, R9 and R10 hold the channel amplitudes, so they feed nicely into the height parameter for drawing a bar. Getting the amplitude for channel A is then as simple as:
This is a simple effect that makes the header logo a little more interesting. Iâm not sure where I originally got the idea - Iâve definitely seen something like it on a few late 80s/early 90s demos, though. All I wanted was to pick random star dots in the logo background and animate them.
Hereâs the header image loaded in ZXPaintbrush with the character cell grid showing. By happy chance, there are four stars which each sit neatly inside a single character cell with enough surrounding space, so they can be used to give an animated âtwinkleâ effect by drawing a cross out from the centre point and back in again.
These dots map to the following co-ordinates, which target the top scanline of each fully-grown star (two pixels up from the centre):
The âtwinkleâ routine itself is simple enough: it adds a pixel on either axis to grow the star, waits a few frames, then shrinks it back down again. The interesting bit was how I made the twinkle order pseudo-random. Remember that my starfield was entirely pre-calculated from a data table generated by a Ruby script, which meant Iâd never actually needed a random number generator in assembly. From Jonathan Cauldwellâs â How To Write Spectrum Games â e-book, I found another great âhackâ which simply walks through the start of the Spectrumâs ROM, picking out random-looking bytes as it goes. As he says, he uses it in most of his games, and it does the job in a really simple way - as long as you stay below the block of structured, repeating data that sits 8Kb into the ROM.
About halfway through writing the intro, I hit a fairly predictable problem: I had run out of memory. In an attempt to keep everything self-contained in one block of code, I was pulling all of the assets (the screen background, the player binary, the music file etc.) into the program itself, and then using the ldir block copy instruction to move each one into its correct location. Since that meant effectively storing every block twice, and the player routine had a hard-coded start address of $C000 , I quickly ran out of room and my code started crashing into the playback routine. The simplest option was to split things out into separate code blocks, load each one directly to the address it needed to live at, and wrap the lot in a multi-stage BASIC tape loader:
This loads the main program, then the player routine directly into $C000 , and finally the background screen straight into screen memory. It does mean the background starts appearing before the demo has fully loaded, but as I imagine most people will be seeing this running in an emulator or on my TNFS site, it doesnât really matter. Plus, at this point I was in danger of disappearing down yet more rabbit holes (I still really want to work out how to do multi-colour border effects!) and Iâd never have got this thing released.
This whole project is a really weird one to look back at. On the one hand, Iâve fulfilled a childhood ambition and have something Iâm very proud of. Itâs also pretty unusual these days to end up with a binary where you can say pretty much what every single byte is doing and the story of how it got there. But on the other hand - I now have an answer for why I donât code in assembly: Itâs because I value (whatâs left) of my sanity! The thing is, in order to write code like this you have to start thinking like the machine itself. You have to visualise the registers and the status flags flapping away, graphics as lines of bits slotted into strange orders, loops and conditionals as binary logic and so on. Getting this close to the hardware definitely brought about a greater sense of attachment to the hardware of my childhood, and itâs easy to see why assembly coders and sceners get so passionate about it. That said, Iâm in no hurry to start re-writing my body of work in assembly!
The projects I really enjoy are those that give me an excuse to learn something for the sheer hell of it, and to slow down a little from the ever-increasing velocity and demands of the modern work world. Going back to Z80 code is probably about the furthest I could have taken this, short of going into hardware hacking. I found it at times an intriguing puzzle, often a frustrating exercise that nearly had me throwing in the towel at several stages. This project has certainly taken the longest to go from the âideaâ stage of any given feature to any kind of meaningful output.
True, I didnât spend every day of the last year working on it - my actual coding time was probably only a few hours over a couple of evenings a week. But Iâve certainly been thinking about it and pondering it most days (as my dogs will attest). The biggest breakthroughs and âaha!â moments usually didnât come from behind the keyboard; they came from scribbles in my notebook and thinking about processor states while doing something unrelated.
It has however given me massive appreciation and respect for the coders who pull this stuff off and make it look easy. And that goes double for those kids and bedroom coding superstars who managed all of this back in the 80s, and had to work it all out by experiment themselves. I only managed to get this far because of numerous books, online tutorials, GitHub repositories with sample code, YouTube videosâ¦ I canât imagine how much longer this would have all taken me if the only resources I had were my Spectrum, a cassette tape recorder and a notepad.
So, as I draw a line under this project - for now! - I raise a glass, and in the words of h0ffman: âShout out to the hackers, graphicians and protrackers.â

title: Education endures amid war in West Darfur
body: Schools across Sudan’s West Darfur state are continuing to operate, with student enrolment increasing despite the challenges posed by the ongoing war, the state’s director of secondary education, Youssef Osman, said. West Darfur is among the areas controlled by the Sudan Foundation Alliance (Tasis), a parallel administration aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudan’s army since April 2023. Tasis announced the formation of a parallel administration in areas under its control in July 2025, with RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti, heading its presidential council and civilian politician Mohamed Hassan al-Taishi serving as prime minister. Osman told Radio Tamazuj on Sunday that enrolment was increasing as parents, guardians and students recognise the importance of education and the lack of alternatives amid the conflict. “Schools are continuing at all levels, including preschool, primary and secondary education. This is because parents and teachers are convinced that there is no alternative to education. As a result, enrolment is high, and we also thank the state administration for making education a priority,” he said. He said the state administration had made efforts to stabilise the education sector and keep schools open despite the difficult circumstances. It had also committed to paying monthly incentives to teachers in public secondary schools, he said, adding that payments for September had been distributed to support teachers and encourage them to remain at work. A teacher in the state said education workers are determined to continue teaching despite the challenges, particularly to protect the future of children and young people from marginalised communities. “We will try our best to provide education to our children. We are here because of them. We know the state is affected by the war, but we remain available to provide education to those deprived of opportunities because of the conflict. We also thank the state administration for the little support we receive,” he said. The teacher said schools are also providing education to displaced people who had fled to West Darfur because of the fighting. Access to schooling, the teacher added, is essential to social stability, warning that a lack of educational opportunities could aggravate social problems. Student Maqbula Abdo Mohammed told Radio Tamazuj that pupils remain committed to their studies despite harsh living conditions and the breakdown of state institutions, describing continued access to education as a source of hope. “We are committed to education in the state, and we thank our teachers for the education they are providing to us despite the war,” she said. Maqbula, a student at El Geneina Secondary School in El Geneina city, also praised the female student who ranked first in the Sudanese Certificate examinations administered under the Tasis government. West Darfur’s education sector continues to face major challenges from the war, including disruptions to schools and the displacement of residents. The post Education endures amid war in West Darfur appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Hanwha Highlights M38/M48 MUSV and Containerized Munitions at AUSA 2026
body: At AUSA 2026, Hanwha Defense USA featured a model of the M38 MUSV made in partnership with Magnet Defense, with the parent design vessel recently arriving at National Harbor just outside of Washington D.C. following previous rounds of testing at sea. Hanwha’s Kevin Schoonover provided insight into the ongoing program, including several of Hanwha’s munitions offering destined to outfit the vessel and other platforms, alongside greater detail pertaining to the partnership with Magnet Defense. Schoonover also highlighted how the M38 is the primary testing vehicle for the class standing at 38 meters long, with future production upgrading to the larger 48 meter standard found on the M48. To this end steel has been cut for the first M48, with production coinciding with continued testing of the original M38. Naval News previously reported on the partnership between Hanwha and Magnet Defense , primarily geared towards breaching the emerging U.S. USV market. Schoonover also detailed how Hanwha handles most of the construction on the vessel along with work regarding autonomous weapons integration, whilst Magnet Defense handles most of the autonomy in regards to navigation and the vessel’s actual operation. Like similar sized USVs, the M38 also features the capability to carry containerized payloads related to multiple missions, including strike, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare. Magent Defense claims the M38 has already demonstrated its range of 17,000 nautical miles on multiple tests, including a trip across the Pacific to American Samoa in up to conditions of Sea State 9 . This has been part of a bid to introduce the M38 to overseas markets, including those beyond the U.S.’s MUSV program and Korean operation. M38’s Weapons A scale model of the 40 foot containerized version of K-VLS II at Hanwha’s AUSA booth. Naval News image. Joining the M38 at Hanwha’s booth, the company showcased offerings for both containerized Multiple Launch Rocket Systems (MLRS) and containerized Vertical Launch Systems (VLS). There are a total of 4 different containerized systems on display, with two systems fitting inside of a 20 foot long shipping containers and the others using 40 foot standard shipping containers. When paired with M38, the vessel can carry up to 4 of the 20 foot long containerized munition packages, 2 of the 40 foot long options, or a combination of a pair of 20 foot containers and a singular 40 foot container A containerized version of the Chunmoo family of MLRS systems constitutes one of the 20 foot options, utilizing the same munitions and launch mechanisms found on the truck based version. This enables carriage of 2 MLRS pods, with each pod containing up to 6 CGR-080 guided rockets, 4 CTM-MR ballistic missiles (with a range of 160km), 4 CTM-160 Anti-Ship Ballistic Missiles, 1 CTM-290 Ballistic Missile (with a range of 290km), or 1 CTM-X Ballistic Missile featuring a range of 500 kilometers. The other containers represent Hanwha’s iterations on containerized VLS systems, with the other 20 foot container featuring a shortened K-VLS compact system, with 4 cells primarily meant for smaller surface to air missile systems such as K-SAAM. The two 40 foot options carry 4 cells of K-VLS I or 2 cells of K-VLS II respectively. The container with K-VLS I can employ Red Shark rocket launched torpedoes (K-ASROC), SSM-700K type surface to surface cruise missiles, and K-SAAM. The container with K-VLS II can utilize the larger L-SAM (intended to replace the SM-2 in Korean service) , and other larger ballistic and cruise missiles. The post Hanwha Highlights M38/M48 MUSV and Containerized Munitions at AUSA 2026 appeared first on Naval News .

title: Russia Strikes Kyiv With Ballistic Missiles After Deadly Drone Attack Kills 2
body:
Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv late Monday, Oct. 12, striking transport and warehouse facilities hours after a Russian drone hit a residential high-rise, killing two people and injuring at least nine.
Ukraine’s Air Force reported that approximately six ballistic missiles targeted several districts of the capital at around 10:10 p.m. local time.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Ukrainian radar detected the incoming missiles, but the military said it had received no advance information about launches from Russian territory.
The Air Force said the circumstances were under investigation, while the missile types had not yet been identified.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed missile impacts in two districts on the capital’s left bank.
In the Dniprovskyi district, a missile struck a transport infrastructure facility. In the Desnianskyi district, another hit a four-story warehouse building.
Emergency services were dispatched to both locations, Klitschko reported on Telegram .
Explosions were heard before an air raid alert was issued, according to Ukrainian media reports.
At 11:17 p.m., Kyiv authorities warned of another drone threat and urged residents to seek shelter.
The missile barrage followed a Russian drone strike on a 25-story residential building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district.
Klitschko initially reported that a Shahed-type drone struck the building between the 12th and 16th floors, setting vehicles ablaze in the courtyard.
Two people were killed and at least nine others injured, according to local authorities. Three of the injured were hospitalized.
A 59-year-old woman was among those killed, while another victim was found dead inside a vehicle near the building, according to Ukrainian prosecutors.
Earlier Monday, debris from a downed drone sparked a fire near a building in the central Pechersk district.
During his evening address, President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the strikes and urged its allies, particularly the US, for increased pressure on Russia.
“It is Russia that continues these brutal strikes. It is Russia that is prolonging the war. Even now, in response to the American proposal, it is sending Shahed drones,” Zelensky said.
“We hope the United States will recognize these signals from Russia and act decisively. Strength is needed to force Russia to end this war,” he concluded.
The strike came amid rising friction between Ukraine and the US.
Instead of increasing pressure on Moscow, as Kyiv has urged, Trump on Oct. 9 announced a diesel arrangement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Russia agreed to supply up to 4.8 million tons of fuel to US and global markets.
The US Treasury then temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel until April 7, 2027.
The move came only three weeks after US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , which granted him the power to sanction all entities and individuals linked to the Kremlin’s war effort, including Putin’s own network.
Rather than using the law’s tools to pressure Moscow – including tariffs of up to 500% on Russian imports and up to 100% on goods from countries that purchase Russian energy – Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel, which may violate the law.
Days after, on Oct. 11, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, although neither Moscow nor Kyiv had confirmed the agreement beforehand.
Concurrently on Monday, Zelensky said there was no indication that Russia was complying with the truce, even though Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian energy facilities overnight.
Meanwhile, Trump defended his diesel agreement with Russia , despite condemnation from both US parties, European allies and Ukraine. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a post on Truth Social .
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Russian mercenaries have operated in the Central African Republic since 2017. Now Russian lessons are coming to three of its public schools.
body: Russia and the Central African Republic (CAR) have signed a resolution on teaching Russian in the CAR’s schools, the Russian Education Ministry’s press office said . Under a pilot program, Russian classes will begin at three schools in the CAR for students in sixth grade and above. The ministry has already supplied the CAR with 500 textbooks for learning Russian as a foreign language. Plans for further cooperation include establishing a Russian-language department at the University of Bangui. Since 2024, teachers from Russian House in Bangui have taught Russian at private schools in the CAR. On October 1, it emerged that Russian had been added to the country’s public school curriculum. From Meduza’s archives After the mutiny What happened to the Wagner Group’s mercenaries in the year since Prigozhin’s ‘march on Moscow’? Mercenaries from the Wagner private military company began operating in the CAR in 2017. In 2023, after the mutiny and the death of Wagner founder Yevgeny Prigozhin, Russia’s Defense Ministry took control of them. As of early 2026, about 1,500 Russian mercenaries remained in the CAR, according to a U.S. congressional estimate . Russia supports CAR President Faustin-Archange Touadéra, who amended the constitution and won reelection to a third term in 2025. In the September 2026 elections for Russia’s State Duma, United Russia received 79% of the vote in the CAR — its best result among all polling stations abroad. title: Son of a Russian Federal Security Service general helps run a company selling mobile data centers amid Ukrainian drone strikes, BBC reports
body: Russian businesses had been preparing for attacks on data centers long before Ukraine began striking them, the BBC Russian Service reported. Yandex, for example, regularly held drills to shut down systems and reroute traffic. Russian companies are also buying mobile data centers in large numbers. According to the BBC, one supplier is linked to the son of a senior general in Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). Demand for mobile data centers has increased since late summer, the BBC reported. Buyers include IT companies and mobile operators, as well as medium-sized and large businesses “that need more computing power than a standard PC.” Suppliers in Russia include Rostelecom subsidiary RTK-TsOD and Yadro, which is part of X Holding. Boris Korolev, the son of FSB First Deputy Director Sergey Korolev, is a deputy CEO of the holding company. In 2026, Yadro launched Borey, a containerized data center. According to government procurement records analyzed by the BBC, a unit costs 18 million to 25 million rubles without servers; with computing equipment, the price can reach hundreds of millions of rubles. The units have been on sale for several months. “The headlines are good for sales — too good, in fact,” an industry source told the BBC. According to the BBC’s sources, people in the industry had been saying since late summer that attacks on Russian data centers were inevitable. Two-thirds of the country’s data centers are concentrated in the Moscow region and St. Petersburg. On October 6, just a couple of days before the first attack on Yandex, Deputy Digital Development Minister Yevgeny Filatov urged companies to move computing capacity “somewhere beyond the Urals, where, fortunately, the strikes haven’t reached yet.” From October 8 to 11, Ukraine attacked three of Yandex’s six data centers: in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, Kaluga, and Vladimir. The strikes disrupted both Yandex’s own services and those of other companies. The data centers that came under attack housed all three of Yandex’s supercomputers: “Chervonenkis,” “Lyapunov,” and “Galushkin.” As of the evening of October 11, the extent of any damage to them was unknown. According to Kommersant, replacing damaged equipment could take about six months. The younger Korolev became a deputy CEO of X Holding in 2023, when he was 27. That same year, Garda, a company in which he held a 20% stake, acquired a stake in the holding company following the death of its founder and owner, Anton Cherepennikov. Whether the younger Korolev retained his stake is unknown, as the company’s financial reports are not public. Journalist Andrey Zakharov believes the ultimate beneficiary of Boris Korolev’s assets is his father, who had previously registered property worth hundreds of millions of rubles in his son’s name. In addition to data centers, X Holding supplies equipment for internet traffic filtering systems known as TSPU. Spending on blocking and filtering traffic continues to rise: The new draft budget would allocate 60 billion rubles for these purposes over the next three years — twice the amount previously planned. It is unknown how much of this money will go to X Holding. title: Kyiv under 'particularly vile' missile attack before air raid alert issued
body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.
Kyiv came under missile attack shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, with powerful explosions reported before an air raid alert was issued in the Ukrainian capital, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Kyiv Independent staff reported powerful blasts in central Kyiv, with air raid sirens and mobile notifications sounding only afterward. At 11:09 p.m., Kyiv Independent journalists reported further explosions in the capital as the attack continued. The cause of the latest blasts was not immediately confirmed.
Ukraine's Air Force later reported that Russian forces had attacked Kyiv with what appeared to be six ballistic missiles at approximately 10:10 p.m. President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 13 that it was five ballistic missiles that hit civilian infrastructure.
Zelensky called the strike "particularly vile," adding that there was no early warning from Ukraine's partners about missiles coming.
"Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
Since last evening and up to now, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different weapons – jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles. A significant portion of these strike assets were shot down. But unfortunately, not all of them. An… pic.twitter.com/lTCF3mB0xL
The Air Force said radar systems detected the incoming missiles during the attack, but that it had received no information about launches from Russian territory. It added that it was investigating why it had received no information about the launches.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed during the national news telethon that the alarm had been sounded only during the missile attack, but said that this had occurred previously, according to Ukrainska Pravda .
He also noted that not only the U.S. shares its intelligence with Ukraine, but other NATO countries do as well, covering strategic aviation, ship movements, and ballistic missile launches.
"There are moments when this information fails to arrive. This is not the first case... If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the intelligence can sort them out. And they will resolve this problem together with our partners," Ihnat said.
At least 12 people were injured in Russian attacks on Kyiv on Oct. 12, including a 17-year-old, according to the Kyiv City State Administration's Health Department.
As of 10:15 p.m. local time, four people had been hospitalized in moderate condition, while eight others, including the teenager, received medical assistance at the scene.
The delayed air raid alert prompted speculation on Ukrainian social media about whether the lack of advance warning was connected to reported U.S. threats to withdraw intelligence-sharing support for Ukraine.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the United States to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
The Kyiv Independent reported earlier on Oct. 12 , citing two Ukrainian officials, that Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said that intelligence sharing between the U.S. and Ukraine was ongoing and had not been stopped, during a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum on Oct. 13.
“You probably ask if we receive intelligence from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation," he said.
The Kyiv Independent has reached out to Ukrainian and U.S. officials for comment.
A Russian drone attack on a private residential building in the Darnytskyi district in the morning injured one woman, the city's military administration said .

title: Opinion| South Sudan should build its digital infrastructure before legacy systems take hold
body: The conventional development path assumes that countries must first establish mature institutions and administrative systems before digitising them. For emerging economies such as South Sudan, that sequence deserves to be reconsidered. Digital infrastructure should not be treated as the final layer added once institutions are fully developed. If designed carefully, it can become part of the foundation through which effective institutions are built. Every modern economy requires reliable systems for collecting revenue, processing payments, maintaining records, reconciling transactions and understanding how money and information move between institutions. These functions may appear administrative, but they are fundamental to how governments operate and economies grow. When such processes remain fragmented or heavily manual, the consequences extend beyond inconvenience. Transactions become more difficult to trace. Reconciliation takes longer. Institutions may work with incomplete information. Businesses face additional friction when dealing with government, financial institutions and one another. Policymakers can also struggle to obtain the timely, reliable data needed to make informed decisions. This is why digital infrastructure matters. The term is often associated with connectivity, mobile networks and access to online services. Those elements are important, but digital infrastructure also includes the systems that allow institutions to identify users, process transactions, exchange information securely and maintain reliable records. Payments sit at the centre of this architecture. A payment is rarely an isolated event. It is often connected to a licence, tax obligation, customs process, public service, commercial transaction or regulatory requirement. Each payment generates information that may need to be validated, reconciled and shared with the appropriate institution. When the payment and the underlying administrative process operate separately, inefficiency is almost inevitable. But when payments, records and institutional processes are connected, governments can gain greater visibility into economic activity. Businesses can transact more efficiently, while institutions can reduce the administrative burden associated with reconciling disconnected systems. For South Sudan, the opportunity is particularly significant. The country is building institutions and economic systems at the same time as digital technologies are reshaping how governments and businesses operate. This creates an opportunity that more mature economies did not always have: the ability to design modern systems before fragmented legacy infrastructure becomes deeply entrenched. Many countries are now spending considerable time and resources replacing or connecting systems that were developed separately over decades. Their challenge is not simply digitisation. It is overcoming the complexity created by institutions, databases and processes that were never designed to work together. South Sudan can take a different path. It can design for interoperability from the beginning. It can establish common principles for security, data protection and accountability before disconnected platforms proliferate. It can build systems capable of expanding as institutions mature and economic activity becomes more formalised. This does not mean attempting to digitise everything at once. Nor does it mean assuming that technology can solve underlying policy or governance challenges. Digital systems cannot compensate for unclear mandates, weak oversight or poorly defined processes. The starting point must always be the problem an institution is trying to solve. What information does it need? Which process is creating unnecessary friction? Where are transactions becoming difficult to reconcile? Which institutions need to exchange information, and under what legal and operational safeguards? Technology becomes useful when it responds to clearly defined institutional needs. This is also why emerging economies should begin with practical, focused implementation rather than ambitious systems that attempt to solve every challenge immediately. South Sudan should also resist the temptation to import digital systems without adapting them to its own realities. Africa does not have a single digital-transformation model. A solution designed for a highly connected market with mature institutions, widespread formal banking and established digital records may not translate directly into an emerging economy. South Sudan’s systems must account for its institutional capacity, connectivity environment, regulatory framework, economic structure and the practical circumstances of the people and businesses expected to use them. That requires collaboration. Government institutions cannot build this infrastructure alone. Financial institutions, telecommunications companies, technology providers, businesses and development partners all have important roles to play. But collaboration must be supported by clear responsibilities, appropriate regulation and confidence in how systems and information will be managed. Trust is therefore not an optional feature of digital infrastructure. It is part of the infrastructure itself. People and institutions need confidence that transactions will be recorded accurately, information will be protected, systems will operate reliably and those responsible for managing them will be accountable. Without that confidence, adoption will remain limited regardless of how advanced the technology may be. The wider economic case is equally important. Digital infrastructure can make it easier for businesses to participate in formal economic activity. Reliable payment and transaction records can improve visibility, reduce friction and create the foundations for stronger commercial relationships. Over time, better information can also support more informed policymaking and help institutions understand how the economy is evolving. For an emerging economy, these are not secondary benefits. They are part of the process of building a more connected, visible and efficient market. South Sudan therefore faces an important choice. It can wait for its institutions and economy to mature before investing seriously in connected digital systems. Or it can recognise that well-designed digital infrastructure can help those institutions mature, provided it is introduced responsibly, gradually and with the right safeguards. The second path is more ambitious and full of potential impact. The writer, Charles Abuy, is the South Sudan managing director of CapitalPay International, a global provider of digital financial services and payment infrastructure. He can be reached by email at charles.abuy@capitalpay.com.ss . The views expressed in ‘opinion’ articles published by Radio Tamazuj are solely those of the writer.
