title: British tanker completes fourteen missions in Saudi deployment
body: A Royal Air Force Voyager sent to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling has already flown fourteen operational missions, alongside air defence also deployed by Britain, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons . Andy Burnham set out the deployment in a statement on the United Nations General Assembly and the international meetings that followed it, describing the Middle East as one of the subjects he had discussed with President Trump in New York. He said: “I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air to air refuelling support. I can confirm today it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.” The deployment was agreed in late September in response to a Saudi request, with the Prime Minister acting on the advice of the Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, and the Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband. Mr Burnham said then that Britain was acting to secure the interests of this country and the wider region, and that pathways needed to be kept open. Saudi Arabia was reported to be running low on interceptor stocks as Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks, which began on 8 September, continued. The attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh came on 8 October, when a Houthi ballistic missile killed three people, among them a Saudia pilot, Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, and wounded dozens more, several of them foreign nationals. A Saudia aircraft was damaged. Operations at the airport have since resumed. Attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports in early October killed three civilians and injured thirty-six, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority, and strikes on Jazan and Najran airports wounded at least three. The coalition said on 18 September that it had intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at King Khalid, and an explosion was heard near the airport the following day with smoke rising from a fuel storage area. Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to deploy forces under mutual defence arrangements signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year, and a Pakistani foreign ministry spokesman has said his country now has a substantial number of forces and resources in Riyadh, acting in defence of Saudi territory without crossing into Houthi-held areas. Voyager is the Royal Air Force’s only air-to-air refuelling aircraft and also carries the strategic air transport role, flying in two configurations, the KC Mk 2 with two underwing pods for fast jets and the KC Mk 3 with an additional centreline hose for larger aircraft. The post British tanker completes fourteen missions in Saudi deployment first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Germany and the EU won’t follow Trump’s lead on Russian diesel, calls for tougher sanctions against Moscow
body: Germany and the European Union do not plan to follow the U.S. example and strike a deal with Russia for diesel supplies, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, according to Der Spiegel. Such a decision is unacceptable to Germany and Europe. Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, so we are maintaining our sanctions against it. Merz said Russia had responded to Donald Trump’s proposal for an energy ceasefire with fresh strikes on Ukraine’s civilian and energy infrastructure. In these circumstances, he said, sanctions against Moscow must be tightened further, and Berlin will continue supporting Kyiv. Criticism of Trump’s deal with Russia extends beyond Merz and his fellow Christian Democratic Union (CDU) members. “First start a war against Iran with no discernible plan, driving up energy prices worldwide — and then make a deal with Putin, who started the war, to cushion the fallout before the U.S. midterms — it doesn’t get more unscrupulous than that,” Der Spiegel quoted Green Party co-leader Franziska Brantner as saying. Merz, meanwhile, is in an extremely weak position: His approval rating has hit a record low, and his CDU is losing regional elections. In the same speech criticizing Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, Merz again promised to cut the electricity tax for all German residents to the minimum allowed in the EU. His party made that promise to voters before the February 2025 Bundestag elections but has yet to fulfill it. title: L3Harris wins record order for GMLRS propulsion units
body: The company will fulfill the order at its new 60,000-square-foot Arsenal of Freedom facility in Camden, Arkansas, scheduled to open later this year. The plant will bring production together and use automation and robotics to streamline solid rocket motor manufacturing. “Securing this follow-on award at the highest quantity in program history demonstrates confidence in L3Harris’ missile propulsion expertise and our ability to deliver at scale,” said Scott Alexander, president of Propulsion Systems, Missile Solutions at L3Harris. “With our investments to expand capacity ahead of need, we’re well‑positioned to meet this surge while maintaining the quality our customers expect.” L3Harris said it has doubled GMLRS solid rocket motor output in recent years through advances in manufacturing techniques and processes. The increase has expanded capacity to supply the United States and allied partners. The company has produced GMLRS propulsion units for decades as the program’s solid rocket motor supplier. It also manufactures the system’s electronic safe-and-arm device and proximity sensor.

title: Yemeni military issues statement on latest Saudi agggression
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – The spokesman for the Yemeni Armed Forces announced that the total number of Saudi acts of aggression—comprising both airstrikes and missile attacks—has reached 2,177 since the new escalation of hostilities.
According to local Yemeni Al-Masirah TV, Yahya Saree, the spokesman for the Yemeni Armed Forces, stated on Monday that Saudi aggressors had carried out 119 airstrikes and missile attacks against Yemen over the past 24 hours.
The spokesman added that the Saudi attacks targeted civilian areas in the capital (Sanaa) as well as the provinces of Al-Jawf, Taiz, Saada, Marib, Lahj, Al-Bayda, and Ibb. These attacks by Saudi aggressors resulted in civilian casualties, including the death and injury of women and children.
Yahya Saree further noted that the Saudi airstrikes were conducted by F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets taking off from the Khamis Mushait and Taif airbases, while missile attacks were launched from the Najran and Jizan regions. The total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks on the country has reached 2,177 since the escalation of the conflict.

title: Britain calls in industry for fleet of drone submarines
body: The Royal Navy has opened preliminary market engagement for the Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle and the AUKUS Signature Payload Programme, inviting companies to register interest before any requirement is set, according to a notice published on Find a Tender at ten past twelve on Monday. “The Royal Navy seeks to improve its understanding of the market and wider ecosystem for Extra-Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) platforms, associated payloads, and enabling functions,” it says. “This activity supports the development of the Type 93 capability and the Royal Navy’s commitments under the AUKUS Pillar II Signature Project.” Registrations are sought from “XLUUV platform providers, payload providers, relevant technology and software suppliers including Autonomy, AI and Mission Management Systems, integrators, through-life support providers, and other relevant suppliers.” Those who come forward may be invited to collaborative workshops, one to one meetings, industry days and written requests for information, and small and medium-sized enterprises are flagged as particularly suitable. “The Royal Navy is initially considering platforms approximately 2 metres in diameter and 12 metres in length, however organisations offering platforms of other dimensions are also encouraged to register,” the notice says, adding that it “should not be considered as a commitment from the Royal Navy to progress with any future procurement activities.” XV Excalibur, the uncrewed submarine Britain already operates, is twelve metres long, two metres across and displaces nineteen tonnes. It was unveiled at Devonport in May last year, as this publication reported at the time, having been built by MSubs of Plymouth under the three-year Project Cetus, for which the Ministry of Defence awarded a £15.4 million contract in December 2022. It joined the Fleet Experimentation Squadron as a demonstrator with no operational role. The Royal Navy controlled Excalibur in home waters from an operating centre in Australia during Talisman Sabre in July 2025, the first British and Australian demonstration of XLUUV interoperability under AUKUS Pillar II. It carried out the first underwater operation of a quantum optical atomic clock that November and transferred to Royal Navy ownership in December. In June the Submarine Delivery Agency awarded MSubs a further £6.7 million for trials and evaluation running to May 2028, work intended to move the programme towards functional payloads. On 13 September, Excalibur fired an American Mark 48 exercise torpedo at the British Underwater Test and Evaluation Centre in Scotland. Britain and the United States described it as the first time either country had launched a heavyweight torpedo from an uncrewed vessel, carried out under Project Broadsword and Trial Iron, both part of AUKUS Pillar II. The Type 93 designation first appeared in February last year, in Project CABOT documents setting out a persistent wide area anti-submarine search capability built around the Type 92 Sloop, an uncrewed surface vessel, and the Type 93 Chariot, described then as a drone submarine. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, confirmed in July that the Defence Investment Plan had announced Type 92 uncrewed underwater sensing platforms and Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels as part of the Atlantic Bastion programme, adding that the number of platforms to be procured and their construction schedules had not yet been determined. He has also told Parliament that the Hybrid Navy will take at least £1.5 billion over four years, and that by 2030 the aim is to have the first large autonomous vessels in service, among them a prototype uncrewed missile platform and extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels carrying payloads developed through AUKUS. The notice states that the programme “directly aligns with the Strategic Defence Review (SDR), Defence Investment Plan (DIP) and AUKUS Pillar II priorities, supporting the transition to a Hybrid Navy through the integration of autonomous and uncrewed maritime capabilities.” The post Britain calls in industry for fleet of drone submarines first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Lithuanian prime minister says more Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers could help safeguard European elections from interference
body: Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius suggested more strikes on Russian data centers when asked at the Warsaw Security Forum how European countries could protect their elections from interference, LRT reported. I think we should ask Mr. Zelensky to strike more data centers in Russia, and that might help. During his remarks, Sinkevičius also urged European countries to invest more in defense and strengthen security cooperation. He said Europe needs to learn from Ukraine’s experience, arguing that European safety will benefit from increased information sharing, joint procurement, joint production, and joint exercises with Kyiv. Sinkevičius said the top priorities for both Lithuania and NATO as a whole were air defense, protection against drones, and countering hybrid threats. Over four days, Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers in Russia. The company’s services are still down. Replacing the damaged equipment will take about six months and will be expensive because of sanctions and a global shortage of computing capacity. title: How many children have been killed in Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine? A new Meduza investigation finds at least 940.
body: The war Russia launched has killed hundreds of thousands of people and harmed millions. Exactly how many are children is unknown. The two sides keep their own counts, but their methods differ, making comparisons difficult. Official U.N. figures also appear incomplete. Meduza examined all available information, checked it against as many public sources as possible, and established a minimum number of children who have died during the war. The answer is in the headline. Caution: This article contains accounts of children’s deaths. What Meduza counted We counted everyone killed who was under 18. This matches the definition the U.N. uses to count casualties in international conflicts. Ukrainian and Russian law use the same age limit. Our analysis drew on data from international organizations and Ukrainian and Russian authorities, as well as: Social media posts by people close to the child Posts by schools and hospitals Official statements from local authorities Law enforcement reports News articles and other public sources Almost every death we counted was corroborated by two or more sources. In some cases involving occupied areas or hard-to-reach places near the front, a statement from local authorities was the only source. We recorded those deaths when the statement specified where and on what date the child died. We excluded reports lacking these details from our database. We classified deaths by where the child died rather than by citizenship, because Russia forced people in occupied areas to obtain Russian documents. For Ukraine, we therefore counted children who died within the country’s 1991 borders — including annexed Crimea and Sevastopol, as well as occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions. For Russia, we counted only deaths within its internationally recognized territory, excluding Ukrainian regions. This distinction follows the U.N. General Assembly’s resolution on Crimea and the resolution adopted after the annexation of four Ukrainian regions . It also prevents some deaths from being counted twice. We do not give the children’s surnames in this article, but we used them in our analysis to ensure an accurate count. In all, we found the full names or first names of 409 children: 372 in Ukraine and 37 in Russia. We most often found their names in posts or statements from relatives, schools, hospitals, rescue services, prosecutors’ offices, courts, and local authorities, as well as news reports and memorial projects. International organizations such as the U.N. do not publish this information. The war Russia launched has killed more than 940 children As of early September 2026, at least 940 children had died because of the war : 873 in Ukraine 67 in Russia For Ukraine, our count began with the figure published by the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission: By August 31, 2026, the U.N. had confirmed the deaths of 835 children. Meduza’s count runs through October 9 and supplements the U.N. data with news reports and official statements about individual deaths. These account for another 38 deaths. Using the same method, we confirmed 67 children’s deaths in Russia. These figures differ from the countries’ own estimates. As of October 9, 2026, the Ukrainian government’s Children of War (Dity Viiny ) website reported 755 children killed . Russia’s Foreign Ministry reported 264 as of June 30, 2026, in its latest statement on the subject . There is a simple explanation for the gap. Ukraine’s figures include confirmed deaths across the country, including occupied parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, but coverage of those areas is incomplete: Investigators often cannot obtain documents or reach the places where children died. Russia’s figures include victims in Crimea, Sevastopol, and other occupied areas as well as within Russia. Our count is also a minimum estimate. The actual toll is almost certainly higher: The U.N. itself cautions that it cannot quickly verify every report of a child’s death, particularly in places where fighting has continued for a long time. The number of child casualties began rising faster in 2026. In Ukraine this July, the number of children killed or injured reached its highest level since the first months of Russia’s full-scale invasion. In Russia, 32 children died between January and early October — more than in any previous full year of the war. Ukraine: 873 killed At least 873 children’s deaths have been confirmed within Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders. Ukrainian authorities’ data show that more than half of the children — 450 — died between February and December 2022. Information about the first months of the invasion remains incomplete. In a report on children affected by war, the U.N. said at least 120 children died in Mariupol between February and April 2022. The actual number could be much higher: Independent researchers have been unable to enter the Russian-occupied city. The exact number of people killed in the March 16, 2022, strike on the Mariupol Drama Theater remains unknown. Hundreds of civilians, including children, were sheltering inside. The word “CHILDREN” was written in enormous letters on the ground in front of and behind the building. The Associated Press later estimated the death toll at around 600. That figure circulated widely but remained unconfirmed. Amnesty International confirmed at least 12 deaths. The human rights organization concluded that more than 12 people had died, but probably far fewer than 600. How many of those killed in the theater were children is unknown. One of the few victims identified by name was 2-year-old Karolina . During the attack, she was on the theater’s second floor with her mother and older sister. Karolina and her parents died; her sister and grandparents survived. Karolina’s last words were: “Grandma, I’m with you.” Children killed in other regions ranged in age from newborns to 17-year-olds. One of the youngest was 2-month-old Uliana . She died in Kryvyi Rih with her mother and two brothers, 2-year-old Demyd and 10-year-old Kyrylo, after a Russian ballistic missile hit their home. On April 4, 2025, a missile exploded directly above a residential neighborhood in Kryvyi Rih, near a playground. Nine children, ages 3 to 17, were killed in that single attack; most were playing in the park when the missile struck. U.N. staff visited the site and saw marks left by hundreds of fragments on swings, slides, trees, and houses. “It’s an unimaginable horror,” said U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk. The mission said the attack killed more children than any other since the war began. On November 19 of that year, Russia attacked Ternopil with drones and cruise missiles. The missiles hit apartment buildings, killing at least 38 people , including eight children, and injuring another 99. In one building, 5-year-old Kamila and 18-month-old Nazar died with their mother. Their father was in another room during the strike and survived; he spent the next three days waiting by the ruins while rescuers searched for his family. In another building, the same strike killed 17-year-olds Artem and Ruslan , who had been friends since kindergarten. After the first explosion, their families left the building and ran toward a shelter. The teenagers did not reach it in time and were killed by the next explosion. Russia: 67 killed Meduza confirmed 67 children’s deaths within Russia’s internationally recognized territory: Two in 2022 Six in 2023 19 in 2024 Eight in 2025 32 from January through September 2026 The children died in 13 regions . Almost half — 30 — died in the Belgorod region , near the front. Another 14 died in the Krasnodar region, seven in the Kursk region, five in the Bryansk region, and three in the Moscow region. These five regions account for 59 of the 67 deaths. During the night of June 30, 2026, a Ukrainian drone hit his family’s house in the Moscow region. The second-floor bedroom, where the boy was with his mother, bore the brunt of the impact. Rescuers searched for Yelisey under the rubble for a long time. He suffered severe burns and died on the way to the hospital . His 6-year-old brother, Matvey, was pulled out almost unharmed, but after the ordeal he did not speak for more than a day. Their parents were admitted to intensive care. Yelisey’s mother had one leg amputated, then the other after she was transferred to another hospital; his father underwent several complex operations . Two-year-old Grisha died on June 12, 2025, in Borisovka in the Belgorod region. His grandmother was pushing him in a stroller around the building that day when a Ukrainian drone hit the apartment building. The child was taken to the hospital with a head injury. Doctors tried for several hours to save him. In Novorossiysk, a Ukrainian drone fell onto a house . An 8-year-old boy died at the scene, while his mother and 6-year-old brother suffered severe injuries and burns. The child was buried in his school uniform : He was due to start second grade in a few weeks. His father is listed as missing in action. Five-year-old Tolya suffered severe burns in a Ukrainian drone attack on a public beach in Kursk. Citing witnesses , Kursk Governor Alexander Khinshtein said the boy had tried to shield his mother with his body. The child died the next day while being transported to a Moscow hospital. We found five other deaths that are unquestionably connected to the war but do not meet the international criteria for counting war casualties. We nevertheless believe they must be mentioned. Three of these five deaths were murders committed by men who had returned from the war. Former Wagner Group fighter Vladimir Vlasov struck his stepdaughter several times shortly after he was demobilized. The girl died at the scene. Artem Buchin, who had previously been convicted of rape and murder and was pardoned so he could be sent to the front, raped his former wife after returning, then killed her and her 7-year-old daughter . Vladimir Alexandrov of Nizhny Tagil, who had also returned from the war, raped and strangled his 11-year-old neighbor Anastasia Yakina. Buchin and Alexandrov received life sentences. A court sentenced Vlasov to 14 years in a penal colony . What Russia and Ukraine say about the children killed Russian officials and state media regularly call those killed in Russia and occupied areas “victims of the Kyiv regime.” This narrative emerged long before the full-scale invasion. In May 2015, a memorial opened in occupied Donetsk with the inscription “ Alley of Angels . In memory of the children of Donbas who were killed.” A granite slab bore 66 names. Russia’s Investigative Committee later described the children as “girls and boys aged 1 to 18” and said they had died in Ukrainian shelling. On the morning of February 24, 2022, when Putin announced the full-scale invasion , he said he was starting the war to protect people “who have been subjected to abuse and genocide by the Kyiv regime for eight years.” Three weeks later, he explicitly linked this argument to children’s deaths: Western countries, he said , “looked away for the past eight years while mothers in Donbas buried their children.” Children’s deaths during the war in Donbas are not a propaganda fabrication. But the Alley of Angels memorial does not name every child killed during that period of the Russian-Ukrainian war: It includes only those whom authorities in the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic declared victims of Ukrainian shelling. Some children, however, died when mines or other munitions of unknown origin exploded. And children killed by shelling from separatists and Russian forces are simply absent from the list. In all, the U.N. confirmed the deaths of 152 children between April 2014 and the end of 2021. Another 80 children died aboard MH17, which Russia shot down; the organization counts them separately. Since the full-scale invasion began, at least 940 children have died in Ukraine and Russia in a much shorter period — six times as many. Some of those wounded were minors: The initial list of the wounded included 16 teenagers ages 15 to 17. All the teenagers who died were legal adults: the youngest had turned 18 four days before the strike. Russian human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova, and propagandists who followed her lead, pointedly described those injured or killed as children when discussing the attack. Kremlin propaganda also claims that AI developed by the American company Palantir deliberately selected the college as a target. Vladimir Solovyov declared Palantir and its head, Alex Karp, directly responsible for the strike. He also blamed them for the deaths of children in Gaza and Iran, calling what was happening “the bloody harvests of Satanists,” and demanded “revenge for the children.” Military commentator Alexander Artamonov said that strikes on children supposedly constitute “a special method of warfare.” Ukraine does cooperate with Palantir. Shortly before the attack, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported using AI to analyze combat data, identify targets, and plan operations. It has also been proven that Palantir’s technology was used in the strike on a school in Iran. But there is no independent confirmation that Palantir was involved in selecting the target in Starobilsk, let alone that it deliberately chose a student dormitory. A few days later, rhetoric about those killed in Starobilsk turned into a direct call for revenge — specifically, according to the propagandists, revenge against children. Military commentator Yuri Baranchik said on the radio station of Komsomolskaya Pravda, the pro-Kremlin Russian tabloid, that in response “the children of Zelensky and Yermak should die.” Host Ivan Pankin pushed back, arguing that children should not be held accountable for their parents’ actions. Baranchik insisted that their deaths would strike a painful blow against Ukraine’s leadership. Russian media have also justified, and even welcomed, strikes on Ukrainian cities that killed children. List of the dead Behind every number is a real child’s life. The list below includes 518 of the dead children. We know the names of 409 of them. In another 93 cases, only the age is known, sometimes approximately. For 16 children, Meduza was able to establish only the place of death. We included in this list only victims about whom we were able to learn at least something. The remaining 422 children in the overall count come from the U.N.’s list — we were unable to find enough information to describe each of them individually. The actual number of children killed is likely even higher. It is worth explaining why Meduza includes U.N. statistics but not Russia’s Foreign Ministry figures. Neither the U.N. nor Russia’s Foreign Ministry publishes a complete list naming the children killed. The difference is in how they verify information and how thoroughly they explain the basis for their overall death toll. The U.N. monitoring mission describes its methodology in detail . Staff compare accounts from witnesses and relatives, medical and court documents, investigation records, photographs, videos, and official statements. Where possible, they visit the site. For a death to be included in the statistics, the combined evidence must provide “reasonable grounds to believe” that the event happened as described in the accounts and documents. This does not guarantee an error-free count, but it is a defined, publicly stated verification standard. The U.N. mission operates under a mandate from the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, rather than the Russian or Ukrainian government, and documents violations by both sides . Its count extends beyond territory controlled by Kyiv: For example, of the 669 children’s deaths confirmed for 2022–2024 in a thematic report , 148 occurred in Russian-occupied areas. Russia’s Foreign Ministry is an agency of the state that launched the war. Its reports focus exclusively on victims of actions the Kremlin blames on Ukraine. This does not in itself make the reports of deaths false — the report’s compilers said they gather data from Russia’s Emergencies Ministry, Health Ministry, ambulance services, and regional authorities. But the U.N. explains how it verifies each death before including it in the count. The Foreign Ministry does not disclose how it checks reports or ensures that the same child has not been counted twice. We therefore cannot verify its overall figure. 1. title: EU States Unanimously Agree to Open 2 New Accession Clusters for Ukraine
body:
All 27 EU member states unanimously agreed on Monday, Oct. 12, to open Cluster 2 – the internal market – and Cluster 3 – competitiveness and inclusive growth – with Ukraine and Moldova, only hours after Kyiv passed a minority education law in response to Hungary’s demands.
The clusters are among six thematic clustersin total that organize the legal and institutional reforms that must be adopted and implemented to join the EU.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs and Defense, Thomas Byrne, announced the decision on X , following months of Hungary vetoing steps related to Ukraine’s EU accession.
“I can confirm that all EU member states have agreed to: open clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine and Moldova, close 3 chapters for Montenegro (17, 18, 19), and close chapter 20 for Albania,” Byrne wrote, calling Oct. 13 another “Super Tuesday” for the thre candidate countries.
The breakthrough finally came through after Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, passed amendments expanding education rights for national minorities and, by doing so, introduced a special status for general secondary schools serving national minorities.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar welcomed the move in a statement on Facebook, saying that the amendments would make it fundamentally easier for Hungarian children in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region to use their native language.
The law effectively creates a special status for schools where most students are taught in a minority language that is also an official EU language.
Parliamentary estimates currently suggest that around 149 schools (approximately 1.2% of Ukraine’s secondary schools) could qualify. The provision, however, will not apply to the Russian language.
Hungary had blocked Clusters 2 and 3 four times, with its fourth refusal on Sept. 8, when Budapest declined to say which legislative steps it expected from Kyiv.
“We are practically negotiating with our Hungarian partners with the EU every day to avoid artificial delays in the negotiation process,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told European Pravda .
The move followed a previous refusal on Sept. 1, when Hungary offered to lifts its veto only if Kyiv demonstrated progress in protecting the rights of the country’s Hungarian minority in the Transcarpathia region.
In June, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Magyar sealed what the Hungarian PM described as a “historic agreement,” formally securing the political, educational, cultural and linguistic rights of ethnic Hungarian communities in Transcarpathia.
Budapest later tied the opening of further clusters to Ukraine turning those commitments into law.
Meanwhile, the dispute has also impeded Moldova’s progress, as the two countries’ EU accession processes remain closely linked.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the EU’s Council, opposed separating the two countries’ accession tracks with other EU members.
Accession negotiations cover 33 chapters grouped into six clusters. On June 15, Ukraine and Moldova opened Cluster 1 – Fundamentals , and Cluster 6 – External Relations on July 14.
Once clusters 2 and 3 are formally opened on Tuesday, two clusters will remain: Cluster 4 – on the green agenda and sustainable connectivity, and Cluster 5 – on resources, agriculture and cohesion.
The European Commission previously proposed limiting Ukraine’s access to EU farm subsidies and markets for sensitive products even after accession , which Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi rejected on Tuesday, Oct. 5. by saying that Kyiv cannot accept permanent restrictions.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Italy eyes MBDA armaments for new Italo-Turkish drone
body: ROME — Italy is holding tests with MBDA to mount the European firm’s armaments on the new Astore Levante drone being built by Turkey’s Baykar and Italy’s Leonardo , the head of the Italian air force has said. The Italian air force is due to acquire six of the drones, which are derived from Baykar’s TB-3 and are being assembled in Italy by LBA Systems, a joint venture between Baykar and Leonardo. The Astore Levante is due to carry Leonardo sensors, but at its unveiling at the Farnborough air show in July it was presented alongside Turkish armaments, including Roketsan’s MAM family of guided bombs and Baykar’s KEMANKES-1 mini cruise missile. Speaking in Rome on Monday, Italian air force chief Gen. Antonio Conserva said he was not ruling out other suppliers of armaments. “At the moment we have not made choices, the natural armament is Turkish but we also have activities with MBDA and small Italian industrial groups,” he said. Conserva confirmed the new drone was set to be certified by the end of 2026 or in early 2027. European certification is deemed a prerequisite for selling the drone in Europe. Mounting European arms will also boost sales efforts in Europe. The Italian air force will initially order three systems, each containing two drones, but Conserva said, “We will see if we go on to expand the capability.” The Astore Levant will replace the Predator MQ1 flown by the air force, Conserva added. As well as being flown on ISR missions and providing armed support for troops, the drones will also be used for training drone pilots, he said. Before the launch in July of the Astore Levante, the Italian navy said in April it was eyeing the TB-3 as a carrier-borne drone to fly off its Cavour carrier, which also hosts Italy’s F-35Bs. The TB-3 is already in service on board the Turkish amphibious assault ship TCG Anadolu. Another TB-3 customer, Indonesia, is expected to base the drone on the Garibaldi, a carrier it has purchased from Italy. Conserva spoke to reporters on Monday at a conference at the HQ of the Italian air force in Rome which gathered air force and industry officials to discuss the future of warfare. Asked by Defense News about the prospect of Germany possibly joining the GCAP sixth generation fighter program set up by Italy, Japan and the UK, Conserva said he was in favor. “We are talking about a strategic partner,” he said. “We would need to find a political and industrial deal. Germany is a great country. We have already collaborated with them on the Tornado which will retire next year, and the Eurofighter which is the backbone of our national defense and deterrence. Whatever emerges I will view favorably,” he added.

title: Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder Full breaks into the AI top tier
body:
Meta released its frontier model Muse Wonder in two variants, and both land among the best AI models available.
Muse Wonder Full scores 56 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, while Muse Wonder hits 52. Its predecessor, Muse Spark 1.3 , sat at 48 points, which makes this a significant jump from what was a mid-tier model.
The biggest gains show up in agentic evaluations, tests that measure how well an AI model can handle complex tasks on its own. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, performance jumped from 33 to 57 percent. Muse Wonder Full places in the top three on six out of ten benchmarks overall, a strong result for Meta, which seems to have recovered after a weaker stretch with its open Llama models. Ad
Meta highlights two new features. "Active Memory" lets the model remember key information across conversations and recall it when needed. "Active Focus" is the model's ability to stick with difficult tasks, try alternative approaches, and ask follow-up questions when something isn't clear. Both are central to Meta's pitch for a personal AI agent that can access calendars, messages, and documents. Ad
Both models support a one-million-token context window and accept text, images, video, and audio as input. Muse Wonder is available through Meta's API and Muse Code , while Muse Wonder Full is currently limited to Muse Code users. Muse Wonder will soon power the Muse app as well, starting with paying subscribers. Over time, Meta plans to build specialized models from it for all users.
Both models show big improvements in coding. Muse Wonder Full hits 68 points on the Coding Agents Index, tying Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5. Muse Wonder scores 63, up from 54 for its predecessor. Ad
Factual knowledge remains a weak spot. On the AA-Omniscience knowledge test, Muse Wonder Full manages only 30 points, and Muse Wonder gets 25. That's well behind Claude Opus 5.5 (46), GPT-6 Astra (43), and Gemini 4 Argon (42), which suggests the Wonder series is built on a smaller base model than its competitors. Low hallucination rates help offset this gap. Muse Wonder Full cuts its hallucination rate from 33 to 23 percent compared to its predecessor, the second-lowest among all models scoring at least 45 index points. Only Gemini 4 Argon (15 percent) hallucinates less often.
Meta addresses a common criticism in its blog post , that Muse models are tuned for benchmarks but fall short in real-world use. The company says Muse Wonder Full does better than expected on unfamiliar tasks that weren't part of training optimization, and credits this to a stronger base model. Ad
On the Vals AI Index , Muse Wonder Full (Max) debuts at fifth place and beats all OpenAI models, according to Vals AI. Only current Anthropic models score higher. Muse Wonder lands at tenth. Ad
The biggest improvements come from coding and math. On ProofBench, a private benchmark for mathematical proofs, Muse Wonder Full solves 94 out of 100 problems, up from 58 for its predecessor. That puts it just five to six points behind the top models (99 to 100). On Terminal-Bench 4, Muse Wonder Full doubled its score while using 30 percent fewer output tokens. Performance on finance and legal tasks stayed at predecessor levels, dropping up to two points.
According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Wonder runs $4.52 per task on the Intelligence Index, nearly three times more than Muse Spark 1.3 ($1.60). Token pricing has climbed too, with $4 per million input tokens and $20 for output, up from $1.25 and $4.25 for the predecessor. Muse Wonder also uses 28 percent more input tokens per task, and those account for 76 percent of total costs.
That puts Muse Wonder below Claude Fable 5.1 ($7.63) and Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98) in pricing, but above GPT-6 Astra ($3.26), Gemini 4 Argon ($1.99), and GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72). No token pricing is available yet for Muse Wonder Full. Both models do use about 10 percent fewer output tokens than their predecessor.
Meta says it trained the models at its in-house Prometheus data center at gigawatt scale. More details are in the model card .

title: Vanuatu Mobile Force lance corporal brings more than carpentry skills to Cook Islands exercise
body:
Unfortunately you are viewing this website on an outdated browser which does not support the necessary features for us to provide an adequate experience. Please switch to a modern browser such as latest version of Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari or Microsoft Edge.
Vanuatu Mobile Force (VMF) carpenter Lance Corporal Nick Kaltoua has been working alongside New Zealand Army engineers in the remote northern Cook Islands, where his knowledge of the Tahitian language has proved just as valuable as his carpentry skills.
He is part of a larger New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) team improving infrastructure and health services across the island of Penrhyn, nearly 1400kms north of Rarotonga, during Exercise Tropic Twilight.
Running annually since 1999, the NZDF Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief exercise in the South-West Pacific, is supported by the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
From Ifira Village in Vanuatu, Lance Corporal Kaltoua has been getting stuck into the tasks including building a new life-skills classroom at Omoka School , one of only two schools on the island, and constructing bases for a number of water tanks.
In such an isolated location, where supplies may be a six-month barge trip away, if the team find something that isn’t up to standard where they can, they fix it. Materials cannot simply be replaced at short notice, so planning for a worst-case scenario was needed, and additional materials are added as a contingency.
Lance Corporal Kaltou a's performance over the first half of the year helped earn his selection for Tropic Twilight.
“I was so happy. I was never expecting this.”
Earlier this year, Lance Corporal Kaltoua worked alongside NZDF tradespeople in Vanuatu, which he said helped him feel at ease when he found out he would be joining familiar faces on this exercise.
Lance Corporal Nick Kaltoua, Vanuatu Mobile Force (VMF) Engineering Squadron, deployed as part of the NZDF team working on construction tasks on Penrhyn
A highlight of Penrhyn had been getting to know the local community after work – heading out fishing, looking for crayfish on the reef at night, and spending time with local families.
The work the contingent has done throughout this year’s exercise will have lasting impacts across the wider Penrhyn population.
More than 50 personnel were deployed, including NZ Army engineers, electricians, medical and dental personnel, and Royal New Zealand Navy hydrography personnel.
They worked on new school facilities as well as maintenance, constructed new water tank and solar still installations to improve water and power supply, provided medical and dental services, and hydrographic surveying for better information about the lagoon and navigational approaches.
Working together regularly helps strengthen relationships between Pacific partners, and Lance Corporal Kaltoua has enjoyed spending the past few weeks working alongside NZDF personnel again.
“Being around them, it’s like we’re just the same.”
Detachment Commander , Major Cam Gurney, said Lance Corporal Kaltoua had been an outstanding member of the contingent, integrating seamlessly into the team.
“His experience and perspective brought significant value to our work in Penrhyn, particularly in the remote environment where adaptability and practical problem-solving were essential.
"His ability to speak Tahitian played an important role in strengthening relationships across the exercise and helped improve collaboration and foster stronger connections between all participants.
“The inclusion of personnel such as Lance Corporal Kaltoua highlights the value of working alongside our Pacific partners.
“These opportunities build trust, improve interoperability, and create enduring professional relationships that strengthen our collective ability to respond to future challenges across the Pacific.”

title: From Uzbekistan to EU: Where Armenian goods are exported after Russia imposes restrictions
body: Changes in the geography of Armenian exports On 10 October, a preferential trade regime for Armenian goods exported to the European Union came into force. Under the EU decision to apply autonomous trade measures, the bloc will liberalise around 80% of imports from Armenia by removing import duties. The measures will cover a wide range of goods, including agricultural products. The European Union has decided to support Armenia in response to restrictions that Russia has imposed on Armenian goods. Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian agencies responsible for enforcing the restrictions cited alleged failures to meet quality standards. However, it later became clear that Armenia’s closer integration with Europe had prompted the measures. Exports of Armenian-origin goods to EU countries have grown for several months. In effect, this trend began before the preferential trade regime came into force. From January to June 2026, Armenia exported more than $516m worth of goods to the EU. This marked an increase of more than 80% compared with the same period last year. Exports to EU countries are now expected to grow further. At the same time, Armenia is seeking other markets. The local outlet Factor TV analysed the results of these efforts. Drawing on data from the Ministry of Economy and the Food Safety Inspection Body, it compiled a list of countries that received significant volumes of Armenian goods. The findings show that products traditionally exported to Russia now go to Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Georgia , Ukraine and Iraq. Preferential regime for Armenian exports to EU in response to Russian restrictions Armenia launches support programme for exporters in response to Russian restrictions Russia’s pressure on Armenia ahead of elections: economy as tool of influence More than 94% of exports went to three countries According to data from the Food Safety Inspection Body, Uzbekistan, Georgia and Ukraine accounted for more than 94% of Armenia’s fruit exports in June 2026: 48% of fruit exports went to Uzbekistan, around 34% went to Georgia, approximately 12% went to Ukraine. Georgia took the lead in July, accounting for around 35.3% of exports. Uzbekistan followed with 21%, Kazakhstan with 13%, Ukraine with 10.5% and Iraq with around 8.2%. By comparison, in June 2025, Russia alone accounted for 86.7% of Armenian fruit exports. The figure rose to 87.2% in July. How Armenia is reacting to export restrictions on Russia: farmers' views and official statistics Russia’s ban on Armenian goods has accelerated efforts to diversify foreign markets. Here’s what is happening. State budget compensation for exporters In response to the restrictions Russia imposed, the Armenian government launched support programmes for local exporters. These include subsidies and cash compensation, including payments to cover export duties in other markets. In June and July, the government paid around 3.96bn drams ($10.3m) in compensation to exporters of strawberries, apricots, sweet cherries, plums, nectarines and peaches. Over these two months, the state covered costs associated with around 90% of the export volume: “The total volume of strawberry, apricot, sweet cherry, plum, nectarine and peach exports reached around 16,752 tonnes. The state budget provided compensation for 15,083 tonnes.” Support programmes also continued in August. The government allocated around 4.52bn drams ($11.8m) that month to support exports and purchases of agricultural produce. This sum also covered costs for exporters of vegetables and flowers. How the compensation was distributed The figures for June and July show that apricots and sweet cherries accounted for 81% of the 3.9bn drams ($10.3m) allocated to fruit exports: The government allocated around 1.86bn drams ($4.8m) for apricots. Sweet cherries received around 1.33bn drams ($3.5m). The government also paid compensation for strawberry, peach, nectarine and plum exports, but the amounts were smaller. Exporters do not receive compensation automatically for every kilogram of produce they ship abroad. They must apply to the Ministry of Economy and submit customs or transit declarations, along with invoices confirming the exports. The ministry reviews each application and pays the compensation if it finds no discrepancies in the documents. Under the government’s decision, compensation rates per kilogram stood at 770 drams ($2) for strawberries, 200 drams ($0.5) for apricots, 250 drams ($0.6) for nectarines and 400 drams ($1) for sweet cherries. For some fruits, the compensation came close to the average market price. In June, for example, strawberries sold for an average of 933 drams ($2.4) per kilogram. title: Speeding up the Unreal editor by… not using unnecessarily secure hash methods
body:
One good trick when trying to look for ways to optimize software is to stay away from areas that are very likely already quite well optimized, and instead focus on areas that might have been overlooked, either because they are too obscure or don’t show up during regular profiling sessions. This tactic worked well in the past, as shown with my optimization of tooltip creation , or the loading of editor localization files .
So when profiling the editor launch (again), this is why I mostly skip over any functions that contain words like “Shader Compilation” or “Shader Source” when I stumble over them in my profiler. The compilation of shaders is a famously long and elaborate process, and I’m pretty sure that very smart people at Epic already spent a lot of time optimizing those areas. That’s the reason why I would, for example, skip the function “Compile Global Shader Map,” even though its runtime would be typically multiple seconds:
This was, at least, true until one day I skipped over it using an unusually high zoom level and saw one of the functions that was called by it:
I am certainly not an expert for hash algorithms, but SHA1 is one of the (very few) hash algorithms that even I know. And seeing this hash algorithm being used to hash shaders seemed somehow wrong to me. That’s because SHA1 is was a cryptographically safe hashing algorithm, originally developed by the NSA (yes, that one). And even though it has been cryptographically broken years ago and actually shouldn’t be used for sensitive information anymore, this origin means that it is – to put it politely – not particularly fast. What does not fast mean in this context? Well see for yourself in this comparison test of a bunch of commonly used hash algorithms that Aras Pranckevičius did a few years ago (actually, it was 10 years ago – I’m getting old). SHA1 was not even included as an actual competitor, but as the start of the article notes just “to illustrate the performance differences.” Ouch. That’s especially annoying since the data being hashed is the shader source code, including all comments and copyright notice:
This means both that we have to hash a lot of data (source files can be quite big) and that there is no reason to hash it using a cryptographically secure hash, since it is no sensitive data.
Therefore, not using a cryptographically safe but fast hash algorithm should be an easy win, right? And the linked article already presented a good alternative, for which I even found an existing implementation in Unreal’s code base: xxHash.
Note before somebody asks: xxHash is not necessarily the fastest hash. Other, potentially even faster hashes do exist, but for now, using a faster hash that is already a used and tested part of the engine we are working on is a much more straightforward option. Changing the used hash wasn’t too complicated, even though I had to change more places in the code than expected, since all places where the produced hash was stored or passed also had to be updated. A nice side effect of this change was that the stored hashes were a bit smaller than before (8 instead of 20 bytes). But, of course, the effect that I made the change for wasn’t about memory, but CPU time. For testing purposes, I opened one of Unreal’s own sample projects, Electric Dreams , in the editor 5 times, both with and without the change, for a total of 10 runs. Profiling was done with Superluminal .
To put the following numbers into perspective, let me note that I will mostly talk about the overall CPU time, summed up over all threads, not just the time on the game thread. This is not done to artificially inflate the numbers, but to make the numbers more consistent and easier to compare. The actual effect on the editor start time is (very roughly) the measured time divided by the number of cores.
In the vanilla version of the engine, a whopping 12.90 seconds were spent in FSHA1::Update. In the modified version using xxHash, this time shrunk to just 1.59 seconds spent in FXxHash64Builder::Update. That’s eight times faster! Mission accomplished.
Normally, this article would now end with a link to a pull request so that anybody interested in the change could integrate it into their own version of the engine while we wait and hope that somebody at Epic would see the pull request and merge it into the main branch. Well, this time I have even better news: The change already got accepted! (not merged however, this seems still to take a few days more) I submitted the pull request just a few days before writing this article you can check it out here . (If you can’t access the link, make sure that your Unreal account is linked to your GitHub account and you are logged in. You can find more information in the official documentation ). Those few days were already enough for somebody at Epic to not only review my change but also polish it up. So let’s take a look some of the changes that were done to my proposed change: One very smart feat that I hadn’t thought of was to wrap the xxHash into another struct, FShaderHash. This doesn’t change the behavior right now but will make it easier to change the hash algorithm again in the future if an even faster one is needed without changing the code in many different places. Fixed a compile error for non-editor builds: That was an oversight on my sight. I had only tested my change in an editor build, mainly because my original profiling was also done in editor. I might need to add non-editor builds to my growing list of checks to do before a pull request in the future. And that was it. If you enjoyed this article and want to read more about game optimization in the future, consider following me on BlueSky , Mastodon or Linkedin where I post all my articles. Or subscribe directly to my blog right below the article.

title: US Army creates robotics technician job to focus on drone warfare
body: The U.S. Army kickstarted a military occupational specialty focusing on robotics and unmanned systems with an induction ceremony this month at the U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School. During the ceremony, 10 warrant officers were formally introduced as 390A robotics technicians. They will now serve as subject-matter experts on all aspects of using robotic and autonomous systems, including programming, building and repairing them, plus integrating them into combat. The 390A inauguration is the result of a lengthy process that has been in the works since 2024, when U.S. Army Special Operations Command announced its aim to train experts in using autonomous systems. The Army deemed it necessary to introduce robotics as a separate specialization to avoid overburdening special warfare operators with having to master an additional, highly complex skill set, in addition to their existing knowledge. “What we’ve determined is it cannot be an additional task or an additional hat for someone on the ODA,” Chief Warrant Officer 5 Jerry Brown, command chief warrant officer for 1st Special Forces Command (Airborne), said in a release , adding that the new specialists will be able to leverage their specific field of knowledge within robotics to help the force as a whole. The new 390A technicians will be assigned to tactical formations at the brigade and group level. As experts in autonomous warfare, they will advise commanders on how best to deploy autonomous systems during operations. They will also be required to think quickly in the field to instantly propose solutions to any problems that may arise with robotics in the field, and to use their expertise to come up with innovative ways of using drones to reach objectives. To prepare them for this role, 390A candidates are required to complete a 19-week course, where they must build drones from scratch that do not require GPS or radio frequencies to navigate. The Army stated in a release that robotic systems assembled during the course will rely primarily on artificial intelligence and machine learning to navigate to targets. Fiber optic cables also provide a way for drones to reach targets while being invulnerable to external signal interference, such as jamming. Known as “tethered drones,” cable-linked unmanned aircraft systems can use artificial intelligence for targeting and navigation while having a direct physical connection to their operator. At the time of publication, the Army had not responded to questions about whether 390A candidates would be learning to build and field tethered drones. “The Army is implementing changes in force structures, adding a multi-domain task force equipped with autonomous long-range fires,” Gen. Christopher LaNeve, Vice Chief of Staff of the Army, said in a statement. “These technical experts will help command teams understand integration across the force. We are scaling this across the Army.”

title: Japan Signs Contract for Ukraine's SkyFall Interceptor Drones
body:
Japan’s Ministry of Defense has signed a contract to buy interceptor drones from Ukrainian manufacturer SkyFall and is working to get them delivered early, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told a press conference in Tokyo on Friday.
The contract gives a Ukrainian drone maker a foothold in the Japanese defense market. SkyFall – a Ukrainian technology and defense company that develops and manufactures unmanned systems – is known for the Vampire strike drone (“Baba Yaga”), the Shrike FPV drones and the P1-SUN interceptors.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The transcript did not specify the contract’s value, the number of drones, the model or the delivery date. Koizumi was responding to a reporter’s question about Japan’s plans to introduce Ukrainian-made drones. Japan’s former Defense Minister Onodera and others visited Ukraine at the end of last month and announced that Tokyo would experimentally introduce the drones.
“The Ministry of Defense has already signed a contract with Ukraine’s Skyfall to acquire interceptor drones, and we are working towards their early delivery,” Koizumi told reporters, according to the ministry’s transcript of the press briefing on Oct. 9.
The minister framed the purchase as part of a broader effort to learn from Ukraine’s battlefield experience. Koizumi said Ukraine has accumulated more experience in “new ways of fighting than anyone else in the world and is improving its sustained combat capability at a rapid pace”.
“From the perspective of fostering the defense industry and the industrial base, there is much we can learn from their rapid feedback cycle, where new drones with improved capabilities are produced every two or three weeks, and they continue to produce them,” Koizumi told reporters.
He added that Japan needs such deterrence and response capabilities and will consider the matter carefully, looking at specific examples.
Meanwhile, Koizumi told reporters separately that Tokyo is not considering transferring weapons, including Patriot missiles that Japan manufactures under license, to Ukraine under the Self-Defense Forces law. He said the ministry has already supplied Self-Defense Forces vehicles and bulletproof vests and has accepted wounded Ukrainian soldiers, and that it will continue to provide any equipment it can.
Olena Hrazhdan is the Business Reporter at Kyiv Post, covering Ukraine’s markets, business, and economic policy. While she reports broadly on economic issues, her core focus is banking, finance, monetary and fiscal policy. Olena previously wrote for leading Ukrainian business media and became a Fellow of the International Monetary Fund’s Journalism Fellowship in 2024.

title: Republic of China Air Force Raises Pilot Retirement Age Amid Acute Shortages for Fighter Fleet
body: The Republic of China Air Force is planning to extend the maximum service age for experienced military pilots to 58 as it seeks to address personnel shortages and prepare for the introduction of 66 new F-16 Block 70 fighters ordered from the United States. The proposed scheme would allow qualified lieutenant colonels and colonels to remain in service beyond their existing career limits, helping the air force retain experienced personnel as it expands its combat fleet. The initiative comes as the Air Force faces persistent operational demands associated with monitoring Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force military activity. The two Chinese air forces are fielded by opposing Chinese governments in Beijing and Taipei, which remain in a state of civil war. Under the new proposal, pilots can volunteer to remain in uniform until the age of 58, compared with existing service limits that generally place lieutenant colonels at approximately 48 and colonels at 52. The Republic of China Ministry of National Defence has also proposed creating 72 additional positions for highly qualified pilots who have served for at least 14 years. These personnel would retain their existing ranks while concentrating on flying duties rather than transitioning into command or administrative roles, allowing the air force to preserve experienced pilots in operational units. The proposal was submitted to the Executive Yuan in Taipei for consideration on September 4, according to the Central News Agency. Defence Minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung said the initiative was intended to prevent the loss of experienced aviators to the civilian aviation sector. Military pilots who reach the end of their service obligations can pursue careers with commercial airlines, where employment opportunities and the potential for longer careers provide a strong incentive to leave the armed forces. The Air Force’s rules generally limit lieutenant colonels to 26 years of service and colonels to 30 years, whereas commercial pilots can continue flying until approximately 65, subject to applicable requirements. The disparity has made retaining senior military aviators a significant personnel challenge. The defence ministry has reported that the air force currently has a personnel fill rate of 87.8 per cent, although recruitment and training remain important sources of new pilots. The ministry stated that recruitment for pilot training reached 96.2 per cent of its target in 2024, 112 per cent in 2025 and 98.6 per cent in 2026. Nevertheless, producing new fighter pilots requires substantial time and resources, while experienced aviators possess accumulated knowledge of aircraft systems, tactics and operational procedures that cannot be quickly replicated through initial training. Retaining senior personnel could therefore help bridge the gap between the introduction of new aircraft and the development of a sufficiently experienced workforce to operate them.

title: Al Ahli overcome Al Wasl in fiery AFC Champions League clash
body: Al Ahli Saudi left Dubai with three points towards their bid for a hat-trick of Asian Champions League titles after a fiery meeting with Al Wasl. Roger Ibanez and Francisco Trincao, two big-money imports to Saudi Arabian football, scored, before Feras Albrikan clinched a 3-1 win in stoppage time. The margin of defeat was harsh on a spirited Wasl side, who deserved more than the lone strike by Pedro Malheiro in first-half stoppage time. Given the gap they were bridging to the high-spending Saudi Pro League side, the home players fully merited the backing they got from their fans on a hostile night in Zabeel. Before kick-off, Ahli’s players stood on the 18-yard line and were serenaded with their club anthem by the travelling supporters. GOAL | Roger Ibañez puts Al Ahli 1–0 ahead against Al Wasl in the 20th minute of their AFC Champions League Elite clash. #AlAhli #AlWasl #ACLElite pic.twitter.com/rIQLOvOu1n — Alkass English (@alkassenglish) October 12, 2026 Around 200 had made the trip from Jeddah, but they were drowned out by the noise of the home faithful. The Ultras Junoon are always loud, but they were particularly rowdy when the Ahli anthem was being sung. The home players responded. Wasl’s start was bright, and they fashioned the first opening, only for Siaka Sidibe to blaze over from the edge of the box. Home optimism was dissipated in the 20th minute, though, when Ibanez headed in the opener for Ahli. The Brazil centre-back, who was called into the Selecao squad by Carlo Ancelotti for the World Cup this summer, is renowned for his leap. Despite common knowledge of his aerial prowess, he was unchallenged at the back post to make it 1-0. The visitors nearly doubled their lead 10 minutes later, but were saved by the post as Eduard Spertsyan’s shot bounced away to safety. GOAL | Pedro Malheiro equalises for Al Wasl against Al Ahli in the 45+3rd minute, making it 1–1 in their AFC Champions League Elite clash. #AlWasl #AlAhli #ACLElite pic.twitter.com/vpwqgX82Os — Alkass English (@alkassenglish) October 12, 2026 Wasl’s defence was being cut open with greater regularity, and they were lucky not to be a long way behind by the break. Their fortune continued when Adryelson, the Wasl defender evaded a red card. After a confrontation in the box, Saleh Abu Al Shamat, the Ahli forward, went down. Replays showed Adryelson had squared up to him, and lightly pushed his forehead towards his opponent. Shamat tumbled to the floor and rolled around as if he was mortally wounded. It was enough of a show to persuade VAR to recommend the referee take a second look at the monitor. Usually, that is ominous for the perceived offender. Justice was served, though, as Abdulrahman Al Jassim, the Qatari official, decided he was right the first time, and stayed with a yellow card. GOAL | Francisco Trincão restores Al Ahli’s lead against Al Wasl in the 58th minute, making it 2–1 in their AFC Champions League Elite clash. #AlAhli #AlWasl #ACLElite pic.twitter.com/rc4l55WrZb — Alkass English (@alkassenglish) October 12, 2026 Adryelson nearly provided the perfect riposte; from the ensuing free-kick for Wasl, he bundled the ball into the net, only for it to be ruled out for offside. The hosts were level by the break, though. In stoppage time at the end of the half, a long range effort from Malheiro, Wasl’s right back, found its way into the net after some limp goalkeeping. Shamat had fully established himself as public enemy No 1. At the start of the second half, he was playing on the wing in front of the hardcore or Wasl’s supporters. They frequently lobbed plastic water bottles in his direction. Rather than fuss, he waved a hand at them, encouraging the fans to bring it on. Just before the hour mark, Trincao ruined the home fans’ fun. The Portuguese forward finished clinically to restore the away side’s lead. Wasl should have levelled shortly after following a rapid counter-attack, but Serginho hit the post with the goal at his mercy. Even when he went off, Shamat caused rancour. After an innocuous incident, he went down clutching his shoulder. The moment Al Ahli’s Saleh Abu Al Shamat picked up an injury against Al Wasl in the AFC Champions League Elite. #AlAhli #AlWasl #ACLElite pic.twitter.com/bXP3RSRJYy — Alkass English (@alkassenglish) October 12, 2026 He looked in genuine pain, and had to be stretchered off on the back of the medical golf buggy. It turned out that his injury was not so severe that he could wave with both arms as he was taken past the Ahli supporters. That added to the fury of the home fans, and even the players were so incensed they threw bottles in his direction as the buggy went past the home dugout. Ahli’s bench sprung to his defence, and the two sets of replacements and substituted players had to be separated. Wasl had their chances as they chased the game, but their hopes were finally dashed when Albrikan scored Ahli’s third in stoppage time.

title: Tiguerones Leader ‘Willy’ Is Living Free in Spain
body: Tiguerones Leader ‘Willy’ Is Living Free in Spain William Joffre Alcívar Bautista, alias “Willy,” the alleged leader of the Tiguerones , one of the most powerful gangs in Ecuador and a US-designated Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO), is living free in Spain, despite still being pursued by Ecuadorian authorities. Willy drew international attention after his gang took over a live broadcast of a television station in Guayaquil on January 9, 2024. That same day, Ecuador’s President Daniel Noboa declared an internal conflict against more than 20 gangs , designating them terrorist organizations, including the Tiguerones. SEE ALSO: Special Series: Ecuador’s War on Gangs Noboa’s government alleged that Willy masterminded the on-air takeover of TC Television while he was abroad, and solicited an international arrest warrant for him on terrorism charges. Ecuador also alleged his involvement in car bombings, contract killings, and extortion. Willy was eventually arrested by Spanish police in Catalonia on October 22, 2024. Ecuador made two requests for his extradition, which Spain accepted on the condition that Ecuador provide human rights and safety guarantees. But those didn’t arrive in time, and Spanish authorities released Willy in December 2025. In March 2026 Willy gave an interview to El Mundo denying his involvement in the television news attack in Ecuador. He told the magazine his life now revolves around a used car business operating from Colombia, and he has hopes of opening a chain of barber shops in Spain. SEE ALSO: The Rise and Fall of El Negro Willy, Ecuador’s Prison-Guard Mafia Boss Willy started his criminal trajectory as a prison guard, eventually founding the Tiguerones. Under his leadership, the group came to dominate extortion and drug trafficking in Esmeraldas and parts of Guayaquil. Initially beginning as a faction of the Choneros , the Tiguerones went independent following internal leadership tensions. They joined a coalition of former Choneros factions known as Nueva Generación (New Generation), and began running drugs for Mexico’s powerful Jalisco Cartel New Generation (Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación – CJNG). The group has fractured in Guayaquil and now competes with other Ecuadorian gangs, like the Lobos , for strategic control in northwestern Ecuador. Ecuador’s government continues to pursue Willy’s extradition . More on Willy’s story in our full criminal profile . The post Tiguerones Leader ‘Willy’ Is Living Free in Spain appeared first on InSight Crime .

title: RAF Fairford incident almost certainly directed by Iran
body: The incident at RAF Fairford is assessed as highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons . Andy Burnham made the attribution in a statement covering the United Nations General Assembly and the international meetings that followed, turning to protective security at bases shared with the United States. He said: “Since Unga, Mr Speaker, we have been in close contact with the US about protective security at our shared bases. I want to thank our police and military personnel for their swift response to the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth. My right hon. Friend the Home Secretary will update the House regarding the incident at RAF Fairford, but I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. “And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.” Iran’s embassy in London called the claims unfounded and malicious speculation, and the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Britain was barking up the wrong tree. Police were called at about a quarter to one in the morning of 27 September to reports of suspicious vehicles heading towards the Gloucestershire base. Armed officers from Gloucestershire Constabulary arrested five men near Whelford, initially on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act 1875 and then on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act under section five of the Terrorism Act 2006. A major incident was declared, a cordon went up and homes nearby were evacuated while Army bomb disposal teams examined three vehicles. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said on 29 September that no improvised explosive devices had been found and that a quantity of petrol had been recovered. He had said a day earlier that investigators were considering whether the activity had been committed by proxies, knowingly or unknowingly acting on behalf of a foreign state. Seven men in their twenties have now been arrested, six of them British nationals and one a British-Iranian dual national detained in Westminster on 1 October. The most recent arrest, a twenty-two year old taken in Westminster on 6 October, was reported by this publication at the time. All seven have been released on bail and nobody has been charged. American B-1B bombers left Fairford on 4 October, with United States European Command saying only that they were redeploying to their home stations and giving no reason. The base is the United States Air Force’s preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe, supported by the 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron. The post RAF Fairford incident almost certainly directed by Iran first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Lockheed’s New PAC-3 Edge interceptor aims for agility
body: The latest iteration of Lockheed Martin’s PAC-3 family of missile interceptors is designed to bring extreme agility to bear against a diverse array of missile threats, Defense News learned. The defense giant unveiled the PAC-3 Edge this Friday and debuted it at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., today. “This missile is capable of being launched from the traditional M903 launcher. It’s capable of being launched from the containerized launchers that are being sought after domestically and internationally, as well as our HIMARS FLEX, which is the offense and defense configuration of our traditional HIMARS vehicle,” Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control Integrated Air and Missile Defense, told Defense News. Lockheed in January announced a seven-year framework agreement to increase annual PAC-3 interceptor production from approximately 600 to 2,000. Designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, the unveiling of the PAC-3 Edge comes as the U.S. military’s reliance on costly interceptors against cheap munitions, particularly those deployed by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, has come under increased scrutiny over the past eight months. The new PAC-3 Edge missile builds on the foundations of the PAC-3 MSE, Lockheed’s baseline missile, and pushes its abilities farther. The Edge system is longer and features a larger diameter, increasing its range. “It also goes higher in altitude and has more agility. It has attitude control motors, which are located near the front of the missile and basically divert the missile in flight,” Reynolds explained. “This has additional attitude control motors that give it additional agility.” While the PAC-3 MSE uses a two-pulse solid rocket motor to speedily approach moving targets, the new system has multi-pulse motor designed by Northrop Grumman. “It has a third pulse to the motor, so that means the motor will fire three times during its flight, giving it additional agility to kill the target,” Reynolds said. The weapon is designed not only for unprecedented maneuverability but to be easily integrated with both present and future missile defense networks. It is compatible with Northrop’s Integrated Battle Command System, or IBCS, a command-and-control network the Army uses to mesh air and missile defense sensors into a central hub. The company intends to begin testing the PAC-3 Edge in 2027 and have it ready to deploy by 2031, although Lockheed aims to have it ready earlier, Reynolds added. “The U.S. Army’s timeline is 2031. We, Lockheed Martin, are trying to pull that in and deliver this capability sooner, so around the turn of the decade,” he said.
