title: Moment when 3rd super tanker strikes sea mine in Hormuz
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – A third oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after striking a naval mine, according to Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps, which said the vessel had attempted to cross an unauthorized route despite warnings.
That was the third super tanker over the past two days that tried to breach the law and cross the Hormuz Strait but hit a mine.

title: Non-medical support during childbirth in Armenia: who are doulas and what do they do?
body: Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women The first certified doulas appeared in Armenia six years ago. Yet few women know that they can turn to doulas for support during pregnancy, childbirth and even after giving birth. Doulas are not medical professionals. They help women manage labour pain through massage and breathing techniques, while also providing emotional support. Women now have a choice about who accompanies them during these hours. Some still prefer to have their husbands, mothers or sisters by their side. Others choose to give birth with a doula. A doula with a woman in labour in the antenatal ward. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova Armenia’s growing number of large families: Statistics, one couple’s story and expert insights ‘They need me’: story of father who was left alone to raise two toddlers after his wife’s death How women in Armenia balance family care, childcare and careers Most doulas enter the profession after a negative personal experience Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova says women decide to become doulas after giving birth themselves. Sometimes they want to share a positive experience. More often, however, they turn to the profession because of a negative experience. “I took a long journey to get to this point. I gave birth twice. My second birth was therapeutic and healing. I realised that a woman’s preparation, knowledge and expectations largely determine how childbirth unfolds. The problem is that women often have expectations that do not match reality. This can lead to traumatic consequences,” she says. Иветта с мужем и сыновьями Yvetta says her husband stayed by her side during both births. The first was a terrifying experience for both of them. The second went differently because they had both prepared for it. This time, they could talk to each other, joke and even dance during labour. She remembers the birth as “a wonderful process”. She recalls that seven days before her second child was born, she listened to a lecture by an American doula. She remembers everything that might prove important during childbirth: “Before that lecture, I was determined not to let anything that happened during my first birth happen again. For eight months, I told my doctor that I refused to give birth naturally. I insisted on a caesarean section. But that one-hour lecture changed everything for me. I realised I could understand my hormones and my surroundings, and that I could control many things. Ultimately, I could simply give it a try. “My second birth went smoothly, without anxiety, and so quickly that after I was discharged, I kept telling my husband I wanted to offer to help pregnant women during labour and reassure them. Of course, those plans never came to fruition because they were unrealistic expectations.” Yet the idea stayed with Yvetta for the next ten years. Eventually, she began working with pregnant women and women in labour, but as a photographer. Her family was living abroad at the time, where maternity photography was very popular. When she moved to Armenia, she expected to find plenty of clients for similar photo shoots. However, she says, almost all women in labour there turned down her offers. “Either they invited me into the maternity ward not to take photographs that would capture this important moment in their lives, but simply because they did not want to be alone. But a photographer cannot intervene; they are like a shadow. Their presence should be as discreet as possible. I realised that, ultimately, I could not help women.” Immediately after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova Yvetta’s dream of becoming a doula came true during the coronavirus pandemic, when many training centres moved their courses online. Yvetta completed a course, passed her exams and received an international doula certification. She became the first doula in Armenia. Who are doulas? Doulas are trained professionals who support pregnant women, women in labour and those who need help during the postnatal period. They prepare women for childbirth and stay by their side throughout labour in the delivery room. Doulas provide informational, emotional and physical support. During labour, doulas help women through massage, pressure techniques and touch. Sometimes they simply offer encouragement; at other times, they explain what is happening in a woman’s body at that moment. They suggest different positions and help women feel comfortable and safe throughout the process. This can increase the likelihood of a positive birth outcome. Yvetta helps a woman in labour manage the pain. According to Yvetta, in countries where many women use doula services, they start looking for a doula in the early stages of pregnancy, sometimes even when planning to conceive: “Since doulas can take on only a small number of pregnant women each month, women book their services well in advance. They try to avoid complications this way, as there may be no available doulas when they go into labour. The situation in Armenia is different. Women who have given birth before usually contact us earlier in their pregnancy. First-time mothers tend to get in touch later, around weeks 28–30, when they start preparing for childbirth.” Yvetta believes women should not leave the search for a doula until the final weeks of pregnancy. Sometimes doulas have to turn women away because the medical facility where they plan to give birth does not allow them into the maternity ward. Armenia’s Ministry of Health has yet to recognise how much the work of a trained doula differs from the support a husband, mother, friend or anyone else can provide. Armenian law also contains no regulations governing their work. There are only five or six doulas in Armenia Most trained and received certification through Doula Link, a platform run by Russia’s Institute for Perinatal Support. They thereby became members of the European Doula Network. This allows them to provide doula services in Russia, Germany, Switzerland, Serbia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Spain, Italy, Israel and Panama. In Armenia, people regard doulas as unqualified assistants. A 2020 order issued by the health minister gives all women in labour the right to have a companion present during childbirth. However, some medical facilities still refuse to let doulas into the delivery room. Moreover, some maternity hospitals charge a fee for allowing a companion to attend the birth. The Ministry of Health does not regulate this practice. Why do women turn to doulas? Yvetta says women in Armenia mainly choose to give birth with a doula because they want someone they trust by their side. They need someone who understands what is happening and what to do, can keep track of the situation and looks after them. They also hope to avoid traumatic experiences, including obstetric violence. “Of course, having a support person present cannot guarantee that a woman will never experience abuse. But a doula is someone who will listen to her and understand her. I am convinced that in 99% of cases involving abuse, doctors do not intend to cause harm. “They often intervene to reduce certain risks. Yet they do not answer the woman’s questions or explain why they have decided to intervene, even when the intervention involves surgery. A doula will at least ask why the intervention is necessary and why it needs to happen at that particular moment. Women feel safer when a doula is by their side,” Yvetta says. A mother with her baby after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova In 2024–2025, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) conducted a study of women’s experiences during pregnancy and childbirth in 16 countries across Eastern Europe and Central Asia, including Armenia. The study found that 67% of the women surveyed had experienced at least one form of obstetric violence. In Armenia, around 55% of respondents said medical staff had performed obstetric interventions without their consent or any explanation. Meanwhile, 32% reported mistreatment by medical staff, highlighting a lack of information or pressure to make them agree to certain interventions. Another 27% reported poor-quality care, such as inadequate staff qualifications. Around 15% of women experienced verbal aggression, while 5% reported physical violence. Eleven per cent of respondents reported various forms of sexual violence, including excessive or inappropriate touching. Why don’t women turn to doulas? Yvetta admits that 80% of the pregnant women who contact her are foreigners who, for various reasons, give birth in Armenia. Local women tend to be more cautious. The main problem, in the doula’s view, is a lack of information. Stereotypical attitudes also play an important role. Many people see childbirth as something women must go through on their own, without any need for additional support. Waiting for childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova “But this is the wrong approach, because every woman in labour is vulnerable. It is very important that, by the end, she feels like a winner because she has brought a new person into the world, rather than feeling broken and miserable after enduring unbearable suffering. Unfortunately, most women still prefer to overcome their fears of childbirth and pain not with a doula’s help, but by paying for a caesarean section. They believe this will solve the problem,” she says. Sometimes women do not turn to doulas because they assume their services will be expensive. Yvetta does not specify how much she charges. However, she says she sometimes helps pregnant women entirely free of charge because she sees this work as her mission. “Being a doula is a calling. This work is first and foremost about your inner world and your heart, and only then about your skills.” She recalls that when she first started working as a doula, she sometimes returned home exhausted and upset. She even considered giving it up. Poor working conditions and hostility from doctors and hospital administrators were the main sources of stress. She also felt distressed when her presence created additional difficulties for the woman in labour. Now she knows which maternity hospitals allow her to do her job most effectively. Some doctors there see doulas not as competitors but as professionals who support their work. Every birth has therefore become a wonderful experience for her. “Now I come home happy because I no longer suffer alongside a woman during labour; instead, I help her avoid suffering. I can see that my work makes a difference. I see a woman who was screaming in pain and fear stop screaming, get up and start dancing,” Yvetta says. Yvetta with the parents of a baby born with her support Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

title: This Is Our First Look At The Wolf Armored Fighting Vehicle That Aims To Replace The Bradley
body: General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS) has offered the first official look at its proposal to replace the U.S. Army’s Bradley Fighting Vehicles, called the Wolf. The Wolf is one of two designs competing to become the Army’s future XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle (MICV). Just earlier today, we published a detailed update on the XM30 competition, including new information about both entrants and the Army’s testing plans, which you can find here . GDLS is showing the one-eighth-scale model of Wolf, seen at the top of this story and made by a company called KiwiMill , at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ is in attendance . Wolf is facing off head-to-head against a version of the Lynx from Germany’s Rheinmetall, supplied via the company’s U.S. subsidiary, American Rheinmetall. It has already been established that Wolf is a further evolution of the GDLS’ Griffin III design, which was first shown publicly at AUSA back in 2018. Griffin III was derived from the ASCOD 2 infantry fighting vehicle, for which Spain was the launch customer, and which is now entering service in Latvia. The U.S. Army’s now-cancelled M10 Booker ‘light tank’ and the British Army’s much-troubled Ajax are also members of this broader family of armored vehicles. A side-by-side comparison of the model of the Wolf, at left, and the Griffin III demonstrator, at right. GDLS/KiwiMill The design of the Wolf, at least based on the model, is substantially different from the earlier Griffin III demonstrator. Wolf’s turret has a broader, flatter, and overall more streamlined shape, which is in line with its remotely-operated design. There is just a single sensor turret on top, along with space for a forward-looking sensor suite to the left of the main 50mm cannon. What may be apertures for additional sensors or other systems are seen elsewhere along the front and sides of the turret. It also has more launchers for smoke grenades around the front edges compared to the Griffin III. A focused look at the Wolf’s turret as seen on the one-eighth-scale model. GDLS/KiwiMill Compared to the Griffin III, the Wolf’s hull has also been much revised, including the elimination of a traditional driver’s hatch in front of the turret ring. The vehicle’s commander (who also acts as the gunner) and driver sit side-by-side deeper inside the hull. Up to six passengers can ride in a compartment further at the rear. For comparison, the Bradley has a crew of three, as well as the ability to carry six passengers. The Wolf’s hull also features side skirts that were not found on the Griffin III demonstrator. A different style of tracks is also depicted on the model. The picture of the model that GDLS shared shows sensors facing outward from a position on the side of the hull toward the front, as well. This makes sense, as the design features a distributed camera system to offer a full 360-degree view of the outside to personnel riding within, the broad benefits of which you can read more about here . Another look at the hull of the Wolf, as seen on the model. Note the outward-facing sensors positioned toward the front, as well as the lack of any traditional driver’s hatch. GDLS/KiwiMill “Because we have a reduced crew from the Bradley [which has a commander and gunner in turret] there has to be greater efficiency in how those soldiers execute their tasks,” Geoffrey Norman, GDLS’ director for U.S. Strategy & Growth, previously noted to TWZ . “The software and menu logic are very intuitive.” Next-generation fire control, sensor, and networking/communications capabilities, as well as improved active and passive defenses, are key requirements for the XM30 program. Both Wolf and American Rheinmetall Lynx-based designs have built-in launchers for loitering munitions, with GDLS having chosen to integrate AeroVironment’s Switchblade 300 more specifically. What we have seen on the Wolf model so far does not appear to explicitly show this particular feature. Wolf and Lynx both also feature hybrid-electric propulsion, which will bring various benefits, especially in terms of fuel economy and electrical power generation, compared to the diesel-engined Bradley. When it comes to the boost in on-board electrical power, “the emphasis from the Army has really been about having margin on the vehicle for future [system] requirements – directed energy, counter-UAS systems, or fill-in-the-blank,” GDLS’ Norman has also told us in the past. A rendering of the Lynx-based XM30 design. American Rheinmetall As it stands now, both GDLS and American Rheinmetall have delivered prototypes of their respective designs to the Army, with initial testing having been conducted at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland. Soldier touchpoints and field evaluations are now set to occur at Fort Hood in Texas between February and March of next year. You can read in more detail about both entrants in the XM30 competition and what is known about their features in our past reporting here . An actual Wolf prototype, seen under wraps, after being delivered to the US Army’s Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland around the end of August 2026. GDLS In the meantime, we have now gotten clear views of both designs vying to become the Army’s XM30 replacement for the venerable Bradley. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post This Is Our First Look At The Wolf Armored Fighting Vehicle That Aims To Replace The Bradley appeared first on TWZ .

title: X-Bow To Supply Rocket Booster For Leidos Low-Cost Cruise Missile
body:
X-Bow Systems on Monday said it will supply the booster motors for Leidos ’ [LDOS] Low-Cost Containerized Munition (LCCM) the company is supplying to the Army.
X-Bow said it expects to begin full-rate production of the solid rocket motors in 2027 following design, qualification and static fires testing of its booster. The Defense Department in May signed three-year framework agreements with Leidos, Anduril Industries , CoAspire and Kongsberg ’s Zone 5 Technologies for their respective LCCMs ( Defense Daily , May 13).
The Army’s initial order to Leidos is expected to be for 3,000 LCCMs. X-Bow’s booster will push the cruise missile out of the launch container and quickly bring it to flying speed.
X-Bow made the announcement during the Association of the U.S. Army Conference.
X-Bow recently completed deliveries of 2,100 rocket-assisted takeoff motors to AEVEX Corp. [AVEX] for the company’s long-range Disruptor drone and is under contract with the Navy to develop and qualify a solid rocket motor booster for the future Navy Modular Missile ( Defense Daily , April 7 and Oct. 7).

title: UAE teacher injured in Riyadh airport attack assured she can complete Umrah
body: A teacher from the UAE injured in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been assured she will be able to complete her Umrah pilgrimage once she recovers. The teacher, whose name was not released, was travelling with a colleague from Abu Dhabi to Makkah via Riyadh when the airport came under attack on Saturday. Saudi Health Minister Fahad Al Jalajel visited the two women in hospital on Sunday when he went to see people injured in the attack and find out about their medical care. One of the teachers told the minister how their journey had been interrupted, according to Saudi state-run television channel Al Ekhbariya. She praised the doctors treating her. Mr Al Jalajel said King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had instructed officials to ensure the women received full support throughout their recovery. “You’re not part of what happened. We know that. For that reason, King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman are telling us to take full care of you, even the recovery, and that you continue on your Umrah,” he told her. Suspension of flights Saudi Arabia has extended the suspension of operations at the airport following the deadly attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels at the weekend. The General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Monday that the suspension would continue while checks on the safety and operational readiness of airport sites were completed. It did not give a date or time for the reopening. Etihad Airways has cancelled all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until October 19, extending disruption to services between the UAE and the Saudi capital into next week. Flydubai has cancelled Riyadh flights until Wednesday, while Emirates and Air Arabia services have been affected. Services to other Saudi destinations have also been impacted. Etihad cancelled four flights between Abu Dhabi and Dammam on Monday, with all services on the route cancelled on Tuesday and Wednesday. Selected Jeddah flights have been cancelled until Thursday.

title: NATO’s top commander outlines ‘Theory of Victory’ to stop attacks and defend allied territory
body: Grynkewich described his “Theory of Victory” as a shared vision for how NATO would deter aggression and defend its territory. It follows the Deterrence and Defence of the Euro-Atlantic Area strategy agreed by all 32 allies, but is not a military plan, he said. “I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable,” Grynkewich said. Preventing war requires clear communication of NATO’s defensive intentions and forces ready to respond to possible attacks, he added. The approach has three stages: block the initial attack, blunt any continuing advance and break the attacking forces’ warfighting system if the offensive persists. Grynkewich said it draws on lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East, with intelligence collection and advanced algorithms helping NATO detect threats and position forces early. Land forces would engage advancing formations and prevent the seizure of allied territory. Air and naval forces, working with space and cyber forces, would seek air and maritime superiority and bring mass and precision against the attacker. Sensors, autonomous systems and coordinated operations across military domains would aim to halt further advances. If the adversary continued the attack or committed reserves, NATO would target the attacking forces and the systems supplying, sustaining and controlling them. “To do this, we will layer high-end and highly effective precision munitions with an overpowering mass of affordable and scalable systems,” Grynkewich said. He described sustained kinetic and non-kinetic pressure to cut off supplies, disrupt command and leave enemy forces unable to continue the attack. The objective would be the tactical and operational defeat of the forces attacking NATO, rather than a strategic defeat of the adversary. “Rather, we are only seeking to stop any attack in its tracks, to deny the ability to seize and hold our territory,” he said. Grynkewich argued that this defensive purpose would leave responsibility for escalation with the aggressor. He said NATO must show that escalation would worsen the attacker’s military and political position, while threats or acts of escalation would strengthen allied unity. He identified long-range precision strike capabilities, sensor networks and a warfighting cloud as investment priorities. Exercises would rehearse the three tasks, with eastern flank land forces practicing how to block attacks and air and maritime forces demonstrating how to blunt them. Grynkewich also praised Poland’s defense spending, industrial expansion, military modernization and focus on societal resilience. He said NATO’s preparations to fight were intended above all to prevent war: “Our first goal is deterrence – avoiding conflict.”

title: Angry at Trump's Russian diesel deal? Here's how you can help Ukraine bomb Russia
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House on April 22, 2020, in Washington, DC. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump had a busy weekend, undermining sanctions on Russia, blaming Ukraine for the war Russia started — again — and insisting that Russian refineries become drone-free zones.
"We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries , because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump said on Oct. 10.
"And (President Volodymyr Zelensky) wants to make problems for the world, he wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel. ... We have a world problem, and the problem is caused by the lack of refineries for diesel fuel. So what does he do? He goes and hits the refineries," he added.
Trump failed to mention the considerable evidence that shows the U.S. war against Iran that he started and cannot finish is the major culprit behind the current shortage of diesel.
The Kyiv Independent has since learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries, despite Moscow's continuing bombing of Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Trump's latest pressure on Ukraine to end the war Russia started and refuses to stop has angered people both home and abroad, even sparking a bipartisan backlash in the U.S. Congress at his decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
Across social media, some people wondered how they could help Ukraine continue to hit Russia.
There are several ways people can help fund Ukraine's drones, and even a few options when it comes to what they hit.
Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (USF), Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and military intelligence (HUR) have all carried out long-range strikes against targets in Russia, including oil infrastructure.
USF does not have a dedicated fundraiser but is supported by donations from United24 and the Come Back Alive foundation. But there is one specific branch of the USF that one can donate directly to.
The 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Aerial Systems was Ukraine's first experimental unmanned aerial systems (UAS) unit, founded in 2022, originally as the 14th Separate UAS Regiment. Since then, it has become the largest UAS unit, specializing in long-range strikes on Russia.
"We are the ones who toss the war over to enemy territory," by striking Russia's military-industrial complex, oil industry, and logistics facilities, the unit says on its website . Over the years, it has struck several Russian airfields, artillery arsenals, and ammunition depots. In 2025, the unit carried out more than 50 successful operations against Russia’s oil infrastructure, such as strikes on oil refineries in Ryazan, Volgograd, and Saratov, inflicting a 38% loss on Russia’s oil refining capacity, the unit says .
Outside of long-range drone strikes on Russian territory, there are several organisations that support mid-range strikes on Russian targets in occupied Ukraine, as well as first-person-view (FPV) drones for use on the front lines.
Founded by Dimko and Iryna Zhluktenko and named after their now legendary dog, Dzyga’s Paw is a Ukrainian charity that equips frontline soldiers with the technology and equipment they need to keep up the fight day in, day out.
Since February 2022, they've raised over $6 million from thousands of donors across 70+ countries, and delivered drones, Starlinks, night vision, and other hi-tech gear directly to 100+ military units.
Come Back Alive is an independent foundation that started equipping Ukrainian soldiers with bulletproof vests in 2014, writing "come back alive" on each of their vests. Today, it is one of the largest providers of equipment for Ukrainian service members all across the front lines, having supplied the military with more than 157,000 FPV drones, over 14,000 units of thermal imaging optics, more than 5,400 units of infantry weapons, 2,400 pickup trucks, over 100 unmanned reconnaissance systems, a Bayraktar TB2 strike UAV complex, and more, according to its website .
Besides supplying equipment, the organization's instructors also train highly qualified military specialists, including sappers, snipers, divers, electronic-warfare specialists, and UAV and UGV operators.
As part of these efforts, Come Back Alive currently raises funds for the Yatagan UAV Operators School , which it launched in partnership with PrivatBank in 2024 within the structures of the Ground Forces. Over the last two years, the school has trained thousands of Ukrainian service members already.
The Sternenko Community Foundation is the charitable organization of well-known Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko and has become the largest non-governmental provider of FPV-drones to the Ukrainian military. According to its website , the foundation has purchased almost 300,000 FPV-drones for the Ukrainian military by mid-October.
In its current "Rusoriz Digital" fundraiser, the foundation seeks to scale FPV-drones using a digital link, allowing them to operate at ranges above 50 kilometers (31 miles) and more resistant to electronic warfare measures. As of today, the foundation has already supplied more than 50 units with the technology and already procured over 10,000 of these drones, for use against Russian logistics behind the front lines.
Unite with Ukraine is led by the Ukrainian World Congress , an NGO established in 1967 and recognized by the UN and the Council of Europe to represent Ukrainian diaspora communities globally.
Together with its partner organizations "Saint Javelin" and "The Last Capitalist," it raises funds for fixed-wing mid-range strike UAVs in support of the several brigades.
The International Unity Movement is a Ukrainian charitable foundation established in 2022, aiming to raise funds across the spectrum of security challenges that Ukrainians face throughout Russia's war.
As part of their work, they support the 423rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment "Scythian Griffins," which carries out combat operations and mid-range drone strikes on the Zaporizhzhia sector. Since its founding in 2024, the unit has destroyed hundreds of Russian vehicles , UAVs, and artillery systems, as well as dozens of tanks and warehouses.
United24 is Ukraine's official government fundraising platform, set up by Zelensky shortly after the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Donors can support a wide range of areas including drones, defense, medical aid, demining, reconstruction, education, and sports.
The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation was founded in 2020 and shifted much of its work toward supporting the military after Russia’s full-scale invasion.
It supplies frontline units with drones, vehicles, communications equipment, electronic warfare systems, optics, and medical supplies, while also running humanitarian programs for civilians affected by the war.

title: Iraq should not pose threat to Gulf states, President of Kurdistan region says
body: President Nechirvan Barzani of Iraq's Kurdistan region has said weapons must be held by the Iraqi government and warned that the country must not threaten Gulf states, as Baghdad enters a new phase following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces. “Iraq should not be a threat to Gulf countries. Iraq should never do that, that is not sovereignty,” Mr Barzani said at the annual Middle East Research Institute Forum in Erbil on Monday. “Weapons should be in the hands of the government,” he added, arguing that Iraq needed to strengthen its ability to exercise sovereignty and take responsibility for its own security. The remarks come as Iraq faces pressure to bring armed factions under state control following attacks by Iran-aligned groups on targets in Iraq and across the region. The US-led coalition against ISIS completed its military withdrawal from Iraq on September 30, with security co-operation between Baghdad and Washington now moving towards a bilateral framework. In a statement marking October 1 as the day of full Iraqi sovereignty following the withdrawal, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said the serious work of dealing with weapons outside state control began now. Mr Barzani said Iraq no longer needed such a large international coalition after 12 years of its presence, adding that the country should develop bilateral security relationships with partner states. “We thank them, but we are happy today that Iraq stands on its feet,” he said. However, he stressed that the Kurdistan region still needed air defence systems to protect itself, following repeated drone and missile attacks. On the wider regional situation amid the Iran war , Mr Barzani said the changes unfolding across the Middle East presented both opportunities and threats for the Kurds, but he believed the opportunities could outweigh the risks. The greatest threat to Iraq, he said, was economic uncertainty, particularly the country's dependence on oil exports . “If the Strait of Hormuz is not resolved, it will be a long-term challenge,” he said, referring to the vital waterway through which a significant share of the world's oil supply passes and which has been effectively blockaded by Iran since the war began. He also warned that Iraq and the Kurdistan region faced challenges in maintaining stable relations with neighbouring countries while navigating the shifting regional landscape. Mr Barzani was more critical of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, saying their actions during the war had placed the Kurdistan region in a difficult position. “The opposition Iranian forces unfortunately behaved irresponsibly and put the Kurdistan region in an embarrassing position,” he said. He said the Kurdistan region's position had been clear from the beginning and that it would not become involved in the war. Reports that Iranian Kurdish opposition fighters were preparing to cross into Iran emerged in early March, after the Iran war broke out. Several media outlets reported that Washington had contacted Iranian Kurdish groups based in Iraq about a possible ground operation, with some fighters said to be on standby near the border. However, the groups denied that their forces had crossed into Iran. Iraqi Kurdish officials also rejected reports of an incursion, amid fears that any involvement could draw the Kurdistan region into the conflict and provoke further Iranian attacks. “It was not our war,” Mr Barzani said. The Kurdistan region shares a border of more than 600km with Iran. Mr Barzani said it was impossible for Erbil to allow its territory to become a staging ground for an attack on its neighbour. He said the regional government had closed the border during the early days of the conflict and deployed forces along it, making clear that it would not allow anyone to use the Kurdistan region to attack Iran.

title: 3 US soldiers awarded Purple Hearts after March missile attack on Saudi Arabia base
body: Three U.S. soldiers were awarded Purple Hearts for their efforts assisting fellow service members despite their own injuries after a missile attack hit their air base during Operation Epic Fury . On March 27, when a missile hit Prince Sultan Air Base in Al Kharj, Saudi Arabia, Staff Sgt. Kalob Mitchell, Spc. Nicholas Cabo and Sgt. Xavier Jones, all with the 6th Battalion, 56th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 1st Cavalry Division Artillery, sprang into action. A 550-pound ballistic missile exploded yards from a bunker on base, filling it with dust and debris. “We’re sitting there talking, and then all of a sudden, we didn’t hear anything, no sound at all. Everything went black, so we were hit,” Mitchell said in a recent release . While expecting just another missile warning, the soldiers were thrown from their position and slammed against the opposing interior wall, forcing all three to lose consciousness. They had their initial medical evaluation later that day at the Role 2 Medical Facility on base. “Woke up, checked on them. They were good. At that time, we heard screams from the opposite side of the bunker. Two Soldiers, I’m not too sure who they were, who had significant injuries; ran over there, applied tourniquets, T Triple C (Tactical Combat Casualty Care), everything,” Mitchell recounted. Mitchell, Cabo and Jones applied a tourniquet to a severely wounded soldier, treated another with a neck injury and helped keep a disoriented soldier safe until it was safe to evacuate the bunker, per the release. Despite their own injuries, the trio continued to assist others, carrying others out to an ambulance and helping a soldier whose leg was severely damaged, speculating that the soldier could have lost their life if not for the group. Capt. Tyler Ritter, commander of 6-56 ADAR, 1st Cav. DIVARTY, received messages from the injured soldier saying, “Sir, your Soldiers saved my life. I thank God every day that these gentlemen survived. Their actions brought great credit upon the 6-56 Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 1st Cavalry Division and III Armored Corps. These Soldiers are my heroes. May God bless them.” Mitchell, Cabo and Jones’ service, described as the “ultimate description of what we mean when we talk about warfighting, readiness, grit and taking care of our Soldiers,” earned them each a Purple Heart during an Oct. 1 ceremony at the III Armored Corps headquarters building at Fort Hood, Texas. “So honestly, it’s kind of cool,” Jones said in the release. “I don’t think any of us was like going for a Purple Heart because it actually sucked. Like that situation was horrible … When I saw it on my STP (Soldier Talent Profile), I was like, man, I never would have thought I would have got a Purple Heart. I never thought I was going to see anything like we saw.”

title: Sudanese refugee killed as fire destroys shelters in eastern Chad
body: A young Sudanese refugee was killed in Adré camp in eastern Chad on Sunday, as a separate fire destroyed temporary shelters and left displaced families without adequate accommodation. Refugees told Radio Dabanga that Chadian police were continuing their investigation into the killing to identify those responsible. The Platform of Civil Associations for Sudanese Refugees in Adré camp , known as PAGES, warned of a rise in armed robberies, intimidation, attacks on civilians and thefts of property in public places and on roads. In a statement seen by Radio Dabanga, the platform urged the relevant government, security and military authorities in Chad, alongside humanitarian partners and civil society organisations in the local governorate, to intervene urgently to address the deteriorating security situation. It also called on residents and refugees to remain vigilant and report suspicious movements and suspected criminal activity to the security services to protect lives and property. ‘Fire leaves refugees without shelter’ In a separate incident on Sunday, a large fire swept through Adré refugee camp, destroying numerous temporary shelters occupied by Sudanese refugees. One refugee told Radio Dabanga that strong winds and the lack of fire engines in the area worsened the blaze. The source also reported that temporary shelters housing Sudanese refugees west of Adré Secondary School were destroyed, leaving the affected families displaced and exposed without shelter. The incidents have added to the insecurity and humanitarian pressures facing Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad. ‘One killed and seven wounded in shooting in South Darfur’ Gunmen killed one person and wounded seven others when they opened fire on a vehicle carrying traders to a weekly market in the east of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, on Sunday evening. Eyewitnesses told Radio Dabanga that the gunmen intercepted a commercial Nissan vehicle carrying traders travelling from the Manwashi administrative unit in Mershing locality. The attackers opened fire on the vehicle near Hamada and Khor Abshe at around 8pm on Sunday, the eyewitnesses said. The attack killed Saddam Abkar Khamis and wounded seven other people. The injured were taken to Nyala for treatment. Several areas across Darfur have experienced rising insecurity and looting , prompting repeated calls for the authorities to intervene and curb the violence. Share article The post Sudanese refugee killed as fire destroys shelters in eastern Chad appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

title: Ukraine is building a patchwork antiballistic defense, one stopgap at a time
body: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine is scrambling to secure enough Patriot interceptors to stop Russian ballistic missiles this winter, piecing together allied stockpile transfers , new production agreements and a homegrown interceptor program as quickly as possible before the cold sets in. The push comes as the world runs short on the weapons Ukraine needs most. U.S. forces in Europe face a “beyond critical” shortage of Patriot interceptors after stocks were moved to the Middle East for the Iran war , a NATO official said in August. Ukraine is also bracing for another winter of Russian strikes on its energy grid, a campaign that increasingly relies on jet-powered Shahed drones too fast for most of the cheap interceptor drones Ukraine has used to stop older models. “Russia uses almost only jet-powered Shaheds to attack Kyiv because the interceptors that we were using in the past against older generations of drones had an interception rate of around 90%,” a manager at Ukrainian interceptor developer Grim Tech told Defense News last month. The faster drones force Ukraine to expend scarce and expensive missiles just as it tries to conserve Patriot ammunition for ballistic threats — the only reliable option against Russia’s even harder-to-stop ballistic missiles, according to Ukrainian officials. “Ballistic missiles are especially difficult to deal with,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a massive aerial barrage on Wednesday night saw Russia fire 70 missiles, many of them ballistic, and waves of Shahed drones at Kyiv and 12 other regions. Soldiers downed 39 of the 48 cruise missiles but only five ballistic missiles, according to Ukraine’s air force . At least 32 people were killed in the attacks, and over 100 were injured, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram . Civilian casualties in Ukraine have risen monthly throughout most of 2026. U.N. monitors verified 372 civilians killed and 2,349 injured in August, second only to July, with long-range missiles and drones causing 47% of the toll. Kyiv is assembling a patchwork of antiballistic air defense solutions, each piece on a different clock: Rounds transferred from allied stocks for this winter, imported systems and licensed production that will begin to matter over the next several years, and Freyja, a Ukrainian-European interceptor still in development. Stockpile swaps The fastest fix depends on allies sharing existing stockpiles, a request Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara put forward at his first Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting with allies on Sept. 8. Kyiv has signed contracts for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles in recent months, but most will not ship for years, Khmara said. He asked partners for 300 interceptors from their stockpiles now, offering newer missiles from those contracts as replacements. “The situation with ballistics is much more difficult. And that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles,” he told allies. Germany answered Khmara’s call by promising an undisclosed number of PAC-2 interceptors from Bundeswehr stocks. Britain committed £100 million through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) for Patriot missiles and other air-defense equipment intended to arrive before winter, according to the British government . But the United States did not include Patriot missiles in the nearly $400 million in expiring Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative money it moved to obligate before the fiscal year ended, a source familiar with the package told Reuters . Surging production of existing antiballistic interceptors “Ukraine is ready not only to produce ballistic missile interceptors for its own needs, but also to strengthen the United States and its allies through joint production,” Zelenskyy wrote on X after a recent meeting with a U.S. congressional delegation in Kyiv. Both Europe and the U.S. are in talks with Ukraine to begin ramping up joint manufacturing initiatives for both the Patriot missile system and the Franco-Italian Aster 30. Zelenskyy said Sept. 25 that U.S. President Donald Trump made a final political decision to grant Ukraine licenses to produce Patriot missiles. But Washington and manufacturers have not publicly identified the variant, Ukraine’s workshare, production site or first-delivery date. Lockheed Martin said it aims to raise its own annual PAC-3 MSE capacity from roughly 600 missiles to 2,000 by 2030, while a $14.7 billion Boeing contract would triple production of the interceptor’s seeker. Germany is scheduled to begin PAC-2 GEM-T production , and Berlin has separately asked Washington and Lockheed Martin to permit PAC-3 MSE production in Germany, but that proposal remains unresolved. France and Italy agreed in a joint declaration in July to authorize licensed production of Aster 30 interceptors in Ukraine before the end of 2026, along with providing Kyiv with four SAMP/T NG systems — becoming their first combat user. France also committed two interim SAMP/T complexes, a GF300 radar before year’s end and progressive SAMP/T NG deployment beginning in 2027. The sovereignty bet: Freyja Ukraine and Europe are looking to a new weapon called “Frejya” as a longer-term solution. Freyja is a Ukrainian-designed ballistic interceptor built around Fire Point’s FP-7.X missile, including an interceptor, launcher, radar and command-and-control network. It’s priced at roughly $1 million per round, about one-quarter of the cost of a PAC-3 MSE, and designed to plug into NATO-standard radars and command posts already in the field. The FP-7.X flew for the first time in early June and is built to kill ballistic targets at roughly 15 miles up using a high-explosive fragmentation warhead rather than the PAC-3’s hit-to-kill collision — which may come in later versions — at a target price of approximately $700,000 per interceptor, or roughly one-fifth the price of a PAC-3. The company says it will build three interceptors a day starting in August. Zelenskyy wants the system up and running within a year, and the coalition is targeting its first real ballistic intercept for the end of 2027. Zelenskyy launched the initiative with nine European countries in Paris in July — and the effort is still growing. Poland joined the group on Sept. 17, a week after Canadian PM Mark Carney told Zelenskyy that Ottawa would contribute its technologies to Freyja along with providing Kyiv with a broader package that includes C$350 million in interceptors. The EU is separately weighing direct funding for the program on top of national contributions, according to Militarnyi .

title: GE Aerospace to double India supplier spending by 2030 amid aviation boom
body:
New Delhi, Oct 12, 2026. GE Aerospace plans to nearly double its spending on Indian suppliers between 2025 and 2030, as the company seeks to expand its domestic supply chain to meet India’s growing demand for commercial aviation and strengthen the country’s aerospace manufacturing and engineering capabilities.

The announcement coincided with the release of a report compiled by Ernst & Young (EY), titled ‘Powering Progress: GE Aerospace’s Economic Impact in India’, which assesses the company's contribution to commercial aviation, defence, manufacturing and engineering during four decades of operations in the country.
The report was unveiled at an industry gathering, ‘India Taking Flight – Aviation, Innovation and the Road to Viksit Bharat 2047’, hosted by GE Aerospace in New Delhi on October 12.
According to the report, GE Aerospace and its partners supplied engines powering the majority of commercial airline operations in India, with a fleet of more than 1,400 engines as of December 2025. These engines have supported Indian airlines in achieving a passenger load factor of 88.2 percent and aircraft utilisation of 12 to 14 hours daily, reflecting the high utilisation of aircraft in the country’s expanding aviation market.
India’s domestic commercial airlines generated approximately $19 billion in revenue in the financial year 2025-26, while the aviation ecosystem supported an estimated 370,000 direct jobs, the report said.
“India’s commercial aviation growth is one of the fastest in the world, and today’s report shows that our commitment here goes far beyond selling engines,” said Vikram Rai, CEO for South Asia at GE Aerospace.
He said the company’s contribution extended from component manufacturing in Pune to engineering and innovation in Bengaluru, adding that increased supplier spending would help strengthen the domestic aerospace ecosystem as India pursues its Viksit Bharat 2047 objectives.



Aviation expansion creates opportunities
India’s aviation sector is preparing for substantial expansion over the next two decades. Government projections cited in the report estimate that annual domestic passenger traffic will increase to 1.1 billion by 2040 from 340 million in FY26, while the number of airports is expected to rise from 163 to more than 350 by 2047.
Meeting the anticipated demand will require an estimated 3,300 additional aircraft, or 6,600 engines, across India and South Asia by 2044.
In July 2026, IndiGo signed a memorandum of understanding with CFM International for more than 1,000 LEAP-1A engines to power 510 Airbus A320neo family aircraft. The proposed order, described as the largest single LEAP engine order, also includes support for establishing IndiGo’s planned engine maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) facility.
GE Aerospace and its partner-engine programmes are expected to power most of the approximately 1,500 new aircraft already on order with Indian carriers. The report estimates that these aircraft could generate business worth more than $5.5 billion for India’s MRO industry.
The projected increase in aircraft numbers is expected to create opportunities for domestic suppliers, component manufacturers, maintenance providers and engineering companies, while increasing the importance of a reliable local supply chain.
Pune manufacturing facility expands capacity
GE Aerospace’s manufacturing operations in India are anchored by its Pune facility, established with an initial investment of $200 million. Since 2024, the company has invested nearly $55 million to expand automation, improve precision manufacturing and strengthen workforce development.
The facility is supported by a network of 17 major domestic suppliers, including small and medium-sized enterprises. GE Aerospace spent approximately $200 million on its Indian supply chain in 2025 and plans to nearly double that expenditure by 2030.
The company’s apprenticeship programme at Pune has trained approximately 5,000 production associates since 2015, with 400 to 500 new apprentices enrolled annually. The initiative is intended to develop the skilled workforce required for advanced manufacturing and aerospace production.
In Bengaluru, engineering development programmes and academic partnerships are contributing to India's research and innovation capabilities. A joint innovation programme with the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, for instance, has produced a locally designed and manufactured Micro Turbomachine.
Defence cooperation supports indigenous capabilities
GE Aerospace’s engagement with India also extends to military aviation and naval propulsion, with its engines playing a role in the country's efforts to strengthen defence manufacturing and reduce dependence on imports.
The company has partnered with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) since 1986 on LM2500 naval engines and F404-IN20 engines used in the Tejas Mk1 light combat aircraft.

The F404 engine family has more than 4,000 engines deployed across 16 countries, according to the company.
A memorandum of understanding signed in 2023 provides a framework for exploring the domestic manufacture of F414 engines for the Tejas Mk2 programme, subject to final agreements and the necessary approvals.

GE Aerospace has also entered into a five-year Performance Based Logistics contract with the Indian Air Force for Apache helicopter engines. Separately, it has agreed to establish an in-country depot facility for F404-IN20 engines, which could strengthen local maintenance and support capabilities.
The proposed expansion of F414 engine manufacturing in India, if finalised, would be relevant to the country's broader objectives of building domestic aerospace production capabilities and developing a more extensive defence industrial ecosystem.
Bengaluru centre contributes to global engine programmes
GE Aerospace’s Bengaluru Technology Centre, established in 2000 with an investment of $200 million, has become a major engineering and research base outside the United States.
The centre has secured more than 1,000 aviation patents and contributed to the design, development and certification of the GE9X, described by the company as the world’s most powerful jet engine.
Indian engineers based at the centre hold significant design responsibilities for the GE90, GP7200, GEnx and GE9X engine programmes. They are also involved in the CFM RISE programme, which aims to improve fuel efficiency by 20 percent while maintaining durability and meeting customer requirements.
The centre’s digital technology team supports the company’s global supply chain, MRO and sales operations through the application of artificial intelligence.
GE Aerospace’s planned increase in domestic supplier spending, alongside investments in manufacturing, engineering, workforce training and defence-related programmes, reflects its strategy to expand its presence in India as the country’s aviation market grows.
The company’s next phase of investment will also test the capacity of India’s component manufacturers, engineering talent and maintenance ecosystem to meet rising demand while supporting the government’s broader ambitions for domestic manufacturing, technological innovation and aerospace self-reliance.

title: Malnutrition deaths reach 1,852 in areas controlled by SLM-AW
body: The civil authority in areas controlled by the Sudan Liberation Movement led by Abdelwahid El Nur (SLM-AW)has reported 1,852 deaths linked to acute malnutrition among children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and older people, warning of a deepening humanitarian disaster as displaced families continue to arrive. Mujib El Rahman El Zubair, head of the civil authority, told Radio Dabanga that famine was spreading across the region, with children, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and older people facing mounting hunger and food shortages. He said deaths caused by hunger and a lack of food were increasing daily. Health services have also deteriorated sharply, El Zubair said, with most health centres no longer operating because of severe shortages of medicines and medical staff. The lack of clean water has further worsened conditions, contributing to the spread of disease , deteriorating sanitation and the threat of epidemics, including cholera, viral hepatitis and malaria. ‘Thousands of children out of school’ The humanitarian crisis has also disrupted education, with an estimated 2,631 displaced children dropping out of school each year, according to El Zubair. He attributed the figures to worsening living conditions and families’ inability to pay school fees or afford basic educational supplies. Only 21 humanitarian organisations are operating in the region, he said, and their work covers only a fraction of the needs of displaced people. Funding shortages , limited resources and gaps in geographical coverage have left many communities without adequate assistance. The continued influx of displaced families has placed further pressure on already overstretched shelter and water supplies. ‘Campaign to raise alarm over famine’ The civil authority has launched a media campaign to highlight the scale of the crisis in Jebel Marra , Tawila and Ain Siro. The campaign aims to raise awareness, sound an early warning, document the crisis through figures and data, and press humanitarian organisations to intervene. El Zubair called on the international community and aid organisations to provide regular food supplies, emergency shelter, safe drinking water and sanitation services. He also urged them to establish medical centres, supply essential medicines and establish schools to ensure that children can continue their education. He called for agricultural support, including water harvesting, storage dams and improved seeds, alongside training in sewing, handicrafts, livestock rearing and poultry farming to help displaced people develop alternative sources of income. El Zubair also called for an immediate end to the war, which he identified as a central cause of the worsening humanitarian situation. He urged the parties to respect international humanitarian law, open safe corridors for aid deliveries , protect humanitarian convoys and hold accountable those who obstruct relief operations. He appealed to the international community and the United Nations to act urgently to prevent further deaths and protect civilians. title: Cube Orange-Powered Aircraft Fly the Tactical Range at the Military International Drone Racing Tournament UK 2026
body:
Australian autopilot maker CubePilot supplied several fixed-wing tactical aircraft for the Military International Drone Racing Tournament at the Royal Military Academy, Sandhurst, England, each powered by its Cube Orange flight controller.
Teams of four pilots from 12 nations competed against the clock, combining speed and precision with tactical judgement and accurate aircraft control. Pilots were required to intercept fixed-wing aircraft, navigate a complex assault course and deliver simulated munitions against multiple targets.
Intercepting a fixed-wing aircraft with an 5-inch FPV drone is far harder than flying a gate course. Pilots must predict the target’s path, close on it and strike under time pressure. The format builds on MIDRT Australia 2026 in Sydney, where pilots jousted with 7-inch FPV drones against Cube Orange-powered fixed-wing targets.
The Cube Orange has triple-redundant IMUs and runs the open-source ArduPilot ensuring the reliability to fly target runs heat after heat.
The Australian Defence Force Drone Racing Team cemented their dominance in military drone racing winning the title of champion nation for the eighth consecutive tournament, with Ukraine second on its debut.
Hamish Glover (Mish), a CubePilot test engineer and Australian Army Reservist, won the overall competition to be crowned the fastest military drone pilot in the world.
“Racing and tactical flying draw on the same core skills,” Glover said. “The reflexes, line choice and split-second decisions you build on a track are exactly what you need to intercept a moving target. The mission is simple: race hard, learn fast and continue to build the skills needed in today’s rapidly changing environment.”
CubePilot is the founding sponsor of the MIDRT series and CEO, Philip Rowse is a staunch supporter of Australian sovereign capability: Australian-designed hardware, flown by Australian-trained pilots.
“Australia has world-class engineers and pilots, and we have to keep investing in them,” Rowse said. “That is what sovereign capability looks like: Australian skill and talent building and flying Australian technology. We backed MIDRT from the start because it develops exactly those people.”
At Sandhurst, both halves of that idea were on show. Australian Cube Orange autopilots flew the targets, and an Australian engineer took the top prize.

title: Sudanese anti-war forces present peace roadmap to regional and international mediators
body: Sudanese anti-war civilian forces have presented a roadmap for ending the war to a regional and international five-party (Quintet) mechanism, as joint meetings began at the African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa on Monday. The talks aim to coordinate efforts to end the armed conflict and address the roots of Sudan’s longstanding political crisis. The participating forces are pushing for a Sudanese-led political process that can deliver lasting peace and restore civilian democratic rule. The civilian delegation brought together representatives of the Sudanese Declaration of Principles forces, the Popular Congress Party, civil society organisations, women’s and youth networks, and prominent public figures. The Quinet comprises representatives of the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the League of Arab States, the European Union and the United Nations. A final document and comprehensive vision submitted by the anti-war forces to the mechanism, obtained by Radio Dabanga, sets out proposals covering humanitarian assistance, a ceasefire and a political process. ‘Proposed 40-member preparatory committee’ The roadmap proposes establishing a 40-member preparatory committee to ensure broad representation in the political process. Under the proposal, 20 seats would go to forces that have not aligned themselves with either side in the fighting. The remaining 20 seats would be divided equally between forces aligned with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and those aligned with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The document calls for an immediate, unconditional humanitarian truce to protect civilians and allow relief supplies to reach those in need without restrictions, paving the way for a permanent ceasefire. It also urges strict sanctions against networks and companies financing the war, particularly those linked to the gold sector , and calls for an arms embargo covering the whole of Sudan. ‘Calls to exclude former ruling party from settlement’ The proposed roadmap rejects granting legitimacy to authorities established by either party to the conflict. It also calls for the exclusion of the National Congress Party, its Islamic Movement and their political fronts from any future settlement. The anti-war forces say a political process must address the roots of the crisis while safeguarding Sudan’s unity and stability and meeting the aspirations of its people for a civilian democratic transition. title: El Burhan orders investigation into deaths of Sudanese miners near Egyptian border
body: Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) Commander and Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council President, Lt Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan, has ordered a fact-finding committee to investigate the deaths of Sudanese miners near the Egyptian border. The committee will include representatives of the Public Prosecution and relevant judicial and security authorities. It will investigate the circumstances of the incident, establish the facts and submit a report on its findings, the council said in a statement seen by Radio Dabanga on Monday. This follows a similar probe conducted in the wake of a reported attack by Egyptian forces earlier this year on June 17 and 18. ‘Conflicting reports on death toll’ Reports on the number of miners killed in Saturday’s bombing differ sharply. The Sudan Doctors Network reported 13 deaths and 28 injuries, while the Emergency Lawyers group reported that at least 72 miners had been killed. The figures have not been independently reconciled. The incident has drawn widespread condemnation, with critics calling on the authorities to end their silence, establish the facts and make the findings public. The council said the leaderships of Sudan and Egypt had remained in contact following the incident, stressing the need to protect lives, preserve relations between the two peoples and establish the facts for public scrutiny. It described protecting the lives, safety and dignity of Sudanese citizens as a fundamental responsibility of the state. It also stressed the need for a serious investigation to establish the facts and ensure respect for the border. The council expressed condolences to the families of the Sudanese miners killed in the incident in the border area between Sudan and Egypt. The accusation casts Kyiv’s refinery strikes as a planned political move against Republicans, and it has spread from anonymous social media accounts to national television and members of Congress, Yarysh notes. Blogger Jack Posobiec, who has a multimillion audience, has urged Washington to immediately stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine and cut off its funding, framing the strikes as an attempt to hurt Trump before the vote. When you cannot fix the problem, try to control the story Yarysh reads the campaign as damage control. The Republicans’ weak position before the vote stems mainly from the economy and a jump in domestic fuel prices, he says, a problem the promised Russian diesel cannot solve. title: WindBorne wins a hefty US Air Force contract for its balloon data
body:
The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by WindBorne Systems ‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup.
WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model. WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model.
The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in. The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data. It can place orders for specific regions at specific times. So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow.
“This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch. He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.”
WindBorne CEO John Dean told TechCrunch in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business. Earlier this summer, the company released the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which it says provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics.
Since the arrival of transformer model architectures and the ECMWF’s release of a massive weather dataset a few years ago, AI weather forecasting has become one of the more productive uses of deep-learning technology. Meteorologists previously relied on expensive supercomputers running detailed equations that approximate how the atmosphere behaves. Now, end-to-end learning can ingest decades of weather data and issue predictions more quickly.
Models built by frontier labs and government agencies are proving more accurate than traditional forecasts, although it is still a jagged frontier, with both types of forecasts required to enable useful understanding of the weather. Google DeepMind’s latest weather model offers important new capabilities, and its cyclone forecasting tools are becoming increasingly central to how the U.S. government responds to hurricane season.
In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the eye of a typhoon . The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go.
“That’s a pretty novel step, and the two ingredients for that are one, having good wind and weather models, and knowing how to navigate them; and two, having a large enough constellation that you have balloons in the right places,” Sushko said. “It’s one of the first times that a deep-learning model was used for actual operational decisions.”

title: your c is not standard c
body:
this is an incomplete list of some incompatibilities between c as it's written in the standard and c as it exists in the real world for people who use gcc/clang + glibc/musl. asm by default, gcc and clang recognize the asm keyword as an extension. this is not strictly conformant, because in standard c, asm is a valid non-reserved identifier. so code which conforms to the standard may not compile with gcc/clang with their default settings. and like, whatever, that's fine, that's why -std exists, but 1. it's notable that compilers aren't conformant by default , and 2. why doesn't the standard just make asm a reserved word? c++ does that; i'm not sure why c doesn't. FLT_ROUNDS the standard specifies the FLT_ROUNDS macro in float.h as follows: 5.3.5.3.3p23 : The rounding mode for floating-point addition for standard floating types is characterized by the implementation-defined value of FLT_ROUNDS . Evaluation of FLT_ROUNDS correctly reflects any execution-time change of rounding mode through the function fesetround in <fenv.h> . notably, the standard requires that the value dynamically changes with the runtime floating environment. gcc, however, always defines FLT_ROUNDS to 1 (rounds to nearest), regardless of the runtime rounding mode: /* Addition rounds to 0: zero, 1: nearest, 2: +inf, 3: -inf, -1: unknown. */ /* ??? This is supposed to change with calls to fesetround in <fenv.h>. */ #undef FLT_ROUNDS #define FLT_ROUNDS 1 clang defines a builtin for this ( __builtin_flt_rounds() ), but gcc doesn't, for some reason. standard pragmas at some point in the future i'm gonna make an entire blog post dedicated to just this, because i kinda find it fascinating. but the super duper short version is this: the c standard specifies five standard pragmas to control the behavior of floating point arithmetic: // added in c99: // switch can be ON, OFF, or DEFAULT #pragma STDC FP_CONTACT ON #pragma STDC FENV_ACCESS ON #pragma STDC CX_LIMITED_RANGE ON // added in c23: // direction can be FE_DYNAMIC, FE_DOWNWARD, FE_TONEAREST, // FE_TONEARESTFROMZERO, FE_TOWARDZERO, FE_UPWARD, or some // other implementation-defined value #pragma STDC FENV_ROUND FE_DYNAMIC #pragma STDC FENV_DEC_ROUND FE_DYNAMIC however, over 27 years after c99 was standardized, gcc still doesn't support any of the standard pragmas . they're just no-ops in gcc. some (but not all) of the functionality can be replicated with command-line flags, but those operate on the entire translation unit, whereas the pragmas can apply to individual functions and blocks. clang mostly supports the c99 pragmas, but still doesn't support the c23 pragmas. there's actually so much more to say about these. i will be writing more about them at some point, but rn i don't really have the motivation cuz it's such a big thing lol qualifiers in function return types the standard requires that qualifiers in function return types are discarded: If, in the declaration " T D1 ", D1 has the form D ( parameter-type-list opt ) attribute-specifier-sequence opt and the type specified for ident in the declaration " T D " is " derived-declarator-type-list T ", then the type specified for ident is " derived-declarator-type-list function returning the unqualified, non-atomic version of T ". The optional attribute specifier appertains to the function type. but clang treats them as significant: $ cat t.c int f(); const int f(); $ clang t.c t.c:2:11: error: conflicting types for 'f' 2 | const int f(); | ^ t.c:1:5: note: previous declaration is here 1 | int f(); | ^ 1 error generated. the two declarations should be identical, but clang thinks they're incompatible. outdated va_start definition on musl for some reason, musl provides its own versions of some headers which the compiler already provides itself. one of these is stdarg.h , which is required to be supported by freestanding implementations and so is virtually guaranteed to already be provided by the compiler. but because it's provided by musl, compilers will use that header instead of the builtin one. this is a problem because musl's header is strictly worse than the builtin header. here's how musl defines va_start : #define va_start(v,l) __builtin_va_start(v,l) this definition is incorrect, because c23 allows the second argument to be omitted. it should be defined like this: #if __STDC_VERSION__ >= 202311L #define va_start(...) __builtin_c23_va_start(__VA_ARGS__) #else #define va_start(v,l) __builtin_va_start(v,l) #endif the result is that, when compiling for musl, c23's single-argument va_start can't be used, even if it's supported by the compiler. see also notes on how glibc and musl handle math errors ( math_errhandling ) oh, apparently it's not possible to portably check for string-to-float conversion errors in standard c : a case where posix arguably specifies a family of functions incompatibly from standard c neither gcc nor clang are compliant with standard c++ : gcc and clang don't store language linkage information with function types in c++, contrary to what the standard requires yet another place where a linux man page is inaccurate (containing a deleted section from this post!)
