title: GUEST BLOG: The hidden constraint behind scaling unmanned maritime fleets
body:
When a U.S. Navy Task Force 59 unmanned surface vessel USV) helped rescue two downed airmen in the Persian Gulf in June of 2026, it underscored something the defense community has known for some time: that unmanned maritime systems are no longer experimental. They’re actually operational assets expected to execute real missions in contested environments.
That shift from experimentation to operational deployment is accelerating. Better platforms, more capable autonomy stacks, improved sensors, and growing investment are rapidly expanding both what unmanned systems can accomplish and the scale at which they can operate.
As programs move from individual vehicles to distributed fleets, a different constraint is beginning to emerge – the growing complexity of integrating communications, mission systems, and disparate networks into a single operational architecture that scales.
Every new vehicle, transport, and mission system introduces another networking assumption. One platform relies primarily on satellite communication (SATCOM), while others communicate over cellular, mobile ad hoc network (MANET), line-of-sight radios, shipboard networks, or whatever infrastructure happens to be available in theater. Individually, each network works, until it doesn’t. Collectively, they create an increasingly fragmented operational environment with fragile routing, brittle configurations, and mission tools that often only work when the network is perfect.
Autonomy doesn’t eliminate the need for command and control
Much of the conversation surrounding unmanned systems focuses on platform autonomy. Modern USVs are increasingly capable of navigating, sensing, and executing mission plans with limited human intervention, but autonomy doesn’t eliminate the need for command and control.
Operators still need to redirect missions, update objectives, monitor telemetry, coordinate across multiple assets, and respond to changing operational conditions – all of which distributed maritime operations depend upon.
The Navy’s unmanned strategy calls for a digital infrastructure that can integrate unmanned capabilities at speed and scale, standardize command-and-control and network interfaces, and enable individual technologies to operate within a broader architecture of networked warfighting systems. In other words, fielding the vehicle is only part of the challenge, but integrating it into the force is what makes it operationally useful.
Once integrated, the challenge extends beyond keeping a vehicle connected. The issue then becomes whether command authority, telemetry, and mission data remain available as communications conditions change. Mission continuity depends on more than keeping a single communications link alive. It depends on making the network resilient enough that operators don’t have to think about which transport is carrying the mission.
The network has become the integration challenge
Scaling unmanned fleets introduces a hurdle that is as much operational as technical. Every communications transport has its own configuration, routing rules, security requirements, and management processes, while every platform manufacturer carries different assumptions about networking. Mission applications often inherit that complexity, forcing operators and network engineers to manage the underlying infrastructure instead of the mission itself.
That diversification creates an expanding logistics burden: As fleets grow, the networking layer becomes increasingly difficult to manage, not because any individual transport is inadequate, but because operators are forced to coordinate many of them simultaneously.
The Pentagon’s Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG) is applying pressure across the broader force by accelerating the fielding of large numbers of autonomous systems. However, increasing the number of platforms will not create true operational scale if every additional vehicle brings another proprietary network, more integration to perform, and an additional sustainment burden. In contested environments, communications links degrade, SATCOM may become unavailable, cellular coverage may disappear, and electronic warfare (EW) may force traffic onto entirely different transports.
Even those adverse conditions shouldn’t require operators to rebuild the network while executing the mission.
Ensuring that a mission continues uninterrupted when a communications link inevitably changes requires, in part, treating the network as a resilient operational layer rather than a collection of independent communications systems.
The goal is not for every link to survive indefinitely, but rather for the network to recognize changing conditions, transition mission traffic across the paths that remain available, and continue delivering data to the command-and-control systems where it can be acted upon.
That distinction becomes especially important as forces grow more distributed. The Navy’s Project Overmatch seeks to connect platforms, sensors, and weapons across naval and joint architectures. Neither can be achieved at scale if network transitions remain platform-specific, manually managed, or dependent on perfect communications conditions.
As autonomous maritime programs expand, several architectural principles become increasingly important:
The defense industry has made remarkable progress building more capable autonomous maritime platforms. The next challenge lies not in making unmanned vessels smarter, but in making increasingly diverse fleets operationally manageable.
The heterogeneous network that connects the future fleet should turn that diversity into an operational advantage, preserving the reach and mission relevance of each platform across changing communications environments. The organizations that succeed will be the ones that reduce networking complexity, integrate disparate communications into a unified operational architecture, and preserve mission continuity as conditions inevitably change.
James Kubik is CEO and Co-Founder of Somewear Labs.
Somewear Labs · https://somewearlabs.com/

title: Iran ready for both diplomacy and war: deputy FM
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi says Iran is finalizing its response to US views on a proposal Iran and remains prepared for both diplomacy and military confrontation.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Deputy Foreign Minister made the comments in an interview with Qatari Al Araby television, where he also said Tehran would continue participating in talks with Washington while maintaining its readiness to defend the country under any scenario.
He said the United States had violated its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, despite Iran’s continued engagement in the negotiations.

title: Russian lawmakers propose tougher penalties for inciting ‘terrorism’ and riots. Online comments advocating mass unrest could mean up to six years in prison.
body: State Duma members Vasily Piskarev and Eduard Valeyev of United Russia have drafted a bill to toughen penalties for public calls for terrorism and mass unrest. The government has backed the bill, TASS reported, citing an official cabinet assessment the news agency obtained. For public calls for mass unrest, the bill would raise the maximum term for court-ordered restrictions on offenders’ movements from two to three years and the maximum sentences of forced labor and imprisonment from two to four years. Calls for unrest made online would carry up to six years in prison. For public calls for terrorism, the bill would also set a two-year minimum and a six-year maximum for an additional penalty barring offenders from holding certain positions or engaging in certain activities. Currently, there is no minimum, and the maximum is five years. The lawmakers said the amendments were needed to “strengthen the deterrent effect of criminal law.” They said public calls for terrorism are often made “in closed groups whose members have no intention of reporting what is happening to law enforcement” or assisting the authorities. For that reason, the lawmakers believe the additional penalty barring offenders from engaging in certain activities should have a minimum term and a higher maximum. TASS did not specify whether the bill had been submitted to the State Duma or when the lawmakers planned to submit it. According to OVD-Info , calls for terrorism under Article 205.2 of Russia’s Criminal Code remained the most common charge in political cases in 2025, with 102 criminal investigations opened under that article. title: What I've been seeing lately (in software)
body:
What is going on in software? You know what Iâm talking about, the stuff with Generative AI. This thing that everyone is frothing talking about. Apparently I am too.
Letâs not talk about that for a minute, and instead look at my little world as of late:
There are people who care. Around me I am seeing more and more people who care about the âart of softwareâ force themselves to not give into LLMs, and we are.. losing slower, mostly. Or not?
Where I feel we are gaining, it is more extremely hobbyist. It is better ideas that are being done with the (little) execution we have. So now, what are these ideas?
This has to come first for everything else to work.
We are normalizing handmade creative output and asserting that the practical merits of a tool cannot outweigh the moral ones; the masterâs tools will never dismantle the masterâs house. @
I feel attacked when someone shows me an AI-generated video, forcing it on my eyes, devaluing good food with cheap sugar and MSG. Diet coke. There is no way out but through, our species is so addictedâ¦
A friend of mine is working on Evocation , a ground-up computing system targeting x86 bytes with Forth. It is difficult work. She does not have many facilities to work with; the ones that do exist are a pain in the ass to use.
Programming is labor. Any particular project requires a lot of it, continuously. Most software systems are inadequately documented â context lives in developer brains.
We do not have the luxury of halting work for a year, to switch to something more important. We need to keep going, nothing can be done without that.
A software community I am part of is fairly young; a few months ago Polyphony was solely a vessel for polyproto , but lately it has been maintaining capacity for at least one more project â slopscore .
Itâs been very nice to see that we can grow a community as substantive as this, and while itâs puny in effect compared to the likes of worm-blossom who are getting funded somewhat consistently.. itâs something! It makes me have faith what we are doing is right: itâs also a social movement.
Hopefully some more time passes, and we see a third project really come to life. We did try, but nothing much has come of it for now.
(Luckily, we didnât explode from 2,320,103 people wanting to learn more about a Helix fork. So we should be able to keep trying.)
Yes, me too. I donât know yet, but EMMA is a good model. Maybe you should ask Dave instead . Might write about this if I figure it out.
A few years ago, I was contributing to rather mainstream projects. Stuff like wireless VR streaming or nixpkgs . This was fun, it felt like the most important place for me to be. I felt free to be one more ant building this Sisphyean castle of low-level dreams.
But I no longer feel aligned with these large commons, the way I do with Wikipedia or Polyphony. Itâs simplyâ¦ inadequate.
The whole world is polarizing lately, and the ruling class seems to understand the degree to which software rules the world. So they will take slop for less whiny developers who donât care about ethics or appearances.
So many developers want to climb up the stairs ladder - again, to dismantle the mastersâ house with his own tools. But this is futile; they donât have to use LLMs! People just do everything for them. In fact â maybe the AI psychosis is good for not feeling like a horrible person!
Look, reader, there are some wonderful things out there being made. David Bushell âs website. Weird websites . Willow! And the Website League is trying to escape its Fediverse tech stack heading for a new greenfield solution. Fluxer is planning to add federation, E2EE and other goodies. Someone made a A DIY electrolysis machine with firmware in Rust.
Little corners of the internet where I feel alive and good about myself. Corners where we just get it, where I can look people in the (maybe-)metaphorical eye.
I want to see this keep going. I want to see post-LLM development grow and get institutional support.
Today, the Dutch government uses Forgejo more @ code.overheid.nl . Thereâs something akin to a flagship instance with Codeberg too, which is run by a German nonprofit ( verein ).
The French government uses NixOS , and theyâre working on replacements for common cloud services . Itâs not everything, and I donât feel it is even close to reaching developers outside European governments and their periphery, but something is happening for sure.
Personally, I look forward to writing complicated software.
The world seems tired of one-more-SaaS to my eyes.

title: Muse Wonder Puts Meta Back at the AI Frontier
body:
Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today.
The Muse Wonder models will be available through an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent.
Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky, with some researchers not sticking around for long.
Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups.
But the company fell behind after delivering several disappointing versions of the model, and as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google rapidly introduced more capable models.
Meta announced the first model from its new lab, Muse Spark, in April of this year. The company has also released a small open-weight model called Muse Glimmer, and says it plans to release larger open-weight models in the future. It did not disclose details of how new Muse Wonder models were built or trained.
Muse Wonder was built to compete with the very best, however. Meta says the largest version of the new model outperforms Anthropic’s second-best model, Claude Fable 5.1, and ranks just below its best, Claude Opus 5.5, on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a widely used aggregated score of model capabilities.
Meta says the model outperforms OpenAI’s best model, GPT-6 Astra, and both Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 on some specialized benchmarks, including ones that measure a model’s ability to work with legal documents and to build software. Benchmarks are not always a reliable measure of real-world performance, but this is still a significant step forward for Meta’s models.
Muse Wonder also includes two novel features designed to help make agents more effective and less inclined to misbehave. The new features, called Active Memory and Active Focus, are designed to keep the model locked into a stated goal and prevent it from becoming confused. This can be a challenge when AI performs complex research or builds a large software project, for example, and can lead to expensive mistakes or compounded errors.
Meta says it has put significant effort into training Muse Wonder to refuse to generate dangerous outputs, such as recipes for building bioweapons or help with hacking. It says the company scores well on several benchmarks designed to measure how resilient models are to those prompts.
A series of recent incidents involving rogue AI agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others also shows how easily powerful AI models can stray when given open-ended commands. Meta did not disclose whether it has seen agents powered by Muse Wonder misbehave in testing or what it has done to mitigate this issue specifically.
Zuckerberg said in a post on X last month that the company had delayed the release of its Muse models to work on safety. Meta also revealed a framework designed to ensure that it scales its models’ capabilities safely in a blog post earlier this month.
Muse Wonder may add more fuel to an already furious race to develop more capable AI, however. It certainly suggests that Meta is once again competitive in the increasingly high-stakes AI race.

title: Ukrainian F-16 flew over Poland
body:
On Monday, 12 October, a Ukrainian F-16 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Royal Netherlands Air Force, flew over Poland. The aircraft passed over Tomaszów Lubelski, later heading towards Wrocław and Legnica. It crossed the Polish-German border and headed towards Belgium.
On Monday, 12 October, a Ukrainian F-16 fighter jet appeared over Poland. It entered Polish airspace near Tomaszów Lubelski. Its presence was reported by Polish Military Radar at 13:28.
The machine flew over several cities, including Wrocław and Legnica. The aircraft crossed the Polish-German border and flew over Belgium. The purpose of the flight is likely a technical inspection.
The aircraft was most likely flying to maintenance facilities. Such plants for F-16AM/BM aircraft—the variants operated by Ukraine—are located in Belgium. It should be recalled that the fighter jets at Ukraine’s disposal are heavily utilised and, at the same time, are already quite worn (the newest may date back to the 1990s, while older ones are from the 1980s). However, they are used intensively in combat to intercept cruise missile attacks and to engage jet drones using their cannons. Ammunition for the latter was recently reportedly supplied by Poland, among others.
Every few hundred flying hours, however, Ukrainian F-16s require an inspection that cannot be carried out within Ukraine. Final assembly of the aircraft now held by the Ukrainians, as well as subsequent modernisations, was carried out in Belgium and the Netherlands at the end of the Cold War (with equipment components manufactured in Denmark and Norway); hence, the expertise to perform the required maintenance is located there. It should be emphasised that such flights require coordination with the Polish authorities, but they have already been conducted on multiple occasions. For example, in August, one of the F-16s flew towards Denmark.

title: ‘Noticeable shift in warfare’: US Army under secretary on the lessons of modern combat
body: The U.S. Army is entering unprecedented territory. Demand for exquisite munitions has skyrocketed as conflicts in Iran and Ukraine — and an ever-tense Indo-Pacific — continue to redefine stockpile demand. So, too, has there developed an insatiable market for cheap systems and interceptors capable of balancing scales that, in regions like the Middle East, have been encumbered by cost-per-kill ratios as lopsided as 114-1 — in the case of a PAC-3 interceptor versus a Shahed-136 drone. If that weren’t enough to consider, there’s the lightning-quick speed of AI integration and unmanned systems into formations, and the reality of having to rethink a simple concept — hiding — that was seldom given a second thought due to the total air superiority of the Global War on Terror. Such frenzied developments, meanwhile, come against a backdrop of new Pentagon policy that aims to eliminate the antiquated red tape of the acquisition process and speed development to the battlefield. A daunting cluster of problems to solve, no doubt. But if encountering such a catalog of to-dos is stress-inducing, one would not know it when speaking to U.S. Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal, who finds himself at the center of many of these discussions. From his office and out on the trail, Obadal oversees the service’s business operations, acquisition strategy, and manpower and personnel systems, among myriad other duties. Obadal assumed the position after a stint in the private sector, which followed a military career that included time as a Special Operations officer, the status of Master Army Aviator and qualifications in nine different aircraft. Obadal spoke to Military Times about how he and the Army are approaching these seismic shifts in warfighting philosophy, and how this year’s AUSA exposition reflects the blistering pace of innovation that catalyzes them. There are many examples of individuals without military experience working in consequential positions within the Pentagon. You are not one. How has your military experience shaped how you approach this role? What I try very hard to do is not let my experience drive the way I do things. I want it to inform the way I do things, whether that’s my experience working with the interagency and seeing how other executive branch agencies operate, my experience in the conventional military or in other parts of the military, doing joint work, working with partners and allies or going out into corporate America. I don’t want any one of those things to be the driver of how I make decisions and conduct myself in the business of the Army, but I do want all of it to come together and inform it. So, it’s certainly very helpful for me when I talk to soldiers or when I look at programs or weapon systems. The biggest thing it helps me with is understanding that there’s no single weapon system that operates by itself anywhere. They are all part of a joint force, and within that, you have a maneuver Army that is reliant — tanks are reliant on infantry, infantry is reliant on fires, all of it is reliant on aviation, medical and logistics. All those components work together as a chain, and you have to make sure every link in the chain is as strong as possible. That’s one of the biggest things that I take away from being in the military: an understanding that all of these things have to work in synergy, and there are no easy solutions. We continue to watch the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran unfold. What do you expect to see at an event like AUSA that reflects what America has learned from them? If you walk around the hall at AUSA, it’ll give you a good indication of the Army’s priorities. Our priorities are reflected in what we’re procuring. Going back several years, when we were in the Middle East and we first saw adversary drones — counter-drone systems became a really important topic. It kind of started in the special operations and then expanded into the larger Army. Ukraine has not just reinforced that counter-UAS is a critical part of operations today; it’s cemented it. So, if you walk around AUSA, you’re going to see an immense number of not only drones but also counter-UAS. That’s a reflection of the procurement and the budget, not just in the Army but in the Pentagon. That’s number one. Number two is software. Being able to see, sense and integrate to understand what your positional advantage is, and understand the adversary and their vulnerabilities. That’s just military operations, but today it’s looking at how we apply the best sensors and best software to bring all of that together to give decision advantage to our commanders. The third one is fires, and when you look at current conflicts, the importance of long-range precision fires is highlighted. So, what you’ll also see at the conference is a reflection of our investment portfolio in our magazine depth, but also the variety of munitions. Expanding out the optionality that commanders have beyond just one or two exquisite munitions, with everything from longer-range artillery, one-way attack and loitering munitions, up into our higher-end missiles. All of those represent our fires portfolio, but that’s just for offensive operations. When we get into the defensive side, we’ll be seeing everything from ballistic missiles down to Group One drones. If you look at those three areas — drones and counter-UAS; software and sensors; and the fires portfolio — and were to roll back the clock to AUSA 10 years ago, the difference is remarkable. At that time, the focus was very vehicle-centric, armor-centric, pieces of kit for individual soldiers. All of those things are important and are continuing to advance, but these newer investment areas represent a noticeable shift in warfare. These conflicts are obviously influencing the speed of acquisition. But that process includes an emphasis on both cost-friendly and exquisite munition stockpiles. What is the best balance to ensure success? The conflicts are definitely influencing and accelerating the way the Army — and certainly the broader Department — are innovating, prototyping, procuring and then fielding different capabilities. If you were to roll back a decade or even less, you would see very traditional models that go from experimentation into writing an initial requirement document, then into prototyping, then selection, then low-rate production and then finally into fielding and high-rate production. That’s years long. That process is very deliberate, and it built our military to where it is today, which is still the most dominant, but with a number of vulnerabilities because of technical innovation in the commercial market that adversaries are able to take advantage of. So, where can we compress this cycle and get it more into a process where we ask the commercial industry to experiment on their dime? A lot of this has to do with private capital being interested in the defense market. They’re making a bet that they can get through some of the experimentation, and then we can follow on with prototyping and quickly get into low-rate and high-rate production before fielding. Fielding then allows us to get immediate feedback that goes back into industry. That is essentially what had to happen in Ukraine because it’s existential to them. So, when we say wartime footing, Ukraine is on the ultimate wartime footing, and there are lessons to draw from there. What are the unnecessary steps in the acquisition process? Where can you smartly accept risk? Probably one of the biggest drivers of speeding things up is acknowledging that we’re willing to accept risk. We know that if we get a tighter innovation cycle, we’re accepting more risk on the battlefield, but we’re also driving down risk on the battlefield because we’re getting it to them much sooner. So, then we get into how that translates to fires. Exquisite versus low cost. It’s a balance, or a high-low mix, essentially, where we have to have both offensive and defensive exquisite weapons. We have to have certain stockpiles to be able to counter the exquisite weapons of our adversaries and have our own effects. Then you get into mass, which comes when we start going beyond the first few days of a conflict, and we’re in protraction. We have to have affordable mass. The cost curve needs to come back in our favor. While balancing the above, how much of a difference has the surge in domestic manufacturing made in having these pre-positioned elements assisting efforts? A massive difference. The Infantry Squad Vehicle is a perfect example. That’s a Chevy Colorado chassis; the drivetrain and suspension are a little different, but it’s nothing unusual. Essentially, it then goes to a detailer that puts the military-specific equipment on top of it. It’s everything that we need it to be. As with anything, it has its vulnerabilities. We’re sacrificing heavy armor and survivability, which we needed throughout the GWOT years, for mobility, transportability and ease of repair. But using this model also allows us to sustain it far more easily because so many of the components are commercial. It especially matters when you get into keeping the ISV — or domestically made equipment — in the decades ahead and needing improvements over the years. With the ISV, as Chevy makes improvements to its chassis and drivetrain, that immediately feeds back into the production line of ISVs. So, we’re now getting upgrades that are just byproducts of the commercial market. With acquisition, there’s a major emphasis on AI. What are you discussing with tech companies to ensure the human-in-the-loop element equates to maintaining final say despite the speed of the tech? Every company that deals with this emerging technology and the military is of the same mindset, which is that the human-in-the-loop factor has to be the default. There are workflows and cycles that human commanders can say, “I need this to run in the background, and I don’t need to see it or be on it.” But when it comes to kinetic kill chains and making decisions on the battlefield, the workflows that enable commanders have to have very hard stops. It’s not just a commander saying yes or no. It’s far more complicated and nuanced. It’s presenting options based on a tremendous amount of computing analysis and saying, “Here are all the courses of action based on the priorities that you gave, based on the environmental factors that the agents have been able to ingest and all of the long-term planning that goes into it. That allows the commanders to then take highly complex tasks like mission planning and distill it down into areas where they can consume it more easily, and then apply what only humans can do, which is context and reason. That context and reason part is what the tech companies that work with us are very focused on enabling, as opposed to taking over entire workflows. Autonomy is important, really, in three areas when it comes to warfighting. Think about combat breaching. That’s one of the most dangerous things we ask a human to do: to breach a linear minefield or barrier. If we can automate that, that removes something inherently dangerous. The second is highly complex, like command and control. How do you distill what would take human staff officers hours or days into seconds, and give a commander not only several options, but the analysis behind it and the confidence in the product being presented? The third is the ability to remove repetitive and mundane things human soldiers are doing. Resupplying via trucks, for instance. If we can automate that, we are removing that task from our logistics soldiers and allowing them to apply their talents to solving real problems with a clear vision and mindset. Beyond weapon systems, something as simple as staging — or hiding — equipment or personnel requires a vastly different strategy than even 10 years ago. How does something as simple as saying, “How do we hide this helo?” impact your conversations with industry? It’s not something that we’ve had to truly consider as an Army for 40 or 50 years because we were guaranteed air superiority. We don’t have air superiority at this point because of long-range fires and precision targeting from space. So, you go back to dispersion, displacement of assets and disaggregation of large headquarters. As you remember from recent decades, a division headquarters would be a massive entity with satellite dishes and other assets in the open. Those days are gone. We now have to consider how we bring in technology from the companies to allow us to displace 10-foot satellite dishes and 20 miles of wire, and actually have small-scale edge compute and transport systems that can disaggregate everyone. That’s incredibly important. Certainly, camouflage comes into play. Other classified capabilities come into play as well, and that’s all just the visible element. Then you get into electronic warfare and the ability to monitor. So, how do you disaggregate some of that? Those are all things that we are actively moving — and coming back to — in a more modern stance.

If we can automate that, we are removing that task from our logistics soldiers and allowing them to apply their talents to solving real problems with a clear vision and mindset. Beyond weapon systems, something as simple as staging — or hiding — equipment or personnel requires a vastly different strategy than even 10 years ago. How does something as simple as saying, “How do we hide this helo?” impact your conversations with industry? It’s not something that we’ve had to truly consider as an Army for 40 or 50 years because we were guaranteed air superiority. We don’t have air superiority at this point because of long-range fires and precision targeting from space. So, you go back to dispersion, displacement of assets and disaggregation of large headquarters. As you remember from recent decades, a division headquarters would be a massive entity with satellite dishes and other assets in the open. Those days are gone. We now have to consider how we bring in technology from the companies to allow us to displace 10-foot satellite dishes and 20 miles of wire, and actually have small-scale edge compute and transport systems that can disaggregate everyone. That’s incredibly important. Certainly, camouflage comes into play. Other classified capabilities come into play as well, and that’s all just the visible element. Then you get into electronic warfare and the ability to monitor. So, how do you disaggregate some of that? Those are all things that we are actively moving — and coming back to — in a more modern stance.

title: GUEST BLOG: Engineering the data ecosystem for decision advantage across CJADC2
body:
The Pentagon’s Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control (CJADC2) initiative aims to achieve decision advantage by connecting sensors, operators, and weapons systems. This massive undertaking is breaking down conventional silos in modern military operations, bringing land, air, sea, space, and cyber domains together into a single cohesive network.
By unifying these disparate nodes, the defense community intends to outpace and outmaneuver near-peer adversaries across the global stage. However, success is not defined by the sheer volume of data moving across the battlespace; it depends on engineering a data ecosystem that filters information to prevent operator task saturation under stress. While establishing complex communication lines between systems provides the necessary foundation, we must engineer the data landscape up front. Ultimately, true advantage relies on our trust in the information we receive – a trust built on rigorous data governance and secure architecture.
In the crucible of high-intensity conflict, our goal is to ensure that more data always translates into better choices. Pumping unfiltered, raw data streams across tactical networks can create a paradox of paralysis, where cognitive overload and operator task saturation become real operational challenges during high-stress scenarios. When a missile defense operator faces hundreds of simultaneous telemetry feeds, engineering must ensure that the critical signal stands out clearly from the surrounding noise. This necessity is magnified as our forces deploy next-generation, high-velocity initiatives designed to track and destroy ballistic, cruise, and hypersonic threats.
Within these fast-moving, multi-axis engagements, decision timelines compress from minutes to milliseconds, demanding a revolution in both our hardware and our data processing paradigms. From a physical perspective, the military must transition to a resilient, mobile command-and-control grid – an objective thoroughly analyzed by the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, which advocates for distributing communications across federated airborne and ground nodes to survive adversarial strikes.
However, while this distributed physical architecture ensures the network survives, it also threatens to flood the human operator with massive, decentralized data streams. To actively protect the operator from sensory flooding, this resilient hardware backbone must be paired with intelligent data filtering. Data quality has a direct impact to our use of artificial intelligence (AI). While AI is critical for accelerating these decision timelines, pumping unchecked data into algorithms creates dangerous vulnerabilities that we must proactively engineer out of the system. Treating AI as an integrated, fundamental component of our infrastructure allows us to manage operational risks effectively. This approach aligns with the directives outlined in the White House's National Security Presidential Memorandum on Artificial Intelligence in the National Security Enterprise (NSPM-11) , which mandates that national security agencies rapidly operationalize trusted AI while enforcing strict risk-management and system-assurance metrics. By ensuring that only verified, clean data flows into these systems, we solve the problem of task saturation and accelerate the speed of accurate decisions throughout the command loop.
Looking beyond our own networks, we must recognize that our adversaries are not passive observers of our digital transformation; they are actively engineering its vulnerabilities. In the next conflict, kinetic strikes and electronic jamming will be accompanied by invisible, data-centric warfare designed to spoof sensors, corrupt AI models, and inject hallucinatory operational signals into the battlespace. If an adversary can subtly poison the targeting data flowing into a high-velocity defense framework, they don't need to destroy our interceptors – they just need to make the algorithm look the wrong way.
Defeating this brand of algorithmic warfare requires shifting our defensive posture from physical armor to software-defined resilience, a reality underscored by an evaluation from the Center for Strategic and International Studies that highlights why software, not just physical platforms, will decide the next war. This is where the theoretical vision of CJADC2 transforms into a tactical imperative. Mission-grade AI cannot survive on inherently trusting, siloed networks; it requires an all-domain ecosystem where data integrity is actively weaponized as a defensive capability.
To achieve this, we must move beyond legacy authentication and embed autonomous "immune systems" directly into the tactical edge. Rather than sequentially authenticating every packet – which introduces lethal latency – these protocols must dynamically cross-examine data across domains in real time. For example, if a ground-based radar feeds tracking data into the network, but an orbital infrared sensor shows no corresponding heat signature, the system must instantly isolate the anomaly, downgrade the data’s confidence score, and quarantine the spoofed signal. Engineering this multisensor consensus into the telemetry level reveals the true utility of CJADC2. Rather than merely acting as a transport layer for the joint force, it forces incoming data to prove its own validity across multiple domains. This machine-speed verification is what ultimately protects our algorithms from spoofing and preserves our decision advantage
This hardened data ecosystem is what drives trust and interoperability across next-generation initiatives like hypersonic defense, missile warning, and advanced frameworks such as Golden Dome. Advanced missile warning and hypersonic tracking are designed to be deeply integrated into a reliable, secure enterprise where the integrity of sensor data remains absolute. The scope of this fiscal and strategic pivot is reflected in the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) FY 2027 Budget Estimates for Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation, which maps out robust investments designed to secure and mature the high-security computing facilities that power modern combat networks. By establishing a secure, resilient data foundation, we guarantee that multilayered defense networks maintain a single, unassailable version of operational truth, even under intense physical and cyber harassment. This structural strength is what enables our joint forces to operate with complete synchronicity, keeping the software environment robust against sophisticated external interference.
Ultimately, achieving CJADC2 decision advantage requires a shift in engineering focus. For too long, the defense industrial base has focused primarily on connectivity and the ability to move data from one point to another. While network capacity and raw speed remain important, the primary engineering imperative needs to change. We must architect data ecosystems not just to connect systems, but to defeat adversarial deception, simplify the battlespace, and sustain mission execution in contested environments. Hardening the data infrastructure provides the path to turning rapid network connectivity into actual, sustainable combat capability across all joint task forces worldwide.
We must move beyond the novelty of AI adoption and focus on the technical discipline of data hardening. The winner of the next conflict will not be the side with the most data. The ultimate strategic advantage belongs to the side that successfully structures its underlying data environment to execute complex decisions with clarity, confidence, and speed.
Ryan Nguyen, Ph.D., is Artificial Intelligence Capability Lead, Arcfield.

title: ‘Ford v Ferrari’ gets a tsarist makeover in ‘Battle of Motors,’ a lavish Russian drama about a race from St. Petersburg to Monte Carlo
body: “Bitva motorov” (“Battle of the Engines”), an adventure film directed by Ilya Malanin and inspired by real events, is now in Russian theaters. Andrey Nagel (played by Ivan Yankovsky), an automobile enthusiast in the early 20th century, decides to test the first Russian car, the Russo-Balt, in the Monte Carlo Rally. He and engineer Dmitry Bondarev (Yura Borisov) set out from St. Petersburg. Film critic Eduard Zhuravlev reviews this entertaining film, which can’t quite avoid patriotic undertones. It’s the early 20th century. Andrey Nagel (Ivan Yankovsky), a young lawyer, racing driver, entrepreneur, and publisher of Avtomobil magazine, has decided to begin manufacturing the Russian Empire’s first homegrown car. But neither private investors nor the Ministry of Railways believes in his venture. Working people can’t afford cars, while the wealthy prefer European models. Nagel nevertheless finds allies at the Russian-Baltic Wagon Works in Riga, where he builds the Russo-Balt with engineer Dmitry Bondarev (Yura Borisov). After spending almost his entire fortune on the car, Nagel decides to prove its quality at the Monte Carlo Rally . He and Bondarev set off straight from a wintry St. Petersburg. Nagel hopes to secure a government order from Emperor Nicholas II (Sergey Volkov), who dreams of showing up his German “cousin Willy.” Nagel is also courting racing driver Lidia (Paulina Andreeva), though their relationship remains platonic. Meanwhile, industrialist Gustav List (Yehezkel Lazarov), a loathsome rival from Benz, sets out to throw a wrench into the Russo-Balt’s progress — almost literally. Actor Ilya Malanin directed this patriotic racing drama. His screen credits include “Tobol” (“The Conquest of Siberia”), “Na rayone” (“In the Hood”), and “Inye” (“Others”). As a director, he made the uplifting dramedy “Nenormalny” (“Extraordinary”) and the Netflix series “Nichego osobennogo” (“Nothing Special”), which the American streaming service shelved because of the war. Besides Gazprom-Media and TNT, the film was produced by Pyotr Anurov’s Kinoslovo and Nikita Mikhalkov’s TriTe studio, which previously teamed up on the blockbusters “Serebryanye konki” (“Silver Skates”) and “Volshebnik Izumrudnogo goroda” (“The Wizard of the Emerald City: Part I”), as well as “Prorok” (“The Poet”), a musical about Pushkin. From the latter film, “Bitva motorov” (also known internationally by the title “Race to Monte Carlo”) inherited a wig-wearing Yura Borisov and almost the entire team: screenwriter Andrey Kurganov, cinematographer Mikhail Khasaya, composer Ryan Otter, and costume designer Tatyana Patrakhaltseva. The blockbuster has the scale of a Hollywood production. Its prerevolutionary Russia is all spotless St. Petersburg streets, gleaming cars, Nagel’s immaculate three-piece suits, and the delightful hats worn by the endearing suffragist Lidia. We also get a detailed look at the workshops of the Russian-Baltic Wagon Works in Riga, where the “Russian Cucumber” is repeatedly assembled and taken apart. An energetic race through the mud outside St. Petersburg looks impressive thanks to judicious slow motion, unexpected camera angles, and rapid editing. The final drive from Russia to Monaco is a full-fledged road movie within the film, taking up a third of its running time (it was filmed in Montenegro). Cars get stuck in the snow, hurtle along winding mountain roads, and fly through narrow European streets. For the film, the production team found authentic period cars or built replicas — about 50 in all. The early 20th century isn’t a favorite period for makers of racing movies, although the 1960s produced two hit comedies starring Tony Curtis: “The Great Race” and “Monte Carlo or Bust!” Structurally, however, “Bitva motorov” is closer to “Ford v Ferrari,” in which two men with different backgrounds and temperaments put up with each other in pursuit of victory. Nagel, a businessman with a taste for adventure, dreams of making history in his own right. He doesn’t want to remain a dreamer with grand but unrealized schemes in the shadow of his grandfather, Andrey Krayevsky, who published Lermontov, Gogol, and Dostoevsky. He’s willing to sell off the furniture in his apartment to fund the venture. Bondarev doesn’t always share his enthusiasm. He’s a hotheaded worker and devoted family man who has already spent time in exile for revolutionary activity. The bromance between Nagel and Bondarev is the heart of a film whose other characters are all one-dimensional. Still, Israeli actor Lazarov, who has worked with Nadav Lapid and Ari Folman, makes an impression through sheer charisma. His German scoundrel List is such a cartoonish villain that he would fit right into “Who Framed Roger Rabbit.” The real List, incidentally, didn’t compete in the Monte Carlo Rally — he was nearly 80 at the time. In real life, Bondarev oversaw Russo-Balt production but didn’t travel to Monaco for the rally himself. Vadim Mikhailov took part in the race, but the film never mentions him. The film ends in both triumph and defeat: The Russians reach Monte Carlo first but finish only ninth on points, winning prizes for endurance and the longest route. Nevertheless, the kindly Tsar Nicholas II appreciates their achievement, pardons the politically suspect Bondarev for taking part in the race illegally, and buys a batch of cars. For a couple of years, the Russian-Baltic Wagon Works becomes a center of automobile manufacturing. The closing titles conveniently omit that Nagel would move to Paris, the factory would be repurposed for military production, and Bondarev would be executed in 1937. At the end, the villain List wonders why “these Russians” risk their lives, freedom, and standing for minor victories, while the tsar says it doesn’t matter how things are judged in Europe — everyone already knows who the real winner is. This gentle patriotism may leave viewers feeling proud of the indomitable Russian spirit. But stepping out of the theater may dampen that feeling a little: Benzes are still on the road. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter . Eduard Zhuravlev

title: Russia’s sabotage of Europe should bring Ukraine more weapons through US purchase scheme, with clear statement of where its red lines lie, NATO’s top European commander says

NATO should respond to the attacks by increasing contributions to the alliance’s PURL weapons program or by sending Ukraine more air-defense interceptor missiles, Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrinform reports . The remark runs counter to a fresh scare. After US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, European officials said that Washington had threatened to halt weapons for Ukraine through PURL, the Financial Times reports, unless Kyiv stopped hitting Russian refineries. Grynkewich’s call to expand the program ran the other way. One of the main goals of Russia’s hybrid operations, from airspace violations to sabotage and cyberattacks, is to break the West’s will to keep backing Ukraine, he stated. The sharpest answer is to prove that assumption wrong, he argued, turning each attack into a reason to send more. The PURL program that lets allies fund US-made weapons for Ukraine, which drew nearly $5.5 billion in pledges before May. Name the culprit out loud, and watch Moscow lose its cover Once responsibility for a specific attack is established, countries should publicly name who did it, Grynkewich noted, so Russia understands it has been exposed and that its network was never as untraceable as it believed. Moscow bets it can escape blame because the West cannot work out who is behind an attack, in his telling. The response, he urged, should be to show that the West can. One voice, not thirty-two, is what Russia actually fears Coordination is the other half. Allies must craft a joint response rather than send Moscow chaotic, uncoordinated signals from individual states, he stressed, and must spell out clearly where their red lines lie. That unity is itself a deterrent. A single, agreed answer tells Russia the alliance is harder to split than its hybrid campaign assumes, and that attacks meant to divide the West only harden its resolve, he contends. title: India sells air defense missiles to Tajikistan, Turkmenistan in Central Asia push
body: NEW DELHI — India has sold its homegrown, short-range surface-to-air missile system called Akash, to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan gaining a foothold in Central Asia as it seeks to expand its defense exports. Analysts say these countries are turning to India to reduce their reliance on Russia, one of the region’s main arms suppliers, whose defense resources are strained by its war with Ukraine. “They are looking for a way to diversify at a time when Russia is no longer active in defense markets as it increasingly looks inwards towards its domestic needs, reducing its capacity to export air defense systems, especially in large numbers,” Aleksei Zakharov, a fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi told Defense News. “As a result, Central Asian countries are looking for possible alternatives.” Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the sales of the Akash surface-to-air missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan earlier this month in an interview with news agency Asian New International. He did not disclose the contract value. India moves closer to a homegrown, long-range air defense In 2022, Armenia became India’s first foreign customer for the air defense system. The Akash system can simultaneously engage multiple targets at ranges up to 25km according to the Defense Ministry. It also incorporates protections against electronic jamming. Calling the system one of India’s “success stories,” Singh said: “It shows the maturing of our indigenous missile design and production system. It is effective in dealing with high-velocity aerial targets.” Indian defense officials have said it was used effectively by the armed forces during the country’s four-day conflict with Pakistan in 2025. Confidence in the missile system got a boost after it was “battle-tested” in a real conflict, according to Zakharov and could encourage Central Asian buyers to consider other Indian hardware, such as artillery and radar systems, as growing geopolitical uncertainty prompts countries to broaden their supplier base. “Certainly this can be an important first step for India’s entry into the defense markets of Central Asia. For those countries, it is also about reducing dependency on any one single source which can be useful if there are disruptions,” he said. “The Indian systems such as Akash are also cost-effective.” In fact, Armenia has emerged as India’s largest buyer of military equipment, signing defense contracts worth nearly $2 billion since 2020, according to reports. Its purchases include multiple-launch rocket systems, counter-drone systems and anti-tank missiles. Analysts say India’s outreach in Central Asia also aims to balance China’s growing influence in the region where Beijing has emerged as a major supplier of military equipment in recent years. India, which has been a major arms importer for decades has been gradually developing its own defense industry and boosting exports, which rose about 62 per cent in the last financial year to $4.1 billion. Indian companies export missiles, drones, armored vehicles, ammunition and aircraft components to more than 80 countries. Its most high-profile export is the BrahMos, a supersonic cruise missile developed jointly with Russia. India has won customers in Southeast Asian countries like the Philippines, where it is delivering a shore-based, anti-ship system. New Delhi has also signed a deal with Vietnam, and discussions are underway with Indonesia to supply the missiles. “BrahMos is a kind of benchmark for our emerging export story. This is one of the high-end strategic systems that we’ve been able to export,” he said.

title: ‘Iran smells weakness’: Burnham challenged over IRGC after airbase plot
body: Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham was urged on Monday to take direct action against Iran if it succeeded in attacking a British airbase. The UK ​announced sanctions against ⁠two Iranian nationals who ⁠the ‌government ​said had been involved in Iranian plots to ​attack ‌Britain, which Mr Burnham blamed on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps . He was told by former deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden that Iran considered the UK its enemy and “smells weakness”. He said Iran had attempted attacks at bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, Akrotiri in Cyprus and Fairford in Gloucestershire. The UK introduced sanctions on the IRGC in July, following the first two incidents and a series of attacks against dissidents in previous years. A successful attack would require direct action, suggested Mr Dowden, who also asked for a pledge of “enhanced support and assistance to allies under constant attack”, noting the targeting of Saudi Arabia in recent days. Mr Burnham said Britain was providing the “most robust response” to the situation and “playing its part”. Under Monday’s sanctions, the head of counter-espionage operations within the IRGC, Ruhollah Bazghandi, will be subject to an asset freeze, travel ban and prevented from running any companies in the UK. The government believes he was directly involved in threatening, planning or conducting attacks against in the UK or against its allies. A key organiser of the Zindashti criminal network, Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, who the government said had been involved in several plots against Iranian dissidents, has also been sanctioned for supporting planned attacks. Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France ​and Germany issued a statement condemning "Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts ‌of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other ⁠hybrid activities against us and our partners". "The UK has also ​concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks ​and proxy actors," ‌the statement said. The developments were announced as Mr Burnham told the House of Commons that it was highly likely that the incidents at RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the US to launch attacks on Iran, were co-ordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC. Seven men have been arrested, and released, over a suspected attack on the base in Gloucestershire. Police said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in vans near the base, and detectives said they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved. The US decided to remove its B-1 bomber aircraft from ​the base after the attack, giving mixed messages over whether there had been direct intelligence of a plot to carry out a drone attack, or whether it had been done out of caution. Increasing danger The British authorities have accused Iran of being involved in numerous plots in Britain. In July, Britain used new powers designed to stop the use ​of state-sponsored proxies to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group accused of being behind attacks at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities and Persian-language media. Mr Burnham said: “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity if Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Iran’s continued attempts to undermine the security of the UK and its allies “through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable”. The Iranian ambassador was summoned for a foreign office dressing down but the Tehran state news agency afterwards described the British allegations as baseless. Iran's ​Ambassador ⁠to ⁠Britain, Seyed ​Ali Mousavi, ⁠denied any Iranian role ⁠in a ​suspected ⁠plot, saying Tehran was willing to cooperate with British ​authorities ‌in ⁠investigating the ​issue. “We are also announcing the designation of two Iranian nationals for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," Mr Miliband said. “This government will never waiver in our commitment to tacking Iran’s unacceptable actions and protecting our national security. We have already designated the IRGC under our new state threats powers, and imposed major sanctions on those responsible for Iran's malign activity.” The Foreign Office said the UK had identified at least 15 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals in the UK between 2022 and 2023, rising to more than 20 in 2025.

title: Lockheed Martin says proven interceptors underpin its expanding missile defense portfolio
body: The company’s latest overview presents operational experience and established technology as the foundation for that work. Lockheed Martin is pursuing upgrades to existing systems alongside new interceptors designed to fill gaps in layered air and missile defense. PAC-3 MSE is a fielded interceptor designed to counter aircraft, missiles and emerging hypersonic threats. It uses hit-to-kill technology to destroy targets through direct impact. In a recent flight test, PAC-3 MSE intercepted an airborne target while integrated with the Army’s Integrated Battle Command System and Lower Tier Air and Missile Defense Sensor. Lockheed Martin said the test brought the service closer to a 360-degree engagement capability. The U.S. Navy has also awarded a contract to integrate PAC-3 MSE into the Aegis Weapon System. That effort would extend the interceptor’s integration into maritime defense. Lockheed Martin and the U.S. government signed a framework agreement earlier this year intended to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity over seven years. The company said a $53.86 billion government contract awarded in July would accelerate production. The manufacturer is working with government and suppliers to streamline processes and expedite deliveries. It said demand from American and allied forces is increasing. THAAD provides terminal-phase defense against ballistic missiles, intercepting threats inside and outside the atmosphere. Lockheed Martin said operational engagements have supplied data demonstrating effectiveness against threats beyond the system’s original requirements. The company continues to improve THAAD’s interoperability and battery-level capabilities, including integration of PAC-3 MSE. It said IBCS connects THAAD to the Army’s broader air-defense picture, giving commanders greater awareness and more engagement options. Lockheed Martin is developing PAC-3 ACE, or Adapted Capability Effector, as a complementary interceptor for American and allied forces. The company said it is designed to counter a range of air and missile threats for less than half the unit cost of PAC-3 MSE. PAC-3 ACE uses existing PAC-3 MSE technologies, components and test data. Lockheed Martin said this approach would shorten flight-test cycles and accelerate fielding. The company introduced PAC-3 Edge on October 12 as its entry in the Army’s Future Interceptor competition. It builds on PAC-3 MSE and incorporates a new seeker, advanced propulsion and control-system upgrades for engagements at higher altitudes and longer ranges. Lockheed Martin is advancing development and testing toward residual operational capability by 2031. PAC-3 Edge is intended to complement PAC-3 MSE and THAAD against air, missile and hypersonic threats. Lockheed Martin is offering QuadStar for the Army’s Next-Generation Short-Range Interceptor program to replace Stinger. Its design combines advanced optics, a high-speed interceptor and a networked architecture, with intended engagement ranges exceeding those of the legacy system. The company is also participating in the Integrated Fires Protection Capability second-interceptor program. The Army awarded it an Other Transaction Authority project agreement late last year for work intended to fill the gap between short-range air defense and Patriot.

title: Army Pacific emphasizes forward deployment, readiness amid Indo-Pacific tensions
body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. The U.S. Army is emphasizing the forward positioning of combat-ready forces across the Indo-Pacific as tensions involving Taiwan, North Korea, and disputed territories continue to shape regional security requirements, Maj. Gen. Frederick L. Crist, commanding general of the 8th Theater Sustainment Command, said during a Warriors Corner presentation at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 conference.
Speaking during a session titled "Posture for Advantage -- United States Army Pacific Command Ready Forward," Crist said the Army's role in the region centers on ensuring that ground forces are positioned to support joint military operations across a theater that encompasses more than half of the world's land area and more than 60% of its population.
He pointed to several regional flashpoints, including tensions surrounding Taiwan, territorial disputes in the South China Sea and East China Sea, North Korea's nuclear ambitions, and border disputes between India and China.
The geographic scale of the Indo-Pacific, combined with the possibility of natural disasters, creates additional challenges for military forces operating throughout the region, he said.
Crist emphasized that the Army cannot afford to wait until a crisis develops to establish its presence and prepare personnel for operations. Instead, forces must arrive at strategically important locations with the training and readiness necessary to carry out their missions.
He cited lessons from previous conflicts, including World War II, Korea, and Vietnam, where the ability to position ground forces and secure key terrain played a central role in military operations.
During World War II, he noted, American forces relied on air and naval power to support ground operations that secured ports, airfields, and other strategically important locations as the campaign advanced across the Pacific.
Those experiences demonstrate the interdependence of land, air, and naval forces, Crist said, particularly when military operations require securing and holding territory.
To address current security challenges, Crist said U.S. Army Pacific is focused on moving forces from its command of more than 100,000 soldiers into forward positions where they can support joint operations and respond to regional contingencies.
The objective, he said, is to ensure soldiers are prepared to carry out their missions when they arrive, rather than requiring additional training after deployment.

title: The Pentagon’s drone revolution: inside the new DRPM-UxS office dismantling military bureaucracy
body:
With veteran reformer Bonnie Evangelista at the helm of procurement, a new Pentagon unit aims to bypass decades of red tape to supply frontline forces with cheap, adaptable autonomous systems.
The United States Department of Defense, long notorious for an acquisition bureaucracy that moves at glacial speed, has launched an ambitious structural overhaul to reshape how it buys military technology. At the centre of this institutional shake-up is the appointment of veteran procurement reformer Bonnie Evangelista to lead acquisition transformation at the newly established Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems office, known as DRPM-UxS. Formed under directives issued by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as part of “Project Agincourt”, the dedicated entity is tasked with consolidating the military’s scattered drone and counter-drone purchasing across the armed services. In an organisation where traditional contract negotiations routinely drag on for upwards of a year, Evangelista’s appointment signals a deliberate shift toward commercial agility and rapid frontline fielding.
The establishment of DRPM-UxS addresses a glaring tactical vulnerability highlighted by recent conflicts: the stark cost asymmetry of modern uncrewed warfare. For decades, the Pentagon’s procurement framework—governed by the rigid Federal Acquisition Regulation—was tailored for multi-decade strategic platforms such as aircraft carriers and fighter jets. Applying these 12-to-18-month buying cycles to software-defined drones, which iterate on multi-week cycles, means equipment risks technical obsolescence before ever reaching operational units. Furthermore, firing multi-million-pound interceptor missiles to neutralise low-cost, commercially modified attack drones creates an economically unsustainable cost-exchange ratio.
To dismantle these bureaucratic bottlenecks, DRPM-UxS has been granted “Direct Reporting” status, allowing its leadership team to bypass intermediate administrative layers across the Army, Navy, and Air Force. Steered by Chief Executive Officer Owen West—who took a temporary leave of absence from directing the Defense Innovation Unit—and supported by interim DIU director Travis Metz, the office reports directly to senior leadership. In his establishing memorandum, Hegseth made clear that the department’s primary objective is not to procure a single, static drone model, but rather to construct a “repeatable procurement system” that pushes capital and decision-making authority directly to warfighters at the operational edge.
In Evangelista, the Pentagon has selected a seasoned insider with a 17-year track record of challenging conventional military buying models. Having held senior roles across Army defensive cyber operations, industrial base policy, and special operations, her most influential work came as Acting Deputy Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer. There, she co-founded the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace, an initiative that replaced multi-hundred-page paper proposals with five-minute commercial video pitches evaluated by expert peer panels. By pre-clearing innovative technology, Tradewinds enabled defence buyers to award contracts in days rather than months.
Evangelista’s overarching methodology requires defence buyers to stop dictating overly prescriptive technical specifications to industry and instead articulate plain-language problem statements. To accelerate requirement generation, she previously pioneered generative artificial intelligence tools that translate warfighter feedback into structured, contract-ready problem descriptions in just 30 minutes. She now brings this flexible approach—leveraging non-traditional contracting mechanisms like Other Transaction Authority—to the uncrewed systems domain.
Crucially, DRPM-UxS is designed as more than a rapid buying mechanism; it is laying the operational foundation for a proposed functional four-star combatant command—the Autonomous Warfare Command—targeted for formal establishment by October 2027. While commercial firms and venture-backed startups gain expanded access to defence spending, suppliers must still satisfy strict cyber standards and supply chain restrictions, including bans on foreign-manufactured components. As history demonstrates, overriding entrenched service rivalries and legacy defence contractors remains an immense endeavour. Whether Evangelista’s agile playbook can permanently overcome the Pentagon’s institutional inertia will be the ultimate test.

title: Mangroves and mud: Inside the Army jungle school’s notorious ‘Green Mile’
body: Aeronaval Base Cristóbal Colón, Panama — A howler monkey looked down from his perch atop the lush canopy before unleashing a bellow so guttural that it seemed to temporarily swallow up the jungle’s hum. To his likely irritation, hordes of uniformed soldiers had gathered beneath the petite primate, filling his muddy underbrush with the heaving sound of heavy rucksacks and the smell of body odor that had been brewing in the moist terrain for days. The soldiers, some wearing days-old green face paint, had congregated amongst the moist fauna to complete their final task in the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama: The Green Mile. The notorious event — in the thick of Panama’s “Green Hell” — is the 18-day course’s culminating exercise, testing participants’ newly learned jungle maneuver techniques, survival measures and fighting skills. By that point in the course, the soldiers had run a days-long jungle reconnaissance and attack operation. That portion of the field exercise was complete, and perhaps to the howler monkey’s dismay, so were the soldiers’ attempts to stay quiet. The course in 2025 returned to Panama at Base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, formerly known as the U.S. Army’s Fort Sherman, decades after it was originally shuttered. The new course is a joint U.S.-Panamanian partnership, with Panamanian instructors leading lessons on jungle survival. With staggered start times, each squad took off running down a soggy, uneven path. Squads in the September course had participants from across the U.S. force, including those from the Army, Marine Corps and Space Force. Some squads had Panamanian soldiers. Other countries, such as Colombia, have expressed interest in sending soldiers in the near future. In classes with Panamanian students, instruction is given in English and Spanish. When the course is English-only, the duration shrinks to 12 days, but without partners, officials say U.S. students can miss out on opportunities to connect with other forces. Spc. Duncan Vaupel, a member of September’s jungle school course, said he talked with and learned from Panamanian troops who described treating soldiers who had lost legs and fighting gun battles in the jungle that stretched into the night. “These guys not only teach it, but they live and breathe it, too,” he said. The squad’s first major Green Mile task was to carry some of the service members’ rucks in a litter made from whatever they could find. Logs or long branches coupled with issued wet weather equipment — a poncho — did the trick. During the course, participants are provided instructions on jungle first aid. They also practice with medical evacuation helicopters, transporting a casualty to some sliver of open sky where a medical team can send a rappel line down to hoist the injured soldier up. Jungle landing zones are few and far between. Sgt. 1st Class Timothy Reeves, a combat medic and an instructor at the school, said that heat injuries are common because of the oppressive humidity and temperature. Animal-related injuries are also widespread, he said. Wild, territorial bees are sensitive to loud noises and will defend their hives by attacking the camouflaged intruders. “We do have wild bees down here that tend to get a lot of the students as they move throughout the jungle,” Reeves said. “I know we’ve had to evac a handful of students before to the aid station for bee stings, scorpion stings and a variety of insect bites.” Once the section of muddy pathway came to an end, there was the sea to deal with. Muddy boot after muddy boot sank into the swirling sand beneath unforgiving waves. Soldiers were instructed to file one behind the other, sometimes sinking waist-deep into the water as they skirted rocky outgrowths and navigated dense mangroves. Fewer troop formations work in a jungle environment, said Lt. Col. Andrew Eagan, who oversees the Jungle Operations Training Center. Wedge formations, for example, do not work, he said. “Here you fight in a column, you fight in a line, and the reason for that is the environment,” Eagan said. “The environment is so punishing.” When the Green Mile took the service members back inland, the soldiers traded the wet coastline for brutal terrain. Their next challenge? A hill so steep that it required crawling on hands and knees. With a grade impossible to climb with waterlogged rucks, the scrappier soldiers scaled ahead, breathlessly anchoring a rope bridge from the top so other soldiers could cling to it as they ascended while lugging the squad’s wet gear. Soldiers slipped, ripping pants and filling scraggly fingernails with brown mud. Weapons became caked with slippery earth as they reached the peak. During Eagen’s interview, he said Panama’s environment was the part of jungle school that U.S. students underestimated most. During The Green Mile, the true magnitude of the jungle’s hazards was revealed — relentlessly. There was no walking down the other side of the hill, for instance. Course participants scooted or slid down on their rears, praying that their nether regions would not cross the path of a black palm — one of the treacherous plants students learn about in the jungle, in addition to the school’s flora and fauna blocks of instruction. With pointy spikes that can reach up to 8 inches long, flaring from every inch of its trunk, soft flesh is no match for nature’s black needles. Other plants, students learn, are edible and can help them survive in such harsh environs. Some of nature’s bounty, however, keeps the jungle students’ digestive systems unusually active. 2nd Sgt. Rubén Rodríguez, a Panamanian instructor for the course, said American students are often particularly hungry. They love to pick and eat coconuts for extra nourishment, he said. Though delicious and healthy in moderation, coconuts can be laxatives in large quantities. The Americans’ frequent snacks, Rodríguez said, send them straight to the jungle bathroom. As the troops progressed through the course, lanewalkers added full water jugs and ammo cans to soldiers’ loads. The extra weight pushed boots even deeper into the muddy ground. Red-faced and exhausted, the squad hoisted the extra weight over and under the first leg of an obstacle course that represents the final, brutal stretch of the Green Mile. The squad dragged themselves — and their equipment — through sticky, brown goop as they low-crawled beneath barbed wire. Soldiers tossed gear over a high wall before hurling their own bodies over after the dumped equipment. Before the finish line, the squad trekked up another uneven hill — even more slowly than any hill they had summited before. Once they hit concrete — and the familiar terrain near the schoolhouse’s campus — the jungle-battered squad had just minutes to sprint the last stretch of what was actually a four-plus-mile endeavor. The instructors imposed a time cap on the event (because what is Army training without the addition of some artificial stress?). As the afternoon sun beat down on the squad, the sprint slowed to a heavy shuffle. One participant, who had been carrying extra weight, stifled a gag as he trod onwards. In a haze of instructor-cracked purple smoke, the squad finished, collapsing in a heap under the shade of a cluster of trees. Some soldiers emptied the water jugs over each other’s heads. Others lay spread-eagled in a lukewarm puddle of mud. Two participants — one with a ripped pant seam exposing a dirty, pale leg — reveled in their success. “It was a good time,” one said, looking at his friend. After a millisecond of hesitation, the friend responded. “Nah,” he said, shaking his head with a smile.
