title: UK’s Burnham Says Russia Interfered in 2016 Brexit Vote, Warns of Similar Activity in France, Germany
body:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “clear” Russia had interfered with the Brexit referendum in 2016, warning that similar activities were currently taking place in Europe – particularly France and Germany.
Burnham made the remarks on The Rest is Politics podcast released on Monday, Oct. 12. Later, he announced that the UK is planning to hold its annual meeting with the EU on Nov. 20, confirming the date in a statement to the House of Commons.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Asked about the Brexit referendum – which led to the UK narrowly voting to exit the EU in 2016 – Burnham said he had raised the question of Russian interference after arriving at 10 Downing Street. “I’ve had the clear answer that, yes, there was [interference],” he said, according to the BBC .
While Burnham did not specify in what form the interference took or how far Moscow’s activity realistically went during the Brexit referendum buildup, he argued the UK had not done enough to inform the public.
“I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas,” he said.
The issue of Russian interference was also brought up during a discussion with German Chancellor Friderich Merz during Burnham’s recent visit to Germany. “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” Burnham noted.
In recent months, Russia has escalated its aggressive rhetoric toward the West.
Russian diplomats have openly and directly threatened NATO over Kaliningrad and the Baltic states over the issue of Russian speakers , prompting concerns that the Kremlin may be searching for a justification for a direct attack on an EU member.
In recent days, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Ukraine’s prominent backer, has also come into focus after Polish authorities reported an alleged plot to assassinate him and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz .
Russia has also stepped up its cyberattacks and hacking operations, with Russian disinformation campaigns now targeting possible contenders in France’s April 2027 presidential elections , according to an analysis by Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications.
On Sept. 24, Marine Le Pen, France’s far-right National Rally leader and a contender in the country’s 2027 presidential election, said that she would end financial aid to Ukraine and withdraw France from NATO . According to Ukrainian analysts, pro-Kremlin narratives have similarly advocated for a future French president to leave the alliance and restore relations with Russia.
Concurrently on Monday, British Foreign Office Minister Stephen Doughty declined to discuss specifics of the 2016 Brexit case.
“Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes,” Doughty told BBC. “They’re engaged in information warfare, they’re spending £1.5 billion [roughly $1.9 billion] this year alone on disinformation and propaganda.”
Following Ukraine’s latest strikes on three Yandex data centers in Russia between Oct. 8 and 11, Russia’s cyber operations and automated online activity appear to have been substantially reduced .
However, Doughty denied claims that Burnham raised the issue as an argument for rejoining the EU. “This is a broader point he is making about Russian attempts to destabilize and interfere in our democracy,” he continued.
Pro-Brexit campaign group Britain Unbound called the remarks “another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016,” the BBC reported.
The group said foreign interference was “obviously unacceptable,” but disputed that it changed the result. “It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped,” it said.
In 2020, Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee reported on Russian activity in UK votes, reaching no firm conclusion on the referendum. Still, it criticized successive governments for failing to assess or counter the threat.
At the time, Russia’s foreign minister dismissed the report as “Russophobia.” The same year, then-Conservative government said it was “almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere” in the 2019 general election.
In his Commons statement, Burnham said he wanted to finalize the agreements previously begun by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
After that, he said, the UK should take a “calm, clear-eyed, rational look” at even closer ties with the EU. During the upcoming summit in November, both sides are expecting to sign agreements on agriculture and food trade, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme.
“If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have,” Burnham said, adding that “sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.”
As an immediate priority, he cited securing a successful outcome during the summit, which he believed would then set up a serious dialogue about the options for bilateral relations in the long-term.
According to Politico , Burnham’s previous option suggestions included rejoining the single market, customs union, or even the EU wholesale.
The meeting, he said, would also prove as a chance to raise the UK’s concerns about “Made in Europe” – EU’s program to favor European-made products, from which some member states want to exclude the UK.
European Council President António Costa issued a statement around the same time, explaining that the three deals could be complemented by agreements on a defense and security partnership, migration and law enforcement. “Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa, who is expected to join the summit alongside European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, said.
This year’s meeting was initially planned for July, but was postponed after Starmer’s resignation.
Meanwhile, Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of reopening settled debates, Politico reported.
“Just like some people thought all of Britain’s problems would be solved by leaving the EU, some now think all our problems will be solved by rejoining. Neither of these are serious positions,” she noted.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Built by Ukraine’s ex-defense minister and unit that wrecked $12 billion of Russian gear, new interceptor downs two jet drones over Kyiv
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A month from idea to first kill. A new interceptor drone built by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov's team with Pavlo Yelizarov, the commander of Lasar's Group unit, soldiers, and engineers, has shot down two Russian jet-powered Geran-5 drones heading for Kyiv, Fedorov says , just one month after development began. Russia's jet-powered Gerans fly far faster than the propeller Shaheds that Ukraine learned to shoot down, and they remain the hardest targets for its air defenses, which catch only about 55 percent of them. The new drone is fast enough to catch a jet drone before it reaches a city, Fedorov noted, adding that the two Geran-5 kills are the first confirmed for the interceptor. Crews from Lasar's Group in Ukraine's National Guard ran the combat trials and downed the two drones within days. Fedorov announced the drone on 12 October, Yelizarov's birthday. A former minister and a legendary commander behind the kill Yelizarov joined Ukraine's Defense Forces in 2022 and, in January 2026, became deputy commander of the Air Force, responsible for small-scale air defense and systems for intercepting Russian drones, Forbes Ukraine reports . He founded Lasar's Group, which destroyed $12 billion worth of Russian equipment. Fedorov, who ran the Digital Transformation and Defense ministries before moving to the private sector, says the interceptor is one of several projects his team continues to develop in Ukraine, combining engineering, military experience, and resources. The next goal: a drone that hunts Shaheds on its own The drone is not finished evolving. Testing continues as the team refines the technology and raises production, Fedorov said, with the next step a fully autonomous version that can detect and intercept Russian drones without an operator. The developers also plan to scale the interceptor's use to protect more Ukrainian cities, he added. The push fits a wider drive: Ukraine aims to build up to 400 interceptors a month to chase the faster Gerans. Read also Ukraine says it hit 12 Russian refineries in September. title: Acting Army Secretary invokes Bible in call for land dominance
body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle invoked the biblical creation of Adam during the opening ceremony of the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 conference, arguing that the Army's fundamental purpose is to control and secure land, a mission he said remains unchanged despite technological developments transforming modern warfare.
Telle drew on the Book of Genesis to explain humanity's historical connection to land, noting that Adam was created from the earth and that the Hebrew word *adamah* means ground or soil.
"Humanity's connection to the land is biblical, and it even transcends faith," Telle said, adding that the struggle to control territory has shaped human civilization since its beginnings. "Controlling and securing land is fundamental to human flourishing and fulfillment."
The remarks formed the basis of Telle's explanation of the conference's theme, "America's Army: Foundation of the Joint Force." He argued that while the Navy, Air Force, and other military branches operate across different domains, human civilization remains rooted on land.
He also pointed to the Army's historical role in shaping American territory, such as Army engineers mapping the frontier, developing waterways, and helping construct the Panama Canal.
Telle described the ability to dominate territory as the ultimate expression of military power. "Our ability to control and secure that piece of dirt is the ultimate deterrent," he said.
He said the Army's modernization efforts must ensure that its personnel retain that advantage against increasingly sophisticated adversaries. Under the Army's current modernization push, Telle said, the objective is to ensure that "when soldiers step onto the dirt, they own it, no question."

title: Army's drone marketplace generates more than $800 million in sales in 4 months
body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. The U.S. Army's online marketplace for drones and counter-drone systems has generated more than $800 million in sales over four months, according to a presentation delivered during Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle's opening ceremony address at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 conference.
The marketplace, available at drones.mil, allows soldiers to search for and purchase uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) and counter-UAS equipment based on operational requirements, Telle said. The system is intended to connect military personnel with manufacturers without requiring them to navigate traditional acquisition procedures.
Telle pointed to the U.S. southern border as an example of how the marketplace is being used to address emerging threats. He said cartels have increased their use of drones to monitor military personnel and identify opportunities to move contraband across the border.
In response, soldiers supporting the joint task force have used the marketplace to obtain counter-drone equipment without waiting for a lengthy procurement process, he said.
"What we did is cut out the bureaucratic middlemen and connected the soldiers directly with the builders," Telle said.
The marketplace operates much like a commercial e-commerce platform, allowing soldiers to search for equipment based on specific threats, compare products, and review ratings submitted by other military users.
Manufacturers can use that feedback to modify designs, adjust production, and manage inventory based on operational demand, Telle said. He added that orders can reach soldiers within days.
A video shown during the presentation indicated that dozens of companies have joined the marketplace, with thousands of products listed. The Army is seeking participation from startups and manufacturers of drone components, in addition to established defense contractors.
The marketplace is part of a broader effort to accelerate Army acquisition by increasing competition and giving soldiers greater access to commercially developed technology.
Telle said the Army has developed a similar marketplace for military test ranges, which he compared to the commercial travel-booking platform Booking.com.
The goal, he said, is to reduce the time between identifying an operational requirement and delivering equipment to soldiers, while allowing manufacturers to respond to changing battlefield needs.

title: Is All Foreign Policy Local? Explaining Georgia’s Shifting Alignments
body: The ruling Georgian Dream (GD) party has turned increasingly authoritarian over the past few years. Faced with a worsening security environment, local legitimacy concerns, and growing international isolation, the party increasingly tied its foreign policy alignment choices to its domestic needs. It nourished the relationships that boosted its legitimacy and contested those that threatened its domestic rule. Several foreign policy alignment patterns emerged as a result. First, Georgian ruling elites abandoned the West as a balancing option against Russia, instead seeing its former partnerships as principal threats to regime survival. Secondly, it chose security bandwagoning with Russia, along with economic accommodation meant to further aid regime survival. Third is transactional and legitimacy-enhancing engagements with the rest of the world — primarily with China, but also with states in the immediate neighborhood and beyond. While GD seems to have so far managed to retain power, it has yet to achieve the ideal multi-aligned state it claims to pursue. The European Union (EU) keeps resisting Tbilisi’s calls to engage without democratic conditionality; the U.S. has yet to clearly respond to Tbilisi’s calls for a reset; bandwagoning with Russia has hit clear limits amid the continued occupation of Georgian regions; and relations with the rest of the world, including China, have served as legitimacy-enhancers rather than achieving genuine strategic depth. More alarmingly, however, this search risks undermining the country’s foreign policy autonomy, limiting its room for geopolitical maneuver amidst the global uncertainty. Authors: Irakli Sirbiladze, Tamta Bezhanishvili, and Luka Danelia Georgia’s Past Alignments Georgia has often defied ideal-type foreign policy alignment categories such as bandwagoning, balancing, neutrality, or hedging . After initial bandwagoning with Moscow in the early 1990s, Georgia has embraced growing alignment with the West. Facing Russian threats and lacking internal capabilities, the country has pursued a NATO membership goal to balance against Moscow. This balancing behavior persisted despite Russia’s aggression in 2008 and a continued absence of Western security shelter. Since coming to power in 2012, Georgian Dream has embraced both bandwagoning and balancing strategies. Even while seeking economic normalization with Russia and avoiding escalatory language, the memories of war and continued occupation of its territories limited the extent to which Tbilisi could bandwagon with Moscow. Balancing logic has persisted as the GD continued political and military cooperation with the West. Georgian Dream chose regime survival over consolidating democracy and pursuing Georgia’s Western integration. That changed with Russia’s full-scale aggression on Ukraine in 2022, which altered the Georgian Dream calculus. To navigate international constraints and weakening domestic legitimacy, the party hardened its bandwagoning with Moscow while softening its strategy to balance against Russia through the West. Tbilisi also sought political partnerships beyond Russia and the West, with a multi-alignment strategy in mind to hedge against uncertainties. What remained certain, however, was that Russia was still the principal threat to the country’s security, leaving Georgia moving back and forth between bandwagoning and balancing options. Changing Alignments in Changing Context In the years that followed, Georgian Dream’s foreign policy alignment choices came to reflect changing domestic and international environments. At home, Georgian Dream has faced an acute legitimacy crisis amid growing autocratization and an anti-Western turn. Internationally, Russian revisionism forced Georgian Dream to make a choice between accommodating or contesting Moscow. The EU’s revived enlargement policy, which links accession progress to democratic reforms, threatened Georgian Dream’s hold on power. The party’s response featured more Westlessness in foreign policy, a hardened bandwagoning with Russia, and an increased engagement with actors beyond Russia and the West. West(-lessness): From a balancing partner to a political threat Georgian Dream’s autocratization and the Ukraine war context have strained Tbilisi’s close ties with the EU and the US. The relationship with the EU is now at its historic low. Georgian Dream’s stark disregard of the EU’s democratic conditionality since 2022 has resulted in a frozen accession process and the suspension of high-level political dialogue between Tbilisi and Brussels in 2024. The political ties with individual EU member states and the UK also suffered. Georgian Dream kept accusing Brussels of domestic meddling and of pushing the country into war with Russia. The partnership with Washington has been similarly tainted. In response to Georgian Dream’s growing assault on democracy, the Biden administration has imposed sanctions on the ruling party’s billionaire founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, and suspended the strategic partnership with the country late in 2024. The Trump administration has not so far reversed the Biden-era decisions. In parallel, the Trump administration’s peace agenda between Armenia and Azerbaijan has taken Georgia out of the geopolitical spotlight, despite Washington’s limited engagement with Tbilisi on connectivity projects and security. Georgia stands as a cautionary reminder that when ruling elites fail to uphold a geopolitical balancing act in a fractured international order, the gradual loss of a country’s autonomy could be the ultimate price. Attempts to fundamentally refresh ties with the U.S. have yet to bear fruit: while the past year saw revived contacts between Tbilisi and Washington, those visits also demonstrated that the aspired “reset” came with its conditions: the Trump administration requested political stability underpinned by political pluralism and a friendly environment for American business, clashing with the Georgian Dream’s autocratic agenda. While the launch of the Trump Tower project in Tbilisi shows Georgian Dream seeking a transactional bargain with Trump, its bearing on official Washington’s policy toward Georgia remains unknown. Georgia’s broader foreign policy and security alignment with the West similarly suffered. Tbilisi’s alignment rate with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) is in decline while its participation in the EU’s international missions has been suspended since 2023. Georgia no longer receives EU defense support, and the country remains outside the emerging European security architecture. Although limited defense and security cooperation with Washington and NATO continues, the scale and scope of practical cooperation is significantly downgraded. This leaves Georgia without a balancing partner or a potential European security shelter against growing Russian threats. Russia: security bandwagoning with economic benefits The Ukraine war led Georgian Dream to embrace a hardened security bandwagon with Russia. The party’s leadership has consistently declared that they are staying militarily out of the war and refused to impose bilateral economic sanctions on Russia. They also abstained from deepening security cooperation with the West. GD chose to stay under the radar instead of taking full advantage of emerging security thinking in the West. This accommodating posture with Moscow came with its economic perks. Georgian Dream deepened its trade and economic ties with Moscow and refused to close airspace to Russian air companies. The Georgian economy benefited from the growing influx of Russian immigrants. Georgia has experienced strong economic growth during 2022-2025, allowing the ruling party to govern amid suspended Western financial support. At the same time, while remaining formally compliant with Western sanctions imposed on Russia, Tbilisi kept drawing scrutiny by drastically increasing Russian oil imports and faced allegations of refining it to export it to the outside world. The scrutiny led to the conditional inclusion of the Kulevi Oil Refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia. In a turbulent and transitional world order, small states face a difficult task of pursuing balanced relationships with all competing powers to maintain both security and autonomy. Driven by party interests, Georgian Dream leadership is failing the task. Georgian Dream also followed Kremlin narratives in contesting the West. While the party has formally and selectively endorsed resolutions supporting Ukraine, it has waged persistent anti-Western disinformation campaigns mirroring Russian disinformation narratives and portraying the West as undergoing an economic and identity crisis. Georgian Dream’s consistent use of conspiracy theories – including the instrumentalization of the peace narrative – to manipulate domestic audiences has amplified Russia’s own anti-Western agenda. The party’s recent campaign to “nip Russophobia in the bud” not only mirrors the Kremlin’s talking points, but also exposes the country to Russia’s future claims of “defending” its citizens living in Georgia. Still, the history of the 2008 war, ongoing Russian occupation, and Moscow’s recognition of Georgian regions as “independent states,” coupled with persistent anti-Russia and pro-Western attitudes among Georgians, tie Georgian Dream’s hands in pursuing a full political thaw with Moscow. The party has refrained from restoring diplomatic relations with Russia or joining the 3+3 initiative, which excludes the West and brings Turkey, Russia, and Iran together with South Caucasus states. The Georgian Dream leadership acknowledges the political costs of formalizing ties with Moscow, as a confident majority of Georgians continue to support EU integration and see Russia as a political threat. These constraints and regime survival calculations thus force the Georgian Dream to value the status quo over an open political tilt toward Moscow. Beyond West and Russia: GD’s legitimacy-enhancing and transactional engagements Georgian Dream has engaged in legitimacy-enhancing and transactional partnerships with China, Iran, United Arab Emirates (UAE), Central Asian states, and the South Caucasus neighborhood. Relations with China have been expanding , offering Georgia’s ruling party legitimacy gains rather than possessing true strategic value for the country. The ties between Beijing and Tbilisi were upgraded with a trade agreement in 2017, elevated to a strategic partnership in 2023, and to a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2026. China is Georgia’s important trade partner; bilateral exchanges between political elites are frequent, while the visa-free regime allows people-to-people movement. Tbilisi has aligned with China’s stance on Taiwan as well as Beijing’s global initiatives regarding development, security, and civilizational values. Still, the relationship lacks genuine strategic depth. China prioritizes close ties with Russia over Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty concerns. In 2026, Beijing exited the strategically important Anaklia Deep Sea Port project, despite the Chinese-Singaporean company winning a bid two years earlier. The defense and security partnership between the two countries is practically non-existent, while China’s societal influence in Georgia remains limited. Growing political alignment with Beijing serves as a legitimacy enhancer for the ruling party – used primarily to showcase its partnership with a major global player amid Western isolation – rather than constituting a genuine strategic partnership. Georgian Dream also increased political engagement with anti-Western and Russia-aligned Iran. The Georgian prime minister and president visited Iran in 2024 and 2026 to attend state events, including the funeral of the late Ayatollah Khamenei. Domestically, analysts have raised alarms over an enabling environment for pro-Iranian networks . Economically, the formal trade between Tbilisi and Tehran is limited, not counting the recent spike in motor car exports, while the US sanctions on Iranian airlines – which Tbilisi enforced – will likely limit the people-to-people movement. The US sanctions on Georgia-registered crypto firms expose the country to the risk of being seen as facilitating sanctions evasion. Growing political alignment with Beijing serves as a legitimacy enhancer for the ruling party – used primarily to showcase its partnership with a major global player amid Western isolation – rather than constituting a genuine strategic partnership. However, the war in Iran in 2026 showed the limits of Georgia’s engagement with the country. Tbilisi’s contacts with Washington, as well as the decision to allow US military transport planes to land during American strikes on Iran and to comply with the US’s recent sanctions on airlines, caused Tehran’s irritation. A series of vague statements by the Iranian ambassador – widely perceived as threats in Georgia – has stirred controversies in Tbilisi. Despite this, the Georgian Dream is likely to continue political engagement with Tehran, putting Georgia out of sync with the West. Georgia’s ruling party further extended its diplomacy across the South Caucasus neighborhood, Central Asia, and the Gulf to project legitimacy and secure economic lifelines. Bilateral ties with neighboring Armenia and Azerbaijan have remained largely untainted, reflecting the neighborhood that values practical stability over democratic standards. Georgian Dream upped its connectivity cooperation with Azerbaijan while being watchful of alternative transit projects such as the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP). Georgian Dream’s engagement with Central Asian states reached historic highs. Since 2024, the ruling party officials have held high-level meetings and visits across Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan to strengthen trade ties, promote Georgia’s role in the Middle Corridor project, and signal the country’s irreplaceable standing when it comes to the connectivity agenda. Georgian Dream’s engagement with the UAE, signing controversial logistics and real estate deals, also features similar transactionality. Overall, these partnerships appear to give the ruling party both economic and legitimacy gains amid its isolation in the West. Party Above Country? Georgia’s foreign policy behavior offers an example of its governing party reshaping state interests to ensure longevity in power. That imperative has come at the cost of Georgia’s national interest, starkly limiting the country’s geopolitical options in an increasingly challenging global environment. In a turbulent and transitional world order, small states face a difficult task of pursuing balanced relationships with all competing powers to maintain both security and autonomy. Driven by party interests, Georgian Dream leadership is failing the task. Three episodes illustrate the trend: First, Georgian Dream chose regime survival over consolidating democracy and pursuing Georgia’s Western integration. Rather than advancing the country’s constitutionally embedded European integration through allowing genuine political pluralism and cooperating with civil society, the party chose to suppress critics, opposition, civil society, and media. What resulted is not only deteriorated ties with the West, but also the undoing of Georgia’s past progress toward democratic development. Tensions with Brussels are even affecting Georgia’s leadership bid in international organizations such as the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE). Second, Georgian Dream’s accommodation of Moscow serves the party rather than the country, as it limits Georgia’s autonomy in the longer run. Economic gains from the party’s engagement with Russia strengthened its ability to foster loyalties, while its authoritarian reliance on and learning from the Russian autocratic ecosystem allowed it to target opponents. But by cultivating various dependencies on Moscow while contesting its Western allies, Georgian Dream leadership leaves Georgia exposed to Russian influence while denying the country necessary maneuverability at times of geopolitical and geoeconomic uncertainties. Fresh reports of Moscow suspending the imports of key Georgian products may illustrate this vulnerability. Third, the ruling party has utilized Georgia’s historic transit identity as a bargaining chip to ensure regime survival. The Georgian Dream has so far been unsuccessful in securing such a bargain with the West. Georgia’s strategic transit location alone is failing to trump the EU’s enforcement of enlargement conditionality, while Washington is placing a premium on the TRIPP project – the result of the rapprochement between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Unbound by enlargement conditionality, the EU has embraced high-level engagements with Yerevan and Baku regarding connectivity, limiting Georgia’s leverage. While existing routes through Georgia still retain significant value, domestic political instability and isolation from the West deny the country the ability to sit at the connectivity table. Friend of All, Friend of None? The domestic legitimacy crisis, external pressures of the war in Ukraine, and the EU’s revived enlargement process have turned the Georgian Dream increasingly authoritarian at home and daring in its foreign policy engagements. In that process, Georgia’s ruling elites have fundamentally blurred the line between partisan and national interests. But the genius formula of ensuring regime survival while seeking multi-alignment — or what the party calls “pragmatic” foreign policy — came with its clear limits. Tbilisi’s attempts to pursue a transactional partnership with the West amid explicitly expressed Westlessness have yet to bear fruit. Local context also continues to pressure Georgian Dream against restoring formal political ties with Moscow or joining Russian-led international platforms. Severed politico-security ties with traditional Western allies and increasing cultivation of economic and political dependencies on Russia and China have denied Georgia necessary geopolitical maneuverability amid global turbulence. At the same time, protracted political instability has relegated the country to the geopolitical margins, further weakening Georgia’s traditional leverage as a transit actor connecting East and West. Today, Georgia stands as a cautionary reminder that when ruling elites fail to uphold a geopolitical balancing act in a fractured international order, the gradual loss of a country’s autonomy could be the ultimate price. Irakli Sirbiladze is a foreign policy analyst and visiting lecturer at Tbilisi State University. Tamta Bezhanishvili is a recent graduate in International Relations from Tbilisi State University . Luka Danelia is a recent graduate in International Relations from Tbilisi State University .

title: Investigations implicate Deloitte, one of the world’s largest accounting firms, in alleged tax-evasion schemes involving Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s Cyprus companies
body: Deloitte, one of the world’s largest consulting and auditing firms, helped falsify documents to conceal Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s wealth and enable him to evade taxes, according to a joint investigation by the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ). The Guardian published a separate report on the same case. The investigations draw on leaked documents and emails from MeritServus, a Cyprus-based corporate services provider previously reported to have managed Abramovich’s businesses. One episode dates to 2006, when Cyprus passed a law requiring companies to publish their financial statements. At the time, Abramovich’s assets were held by the Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. Its balance sheet listed $672 million in assets: a mansion in the English county of West Sussex, an apartment in London, an estate in southern France, helicopters, private jets, and yachts, including the 115-meter (377-foot) Pelorus. Abramovich reportedly owned all these assets at the time. Abramovich’s aides and MeritServus decided to transfer the assets to Amiscan’s parent company in the British Virgin Islands, where companies did not have to disclose their financial statements. According to the investigation, they backdated the paperwork to make it appear that the transfer had taken place in 2003. Deloitte’s Cyprus office reviewed the documents and deemed them sufficient to remove the assets from Amiscan’s financial statements, leaving it with just $75,000 in assets. The Guardian reported that emails in the leaked files show Deloitte Cyprus employees took part in discussions about this scheme to make the assets “disappear.” Deloitte signed off on Amiscan’s financial statements with the valuable assets removed. Deloitte headquarters in Limassol, April 2023 Another episode described in the investigations involves the Cypriot company Kravin Investments. In May 2003, its accounts held about $2 billion that Abramovich had received from selling assets in Russia. Some of the money was lent to other companies. All these funds should have been subject to tax in Cyprus. But documents show that Abramovich’s advisers soon began devising a plan to “eliminate” tax liabilities that could be “very large.” They decided to alter Kravin’s financial statements and accounting records for 2003 and 2004 retroactively. The documents made it appear that Kravin did not own the funds but merely managed them on behalf of its parent company in the British Virgin Islands. This allowed the advisers to claim that the Cypriot company had no taxable income. Citing the leaked correspondence, the BBC reported that Abramovich’s advisers devised the tax evasion plan after meeting with Deloitte representatives. Another scheme concerns Electus Investments, a Cypriot company linked to Abramovich. Its accounts held $10 billion. Leaked emails show that in 2006, MeritServus proposed backdating documents to make it appear that a company with the same name in the British Virgin Islands had owned these assets since 2003. As a result, when the Cypriot company’s financial statements became public, its accounts showed just $145,000. Abramovich’s lawyers denied any wrongdoing and said he had relied on advice from his advisers and Deloitte’s Cyprus office. Deloitte Cyprus said it had always complied with local law. It said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents and correspondence cited by the journalists concerned events from 20 years ago and were “no longer accessible.” At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

title: Open architecture is 'non-negotiable' for all future Army systems, Acting Army Secretary says
body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. The U.S. Army will require open architecture in all future equipment purchases as part of an effort to improve interoperability between battlefield systems, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said during the opening ceremony of the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 conference.
"Everything we buy from here on out will have open architecture. It's non-negotiable," Telle told attendees, arguing that proprietary systems have prevented the Army from sharing data across platforms and integrating new technologies into existing networks.
Telle identified interoperability as one of three major acquisition problems the Army is working to address, alongside lengthy procurement timelines and an acquisition structure organized around individual platforms rather than operational requirements.
He said the Army has allowed data to become trapped within proprietary systems, forcing the service to depend on contractors to access and exchange information between equipment.
As an example, Telle pointed to the Army's effort to field thousands of lower-cost interceptors designed to defeat incoming missiles and drones. Those interceptors must be able to communicate with the Army's broader command-and-control network, he said.
"If the data is trapped behind proprietary modes, and we have to call a contractor to decode the data, our super intelligent command and control doesn't matter," he said.
For existing equipment, the Army has launched an initiative called Operation Jailbreak, which Telle described as an effort to overcome interoperability barriers across legacy systems. Under the initiative, engineers from companies that had not worked together were brought into a single location to address integration problems over a period of weeks, he said.
Telle argued that the approach could reduce the time and expense associated with connecting existing systems, rather than requiring prolonged development efforts to achieve interoperability.
The push for open architecture is part of a broader effort to change how the Army acquires and integrates technology. Telle said the service has reorganized its acquisition structure around a smaller number of portfolio acquisition executives, bringing soldiers, engineers, manufacturers, testers, and logistics personnel together to address operational requirements.
The goal, he said, is to make decisions about technology integration, manufacturing, and supply chains earlier in the acquisition process while ensuring that systems purchased by the Army can function together on the battlefield.

title: Why the government's own case for MOSA – technology refresh – is the one benefit programs most often leave on the table
body:
The U.S. Department of Defense’s (DoD)’s own benefits list names technology refresh as a primary reason the modular open systems approach (MOSA) exists. But because the mandate is outcome-based, verified only at the interface, and never priced as a deliverable, it is easy to meet on paper but under-deliver in practice. MOSA cannot be certified into existence by naming a standard, and its refresh benefit is not free. It is delivered by the architecture beneath the interfaces via independence inside the mission computer and a deterministic backbone across the platform, and technology refresh is exactly where that choice gets rewarded or punished. Programs that treat MOSA as a compliance checkbox will pay for integration on every upgrade, but programs that architect true independence from day one only pay for integration once and harvest the savings forever.
The modular open systems approach (MOSA) is a statutory requirement mandated by the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD). The department lists several reasons for requiring an open approach, but of the five primary benefits the DoD seeks to achieve through MOSA, “technology refresh” sits near the top; the OUSW (R&E) engineering office states MOSA should let a program field new capability or replacement technology without changing every component in the system.
Moreover, MOSA is codified in 10 U.S.C. §4401 for major defense acquisition programs, and the December 2024 Tri-Service Memo elevated it to what the services called a warfighting imperative. A prime cannot simply decline to do MOSA.
And yet the same policy that mandates MOSA also says, plainly, that there is no single way to implement it. That single sentence is where the refresh benefit tends to leak away, and it is worth understanding why before a program commits to an architecture it will live with for the next three decades.
[Figure 1 ǀ The two axes of MOSA technology refresh: independence inside each mission computer and independence across the platform.]
Mission platforms are built to last. The aircraft, ground vehicle, or shipboard system fielded today may still be flying, driving, or sailing in twenty or thirty years. The silicon inside it will not. Processors, GPUs, I/O standards, threat models, and mission software all turn over on a far shorter cycle than the platform that hosts them.
That mismatch is expensive. Major acquisitions now average nearly twelve years, with roughly $49.3 billion in cost growth spread across thirty programs. A meaningful share of that growth is not the cost of new hardware; it is the cost of everything the existing architecture forces a program to re-touch, re-integrate, and re-certify when one thing changes.
MOSA is meant to reduce the mismatch. But the way most programs implement MOSA actually perpetuates the cycle, adding time and costs.
Here is the tension at the center of MOSA, and it is baked into the policy itself.
First, MOSA is a strategy, not a standard. The DoD defines it as an integrated business and technical strategy built on modular design and open interfaces “with which conformance can be verified.” The part that gets verified is the interfaces and the standards they conform to – not the architecture behind them.
Second, the enforceable specifications are not MOSA itself but the domain substandards that implement it – like the Future Airborne Capability Environment, or FACE Technical Standard, for avionics software; the Sensor Open Systems Architecture, or SOSA Technical Standard, for sensor systems; or OpenVPX on the hardware side. These are real, testable, conformance-checkable standards. But a program can hold a valid FACE or SOSA conformance claim and still run a tightly coupled architecture underneath it. Conformance is not the same thing as capability.
Third, “no single way to implement” is a double-edged instruction. The outcome-based latitude is genuinely useful, as it lets programs tailor MOSA to their missions rather than forcing a one-size design. But it also means the minimum a program must do to satisfy the mandate sits well below what actually delivers refresh benefit number two.
Lastly, MOSA has no line item. There is no priced MOSA module a prime can drop into a proposal and point to. The deep architectural work carries near-term cost, and its payoff does not arrive until a refresh years down the road. In a competition graded heavily on near-term price, the rational move is to do the minimum: Satisfy the letter, cite the conformance, and defer the architecture.
Put those four together and the outcome is predictable. The mandate gets met on paper, but the refresh benefit is tough to materialize. Closing that gap is an architecture decision, and it plays out along two axes: how independent functions are inside a mission computer, and how independent they are across the platform.
MOSA initiatives are usually discussed in terms of standards and interfaces. That is necessary but not sufficient: True modularity requires more than a set of interoperable, standards-conformant components – it requires an architecture that supports independent deployment, independent sustainment, independent assurance, and independent security boundaries.
Those four types of independence are what determine whether a refresh is contained or catastrophic:
None of these are guaranteed by an interface standard. They are guaranteed – or not – by the architecture beneath it.
There is a simple way to tell whether an architecture will deliver independence when it matters: ask the vendor. If the lowest-criticality partition on the processor fails in the worst way imaginable – a runaway thread, memory corruption, a malicious actor with root – what changes for the highest-criticality partition? (Figure 2.)
[Figure 2 ǀ Isolation by construction: A catastrophic failure in the lowest-criticality partition leaves the safety-critical partitions unaffected.]
In many architectures the honest answer is “something.” Maybe latency, maybe scheduling, maybe a shared resource the safety case never fully accounted for. The architectures that survive decades of refresh are the ones where the honest answer is “nothing.” That isolation is a property of the layer beneath the operating systems, delivered by a small, rigorously designed separation kernel hypervisor that partitions CPU time, memory, and I/O – and increasingly, GPU resources – and hands each guest a strictly bounded view of the hardware. It is what lets a program drop in a new or modified component and trust that the safety case underneath is unchanged.
That trust matters most for the refresh you cannot avoid: Accelerators, high-bandwidth I/O, and AI or perception workloads that were never designed with bounded latency in mind. When an inference workload runs on a shared GPU, the timing of every other GPU-touching task becomes a question instead of a guarantee – and for a safety-critical display or a real-time control loop, a question is not good enough. Bringing accelerators into the mixed-criticality story properly requires time-bounded execution for heterogeneous compute: scheduling that gives GPU and AI workloads predictable latency, not just good average throughput. Get that right, and new compute capability arrives as an addition rather than a re-architecture.
Isolation inside a box only solves half the refresh problem. A large share of real refresh cost lives between the boxes in the wiring, the point-to-point interfaces, and the re-verification triggered every time a line-replaceable unit (LRU) is added, moved, or replaced. Classic federated architectures make that expensive by design: change one node and the integration ripples outward.
A time-sensitive networking (TSN) digital backbone changes the economics of platform integration by replacing bespoke interconnects with a common, deterministic Ethernet fabric. The network becomes the integration contract: Each function joins as an endpoint with defined and enforceable requirements for bandwidth, latency, timing, and stream reservations. Think of it as a digital highway with strict traffic rules, where every workload is given predictable access to network resources. When a radar, sensor, or compute function is added or upgraded, it can be integrated at the network edge and verified against the existing certified network schedule. Rather than requalifying the broader platform, testing can focus on the new or modified capability and its impact on the backbone. The fabric becomes the abstraction layer that enables capabilities to be added, replaced, and upgraded more independently. (Figure 3.)
[Figure 3 ǀ On a TSN backbone the network schedule is the integration contract; a refresh is verified as an increment against it, not as a platform-wide requalification.]
Why does this setup work? TSN brings far more than bandwidth. Plain fast Ethernet offers throughput and nothing else, whereas TSN adds a determinism layer of time synchronization, time-aware traffic scheduling, frame preemption, per-stream ingress policing, and redundancy that enables safety-critical and noncritical traffic share one fabric without the low-criticality flows stealing latency or bandwidth from the high-criticality ones. That is the network-level analog of the separation kernel’s failure test: A new or misbehaving endpoint cannot degrade a safety-critical stream, so adding a node does not reopen the timing case for the ones already there. Mixed-criticality is enforced on the wire, by construction.
The U.S. Army’s HADES [High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System] aerial intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) program is built on exactly this idea: a MOSA aligned TSN digital backbone whose stated purpose is to accelerate capability insertion and enable rapid upgradeability, reconfigurability, and cost-effective lifecycle refresh. It combines a deterministic 10-Gbit TSN fabric built to the IEEE 802.1DP aerospace profile; SOSA conformant 3U-VPX nodal access units and TSN switch LRUs from one vendor; and a DO-178C DAL A, FACE conformant node operating system from another. Independent laboratory work points the same way: A VFS Forum 80 paper demonstrating a TSN-based zonal architecture on multivendor COTS [commercial off-the-shelf] hardware argues that TSN truly meets MOSA requirements while delivering size, weight, and power (SWaP) savings and both hardware and software modularity.
Two features of that pattern do the real work on a refresh. The backbone is inherently multivendor and COTS-based, so severable modules can be competed and sourced from independent suppliers, which directly serves MOSA’s competition, interoperability, and cost-avoidance benefits alongside refresh. A zonal layout lets functions be re-homed to different compute nodes without re-cabling, so a refresh can redistribute capability rather than rip and replace.
The two axes are complementary, not competing. The digital backbone handles independence between nodes, while the separation architecture handles it within each node. HADES illustrates the pairing: A TSN fabric to move modules onto and off the platform, and a partitioning node OS to keep mixed-criticality functions independent inside each box. The backbone gets modules to the box and the separation architecture keeps them independent once they are there. Neither layer alone delivers the refresh benefit, but together they accomplish it.
Neither axis is free, and neither is automatic. TSN determinism depends on a correctly computed network schedule and conformant endpoints. The schedule itself becomes a certification artifact and a real tooling burden. Programs that treat “we use TSN” as a box-check inherit the same underdelivery trap that afflicts MOSA generally. The determinism has to be architected to contain interference, exactly as the separation kernel’s isolation does.
The hardest thing about MOSA in a proposal is that its value is invisible until refresh. The way to make it visible is to price it against the cost it avoids.
Partial recertification, or delta-certification, is how you capture those savings. It works in two places: Inside the box, clean functional separation means a change recertifies only what changed, not the whole system, potentially cutting certification and recertification cost by as much as half. Across the platform, a certified TSN schedule means a new endpoint is verified against a bounded contract rather than triggering a platform-wide re-qualification. This is the figure a program office can finally put against MOSA benefit number 2 (technology refresh) and benefit number 4 (cost savings and avoidance). Delivering a well-understood partitioning model such as ARINC 653 on a modern separation-kernel foundation reinforces the intra-node half: a cleaner certification story, less custom glue code, and headroom to scale over the life of the program.
Two more levers tighten the case and add early value: Virtual integration enables teams to develop and validate a refresh before the target hardware exists, thereby taking risk out of the schedule. Additionally, continuous software composition analysis (SBOM [software bill of materials] visibility plus CVE [common vulnerabilities and exposures] management) keeps a refreshed system compliant in the field across decades, filtering out irrelevant vulnerabilities so sustainment teams can patch what actually matters.
Michel Genard is chief strategy officer and board member at Lynx Software Technologies, where he leads strategy for safety-critical and mixed-criticality computing platforms. He has over two decades of experience in embedded systems, avionics, and defense software architecture.

title: Clearing chat history helps AI agents find better solutions
body:
Long-running AI research agents can plateau despite additional compute, a Microsoft Research study finds. Accumulated conversation context can constrain their search, keeping them focused on similar solutions instead of exploring better approaches.

Microsoft researchers studied what they call "Autoresearch agents," AI systems that repeatedly propose solutions, evaluate them, and refine them based on feedback. Eight independent runs of the same agent on the same task plateaued at significantly different performance levels, with final scores ranging from 68.3 to 100.0. These gaps persisted even with substantially more compute, according to the paper.
Agents get stuck in "idea basins"
The researchers plotted solutions from all runs on a two-dimensional map that places similar solutions close together, then compared them. Solutions from a single run almost always stayed within a small region of the map. The authors call these regions "idea basins."

The agents spend a large share of their remaining compute budget refining solutions within a less productive region instead of finding better approaches discovered by other runs. This pattern persists even when the agents periodically compress their conversation histories.
Clearing chat history lets agents explore new approaches
The proposed method, "Fork-and-Flush," combines two mechanisms. In "forking," the agent splits into K parallel branches, each inheriting the previous workspace and all generated files. In "flushing," each branch loses its entire chat context but keeps the workspace, allowing it to start a fresh conversation and build on prior work.

[caption id="attachment_41448" align="alignnone" width="1100"] On the left, a single run (gray, dashed) keeps refining solutions within the same idea basin. Fork-and-Flush starts parallel branches with fresh chat contexts, keeps the best branch, and discards the rest. On the right, a branch with fresh context moves into a different idea basin and achieves a higher score. | Image: Cai, Ziakas et al. (2026)[/caption]

A branch that keeps the parent process's chat context tends to return to the same idea basin because the previous reasoning steers its next steps. Fresh context restores diversity in the search. The conversation history is lost, but the code, files, and saved results remain in the workspace.
A 66 percent higher normalized average score on the same compute budget
The researchers tested Fork-and-Flush on 13 long-running tasks, including polyomino packing, job-shop scheduling, and cryptanalysis. The tasks also included compressing a CIFAR classifier and optimizing a VLIW kernel. Individual runs lasted from several hours to over 100 hours. The agents used GPT-5.6-terra and GPT-5.5 through the GitHub Copilot CLI.

On the same compute budget, Fork-and-Flush achieved a min-max-normalized average score of 0.78, compared to 0.47 for single runs and 0.54 for best-of-4. The paper reports relative gains of 66.0 and 44.4 percent, respectively. The method achieved the highest mean score on 12 of the 13 tasks.

Fork-and-Flush also produced more consistent results, with normalized standard deviation falling to 0.16 from 0.26 for single runs. Simply clearing the chat context without branching improved results by 22 percent.

Stronger models may still need context resets
The researchers also tested whether more capable models avoid idea basins, using MAX-3-SAT problems across three model sizes, Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, and 27B. Variance between runs followed an inverted U-shaped curve, peaking on tasks at the edge of a model's abilities, roughly halfway between random-guessing performance and the reference solver's performance.

[caption id="attachment_41447" align="alignnone" width="838"] Results vary most on tasks at the edge of a model's abilities, with some runs succeeding and others falling well short. Models almost always succeed on very easy tasks and fail on very hard ones. This pattern holds across all three model sizes tested. | Image: Cai, Ziakas et al. (2026)[/caption]

The authors argue that open research problems sit, by definition, at the limits of models' abilities. They expect the variation Fork-and-Flush exploits to persist as models improve, with the boundary simply shifting toward harder problems. The results suggest that regular context resets could remain useful even for frontier research agents.

title: New Coyote Anti-Drone Interceptor Swaps Jet Engine For Rocket Power
body: Raytheon is developing a new iteration of its Coyote Block 2 counter-drone interceptor powered by a solid rocket motor rather than a small jet engine. This pushes the Block 2C+RM version, which also comes with a new seeker and warhead, into the surface-to-air missile side of the interceptor spectrum. With a significant boost in speed, range, and terminal intercept performance, it is designed to address evolving one-way-attack drone threats. The Coyote Block 2 series is already a combat-proven system, with more than 600 kills in the course of operational U.S. military deployments to date. The unveiling of the Coyote Block 2C+RM came today around the start of the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ is in attendance . The rocket-powered version has been in the works for some 15 months now, and three successful live test launches have been conducted. That followed static test fires of the new rocket motor, which an unnamed subcontractor is supplying, and other testing. A look at the general design of existing jet-powered Block 2-series Coyote interceptors. Joseph Trevithick The Pentagon and the U.S. Army have been engaged with Raytheon (now formally RTX) on the development of the Block 2C+RM, but whether there are formal U.S. military contracts to buy this version now is unclear. The U.S. Army is the largest known operator of Coyote Block 2-series interceptors now, with previously stated plans to buy at least 6,000 of them between Fiscal Years 2025 and 2029. We will come back to this later on. As mentioned, existing versions of Coyote Block 2 are powered by a turbojet engine. A small rocket booster is also used to launch these interceptors, but does not propel them through the entire course of their flight. A side-by-side comparison of an earlier rocket-boosted, jet-powered Coyote Block 2, at left, and the new Block 2C+RM version, at right. Raytheon With the rocket motor, “you get upgraded propulsion for faster launch and higher velocity flight,” Tom Laliberty, President of Land & Air Defense Systems at Raytheon, told TWZ and other outlets during a press call last week ahead of today’s announcement. “In terms of range and so forth, I can’t really get into any specifics about that, for obvious reasons.” “What I would just say is it’s significant in terms of the range difference, and in the [sic] what I call end-game capabilities of the missile, where velocity might come into play,” he added. “Then with the seeker [and] warhead [upgrades], it really gets after the sort of more cutting-edge drone capabilities that we’re seeing from the adversary.” Laliberty also did not elaborate on the specific improvements to the seeker or warhead. Existing Block 2-series Coyotes use on-board radio frequency seekers to find their targets in the terminal phase of flight after first being cued via radars and other sensors on the ground. They also carry blast-fragmentation warheads . During last week’s call, Laliberty was asked about whether new faster-flying jet-powered one-way-attack drones, like Iran’s Shahed 238 and Russia’s Geran-4 and -5 derivatives , had prompted Block 2C+RM’s development. He was also queried about Block 2C+RM’s ability to defeat traditional cruise missiles. A jet-powered Shahed 238 kamikaze drone, or a mockup thereof. Iranian State Media “Unfortunately, I can’t get into the specific threats, but I can tell you the intention is to have this cover all types of Class 3 drones,” he said in response. “If you think about the Class 3 drone kind of ‘spectrum,’ there’s a pretty good overlap there with the capabilities of cruise missiles, as well, right? So it all depends on the specific[s] of the cruise missile.” The U.S. military defines Group 3 drones, whether they are weaponized or not, as designs that weigh anywhere from 56 to 1,320 pounds, are able to fly up to an altitude of 18,000 feet, and reach a top speed of no more than 250 knots. The Shahed 238’s combustion engine-powered predecessor, the Shahed 236 , is a prime example of a Group 3 kamikaze drone. The claimed top speeds of the jet-powered derivatives (approximately 270 to 320 knots) actually push the upper boundaries of this broad middle-tier category. TWZ regularly highlights the additional challenges that jet-powered kamikaze drones like the Shahed 238 and Geran-4/5 present. We also routinely note how the line between longer-range one-way-attack drones and cruise missiles has become increasingly blurry . The Block 2C+RM itself also further blurs the definition between a drone-like counter-drone interceptor and a more traditional surface-to-air missile. RFE/RL takes apart a Russian Geran-4 drone to uncover what makes the jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) faster, harder to intercept, and capable of operating deep inside Ukraine — from its turbojet engine and advanced camera to foreign-made communications and navigation… pic.twitter.com/WGNdlpS9w1 — Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (@RFERL) September 25, 2026 The conflict with Iran , as well as other crises in the Middle East in recent years and the ongoing war in Ukraine , make clear that even slower-flying Group 3 kamikaze drones present real dangers now. Those threats are magnified when these one-way attacks are employed in large volumes and/or in complex attacks mixed in with ballistic and cruise missiles . As noted, Raytheon has highlighted how Coyote Block 2C+RM also has a faster overall response time compared to its predecessors, offering additional flexibility for engaging incoming waves of drones. The new version also works with all existing four- and eight-cell launchers, which can be variously mounted on vehicles and static positions on the ground , as well as on ships . As mentioned earlier, the U.S. Army is the primary operator of Coyote Block 2s today, with the interceptors being used in both vehicle-based and palletized versions of its Low, Slow, Unmanned Aircraft Integrated Defeat System (LIDS). The U.S. Air Force has also been at least involved in the operation of fixed-site versions of LIDS at forward-deployed locations. The U.S. Navy has integrated launchers for Coyote Block 2s on several Arleigh Burke class destroyers , as well. A promotional shot showing the fixed-site version of the LIDS launcher and radar components, as well as a vehicle-based version of LIDS in between. Raytheon A promotional shot showing the FS-LIDS launcher and radar components, as well as an M-LIDS vehicle in the middle. Raytheon An annotated image showing an eight-cell Coyote anti-drone interceptor launcher on the US Navy’s Arleigh Burke class destroyer USS Carl M. Levin . This is a new type of naval launcher that first emerged earlier this year. USN It’s also worth noting here that Coyote is generally described as a lower-cost interceptor, with a unit cost reported in the past to be around $100,000 . How the new rocket-powered version will compare to existing types price-wise is unclear, but this is an increasingly important factor for the U.S. military and others, especially when considering the cost curve against the expected target set. As an example, the estimated cost of a Shahed 236 is in the $50,000 range . To be clear, Coyote Block 2C+RM is still in development, and when it might start to enter operational service with any user remains to be seen. “We’ve got additional tests scheduled into the first half of next year, and we’re working with the Department of War,” Raytheon’s Laliberty said last week. “We’ve got an ongoing investment from Raytheon, but now essentially received some government sponsorship as it kind of transitions into the program of record, and that’s still kind of ongoing with the Department of War in terms of how all of that is going to be structured. Certainly, in follow-on contracts for Coyote, this can be cut in.” Raytheon has no plans to stop producing jet-powered Block 2 versions, either, at least for now. Beyond the U.S. military, there are now contractors to supply these interceptors to Qatar and Jordan. Another picture of a Coyote Block 2-series interceptor being built at Raytheon. Raytheon The Block 2 series is just one part of the larger and still growing Coyote family of drones. A separate series of Coyote Block 3 drones , which evolved from the original electric motor-driven pusher propeller Block 1 design , is also steadily expanding. This includes versions configured as loitering munitions and as counter-drone interceptors carrying still unidentified “non-kinetic” payloads . The U.S. Army is already in the process of acquiring Block 3 types in addition to Block 2 interceptors. A pusher-propeller Coyote Block 3NK non-kinetic interceptor seen being launched with the help of a rocket booster. Raytheon As an aside, the U.S.-based subsidiary of Germany’s Rheinmetall is currently competing in the Army’s XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle (MICV) competition with a design that will be capable of employing Coyote Block 3. The launchers on American Rheinmetall’s Lynx-based XM30 offering will also be able to fire anti-tank guided missiles like the TOW and Javelin . You can read more about the XM30 competition and the other design in the running, General Dynamics Land Systems’ Wolf, here . More broadly speaking, Coyote Block 2C+RM will be entering a hugely expanding market space for lower-tier and lower-cost counter-drone interceptors globally. The U.S. Army alone is already pursuing several new lower-tier anti-air interceptors to expand its capabilities against Group 3 drones, as well as other types of uncrewed threats and cruise missiles. If nothing else, the newly unveiled Coyote Block 2C+RM reflects continued high demand, broadly speaking, for new interceptors, and more of them, to address ever-more capable longer-range kamikaze drones. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post New Coyote Anti-Drone Interceptor Swaps Jet Engine For Rocket Power appeared first on TWZ .

title: How would NATO defeat a Russian invasion? Its top commander envisions a wall of drones, a counteroffensive, and missile strikes deep behind Russian lines.
body: Alexus Grynkewich at a forum in Warsaw, October 12, 2026 General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said NATO forces would destroy “anything and everything” involved in any Russian attack on the alliance’s territory. He presented his “theory of victory” at a security conference in Warsaw. Bloomberg reported a week earlier that Grynkewich would present a “quick victory” strategy for responding to a Russian advance on the alliance’s eastern flank. Reuters reported that he did not explicitly mention Russia in his speech, but his message was clearly directed at the Kremlin. Grynkewich said NATO is a defensive alliance but will thwart, repel, and crush any attacks on its members: If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. […] We will, ​in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile. In Reuters’ assessment, the general signaled to Moscow that, if necessary, NATO would launch large-scale retaliatory strikes against both the forces directly involved in the attack and facilities beyond the area under attack. “Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” Grynkewich said. “This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force.” He said that if NATO territory comes under attack, its forces would not allow the enemy to gain a foothold on the alliance’s territory. The aim, he said, is to reduce the enemy’s offensive capabilities until it can no longer continue fighting. Grynkewich believes this approach should underpin a deterrence strategy in which any escalation by the aggressor backfires. Grynkewich said a key factor in deterring Russia is consistently and unambiguously showing that NATO is ready to repel any aggression. From Meduza’s archives ‘This has to happen in the next 5–10 years’ With a growing Russian threat and Trump raising the stakes, NATO scrambles to lock in new defense plans ‘Putin’s less afraid of war than of peace’: What independent military analysts have to say about the risk of Russia invading the Baltic states The Wall Street Journal reported details of Grynkewich’s “theory of victory.” The plan calls for creating an extensive “autonomous zone” on the eastern flank, where drones and “ground robots” (probably ground drones) could hold back a Russian advance without heavy losses among NATO troops. At the same time, long-range missiles would strike Russian command posts and air defense systems in the Kaliningrad region, near St. Petersburg, and in Belarus. The strikes are intended to undermine Russia’s ability to control the skies and allow the U.S. Army’s V Corps and other NATO ground forces to counterattack. NATO aircraft would also need to strike Russian reinforcements quickly as they move toward the battlefield, along with other targets in the rear. A system allowing NATO allies to share classified targeting data instantly through cloud infrastructure would make these strikes possible. Some elements of the system have already been tested in the Middle East during the U.S. attack on Iran. The German tabloid Bild reported on a similar NATO plan in mid-August 2026. The article said NATO has a plan for a military response to a Russian attack on the Baltic states. Among other things, it calls for the alliance’s missiles and drones to disable Russian missile systems, including those in Kaliningrad. The Wall Street Journal reported that while Grynkewich was speaking in Warsaw, more than 20,000 military personnel from various NATO countries were taking part in a 10-day command-post exercise called “Steadfast Duel.” The exercise was intended, among other things, to simulate one million NATO troops repelling an invasion from the east by an army of comparable size. The newspaper reported that other exercises also rehearsed strikes with ground-launched missiles to disable enemy command posts. In late September, Russia’s embassy in Ireland claimed its diplomats were receiving information about NATO preparations for an air and naval blockade of the Kaliningrad region. The diplomats said that if this happened, Russia would be prepared to use any weapon, including nuclear weapons. The same warning appears in a document Russia sent to NATO that Reuters obtained . In it, Moscow accuses the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carries “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.” Vladimir Putin later made a similar statement: If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case, we mean Kaliningrad, perhaps other territories as well — then, of course, Russia’s use of all the weapons at our country’s disposal will inevitably and immediately be on the table. That is inevitable. In its written response to the Kremlin, NATO said none of the alliance’s exercises or activities pose a threat to Russian territory. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

title: Deployment of 39,000 troops foiled enemy ground invasion plan
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – The commander of the Iranian Army Ground Forces said the deployment of more than 51 combat units and the repositioning of 39,000 army personnel during the Ramadan War thwarted the enemy’s plan for a ground invasion of Iran.
Brigadier General Ali Jahanshahi said army units were deployed across various parts of the country, from the southwest to the West and East Azarbaijan provinces, as well as to Sistan and Baluchestan and the Makran coast. Despite difficult weather conditions, the units carried out their assigned missions.
He said the enemy had expected that airstrikes and the assassination of commanders would pave the way for proxy forces and terrorist groups to enter Iran. However, the rapid and extensive deployment of army and Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) units along the borders thwarted the plan.
Jahanshahi said that following the 12-Day War in 2025, Iran’s armed forces reviewed battlefield experience, revised operational plans, reorganized combat formations and strengthened defensive positions.
He said combat-readiness exercises at military bases and the reinforcement of border units were among the measures taken to counter potential threats.
The commander said the Ground Forces were prepared to counter any act of aggression, citing their mobile assault brigades, rapid-response forces, special units and mechanized forces.
General Jahanshahi added that army personnel considered the defense of Iran’s territorial integrity their duty, stressing that the armed forces had assumed responsibility for protecting national interests and ensuring the country’s security following the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
